chapters.title: Subhadra
paragraphs: Subhadra Here of a lovely dark and there arid with their frightful extent, filling up the quarters at different places with the murmur of brooks, and interspersed with holy places, hermitages, hills, rivers, valleys and woods—these are the tracts of the Dandaka forest meeting my view, the sites of which have been familiar to me.⟨fn:113⟩ This description captures the beauty of the place where river Subhadra meets the sea. At the mouth of the river there had formed a sandy island. The river formed two streams before it merged with the sea. The swirl of water made soft music akin to the ringing of silver bells, or like the soft, sweet tones of Kumud’s voice. At high tide the sea would submerge the island in knee-deep water. During the four months of monsoon the island remained submerged. It had no name; people simply called it the ‘Island’. To the north of the river, the area adjacent to the foothills of Sundargiri, was a large flat ground while on the southern side were sandy ravines so deep that only the tops of the trees that grew in them were visible. Lush, green grass grew the year round on the river banks. A thick canopy of trees covered the slopes of Sundargiri, and its higher reaches were hidden by clouds. From the mountain top one could see the vast sea swelling beyond the horizon—an expanse that challenged the human eye: ‘look as far and farther as you can, and also look within to know your own limits.’ The river meandered through the ravines on the east and almost disappeared into their depths. A platform was constructed in the middle of the island. A bamboo shaft was fixed onto the platform over which a small flag fluttered. Just below the bamboo was a small tent-like structure made of ochre- coloured khadi. During the dry season a sadhvi lived there. She had made an idol of the mother goddess of the island. Bharvads, Rabaris and other cattle-rearing communities brought their cattle to graze on the river banks. People of the nearby villages also visited the island. They came on festive days, Sundays and other religious days. Some came daily in the morning and evening and worshipped the island mother goddess at a spot where natural beauty was imbued with religious sentiments. The sadhvi was young and brimming with youthful zeal. But her mind was saturated with the aesthetics of ascetic life. She was so imbued with devotion that no worldly desires or bodily passions touched her. On the day that Kumud Sundari drowned in the river, the sadhvi was on the island, singing to her goddess, while some women devotees danced the garba. Mother Birdari descends Mount Sundargiri Wearing new clothes and tinkling anklets, Dazzling as the stars at dawn, Which adorn your shapely ankle rings. The sun rises as a mirror to you, Mother Birdari; Sparrows and swans play at your bejeweled feet. The Mother comes to bathe in the river. We are the daughters in whose heart you reside, Mother Birdari. You are omnipresent and yet contained in our hearts. A brahmin woman devotee’s eyes were riveted on the river. ‘Sadhumata, what is that?’ she addressed the sadhvi, pointing at the water. The sadhvi placed a finger on her lips, signaling her to remain silent and carried on with her garba. She sang a new garba.

You appear before us at high noon, Mother; As the tide swells, you appear more youthful and beautiful. Mother Jobanvanti, the sun worships you: The sounds of the river and the sea play like temple bells and drums. All ten directions seem aflame with the dance of your devotees. Brahma himself bows to you, singing paeans to Shakti. The world is on fire, Mother; protect your daughters: What do we do with Brahma and all the other men? The daughter finds solace in the Mother. Safe in your lap we are free from the cycle of birth and rebirth; Unafraid of death we cross this worldly sea. That was the day of the high tide. Sea water rushed through the inlet towards the island. As the water lapped the feet of the dancing women, they all got up on to the platform. The garba and the dance stopped. The sadhvi’s attention shifted to the play of water. As she looked on, something floated up towards the platform but was dragged back into the river—it was at a point where the river and the sea struggled with each other. The women initially thought it was a magnificent fish of the sea. The floating fish-like form was covered in red. The brahmin woman looked closely and said, ‘Mataji, I do not think it’s a fish. It is a woman’s dead body.’ One woman tucked in her clothes and jumped into the water; a few others followed. They swam swiftly towards the floating body. The sadhvi spoke: ‘The power and the glory of the Goddess are such that all things brought in by the sea and the river come to rest near her. Nothing drowns in her presence. Mother Goddess never allows any harm to come to her daughters. Even from this far from our platform we can see that girl afloat in clear water. If the Goddess so wills, she will survive.’ One woman cried out, ‘God, save her!’ The sadhvi immediately chided her, ‘Don’t say God! Do you not know that in the presence of this Goddess men turn into women? Brahma the Creator plays in the cradle at Mataji’s adobe. Any mention of male gods is prohibited here as it is shunned by the Goddess. God and goddess are not distinct: they are one. But a woman cannot open herself and be transparent before Narayana, the male form. A woman cannot give up her shame. Hence Brahma becomes Vidhatri, the Goddess of Destiny, Vishnu becomes Lakshmi and Shiva transforms into Uma. All male gods are a form of Narayana. The power of these gods is Goddess Narayani. You and I are born as women and from the moment of our birth we are in the lap of this Mother Goddess. Hence, no man or god’s name should be uttered in this place made sacred by her presence. Look, here they come with the girl. In this place the Goddess brings to life even those of her daughters who have died. This girl too shall live.’ ‘It is true; an ascetic woman sees the whole world, including the gods, as feminine,’ a woman commented. ‘Yes,’ said the sadhvi. The women swam out of the deep water and walked towards the platform; two of them carried Kumud Sundari. She seemed dead. She looked as delicate and beautiful as the grass that grew on the bank. The water draining from the bodies of the women made shallow streams which erased the marks left by their feet on the soft sand. Kumud lay inert in their arms; her garments clung to her, marking the contours of her body. In this sacred space of the goddess, the impure, obtrusive male gaze had no place. It was as if Kumud’s body knew this and displayed her beauty with even greater abandon. Water streamed from her clothes, draining all her pain, suffering, desire and attachment to action. The one blessed by the goddess is released from worldly pain. Everyone has to be carried for cremation after death so that their soul can become one with the divine. The women carried Kumud Sundari as the dead are carried. She was pulled to this place by divine will. The great poet has described how the loving embrace of mother earth enveloped Shakuntala as she emerged unrecognised and insulted from King Dushyant’s palace. Poor wretched Kumud had also tried to run away from similar pain and suffering. She was brought before the eternal mother goddess who never abandons anyone seeking her sanctuary. No one in Suvarnapur could have fathomed the ways of destiny, but some might have heard what the wind whispered. She tossed her arms, bemoaned her plight, Accused her crushing fate—
... Before our eyes a heavenly light In a woman’s form, but shining bright, Seized her and vanished straight.⟨fn:114⟩
chapters.summary: On an island where a sadhvi and devotees worship, a mysterious body, believed to be Kumud Sundari, floats ashore, stirring hope for divine intervention.

chapters.title: Sarasvatichandra's Initiation
paragraphs: Sarasvatichandra’s Initiation Those knowing the knowable, and resting in all pervading spirit, and acquiescing alike to their wants and gains enjoy lives of perfect tranquility.⟨fn:115⟩ Sarasvatichandra craved the ascetic life. He deliberated over the decision. In order to please Vishnudas—the man who had given him new life—he adopted ochre robes. He wore an ochre dhoti, an upper garment and ochre headgear. At the moment of his initiation, calls of ‘Alakh!’ echoed across the hills of Yadu Shrunga. Amidst all this, a delighted Vishnudas whispered the verse quoted above from the Yoga Vasistha in Sarasvatichandra’s ear. Sarasvatichandra repeated the verse after him. Vishnudas accorded to him the highest order among his followers. On that day, the ascetics decided not to engage in their usual study and contemplation, nor did they go out to seek alms. Each one went on an excursion to a place of their liking. Viharpuri and Radhedas took Sarasvatichandra on a tour of all the major hills of the mountain. They had gone out on an excursion early that morning as well. At that time there was curiosity, many questions and even banter among them. That easy playfulness of Viharpuri and Radhedas had now given way to a somber, almost worshipful attitude towards Sarasvatichandra. Their Guru Vishnudas had accorded their companion the highest degree, and their hearts were filled with devotion towards the master and the chosen one. Their demeanour was that of humble followers. They adjusted their pace to Sarasvatichandra’s slow, deliberate walk. They walked in silence and had not uttered a word, not even to ask a question. They were convinced that their Guru could predict the future. Their devotion to him was so deep that any doubt about his word was a sign of lack of faith and evil lurking in their minds. If they had any question, it was about the attire that Sarasvatichandra had adopted. They were curious about his early life, the merits that he had accumulated and the glorious future that awaited him. The followers of Vishnudas wore only a loin cloth, smeared ash over their bodies and applied sandalwood paste on their foreheads. They wore their hair in a roll. Attired in his ochre robes, the fair Sarasvatichandra flanked by the two dark-skinned ascetics in loin cloths looked like Mahadev with his gana or like Rama flanked by Hanuman and Sugriva. His companions felt blessed and content in his presence. ‘Viharpuri, where are we going?’ Sarasvatichandra asked. Viharpuri came forward, bowed his head slightly and replied, ‘Maharaj, at dawn we had gone to the western side. Now you have come to the hills on the eastern side.’ ‘What is that water body in the east?’ ‘We are on the highest peak. There is a large sandy area between this mountain and Ratnanagari. What you see is not water but an ocean of illusion; it is a mirage.’ Sarasvatichandra caught his hand and exclaimed, ‘Oh, so this is the fabled Mrigjala or mirage?’ His fingers went to his lips in awe as he murmured, ‘A lake full of illusionary water!’ Viharpuri: ‘Yes, mere illusion. Hundreds of thirsty deer chase it and still die thirsty.’ Sarasvatichandra let out a deep sigh. He bit his lower lip pensively and said, ‘Viharpuri, Radhedas, let me contemplate this mirage, a perfect representation of this illusory world. My pilgrimage to the sacred abode of the Master is now complete. Let us all sit on this hill for a while.’ Not a word escaped them. As Sarasvatichandra’s eyes were riveted on the mirage, thoughts flooded his mind.

My wealth was as illusionary as this mirage. I have forsaken it. Kumud: as beautiful and alluring as this illusion, you, too, had occupied my mind. Even you I have abandoned! But— Where are you? Where am I? For the present this experience gives me joy—I will empty my mind of all thoughts of you. I have adopted these ochre robes. I have made this ashram my abode. If we had married, we would have suffered deep pangs of separation at the time of death. So we will make the pain of death and separation a fact in the present itself. Wise are those who adapt and make their own that which is to come in the future. Kumud! Chandrakant! One becomes the cause of pain and pleasure of many others. I am the cause of your pain just as the dead cause pain to those who are left to mourn. And yet that is no sin committed by the dead. But suicide—that is a sin. I, too, have committed suicide of a kind. Do not all ascetics, warriors who are martyred in wars and those who cross the seas in the quest of riches commit suicide of a kind? If so, why should they be freed from such sin? A body surrendered on the righteous path earns merit, but a body squandered on the path of evil is sheer waste. This world, like the body, exists because of the soul, is joined by one spirit. It will cease to be when the soul so desires. All individuals and distinct beings are parts of the universal being. What I consider to be my body is also part of this great being, and hence it is not mine. My body is part of the body called family; for a moment it was joined with Kumud. My body is a fragment of this country; it is a part of human life. All those beings are mine just as this experiential body is a part of them. Any expenditure of the body on the righteous path is not wasteful. An expenditure of a part benefits the larger being. It is a means to an end. In the real sense there is nothing like suicide; the soul is immortal. Truth is that no weapon can wound it; no fire can burn it to ashes. The soul emanates from the great being and permeates individual bodies that grow and wither. It resides in the body but is not confined by the body’s limitations. There is no soul outside of the great soul. Sarasvatichandra! For which great and righteous cause have you expended your body?

His mind was caught in a whirl of self-examination. My righteous cause, my act for the benefit of the world, for the people—where is it? In what does it inhere? Life is real! Life is earnest!⟨fn:116⟩ What is the Meaning of life? While the sound whirls around Down, down! As the fawn draws the hound, As the lightning the vapour, As a weak moth the taper; Death, despair; love, sorrow; Time, both; to-day, to-morrow; As steel obeys the spirit of the stone, Down, down!⟨fn:117⟩ The scholars of the city of Bombay, rulers, poets, servants of the country, Laxminandan’s wealth, Chandrakant’s friendship, Kumud’s love—I have descended below all these noises and snares. The first step in the decline to the nether world was Buddhidhan’s Suvarnapur; the second step was his administration; the third was in his household; the fourth step was among the outlaws and Aarthdas; the fifth step was the night spent in the forest with the snake. Now I am on this sixth level of the nether world. Now I have to shake off the residual attachment. What awaits me in the nether world? I am descending into the belly of a great python that is this world. But for which righteous cause? Poet Bhavabhuti said that Sita, as she immersed herself into the Ganga, had a vision of the Ganga and Vasundhara—mother earth. To which deep waters will the maker of my destiny take me? Will I, too, come face to face with Vasundhara? O’ mirage, my eyes rest on your beauteous, alluring, glittering expanse. Am I not fortunate that I can gaze at your beauty from afar and not chase you? O’ Vasundhara! Bearer of this earth!

Suddenly a fragment of a letter floated on the breeze towards him, and broke his spell. Sarasvatichandra picked it up, and was stunned. ‘An envelope addressed to Chandrakant! This is Bulwer Sahib’s handwriting! Chandrakant, you? Here?’ He turned to them and asked, ‘Viharpuri, how could this fragment have reached here?’ The two came forward with folded hands. The English orthography was beyond them, but they considered various possibilities. Radhedas spoke up, ‘Navinchandraji, some three or four days ago some of our ascetics had gone among the people to spread the message of Alakh. On their way from Ratnanagari to Bhadreshwar they had found a bundle of papers, and brought it with them to the Ashram. They must have taken this path and this letter may have slipped out of the bundle unnoticed.’ Viharpuri: ‘Yes, that must be it. Otherwise it is impossible to find such writings in these parts, Maharaj! Can you decipher this writing?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Yes. Will I be allowed to see that bundle?’ ‘Guruji has said that all esoteric and secret texts of the Ashram should be made available to you. This bundle is insignificant. Maharaj, do we have the right to know what this letter contains?’ These affectionate words brought tears to Sarasvatichandra’s eyes. ‘Dear Viharpuri, you have done me an immense favour. Like you, I have another dear friend who is wandering around Ratnanagari, searching for me. This letter is addressed to him. That bundle of papers must be his.’ ‘Excellent, Maharaj! We shall welcome that good man as well. If you permit me, I will go to him immediately.’ ‘What will you not do for me out of affection? It is not possible for you to go there. Your service to the Guruji is unmatched, Viharpuri; no one can take your place. Hence, any other member of the ashram could go to Ratnanagari. My friend is a guest of the minister, but the minister must not know of this visit. And no mention should be made of my presence here. My friend needs to be dealt with cleverly and invited to visit the ashram. That is what I would like.’ ‘That we can do with ease.’

‘My friend is called Chandrakant. He has come from Bombay. If he declines the invitation, I will give you a sign which only he will comprehend.’ ‘What should that sign be?’ ‘This should be told only to Chandrakant.’ Owing to neither goddess nor woman, My friend has withered. The moon wanes, pining For the moonbeam. Viharpuri heard him with closed eyes and said, ‘Maharaj, I have committed the verse to memory.’ Sarasvatichandra composed more verses and recited them. The mountain tops kiss the rain-soaked sky; There the pious sadhus awaken the unmanifest. The road leading to an unending mirage Is an alluring one: It is the chosen path of the renouncer And does not glisten with the dazzle of illusion. There is not even the subtle fragrance of Kumud there. Your ancestors live among the immortals there. Even now the echoes of the first words resound there. I have forsaken the glitter of Indrapuri, Forsaken Kumud, and all that binds me. I have adopted the ochre of renunciation And roam unattached but melancholy. In my heart, you know there is a light: I offer to it the teachings of masters. A new wind blows and a soft light emerges. Slowly my eyes open to the rising sun. A sacrificial fire dawns upon this mountain. In absence of he who presides over the sacrifice It remains incomplete. Viharpuri had shut his eyes to listen attentively, but the disappointment at not having been able to memorise the poem was apparent on his face. Sarasvatichandra was sensitive to this and said, ‘Viharpuri, I will write down this poem for you, which will make it easier to remember.’ Viharpuri was clearly pleased. Sarasvatichandra told them, ‘Now you go and make these arrangements. I will come later.’ His companions left him and before long the two had disappeared among the hills and the foliage. It was four in the afternoon. The sun was going down behind the tall mountain trees. The plane on the eastern side was more clearly visible now as the sun had moved westwards. Sarasvatichandra got up and looked at the vista before him. On one side was the mirage, on the other side verdant forests, crisscrossing roads, circular ponds and rivers like a woman’s body—hidden from view but suddenly revealing itself. Sarasvatichandra looked at this picturesque scene, and exclaimed, Woods over woods in gay theatric pride. And a little while later, Amidst the stores shall thankless pride repine? ... Creation’s heir, the world, the world is mine!⟨fn:118⟩ The scene before him was laid out like pieces on a chess board, or the intricate embroidery on a woman’s blouse. As his eyes rested on Ratnanagari and the ramparts of that city, a new world became manifest in his mind’s eye. An image of Kumud Sundari appeared before him from the north. Another, which took the form of Vishnudas, appeared from the south. Both came and stood on either side of Sarasvatichandra. ‘Each house is laden with golden boughs,’ said Kumud. ‘The virtuous meet the righteous on every path,’ said Vishnudas. Sarasvatichandra stood still as a statue. The two forms disappeared, but their voices persisted. ‘The company of the wise, even for a moment, becomes the boat on which to cross the ocean of samsara.’

These conflicting, contradictory voices confused him. He began to walk away from the ashram; and then, to walk back towards the ashram. Kumud’s image reappeared. Walking beside him, she sang, My beloved adorned in ochre, the enchanting yogi, He is a renunciate, his garb is dear to me; Kumud walks beside Chandra yogi, Beloved, we shall be one in love and play with abandon Amidst Sundargiri’s verdant beauty, In its cool shade together we shall cross the sea of sorrows. In that narrow space between rocks, In close proximity, we shall speak of knowledge. Having forsaken the false world, We shall imbibe the nectar of truth, Bereft of luxuries, we shall soak in togetherness. Sarasvatichandra was enchanted with Kumud’s song. He extended his arm to hold her, but the image vanished and his hand grazed against a boulder instead.
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra embraces his ascetic initiation, contemplating life's illusions, but a mysterious letter and a vanishing vision of Kumud stir his new resolve.

chapters.title: The Garden of Beauty and Kusum's Coming of Age
paragraphs: The Garden of Beauty and

Kusum’s Coming of Age She seems a flower whose fragrance none has tasted, A gem uncut by workman’s tool, A branch no desecrating hands have wasted, Fresh honey, beautifully cool. No man on earth deserves to taste her beauty, Her blameless loveliness and worth, Unless he has fulfilled man’s perfect duty— And is there such a one on earth?⟨fn:119⟩ The verse captures Kusum’s unsullied beauty. This was also the cause of Gunasundari’s anxieties. She was worried about both her daughters, albeit for very different reasons. She felt weighed down by the burden of this anxiety. Gunasundari had come to understand that for a mother the greatest pain was the suffering of a daughter. As a young bride she had been weighed down by the responsibilities of a large joint family, a burden she had borne with the generosity and largeness of heart expected of a householder. She had a natural, inborn quality of forgiveness, the forbearance of an intelligent woman and the patience and wisdom of the brave. With these qualities she had harnessed herself to her husband, run with him and become a co-sharer of his burdens, a partner. The family matters had been resolved. Gunasundari had remained alert, and her body supple and firm. Just around the time she had at last managed to disentangle herself from the web of the joint family, her husband had grown in both power and wealth. Her days of hardship seemed over. As the wife of the minister of Ratnanagari, Gunasundari enjoyed influence and riches. But now she was crushed by worry for her two daughters. The burden of a joint family and the hardships of a small income were nothing compared with the terrible weight of the sorrow and guilt that she now experienced. Kumud Sundari was born at a time when her parents were struggling with their household responsibilities. She was then married to a man who possessed no faculties to appreciate and enjoy the beauty of Kumud’s mind. While on the other hand, there was no man who could take delight in Kusum’s beauty. Gunasundari could not decide which of the two was a greater cause of worry for her. On her return from a visit to Mena Rani, she collapsed into an easy chair, covered her face with her sari and wept silent tears. Soon, gaining a measure of control over herself, she wiped her tears and spoke a verse in anger and in pain, as if seeking justice and reprimanding Pramaddhan. The natural place of a sweet-smelling flower is on the head: and not under trampling feet.⟨fn:120⟩ Pramaddhan, you failed to recognise virtue—how could you have taken pleasure in Kumud? The sweet, soft water of the river when mingled with the sea becomes salty. Those who understand virtue are capable of recognising and respecting it in others, or else virtues turn into defects. I have sinned. I have sinned greatly by sending my precious daughter, sweet as a river, to meet with the salinity of the sea. How can I possibly blame the sea? Salinity is its nature. We her foolish parents were enticed by the sweetness of her in-laws and gave her to a husband as salty as the sea. The stupidity was ours, and Kumud paid the price for it. Such is the nature of parental duty. Oh God! Tears flowed from her eyes. Suddenly Gunasundari remembered Kusum’s inclination to remain unmarried, an intent she had voiced once again on their way back from Mena Rani’s garden. That was an additional cause of concern. Gunasundari sighed a deep sigh; she was weary of pain, of anxiety. She got up restlessly and sought solace in the beauty of her garden. In keeping with his status as a minister Vidya Chatura had moved into a new palace. This palace was situated on the outskirts of Ratnanagari and was surrounded by a large garden. Gunasundari had assumed the responsibility of decorating the palace and laying out the palace gardens. She combined in her decoration Sanskrit aesthetics with Western ideas of beauty. She read new books, learnt from the various distinguished guests who visited the palace and constantly added and changed objects in her house as per the demands of their status as also with the changing times. Gunasundari’s garden, which combined the best features of the gardens of the Ratnanagari nobility and the latest trends of Bombay, provided for all contingencies and needs. The layout of the garden was according to the seasons— summer, monsoon and winter—and the play of light and shade at all hours of the day—morning, noon and evening. It provided spaces for night-time soirees under the moon, places to sit in the company of friends, spaces for meeting general public, secluded spaces for women to gather and solve their intricate problems, solitude and privacy for couples, for occasions joyous and sad; it also provided spaces for the minister’s quiet, contemplative moods. There were fountains, springs, small ponds, dense foliage, meadows, and the landscape approximated the contours of deep caves, ravines and hillocks. It was said by the people of Ratnanagari that in Gunasundari the minister had a wife who enhanced his glory and wealth manifold. King Maniraj had named the garden ‘Saundarya Udyan.’ In that garden, Vidya Chatura received the king and the humblest of citizens, scholars and idiots, the young and the elderly. All were received with the utmost courtesy, and through these meetings the minister got a grasp of the pulse of the people, understood their aspirations and grievances, found ways of encouraging their pursuits as also keeping them under check. Love and fear were instruments of power and through them he strengthened the reign of Maniraj. He endeavoured to create in Maniraj affection for his subjects—the affection that a householder has for his beloved—and helped him cultivate the enthusiasm and capability to fulfill the desires of his beloved people. Vidya Chatura tried to lead his people towards higher goals and in time he acquired renown as an able charioteer of the state. Gunasundari—though unseen by most—possessed all the capabilities of being a true and equal partner in dharma to her husband. Her heart was the fecund field in which the seeds of her husband’s aspiration were first sown; the Saundarya Udyan was only an outward manifestation of that. The planning and laying out of the palace garden had taken three years. Kumud, born during the years of struggle and hardship for her parents, was then already on her way to her in-laws’ house; the garden was still incomplete when she left for Suvarnapur. Kumud had enjoyed the garden during that ever-so-brief period of her betrothal with Sarasvatichandra. With his disappearance, she parted company with the garden as well. The same goddess of destiny, who had darkened Kumud’s fate, shone a benevolent light on her younger sister Kusum. Gunasundari, burdened by the duties of a large family, had been unable to play a conscious role in Kumud’s upbringing, but she showered care and attention on Kusum. The minister’s palace had separate women’s quarters. Adjacent to the women’s quarters, a special garden was made for Kusum. This secluded garden had all the facilities necessary for Kusum’s physical and mental development. It had spaces for study, for physical exercise, for pleasure and all that which may be required for her development as an unsullied but independent young woman. And yet care was taken to ensure that independence did not turn into unbridled youthful passion; Kusum was shielded from undesirable influences and urges. Care was taken to ensure that she did not read books that would inflame her passions. Influences which were thorny or weed- like had no space in Kusum’s garden. The garden was so designed that all parts of it—even the most shaded nooks and crannies—were visible to Gunasundari from her easy chair or her swing. Both hers and Sundargauri’s windows had a clear view of the garden and its occupant. The attempt was to allow Kusum to grow independently without going astray. Weary of her sorrows and cares, Gunasundari sought solace in the pleasing vistas of the garden. She stood at her window and gazed at Kusum’s garden. Just as the sight of the moon inflames the passions of one suffering the pangs of separation from the beloved, the sight of Kusum heightened Gunasundari’s anguish. What was innocent Kusum doing which so distressed her mother? Just below Gunasundari’s window was a pavilion. Its sides were made of wooden lattice work. A dense canopy of trees and creepers formed a roof over it. The lattice work was almost completely covered by the various vines and creepers that grew around it. The blue, white, yellow, deep purple and red flowers of these creepers made delightful patterns. On either side of the entrance to the pavilion were rose and mogra bushes. To offset the predominance of green, the furniture inside the pavilion was made of blue, red and white glass. There were some chairs, a bench and a table. Kusum liked to spend time with her books inside this pavilion. Right in front of the pavilion was a pool of water. Marble steps from two sides led to the water, while the other two sides were screened with brass lattice work. Gunasundari looked out of her window and found Kusum standing near the brass screen. She had worn a petticoat of fine cotton fabric which she had tucked in-between her legs, exposing her thighs and legs. Her long legs were as smooth and delicate as a plantain stem. The petticoat was of a golden hue, also the colour of her skin, and the garment and the body appeared as one. The gathers of her petticoat gave the appearance of creased plantain leaves. The ends of the drawstrings that held the petticoat were tied in a flowery knot just below her lotus-shaped belly button. The tightly strung petticoat thrust up her delicate breasts. Her whole golden body glistened like the sun at dawn. Kusum looked so alluring and desirable that no onlooker would have been able to take his eyes off her. Her tight blouse, made of the same fine cotton, was held together not by buttons but a silver chain that sparkled in the sun. But the chain did not succeed in either hiding or containing her breasts within the blouse; her small, delicate breasts were pert and firm without any support. Her hands covered her face, as if to suggest that there was no man worthy of partaking in the pleasure of her beauty. As her mother examined her beautiful young daughter’s body, her eyes caressing her from head to toe and back, she felt greatly perturbed. Gunasundari muttered to herself, Oh God! Have you made a man worthy of her? I cannot see any. Why did you make her so beautiful? Unmindful of her mother’s gaze and worry, Kusum draped herself around a tree. Her long, shiny, black hair covered her back. In one swift movement she climbed up the tree and positioned herself on a branch. Like the sprays of a water-laden cloud she dove into the pool and disappeared under water. After a while she resurfaced and floated on the water like a ‘jolly- boat.’ She made delicate strokes with her hands. She swam, she floated and she splashed water on herself and all around the pool. Her long, black tresses acquired a life of their own and floated on the water after her. Gunasundari was certainly delighted with her daughter’s artistry in water, but her joy was tinged with sadness. Unaware of her mother’s tears, Kusum continued her play in the water. Just then Sundargauri came up to her sister-in-law and said, ‘Chandrakantbhai seems mired deep in sorrow.’ Gunasundari snapped out of her thoughts. From a room nearby, she overheard Chandrakant talking aloud to himself in a melancholy voice. ‘Sarasvatichandra, you led a carefree life but were suddenly possessed by other ideas. The woman you loved and cared for deeply was given to one unworthy of her. Like a flower in the hands of a monkey. None else but you are responsible for this. Oh God! A perfect pair was broken. Each day greater distance separates them. Those once parted will not come together again.’ Leaning on Sundargauri’s shoulder, Gunasundari pressed a hand to her chest, heaved a deep sigh and listened as Chandrakant continued his soliloquy: ‘A pair like that can only be made once. Now it is impossible even to think of another pair coming together.’ O’ aesthete, where will renunciation take you? Will it make a wanderer of you and have you lose your way? In all your wanderings, Where would that doe-eyed beauty be? The flower captured the bee at dusk; It flew away at dawn never again to be caught. Even the god of love and desire is powerless When both are married to a life without care. ‘Wretched Laxminandan! In your old age you invited trouble on yourself and your son. Your son did not want to marry; he agreed to marriage only to make you happy. But he soon realised that his marriage will give you no joy, and he escaped the net he was about to fall into. Now where shall I look for him?’ As the image of Sundargiri flashed before his mind’s eye, Chandrakant grew silent for a while. Gunasundari said, ‘Sundarbhabhi, this sad soliloquy will neither give solace to him, nor to us. It may be possible to find Sarasvatichandra, but that will not solve the problem that is Kusum. If one person is unwilling, one may well arm-twist and convince the other. But in this case both will be unwilling and difficult to budge. Sarasvatichandra is like a son to us; we feel his pain. We should for that reason alone search for him, but it is pointless.’ ‘Bhabhiji, someone like me can lose patience. But it is surprising that someone as experienced as you, someone who has been a source of such immense patience and strength for us, should lose heart. Both of them are inebriated with irresponsible youthfulness. This is just a passing phase; it will change with the seasons. I am not worried about that. What worries me is that someone who loves Kumud so deeply may not be willing to wed her sister,’ said Sundargauri. Chandrakant now resumed his soliloquy, and both women listened keenly. ‘Kusum Sundari’s resolve to remain unmarried is simply delightful. She is as carefree and innocent as a deer in the hermitage of a sage. She is incapable of seeing the vicissitudes of a householder’s everyday life. She is enamoured by the dream of an unattached, carefree existence. She is astute enough to know and be wary of the follies of a life of pleasure. She is possessed of the reason and intellect to find the means of fulfilling her aspirations. She is observant and capable of participating in a new game. She is playful; she can toy with my friend or entice him to make her his playmate.’ Gunasundari stood transfixed listening to him as Sundargauri held her tightly. ‘But all this is against custom. A political person like Vidya Chatura is unlikely to be moved by such theories. It is no less surprising that Kusum is still unmarried. If a man as learned, as wealthy, brave and firm of conviction as Vidya Chatura were to be in the liberated atmosphere of Bombay, he would certainly not confine a bird as free and as beautiful as Kusum in the cage that is marriage. I and others like myself would be tempted to see her take flight and soar high in the sky. But the people of our native states are like fish in stagnant water and would find such aspiration unnatural and against custom. Dear Bombay! My liberated Amravati! Conceited kings and their ministers would never comprehend the joy of someone like me who, though poor, has the divine right to swim freely in the great ocean of life that is Bombay. They consider me and others like me as childish, crazy, stupid and ignorant! I consider kings, their ministers and other men of wealth as worthless as mattresses made of lumpy, filthy cotton! And I consider their wealth and power as worthless as the dust of my feet! Awake, my St. John! leave all meaner things To low ambition, and the pride of kings.⟨fn:121⟩ ‘Sacred Bhartrhari, your words resonate in my heart. Do not despise wise men who have obtained the highest good; wealth, worthless as grass, stands not in their way; a lotus-fibre cannot present any obstacles to elephants whose temples have been darkened with a stream of fresh rut.⟨fn:122⟩

Chandrakant bit his lips, his brows creased and his feet resolutely struck the ground. ‘Well, I feel my heart elated and buoyant. Poor as I am, I must find out my noble bird from its most hidden recesses and rely upon my own strong arm, single and unaided, rather than suffer further delay at the hands of the proud indifference that reigns supreme within bosoms where my own dear business has no status!’⟨fn:123⟩ Sundargauri understood nothing of what was said and what she heard. Gunasundari was pensive. Hitherto she had remained untouched by the allure of power. Her affection for Sarasvatichandra allowed her to view this criticism sympathetically. She felt no anxiety or compulsion even to defend her husband. Then she heard Chandrakant laughing aloud as he said, ‘If I could, I would ask the minister. Does she, till marriage only, keep her vow As hermit-maid, that shames the ways of love? Or must her soft eyes ever see, as now, Soft eyes of friendly deer in peaceful grove?⟨fn:124⟩ ‘Here is an angel that can shake to the roots the foundations of society in my beloved Bombay, and revolutionise the fortunes of her sex in that my city of Gods, if only he would stoop—stoop to conquer her. ‘That’s pretty nearly impossible: He won’t stoop any longer.’⟨fn:125⟩ All of a sudden Chandrakant’s soliloquy stopped. As he sank deeper into the easy chair, a silent voice from within reprimanded him: I have committed a serious blunder. This loud soliloquy is a bad habit, out of place, out of time and out of tune in this land of intellectual and sentimental bondage. Nay! We Bombay fools have loose and quarrelsome tongues and restless verbosity from which these men here, who study and practise the ways of the business of life, are quite free, and their art is worth acquiring. There, too, my noble friend has got this noble art by birth and by instinct, while the pest of pauperism has left me a low-bred fool. Suppose my wild utterances have assailed the sacred ears of my sweet hostess, what a wretched and ungrateful idiot must I have proved myself to her mind and how must I have marred its sweetness with my sour effusions?⟨fn:126⟩ Chandrakant was angry with himself, and rightly so. Gunasundari seized this opportunity for some banter and entered his room, followed by Sundargauri. ‘Chandrakantbhai, there can be no food without salt. Absolute sweetness is liked by none. We in the native states eat our sweets mixed with the savouries that the likes of you bring. Therefore, there is no question of blaming either yourself or us.’ Chandrakant was taken aback. His fears had proved correct. He did not know what all he had said aloud, and how much she had heard. Before resolving this quandary, it was necessary for him to respond to the intelligent woman standing before him. ‘Gunasundaribehn, when I think of my friend Sarasvatichandra, I am filled with pride for Bombay. But the moment I consider the crudity of brahmins like myself, my pride melts. Moreover, the sophistication that I had acquired in the company of my friend is wearing thin ever since he disappeared. My condition is like that of a camel raised by a lioness.’ ‘What is that?’ asked Gunasundari. ‘There is a story in the Panchatantra about a camel raised by a lioness. One day, the camel went to the lioness and spoke glowingly of his own bravery. The lioness replied. You may be valiant, intelligent and highly noteworthy; But the race that you are born in does not slay elephants.⟨fn:127⟩ ‘The camel realised his own unworthiness and ran away. However hard I may try, I will never be able to cultivate the mannerisms of the high- born. In my crudity, I end up insulting even those whose favours I have received. I have to make an attempt to behave like the well-bred. But if I try to imitate them, I become unnatural and lose what is my own by instinct. I feel that I should, like the camel, run away from here.’

Gunasundari laughed and said, ‘You are not as lucky as the camel. The camel returned to its own kind, but you seek Sarasvatichandra. The example of the camel is therefore inappropriate.’ ‘He has a unique quality. He loves me for my crudity. His affection for me remains undiminished. I have no control over my mind as it seeks him. I roam after him like a satellite orbiting a planet,’ a mellow and sad Chandrakant replied. Gunasundari took pity on him. ‘Chandrakantbhai, we, too, would be unworthy of receiving the rays of that moon if we allow this loved one to go away when his quest is still unfulfilled. Do you think my heart does not burn with worry for Sarasvatichandra?’ Gunasundari could not speak any further as tears flowed from her eyes and the hand raised to wipe them became wet with tears. Chandrakant’s heart melted. The nectar-like words of this wise and compassionate woman had given him new reason to live. Kumud’s mother shared his grief for Sarasvatichandra! Chandrakant realised that the family of his host was by no measure an ordinary one. Gunasundari composed herself and said, ‘Chandrakantbhai, I do not have a son. God gave me a son, one as worthy and superior as Sarasvatichandra; I lost him because of my own misfortune. Kumud’s tragedy has been a source of great anguish. But then daughters and women are born to misery and tribulation. So be it! I could have rejoiced in Sarasvatichandra’s happiness. In times of misery and torment, he would have given me solace and comforted me as a son would a mother. During the few days he spent with us, he tied strings of affection around us. Would he not have cared for us in our hour of crisis and sorrow? Do you think he would not have shared our pain and grief? Do you think he would have treated me with disdain had I told him that it was up to him to remedy my misery? I do not know if I speak out of selfishness or affection? I opened my heart to you as you are a friend of my son.’ Gunasundari’s face was smeared with tears. Chandrakant felt her agony. She continued, ‘Chandrakantbhai, I speak selfishly because where there is love, there is also selfishness. If there is a selfish desire, it is only that I should be able to share my grief with my son. His sorrow pains me, and I rejoice in his joy. Call it love or call it selfishness, but my heart aches for Sarasvatichandra. So well-bred and high born! Where is he? Has he ever experienced heat and cold? Kusum’s father blames Sarasvatichandra’s temperament. But I feel differently. A man who has slept on the softest of silken mattresses, who is unused to any harshness or discomfort, now sleeps like Bhishma on a bed of arrows. What must he be going through? No one ever said a harsh word to him. His friends care for him. But his father struck hammer blows on a heart as delicate as his. Should it not be expected that he would feel hurt and take exception to it? His story has become an illustration for the world about the pain and suffering caused by a step-mother. He was no less devoted to Guman. But Guman’s affection for him proved a mere charade. How was he to believe that my affection for him was real? The truth is that just as I am consumed by worry for my two daughters, my heart is also heavy with concern for your friend. Chandrakant, the world believes in blood ties, in kinship; but in case of Sarasvatichandra this has proved false. Those like you, who are not tied to him by blood, truly feel for him. What is true for you is true for me as well. If our hearts were transparent, I could have shown you exactly how I feel.’ Chandrakant realised his folly. Hitherto he had believed that his affection and concern for Sarasvatichandra was matchless. Gunasundari’s rare capacity for empathy and her untainted womanly affection combined with the power of her intellect dawned upon him. His haughtiness vanished. He wiped his tears and said, ‘Gunasundaribehn, it gives me great joy to know that my motherless friend does indeed have a mother. I share your grief. Hitherto, in my conceit I believed that no one but me cares for Sarasvatichandra. My pride has melted. It gives me immense solace to know that you share my grief. I am poor and without any means to support my search for my friend, a search which has begun to exhaust me. But your support strengthens me. You have given me the faith to renew my belief that Sarasvatichandra’s mother Chandralaxmi is alive and with me, and that my search for her son has her blessings. You have given me this beautiful vision in your lovely garden, the Saundarya Udyan.’

Before Gunasundari could respond, Kusum walked into the room in strange attire and grabbed everyone’s attention much like a resplendent chandelier in a hall. The glow on her face and hair suggested that she had just bathed. She had worn a chunari in the manner of Multani women and a nose ring with a single pearl. She carried a hundred-petalled lotus, plucked from a ‘river’ made in her Kusum Udyan. The lotus rested on her left shoulder as she held its long stem in one delicate hand; it gave the illusion that on either end of the stem was a lotus. In the other hand she carried a book, her finger marking a page. Kusum floated in and stood right at the centre of the room, unconcerned about what had been going on before her arrival. She pretended that they had gathered without purpose and that she had caused no interruption. She was like sudden rain that comes un- summoned when the sun is shining brightly in the sky. Kusum did not even glance at her mother and aunt and focussed all her attention on Chandrakant, addressing him the moment she entered the room. ‘Chandrakantbhai, I need you. Sarasvatichandra had given me this book of his when he visited us. He had composed a new poem, which is not included in the book. The loose sheet on which he had written the poem was in it. I found it before Kumudbehn left for Suvarnapur. If I had shown it to her, she would have explained it to me. But I did not do so as I did not want to cause her pain. I would like you to explain this poem to me.’ ‘Give it to me,’ said Chandrakant. Holding the piece of paper with his friend’s writing on it, Chandrakant felt as if he had met and held his dear friend. He read the poem, and was stirred. ‘Oh God!’ he said aloud. Then, composing himself, he said, ‘Kusumbehn, I will explain the meaning to you on two conditions: first, you must sing the poem; and second, you must tell me what your own understanding of it is. Gunasundaribehn, this poem is a favourite of my friend; it contains his philosophy of life.’ Chandrakant gave the poem to Gunasundari. Kusum grew impatient and said, ‘Why did you give it to Gunial? She will take more time to read it than you would have taken to explain it!’

Gunasundari continued to read as Sundargauri leaned over her shoulder to look at the poem. An amused Chandrakant said, ‘How can I explain unless my conditions are met?’ ‘Chandrakantbhai, why did you have to put conditions? Let’s be done with it!’ Kusum’s youthful eagerness could not brook further delay. ‘My conditions remain. If you accept them, I will do as asked.’ ‘All right. What if I recite and not sing?’ ‘No, the condition has to be met fully.’ Kusum blushed. Her bashful coyness coupled with her eagerness made her even more attractive to behold. Chandrakant gazed at Kusum; her beauty was as soothing and radiant as moonlight, he thought. He mused, Sarasvatichandra, why have you forsaken this world of beauty? Where do you hide? Oh, if only like the Theosophists you could send your body over to see and partake of the delight in this beautiful spectacle! And behold how, like Alladin’s jinn, your thoughts have created new worlds! Kusum’s intellectual eagerness proved to be more urgent than her demure reticence. She tried not to think about how shy she felt and made a feeble attempt to sing. Her hesitation and eagerness were both apparent. Chandrakant looked at her and thought, How enchanting those quivering lips are! But before Kusum could begin to sing in earnest, Sundargauri let out a laugh and whispered in her ear, ‘Kusum, dearest Kusum, even a lump of sugar is not as sweet as the sweetness of self-interest.’ Kusum pushed her away angrily, saying, ‘Kaki, must you remind me of it?’ Sundargauri turned to Chandrakant and said, ‘She agreed to sing only because she wants something from you. There is a saying that one becomes a beggar for sweets. It is just that and nothing else!’ Kusum’s shyness disappeared. ‘So be it. Chandrakant is like a brother to me. I will obey his wishes if only to learn from him. And I am also willing to be called a beggar greedy for sweets. Anything else?’

Sundargauri was defeated. ‘All right, then sing. Chandrakantbhai will test you. The one who abandons shame and makes a virtue of it becomes a master of her kingdom.’ Kusum laughed. ‘Yes, that is true. I am king of all that I survey. Chandrakantbhai, hear me sing, this is for you. As it is, Kaki thinks I am crazy and she only distracts. I cannot sing a song written for a male voice. So allow me to just recite.’ ‘That is hardly an excuse,’ Chandrakant replied. ‘All right, I will sing. But you cannot fault me on the choice of raga.’ ‘Not even if it is wrong?’ ‘I cannot sing ragas suited for a male voice.’ ‘But that is a lacuna in your training.’ ‘You begin, I will join in.’ ‘That was not part of the condition.’ ‘All right. If a sister makes a mistake, it should be a matter of shame for her brother.’ Sundargauri realised that this banter was going nowhere, and butted in, ‘Sing, my dear, sing. You are hell bent on singing. Who can stop you? Sing so that we also know what Kusum is capable of.’ ‘Hunh! I don’t need to respond to you. It will only delay my acquisition of sweets. Chandrakantbhai, this is for you.’ Kusum looked down and closed her eyes. She knew the poem by heart. Her song combined the natural melodiousness of her voice and her youthful exuberance. She sang in a steady voice. While the sound whirls around, Down, down! As the fawn draws the hound, As the lightning the vapour, As a weak moth the taper; Death, despair; love, sorrow; Time both; to-day, to-morrow; As steel obeys the spirit of the stone, Down, down!

Through the gray, void abysm, Down, down! Where the air is no prism, And the moon and stars are not, And the cavern-crags wear not The radiance of Heaven, Nor the gloom to Earth given, Where there is One pervading, One alone, Down, down! In the depth of the deep, Down, down! Like veiled lightning asleep, Like the spark nursed in embers, The last look Love remembers, Like a diamond, which shines On the dark wealth of mines, A spell is treasured but for thee alone. Down, down! We have bound thee, we guide thee; Down, down! With the bright form beside thee; Resist not the weakness, Such strength is in meekness That the Eternal, the Immortal, Most unloose through life’s portal The snake-like Doom coiled underneath his throne By that alone. ... Ye congregated powers of heaven, who share The glory and the strength of him ye serve, Rejoice! henceforth I am omnipotent. All else had been subdued to me; alone The soul of man, like unextinguished fire, Yet burns towards heaven with fierce reproach, and doubt, And lamentation, and reluctant prayer, Hurling up insurrection, which might make

Our antique empire insecure, though built On eldest faith, and hell’s coeval, fear; And though my curses through the pendulous air, Like snow on herbless peaks, fall flake by flake, And cling to it; though under my wrath’s night It climbs the crags of life, step after step, Which wound it, as ice wounds unsandalled feet, It yet remains supreme o’er misery, Aspiring, unrepressed, yet soon to fall: Even now have I begotten a strange wonder, That fatal child, the terror of the earth, Who waits but till the destined hour arrive, Bearing from Demogorgon’s vacant throne The dreadful might of ever-living limbs Which clothed that awful spirit unbeheld, To redescend, and trample out the spark. ... Drink! be the nectar circling through your veins The soul of joy, ye ever-living Gods, Till exultation burst in one wide voice Like music from Elysian winds. And thou Ascend beside me, veiled in the light Of the desire which makes thee one with me, Thetis, bright image of eternity!⟨fn:128⟩ They listened to her with rapt attention, soaking in the poet’s words. Kusum seemed content. Chandrakant broke the silence, ‘Behn, the poet’s muse would have rejoiced in your singing. The poet wasn’t here among us to hear your song. If he were, he would have said whether or not it stirred his being. I am after all a poor wretch; what was presented delighted me. There can be no other test of it. Now, the second condition.’ Before he could complete the sentence, Kusum said, ‘I will be back,’ and darted out of the room with the swiftness of a foal. When she returned, she had with her a flat, wide box. She said, ‘Chandrakantbhai, you did not specify that I must explain the poem to you in words. I have painted some pictures that depict the poem.’ ‘Your melody gave joy to our ears; now our eyes will feast on your paintings,’ he said. ‘Kusum is interested in many things. If she finds no teacher, she learns on her own. Her father has instructed that we should assist and further her endeavours. If she does not find a generous and noble partner to match her aspirations, she is certain to suffer. Her aspirations give me sleepless nights and I worry during all my waking hours. It is against our custom to train our daughters in the high arts. But the master of this household thinks otherwise; hence we do what we can as one would support a beautiful, delicate creeper,’ said Gunasundari. ‘I must perform penance for my unjust criticism of what I perceived to be the narrow, restrictive mentality of our native states. A land where the wealthy provide opportunities for learning and for cultivation of the high arts to their daughters—something that our people and customs regard as dangerous—if only this land could inculcate courage in our people and give them back all the weapons they have lost, they will earn high merit—the kind of merit that has accrued to the English. The English have banished the slavery of black people; freedom is dear to them. In this temple of yours, you worship freedom. Vidya Chaturabhai’s god-given wealth is being spent on an admirable and noble endeavour. Gunasundaribehn, the master of this house in his wisdom expressed his desire, and you with your virtue and intelligence have nurtured it. The fruits of your nurturing care are apparent to me. I can see that the patriotic fervour and nationalist aspirations of my friend are being realised here. I am so very pleased. Kusumbehn, let us see your paintings.’ Kusum opened her sandalwood box. The fragrant box was lined with red velvet. She took out a painting and gave it to her mother, who was still rejoicing in her husband’s praise. Gunasundari looked at it before passing it on to Chandrakant.

Gunasundari had had several occasions to meet and spend time with the wives of English officers. Kusum had learnt the general principals of ‘perspective drawings’ from them. She had made some progress by imitating the works of English masters and by the use of her own imagination. The first painting was done on canvas. The picture was divided into two parts. In the upper portion of the canvas she had painted clouds, rivers, oceans, horses, carriages of the wealthy and scenes of an army. All these were painted with a high degree of precision. The sharp rays of a bright sun gave light to this part of the canvas. Below this, a half circle drawn from left to right suggested the surface of the earth; this dark part symbolised night. A female figure clad in black garments personified ‘Rajni’ or night. Rajni seemed intent on emerging out of the darkness; her untied hair formed a ‘halo.’ Chandrakant looked at the painting wide-eyed. He re-read the first half of the poem. Kusum: ‘Chandrakantbhai, the upper half of the painting is busting with activity. It represents the large forces of nature and is radiant with sunlight. The bottom half represents night. She is trying to emerge from the darkness out into the light; the halo around her head is symbolic of that. Night is eventually transformed into light and day. This painting is a representation of the poem. But I do not understand the true inner meaning and intent of the poem.’ Gunasundari: ‘Kusum, that you will understand only when you experience life.’ Kusum: ‘Everyone can learn from experience and life. The true test is to understand without the experience of it. Chandrakant: ‘Let me narrate that experience. The day and sunlight represent Sarasvatichandra’s life in Bombay, and the darkness is his life after that. So long as he was in Bombay, knowledge, wealth, riches, friends, parents and the world glowed before him. Now he lives in the darkness of night.’ Kusum: ‘Why does night follow day? How can night transform itself into day?’

Chandrakant: ‘Human beings are born on the earth and return to the earth. “Dust thou art, to Dust returns.” That dust is our real night. Life is like day, but it is merely an act in this play. Night is the reality of this play, while day is only the delusion of it.’ ‘It is the time between birth and certain death,’ murmured Gunasundari. Kusum had a sudden flash of brilliance and her eyes lit up. She placed a finger on her lips and said, ‘Yes, of course! That is why it is said: Dust thou art, to dust returnest, Was not spoken of the soul.⟨fn:129⟩ ‘Dust, the earth is our only true friend and repose at the moment of our birth and death. Only those who befriend the night can see the truth. The day is mere illusion. You described Sarasvatichandra’s life in Bombay as day, and his later life as night. Are they distinct or are they emanating from the same matter?’ Chandrakant: ‘It is God who grants us the day and night of our lives, just as it is He who grants us days of comfort and hardship. Wealth has been called slippery, unsteady. The ochre colour of your garment is not permanent; similarly wealth is also impermanent. This impermanent, transient colour dazzles our eyes and creates chimeras. But hardship, the night is the only true colour.’ Kusum: ‘Ah ha! Let me say it differently. It was day and light for Kumud as long as she was engaged with Sarasvatichandra. But Sarasvatichandra ran away, and Kumud had to go to Suvarnapur. Then she was caught in the grip of night, and now she has descended into the lap of Rajni.’ Tears flowed from Gunasundari’s eyes. The childish girl in her enthusiasm saw nothing and carried on, ‘Here’s another example. As long as Maharaj Mallaraj was alive, it was day for Mena Mata. From the day he died, Mena Mata lives in this world as one would live in a crematorium—that is night.’

Chandrakant: ‘That is so.’ Kusum: ‘For all of us, the day must set and the night must emerge. So long as one is unmarried it is night. Marriage is like day. But widowhood means night. Like day, marriage is a charade; night is the real thing. Explain further.’ Chandrakant: ‘We have dealt with the painting you gave.’ Kusum: ‘Here is the next one.’ Sundargauri snatched the painting from Kusum’s hand and said, ‘No, Chandrakantbhai, we do not want to see these paintings nor do we want you to explain the poem to her. No matter what the issue, she always brings up the talk of wanting to be a spinster. She is possessed by this idea. We do not need to encourage her.’ Kusum glared at her aunt and said, ‘Kaki, are you giving it back or not? Then you will say that I shoot my mouth off.’ Sundargauri: ‘What can you say that you haven’t already said? Sri Krishna was tied to a stone mortar. We are going to tie you down and get you married. No more mollycoddling and pampering.’ Kusum: ‘No one has been indulgent to me. I speak when I am pushed. You lead a life of darkness, and yet you push me towards the illusion of day. Why? If you push me any further I will say even more.’ Gunasundari: ‘Sundarbhabhi, she has lost her head. Let her do what pleases her. Let her put up a show. We shall also see what she is capable of if left to herself. Finally, it is for you, me and her father to decide.’ Kusum: ‘Gunial, even you? You, too, have joined Kaki’s bandwagon!’ Chandrakant: ‘Behn, let’s get back on track.’ Kusum: ‘Yes. They are only a distraction. Here, take this.’ And she snatched the painting back from her aunt and gave it to Chandrakant. The painting was dark, the colour of night. There was a canopy of stars, the outline of a mountain and the blurred lines of trees. At the centre of the painting was the figure of a man asleep, dreaming with a faint smile playing upon his lips. In a corner was drawn a woman, also asleep, clutching her sarangi to her bosom. Another female figure stood holding a lantern to the face of the sleeping woman.

Before Chandrakant could take a proper look at the painting, Kusum spoke up, ‘This painting depicts night. On top there is a canopy of stars. The darkness is accentuated by the outlines of the mountain and the trees. This man is dreaming a strange dream. The woman, who is actually the form that illusion takes, is asleep clutching her sarangi. The other figure is night who is holding a lantern to her face; its light makes her features so blurred that they cannot be seen. Night tried to assume the form of day and met with this accursed condition.’ Chandrakant: ‘Now that you have explained the first part of the painting, the rest will explain itself.’ Kusum: ‘From dust to dust ... that dust is night. But why the stars?’ Chandrakant: ‘What would one see if one were to look up at the sky on a night like this?’ Kusum: ‘On an uneventful, ordinary night one would be filled with good thoughts. Because, as someone said: The midnight moon serenely smiles. O’er Nature’s soft repose; No low’ring cloud obscures the sky, Nor ruffling tempest blows. Now ev’ry passion sinks to rest, The throbbing heart lies still: And varying schemes of life no more Distract the labouring will. In silence hush’d, to Reason’s voice, Attends each mental Power: Come, dear Emilia, and enjoy, Reflection’s favourite hour.⟨fn:130⟩ ‘But such thoughts come to one only when one is happy under a starlit sky. A person loses her reason on dark nights of sorrow. I have been a witness to that.’

Chandrakant: ‘Where?’ Kusum: ‘Let it be. I don’t want to say. But I have recently seen the state to which even the wise are reduced in times of grief.’ Gunasundari: ‘You were about to take my name.’ Kusum laughed and said, ‘Now that you have said it, yes.’ Sundargauri: ‘Let me tell you what a grief-stricken person remembers. There is a saying that one remembers a jeweller in times of happiness while in times of grief, it is the name of Ram that comes to us.’ Kusum: ‘Oh ho, Kaki! You are not literate, but you are wise and experienced. Does that mean that Mena Rani did not sing prayers to Shiva in times of happiness?’ Gunasundari: ‘No.’ Kusum: ‘So one remembers God and has similar lofty thoughts in times of sorrow.’ Chandrakant: ‘The stars appear small to us, but in fact they are quite large.’ Kusum: ‘That is true. But why does he describe trees and mountains as contained by the darkness?’ Gunasundari: ‘That day, your father recited a poem by Tennyson. Do you remember what sorrow says?’ Kusum: ‘Yes she says: ‘The stars,’ she whispers, ‘blindly run, A web is woven across the sky; From out waste places comes a cry, And murmurs from the dying sun⟨fn:131⟩ ‘But for Sarasvatichandra the dark night of sorrow represents truth, while for Tennyson it is untruth.’ Chandrakant: ‘Oh, do recite the previous stanza!’ Kusum recited:

O Sorrow, cruel fellowship, O priestess in the vaults of Death, O sweet and bitter in a breath, What whispers from thy lying lip?⟨fn:132⟩ ‘The poet considers the lips of sorrow as lying.’ Chandrakant: ‘But he also calls her the priestess in the vaults of death. So does Sarasvatichandra.’ Kusum: ‘So he does. Let me explain. The illusionary mountains are not destroyed by the dark, they just appear invisible. The stars which are unseen during the day appear at night. Then, both day and night conceal some illusion, propagate some lie. But the visage of the night is ennobling, hence, it is said, “Oh night! Lift your veil.”’ Sundargauri: ‘The Gita says, when it is night for all other beings, the disciplined soul is awake; and when all other beings are awake, it is night for the seeing ascetic.’ Chandrakant: ‘Kusumbehn, your Kaki is right. The day is filled with hustle-bustle and noise of all kinds, while the night is silent. The disciplined soul of the yogi is awake when it is night for others. Yogis are of three types. The lowest among them retain worldly desires. Just like the rest of the world, these ascetics are also trapped by the residual desires alive within them, and they take pleasure in this entrapment. Their inebriated mind suffused with ego sings its own praise. Night gives a boost to their ego. Whatever boosts the ego is intoxicating. Such ascetics sing egoistic songs all through the night.’ Kusum: ‘Right. Emperor Babar faced a lot of hardship in his childhood. It is said that he used to go up the mountains, compose poems and sing them. The songs of these ascetics must be similar.’ Chandrakant: ‘He had no desires, no attachments at that age. Yesterday, you recited a verse of Bhartrhari: “The world has been maddened by drinking the intoxicating wine of delusion.”⟨fn:133⟩ If someone feels a similar intoxication...’

Gunasundari: ‘She will learn that at an appropriate time. Let us speak of the second order of ascetics.’ Kusum was about to give a retort to her mother, but checked herself and said, ‘The second order of ascetics have poets such as Emperor Babar. They are moved by the beauty of the night, and they have strange dreams which they chase. That is why it is said that the heart runs after the vision of dreams. Do those who take intoxicating drinks have sharp intellects? It is said in Magha: The mellifluous female of the bee had her audacity augmented For she was drunken with the wealth of honey from the spring creepers⟨fn:134⟩ Chandrakant: ‘That only causes inebriation.’ Kusum: ‘That is right. Because the next line says: Roused to flowering by the coming of the spring and with her repeated Buzzing, she sang a muted, slurring sound though the air.⟨fn:135⟩ She immediately realised the meaning of the verse and became silent. Deeply embarrassed, she cursed the knowledge of Sanskrit, ‘Oh, this wretched Sanskrit! One tends to get carried away and recite verses that are inappropriate and embarrassing. If one is not careful, this shringar may even lead to marriage!’ Then in an unnaturally loud voice, she added, ‘Chandrakantbhai, do tell me about the third type of ascetic.’ Chandrakant: ‘The third type of ascetic actually lifts the veil on the night and he wanders through the night having left behind all his wealth and similar such attachment.’ Kusum: ‘Just like Sarasvatichandra.’ Chandrakant: ‘That is for you to decide.’ Kusum: ‘But I cannot show you any more paintings.’ Chandrakant: ‘Why not?’

Kusum: ‘Because I will have to redraw the male and female figures.’ Chandrakant: ‘Why so?’ Kusum: ‘Now that I understand the meaning, I realise my error. I will have to think as to what kind of changes need to be made. A poem describes two kinds of eyes and two types of seeing; I will have to capture that in the painting.’ Chandrakant: ‘Which poem is this?’ Kusum: The world beholds her beauty with eyes open, The world delights in her beauty with eyes closed. Gunasundari: ‘Whose poem is this, Kusum?’ Kusum was embarrassed and would not look up. ‘I have a fragment of a letter that Sarasvatichandra wrote to Kumudbehn.’ Sundargauri: ‘Aren’t you ashamed? Have you now taken to stealing letters of your sister?’ Kusum: ‘It was a mistake, I admit that. But how can you charge me with stealing? She was careless with the letter, and I read it. Should I leave my eyes someplace else when I walk around this house? Yes, I admit that I should not have read the letter as soon as I realised that it was meant for Kumudbehn—to that extent I erred.’ Sundargauri: ‘You can split hairs endlessly, but you won’t acknowledge an apparent wrong!’ Kusum: ‘Then just give up on me now. Forgive me; what is done cannot be undone. But Chandrakantbhai, I will paint the eyes that can see when open as also when shut. Kaki will object, but after all I am young and am tempted by such things.’ Just then a servant came in. Vidya Chatura had invited Chandrakant to his maternal uncle Jarashankar’s house for a meal. Rana Khachar had come to see the ailing Samant Mulu. Maharaj Maniraj had called a meeting of his officials to meet Rana Khachar and to discuss political issues. Chandrakant was also invited to that gathering. Chandrakant got up to change his clothes. The thought of the impossible possibility of the coming together of Sarasvatichandra and Kusum was uppermost on his mind, and with a heavy heart he set out to meet the minister of Ratnanagari. The women went back to their quarters. Sundargauri teased Kusum, pulled her hair, kissed her and said, ‘You sang about the desire of lovers. It is certain that you are going to marry Sarasvatichandra.’ The young girl, still intent upon remaining unmarried, was both embarrassed and angry at the suggestion. She pushed her aunt away and went to her reading room. Gunasundari, even more perturbed by her daughter’s unbridled charm, walked out into the garden to nurse her worries.
chapters.summary: Gunasundari frets over Kusum's blossoming beauty and her surprising recitation of Sarasvatichandra's words, hinting at an unexpected connection that deeply concerns her mother.

chapters.title: Do We Need Native States? An Acrimonious Debate between State Officials and Visitors from Bombay
paragraphs: Do We Need Native States? An Acrimonious Debate between State Officials and Visitors from Bombay What nature has disjoined in one way, wisdom may unite in another.   —Edmund Burke Mallaraj had taken a deliberate decision to align with British rule. This fiercely independent ruler had to swallow many bitter pills, but until his last day, he neither regretted his decision nor saw it as a mistake. He had not been able to explain the logic of his decision to anyone. Both Samant and Muluraj had remained unconvinced of this decision. Mallaraj had not received any English education, but he had given English education to his son Maniraj and had appointed Vidya Chatura as his tutor and later as a minister. He had also trained Vidya Chatura in the principles of his own statecraft. Mallaraj believed that this inheritance was a thousand-fold superior than all the wealth and riches of the state. The fortunate people of Ratnanagari derived the fruits of his deeds. After Mallaraj’s death, Ratnanagari had Maniraj as ruler, trained in virtue and statecraft by his father. It was as if one flower withered but from its manifold layers, a new bud emerged. Vidya Chatura took Jarashankar’s place. It is the duty of a ruler to ensure that the state is never bereft of able leadership, and he must train and cultivate leaders at all levels of administration. The new king and his minister not only nurtured the seeds sown by Mallaraj, they gave them fertile ground to flourish. Ideas which had remained mere intentions were experimented upon and proven ideas were put into practice. Mallaraj had espoused a principle that just as the bride must come from outside the circle of incest, the minister of the state should not be a hereditary position and he should preferably be an outsider. He believed that the right of primogeniture and royal lineage were beneficial to the state; but the same principle, when applied to the post of the minister, sapped the state of creative potential and could become the cause of rot in the state. Despite this belief, Mallaraj had taken a calculated risk and appointed Jarashankar’s nephew Vidya Chatura to succeed him as minister. He acted with caution as foreign rule was sweeping across the country. He felt that any new experiment should be avoided. Vidya Chatura knew well the forces which had worked in his favour and got him the ministership. He did not want to fail his young king. He wanted Maniraj to have a choice in the appointment of the next minister, preferably unrelated to him and not a native of Ratnanagari. He had appointed some able outsiders to subordinate positions. This arrangement, he hoped, would enable him and his king to test their abilities and choose the most appropriate person as the minister when necessary. These men were all intelligent and had the experience of working in other states. Vidya Chatura generous, unselfish and conscious of his duty towards the state, never hesitated to create opportunities for them and gave them exposure to various aspects of the state administration and new ideas about statecraft; with this view he had invited this select group to the meeting with Rana Khachar. Chandrakant, too, was invited to this special gathering; so was Vir Rao Dhampate, a patriotic Dakshini from Bombay who happened to be visiting Ratnanagari. Vidya Chatura wanted officials of the native state to experience for themselves the forceful advocacy of independence that residents of Bombay were known for. This was also his way of getting to know the visitors to the state. Rana Khachar was an old-style ruler and held on to traditional ideas of statecraft steadfastly. Vidya Chatura wanted to expose him to newer ways of thinking and hoped that a ruler like him would play a part in bringing together various native states.

One of the officials selected by Vidya Chatura was a bania named Pravindas, the native of a state neighbouring Rana Khachar’s state. His father was a trader, but Pravindas had studied in an English school and worked as a mamlatdar, or revenue officer, in a few states. His honesty had benefited both the rulers and the people of these states. Vidya Chatura had met him on a few occasions on his way to Bombay. He had immediately recognised his integrity and calibre, and attracted him to work for Ratnanagari. Pravindas was a recent appointee and was put in the recovery department of the state. Vidya Chatura handled this department and, at an appropriate time, hoped to make Pravindas its head. Vidya Chatura had invited from Bombay Shankar Sharma, an experienced jurist and expert in English laws. In a game of chess it is sometimes necessary to sacrifice a rookie to take the opponent’s king. Similarly, a state must be prepared to make some sacrifices to secure justice. These principles are well known, but men greedy after power tend to view them with disfavour and disregard them. Vidya Chatura however nurtured and cultivated these principles and encouraged Shankar Sharma to follow them. As minister, Vidya Chatura was quick to nip in the bud any sign of fear, favour or intimidation. Ratnanagari had vast forest wealth and several ports. Vidya Chatura had personally selected experts of the field from Bombay and employed them. The education department, usually relegated to the lowest priority and manned by poorly paid and despised officials in almost all native states, was headed by an able scholar who was paid a high salary. The minister kept constant but benevolent watch over the department. Apart from Pravindas and Shankar Sharma, officials of these departments were also invited to the special court. Mallaraj had commenced the construction of a grand palace outside the city of Ratnanagari. Maniraj improved upon the design and completed its construction. He named it Malla Mahabhavan. The front hall of the palace was named Vidur Bhavan. The special court was to be held in this hall. All walls of Vidur Bhavan were covered with maps—maps of the state, of all parts of India and even various countries of the world. It also contained a vast library, which had biographies of political leaders, past and present, of all lands. The library had a selection of speeches and writings of leaders. These were systematically arranged according to the country. If one section held books from England, the second had books from Germany and the third from America and so on. The library also had leading newspapers and magazines from Europe, America, India and other countries. Beautiful couches and chairs were placed in the middle of the hall for meetings. The invited guests looked at exhibits and browsed through books and magazines as they awaited the arrival of Maniraj and his officials. Shankar Sharma, Vir Rao and Chandrakant sat around a table. Chandrakant remarked, ‘What a great collection of books! A king who merely comes into this garden of books and smells their fragrance is sure to gain wisdom.’ Vir Rao laughed. ‘Hah! This is only for show and display! It’s a mere pretence. The native states are rotten! All is rotten at the core in these states! Don’t be taken in by this show like a simpleton!’⟨fn:136⟩ Shankar Sharma was startled by these sharp words. Pravindas signalled to him to keep quiet. Other invitees gathered around their table. Chandrakant was no stranger to such opinions, but he found them misplaced and smacking of ingratitude, especially given Maniraj’s hospitality. He joined the debate, ‘Mr. Dhampate, even if your opinion had some merit, its utterance here is out of place.’ Vir Rao: ‘You can butter them. I speak what I think. You see, I do not care a fig for these foolish and dishonest forms!⟨fn:137⟩ “One should not speak truth that goes against the people’s perception” is a convenient principle of honesty for the cowardly. Why should the warriors of truth care for what the world thinks?’ Vir Rao made a sound of disdain. Shankar Sharma laughed and gently said, ‘But one accused of libel cannot get away by saying that he speaks the truth. That is no proof of innocence.’

Vir Rao stretched himself up to his full height and said, ‘Mr. Shankar Sharma, your jurisprudence is futile before our science of truth. Politics is full of lies and even your justice is filled with untruth. Morality and justice can get caught in the web of lies, but that does not frighten the warriors of truth.
