In a real sense dharma, law, justice and religion all rest on the foundation of truth; human life and all its higher aspirations rest on truth. In one of our compositions, Dharma says: morality rests on religion and religion is based on truth. ‘Even Western scholars have expressed similar ideas. The flame of truth—like the flame of fire—shall burn brighter and stronger, and false religion masquerading as truth will melt in its fire. The warriors of truth shall fight to overturn the false polities of rotten states; they will become martyrs to truth that shall emerge triumphant. The warriors of truth are not required to consider place, time and consequence. They will speak their mind. That is our truth, and Damn your states and politics for preventing all the dictates of truth!’⟨fn:138⟩ Pravindas went cold as these abuses rained on them. Other officials depending upon their disposition were angry, amused or filled with disdain. They were all stunned by this forceful advocacy. They did not know that Vidya Chatura and Maniraj had come in unannounced and heard the entire exchange. Approaching from behind, Vidya Chatura quietly placed a hand on Vir Rao’s shoulder. Vir Rao looked up and rose to greet the minister. He did not care what the minister and the king thought of his outburst; he was in any case not given to guilt or embarrassment. He shook hands with Vidya Chatura and, turning towards Maniraj, said, ‘Maharaj, kings and commoners are all alike as humans. Humanity is higher than royal power. This order is based on truth. Even you would admit that. But our lawyer friend Chandrakant argued to the contrary, and hence I had to battle him.’ Maniraj laughed as he shook hands with Vir Rao and said, ‘The purpose of Vidur Bhavan is to provide the space for such verbal duels, and we welcome persons like you in the debates. Muluraj will shortly escort Maharana Khachar, and should be here soon. They, too, will benefit from your forceful advocacy. Let us all sit in the meeting room while we await their arrival.’ All of them walked towards the meeting room. Just then the ushers and the trotting of horses announced the arrival of Rana Khachar. All went to receive him. Maniraj led Rana Khachar. They seemed happy as they exchanged pleasantries. The two rulers sat on an ornate golden couch; on one side of Maniraj sat Vidya Chatura, followed by Vir Rao, Chandrakant and other officials of Ratnanagari. Rana Khachar was a lean, tall man. His deeply lined face showed his age, but his long, sharp and sparkling eyes showed his determination, resolve and betrayed his Rajput pride. His twirled moustache reached up to his ears and showed some grey hair. His lips were thin and long. His proud eyes and lips betrayed his contempt for the world. Even his smile had a razor’s edge. Rana Khachar was Maniraj’s father-in-law. They presented a study in contrast—one was mild and soothing as the moon, the other fiery as a comet. ‘Ranaji, these are our guests from Bombay,’ Maniraj introduced Chandrakant and Vir Rao to Rana Khachar. ‘Well, that is apparent from their faces,’ replied the Rana. Maniraj: ‘The Dakshini gentleman is Vir Rao. He believes that the native states are rotten at the core.’ Rana Khachar: ‘If he feels that, it must be so. What are we to do? The termite of Bombay eats away the core of our native states. The price of hosting such guests is not small,’ Rana Khachar’s tone mocked Vir Rao. Vir Rao’s eyes showed his anger, but he chose not to respond. Instead, he whispered to Chandrakant, ‘Look! Look! Not only does the devil coil and sting like a serpent, but he can breathe venom, too!’ ‘He only pays in kind!’ Chandrakant replied with some relish. ‘Me, he pays in kind? You say so?’ Vir Rao puckered his lips. ‘I believe he thinks so,’ Chandrakant smiled.⟨fn:139⟩ ‘Chandrakantji, you are carrying on a private conversation. Do share with us the nectar of your wisdom,’ Maniraj egged them on.

Vir Rao: ‘Then listen, Maharaj. Bombay has termites, but it also has reform. Termites go where they find clientele. If the native states attract nothing but termites, these states must be diseased.’ Maniraj: ‘Let us put aside the question as to which of the native states are diseased, and which are not. But if you can show us a remedy for the disease, it would contribute something of value to the debate.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘According to Dhampate Sahib, the disease has spread everywhere.’ Maniraj: ‘If that is the case we should for the sake of argument accept that we, too, are diseased. But this acceptance is not the cure of the disease. What is the remedy?’ Vir Rao: ‘Maharaj, as far as I am concerned, the disease is now incurable. The states must be stewed in their own sweet juice.⟨fn:140⟩ It is said: When the body has lived its duration and been caught up in disease therein, the medicine is the water of Jhanvi, and the healer is Narayana.⟨fn:141⟩ Shankar Sharma: ‘Vir Raoji has rung our death bell. He has pronounced the death penalty. We should hear if the lawyer has any solution to this problem.’ Pravindas: ‘Bhai Sahib, have patience. If our neighbour has piled up food grains, we will be able to borrow some in times of famine. We should ask about the condition of states where jewels like Vir Rao are to be found.’ Vir Rao: ‘What do you want to ask? Native states are the impediment in the growth and welfare of natives under British rule. Whenever the question of the ability of natives for Home Rule is discussed, the British officials invariably point an accusing finger at you. They say that the native states provide an “object lesson” in the type of misrule and anarchy that self-governing natives invariably create.’ Pravindas: ‘But Rao Sahib, we are on our death bed; let us await our certain death. But do please tell us as to what kind of life still breathes in you.’ Vir Rao: ‘How are we to show that? If there were to be a Governor General like Dalhousie who would merge all the native states within the British Empire, you would see the life that stirs within us. But just as the divisions of caste come in our way at every step, the conditions of native states push back our aspirations.’ Rana Khachar was evidently displeased. Shankar Sharma: ‘What is it to us whether you burn in the destructive fires of Holi or have the festive prosperity of Diwali? Is it just to seek our destruction, so that you could rise and shine? Rao Sahib, you have swept aside all considerations of morality, law and religion.⟨fn:142⟩ Vir Rao: ‘He who would rush into the front ranks must tread upon somebody’s corns.⟨fn:143⟩ Why should the welfare of the nation not be secured by the death of some native states, already groaning in pain of disease and awaiting their death? The people of those states would be happier, and it would also aid our efforts. If morality, law and religion become impediments for the attainment of this great goal, these obstacles must be removed. When a kshatriya goes to battle, he kills a cow that impedes his advance and atones later after securing victory.’ The assembly shuddered at these words. They looked at Vir Rao with disdain and dejection. Vir Rao ignored them. Vidya Chatura: ‘Rao Sahib, we shall for the present not go into the deep and complex subjects of law, morality and religion. We shall discuss history, the question of means and ends and the future. Do you believe that we are not part of the Empire to which you belong?’

Vir Rao: ‘That’s it.⟨fn:144⟩ Of course, we are both part of the Empire, and that is why I say that when a part of the body is diseased and begins to rot it is best to cut it off so that its poison does not spread to the rest of the body. Only a part of the body is diseased, but it endangers the whole of it. That is the truth. Religion, law and morality are based on the foundation of this truth. For the good of the body, the diseased part must be severed.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Then you must find out to what extent we harm you and to what degree we contribute to your welfare?’ Vir Rao: ‘What is the need? The native states cannot be reformed. Kings are misled by the machinations that plague the core of their kingdoms. Even when one of our good men goes to the native states, he becomes rotten because of the machinations. Its germs come and plague us. The story of your states is that of the contagious disease that infects one eye after another. They are rotten and they spread their rot. Their subjects are unhappy and victims of tyranny. The rulers waste money even if they have to incur huge debts. They are greedy and stingy when it comes to spending money for the welfare of their people. They either hoard their wealth in their basements or waste them in their debauched ways. The people remain paupers! The people living under native states will get neither education, nor freedom. They will be denied industry, happiness and even humanity. Kings and their officials will become thorns in their sides if they wish to pursue any higher aspirations. The kings will always remain backward in this age of reform and force their people to remain backward like them. The native states benefit no one; they only cause harm. They are doomed and shall cease, and the sooner the better.⟨fn:145⟩ No one in this world has any use for them. When these states are destroyed the rulers will regain their humanity and will become partners in our great endeavours. This is the only way to resurrect these rulers and those living under their rule. All else is futile.⟨fn:146⟩ The sooner these states die, the sooner they will find release and possible rebirth.’ Pravindas: ‘The English drain away your wealth. Our wealth not only stays with us, it also nourishes you. What about that?’ Shankar Sharma: ‘For you, there is only one school that gives you lessons in statecraft and state policy. And this school happens to be us, the native states. The only place where the English officials relate to the natives on a basis of equality is also the native states. What about all these?’ A young official seated at the very end spoke up, ‘In British India, all of you will always remain “plebeians,” while all the “patricians” are among us. This is the only place where you can leave behind your lowly upbringing and acquire the cultivated culture of the high born. What about that? Every word of yours betrayed your birth. But for the native states where will you learn refined tastes?’ Muluraj mocked Vir Rao, ‘Rao Sahib, you have found a nice way of sending native states to heaven. Maharaj, do Bombay’s cattle sheds only have gentlemen like him, or does the city house other animals also?’ Vir Rao turned red with rage. He was about to give a sharp retort when Chandrakant joined the debate to prevent it from turning ugly. ‘Muluraj, our Rao Sahib is the author of many books and he also edits a newspaper. He has no personal experience of native states; his views are based on what his reporters from the native states write. Maharaj, if Vir Rao has disdain for the native states, my friend Sarasvatichandra has nothing but affection for them. I have no personal experience, but I have heard many stories from my friend and I have discussed the conditions of native states with him. Hence, my views are not mature and well-considered. But I see no fault in expressing them.’ Maniraj: ‘Please speak without hesitation; we are truly eager to know our faults and all that ails us.’ Chandrakant: ‘I feel that among us there is a large class of commoners. But what we need is a class of nobility, an aristocracy that has the money and the power to mediate between the people and the rulers. British rule has churned us, which, like the churning of curd, will dissolve us and break the power of the native states, and they will ultimately merge with British India. In Bengal, large landlords are often addressed as raja. I feel that our rulers will become the aristocracy required to mediate relations between the commoners and the rulers. Rulers have many constraints and are often unhappy. Once they merge with the rest of us, they will be autonomous and happy, and they will become instrumental in securing the welfare of the nation.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘How will it benefit you if the rulers cease to be rulers and are constituted as a class of aristocrats?’ Vir Rao: ‘Sir, he has said exactly what I said, but this Gujarati bhai smoothened and softened the blow with butter.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘No, Rao Sahib. You seek the destruction of kings and of nobility. You want to reduce all of them to your level—to be as sky-clad as you are. Chandrakantji has faith in the aristocracy. You seek the destruction of the rulers; he does not. He believes that a change in the character of the rulers is the destiny of these changing times.’ Vir Rao: ‘Yes, but it is all the same.’ Chandrakant: ‘No sir. You journalists cannot fathom the power of English law and diplomacy. When the Roman Empire ruled the world, Pax Romana was established. All dissensions ceased.⟨fn:147⟩ Just as all other animals run for cover as soon as they see a tiger, the small states ceased their infighting faced with the might of Roman law. In India as well, Pax Britanica is about to usher in that age. It is true that the native states are not subordinate to our high courts, but they are not independent from “International Law.” And each moment the will of British rule is enforced. The internal dissensions of the native states help that process. Faced with Pax Britanica our rulers have become noble aristocrats. They are being transformed, and ultimately a class of aristocrats will be created.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘Do you believe this to be inevitable even if the native rulers were to reform themselves, to become pure and virtuous?’ Pravindas: ‘Do you believe that we lack the intelligence to avoid that fate?’ Chandrakant: ‘Pax Britanica will cause the decline of all other powers. When the sun rises, all light, be it that of the stars or the moon, fades. Just as Arjun saw the Kauravas and Pandavas disappear in the universal form of the Lord, all kings—be they pure or impure, wise or foolish—will cease to be in the face of Pax Britanica. The British not only retain the authority of adjudicating disputes between native states, but also those that arise between them and the native states. The laws that they have formed are also appropriate to these times of transition. The native rulers hold the scales of justice so far as their subjects are concerned, but if they fail to hold them in a fair and just manner they will slip into the firm grip of the British. In such times the people of the native states will prefer to be ruled by the British rather than by the native princes. Just as a woman harassed by her in-laws sometimes takes the drastic step of running away with a foreigner, the people too would seek British rule. Our native rulers are no longer kings; they have been reduced to local officials appointed by the British. “They are already reduced to what Herbert Spencer calls local Governing Agencies.”⟨fn:148⟩ ‘In these times of transition, in the age of industry, people of smaller states will merge into larger ones and at such times the traditional rulers of these states will become “Lords and Nobles—a noble aristocracy.”⟨fn:149⟩ Soon you will see yourselves reduced to our “local boards” and “municipalities.” Eventually you will cease to be.’ Pravindas: ‘How will that benefit you?’ Shankar Sharma: ‘Do you know of any such example?’ Chandrakant: ‘The barons of England have been reduced to dukes and counts. That’s an example for you! Is the condition of your Bhayat any different? Eventually, the native rulers will become Garasias of the British. That will be to our advantage. We the people of British India have no accumulated capital. We have no scope for establishing industries. We have to make a great and consistent effort in order to secure even small concessions from the British. The Congress and its activity bear testimony to this. In Bengal, the landlords have the leisure, the wealth and enthusiasm. Bombay province has trade and commerce, but it is not controlled by the scholarly class. If they pursue wealth, they have to forsake the leisure of scholarly pursuits. The traders tend to invest their money and effort in enhancing their trade. Those who have the wealth and opportunity lack in industriousness. If the native rulers were to become like the landlords of Bengal, Bombay province will have a class of landed aristocracy. This is clearly on the cards. When this happens, we, the scholars, will enthuse this class with ideas and like the barons who fought for the masses of England and secured the Magna Carta⟨fn:150⟩ our country, too, will get a class which shall fight for the people. We want the government, the rulers and the subjects all to benefit. That is our vested interest!’ Pravindas: ‘Do you actually hope that like the barons of England we, too, should commit the folly of raising arms against the Crown?’ Shankar Sharma: ‘Do you harbour such seditious thoughts? You have been so blinded by your enthusiasm that you cannot see the treachery and sedition inherent in your thought. Or else you consciously harbour thoughts of sedition.’ Vir Rao: ‘Bhai Chandrakant, you buttered them, but the end result was the same! Regain your senses and admit that these great souls are so impotent that they have neither the courage nor the sagacity to act as responsible noble men. Not just that, they lack even the humanity of poor like us. In England, if the commoners were not raised to the peerage and made earls and dukes, they, too, would have lost all nobility just as the old nobles have lost theirs. But how does one even begin to compare that country with ours? They are able to regain their balance as they are about to fall, but our people fall before they can even stand on their feet. How do we hope that one day they will stand up? Now we have to perform their last rites so that their souls can be freed from this bestiality and be born again as humans! Look at this judge of ours from Bombay. His autonomy and humanity are afraid of sedition! Hey Ram! Hey Ram!’ The Rajputs seethed with anger, blood rushed to their eyes and their foreheads creased in deep furrows. Only Maniraj retained his equanimity. Shankar Sharma was stunned. One old official of Ratnanagari seated in the last row spoke up in a steady voice, ‘The proof of one’s caste and family lineage becomes evident at the moment of utterance.’ A Garasia of Maniraj spoke without betraying any emotion, ‘There is no cause for anger if in this Vidur Bhavan—named after a man who was born to a slave woman—a person should speak words expected of the low born.’ With the exception of Maniraj and Vidya Chatura, everyone laughed. It was Vir Rao’s turn to seethe in anger. Chandrakant intervened, ‘Those who hit hard must be prepared to be hit hard!⟨fn:151⟩ Bhau Sahib, you must accept the statements of these gentlemen as part of this debate just as they accepted yours. Equanimity is necessary in a debate, or else we will defame Bombay.’ Vir Rao: ‘It was mistake that I intervened in a debate that was being led by you. It is greater pleasure to see how you measure up to them.’ Chandrakant: ‘As you please. I am required to answer many questions. But before that I must respond to you. You were responsible for some of the unpleasantness that ensued. The pleasure of a debate is not enhanced by abuses and curses. A debate has to be conducted not by rhetoric but by subtle inflections of meaning, by statements that are sharp, masked by humour. Such a debate not only gives pleasure but also generates high discourse and leads all towards truth. You have experienced this art during your interactions with our noble friend Sarasvatichandra. The officials of the native states will also teach you courtesy and the art of debate. I must admit that despite conscious attempt, I have acquired only rudimentary competence in this art. It is likely that someone like you, who has obvious disdain for the finer aspects of a debate, would have remained a stranger to this art. But, unlike these gentlemen, I do not dislike you, because I have the same follies as you. Today you may not feel defeated, but you received some hard kicks. This will perhaps allow you to admit that probably there is some problem with our manners. You describe my desire to be free from this folly as an act of “buttering.” I take exception to this. If it is indeed buttering then it is both delicious and nourishing. This butter can produce “ghee.” This butter is a product of pure milk. So long as the milk is not contaminated by waters of untruth and has not turned sour, the butter that comes from it remains fit for consumption. You Marathas consider abuse as good manners, but among us there is another view. You disregard the nobility and goodness of kings, but you must admit that it is their nobility that allows them to retain their poise even when you abused them and continue to treat you as an honoured guest. Nobility has three aspects: forbearance, forgiveness and generosity. Maharaj Maniraj embodies all these qualities. This object lesson should teach you that at least a part of your argument stands demolished. The nobility of your rulers is not as fragile as you would like us to believe. It is not so easily destroyed. ‘I need to respond to you and Shankar Sharma on the question of sedition and treachery. Vir Rao considers even the thought of treachery as dereliction of duty, while Shankar Sharma is unduly perturbed by it. ‘Vir Raoji, you rely upon the Shastra for thought and conduct. Firstly, this Shastra itself is false. You do not advocate that one should follow the Shastra in every instance. No father desires to know the intimate details of his son’s bed chamber, no matter how obedient the son is. All of us dread the possibility of exposing a certain half of our bodies. Similarly, our intellect refuses to see and acknowledge certain truths. Vir Raoji, you must admit that even you would refuse to recognise and acknowledge certain facts. Your argument is based on a false premise. Your position can lead to great calamities. Your caste fellows, journalists and the Marathas of British India bear testimony to this. Bulwer Sahib has grown tired of repeating that so long as the English and the natives consider each other foreigners and fail to build relations of brotherhood, India will not emerge out of the mistrust between the rulers and the ruled, and this will do good to none. Anyone who becomes an obstacle in this path of trust and welfare is a traitor. You do not realise that your words smack of treachery. You consider yourself patriotic but you advocate treason. The fact remains that the English are not capable of entirely giving up their selfish nature and they harbour a deep mistrust of the natives. But which native can deny that there are noble exceptions to this? The English who have laid the foundations of the Congress bear testimony to this. Rippon is a living example of this. More natives speak English compared to the British who understand our native tongues. Similarly, they may or may not understand our hearts and minds, but a native who makes the slightest efforts would easily grasp their mind. The one who has better understanding has a higher duty. A large section of the British may not in fact trust us, but it is up to us to make an attempt to enhance their trust in us. As we become more able, our duties and responsibilities correspondingly increase. Your statements are a breach of this principle, and the ruling classes of the native states unnecessarily invite the charge of the mistrust on themselves. This is like the horns of a cow that can neither be consumed, nor give any joy or provide nourishment.⟨fn:152⟩ Any attempt to bite into them can only result in the teeth breaking. This stupid and meaningless attempt is the result of your speech. So long as you cannot control your speech, you will bear the sin of treachery. You will not only fail to enhance the trust of our foreign rulers but in fact you will give them reasons to mistrust us. They will become even less generous and less noble, and we will be destroyed like the shalmali tree.⟨fn:153⟩ ‘You complain that caste divides our native states. But is our Bombay or Poona any different? Do we not discriminate between Dakshinis and Gujaratis? Are not the Dakshinis divided among prabhus and brahmins, between brahmins and Marathas? Are not the brahmins divided among deshastha and kokanastha? Are the chitpavans not different from the karadha? Do these differences not create havoc among us? Have they not destroyed the reform movement? The fact remains that some patriots like you fight against these distinctions and inequities, but the people who oppose you include gentlemen with B. A. and M. A. degrees; they include lawyers, doctors, ministers and rulers as well. The waves of opposition have not hitherto travelled from Gujarat to Maharashtra. But we Gujaratis learn from your patriotic fervour and are now aroused. Hence, you should give us the benefit of your experience so that we can rid our politics of caste divisions. The energy that you expend in futile endeavours of abusing our rulers and the British government could be better employed in eradicating caste distinctions among our own kind. If you can do that, you shall see that native states, too, will follow your lead. Vir Raoji, if we are scholarly and apparently reformed, we should provide object lessons to the illiterate native states by our exemplary conduct. This is our duty, if our learning and scholarship are true. An object lesson will always be more effective than hundreds of abuses. If we consider ourselves superior to others, it should be reflected in our conduct from which others can learn. If we fail to do so, it proves that our perceived superiority is false. That is the fact. What is the use of our wild talks and odious comparisons which only irritate others and lower ourselves?’⟨fn:154⟩ Maniraj: ‘Chandrakantji, Vir Raoji, you are both our guests. It is our practice in Vidur Bhavan that we learn from the truth of our visitors and disregard all else. Our minister will certainly learn from the truth of Vir Raoji’s statements. If you find his enthusiasm unbridled and without restraint, you will have other opportunities to rein in your comrade. But for the present allow us to test our ability to comprehend the fearless thoughts expressed by him and you alike. Allow us to contend with the views that you have both so eloquently expressed. Disregard our status and authority and let your mind be as clear as crystal,⟨fn:155⟩ allow your thoughts to flow freely, permit the song of freedom to burst forth in all its exuberance, let all flowers bloom. Do not allow our royal lineage to be our enemy and deprive us from partaking in this exalted scene. This Vidur Bhavan has been created so that we can forget—for a short while—our royalty and be as commonly human as you. Humanity, so natural for you, is a rare privilege for us.’ Chandrakant smiled and said, ‘I submit to my friend that this rare hospitality is also an expression of nobility. I feel that he has got the answer to his poser that native states are bereft of all nobility. A discourse on nobility would have remained inconclusive if I had failed to illustrate both nobility and its absence. Now that it has been made apparent to all of us, I need not labour that point. ‘Before I conclude, I do wish to state that this object lesson proves my contention that native states will give us a class of nobility and aristocracy. Vir Rao considers native states to be the miscarriage of nobility. And that is his error. Foreign rulers, with their deep mistrust of natives, are incapable of this generosity and nobility towards us. In their limited vision, all natives are eager to turn traitors. But there is no reason why the native states should share in this nightmarish vision. The distinction of native and foreigner is both false and misplaced in the context of our native states. Similarly, the fear of sedition is also misplaced and false. It is not necessary to elaborate this point any further. Not only because the British are ultimately the sovereign rulers over our native states, but primarily because of the foresight, nobility, generosity and forgiveness that rulers such as Maharaj Mallaraj have embodied. The result of these qualities is for all of us to observe and learn from. When not only Samant Raj but almost everyone saw Muluraj as a rebel and a traitor, Maharaj Mallaraj saw a patriotic soul; he nurtured and nourished those seeds and today that former rebel is a patriot and a pillar of this state. Muluraj’s devotion to the state has given a new lease of life to his ailing father and he is with us as part of this august assembly. Mr. Shankar Sharma will learn from this illustration and recognise that the native states need not harbour fears of sedition. The freedom of Bombay, which has withered, will be nourished in this state. He will realise that some day he might be called upon to judge the tyrannical conduct of powerful men, but he will not have to adjudicate a matter of anyone having committed a seditious act towards this throne from which rulers such as Mallaraj and Maniraj have ruled. Anyone accused of sedition will be given a punishment of a different order by this state. A diseased person will be punished not by the sword but by the life-giving potion that nourishes latent patriotism.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘I did not mean that our state has any fear of traitors from within. But you seem to incite us to rebellion against the sovereign power.’ Chandrakant: ‘Clearly, for us Swaraj is something to be obtained by sedition. Hence, you thought of rebellion and misinterpreted my statement. The fact is that the nobles who asked for the Magna Carta were armed. But I sought your assistance in obtaining a Magna Carta  for us after you have been disarmed and have ceased to be rulers. I sought your help not because you can wield weapons, but because you have wealth, because you have close ties with the British and because you have mastered the art of diplomacy. I sought your assistance because you have exercised great power over the minds of our people and know how to rule their minds. In this day and age this is the only real power. And this power actually works against rebellious and seditious ideas. This power can destroy the odour of sedition.’ Pravindas: ‘You may think what you like. But why should we disregard our own interests, deprive our people of the wealth that we have accumulated for their welfare and spend it on your fancies? Please explain to me as to how you have come to believe that you are the sons-in-law and nephews of the native states and have claims on us.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘Money is not the only thing. Among us the son-in- law is considered to be the additional tenth planet that could cause us grief. Who has given you the rights to make claims on our resources, abuse us, humiliate us, give us grief and keep a sword hanging over us? Why should we be forced to accept the barking that your newspapers do every morning?’ Vir Rao: ‘Bhai, we are neither your nephews nor your sons-in-laws. But we occupy the place of your family priest. So when you neglect your duties, we get your people, who are as meek as the women of your households, to make noise and complain. The times are such that you would submit more readily to the charms of your women than to the advice of your priest. In this dark age, dharma has become the preserve of women; they are the upholders of dharma.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘Now, this is a new fad.’ Vir Rao: ‘There is nothing new about this; this is old, tried and tested. In your weddings women sing songs about how they have reined in their men. The only thing they need to decide is which part of your nose has to be pierced to put in the reins. We, the priests, encourage them; it is our duty to ensure that dharma does not desert your households and realms.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘And it also fills your bellies.’ Vir Rao: ‘Sahib, the nobility of my tongue seems to have affected your speech as well! I feel elevated. Bhai Chandrakant, please respond to this charge.’

Chandrakant: ‘It is a great error to think that your interests are different from ours. If you think from the point of our people, the interest of the people of this entire Indian subcontinent is one. Just as caste discrimination hampers the attainment of one common objective, a parochial, regional view is also an obstacle. If you consider the rulers, from the point of view of the rulers, the native chiefs and fiefdoms are all part of the Empire. We are a mere wheel in this enormous machine. It is necessary that all parts of a machine work in harmony. If there were to be an attack on our borders, will either you or us or even the English take a different view of the matter and act to the detriment of our people? When the people of the subcontinent face famine or when questions of the spread of railways and education are considered, would we only fill our plates and watch the others suffer? Do you think that a calamity would make distinction between us and you and favour one over the other? If my roof catches fire it is certain to spread to my neighbour’s house. If there be wealth in my house, my neighbour would be able to lay claim over it in times of distress. The unsullied interest of all of us—whether it is the English, us natives or you the rulers—is one. ‘With each passing day, the peoples of the world are coming together in a federation. The political process is bringing people closer to each other and ultimately commerce and industry shall emerge primary.⟨fn:156⟩ You and we should give up any thoughts of being separate.

The political processes—the federation⟨fn:157⟩—is bringing the people of the old world together; the people of the new world are coming closer and ultimately the peoples of both the old and the new world will be unified. By the same logic, you, we and the English will become one people. The political union will eventually result in the unification of people. The English, the natives and the people of the native states depend upon one source for their livelihood. When people realise this, when they open their ears and hearts to this fact, then their intellects will also work towards oneness. All hearts will resound with the same voice and the bodies will work to the same rhythm. British India is a colony of England, and the native states are colonies of British India. This relationship has already been established. This relationship will be strengthened and reinforced. Our newspapers will provide you with wisdom, they will scold you but will also support you when you face injustice. They will praise you when you do well. Those who serve our land will also serve you and will demand their price from you like they do from us. We cannot get rid of you. You cannot be free of us. The footsteps of the inevitable future can already be heard. Each of us will have to welcome that future. Whether you like it or not, you are destined to receive that future with open arms.’ Vir Rao joked with Chandrakant and said softly in his ear, ‘Your long discourse has put the assembly into a deep, Kumbhakarna-like sleep. A woman seeking to seduce an impotent man is ultimately frustrated!’ Chandrakant could not suppress his laughter. ‘Maharaj, when Vir Rao is angry he makes his opponents angry; but when he laughs all laugh with him. Pravindasji, the noble men who invite the likes of Shankar Sharma from Bombay to Ratnanagari and set up a mutually beneficial encounter will one day unite the Indian subcontinent. When that happens, this entire land will become fragrant and they will nourish all the trees of this garden. We are all joined together in this great endeavour!’ The last statement melted the bania’s heart. Pravindas raised another question, ‘Chandrakantji, let that be. But I do not believe that the British will rob our rulers of their royalty and reduce them to mere nobility. It is in the interest of the British that we remain separate and disunited. This clever class of merchants will not fail in this. That is my conviction. The British can make use of the armies, the wealth and the authority of the native states. A mouse digs a burrow but the snake occupies it. By the same logic, the British will not waste this great opportunity. They are not foolish. We also stand to benefit. The British are promise-bound to help us against the aggression of other empires, and also against our own internal conflicts and dissensions. They have to protect us from the divisive influence of the people of British India. We are part of the great Empire that you speak of, but our self-interest lies in furthering each other’s authority and not in diminishing it.⟨fn:158⟩ This is a great task. We have through our traditions gathered great experiences; we shall add to those new arts that we shall learn from English education. The English will treat you the way a mother-in-law treats her daughters-in-law. We occupy the place of a sister-in-law vis-à-vis you. As it happens, the mother and daughter will come together to ill-treat and subjugate you, the daughter-in-law. And that shall be your fate. God willing, all of us will live together in harmony. But in any case the Paramount Power stands to benefit by protecting us. They will not cause the erosion of royal power. We are born with good fortune.’ Vir Rao: ‘Given the machinations and the short-sightedness of the rulers it is unlikely that the foresight and the arts required to realise your scenario will ever be attained. It is futile to hope for it. It is likely that they are noble and will remain so, but learning has never been and will never be the preserve of the native rulers. How are they going to suddenly acquire it? The Paramount Power has the mastery over learning and various arts. But when the roots are destroyed, how are the branches to survive? Can this great learning be obtained just by collecting a few books?’ Pravindas: ‘Bhau Sahib, why do you forget that we have not invited European learning; it has come to our land on its own wings. Whether the native states welcome it or not, whether we have affectionate regard for it or not, it will become part of everything we do. There is a saying that a bard and a brahmin come uninvited. Even if one asks them to be at the village square, they invite themselves to our homes. You who advocate European knowledge are the new brahmins, and newspapers are your bards. These forces will gradually but surely make their way into our lives.⟨fn:159⟩ And once it enters our lives our children will submit themselves before it and learn this new art.’ Chandrakant: ‘Bhai, it is not my experience that the interest of the Paramount Power lies in our survival. But let us for the sake of the argument assume that it is so. Let us accept that European learning will come upon you with its own force and capture your intellect. Let us also assume that it will dispel the present darkness and give you the resources to develop and nourish your royal authority. Even then you will admit that the English will always be fifty times more advanced and developed compared to you. They will travel much further, and you will forever be following after them. This effort will tire you out and eventually you will abuse the English. A student who is coerced into learning does not go further either in learning or in life. A fast walker, walking along with a slow paced one, eventually loses patience and leaves behind his burden to walk his own path. The slow one belongs neither to the home nor to the world, but wanders aimlessly. He meets a sorry fate. It is said that a short one walking with a tall fellow is certain to come to grief. Today, Europe is moving with such force that your condition will inevitably be the one that I have just described. The inherent nobility of your character will not desert you, but our princes will lag far behind in the acquisition of new arts. Their fall from royal power is certain. In this instance at least their accumulated merit appears to be fast running out. They will eventually become commoners. It is said that when the gods exhaust their merit, they are born as humans and take birth in meritorious families. Similarly, the princes will be transformed into landlords.’ Pravindas: ‘Both of you are ‘pessimistic’ when it comes to the native princes, while we are ‘optimistic’. The English whom you regard as selfish, mired in vile diplomacy and intent on opening the latent volcano that will engulf us are not so in our estimation. We regard them as the harbingers of hope and justice. We see them as the source of the divine Ganga that nourishes our highest ideals. It is true that we as their pupils will take long before we can actually walk beside them. Our teachers in the art of politics will certainly not reveal all their secrets to us and they will prevent us from acquiring mastery in their arts. Their lack of generosity will certainly be an obstacle in the path of our independent development. Some of our un-enlightened rulers will fall way behind the rest of us. But the spring of goodness always gains current, it does not dry up. This is our duty. The cultured sections of our population accept this.⟨fn:160⟩ This class of people is growing. The

English have a paternal feeling towards us; they want us to progress. But we have the soft heart of a mother. This soft-heartedness prevents us from making progress and attaining the true fruits of the paternal efforts. It is like a child who goes weeping to his mother when the father sends him to school. The mother invariably melts and lets the child stay away from school. But eventually the father gets his way. The paternal feeling is quite evident among the British ruling classes and soft-hearted that we are, we will ultimately submit to it.’ Chandrakant: ‘If that indeed be the case, in what direction do you see this development taking you?’ Pravindas: ‘In 1871 the smaller states of Germany formed a union and joined the Prussian Empire.⟨fn:161⟩ We will look after our internal affairs, and the Paramount Power will not interfere in these matters. When the Paramount Power enters into war or participates in peacetime diplomacy, we, the native princes, will assist them as their fiduciary. We will learn from these experiences. Just as the German Emperor has been able to challenge France with the help of smaller states, the English, with our support, challenged Russia. The Paramount Power views you with suspicion and is always alert that you do not take up arms. The Paramount Power will trust us. But if we join your ‘bad company’ like that parrot who befriended the crows, the government will also come to mistrust us, and our condition will be as sorry as that of that parrot. I can clearly see when I calculate the advantages and disadvantages of associating with you that the disadvantages far outnumber the advantages you have enumerated.’ Chandrakant: ‘Instead of calculating cost and benefit it would be more fruitful to see the present trends and arrive at the scenario for the future.’ Pravindas: ‘Now you are speaking like a fortune-teller. I desire to be the doctor of our maladies. You are caught in the web of ‘‘fatalism’’ in the name of ‘‘science.’’ I accept the ‘‘will’’ and seek my ‘‘duty.’’ I see a beneficial outcome. You are a closet fatalist, while I have faith in the will and industry of man.’ Chandrakant: ‘Whatever it is, we should not confuse the topic of our debate. If a human being can discern the truth of the future, it is his duty to act on the basis of that truth. Is it your duty to close your eyes and wield your sword guided by the whims and fancies of your mind? Germany, united by the prospect of a common enemy, will disintegrate the moment the threat of that enemy disappears. One scabbard cannot hold many swords. One woman cannot have multiple husbands. If there are many claimants to power, the strongest among them would annihilate the others and assume all power. Your authority will be consumed by the British. Arjun saw the universal from of the Lord and realised that all forces finally merge in Him. This realisation showed him his duty. You should also see that your powers are merging into the giant belly of the Paramount Power. If you realise this, it will help you understand your duty. The political forces are such that gradually smaller states will merge into the larger ones. The glory of the sun makes the light of the moon and stars appear feeble. Eventually even the unification of people will be attained. This will be the final destiny of both the ‘‘federation’’ and the ‘‘colony.’’ This is what happened to Rome; the same will be the fate of Germany. That is also the destiny that awaits you. You are being dragged towards the mouth of such a force.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘You fail to observe these forces from a pragmatic point of view. You fail to distinguish between various streams. The fact remains that the unification of Germany was not accomplished due to one specific cause. Hence, its eventual fate will depend upon how it functions. It may even result in a process you just described. You accept that all around us civilised nations are coming together in some form. But the people of these nations do not become one people. And such unification of people in this country is an impossibility. People come together as a political body as a republic or as a monarchy. You, those who live under British rule, are not likely to form yourselves into a single unified political body. We, the native states are a political body. It is impossible to visualise a situation where we align with you—who have neither a body, nor a head. The dream that you cherish that you can unite with us and form a political body is not something to be entertained during waking hours. This dream is dear to you because of your felt need to align with us. But you and we belong to the same gotra and our union is prohibited. The English will not allow that to happen.’ Vir Rao: ‘They will not allow the two of us to marry, but they will rob you of all your clothes, and you and us will play in our loin cloth like bum-chums. The area between Himalayas to Kanyakumari will be our vast playing field. The government will use its power to ensure that we play in the spirit of the game and do not fight. In India, the English rule as the representative of their monarch. The history of England bears testimony to the fact that a powerful monarch reduces the aristocracy to the level of commoners. During the reign of Charles I, the barons who sought Magna Carta were reduced to dust by the power of the Tudor kings, and that time Cromwell and Hampton spewed venom on behalf of the people of England.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘That time has long passed into history. At present, dreams of rebellion have made way for ideas of national justice. In this the nobles become the pillars of the state. Unparalleled military might—far greater than the great war of Mahabharata—has been accumulated, which is intent upon destroying all human aspirations in Europe. It is the art of diplomacy that thwarts the ambitions of military might. When all other nations aspire to military might, the English have taken to the art of diplomacy. It does not waste its resources in becoming a mighty military power. The age of diplomacy and peaceful resolution of conflict is upon us. As this art deepens, as its force becomes more obvious, the rulers will give up the demonic dreams of rebellion and worship the godly means of the age of peace.⟨fn:162⟩ ‘Vir Raoji, now the politics of war has given way to politics of commerce and economics. Political greed will make way for commercial greed. The English are a nation of merchants. They will not give up the temptation of trade with us and allow their greed for territory to overpower commerce. The capacity for justice will gradually merge in the power of commerce. The age that Pravindas wants to bring upon us through human endeavour is already upon us. The English are harbingers of that age. They consider the power of native states to be insignificant. They will preserve the nominal authority of the native states so long as it can be preserved and extract commercial advantage from it. Even a daemon that thrives on human flesh prefers the seductive charms of a woman’s beauty to the taste of her flesh. The condition of native states under the British will be something similar. The English political class does not consider native rulers as their competitors but they see us as their fiduciaries and seek our advancement. They seek to join our authority with their power for mutual benefit.’⟨fn:163⟩ Vir Rao: ‘That implies that the British are the man and you are the woman, and the two of you are set on the course of blissful matrimony, isn’t it? Chandrakant, we must bow before this virtuous, faithful woman and seek her forgiveness. We told this seductress that her husband would seek to devour her, but they seek pleasure of each other’s flesh! We have committed a sin. She might even curse us! Oh pious Mother, please forgive our crime!’ Shankar Sharma: ‘Vir Rao, you may continue to speak like the severed fifth head of Brahma. I made the error of speaking of lofty ideas in the language of everyday usage. I employed a wrong simile. If that is the case, it is the task of the lettered and the cultured to improve upon it. The point is that the Paramount Power and the native states are enjoined by forces that are not transient. Unlike the unification of Germany, we are not joined with the British by transient and present interest. Our interests are permanent.’ Vir Rao: ‘In your simile, the desire that you allude to will disappear with youth. And to that extent it is transient. What will happen to you when you and your husband lose the flush of youth?’ Shankar Sharma chose to ignore Vir Rao, and continued: ‘Chandrakantji, eventually the native states and the British government will form a federation on the model of the United States of America. So long as we remain backward in Western political forms and methods, that federation will not materialise. The English are foreign rulers. Given their obvious self-interest they will never be able to secure the happiness and prosperity of our people. But the native rulers with the minimum of efforts will be able to make their subjects happy and prosperous. And they have already made beginnings in this endeavour. Some general goodness, some high aspirations and the ability to imitate the British—these are the only three qualities required to make our people happy. If these factors are present we can prove that native rulers will make their people happier than those living under British rule. With each passing day these qualities will flourish among us and then, as compared with you, our people would lead better lives. Unlike in British India, we shall not discriminate between natives and the English in matters of justice. Our wealth will not be drained out of the country; a petition by our subjects will not be considered an act of treason; our people will not be suppressed because they shall express themselves freely. It is your misfortune that the government that rules over you has no superior. But we are watched by the British. Even out of fear, out of a desire to prevent our people from taking their complaints to the British, we shall reform ourselves and our government. The British will not, even after great effort, understand the customs and habits of our people. We understand them instinctively and can satisfy the wants of our people. And so doing we shall progress. When this is accomplished, the people of England and the British government will accept our prestige and authority. Should there be any doubt regarding this? When we progress, would the government not think twice before showing the stick to us? The English masters will feel shy of their own conduct, and public opinion in England will make them even more ashamed of their conduct. They will have to put away their sticks. The government with its paternal attitude will learn that a son who attains the age of maturity has to be treated as a friend. Do you believe such a thing to be not possible? At such a juncture the government will respect our wisdom and accept our opinion. They will feel ashamed of sitting in judgement over us. Once we treat each other with equality, our bonds will grow stronger. It is not impossible to dream of a situation in India akin to the United States where all constituent units work with the principle of majority. Once the native rulers realise that their interests are best served by the welfare of their people, they will also progress. A native ruler who develops and progresses will naturally command the respect and goodwill of the English people. ‘The maturity of our own moral and intellectual altitude, whenever we reach it in the distant future, will not fail to command respect and love in the highest circles among Englishmen, if English instincts will have survived the period. The princes that will have led their subjects to a climax of genuine prosperity, a vision which a foreign government will have tried in vain to conjure up before their Indian subjects, will present a divine spectacle which will make your English rulers blush with an awakened consciousness of their own inner frailties! That will be the moment that will call them to the presence of a higher ideal, and I believe that also will be the beginning of an epoch when the Government will see the necessity of looking after your aspirations as if they were your kith and kin and not as your more powerful rivals and competitors. In the existence and growth of the native states not only are the subjects interested, but the rest of India and its rulers will find to this extent their own fortunes involved.’⟨fn:164⟩ Vir Rao was delighted. He got up and shook Shankar Sharma’s hand and said, ‘Thank you, my friend, for having an ideal so beautiful! I shall now be proud to claim you as my fellow townsman of Bombay.⟨fn:165⟩ ‘Chandrakant, I am happy that I have been proved wrong in case of Mr. Shankar Sharma, but our irreconcilable differences remain. The picture he has painted of the heavenly river is beautiful and divine, but it is not likely to give even a drop of drinking water. “It is all utopia, you see!” Mr. Shankar Sharma, please forgive me! The man convinced against his will, Is of the same opinion still.⟨fn:166⟩

‘Your framework does not sit well with my temperament.’ Rana Khachar took out his watch, looked at the time and said, ‘Vidya Chaturaji, all these pearls that you have collected are interesting, but do please bring it to some conclusion.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Yes Maharaj, it is about time. Vir Raoji, I would not be surprised if the native states indeed meet the fate you have envisioned. But the fact remains that all four of you learned men tried to cast the birth charts of the native states as per your calculations. And yet all of you would contest the charge of having faith in astrology. It is easy to paint these scenarios based either on astrological calculations or in the name of destiny or popular perception. No one can say with certainty as to how they will come about. Human intellect cannot discern the will of God. Truth is the basis of all religions. Just as these statements are true, so is it true that human beings have the capacity to discern some aspects of truth from the past and the present. Any statement about the future has the validity of a dream. The truth of this forecast is merely “speculative”. It is like groping in the dark. It would be wrong for us to base our conduct on mere speculation. ‘It is proper to ask these questions in a historical enquiry. A historical enquiry can enlighten us just as lightning in the sky lights up deep gorges hidden by tall mountains. It opens up new vistas. It is essential for scholars and kings to have such a vision because both must study the past in its proper context. Such minute examination of the past also allows them to perform another duty: to endeavour to change the present and ring in the new. The king and the scholar can discharge their duties only when they can dispel fatalistic tendencies. When an enemy declares war, at times of famine or when the sovereign movement of time and fate turns against one, a king satisfied with the condition of his state is certain to be destroyed. But a king who sees himself as working on behalf of his people makes all attempts to battle the forces arrayed against him and secures the welfare of his people, and so doing he performs the duties of a king. It is our duty to cultivate such vision and make such endeavour to secure our people’s welfare. ‘Subjects must live within the limits of time and space as defined by a dutiful and righteous king. They must preserve and protect righteous conduct. They have to search the history of their present condition and envision a future, and to this extent they must believe in fate. They must find the meaning of their life and perform their duties bound by fate and in obedience to their rulers. At present the English rule over the native states as a sovereign. The sovereign has to consider the benefits of all rulers such as us and frame policies. It is our duty as a vassal of the sovereign to follow them both in times of conflict as also peace. We have to locate our duties towards our people within that framework. Like our people we, too, are bound by the conditions that our sovereign creates and to that extent we, too, must follow what is ordained for us by fate. Our sovereign has to consider the flow and movement of the entire human civilisation; he provides us with this analysis and it is our duty to follow the policies so laid out by the sovereign power. If we transgress the limits set by the sovereign, we defy the limits of our duty; but if we do not transgress the sovereign will in order to secure our people’s welfare, we would have failed in our duty towards our people. When our people rise above their present lot, we shall build the edifice of our duty and conduct on the foundation of truth that you speak of. But for the present, and especially in relation to the sovereign, we shall consider that truth to be a mill of darkness. We shall follow—like the battalions of an army—the traditions set by the sovereign. If we fail to do so, we shall incur the great sin of becoming an instrument of disturbance and destruction of the fate destined for the Indian subcontinent by God. These in essence are the duties of the native rulers. ‘If we are destined to meet the sorry condition of a widow as predicted by Vir Raoji and Chandrakantbhai, we have no reason to strip ourselves of all ornaments and break our bangles in anticipation of that eventuality. We shall also not remain indifferent to our possible widowhood. Pravindas and Shankar Sharma have dreams of our great future and fortune. Only a great effort and an equally good fortune can ensure that their dreams turn to reality. We cannot see any beginning of that effort. These two learned men have envisioned a goal; it is likely that someone else will think of means to attain this end. We can make the effort, but its outcome is in the hands of the sovereign and the almighty God. Your debates and diagnosis help us to this extent.’ Vir Rao: ‘Do you accept subordination of the sovereign irrespective of whether their commands are just or unjust? Do our newspapers make an error while seeking to point out the unjust policies of the British and in taking your side?’ Chandrakant: ‘Do you accept that in matters relating to your relations with the sovereign, the sovereign, though an involved party, also assumes the role of the judge? Do you not consider that such a situation will gradually wither away your rights?’ Vidya Chatura smiled and said, ‘No. I do accept that it is improper for the sovereign to act as a judge in matters involving them and us. I also accept that such conduct leads to the erosion of our rights. But so long as we find someone as liberal and clever as the British to occupy the seat of judgement to adjudicate matters relating to the native states and people of the Indian subcontinent, we must uphold the destiny of the present system as members of the Empire. If we fail to do so, there would be anarchy, which would affect both the sovereign and us. A certain and inevitable slide into the abyss of anarchy can be prevented only by upholding the dignity of the seat of justice. This dignity is derived from learning, intelligence, a sense of righteous conduct and power; and this authority must therefore vest in the most superior ruler of the sub-continent. Who, with the exception of the present sovereign, commands such royal authority? The English officers are not free of many small and not so small follies; despite these if we were to consider the qualities required of a sovereign, the British are the most superior. The follies are inconsequential if we compare them with the benefits of the qualities. We must ensure that these qualities are not eroded while we challenge their follies and mistakes. This can be achieved only by our cleverness, our intelligence, our mental resolve, our autonomy and our forbearance. But these attacks must be mounted with the same sense of devotion and loyalty that guides a minister when he seeks to correct his king. In this respect, we the native states and the people of British India share a common ground. We can help and assist each other so long as neither of us violates our duties towards the sovereign. I do in fact see such mutual cooperation as our duty. The views expressed by Vir Raoji and Chandrakant on this issue point the right path of conduct. ‘Human nature harbours both nobility and evil. If we make an endeavour to protect and preserve ourselves from the evil aspects of the English officials—and unlike Pravindas we should not see this effort as motivated by purely selfish reasons—with the help of the merchants, leading men, scholars and newspapers of British India, we may in fact succeed in bringing to the fore the sovereign’s noble character and thus secure large benefits and boons for our people. In so doing, we shall not have committed an act of treachery. This is not impossible to attain. This is also right conduct and action. If the native states acquire the fitness and capacity for this, then your verbose and supplicant Congress and we can come together and form a joint council presided over by the sovereign. Our “federation” would be different in character and impulse from both the German and the American federations. But if this ability does not emerge or it fails the test of intellect or is defeated or instead of patience and right conduct we play the game of dice with vile haste and wrongdoing, the condition of the native states is certain to be sorrier than it is now. There are only two possible fates before us: we awake and arise, or be destroyed. It is impossible to predict with any certainty the fate that awaits us. The only thing we can fathom is that those who fail to keep pace with this restless activity and ceaseless change will be consigned to darkness and be trampled under the galloping forces of time.⟨fn:167⟩ This is our common destiny. ‘This is the direction in which fate is leading our age. English diplomacy understands the flow of our times and it fashions a new age. They will persist in their attempts. That, too, is our fate. If we fail to see the tide, if we try to resist it, we shall be drowned. That would be our misfortune, but it would be of our own making. However mighty and forceful that tidal wave might be, we will have to learn to swim in its waters, go below it or stay above; no matter what we do we shall have to remain afloat with skill and perseverance. We will have to master this art with our own efforts; whether we succeed or not is the will of God. It is beyond human capacity to predict what course time will take. If humans begin to have such faith in fortune-telling they would give up the path of “free will,” become fatalistic and forsake all human endeavour. Such predictions are not against morality or religion, but we are not duty-bound to believe them. Instead of believing in such predictions, we should make all humanly possible effort in acquiring the means to attain the end that we desire. This is our duty. This duty is also practical religion. Both commerce and politics depends on such practices. ‘The Shanti Parva describes this as the permanent, immutable duty of a king. It is the king’s duty to ensure that fatalism does not violate human endeavour. This is pragmatic conduct and remains a friend of the king even against the vagaries of time. ‘The four of you made dissimilar forecasts, two of which are optimistic, while the other two are pessimistic. It is the duty of a wise politician to take advantage from all of them. These predictions are based upon the assessment of the present and hence contain elements of truth. What one man sees, the other does not. Optimism and pessimism are two sides of a shield. Pravindas and Shankar Sharma see a golden future, while Vir Rao and Chandrakant see the future as corroded. All their views are reflections of British politics. ‘The British Empire exists as a system of both Hopes and Fears for the Native States as for all Natives as well, and on them it mostly lies to choose whether they will have the Hopes or the Fears, and the unknowable resultant of all varieties of the individual wisdom and working of each state, great and small, forward and backward, within its own isolated sphere. Government sees the working of all of them; it is in touch with all of them. Each of our states on the other hand sees only that point of Government which affects its own isolated individuality, and is blind to the rest. It is this inequality of vision that makes the states unequal to the comprehensive operations which the present system calls upon them to perform; and until this inequality is pronounced incurable or begins to perceptibly abate throughout, neither our fears nor our hopes can be looked upon as a constant factor.’⟨fn:168⟩ Vidya Chatura turned to Rana Khachar and said with a smile, ‘Maharaj, these gentlemen comprehend English much better than they do Gujarati. I had to explain the point to them in their own language, hence I spoke in English. Please forgive me for that. I simply said to them that our homes have holes in them; the British government sees all that we do, and hence our internal dissensions must subside. If we are destined to have the wisdom to see the functioning of the government in its totality and look after our own affairs, we shall someday have some success vis-à-vis the government or else the government will continue to rule over us. ‘Pravindas, we need not go far and wide. You know the history of Suvarnapur under the rule of Jadsinh. So long as the native states do not remove, root and branch, the immorality, corruption and intrigues that characterised Jadsinh’s Suvarnapur, so long as the majority of rulers and their ministers do not follow the path of virtue and good conduct, so long as they do not understand that their self-interest lies in securing the welfare of their people, till such time the danger of Vir Rao’s prediction coming true looms over our heads, and when these corroded states fall and are swept away they will drag along with them even the good states. Krishna and Balaram were dragged into the self-destructive war of the inebriated Yadavas; Bhishma perished along with the other Kauravas; a similar fate will befall us. The states smug in their own goodness are faced with this danger. In politics we have to guard against the fire engulfing even a distant neighbour; this dangerous truth is contained in Vir Rao’s prediction.

‘If native rulers could become free of immorality and vice, they would become the noblemen of Chandrakant’s imagination. But morality and virtue can help private families; they are not sufficient to secure the welfare of rulers. If a king be like Yudhishthir, he would lose Draupadi in a game of dice. ‘In addition to the dharma and virtue of Yudhishthir, the royal persona also requires the power of Bhim and Arjun’s art of warfare. Those native states which lacked the power to support the sovereign in times of war are not likely to receive support from the sovereign in their effort to regain their glory and power. Rulers will cease to be rulers and be reduced to local officials. If, in times of peace, the rulers do not possess the wisdom to follow the views of the sovereign on the question of the Empire and if they do not possess the power and the art of following the English officials in implementation of their policies, then the subjects of native states would follow the caravan of the English merchants and the rulers would lose the power of even local administration. In this instance, Chandrakant’s forecast would come true. ‘If the rulers, reduced to such a condition, do not join the people of British India and act as noblemen should, they would in their pettiness and sloth prove Vir Raoji correct. Having lost royal power, the kings should not squander nobility. They should recognise that the people of British India and they are one people; the same blood flows in their veins and both are required to assist each other in times of crises and make a joint effort to rise. Hence, it is desirable that we in the native states should cultivate with British India the type of relationship that Chandrakant envisages. ‘These are the remedial measures required to deal with the pessimistic scenario; similarly there are constructive measures that are required for the optimistic view to prevail. While fulfilling our obligations to the sovereign, our wealth and power have shrunk and withered, and these constructive measures would enable us to retain some autonomy.’

Vir Rao laughed and said, ‘Sahib, do not forget your obligations towards the sovereign—otherwise in terms of Shankar Sharma’s definition you would be committing treachery.’ Rana Khachar: ‘Pradhanji, Vir Rao is not going to spare even you.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Even if he wants to spare me, I do not wish to be spared. Vir Raoji, whether it constitutes treachery or not, you will admit that small traders can never match large merchants. They have to join a “joint stock company” if they want to be part of large ventures; and such a company would require the leadership of large merchants like the English.’ Vir Rao: ‘What will a company of rulers ever achieve? And if they can do something, why can’t the small rulers achieve something? Why do they have to go looking for the sovereign?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Two great empires on either end of the Himalayas are waiting to crush this country. The first task is to defend ourselves against that attack; this cannot be done without a sovereign power.’ Vir Rao: ‘A new master would replace an old one. For a community that allows its widows to remarry, widowhood should hardly be a matter of grief!’ Vidya Chatura laughed at this analogy and said, ‘Is it wise to abandon a husband with whom we have lived for so long, who has cared for us, and with whom despite our quarrels we continue to co-habit? Is the desire for a new husband a mark of wisdom? If that husband were to go away, you and we alike would be widowed. Experience should have taught you that what ails you ails us as well.’ Chandrakant: ‘Vir Rao, now even Pradhanji speaks your language, which should make comprehension easy.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘I will formulate this differently in my own way. Vir Rao, you say that if not the English we would get someone else to become the commander who will steer us clear from all the dangers that await us. But we also have constructive tasks to perform, and our company is unlikely to get a leader as able as the English. The creative and constructive energies of the native states and the English have merged together like the Ganga and Yamuna. This is without precedence for any empire. Neither your, nor our creative energies would find the autonomy to grow even in a democracy like the United States. If that be the case, we should not bring any other empire into our discussion. These other powers seek to promote the interest of their own people to the exclusion of all else. The interests of the English people are ever present before the English rulers, but they occupy the place of a mother goddess for people of many states; they know how to nurture and raise the children of others along with their own progeny. The constructive energies of this generous people and your own creative energies can and in fact do merge into each other. Similarly, we are under pressure to allow unfettered development of the creative energies of our own people. We will learn to nurture and tend to the garden of our people’s creativity. Gradually, a new world will emerge out of our constructive actions. That is our principal hope. The tree of hope will flower and bear fruit when many native states adopt a constitution like the one that the state of Mysore has, if not a superior one. ‘If our hopes come to fruition and our native rulers become as capable as the rulers of the British Crown’s colonies, we would reach the zenith of our aspirations. The exercise of our power would be limited to our own people; our responsibility would be to shower them with generosity and expertise, in which effort the British Government would support us, encourage us, teach us the art of governance and not be tempted to interfere. If our people rise to that level, the English officials would not dare to push their own agenda in the everyday affairs of our states. Moreover, in such a state of affairs we would be compelled to inform our people regarding the commands and dictates received by us from the English officials; this would ameliorate the charge made by native states of the covert pressure and intrigues that they are subjected to. If any sense of selfhood survives in us, we would be able to undertake this effort on the strength of our own abilities. No enemy other than the weakness of our own hearts can impede our efforts. When we become capable of this, our condition would be superior to those “colonies” with “Responsible Governments”⟨fn:169⟩ because the government retains “vetoing power” over these colonies, but powers over us. ‘We are self-governing “colonies” of Britain. The native states cannot become autonomous constituents of a union, like the one in United States, because in absence of native rulers, the reign of the British would be established over all the territories. One cannot even dream at present that the British would grant rights of self- government to the people of the native states. This part of Shankar Sharma’s argument is mere day-dream. ‘The British would have us aspire to become like the Crown’s colonies or like the constituent units of the German Empire. The German Emperor has the power to declare wars or ask the constituent units to bear the expenses of such a war. The English do not exercise such unqualified powers over us. We can follow and assist the sovereign power if we have the resources and the will to do so. The British have assumed for themselves the right to negotiate with foreign powers on our behalf; this they have done on the condition that their armies would protect us against external aggression. Even under such exigencies, we are not bound to supply them with armies. We have more autonomy compared to other British colonies and even the constituent units of the German Federation and the United States. If we were to help and assist the British we would be doing them a favour. ‘If we do not allow our people to rise to the level of the people in the best British “colonies,” our subjects would in comparison find themselves inferior and feel the shame of it. Such a scenario would prove Chandrakant right. We have to ensure that our people do not live with a sense of shame. ‘If we fail to provide assistance to the British, sooner or later they would assume powers similar to those of the German Emperor, and the predictions of Pravindas would come true. Maritime trade, railways, electricity and support for the security and integrity of the Empire are among the many subjects where we provide voluntary cooperation to the British. If we fail in voluntary cooperation, we would be eventually forced to submit to even harsher conditions. ‘It would require considerable constructive effort before we could reach a stage where the judicial authority of the sovereign is transferred to a chamber of princes. We are yet to reach a stage where we could even begin some efforts in this direction. We do not know if we would be able to organise ourselves for such an effort. That only God knows.’ Vidya Chatura concluded his discourse. Maniraj gave flowers and fragrant betel nut to everyone. As the assembly dispersed a messenger came and gave a note to Muluraj, who in turn handed it to Maniraj. Maniraj read the note and, in a voice stricken with grief, said to his minister, ‘Pradhanji, you must rush home.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Maharaj, the news must be about Kumud. My flower has withered.’ Maniraj: ‘The note says that your esteemed father has returned home.’ Rana Khachar: ‘Were they not able to find Kumud Sundari? Vidya Chatura, I know that separation from a daughter causes deep pain.’ Maniraj: ‘Pradhanji, you must return home without further delay. Give solace to your family. I will join you soon. Pradhanji, those who know your forbearance need not say much; it would be preposterous to even imagine your grief and compare it with mine.’ Maniraj’s eyes were moist. The assembly turned sombre and mournful. After a few minutes of silence Vidya Chatura said, ‘Maharaj, our Kumud cannot be traced, while Pramaddhan is no more. Both Buddhidhanbhai and we have suffered bereavement; the light has gone out from our lives. His grief is greater compared to mine. When I think of that I forget my sorrow.’ The assembly walked Vidya Chatura to his carriage. Maniraj, Muluraj and Rana Khachar got into the royal carriage. For some time no one spoke. Rana Khachar eventually broke the spell and said, ‘Maniraj, there is no harm in holding such debates. These verbose people do not cost us anything as compared to the dancing girls, and that in itself is a benefit. I am happy that you listen to them without expressing your views. But you must be careful that this bookish knowledge does not cast a spell over your mind.’ Maniraj: ‘Pradhanji with his vast experience filters them out like a sieve, and the residue is removed by association with rulers like you.’ Rana Khachar: ‘That is good. The discussion regarding the policies of the English rulers was useful. Some of their officials are good, while others are bad and create trouble for us. Have you thought as to what one should do with them?’ Maniraj: ‘Truly speaking I have not had the occasion of being in a situation of conflict with them so far. The late Maharaja has shown us ways of avoiding such conflicts, and by following his tradition we have hitherto secured our welfare. But should an occasion arise, we shall consult you and the policy that you suggest shall illumine our actions.’ Rana Khachar: ‘It is truly God’s grace that you have so far not had to battle it out with the British officials. But such comforting times will not last for ever; hence listen to my advice. The Queen, the Viceroy in Calcutta and the Governor are very far from us. It is the local officials who matter; if two are good, two others are bad; if two are wise, two are stupid. They are unpredictable; if one goes in one direction, the other goes in the opposite direction. They force us to be like them.
