The good thing about them is that they work through memorandums and files; if one sends a bad report the other one sends a favourable memorandum. Why can’t our conduct be such that they become favourable to us? We should ensure that officials, at least some of them, write reports favourable to us. The government’s mind is in the files; two good reports nullify the effect of bad ones. They might even be persuaded to think that bad reports were written by those who nursed a grudge against us. If we can ensure this, the victory is ours. ‘If an English sahib jumps up and down in rage, we should tell ourselves that he would go away in a few days while we are here to stay; so let him be drunk on power for a few days. We should somehow deal with their madness, but not retaliate. Even the stupid ones among them are good at writing reports; we can never match them in drafting memorandums. One should stay away from those who possess the power of knowledge as they can kill without a weapon. We should not believe that they cannot hurt us from afar.⟨fn:170⟩ They have the ears of the government, and they can hit us when our eyes are elsewhere. ‘Before challenging them we should pause to consider the extent of our reach. We should not jump into a river that we know we are incapable of swimming across. We should not take away a thing from one who can snatch it back from us. We should not cut a tree that cannot be uprooted, root and branch; we should not attack one who cannot be beheaded.⟨fn:171⟩ Maniraj, though we no longer fight with swords, we should rely upon this wisdom even while sparring with pen. Sahibs are like the first-born sons of the government, and parents never see the faults of their sons. Even if they know them to be at fault, they will scold us to save their children from punishment. The Kaurava elders knew all that was wrong with their sons, but they did not counsel them. The Pandavas were ultimately born to others and hence were subjected to rage. When Vyasa forbade the widowed Gandhari from cursing the Pandavas, she went ahead and cursed Krishna that the Yadavas would be annihilated in a fratricidal war. A child who takes a complaint to the mother of a stronger child usually comes back abused. Sri Krishna who participated in someone else’s war came back with a curse. If we fight with the Sahibs, our defeat is certain, and it would harm our relatives also. If you ask me, this pen pushing and memo writing is like the abuses of women and the war cries of banias. We will never master that. The battles of Rajputs are a thing of the past. ‘Even after all caution, if some officer were to become unbearable and required to be uprooted, one should weigh the chances of success before making the final effort. Sometimes when twigs are burnt they make no fire but spew out smoke. We should not do that. If we start a conflagration, it should be visible to all and its flames should scald those who come near it.⟨fn:172⟩ Your late father was right in saying that a king who raises his hand in futile effort loses a part of his royal authority. Dhritarashtra, blind, incapable of justice and compassion, did nothing to prevent Draupadi’s insult; but when he saw God’s wrath, he granted freedom to the Pandavas and honoured Draupadi’s word. Similarly, the government would pay no heed to our petty complaints against its officials, but will be forced to protect us and chastise them when their misdeeds become gross. At such an opportune moment we should present all evidence and use all royal authority; but till such time we should bear with some harassment. ‘Frequent complaints often lead to irritation in the minds of the superior authority. Hence, we should tactfully get our way with the officials and lodge complaints only at a critical juncture. In our dealings with clever and experienced officials we should present our case as if we are in fact implementing their policies. When a cuckoo lays eggs in a crow’s nest, and the crow cannot distinguish between her own and the cuckoo’s eggs, the crow does not complain about the cuckoo. Similarly, if we were to present our case as if it were the government’s own desire, the officers would not hold any grudge against us. We shall get the advantage of their cleverness without us having to plead for it.

Our sons can learn the Kshatriya art by being in their army; this is one such example. ‘One should, to the extent possible, not invite conflict with cunning and powerful officials. If their destruction is both imperative and desirable, we should play the trick of the wild boar and get under their horses to attack them. An officer who makes the mistake of allowing a wild boar to attack his mount is not likely to get much sympathy from the government. One should not forget that this game is dangerous and that we are always in danger of being pierced by the officer’s lance. ‘To the greedy officers we should appear like a mountain of gold. They come from afar in search of gold; the climb to the mountain often tires them and they are grateful with a nugget of gold. But one should never make the mistake of offering any gold to them because they might just be admiring the beauty of the mountain without any desire to possess the gold. There are officials who like us because they are enamoured of our glitter and glory. We should appear before them in full splendour. ‘If we are not resourceful or tactful enough to appear as a golden mountain, we should show ourselves as denuded of resources and riches. They would not cast a greedy eye in our direction because to them we would be paupers. They would not even employ a spy to keep an eye on us. This is another way of dealing with them. ‘These approaches are to be employed for officials who are clever. But with foolish officials we should become actors and put up shows for them; we should do what Vir Rao describes as “buttering.” ‘If the officer is wise and virtuous we should have devotion for him in our hearts, but our outward conduct should be of an equal friend. We could submit to him internally, but we should not lower our prestige before our own people by being submissive. If we know where to look, the world is full of gardens of gold. The brave, the wise and the one devoted to the service of others know how to pluck flowers from there. All the princes and all the people served Emperor Akbar. If the Sahibs are great souls, there should be no hesitation in becoming their devoted friend. In all other cases it is the duty of the king to pay them back in the same coin. People can afford to be obstinate and invite self-destruction, but a ruler cannot do likewise as his conduct affects the lives of other people. ‘Thus we should modulate our conduct according to our assessment of the other’s character, and employ means such that it secures our welfare. This is also a duty enjoined upon a king by Bhishma in his discourse to Yudhishthir. When the British officials bring difficulty upon us, we have to assume one of the six characters: those of the cuckoo, the wild boar, the mountain, a desolate and denuded palace, an actor and a devoted friend.⟨fn:173⟩ ‘Maniraj, your Pradhan was correct in saying that fate and providence are forces that our people need to contend with, but rulers in their endeavour to secure the welfare and security of their people can believe only in human endeavour. A king who believes in fate is certain to be destroyed. Destiny and satisfaction are attributes fit for brahmins and women. It is the right and the duty of a king to create and alter the destinies of their people. Hence, a ruler is considered to embody an element of the divine. Maniraj, you must remember that we are required to play many parts and master many arts with the changing times. Time is the pair of horses that we rein in through our statecraft. Never allow fate to frighten you in laying down the reins.’ The son-in-law heard the refined wisdom of his father-in-law, which manifested not only through his words but also in the excited palpitations of his heart, his fierce piercing eyes and steady grave tone. Muluraj, who had vowed to bring the two former enemies together, realised that his pledge was now fulfilled and the patriotic seeds sown by him had borne fruit. As the mounted guards and the royal carriage passed through the grand gates of Maniraj’s garden palace, it seemed as if the late king Mallaraj showered his blessings upon the three royal personages and that his pious, clever and noble statecraft had found a fertile soil in their hearts. A righteous king who nurtures virtue in statecraft enjoys the pleasure of heaven on earth; his deeds benefit his successors and give immortality to the soul of the deceased king. It is said that those whose merits are limited reside in the land of the dead, but this saying does not apply to a king whose glory is immortal and inexhaustible.
chapters.summary: Minister Vidya Chatura convenes a special court, where visitor Vir Rao from Bombay ignites an acrimonious debate, fiercely questioning the purpose of native states.

chapters.title: A New Night
paragraphs: A New Night The meanest vesture glows On beauty that enchants: The lotus lovelier shows Amid dull water-plants.⟨fn:174⟩ My love within a forest walked alone, All in a moonlit dale; And here awhile she rested, weary grown, And from her shoulders threw the wimpled veil, To court the little gale. I peering through the thicket saw it all, The yellow moonbeams fall, I saw them mirrored from her bosom fly, Back to the moon on high.⟨fn:175⟩ ‘D ulari! O’ my sweet Dulari! Behold the grace of the Divine Mother!’ The ascetic came out of her hut and embraced and kissed the young woman seated on the platform of the temple on the island. The young woman’s eyes were riveted on the sea. ‘Chandravali behn, I fervently meditate, but the man in my heart remains captured in it,’ the young woman wiped her tears with a handkerchief and continued to look out to the sea.

‘Which of the two refuses to leave your heart?’ Chandravali sat beside her and asked. ‘The man to whom I was given in marriage would be happy at the news of my death; for that reason I am happy to be here in the abode of the Goddess. But the great soul who cut me off from his life, but has not been able to dislodge me from his heart, remains etched within my greedy, wretched heart as well. Oh, he renounced his wealth, his family and even me for my own good. I would get some respite only when the light of the Goddess illuminates my dark heart.’ A deep sigh escaped her. Dear reader, you would most certainly have recognised the one who said these words. Chandravali and the other women had saved the drowning Kumud and their care and ministrations had revived her. For the past four days Chandravali had sought to soothe Kumud’s troubled mind. The clothes that were on her body, a reminder of her life as a householder, were thrown into the river and she was given a silken garment sanctified by the goddess. This frail, grief-stricken woman looked ever so beautiful in her new clothes, which fluttered in the westerly sea winds. Kumud had not shared her identity or those of her father and father-in-law with Chandravali. She had not uttered the names of Pramaddhan and Sarasvatichandra while sharing her story and grief with Chandravali, who had heard her with great compassion and patience. Chandravali had given her a new name: Madhuri. ‘Madhuri, the water that flows towards this island is the door to heaven. Those who enter this sacred land leave behind the cares of earthly existence. Just as one man has left your heart, the other too will leave. Have faith in the Mother.’ The fading light of the setting sun cast a shadow over Kumud’s face and the gloom of her heart darkened her visage. She gave no response and continued to look at the moonlight now slowly spreading over the water. Chandravali: ‘Madhuri, look at the moon rising behind you. How resplendent it is!’ ‘Chandra? Is he right behind me?’ Startled by the utterance of the word Chandra, Kumud turned around, but all she saw was the moon. She turned away from it. Her face turned red with shame. She composed herself and said, ‘Chandravali behn, Damayanti had prayed to the gods to grant her the power to win over Nala’s heart. Similarly, this man prayed to me! And yet, he abandoned me for my own good. Would you call this man mired in this world or an ascetic? I will also emulate the purity and piety of his heart. I will rid myself of his thoughts and meditate upon the sacred feet of the Mother.’ Chandravali: ‘Daughter, that is truly praiseworthy. Do not make the mistake of believing that the Goddess is present only in this sacred spot. She is omnipresent and lives in the hearts of all her daughters. We worship her idol to feel her proximity and presence. We have to understand her in other forms as well. The Goddess is the embodiment of the feminine principle. She is also the formless one, represented by the litany of her names. Incessant meditation upon her idol would enable you to forget this world. You would come to understand her formless self, and her power would lodge itself securely in your heart. Once you attain this state you would experience her presence everywhere and at every moment; she would reveal herself to you.’ Kumud Sundari’s attention wavered and her eyes once again came to rest on the roaring sea. Chandravali tried to distract her. ‘Daughter, this is the time of the Navaratra, the period of nine nights when we worship the Mother. The women of Surgram will be here shortly to play the garba and seek the Mother’s blessings. All of us will sit around the lighted garba and sing to the Mother and feel the essence of her presence.’ ‘Chandravali behn, I will certainly join you, but till such time I will try and soothe my mind in this cool breeze while watching the moonlight dance on the water. I do not wish to hinder the worshippers by my distracted state. Behn, I am a lot of trouble to you, am I not?’ Kumud looked at her with a sorry face. ‘It is the right of the daughter to let off steam before the Mother. Madhuri, you too will sing, won’t you?’ ‘Why would I not sing? But my song might just express the man who is in my heart. Would that not be an insult to the Mother?’

Chandravali thought for a while and held out two fingers before Kumud. ‘Pick one, let us see what happens.’ Kumud gingerly held one finger. ‘Behn, the Mother has spoken. You may sing what is in your heart.’ ‘You may go now. I shall try and memorise the song,’ replied Kumud. Chandravali withdrew to her hut. Soon the women began to gather. The sounds of their chatter merging with the breaking of waves played on Kumud who sat still, seeking to calm her troubled mind. She had escaped the noise and tumult of the life of a householder and found refuge in this quiet, solitary place. Along with the roar of the waves she heard the name that had come to be etched in her heart and yet remained unspoken; it enveloped her. This shower of mercy doused her parched heart. Kumud sat up straight. Moon rays, delicate and beautiful, soothed her. She remembered her mother-in- law, beauty incarnate, as soothing and gorgeous as the moonbeams and the delicacy of whose soul matched the grace of the moon rays. She berated herself. There is no one as ungrateful as me. My mother-in-law was the only one who applied balm to my seared heart, who enveloped me in her gentle, healing embrace. I gave her grief in return. How I wounded her! How I spurned her love! How difficult must her life have become? How must she pass her days? God granted her bliss, and I, the evil one, cast the coals of my misfortune on her. I, like the black serpent, bit the one whose heart was generous and pure. She is like the Mother Goddess Jagdamba, and I sinned against her. Gunial! True, you gave me birth. But the love and protection given by my goddess-like Devi is beyond even your dreams. You cannot ever match what she did for me. For my sins Gunial, you would vow never to even look at my face. But if I were to go back to Devi having committed these thousand crimes, she would embrace me as if I were her life. She loved me more than her own son and daughter. O’ Goddess, I have come to you seeking protection. Please show me a way whereby Devi is not robbed of her life. I am incapable of finding this path. What was I thinking when I fell into the river? Or did the outlaw drag me in? Did I fall in unmindful of where I was? Did the river bank cave in? I remember nothing, I cannot think clearly, even my imagination fails me. Kumud’s head hung low, heavy with melancholic thoughts. The sounds of the crashing waves broke her reverie. Her thoughts assailed her anew. Alakh behn! Alakh behn! What have you done to yourself? I know your grief. I can imagine how you wailed. But pray do not quarrel with your brother. I know you would have fought with him and taken him to task. But let that poor man be. I did this so that he could pursue his happiness unhampered. We shall rejoice in the soft sounds that surround, I shall play a leisurely dance on its waves. When I explained these lines of Kusum Mala to you, you too danced with joy. I remember how coy you felt when your father peeped in from the window and saw you dance. O’ Pitaji! You worked tirelessly, faced dangers to your life to secure power and happiness for your family, and when you were about to reach ashore, I sank your ship. I left the glory of your home and came to this place. Unfortunate and wretched, I have sullied your name, drowned your aspirations. Her mind ran in another direction. Will you drown as well? Will you not return to your home and world? Did I bring misfortune upon you as well? Some swim by the utterance of a name, Others drown and take others down. I, like a Chandal, drown and sink others, I am the outcaste wherever I go. A virtuous one by her presence Brings a creeper to bloom; My inauspicious breath Withers flowers in bloom. O’ mother mine! Why was I given life? Why did you not carry a stone instead? Even death is denied to me, I, born of your blood, am ill fate incarnate.

A half-moon had risen in the sky; white clouds fleeting past concealed it before the moon pierced through them again. Far at sea a ship sailed, the waves playing with it. The young woman’s eyes flirted with the play of light and shadow in the sky and the ship swaying upon the waves. The cloud covers the moon and conceals its light, while the waves have the power to drown the ship. If they are fortunate enough to be drowned by the elements, why can’t I be equally fortunate? Who will stop me if I were to walk into the sea? Alarmed by this thought Kumud looked back. The moon shone into her eyes; no other image could be held by them. She laughed, but her laughter was bereft of joy, empty and withered. Now I am all alone. A poet as romantic as Shelly desired to sleep amidst the sea waves. Sarasvatichandra, it was you who told me this. From where am I, poor and helpless, to get a boat? The Creator will come to my aid. She walked into the water, which played with her heels. Yes, if I were to walk a little further, the water will reach up to my knees, and then up to my waist. Gradually it would come up to my shoulders and eventually it would flow over my head. And this unhappy, sorry Kumud will cease to be. Fate had decreed that I should grab food received by Chandravali as alms; even this sin I have borne. Now is the time to be free from all sins, from every sorrow. I came to the abode of the Goddess, and this is the path that she has shown. I drowned in the river and found myself on this island; but there are no islands in the sea. I was saved because it was daylight and the women saw my floating body. No one will see me in this dark. Kumud Sundari stood in the water, her sari tied between her legs. She glanced back at the temple, looked up to the sky and pleaded with folded hands, ‘O’ Mother! Some call you God, others know you as Goddess. You are the reason for my birth; you gave me the fleeting joy of being with a great soul and ultimately you gave me the wisdom that I am unfit not only to receive your grace but also unfit for this world. This poor, wretched, orphan girl has neither the right nor the capacity to live in this pure world that you have created. I seek a place at your feet, pray do not shun me. Taking one’s life is considered a sin to be punished by torture and hardship. For me life itself is a torture that cannot be matched by anything that hell has in store for me. Mother, Yama rules over the space outside of your abode, death is ever-present. Once consigned to hell one does not commit any more sins. Once the period of punishment ends, one returns to your bosom. Mother, bless me that I have the forbearance and patience to endure this. Mother, I am in pain, I have fallen, I have sinned. No one needs me; I am eager to come to you. I want deliverance from this world. Mother, I seek your forgiveness, I seek your protection and I see an end to my sorrows. She stood facing the south. The ravines and trees in the distance seemed like hills. That was the direction of the kingdom of death, the land of Yama. She bowed in that direction and sang: There is light here, darkness afar, This is life, that passage of death This is the world, that abode of Yama, Cruel is the world, compassionate is Yama. Yama, the refuge of the orphaned, I bow to thee. O’ Dharmaraj Yama, in you I have solace. O’ Dharmaraj, take me to thee. She then turned to the north, where Ratnanagari was situated. She wept as she bid farewell to her family and the city. Beloved mother, father, you reside in the North, My last pranam to you, the very last. O’ dear father, o’ father dear, My last pranam to you, the very last. You abide in rectitude, do forget Kumud. O’ dear mother, o’ mother dear, Your heart will break, o’ it will break for certain; When you think of your meek Kumud. O’ mother do forgive me, pray do not grieve, My father, sad and soft-hearted, Give him solace, o’ mother.

Alone, unknown, lost, Kumud will sleep in a watery bed Leaving mother and father with a wail in their hearts. O’ father dear, o’ mother dear, You shall rain tears, your hearts shall weep, A daughter dies once, not again and again. O’ mother, pray forgive me, Do not grieve. My father, sad and soft-hearted, Do not forget an abandoned daughter. Kumud, bathed in her own tears, stumbled and fell down in the shallow water. The sudden fall seemed to awaken her. She stood up, wiped her tears and walked into the water. She touched her heart as if to seek courage and said aloud, ‘Mother, you have come to my aid, and Yamaraj, you hold my hand. I have gained courage, my deliverance is certain.’ One more Unfortunate, Weary of breath, Rashly importunate, Gone to her death! Take her up tenderly, Lift her with care; Fashion’d so slenderly Young, and so fair! Look at her garments Clinging like cerements; Whilst the wave constantly Drips from her clothing; Take her up instantly, Loving, not loathing. Touch her not scornfully; Think of her mournfully, Gently and humanly; Not of the stains of her,

All that remains of her Now is pure womanly. Make no deep scrutiny Into her mutiny Rash and undutiful: Past all dishonour, Death has left on her Only the beautiful. Still, for all slips of hers, One of Eve’s family— Wipe those poor lips of hers Oozing so clammily. Loop up her tresses Escaped from the comb, Her fair auburn tresses; Whilst wonderment guesses Where was her home? Who was her father? Who was her mother? Had she a sister? Had she a brother? Or was there a dearer one Still, and a nearer one Yet, than all other? ... Where the lamps quiver So far in the river, With many a light From window and casement, From garret to basement, She stood, with amazement, Houseless by night. The bleak wind of March Made her tremble and shiver; But not the dark arch,

Or the black flowing river: Mad from life’s history, Glad to death’s mystery, Swift to be hurl’d— Anywhere, anywhere Out of the world!⟨fn:176⟩ ‘Sarasvatichandra, my beloved, unlike your Hamlet I do not fear death.’ To die, to sleep— No more; and by a sleep, to say we end The Heart-ache, and the thousand Natural shocks That Flesh is heir to? ‘Tis a consummation Devoutly to be wished. To die, to sleep, To sleep, perchance to Dream; Aye, there’s the rub, For in that sleep of death, what dreams may come, When we have shuffled off this mortal coil, Must give us pause.⟨fn:177⟩ Her voice faded. She walked with measured, resolute steps. Her gaze was steady. The waves did not make her unstable. She had found her own rhythm, her own ballast. The forces of the world had no power over her to curtail her freedom. Her eyes shone bright with determination, her teeth dug into her delicate, petal-like lips. She walked with head held high, her chest thrust out. With her mind and her body firmly under control she walked into the water. Only her tears refused to obey her commands; they poured from her eyes, each tear drop taking the form of Sarasvatichandra. Moonlight cast her shadow over the water. She and her shadow steadily moved on with the sea rising at every step and crushing her delicate breasts. She heard a strange voice. It was not the voice of the divine speaking from within; it was distinctly a sound from without. It was not a human voice as no voice could be heard in the roar of the sea. For a moment it seemed to come from the moon, or from the stars; then suddenly it seemed as if the winds had carried it from beyond the darkness that enveloped her, and now it played upon the waves as if it had come from the depths of the ocean. The music of that sound and its song entered her ears; it merged with the water and encircled her; it palpitated with her heart, she breathed in that voice; she could feel it on her lips, she could see that sonorous sound. Its call was irresistible. Kumud submitted to the call and walked into even deeper waters. Her being and her surrounding were filled with the song. You walk slow and steady, The Goddess desires you to return. Daughter, your heart singed by a demon, Come to Mother for everlasting peace. The ocean’s waters are cool and deep, But only Mother is a succour for the fire within. You prepare to rest on the ocean’s bed; The immortals laugh at your resolve. The stars are startled by your sweet call, The night weeps at your tears; Open yourself to them. Chandra, high and solitary, Stands guard to the promised Kumud. Daughter! Why be afraid? Mother is your succour. Come out of the ocean, Into the bosom of the Goddess. Her nectar-filled eyes await you, Why care for the world? Wipe your tears daughter, Let your heart be soothed. The kumkum on your forehead is your destiny, The hand of the Goddess protects you. You bite your lips, your eyes water, The Goddess weeps with you. Your sorrows are about to end. Into Mother’s embrace daughter return. The ocean vast as the sky Roars day and night, How can your delicate petal body Find repose therein?

Forsake the ocean, return to Mother’s lap The body and attachment are illusion, Only Mother is eternal. Kumud hesitated for a moment; her feet refused to obey her command to move but she plodded on. She could neither comprehend the source of the song, nor its meaning. But the song captivated her. Like a deer who, captivated by the song of a young peasant woman, forgets to graze, Kumud too forgot her resolve. As she tried to walk resolutely into the water, something obstructed the movement of her feet. There was a sudden splash of water behind her, and Chandravali grabbed her from the waist. She spoke in an affectionate but firm voice. ‘Madhuri, Madhuri my daughter. Can’t I trust you at all? In the name of the Goddess, I ask you to turn back.’ Kumud was by now surrounded by three-four other women. She turned around, embraced Chandravali and wept. ‘O’ mother! What am I to do and where am I to go? Chandravali behn, your affection for me is greater than that of my own mother. I have gone numb. I cannot bear it anymore.’ Her wails reached skywards. She was taken back to the temple and made to change into dry clothes. The women, instead of worshipping the goddess, ministered to her daughter. Kumud was so ashamed of herself that she hid her face in Chandravali’s lap. Occasional sobs escaped her, the only sign that she was alive. Some eight or ten women clustered around her. They realised that she was beyond any words of solace that they could offer. They chatted about all manner of things, none of which caught Kumud’s attention. One ascetic related the recent events, ‘Chandravali Maiya, a guest has appeared in the abode of our Master. Our Master has shown great favour and partiality towards him.’ ‘Bhakti Maiya, who is the man who has gained the Master’s favour over his old disciples? Chandravali asked. Kumud’s heart suddenly became anxious for the response. ‘The guest is called Navinchandraji.’ Kumud sat up, electrified. Bhakti continued, ‘The Master saw him at a propitious moment in the forest. His intelligence and scholarship have won over the Master.’

Chandravali saw that Kumud was revived. She suggested, ‘We should commence our worship. Madhuri Maiya, the Mother Goddess embodies creation; the same energy is present in this idol. Since the time of Matsyendra Nath and Gorakh Nath this sect of jogis is known as the Nath Panth. The disciples of these two great masters have ordained a practice of worship for those of us who have not evolved to higher forms of comprehension. It is called Pata Yoga. We imagine a pure white, unsullied piece of cloth on which we project the image of the divine as we perceive through our senses and meditate upon it. Once we gain a certain degree of control over our minds we imagine a shorter piece of cloth, as if we have cut away its sides. We again project the same aspects on the cloth, albeit in a smaller form; following the same method we keep imagining a smaller span till the image disappears and the divine becomes formless. But ordinary persons find this exercise difficult and hence they install an idol attributing to it divine essence. For ordinary folk the saints prescribe idol worship. The masculine principle is imagined as the linga of Shiva or as shaligrama. But even this abstraction is beyond the comprehension of some, and so an idol complete with all human features was prescribed. For us women, the worship of masculine form is prohibited and hence the Goddess was imagined. Place all your desires, all things of beauty, your family and the man who has captivated your heart in the image of the Goddess and meditate upon it. This would make your life bearable. Devote your self to the Goddess such that all your desires melt and merge into her. ‘Madhuri, I have shown you the path of devotion; I have revealed to you the mystic nature of the Mother. You will be able to see the man of your heart and, with the grace of the Mother, gain all happiness. A daughter does not require external aids and bodily mortifications to worship her mother. The gopis left behind all their men and followed Krishna. Similarly, leave behind all things that your senses are attached to and devote yourself to the Goddess. What was Mira’s devotion like? She waited upon Sri Krishna, pining for him. The gopis, who had installed the call of Krishna’s flute in their hearts, felt his presence everywhere at each moment. Krishna and Lakshmi, Shiv and

Parvati are not distinct; they are one. Like the gopis who felt Krishna’s presence you too should feel the presence of the Mother and submit everything—your parents, the man you love, Sri Krishna, all things of beauty and all your desires to her, and in so doing you shall find them. You do not have to jump into a well or a river or offer yourself to the sea. The well, the river, the ocean, your life and death have all merged into the Mother. All your desires, all your search, your restlessness, all that is you is now to be placed at the mercy of the Goddess and you shall swim across the ocean that is life.’ Chandravali’s face shone with a new light as if the goddess had bestowed her light to the devotee. She spoke with force and her words rang true. Finally Kumud said, ‘Chandravali behn, you are right. I came out alive because that is what the Mother willed. I will not seek death. I shall submit to the Goddess.’ Bhakti Maiya: ‘If that is so, you must take the lead. Sing a garba in praise of the Mother wherein you place all your desires at her feet.’ All the other women urged her to do so in unison. Kumud did not respond immediately. They waited for her to respond. Kumud had closed her eyes. She opened them as if she had come out from deep sleep. Her eyes were transfixed at the feet of the goddess. She folded her hands and began a song. She cried as she sang. Her tears and her song became one, indistinguishable from one another. All the women joined in her song, and with her song they shared her pain, her sorrow and her tears. Mother, a yogi met me and said, I am the bee, you the lotus; He held me captive. She remembered the time that she and Sarasvatichandra had spent together in her parental home. She recalled their private moments and all the letters they had exchanged. Her song betrayed her anguish and her longing. He spoke sweet, soft words Foolish me opened my heart, and

He made it his abode. The verse that he had written for her at the moment of his departure had become etched in her memory. That verse became her song. One night the yogi revealed himself, And said: ‘I am a renunciate. You, born of mud, are ill-starred; Our togetherness cannot be. Your petals shall remain shut at night; My wings cannot rest. Be content, poor wretch; Your petals shall remain shut.’ Mother, saying this he went away. He bewitched me, robbed me of my peace. Mother, he visits my dreams; I long for him. He holds my saree without shame, and yet a yogi? I gave up all attachments to be free from his world. I jumped into the river and the great ocean, All ships sink, but wretched I did not. My fate! Does not allow even the solace of death, Is this your justice, Mother? You are the Mother. What am I to do? Why did you save a weeping, wailing One such as me? My heart does not do my bidding, Why live at all? Your meek daughter seeks only death, Why does Yama deny even that? Kumud continued to weep long after the song was over. Then abandoning her restraint, she wailed aloud, pleading with the goddess in words wet with tears. ‘O’ Mother, I sought death to be free from the sorrows of the world that you have created. I was given to two men who had no use for me. When I sought death, Yama had no place for me. Mother, one forsaken even by death has no place but to seek refuge at your feet. My long-suppressed pain finds words in your presence, please forgive me. I have no one to call mine in this world. You are the only shelter for this orphan. It is true that the world is an illusion. You alone are true. You are the beginning and the end for women as worthless as me. You are the strength of the orphaned, feeble, wretched women. O’ Universal Mother, when strong winds uproot mighty trees, delicate creepers that break at the mere touch of nails survive the storm. I, too, survived and found love and support from these compassionate women. Jagdamba, this can be only because of your grace. I would prove myself even more unworthy and ungrateful if having recognised this I fail to submit at your feet. Whether I submit my life and world to the small feet of your idol or submit my being to the formless you, both would allow me to be one with your light and forget the sorrows of this world. At this moment I feel your presence; I feel the weight of my sorrows lift. May your grace always be with me so that this experience of being free from pain does not become a fleeting one. Mother, let this not be as transient as the desire for renunciation that one feels in the cremation grounds, or as momentary as lightning in the sky. I do not wish to plunge back into the darkness that the world is. I do not want this experience to be as illusionary as a mirage. I seek your blessings: grant me a boon that is not like the joy of a dream certain to vanish upon waking.’ Kumud appeared composed. She was no longer weeping, but her face remained stained with tears. Her voice was steady and grave. She felt a new strength in her heart. Infused with new life she was no longer a sorry, wretched, helpless woman. She seemed to have tapped an inner strength and resolve. Her eyes, face and forehead were radiant with new light. Chandravali was quick to see the transformation. She seized the moment and said, ‘Madhuri, you experienced the Mother as an embodied one. You felt her presence in and through this idol. Now we shall invoke her eternal and formless presence. Listen to us and let it fill your heart.’ Chandravali sat facing the idol. All the others joined in her singing of the Devi Mahatmaya and clapped to the rhythm of the song. You are the nectar of the gods, O imperishable, eternal one; you abide with the threefold syllabic moment (matra) as your very being.

(You are) the half-matra, steadfast, eternal, which cannot be uttered distinctly. You are she; you are Savitri (the Gayatri mantra); you are the Goddess, the supreme mother. By you is everything supported, by you is the world created; By you it is protected, O Goddess, and you always consume (it) at the end (of time). At (its) emanation you have the form of creation; in (its) protection (you have) the form of steadiness; Likewise at the end of this world (you have) the form of destruction, O you who consist of the world! You are the great knowledge (mahavidya), the great illusion (mahamaya), the great insight (mahamedha), the great memory, And the great delusion, the great Goddess (mahadevi), the great demoness (mahasuri). You are the primordial material (prakriti) of everything, manifesting the triad of constituent strands. The night of destruction, the great night, and the terrible night of delusion. You are sri, you are the queen, you modesty, you intelligence, characterised by knowing; Modesty, well-being, contentment, too, tranquillity and forbearance you are. Terrible with your sword and spear, likewise with cudgel and discus. With conch and bow, having arrows, sling, and iron mace as your weapons. Gentle, more gentle than other gentle ones, exceedingly beautiful, You are superior to the high and low, the supreme queen. Whatever and wherever anything exists, whether it be real or unreal, O you who have everything as your very soul. Of all that, you are the power (sakti); how then can you be adequately praised? By you the creator of the world, the protector of the world, who (also) consumes the world Is (there) brought under the influence of sleep (nidra); who here is capable of praising you? Since Visnu, Siva, and I have been made to assume bodily form

By you, who could have the capacity of (adequately) praising you? May you, praised in this fashion, O Goddess, with your superior powers Confuse the two unassailable Asuras, Madhu and Kaitabha, And may the imperishable lord of the world be quickly awakened, And may his alertness be used to slay these two great Asuras.⟨fn:178⟩ They sang late into the night. Finally each one paid her obeisance and laid her desires at the feet of the goddess. They slept on the platform of the temple with the moonlight as their cover. The pulsing sound of the sea waves calmed their minds as they surrendered to sleep. While others slept, Kumud lay awake. She transferred the image of Chandra installed in her heart into the moon, and remained captivated by this vision. She thought of Navinchandra, whom Bhakti Maiya had mentioned. Chandravali, sensing Kumud’s restlessness, woke up. She turned towards her and asked, ‘Madhuri, are you still awake?’ ‘Chandravali behn, my heart desires a pilgrimage to Yadu Shrunga. Perhaps I could go with Bhakti Maiya?’ Bhakti, alert to the conversation, said, ‘Chandravali Maiya, permit Madhuri to go with me.’ Chandravali: ‘But will her dainty feet carry her up the mountain? She is certain to tire out and you will have to halt to give her rest.’ Kumud: ‘Will not the Mother give me strength?’ Bhakti: ‘Most certainly. And if your delicate feet cannot carry you up the mountain, we shall carry you as easily as one would a flower bud. Oh beautiful Madhuri, even our ugly bodies would look beautiful in your company. Beauty makes everything that it touches equally beauteous. Chandravali Maiya, you must grant her this wish.’ Chandravali: ‘Your words reflect your affection. But, Maiya, I dare not allow Madhuri out of my sight. Her heart is still not free of pain. You saw that today she was saved only by the grace of the Mother. I fear that solitude would re-ignite her death wish. Let her be with me for the time being.’ Kumud: ‘Chandravali behn, Mother rid me of the death wish; she will also ensure that such thoughts do not come anywhere near me. I feel I can trust my heart once more.’ Bhakti: ‘Maiya, we will look after her, care for her. Goddess Lakshmi resides in the beauty of Yadu Shrunga, and she will breathe new life into Madhuri. We would not let her out of our sight even once.’ Chandravali: ‘All right. But remember, my life is in your hands.’ Kumud, having had her heart’s desire fulfilled, fell into deep sleep. The cool rays of the moon played on her body unhindered, unabashed. They entered her heart, every pore of her body and created a new world all of their own. Kumud entered a world of dreams. She saw herself seated on the platform of the temple watching the sea. A storm raged over the sea, the waves rising two heads high. A gale of wind matched the fury of the sea. The sky looked heartless. A small boat being flung hither and thither struggled to stay afloat. It rose and fell with the waves; its hull seemed on the verge of breaking. The wind tore through its sails and broke the gaffs. Kumud Sundari watched nervously. The boat carried her life as its cargo; if it were to sink her life would find the bottom of the sea. Her heart watched the fierce, tottering movement of the boat. The moon, the only source of light, held the scales of life and death in its hands. Troubled by the dream Kumud sang in delirious sleep. Her song woke up the women around her and they heard her with eagerness, anxiety, love and pain. Woman, your ship is going to sink, Mother, bring it ashore! The seas are stormy, a tempest rages, From the shore I watch the ship disappear. It carries gems, Merchants await the cargo, I saw it set sail, promising to lay anchor soon, And yet, having kindled hopes, it disappeared. It breaks the hearts of all whose cargo it holds.
Mother, your sailors have given up. Mother, I beseech you, save it! I shall offer you kumkum. Or else my life will go with it.
chapters.summary: On a sacred island, Kumud, rescued and renamed Madhuri, grapples with her past, seeking solace from the Mother Goddess and a new path forward.

chapters.title: Sarasvatichandra's Anguish
paragraphs: Sarasvatichandra’s Anguish And the Raven, never flitting, still is sitting, still is sitting On the pallid bust of Pallas just above my chamber door; And his eyes have all the seeming of a demon’s that is dreaming, And the lamp-light o’er him streaming throws his shadow on the floor; And my soul from out that shadow that lies floating on the floor Shall be lifted—nevermore!⟨fn:179⟩ Vishnudas and his disciples had gone down to the villages to spread the message of Alakh. Sarasvatichandra was left alone with the bundle of letters that Viharpuri and Radhedas had found. The outlaws had ambushed Chandrakant and stolen all his possessions. They had no use for a bundle of letters. Viharpuri and Radhedas had found this bundle and given it to Sarasvatichandra. He was immersed in the letters, which gave him joy equal to meeting his friend. Chandrakant and Sarasvatichandra were very close friends. Despite this Chandrakant had never given him an inkling of his difficult pecuniary condition and the problems of his large household. He did not want to sully Sarasvatichandra’s world with his petty problems. The letters were full of domestic issues and economic hardship. These exchanges gave Sarasvatichandra his first glimpse into the personal life of his friend. It cast a shadow on him; he was surprised, stunned and pained by what he had read.

Oh Chandrakant, you are burdened by so many problems. And yet you gave me no inkling of them! I witnessed the pain of beloved Kumud, but I can only read about your problems. Dear friend, you kept a distance from me! Sarasvatichandra, you have experienced no hardship. Wherever you went there was the grace of Annapurna, the goddess of bounty and plenitude. You have not had to worry about your meals. But this is something unusual! He got up, walked around with the letters clasped to his heart. Tears rolled down his eyes. He sat on a boulder and read one of the letters. Dear Chandrakant, You have set out in search of Sarasvatichandra. But with the exception of Gangabhabhi, no one in your family appreciates this. The expensive life of Bombay and the earning of an honest man are as friendly as a rat and a snake. Your mother keeps niggling that Sarasvatichandra has given you nothing and has nothing to give now, and you have gone looking for him spending your own money and that too by stopping all work which brought some money home. The routine expenses of your household can be barely met with your income. Now that you do not bring in money and spend out of your savings, the family is forced to cut corners and all of them abuse Sarasvatichandra as he is the cause of this. If you ask me, I see your behaviour as contradictory. You should control your family members and prevent them from spending money haphazardly. But this is likely to invite further conflict in the family. But in order to save a few rupees either you should learn to ignore their demands, or you should shout and scream at them once in such a way that all of them shut up forever. They will call you names, but that would solve the problem for life. It is futile to hope that they will reform themselves and learn to spend your money with caution. You should consider it a grace of god that so far they have not learnt to borrow money on your name. There is yet another way. Before he left Bombay, Sarasvatichandra gave you a large sum of money. You have hitherto not used it in false pride of your virtue. You should give up such pride and use that money; this is certain to make everyone happy. If you do not want to do this yourself you can send me a power of attorney, which authorises me to withdraw money from the bank. When Lakshmi comes to you with wealth, you cannot ask her to wait at your doorstep because you want to wash your face. I am not as educated as you are, but I have more experience of the world. I have taken the liberty of advising you because of our mutual affection. But if you still want to hold on to a buffalo’s tail, it is your choice. We shall watch the fun. Your childhood friend, Sansarilal. Chandrakant had made notations on the margins of many letters; these were either a summary of his response or his reactions to the letter. Sarasvatichandra read Chandrakant’s response. The stone-hearted people of my house will not understand Chandrakant’s longing for Chandra. If they covet someone else’s wealth, they will be equally greedy with each other’s wealth. This we should know from our experience. Given our poverty, if there is a possible source of money, the household bugs will begin to bite. We are not like the English who throw away their parents but invite sisters-in-law to their homes. We follow our duty of compassion. The hungry and the greedy will feed on us so long as we have something to offer. One can only draw water from a well which has water. One should acquire the equanimity of a renouncer and watch the gluttons gorge on food and the famished die of hunger. This is the conduct of one who has cultivated the art of being a witness. Outsiders rob our country and the family robs our household; one’s destiny is to witness this denudation like a renouncer who regards the sky as his covering. One is powerless before the might of the outsider. But one who has breathed in the fragrance of Sarasvatichandra’s friendship will not take out his anger on his wretched family, like a mother-in-law scolding her daughter-in-law. A friend of one who could kick away immeasurable wealth will not bark and bite like a dog to grab a morsel of food.

Deeply moved and excited by this, Sarasvatichandra sang out: Open here I flung the shutter, when, with many a flirt and flutter, In there stepped a stately Raven of the saintly days of yore; Not the least obeisance made he; not a minute stopped or stayed he; But with mien of lord or lady, perched above my chamber door— Perched upon a bust of Pallas, just above my chamber door He remained absorbed for a while. Then he took out another letter, but instead of reading it he crossed his arms across his chest and recited: “Though thy crest be shorn and shaven, thou,” I said, “art sure no craven, Ghastly, grim and ancient Raven wandering from the nightly shore— Tell me what thy lordly name is on the Night’s Plutonian shore!”⟨fn:180⟩ He raised the index finger of his left hand and sang his own composition: Men of sterling virtue face hardships untold! Why speak of their sorrow when my wealth lies unused! He read another letter. It had neither salutation nor a signature at the end. He recognised the uncultivated hand of Chandrakant’s wife, Ganga. Your letter has reached. Your sister opened it and read it before giving it to me. No one liked that you wrote me a separate letter and paid for extra postage. So I gave this to Sansarilal to post. Now on I would not be able to do even that. Because all the virtuous women of the house talk about me and Sansarilal as I go and hand him the letter. I pay no need to their backbiting, but poor Sansarilal also gets dragged into this. There is nothing that your family is incapable of doing. I swallow the insults; but you have done so much for them and yet instead of gratitude you get brickbats from them. They feed on you and yet they dig ditches to trip you up; this is unbearable. I give it back to them when they speak ill of you. I am more than a match for all of them put together. I work hard all day long, do all the household chores, but they can’t spare the money to buy me a piece of cloth. They need everything, but for you and our daughter Kiki they do not even have a quarter to spare. Such are their calculations. I do not want to say more; otherwise you would say that my complaints and grievances follow you everywhere and give you no respite even in a foreign land. I have said enough for you to understand my situation. Your family is critical of even Kiki going to school. They say that a girl need not go to school; she should stay home and learn household chores. Everyone wants to be fed on their time; no one cares if Kiki gets late for school. She has been asking for school fees for two days, but no one has had the time to give it to her. The school threatened to cancel her admission, so she wept and pleaded for the fees. She was scolded for asking, and I lost my temper and had a raging battle with them and got her fees. Do not worry about me; I did not cry. Your family is planning to get Kiki engaged. The family of the proposed groom is not likely to meet your approval, and that has slowed things down a bit. They wanted to finalise the arrangements without consulting you. I was as alert as a crow and had another battle with them; for the time being the matter has been put on hold. That family has promised their daughter to your sister’s son in exchange of Kiki marrying their son. That was the plan, but for the time being I have ensured that it gathers dust. You should be content with so much news. If I give you any more it will cause you constipation, and eventually I will suffer because you are the only one who cares for me. Who knows which wretched whore created this life of a householder in her spare time? Let them say what they like. If the money runs out, I will fast and ensure that others do likewise; but do not come back without the one for whom you are searching. If he tries to run away again, show him this letter and tell him that in every house there are women like Ganga who bear hardships and yet can match any trouble. Tell him that what he got was only a pinch, a thousand times less than what we women suffer every day. If men like him are so delicate and run away, all the women of this world created by Brahma will have to remain unmarried. That barrister punished Kumud Sundari for what his father did to him. Is this his sense of justice? Other lawyers will now cite his example. Kumud Sundari suffered silently, but Ganga will catch him by the scruff of his neck. Sarasvatichandra forgot his sorrow and laughed aloud, saying, ‘Gangabhabhi, you are the strongest!’ But as his laughter waned, the shadow of pain and gloom reappeared on his face, and he was lost in thought. Chandrakant, despite my laughter the pathetic condition of your family fills me with gloom. Gangabhabhi, do you wish to tell me that all the women in India in every household suffer like you? If that is so, my pain increases a thousand-fold. Do such conditions plague every household? Sarasvatichandra! Gautama Buddha understood the human predicament by the scenes that he witnessed. Sarasvatichandra, a cloud of your own sorrow now covers the entire sky, causing darkness all around. Oh God! Beloved Kumud, my abandonment not only made you suffer it has caused suffering to all women; all of them have been left weak and unprotected. If I had you as my wife and co-worker, we could have reached out to other women and included them in our work. I could have helped alleviate the suffering of many women like Gangabhabhi. Such an endeavour cannot be undertaken without you and my father’s wealth, and I renounced both! Gangabhabhi’s prose, uncultured though it is, has the force and power of a woman’s aspirations and her desire for freedom. What can education not contribute to this potent force? Deprived of nurturant care, The women of my country Neither flower, nor bear its fruits! Their spirits unnourished by beauty and enquiry! My wealth alas remains unused. Chandrakant! Thy noble bust at my chamber door! The ominous raven that perches on thy head! And it casts a shadow from which my soul

Shall be lifted? Nevermore! Shall be lifted—nevermore! He read Chandrakant’s note on Ganga’s letter. You should fear no one and have no mercy on me while giving me the news of our household or while opening your heart before me. It is the inalienable right of a husband and wife that they should open their hearts to each other. It is also their duty according to the norms of right conduct to shun anyone, including parents and even Brahma himself, who places obstacles in this. Failure to discharge this duty results in the nullification of marriage. Parents lose their right over their children, at least to this extent, when they marry. Therefore, you should not pay heed to anyone. We also have duties towards our children. Hence, in matters pertaining to Kiki’s engagement and education you should do exactly as I have decided. You should listen to no one, be headstrong and do exactly as you please. Some husbands torture their wives at the behest of their mother, while some men disregard their parents by submitting to their wives. Men of both these types are irreligious and unjust. Duty and right conduct lies in being just to both the parents and the wife. But pure justice is not possible in absence of mutual trust; and even if the decision is impartial it is often difficult to implement it in the right spirit. Ganga, my wife, I have given you education sufficient to understand this. The way you can open your heart to me, no one else in the family can. Hence, it is impossible for me to be impartial and do justice in matters concerning you and the rest. You would remember that when you were still very young, I made efforts to ensure that you and the family learn to trust and love one another. Now that you are a mature woman you are free to determine your relations with them; you decide whether to care for them, reform them or teach them a lesson. It all depends upon your cleverness and your will. I do not wish to interfere in the matter. You shall reap what you sow; you will be responsible for your happiness as also your sorrow. I cannot be held responsible for that. The Shastras say that a son, when he turns sixteen, should be regarded as a friend; but a wife is a friend from the day she enters her husband’s house.

Ganga, following the customs of our people I treated you like a child till you turned twenty; I played with you and sometimes made you weep as well. But after that I have no rights over you. You have been given total autonomy. Therefore, neither you nor anyone else should expect Chandrakant to adjudicate in matters of your internal bickering. Our friendship is lifelong, and I am prepared to listen to everything you have to say and advise you, if you so desire, on any matter. You are free to ask for anything that you want. Now that you are a friend, it is not for me to decide whether what you ask is wise or unwise. Because I do not believe in the principle that whatever men desire is wise and all that women want is unwise. It is against the idea of friendship within marriage to confine a mature woman in the constricted world of her husband. Treating women as if they were immature and childlike will do no good to the world. Because women are capable of being wiser than men. And if men and women as friends and as partners in marriage wish to lead a pleasant conjugal life they must open up before each other, share wisdom and instead of establishing a principle that men must follow women or women must submit to men, they should do what is right. Ganga, I do not believe that you are wiser than me, but you certainly are an adult and hence I have resolved that you will manage your own affairs. In case of a quarrel you and my family have to decide as to how it has to be resolved. Either you fight or tactfully resolve the issue. I do not wish to be mired in this; it is a matter for you and them to resolve. You manage the house, and I shall not interfere. I will manage my worldly affairs and will not permit any interference. I will provide for the house but if my resources run dry, you cannot be blamed. You are right about Sarasvatichandra. Most people think that he ran away because of a quarrel with his father, but you have understood the cause of his renunciation. The worldly matters which bother us and make us uneasy he understood before marriage and left them behind. We understand them in hindsight and repent after the fact of marriage. But his folly was that he proved selfish and thought of his own interest and not of Kumud Sundari. We bear the burdens of the family, deal with all its problems and within the limits of our capacity give each other joy. Why could he not have done that? How happy Kumud Sundari would have been with him! He gave undue importance to Laxminandan’s criticism. Not being a man of the world he did not realise that in every instance words do not reflect true feelings, and that momentary passions do not endure for a lifetime. I have heard that Laxminandan is now repentant; one does not know what will happen to him. If Sarasvatichandra were to return it is likely that he would get his share of worldly problems; I am not perturbed by that. But his return would create possibilities of the betterment of others. Ram and Sita suffered hardships, but Ravana was destroyed, which was good for the world. I want to bring back Sarasvatichandra to make this world a better place. Therefore my dear Ganga, I will not return without Sarasvatichandra. And until we return, my family is your headache; you can be happy or fight like the Yadavas till the bitter end. I have addressed you respectfully as tamey instead of tu in the letter. This will anger you, my family will show its disdain for this and others will snigger. But I am quite accustomed to these, and Ganga you know that. I have written you a long letter so that on my return to Bombay I do not have to face your barbs about it. Sarasvatichandra sighed. He was not willing to believe that his father was pained by his departure, but his affection for his father brought tears to his eyes. ‘Father, why aren’t you happy? What worries you now?’ he said aloud. He fell on his knees, raised his arms skywards and sang with tears in his eyes. Father, you are omnipresent; You bound us by chains of love And joined our hearts to one another. He who sired me, He who tempered my heart, He to whom I am beholden, He who made my childhood bliss, He who fathered me, God, grant him joy. You are his father too;

Your affection for me is unparalleled; I beseech you. I have not forsaken your love, I have not forsaken my duty as a son, I have not berated my father in anger, I hold no prejudice against him. I have merely made it easy For him to pursue his happiness. O’ Father of all earthly fathers, Grant him peace and happiness. To follow the path of duty, To give him joy and freedom, I abandoned my love and his wealth. I abandoned my beloved And embraced a pierced heart; In a moment I did all that to secure his happiness. Father, you know all that is in one’s heart, You know what enlightens my heart, You know the beauty therein. Oh love! You imagined it, you inspired it; You untied and freed me, Bring my efforts to fruition, Grant him joy. My body desires hardships, My heart longs for pain For the happiness of my father, For his peace. Lord, I beseech you with my tears. Fulfill this wish of mine! Sarasvatichandra wiped his tears and addressed Kumud. ‘Beloved Kumud! You became the oblation of his sacrifice. Pramaddhan, this oblation has been offered to you—may she find a place in your heart! Beloved Kumud, Chandrakant’s pain is the pain of all men; you embody the suffering of all women.’ In this unfortunate country of mine, Fecund though the earth be,

The women of my country neither flower, Nor bear its fruits; Denied the warmth of the sun, They remain infertile, My wealth remains unused! He picked out another letter. It was written by Chandrakant’s elder brother, who was barely literate and wrote accounts at a clothes merchant’s shop. Sarasvatichandra glanced through the opening lines and read the main body of the letter. Brother, I as an elder should not talk ill of those younger to me. But one writes when the heart burns. Your wife detests our mother’s instructions. So long as they do not harm, the younger ones should be allowed to dance to their own tune. But in money matters men should have the final word. We earn little in pais and annas; our hearts cannot bear expenses in silver coins. You earn a lot and spend as much; it is fine so long as you are the only one doing that. But when your wife also begins to spend like you, then eventually you and I would even out. Secondly, you reformers want mature and educated husbands for your daughters; but we know that young ones will one day grow up and the educated are found begging on the streets. So we give our daughters in a family with means so that we do not have to worry about our daughters going hungry. Therefore, think carefully about Kiki’s marriage; if you follow your wife’s advice, your daughter will see hunger. These days the Queen rules over every house. I know that whatever I say will sound discordant to you like the trumpet breaking the rhythm of drums. Even then, I blow my trumpet because my heart burns for you and forces my hand. Chandrakant had made jottings on this letter as well. Brother, you are right. But what am I to do? You got me married in my childhood to a wife you now call a drum. I have lived with her ever since. Today you are tired of her. It is true that I have joined the ranks of reformers. If you had not educated me I would not have joined the reformers. Like you I, too, would have earned fifteen rupees. So we would both have been equal and happy. You thought like a bania and gave me English education. Hence, I earn more. I have kept my bags open for you. We reformers are loyal subjects of the Queen. We would be accused as traitors if we did not give a free rein to our wives and daughters. The reformers would banish us beyond the black waters. So mother and you can spend as much money as you want; no one will hinder your spending. But when my wife spends money, neither you nor our mother should say anything. This is the way things are; you have no cause for complaint. Enjoy yourselves. When I run out of money you will have to give me nothing, and I will have nothing to give you. You educated me for twelve years and everyone lived off my earnings for twelve years. We begin afresh in the thirteenth year, as I have repaid all that was spent on educating me. This is how things are. For twelve years, with God’s grace we had money. The money belonged to us jointly. And if the wheels of fortune were to turn against us and we were to become paupers, you, too, would face the consequences. I am unaffected by all this. I know where I came from and where I am going to end up. With your blessings from birth to death I am one with the supreme bliss. So please do not worry about me and stop blowing discordant notes from your trumpet. I will listen to you regardless even if you were to make enough noise to drown the drumming of my wife. I will hear everything you say. I am not going to harass you because someone wants me to, nor am I going to make things difficult for her to please you. You are my elder brother, and I will serve you in every possible way you demand. The age of Parashuram, when the young ones were punished to keep the word of the elders, is over. This is the age of Queen Victoria, and your brother has learnt that one’s conduct should be appropriate to time and place—and I am not about to forget this easily. Sarasvatichandra held the letter in one hand and placed the other hand on his heart, and said aloud, ‘Oh God! Chandrakant, you do not allow your brother to see your pain; you mock and you laugh. But notwithstanding your wounds, from deep within one can hear the sounds of a furnace. Your laughter springs forth like a fountain, but beneath that I can see your bleeding heart. Oh dear God! Chandrakant, your pain defeats the world and proudly soars up in the sky!’ Thy deep-seated proud pain is the raven— Of which it was so truly said— Not the least obeisance made he! And it has Perched upon my bust of Pallas Just above my chamber-door! He picked up another letter, written by the poet Tarang Shankar. Dear friend and fellow traveller, the one whose mind is imbued with all the rasas, As desired by you, I do keep an eye on your household. You have wisely and correctly said that in this world filled with worries, no one is free of them and hence neither of us can be free of them either. I would be repeating myself if I were to write about the situation of your household. But it is my duty to observe and report on the field assigned to me, hence this letter. The letters from your brother and Gangabhabhi would have given you all the news that you should have. I need to tell you that all the members of your family are selfish and are incapable of acting in a just manner in their dealings with you. One cannot expect any compassion from them. At one point I believed that this was a condition unique to me; but with experience I learnt that this condition prevails in every household. At the first whiff of this evil, that clever Sarasvatichandra promptly renounced the dry worldly life. But you are the only one I know, who like Shiva has made the snakes his ornaments and lives in the world as the Lord lives happily in the cremation ground. I have reached a conclusion that in this world pure, selfless love does not exist. The world is devoid of any aesthetic delight. Human beings show affection for poets because they can find aesthetic delight in a poem, a quality which the world is devoid of. If there were pure aesthetic pleasures in the world, why would only poets take delight in them? Who would crave for what can be conjured up with words if the thing itself were available!

Dear Chandrakant, Gangabhabhi is no exception to this rule. You have been generous with everyone in your family. Consequently, no one knows as to when your resources would dry up, and even if your resources were limitless no one knows how long you will live, and at such a time whatever they have grabbed would become theirs and the one who has nothing will suffer as no one would care for that person. This is what they believe and hence they are all busy in selfish acquisition. It is natural for a man to be partial towards his woman, which is not the case with you. I fail to understand as to how a woman for whom you have no special affection can respond to your heart? Uncultivated minds cannot respond to undemonstrative affection. Even if they do, it cannot be sustained. Gangabhabhi will remain selfish so long as she is tied to her children and has her own interest at heart. If you do not become a partner to her and favour her in matters where her self-interest is concerned, it would be futile for you to expect deep love from her. Other members of your family cannot rid themselves of their self-interests and the partiality that goes with it. They want to secure the future of their children. And yet they expect that Gangabhabhi should have no such aspirations and desires for her own children. “Do unto others as you would have it done unto yourself.” So long as our families do not understand this English maxim, you should remain partial towards Gangabhabhi. This is the only means of securing her love and your mutual happiness. So long as you do not adopt this means, the anarchy and disorder in your house is bound to increase every day. I keep my family life orderly through such means. I am abused by those whom I seek to bring to order, and those I am partial to are also partial towards me; but by such means I also secure my happiness. You are impartial to all and are abused by all; yet disorder and anarchy prevail. My way at least secures my happiness. If you ask me, one scabbard cannot hold two swords. Therefore, the British custom of keeping the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law apart seems to me the path of happiness. True love is absent among them, as also among us.

I have organised my family life around such principles. The Vedantis describe the world as full of sorrow; I call it bereft of aesthetic delight. The Vedantis believe that the world is devoid of ananda, of bliss, and hence aspire to the state of bliss. For me the world is devoid of aesthetic delight, and hence I strive for that state. In everyday life the Vedantis and even the renunciates fail to act without attachment and prejudice; they fail to attain bliss but merely prattle about it. I am also incapable of renouncing this world. I fail to attain the pure ideal of aesthetic delight and instead sing songs of it. Chandrakantbhai, I write about my experiences only so that they give you some solace. But if you were to meet Sarasvatichandra, please do not share these with him. His life so far has been like that of Prospero’s Miranda, or the young Buddha. Do not let the world blot that pure vessel of aesthetic delight. If he were to ask about the condition of Bombay, tell him that for us Bombay has always meant our group of friends. Tell him what the poet of Bombay has to say. The garden weeps with the gopis, o’ Krishna; Why have you forsaken us, Chandra? The water lilies with withered faces Gaze at the sky and ask, “Where is our bee?” Aesthetes, poets and scholars pure Come together with a question: Where is our noble Chandra? Radhika, leaving her companions Roams the paths of Vraja, asking, “Where is that cheat?” Patriots, poets, scholars and declaimers, You forsook them all, o’ Chandra of Kant, Where are you? Kant, search him out; Kumud longs for him: “Where is the dark one?” Scatter the winds, set them after him; The bird takes flight, o’ Chandra, You who forsook wealth! O’ winds, dispel the dark clouds, The soaring bird asks the moon: Have you seen Chandra?

O’ Kant, let the winds dispel these clouds of gloom, Tarang waits with a pounding heart: Where does our moon shine? Dear Chandrakant, it is affection for Sarasvatichandra that made a Persian composition ring to the tunes of my sarangi. I try to love my illiterate and dry wife; I build castles of “gallantry” and “chivalry,” but her selfish heart detonates my creations. At such times, I recall Goldsmith. And love is still an emptier sound, The Modern fair one’s jest; The earth unseen, or only found To warm the turtle’s nest. “For shame, fond youth, thy sorrows hush, And spurn the sex,” he said: But while he spoke, a rising blush. His love-lorn guest betray’d. Surpris’d, he sees new beauties rise, Swift mantling to the view; Like colours o’er the morning skies, As bright as transient too. The bashful look, the rising breast, Alternate spread alarms: The lonely stranger stands confess’d A maid in all her charms. “And, ah! Forgive a stranger rude A wretch forlorn,” she cried, “Whose feet unhallow’d thus intrude Where heav’n and you reside. “But let a maid thy pity share, Whom love has taught to stray; Who seeks for rest, but finds despair Companion of her way.”⟨fn:181⟩

Unable to find a woman’s love, I search for her in my poems, I praise and raise her to the seventh heaven and bow to this imagined beauty. But the real women of this world are shrews. I get evil pleasure in the knowledge that you too are in the same class as me. I consider Sarasvatichandra fortunate that he was saved from such impossible love. I am quite enamoured of his cleverness. Wherever he is, his heart could not be sullied by the muck of this world, and will remain pure. I would consider my sojourn to this world fulfilled if I can come face to face with even one person whose aesthetic pleasure has remained unsullied. Chandrakant had made detailed jottings on this letter as well. Philosophers like Hobbes and disciples of the Nyaya school of philosophy ensure that there is no contradiction between their conclusion and their experience and knowledge. But you have proved that poets are capable of reaching one kind of experiential state and retaining poetic sensibility of a different kind. Sarasvatichandra is a poet like you, capable of swimming in opposing currents of experience and high aesthetic sensibility. For someone like me bereft of any poetic sensibility, it is interesting to watch the interplay of two poets. I recall now you once explaining to me that the life of Krishna is also filled with similar contradictory impulses. Yours is a true description of the anarchy of my household. I and your sister-in-law are as implicated in this disorder as the rest of my family. Despite this you ask me to show favour and preference for your sister-in-law. This too is a miracle of your poetic disposition that allows you to juggle contradictions. Oh king among poets! The time is not yet ripe to emulate the English custom of showering favours on our wives. So long as we have not resolved to drive out our parents, we must follow the principle of rising above partiality and favouritism. We like a giant bird have to carry our parents on one wing and wife and children on the other; our body keeps them separate and divides them so that their conflict does not destroy them. We must rise and soar high with them on either wing—this is my idea of rising above prejudices. The burden that I carry is likely to be inert and devoid of any feelings towards me; but my interest lies in bearing their burden and still rising above prejudices. I cannot, unlike you, compose poems about this. If I were a poet, I would not have allowed Sarasvatichandra to run away. I grant complete freedom to all members of my family. If I were to die, my family would be forced to live with each other, negotiate on the basis of their self-interests and deal with each other with either tact or force. I am training them to do so. At the moment this training brings nothing but grief and conflict. But I hope that eventually all of them will learn to protect and nurture each other and be happy together. I have drunk the nectar of freedom and I endeavour to give others a taste of it. I use the force necessary to ensure that no one in the family succeeds in destroying the freedom of others. If, in so doing, I were to lose all my money, I shall remain indifferent to it and even be able to laugh about it as the family would have proved incapable of order and harmony while we have money. They will be forced into poverty. Poverty has its own nectar which will imbue the hearts of my family. Such poverty would peel off the dirt and shrill discordance of the jewels of my family and make them harmonious, melodious and shining. And when this happens, oh king among poets, it would truly be of interest to me. Pure love and unsullied aesthetic desire are to be found in a mind that has either embraced poverty or become content otherwise. It cannot be found among those who are neither here nor there but somewhere in between. If I fail to attain that equability I would happily embrace poverty. Sarasvatichandra has flown away, abandoning what could have been easily within his reach. But he is likely to be disaffected with what he finds; hence I have set out in search of him. My poverty and Sarasvatichandra’s dreamland are both means for the welfare of this country. Therein lies the welfare of all: you, me, him and everyone else. Poor Kumud Sundari! She got a glimpse of that inner world of Sarasvatichandra through his letters; she tasted that nectar and just as she was about to settle on his wings and soar high, she disappeared behind darkness as impregnable as death itself. She is beyond reach!

Oh prince among poets! You say that no one in my family is capable of pure love and their selfishness has dried up the fount of affection. This is true. But the feelings of a noble mind emerge through self-volition; it does not expect affection from others. Parents’ love for their children does not rest upon their children’s capacity to return their love. Our love for the country does not depend upon the country’s capacity to love us in response. Our love for God is of a similar nature; we are drawn automatically towards Him. The affection we have for our illiterate families is also similar; it is out of self-volition. It does not arise and is not sustained by the other person’s capacity to respond and reciprocate in equal measure; it arises out of our consciousness. It is futile to hope for selflessness and detachment in our families. Our tradition says that the Creator loves all beings. This applies not only to scholars but also to our illiterate, small- minded families. Hidden beneath layers of selfishness lies the possibility of selfless love; we are required to find it, cleanse it and benefit from it. This is the path of high-minded aesthetes in search of love. Our minds are caught in petty concerns, in small desires and attachments. These attachments disappear when knowledge and aesthetic concerns arise in our minds; other images take their place. It is an injunction upon the wealthy that they should have compassion for the poor and not live in conceit of their wealth. Similarly, those who worship Sarasvati, the goddess of learning, are required to have compassion for the petty and impure desires of the illiterate.
