Men of religion have said that pity or compassion is the root of religion; poets like you should add that pity is also the root of love. It is said of such great souls that: What goodness is there in the kindness shown by a man towards those who have obliged him? One who is kind towards those who have done him wrong is described as a virtuous person by the good.⟨fn:182⟩ The more I realise that my family or my wife is selfish, the more I try to increase my love for them. God, for some reason, willed our relationship; the reason for this is mysterious and known only to Him; but those whose hearts are moved by friendship and compassion should see the manifestation of the self in all beings. In my view this principle should be initially applied to those who are nearest to us. “With the disappearance of the attachment of the body and with realisation of the supreme self, to whatever object the mind is directed, one experiences Samadhi.”⟨fn:183⟩ I try to cultivate this disposition: Charity begins at home.⟨fn:184⟩ Sarasvatichandra put aside the letter and looked up, deep in thought. Kumud Sundari! Our love was pure. Love that rests on compassion is mere affection. The love of equals is friendship; conjugality is also a form of friendship. Chandrakant, I see that your attempt is to bring conjugality within the ambit of compassion. I see that you are disappointed with the idea of conjugality based on friendship. Chandrakant! Tarang Shankar! If the picture of conjugality and family life that you present is prevalent across our society, our country is in certain decline. Your high ideals are attempts to emerge along with your family out of this quagmire. What is more beneficial: the pain of Indian scholars or the battles that reformers wage against our people? On one side the reformers loudly proclaim their war cries against society, give refuge to a few brave men, proclaim the victory of reform and even establish a few reformist societies; while on the other hand these scholars committed to the welfare of their families make silent, unpublished attempts to bring up their families and suffer in the process. The fact is that Gangabhabhi is not yet ready to participate in the meetings of the reformist society; she can neither compose books like our leading reformer Uddhatlal’s wife Srimati, nor can she prate English phrases. Uddhatlal succeeds in elevating his wife and daughters; let us suppose that they rise a hundred feet higher, while Tarang Shankar and Chandrakant’s efforts make their entire families rise by ten feet. To what extent is their example imitated and followed by others? Among these two kinds of efforts one might be more fruitful and beneficial than the other, but without doubt Chandrakant’s effort is selfless and for the benefit of others. This effort is not known. Srimati’s learning smacks of Uddhatlal’s selfishness. Chandrakant and Tarang Shankar meet with failure in their heart’s desire for conjugal friendship. Men and women who are not scholars often find this friendship effortlessly; Buddhidhan and Saubhagya Devi exemplify this. But it is impossible for this friendship to emerge between an educated man and an illiterate woman. What is possible is affection, and that Chandrakant has for Gangabhabhi. Chandrakant, in order to give to his family, gave less to Ganga and denied himself the possibility of conjugal friendship. “Those are the noblest persons who, giving up self-interest, bring about good of others.”⟨fn:185⟩ Chandrakant, you have renounced selfishness. This goodness is entirely yours. Is there no other way of securing your family’s welfare without denying yourself this noble ideal? Is there no way of securing a family’s happiness without crushing women in the process? Kumud Sundari, please forgive me! I left you and with that I forsook happiness. Today, I realise that many scholars live a life devoid of any joy. My own joyless condition has enabled me to understand their state. Dear father! Beloved Kumud! If Buddha’s renunciation was not against religion and morality, if it did not violate norms of right conduct, my renunciation is so little that it cannot be compared to his. Dear Chandrakant! Your feelings for your family do not permit you to nurture dreams of love in the temple that you have created. Buddha, moved by compassion and affection for the world, renounced a life enriched with love. I ran away at a time when a life filled with love approached me. What have I lost by that act? Friends like you, who have none of the riches I had, have a remarkable capacity to endure family conflict, while I trembled at the mere hint of such a conflict. Beloved Kumud, the man who was so easily shaken was unfit for your love. I broke your trust; you had to face many hardships because of me.

I have now begun to see, somewhat hazily, the possible penance that I could perform. There was a day when all of creation appeared to me filled with Kumud’s joyous presence. There came a day when Kumud’s pain filled the world and I sang, “You alone abide in my heart.” Now I shall dismantle that world of illusion and like Lord Buddha perform my penance. That I can perform. Kumud Sundari, Buddha heartlessly abandoned his beloved for the welfare of the world. I had sent you a poem on his great renunciation. Today, it is my turn to take a lesson from the same poem. And a day will come when I, like that great man, will come to you and beg your forgiveness. He got up and walked around, gazing at the mountain tops. He recited the words of Buddha. “I will depart,” he spake; “the hour has come! Thy tender lips, dear sleeper, summon me To that which saves the earth but sunders us; And in the silence of yon sky I read My fated message flashing. Unto this Came I, and unto this all nights and days Have led me; for I will not have that crown Which may be mine: I lay aside those realms Which wait the gleaming of my naked sword; My chariot shall not roll with bloody wheels From victory to victory, till earth Wears the red record of my name, I choose To tread its path with patient, stainless feet, Making its dust my bed, its loneliest wastes My dwelling, and its meanest things my mates. Clad in no prouder garb than the outcasts wear, Fed with no meats save what the charitable Give of their will, sheltered by no more pomp Than the dim cave lends or the jungle-bush. This will I do because the woeful cry Of life and all flesh living cometh up Into my ears, and all my soul is full Of pity for the sickness of this world:

Which I will heal, if healing may be found By uttermost renouncing and strong strife. For which of all the great and lesser Gods Have power or pity? Who hath seen them—who? What have they wrought to help their worshippers? How hath it steaded man to pray, and pay Tithes of corn and oil, to chant their charms, To slay the shrieking sacrifice, to rear The stately fane, to feed the priests, and call On Vishnu, Shiva, Surya, who save None—not the worthiest—from the griefs that teach Those litanies of flattery and fear Ascending day by day, like wasted smoke? Hath any of my brothers escaped thereby The aches of life, the stings of love and loss, The fiery fever and the ague-shake, The slow, dull, sinking into withered age The horrible dark death—and what beyond Waits—till the whirling wheel comes up again, And new lives bring new sorrows to be borne, New generations for the new desires. Which have their end in the old mockeries? Hath any of my tender sisters found Fruit of the fast or harvest of the hymn, Or brought one pang the less at bearing-time. For white curds offered and trim tulsi leaves? Nay; it may be some of the Gods are good And evil some, but all in action weak; Both pitiful and pitiless, and both— As men are—bound upon this wheel of change, Knowing the former and after lives For so our scriptures truly seem to reach, That—once, and wheresoe’er, and whence begun— Life runs its rounds of living, climbing up From mote, and gnat, and worm, reptile and fish, Bird and shagged beast, man, demon, deva, God, To clod and mote again, so are we kin To all that is; and thus, if one might save

Man from his curse, the whole wide world should share The lightened horror of this ignorance Whose shadow is chill fear, and cruelty Its bitter past time, yea, if one might save! And means must be! There must be refuge! Men Perished in winter-winds till one smote fire From flint-stones coldly hiding what they held, The red spark treasured from the kindling sun. They gorged on flesh like wolves, till one sowed corn, Which grew a weed, yet makes the life of man; They mowed and babbled till some tongue struck speech, And patient fingers framed the lettered sound. What good gift have my brothers, but it came From search and strife and loving sacrifice? If one, then, being great and fortunate, Rich, dowered with health and ease, from birth designed To rule—if he would rule—a King of kings; If one, not tired with life’s long day but glad I’ the freshness of its morning, one not cloyed With love’s delicious feasts, but hungry still; If one not worn and wrinkled, sadly sage, But joyous in the glory and the grace That mix with evils here, and free to choose Earth’s loveliest at his will: one even as I, Who ache not, lack not, grieve not, save with griefs Which are not mine, except as I am man; If such a one, having so much to give, Gave all, laying it down for love of men, And thenceforth spent himself to search for truth, Wringing the secret of deliverance forth, Whether it lurk in hells or hide in heavens, Or hover, unrevealed, nigh unto all: Surely at last, far off sometime, somewhere, The veil would lift for his deep-searching eyes, The road would open for his painful feet, That should be won for which he lost the world, And Death might find him conqueror of death. This will I do, who have a realm to lose,

Because I love my realm, because my heart Beats with each throb of all the hearts that ache, Known and unknown, these that are mine and those Which shall be mine, a thousand million more Saved by this sacrifice I offer now, Oh, summoning stars! I come! Oh, mournful earth! For thee and thine I lay aside my youth, My throne, my joys, my golden days, my nights, My happy palace—and thine arms, sweet Queen! Harder to put aside than all the rest! Yet thee, too, I shall save, saving this earth; And that which stirs within thy tender womb, My child, the hidden blossom of our loves, Whom if I wait to bless my mind will fail. Wife! Child! Father! And people! Ye must share A little while the anguish of this hour That light may break and all flesh learn the Law. Now am I fixed, and now I will depart, Never to come again till what I seek Be found—if fervent search and strife avail.” ... “Pleasant ye are to me, sweet friends!” he said, “And dear to leave; yet, if I leave ye not What else will come to all of us save eld Without assuage and death without avail? Lo! As ye lie asleep so must ye lie A-dead; and when the rose dies where are gone Its scent and splendor? When the lamp is drained Whither is fled the flame? Press heavy, Night, Upon their down-dropped lids, and seal their lips, That no tear stay me and no faithful voice. For all the brighter that these made my life, The bitterer it is that they and I, And all, should live as trees do—so much spring, Such and such rains and frosts, such winter-times, And then dead leaves, with maybe spring again, Or axe-stroke at the root. This will not I, Whose life here was a God’s!—this would not I,

Though all my days were godlike, while men moan, Under their darkness. Therefore farewell, friends! While life is good to give, I give, and go To seek deliverance and that unknown Light!”⟨fn:186⟩ An image appeared from the rocky walls—Kumud Sundari! But she disappeared soon after into the wall on the other side. A large branch of a mighty tree hung low. Sarasvatichandra saw among its foliage the image of his long lost mother, Chandralaxmi. He had memories of her from a photograph seen at his father’s house. He was stunned and moved to tears by her vision. He stood with folded lands. Before he could decide what to say or do, the image of his mother began to speak. She spoke eagerly; her speech was delicate and soothing like the cuckoo singing from the tree. The mother pleaded with her recalcitrant son. My son! Return home, at least once. Your father, though unworthy, is my life. I watch him from the high heavens; His tears have not dried. Do not go to him in your Ochre robes, he Will weep and wail till his heart breaks, Till life leaves his body. I died in your infancy. You are his only solace and succour. His love for me was deep, and remains so; Your father’s heart is Delicate and soft. My son! Be good, return home. I weep in the other world, as your Father cries for you. Neither Guman nor Dhurt are his; He weeps alone; son go back to him. He forgave my crimes As you would forgive me, Forgive your old father, he weeps.

Son, do not be irate! Go home! Go home! Embrace your old, perturbed father, Hold him to your heart. Son, do not be adamant, Go home. Go! Your old father weeps—clasp him To your heart. The image disappeared. Sarasvatichandra put his face in his hands and wept. He composed himself, wiped his tears and recited the lines of Buddha’s renunciation. Wife! Child! Father! And people! Ye must share A little while the anguish of this hour! That light may break and all flesh learn the Law. Now I am fixed, and now I will depart, Never to come again till what I seek Be found—if fervent search and strife avail.⟨fn:187⟩ He gained some measure of control over his emotions. He sat down on a boulder and took out another letter from the bundle. This one was written by Uddhatlal, the editor of Gurjar Vartik. Dear Chandrakant, I have received your letter. If we were to say that Sarasvatichandra, through his wealth, his learning, his enthusiasm and effort had done great service to the community of scholars and patriots of our city, we would be falling short in the description of his worth. Any good man can do favours unto others. But our friend had become one with all our endeavours. He was as integral to them as the law of gravity is to all atmos. The country needs scholars, patriots, men of wealth; it needs thinkers who encourage others and become catalysts; we need action-oriented men; we need reformers and popular leaders; we also need men favoured by the British; we need liberal and generous men; we need these and many other types of men. But all this is not enough. It is possible that a wealthy man has no sense of public duty, has no learning; what use is such a man? What is the use of a learned man who has to struggle day and night to acquire a few utensils for his house? Our Narmad has said in melancholy mood: If such is the state of the house, what is to be done With a vast intellect and broad vision! Dalpatram has said: Brothers, a man with a bad wife Has many burdens to bear. Navalram has said: Man plays with geography and astronomy, While woman’s mind burns with the kitchen fire. My fellowmen! Tell me, What sort of mismatch is this? Therefore, we require men of learning who are so wealthy that they are enthused by all aspects of national welfare. Only one person, born in the family of Laxminandan came close to this ideal, but he disappeared and vanished. Oh, he was to be united with a gem like Kumud Sundari! But that, too, became a distant dream. If that learned young beauty had united with our connoisseur, what joy they would have showered on our people! But your households torn asunder by strife—you in your false pride name it Indian family values—should be destroyed root and branch. This household and joint family system, which is evil and a collection of stupidities, snatched away a rare jewel from our hands and threw it into the sea! Now Chandrakant, you make futile dives to its bottom to retrieve it! If Sarasvatichandra were to be found, it would be of great benefit to humanity. But it is impossible for him to marry Kumud Sundari. One arc that could have saved and help raise the lot of our women has broken and drowned. I hope at least now you will admit that our joint family system is the worst plague that destroys our countrymen all throughout the land and eats up all that is fair and fruitful in the world of our hopes.⟨fn:188⟩

Let’s take the question of social reform. Do you want to bring child marriage to an end? So long as persons of old values who are also illiterate live in your house and destroy your right over your children, this cannot be achieved. Do you want widows to remarry? So long as you feed and fatten such men with your wealth none of this will be possible; your own power is no greater than that of a poor widow. Do you wish to educate your daughters? Do you want to take your wife away from the smoky kitchen and the ash heaps that shine utensils, and introduce her to the enchanting world of learning? Do you want your wife, daughters and daughters-in-law to share in the general comforts and good life that you have? Or do you want the possibility of spending your income, your abilities and independence in a manner that secures your welfare and by so doing make your English education truly meaningful? I declare that so long as you live in a joint family, submit to their foolish demands and allow their vile desires to shackle your arms and feet and hamper your independence, you will not be able to do any of the good deeds that you aspire to. Countless bees live in one hive. Like them why did we adopt the custom of three generations, including daughters-in-law, living under one roof? How has this benefited us? How are we going to ensure that daughters-in-law and our own daughters will live with each other in harmony and affection? We have an ancient saying: a nanad is one who is never happy with her brother’s wife. This phrase, coined thousands of years ago, tells us that sisters-in-law will always, invariably quarrel and impede each other; they are like the moon sign occupying the twelfth house in a horoscope. If this is as it is described, a mother who is also a mother-in-law will always favour her daughter over her daughter-in-law. It is easy to understand that she would smile at one and scowl at the other. You can understand that a man who is both a brother and a husband is crushed from both sides, like a betel nut placed in a nut-cracker. You will argue that the educated among us have elevated our wives to the level of ‘madams’ and begun to disregard our parents. But parents are enthusiastic about a son’s marriage; however the moment he looks at his wife with affection and care, his sister’s tongue turns poisonous. This is customary among you. Take it: this is a New Year’s Day present of a toy that was made by your artist before English education was born in the land!⟨fn:189⟩ On one hand he is expected to shoulder the burden of the entire family; on the other there is child marriage and the remote possibility of love. Does it surprise you that a man squeezed from either side pushes away that elusive possibility of love to lessen conflict in the house? The fact is that independent-minded and powerful men succeed in shedding the burden of family and hold on to the possibility of love. But people disparage and censure such men as hen-pecked and sinful. The burdens of a joint family and public opprobrium push in one direction; there are a rare few men who can be indifferent to it. I do not deny that in some such households the daughter-in-law rules over the mother- in-law. I am willing to go a step further and admit that those men who begin as ‘mama’s boys’ end up—either in reaction to or out of selfish desire for happiness in the company of wife and children—as hen-pecked husbands. And those daughters- in-law whose youth was denied to them by the evil designs of mothers-in-law turn against them the moment they attain an upper hand and make their old age a miserable existence. People regard this as tyranny and sin, but I call it meeting one’s just deserts—injustice for injustice—something that is divinely ordained. This pattern is also age-old. But are we bound to perpetuate it? I do not see any reason for it. Husband, wife and unmarried children constitute a family. This is the natural composition of a family. Many such families come together to form a heterogeneous, uneasy unit called a joint family in which evil and stupidity ferment. We are required to take pride in the values of a joint family. Such arrangement might be acceptable to Chandrakant, but I see it not as a natural arrangement but a deformity of corrupt practices. Even you, Chandrakant, would not argue that we should sustain corrupt practices just because they are traditional and customary.

This practice of heterogeneous units forming a joint family is a sign of the barbaric condition of our ancestors, which we have retained. You have read the works of jurist Sir Henry Maine. After years of research he has concluded that in the ancient past the social organisation was ‘tribal’⟨fn:190⟩ and the evolutionary reform of Western social forms has transformed these tribal forms into ‘territorial’ forms of social organisation. In earlier times people were linked to each other through tribal forms, which are now forged through territorial principles. In earlier times people formed a country; now different people belong to nations. In earlier times the world was seen as composed of the Aryans, Dravidas, Mlecchas, Yavans, Rakshasas, Semitic people, Tutons, Celts and the French people; now we understand the world through territorial and geographic units like Hindustan, England, France, China and such like. In short, in ancient times barbaric people held on to pride in one’s family or one’s race; in this age of reform we have cultivated pride in one’s nation. Our castes and joint family system are remnants of our barbaric state when we cultivated family or racial pride. Those who succeed in destroying it will secure happiness; those who cling to it will be destroyed. When they disappear, the residue of the past will disappear with them. To paraphrase Sir Henry Maine, in ancient times the social formation was tribal with families as its constituents, while in the age of reform the uniting principle is territorial with individuals as its constituent units. A family as a clan is somewhat smaller in its organisation than a caste while people as a whole are the largest unit. Racial pride and pride in one’s family are residual elements of the past, while pride in one’s nation is the fount of the age of reform. In ancient times people were ‘nomadic.’ They moved from place to place and hence they did not belong to a specific territory. A huge population, composed of many clans, came to be called the Aryans. They moved and dispersed like sea waves to many parts of Europe and South Asia. Europe, Persia and Hindustan came to be settled by them. Our kshatriyas, brahmins and vaishyas formed themselves into castes and settled in this part of the world. The brahmins preserved the caste organisation as also its constituents like gotra. Many families formed a clan. This was the principle of social cohesion. As people migrate these bonds weaken; new areas and new cities emerge giving rise to many brahmins or vaishya jatis. Our present caste system is neither tribal nor territorial but a hotchpotch of both. Our joint family system has survived as beads of a social chain. You wish to preserve them, I aspire to destroy them. You would argue that in a family each member supports the other selflessly and that this noble ideal should be preserved. First, your principle of ‘altruism’ is ephemeral like smoke. It is an ideal only in name; from ancient times this ideal has been exception and continues to remain so. It is a ‘utopia.’ I cannot see it either in your house or any other house. It exists as a mental construct in someone like you. Secondly, this utopia is unscientific. It is against the principles of economics. The scientific principle of the creation of wealth and its growth and maximisation demands that each human being should have the possibility of developing their capacity for labour—both physical and mental—to its fullest potential. This potential is not attained so long as the person’s labour is not fully rewarded. Our tribal sense of family justice demands that one person earns through the sweat of his brow and others benefit from the fruits of his labour. Your sense of family justice destroys root and branch the principle that labour creates wealth and its growth depends upon an unhindered capacity for productive work. My dear Chandrakant, your sense of family justice has perturbed your mind. Your body has still not withered, but it will one day. This joint family nibbles at you; it is the cause of your troubles, illness and disease. Your attempts to dull your nerves by drinking the opium of ‘philosophy’ and pursuit of knowledge are futile. Your pride may last for a few days, but eventually it will desert you. Whatever your fate may be, have you ever considered that countless wretched men are incapable of being philosophical? Have you considered how badly mauled they will be till such time that they cultivate this disposition? So long as this barbaric joint family system is not destroyed, gems like Chandrakant will not shine forth in their glory. That hope is futile. People who subsist on the labour of men like you are like cattle; they will graze in your field but unlike cows and buffalos they will yield no milk. They are like bulls, unproductive and merry. They will only harass and cause trouble for poor helpless cows and buffalos. They will never acquire the capacity for creation of wealth through labour, something which all free men are capable of. Any compassion for your family and giving of alms to such able-bodied beggars is detrimental to both the giver and the taker. It is a path that invites destruction. You still follow the barbaric and corrupt practice of sharing Draupadi equally among five brothers to honour the injunction of a foolish mother. You share your wealth equally. Even scholars like you revel in it! The English education that you have received is like desert rain. Sarasvatichandra did not have the courage to discard false affection for his family and to this extent he proved a coward because he should have kicked away Laxminandan’s wealth and married Kumud Sundari. He failed to do so. This would have been the best option, which he proved incapable of. He chose the middle path and escaped the snare of family before it could catch him. I must congratulate him for this clever move! Please show him this letter and urge him to move away from the middle path and follow the best option. This is the essence of economic principles. Now let us examine ethics. But which school of ethics should we examine? All shastras prohibit theft and falsehood. Is the composition of your joint family system such that these two elements are precluded? The day Kaikeyi succeeded in getting Dasharath to command Ram to give up his claims to the throne, a truthful pledge was used for theft in broad daylight. Every joint family has a ‘patriarch.’ The immorality done unto Ram was done by the patriarch. Similar immoral acts were done under Dhritarashtra. Brothers, their sons and daughters-in-law, daughters and their children all suffer combined destinies; their machinations and prejudices have remained with us from the times of Kaikeyi and Dhritarashtra. The immorality of the game of dice and the war between the Kauravas and Pandavas are being waged in our homes either openly or in the secrecy of families. Who can claim in a country where families are plagued by the disease of evil agitation, where purity and peace have no place, that the joint family system is moral and ethical? Which man who has experienced this would ever make an ethical argument? English family life precludes the possibility of such strife within a family. Among them a mother is never given the opportunity to favour her daughter and harbour prejudice against the daughter-in-law. Among them the thieves are not harboured within the family. Outsiders cannot hamper and impede the love between husband and wife and the affection of parents for their young children. English families, limited in their members who are united by common interests, experience the morality and peace of a householder’s life. There is no scope for theft, cunning and mutually destructive prejudices and anger. Even humble hut- dwellers can enjoy heavenly riches. A Hindu who earns five thousand rupees cannot dream of the comfort, the happiness, the peace and moral life that a European who earns only fifty rupees enjoys in his small cottage. A European acquires these almost effortlessly, and his joy grows daily. He has the scope to further his bodily welfare, his joy, his love, his religion and morality; because he does not know the joint family system that destroys these. That man is not one of many beads in a social chain; he belongs to no clan or caste, and he is not a thorn in a joint family system. He flowers within the territoriality of his existence. Bereft of caste and devoid of thorns, the two halves— man and woman—come together to plant a new family tree. Dear Chandrakant, if you were born among the English, you would have shined forth in a very different family domain. Those members of your family who have become a burden and whose corrupt practices make others equally sullied would have also become meritorious and contributed to the merit and joy of others if they had been born in the land of English. Self-interest, altruism and welfare of the country are all simultaneously secured among them. Our joint family, like a locust, eats away bountiful trees like Sarasvatichandra and Chandrakant. Is that an ethical life? Is there anyone who cannot see the answer in a pure, unbiased judgement?

My dear Chandrakant! Our joint family system has but a blasting influence on the growth of our individuals, on our economic and moral conditions, and even on our national and political growth. It has kept our beings stunted in intelligence and action. It has turned our best sentiments into cruel mockeries and machines for grinding down the nervous systems of our young men and women in all ranks of life. Our idea that the world is misery is special to India, being born of this our special national engine for destroying all warmth of youth; and lo! We are all only old men or children in India in spite of our ages! And for any reform, woe be unto every idea of your social or domestic reconstruction or even improvement so long as you have not touched the root of the disease and said: Down with the joint family!⟨fn:191⟩ Dear Chandrakant! I am a ‘radical,’ an ultra reformer and therefore, I have adopted the name Uddhatlal, given to me by people in hatred. I have arrived at this principle after a great deal of experiment, deep observation and much deliberation. This principle has taken firm root in my heart. It is necessary to become Uddhat—haughty, vain, arrogant, rude and ill- behaved—to raise our people out of the foolish and evil disorder of our country. We cannot be elevated without some form of haughty, intemperate behaviour. If we want to see the fruits of our education and our intellect in our own lifetime, we have no option but to cleanse our land of all the dirt that has accumulated in guise of tradition and custom. We must begin this effort of eradicating idiocy and evil conduct from our own homes. You may ask me, what have I done? Here it goes! The twin principles that a son must obey his parents and be grateful to them are prevalent among us. Its prevalence knows no limits. You must have read that at one time among the Vaishnavas a practice prevailed that devotees of the Vaishnav Maharaj gave their body, mind and wealth in the service of the Maharaj. Even bodily submission by a devout woman to a Vaishnav Maharaj was not considered a debauched act. This is the object lesson of the proposition that even a good idea, exercised without limits and fetters can lead to excesses. By the same logic the maxim that one should obey one’s parents has come to be misused. Let us take some examples. The moral authority of parents is required in infancy and childhood. But once that age is passed such commands are both ill-placed and illegitimate. These commands have to be obeyed not for the good of the parents but to secure the welfare of children. And as children grow up and mature they grow not only in body but also in mental capacity. It is true that children do not have the same depth of experience as their parents. But if that is the only justification for complete obedience, parents would always have more experience than their children because of their respective age. By this logic parents would command obedience till the end of their lives. Most certainly, our Shastras cannot form a maxim that is apparently so stupid and evil. Our Shastras say that a son, once he attains the age of sixteen, should be regarded as a friend. This is a true maxim. Why should we regard a sixteen-year old son as a friend? What does such conduct entail? A father’s right to command ends and a son’s independence commences at that age. If a father’s experience was the basis of his right, this principle would never have been formulated. If a father’s right to receive obedience were to be based upon all the love and care he has lavished upon the son, this principle cannot be realised. If so, what then is the reason for this age limit? Till the age of sixteen a son’s intellect is not fully mature and till such time it was a father’s right to issue commands and demand their obedience for the sake of securing the son’s interest. That reason is nullified at the age of sixteen when the son attains maturity. The Shastras consider the age of sixteen mature enough to grant independence to a son and take away the father’s right of demanding obedience. Any command given by the father after this age is a violation of the injunctions of the Shastras. It is in the interest of the son that he exercises his autonomous judgement. If the father is wiser than the son, he should counsel like a friend. A father who violates this principle is evil; there can be no doubt about this. Intellect is a gift of God; He grants more to some and a little less to some others. Whatever it may be, it should be regarded as God’s light.

The recitation of the Gayatri Mantra acts as a reminder of this to all who are twice-born. This flame may give bright light or burn dimly; only God and the king have a right to arrest this light or limit its reach. Once this light acquires an autonomous existence, a father who tries to snuff it out by the exercise of his authority engages in an evil act of destroying its life. It is likely that sometimes a son does not possess a sharp mind and unguided exercise of his judgement may cause him harm. Even in such cases a father does not have the right to issue commands and demand obedience. If this were to be regarded as a legitimate ground for paternal authority, all of us are given to regarding ourselves as wiser than the rest, and by that logic all fathers would consider themselves wiser than their sons and sons would never gain the autonomy of judgement. It is for such reasons that the wise law-givers of the Shastras gave an injunction that by the age of sixteen a son’s intellect must mature and with that the exercise of paternal authority must cease. The age could vary, from sixteen to eighteen to twenty depending upon the place and customs, which could be determined by the Shastras or by royal authority. This authority must not be given to fathers who are greedy to extend their reign over their sons. The age may vary but this principle must be adhered to. A daughter, the moment she becomes a woman, restricts physical proximity to her father; she becomes untouchable even by her father. Similarly, a son when he attains manhood should be regarded as immune to father’s intellectual influence. This principle should be adopted for the welfare of our people. All civilised countries have adopted this principle. The Patria Potestas⟨fn:192⟩ of Rome was destroyed on the basis of this idea. Something similar happened in England. We have also adopted a maxim of limiting the age of maturity. It is our strange fate that in modern times this injunction is not followed, and parents retain the greed to seek obedience from their elderly son; they accuse sons of ungratefulness when they seek or assert autonomy. Consequently even intelligent sons have to submit to the stupidity and cunning of their fathers. Their wives are forced to live in a world dominated by their mothers- in-law and sisters-in-law. This is the result of the ethical or rather the unethical principles of our family lives. Uddhatlal has kicked away these principles. I have, beginning with my own family, begun an endeavour to raise the lot of our helpless generation. My father spent money on my education. I am told I should be grateful for that. Your courts of justice have equated money spent on a son’s education to breastfeeding. The gratitude one is expected to feel for education is in no way greater than the gratitude one has for being breastfed. Breastfeeding one’s own child is like watering a plant one has planted; watering of a plant presupposes the sowing of a seed. Breastfeeding is thus a duty tied to child-bearing. A mother who conceives and gives birth to a child but fails to breastfeed the child fails to discharge her duty as a mother. A mother needs to be thanked not for feeding us at her breast but for giving birth to us. A mother who makes her child’s life deliberately unhappy deserves no gratitude; she should in fact be subject to criticism. This is not a gift of life, a life of love, but the act of an enemy. A father who fails to provide the nourishment of education is by the same logic an enemy. No gratitude is due to him for providing education; one has to be grateful to him only if he has made special efforts to make our lives successful. But a father who harbours animosity towards his son, acts in a way that is detrimental to the son’s interest and cries when the son dies has no love for his son. It is like describing ash as fire. Laxminandan’s wailing is of this type. My parents gave me education but did not discharge any other parental duties. I believe that my child marriage was an act that an enemy would perform. They in their foolishness did not see this as an act of animosity but an act of love. Therefore, I am willing to place this act, though an act of an enemy, in their favour and consider it as part of their parental duty. Sarasvatichandra fortunately realised that his father’s discharge of parental duty was in fact detrimental to his own interest. He is sharp and clever but clearly lacking in experience as he could not turn it to his advantage. My father educated me, arranged my marriage and fed me. He spent roughly three thousand rupees in discharge of his parental duty. Even if we calculate compound rate of interest, he has spent seven thousand rupees on me. The day my parents became a hindrance in my duties towards my wife Srimati, I saw that as a violation of parental obligation. Their conduct was that of an enemy. It was no longer possible for me to live with them. I saw the continuance of joint family as irreligious and immoral. I believe that in matters of food and social conduct a bold, truthful man secures happiness. I followed this maxim and set up a separate household. My father, in discharge of his parental duty, has spent seven thousand rupees. I do not have that kind of money to return the sum to him immediately. But I pay him the amount that he would have earned as interest on this sum every month. I have to cut corners and face some hardship for this, but I will continue to pay them so long as I live. I do not have seven thousand rupees, but I have taken a pledge that I shall return the amount to them the day I get it. I have informed my parents of this resolve. I do not consider that I am duty-bound to do anything more. There was a law in Athens that a son who had not been educated by his father was not obliged to provide food and clothing to his parents in their old age. Among the English a son starts a separate house the day he gets married and is free of all obligations towards his parents. We, on the other hand, celebrate total submission of a son to his parents. This custom, which is as old as Kunti, survives till today. It is a residue of the tribal way of life that still survives among us. Dear Chandrakant, unlike Sarasvatichandra, I do not submit to such impulses. I discharge my duties in an unimpassioned, objective manner. I cut away the excessive bondage masquerading as morality with a sharp-edged knife. I also stay away from excess of freedom. I weigh my actions on the scale of righteous conduct. I act without hesitation once I decide the path of right action. You comprehend all this; your understanding is no less than mine. You know what ails you, but stay away from its remedy. You are a ‘Let-Alonist.’ You stay away from social opprobrium. You allow the bondage of family to grow like a spider’s web. You suffer as a result and will continue to suffer in the future. You will not be able to secure either your joy or the welfare of the country. I quote a dialogue from Lytton’s novel for your reflection. Among us there is a saying that one need not drink saline water from a well just because it was dug by one’s father. Now over to Lytton: “My dear Ma’am!” said the Parson, “There are many institutions in the country which are very old, look very decayed, and don’t seem of much use; but I would not pull them down for all that!” “You would reform them, then?” said Mrs. Hazeldean... “No, I would not, Ma’am!” said the Parson stoutly. “What on earth would you do, then?” quote the squire. “Just let  ’em alone,” said the Parson. “Master Frank! There’s a Latin maxim which was often in the mouth of Sir Robert Walpole, and which they ought to put into Eton’s Grammar: ‘Quieta non Movere.’ If things are quiet, let them be quiet! I would not destroy the stocks because that might seem to the ill-disposed like a license to offend; and I would not repair the stocks because that puts into people’s heads to get into them.”⟨fn:193⟩ Chandrakantbhai! You are like this Parson. You must stop this adverse current, if not reform it. Shri Krishna could afford to sit aside and watch the Yadavas self-destruct. He could do so because his work was done and he was waiting to get back to heaven. But you still have to fight the battle of the Mahabharata. You cannot afford to be such a great soul. I have written a longish letter because if you were to meet Sarasvatichandra and if he were to refuse to return to Bombay, give this to him. He is a clever and thoughtful man, but he needs to garner experience. Sarasvatichandra read the letter. He seemed dejected. He began to read Chandrakant’s response. Dear Uddhatlal! The image that you paint of our disorder and chaos is not false, but it is an incomplete picture. Our families follow tribal principles; we have a joint-family system which is the bedrock of our social formation. In Europe every individual looks for a personal utopia. Among us we do not have personal, individuated utopias. Those men and women who bear the burden of the family are crushed under it and become feeble; their families harbour and conceal many social evils. The image that you have painted hitherto is acceptable to Chandrakant. Reforms are impeded at the very source. You argue that it is the evil of joint family that impedes reforms. Even this argument is acceptable. But there are certain lacunae in this image which I wish to supplement. If members of the joint family were to realise that their welfare is best secured by the welfare of those men and women who bear the family’s burden and provide for it, the reasons for which you wish to destroy this system would disappear to a large extent. Those families which have realised this do not harm each other in futile, meaningless conflicts. This realisation comes with general education, some reflection and reposing trust in the person who bears the burden. You know well how education can be furthered. With education comes a capacity for reflection. Experience and wisdom also contribute to the reflective capacity. It is up to us to gain our family’s trust. There are people who possess this art. I have learnt much from my hostess Gunasundari. The person who seeks confidence should have pure intentions, unsullied affection, forbearance and generosity and many other similar virtues. It is true that such virtues are not easy to cultivate and are not found in most. And yet, I must assert that such virtuous persons are found in this country and are not as rare as it is assumed. I do not deny the benefits of a nuclear family consisting of husband, wife and their unmarried children. I am not in a position to challenge your assertion that the disappearance of the joint family system and its replacement by nuclear families will lead to the welfare of our country; but I can assert that you have not arrived at this principle after appropriate research. I also submit that such a man will obtain one type of happiness, but this also makes him vulnerable on other counts. It is a different matter to investigate whether the benefits outweigh the costs or not. It is likely that we might come up with the situation of the blind men and the elephant. Instead of dismissing the experiences of all blind men as false, we might arrive closer to the truth if we add up their experiences. These days we have instituted the practice of insurance; we even insure expenses for marriages and death rituals. These insurances are issued by insurance companies. We know of instances of women who gave their body and wealth for the family; and after their death other members of the family look after and raise her children and provide for them, if not forever then for a short time. If such instances are true, then it is possible to argue that the deceased had obtained insurance without actually having purchased one. This mode of insurance bears fruit after her death and compensates her effort. However, the fact is that not everyone obtains such results; the occasion does not arise. And at the same time very few actually receive the annuity on their insurance. If all those who obtain insurance were to claim insurance benefits, the companies issuing them would go bankrupt. Our joint family system is a form of insurance. You will comprehend this only if you follow the logic of my argument. In families not all members sit idle and unproductive. Each one according to capacity and intellect helps and serves the others. They do work which would otherwise require servants. It is true that one cannot have the same degree of control over family members as we do over paid servants. Despite this control, one can never trust a servant as much as one trusts one’s family. Not just that, family is a type of fortification. This protection provides security to our women against lecherous men from outside. In Europe such protective walls do not exist, and it gives rise to many fears about immoral conduct within a family. You will understand this if you visit Europe. Dear Uddhatlal, hitherto I have not had the misfortune of judging whether the loss of trust and confidence in the women of one’s family is a cause of greater turbulence or whether the conflicts of a joint family are more disturbing. I do not say that your arguments are patently false. I am merely adding a different tonality to the picture you have painted. You will certainly not argue that our tribal joint family system is detrimental to the country. The economic principles, which were hitherto considered impregnable in Europe, have been breached by the ‘socialists.’ In Europe, we find an extremely rich man and a poor man being neighbours. A rich man spends money which could buy heaps of food on frivolous pleasures, but we find his neighbour starving. Today in Europe parties have been formed which seek to eradicate such glaring inequalities by the redistribution of wealth. These parties go under different names, but kings and noblemen and all advocates of a conservative social order tremble at this possibility. We need not speculate as to what extent these parties will succeed in shaking up the established order or what force they will be able to exert. But I do see the socialist aspiration being fulfilled, albeit in a different form, in our country. One man’s earning is used to provide for many family members. The practice of feeding one’s caste members might have taken root with the idea that the money of the rich is spent on members of his caste. In these arrangements, I see socialist ideals being realised among us. I cannot argue that the ideals we have attained should be forsaken so that we could attain a social condition similar to the one prevalent in Europe, because the socialist ideology is smouldering like a volcano underneath the European social order and is threatening to destroy it. Our country is poor. Our people have become feeble. We are ruled by a foreign power. Our laws and our wealth are subject to decisions made by outsiders. At such a time, if your aspirations were to be fulfilled and if all able men were to walk out of all families in this vast land spanning from the Himalayas to Setubandh Rameshwar, how deep would be the anguish, how dangerous that anarchy! All around us there would be poverty; people would be orphaned. My imagination fails me in painting a picture of that disorder. I leave the judgement to you as to whether such anarchy is desirable or not, and wherein lies our duty and right conduct. Dear Uddhatlal, whenever I think of adding something to the wealth that is exclusively Ganga’s and mine, whenever I think of earning behind the backs of my foolish loved ones, these images of our people rise before me. My affection for my family gives rise to a sense of patriotism, which in turns strengthens my bonds with my family. My mind thinks many thoughts and my heart experiences many feelings. But eventually, dear Uddhatlal, all my wanderings bring me home! When I think of my home, of our society, my heart churns, but no amount of churning produces any butter. Because the result of such heart-churning is Sarasvatichandra, who has disappeared. The churning of my heart has proved futile. Why? Because I know something about Sarasvatichandra’s aspirations. If these aspirations were to be fulfilled, then the aspirations that you and I have, with our different ideologies, will be actualised. There is a way of bringing together our aspirations. The futilities of the joint family system that you point out were known even in ancient times. Elders went to the forest, accepting Vanaprastha. This was done to save the family from such futility and conflicts. Even Dhritarashtra accepted Vanaprastha. In our age the problems have compounded, but at the same time we have many more remedies. Our younger generations, exposed to the English kind of individual freedom, sing a different tune while our elders continue in their age-old methods. The cacophony that these two disharmonious tunes produce is the conflict and discord in our families. With the passage of time this discord will disappear because the older generation is certain to die. The younger generation of today will assume the role of the elder. Their past experience will teach them not to sing a discordant note and create problems for the new generation. Till such time the present discord and caste system are necessary, but they are not permanent. We should remind all those who suffer because of familial strife and discord that this condition is temporary and transient. In our times, sons and brothers migrate to distant lands while elders stay home. This is the new mode of Vanaprastha. In the older system the elders went to the forest while the sons stayed home and provided food and clothing to the elders who had accepted to dwell in the forest. In our times the sons migrate while the parents stay back; the sons provide for their parents from a distance. When both the older and younger generations live in the same place, discord and strife prevails. Some of them adopt the path that you have chosen. Some others like me and Tarang Shankar find other ways of dealing with it. There is no dearth of people who find either one of the two options. But Sarasvatichandra found a unique solution; he joined neither your caste, nor mine! ⟨fn:194⟩Dear Uddhatlal! Subject to all these things that I have said here, I plead unreservedly and fully guilty to the charge you have framed so pointedly against me! I could have raised my Ganga and my children to the position which was due to them from an EDUCATED paterfamilias. But the existence of a wider family and my deference to the feelings of the other heads of that family have made me sacrifice higher interests of my own wife and children. I may be wrong; I may have sinned. But I may also be right and I have tried to err on the safer side—safer so far as the fortune of our people may be measured by that of their numbers. I am not quite what you call a Let-Alonist. The Hindu ideal is eminently socialistic in life and practice, and though I am no socialist in aspirations, I feel it a duty to give fair scope to the free operation of that ideal side by side with the forces of Western Individualism which are stirring our souls, so that both may by the laws of natural selection adjust themselves to each other and bring about a happy combination of the special blessings of each. The main feature of our Hindu socialism is that it is Protective. It protects the purity of the sex from outside influences which operate elsewhere and are always at the mercy of accidents and intrigues. It protects the weak, the infants, the women, and the aged from starvation and its consequential crimes. It protects the family wealth from the whims and follies of profligates and imbeciles at home and from the operations of rogues abroad, by a domestic organisation of people who can watch like dogs and guard like sentinels. It protects and protects. Our Western individualism is on the other hand essentially Progressive, and progress is safety in these days. To explain my whole being in a sentence, I am breathlessly watching the confluence of socialism and individualism, wish welfare to both, am anxious to guard against socialism becoming oppressive and individualism becoming aggressive, for what is protective has a tendency to become oppressive and what is progressive has a tendency to become aggressive. The sacrifice that one has to make in order to secure a combination of the two boons, without their abuses, is mine, and the blessings of full individualism are yours. I sincerely love you for the noble blessings with which you have surrounded yourself. But for poor me, dear friend, it is the essence of my sacrifice that I must abstain from securing them to myself until I am able to share them more or less with the whole group of my dear and poor joint family. This means poverty, patience, forbearance and even suffering for at least one generation, and I am prepared to wait so long or even longer. Perhaps, nay probably, we shall agree with our sons more in the new generation than our elders do with us in this. That’s my hope built upon the fact that, unlike our elders, we have had the same education that our sons are receiving now.⟨fn:195⟩ Sarasvatichandra kept the letter back in the bundle, put the bundle aside and stood up. As he walked back and forth from one rocky wall to another, he thought about all the letters from his Bombay friends. He seemed pensive, disturbed, even somewhat confounded. His confusion formed itself into a poem which flowed out of him along with his tears, tears of joy as also of sorrow. His face was lined with pain, his heart full of yearning. Quite unaware of his actions, he picked up a rough sheet of paper and wrote on it with a thick-nibbed pen. The compassion, love and pride latent in Sarasvatichandra’s heart poured forth as he wrote. Dear Chandrakant! Dear brother, I see your life unravel before me: Full of sorrow. My eyes have opened: I see your pain as mine! Pain, like a demon, Eats away at your heart. Pain assumes many forms; It encircles the scholar who stands in its midst.

The brave one disregards pain, Does not blame fate, Harbours no anger. You stand alone in the worldly Forest to hunt the animal That is pain. Your mind in a whirl, dear Learned friend, wastes away. Dear Chandrakant! You struggle to make ends meet; You refuse the money I gave; You strive to accumulate some wealth; You disregard the follies of your dear ones. The anger was now apparent on his face. Your family, a colony of leeches, Has no regard for your pain; They drain your wealth, They shout and shriek, Allowing not a moment of repose! Your family is selfish, and your wife is no exception. And yet you remain steadfast, You retain your affection And bear the hardships; Dear brother, you are an ascetic. Dear Chandrakant! You do not open your heart to me; Your wounds remain hidden. Tears rolled down his eyes as he wrote. Futile is my life, futile my wealth, Futile my renunciation—I failed to see your poverty. Sarasvatichandra felt a profound dislike for himself. He sat down, then again got up restlessly. He placed the page against a tree trunk and wrote: You are a rare gem, A hard won boon for the country,

But for generosity’s sake, You remain hidden in a heap of dirt. Oh brother! Your pain breaks my heart! I have sinned against a friend, against my country, and I bear witness to it! Dear Chandrakant, is there no way out? There are many wealthy men, But their ignorance is limitless, Wealth and dirt are alike for them; They drown their wealth in the sea; They drink and sin with their money; Fools waste their money on lowly things. As men dance to the tunes of a courtesan, Goddess Lakshmi makes them dance and still eludes their grasp. But all these wealthy men are illiterate and foolish. How can one blame them? Are there no scholars who have enough money for altruistic goals? If there are learned men who have wealth but do little with it, how can I blame those who are wealthy and stupid? How can I blame the stupid? Why should I wade through the dictionary of stupidity? There are scholars like me who have wealth, but for what purpose? Wealth makes them blunt, inanimate; they forget all their education and learning. And I am learned and still foolish! How can I blame others And fill books with their criticism? Lakshmi resides in my house; Sarasvati has blessed me; And still I have not a Thought in my head! I left home to see the world But failed to look around and within me. Dear friend! I see what lies in your heart; my heart weeps for you. I have awakened from my dream. Dear friend, now all your worries will disappear. The condition of one Chandrakant allows me to see that of many Chandrakants. The pain of one is the pain of many. Knowledge is not wealth; not just that but among us Goddess Sarasvati and Lakshmi are said not to co-exist. I had an object lesson in this. Chandrakant offers Ganga as an oblation to the family sacrifice. Uddhatlal, in his intellectual excitement, wants to make Srimati his partner; he destroys the web of joint family and sets out on a path of rebellion to eradicate and cleanse that system. Tarang Shankar loves his wife but cannot get rid of his family; he searches in vain for poetic sensibility in the world around him. Gangabhabhi! Parvati could not bear Shiva’s insult. You are as virtuous as her; you have true feelings for your husband, but they are concealed under your selfishness. This dirt of selfishness can be swept aside by a broom called wealth, one thing that Chandrakant does not possess. As these new ideas flashed across his mind, Sarasvatichandra saw new vistas and new worlds open up before him. He trembled with excitement as his tumultuous thoughts found words to express themselves. He addressed himself to the predicament of Chandrakant and Tarang Shankar. Men of sterling virtue Face many hardships. What to speak of the poor? My wealth remains purposeless. Hidden by the dirt of poverty, Men of virtue remain paupers. No one looks for men of virtue. The remedy lies in my wealth, which remains purposeless. He compared Uddhatlal and Chandrakant. Leonine men of my country Remain caged by sorrow; No one frees these brave hearts. I mourn the futility of my wealth. He thought of Chandrakant’s wife, Ganga. The earth is fecund with juices, But women remain barren, unnourished. They cannot flower without a

Gardener to tend to them. There are gardeners, but they are poor. How can a withered gardener nourish? My wealth remains unused! Beloved Kumud! You remained without a gardener’s care! There is wealth, but no gardener to tend it. I am the cause of your misfortunes. Kumud, my beloved, I love thee. My friend, I love thee. You and your virtues multiplied by many can flourish with my wealth. Shiva gave up his body; I shall give up my wealth. My heart sees a new horizon, But not the pitiable condition of men of virtue; My renunciation now has a meaning; I have seen much that was hidden before. For the sake of my countrymen, I will return home. He sat down on the ground, his flowing robes spread across the length of his body. Suddenly, he grew conscious of his clothes; the poem seemed to be running away from him. He got up at once. Sarasvatichandra! All those desires and aspirations do not match with these clothes. You left home because of your own stupidity. Your follies brought you here and made you aware of the condition of our country. Now, at this point, to return home, to reclaim the wealth already given to Dhanbhai, to renounce the clothes of renunciation! Is this greater stupidity or wisdom? Is this moral or immoral? Is this righteous conduct? It is said the non-commencement of something is the first sign of intellect, and the second sign is to remain consistent to the commitment already made. I failed the first test of intellect, but I must remain steadfast on the second. I have committed myself to this stage—by folly or by fortune— and I shall at least be consistent with myself and stick to what I have accepted. That saves me an amount of thought and vexation.⟨fn:196⟩ It is sinful to take back wealth that is already gifted.

I leave it to God to find someone who will make the efforts to secure the country’s welfare through wealth. I had the means to make this effort, but I no longer do. That, too, is the will of God. I will find new means for the new path I have adopted. I do not wish to pick up arms which I have already discarded. Kumud, the vow that I took for you will not be broken. My renunciation and acceptance of the life of a mendicant are my penance for the sin of pushing you into the well of grief. Is there anything in the world which can tempt me to return home? Are altruism and compassion enough penance? Will my sins be washed? Kumud Sundari! It was my wanton behaviour that pushed you into sorrow. I will atone for it as I have promised. And like Buddha, I will come to you one day unannounced as a renouncer and seek your forgiveness. With my limited abilities I will work for the welfare of our people. Chandrakant, before I left Bombay, I believed that one can secure the welfare of the country, the people and self-realisation without wealth. You argued for the necessity of wealth and I argued against it. I believed in my arguments and gave up my wealth. Your arguments were rooted in experience. I now realise that my arguments were stupid. I lost the means to come to your aid. What has been done cannot be undone; I cannot go back on the pledge I have taken. Now I must dedicate this body to the great effort. At this point I want to hold on to the fatalism that our people revel in. My determination to remain true to my pledge appears consistent with our belief in fate and destiny. Tarang Shankar! You teach that love like illusion is false. If I give up the dream of securing Kumud’s love it would be appropriate for a renouncer; I do not deny that. But Buddha obtained his wife Yashodhara’s pardon, and until I secure Kumud’s pardon, I cannot gain the equanimity of Buddha. Buddha’s renunciation did not compel his queen to marry someone else. Kumud, you were given to Pramad and met with unbearable pain. I was the sole reason for it. I believed that since we were not ritually married I had the right to break a union that our hearts had accepted. This was my sin. Dear Chandrakant, I will remain steadfast to my pledge and till such time that Kumud’s generous heart has pardoned me unconditionally I will remain in the garb of a renouncer and keep the flame of love alive in my heart, even if it were to scald me. Oh my soul, I gave misery to the beloved. I cannot be a householder, Nor can I be a renouncer. Body smeared with ash, Heart smouldering with grief, This renunciation is like A volcano ready to erupt. His forehead, his eyes and lips gave testimony to a fierce and unshakable resolve. She appeared unseen, Kumud’s fragrance permeates The forest air. Such is my fate! Chandrakant! Chandrakant, forgive me! Till such time that I obtain Kumud’s pardon, this renunciation will be a fiery ordeal and only after that shall I have peace and equanimity. Once I attain a sense of equanimity and quietude I shall remember this country of ours and find ways of securing its welfare without wealth. I will put into practice my dream. Sarasvatichandra looked at his ochre robes and, holding them in his hand, addressed his robes aloud: ‘Oh ochre robes of my renunciation! I shall not insult your dignity. I was taught at the time of my initiation that one should live in the world in a natural state. In case of Kumud I deviated from the path; I caused my own fall. This fiery ordeal has to be my state. I will purify my mind with the fire of renunciation; this is not contrary to the conduct of a renouncer because this is in accordance with my initiation.

Just at that moment, he heard Kumud’s voice. My beloved has worn the ochre garb: O’ the beauty of the renouncer! His garb is dear to me! He now aspires to the Truth divine. He looked around, but Kumud was nowhere to be found. He said aloud, ‘Oh, my innermost thoughts express and manifest themselves! They perturb me. But I believe that such disquiet is part of my penance and shall allow it to express itself unhindered.’ Once again he heard Kumud. Kumud became a renouncer With her Chandra, Beloved! We shall play a new Game of love. Sarasvatichandra spoke to that voice. ‘Oh beloved, melodious voice! I do not aspire to this beautiful, enticing dream of love. That dream itself is sinful. Oh unmanifest voice, this dream would invite tribulation. Stop calling to me and instead berate me for my evil actions.’ The answer came from somewhere else. An ascetic came to the window of the monastery and called out, ‘There is but one God— the one who grants bliss!’ This call reverberated all around and the monastery walls, the sky, the spring, the trees all answered, ‘He is the giver of bliss.’ Sarasvatichandra’s heart also responded to this call of bliss. He turned towards the window and saw the ascetic approaching him, his face radiant with joy.
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra grapples with anguish after reading letters exposing Chandrakant's secret family struggles, finding himself torn between his vows and an ethereal voice.

chapters.title: Twin Sisters: The Spinster and the Widow
paragraphs: Twin Sisters: The Spinster and the Widow The husbandless woman exists in two shapes. She is either a spinster or a widow. Most nations permit both institutions to grow up side by side with each other with the result that the reciprocal proportions of the numbers of the two classes undergo fluctuations on principles very similar to those of the two metals of a double currency under the guidance of economic laws. Social science is interested in noting how these fluctuations tell upon the general welfare of the nation. The poet of domestic charms falls in love with the different features of the lights and shades of the twin sisters—the spinster and the widow. There is also a cynical way of subjecting both creatures to a camera observation and comparing the shadow of the two reflected upon its plate. This is especially useful in a country like India where the Hindus have chosen and contrived to escape the fluctuations of a domestic double currency by keeping the widow a permanent coin and excluding the spinster altogether from their mint. The propounders of justice and of the equality of the two sexes may well protest against this gross injustice to the weaker sex. But apart from that, no small interest gathers round the questions whether India, with this monometallism for her social economics, is really a loser on the whole, and whether the world of bimetallists has gained anything substantial, or to be more serious and less offensive to the fastidious moralist, whether the world has gained on the whole by its submission to the ordinary laws of nature, and India has suffered by working out this artificial system within its families.⟨fn:197⟩   —Anonymous Vidya Chatura’s family came together. Their elder Manchatura counselled them to give up hopes of finding Kumud. Buddhidhan’s letter brought news of Pramaddhan’s death. In one day they received the news of two deaths; their poor daughter and foolish son-in-law. Vidya Chatura’s ministerial palace was shrouded in gloom; it was akin to the darkness of a moonless night with black, rain-laden clouds covering the sky. Before they could mourn Kumud’s loss and hurl accusations, abuses and curses on Pramaddhan, the news of his death reached them. The flow of abuses and curses dried up. Kumud came to be considered fortunate because she had died before becoming a widow; this thought worked as a balm and assuaged their grief somewhat. Maniraj grieved with them, consoled them. Friends, family, caste fellows, officers, the staff of the royal household, leading men of the state came to give solace and share in their grief. These customary visits for offering condolences dispersed and fragmented their grief a little. At the end of the day, tired and drained out, all of them took to their beds. When Vidya Chatura focused on God’s will, his sleep deepened. When he thought of Kumud’s virtues and her misfortune, sleep eluded him; at times his grief and tears poured out in his sleep. When he thought of his fondness for his daughter, sleep took the form of an ache; only when he assuaged his grief by thinking of the futility of life itself could he surrender himself to sleep. For Gunasundari the only solace and consolation was that her daughter did not die a widow, but the tears would flow afresh whenever she thought of all her virtues. She could not sleep at all. She wept all night. Sometimes she lay down and cried; sometimes she sat up in her bed and wept. She and Sundargauri held on to each other and wept inconsolably.

As the days passed, their grief became less immediate. Everyday life asserted itself, blurring and blunting their memories. The family’s grief took their attention away from Kusum. Gunasundari remained preoccupied with her social obligations and rituals. Kusum spent more and more time alone. Her heart and mind were filled with all these new experiences, new thoughts and newer worries. She was eager to chart a very different course for her life. These anxieties and aspirations took possession of her. Kusum’s preoccupation became a cause of Sundargauri’s worries. Gunasundari was a wise and learned woman, but the shock of Kumud was too much for her to bear. She went about with a vacant look, paid scant attention to the running of the household and had no mental space to worry about Kusum. Sundargauri constantly remained by Gunasundari’s side, but her eyes followed Kusum. Sundargauri had no time to grieve as her time was spent consoling Gunasundari and in her attempts to control Kusum’s self-willed aspirations. This was an opportunity for Sundargauri to repay in some measure the lifelong debt of gratitude she felt she owed to her sister-in-law. She showed no lethargy in this. Kusum walked around unescorted in her garden, the pond adjacent to it and on the pathways during the early hours of the night. Her mind was in a whirl. Marriage means a certain abasement and capitulation. Kumud behn! You passed away and Pramaddhan died! If both of you or you alone had lived your pain would have been unbearable! The only reason for this pain was your marriage. Marriage is an enemy of women. Gunial takes consolation from the fact that death saved you from the pain of widowhood! Why should it be so! Kumud behn, you would have been happier had you not married and not faced the prospect of widowhood. Death demands mourning; it leaves behind grief. Similarly cessation of marriage leaves behind the shadow of widowhood. If the shadow is so evil, how undesirable would marriage itself be? Your death was preferred over your life as a widow. Hence, I will accept neither marriage nor widowhood! Kaki is determined to get me married and push me into a ditch. But Gunial is silent on this issue. It is only because of father that I am still unmarried! Kusum ran swift as a gazelle, passed a line of roses and sat down on a blue glass seat facing the pool. Sundargauri saw her run. She went up to her and said with concern, ‘Daughter, is it good for a woman of your age to run around like this? You are no longer a child!’ Kusum: ‘It might be wrong for a married woman to run around. But an unmarried woman can run, whatever her age.’ Sundargauri: ‘Is your marriage so far into the distant future? Do you have any idea as to how concerned Gunial is about you? Kusum, you must grow up and be wise. If you do not lessen your mother’s worries at such times, when will you do so?’ This barb found its mark. Kusum softened and grew serious. All human beings submit to a certain sense of limits, some sense of regulation. Evil-minded persons are restrained by the prospect of punishment. Fools need a series of mishaps and difficulties to obey certain limits. Clever and pious but inexperienced persons can see far and, at the first sign of approaching difficulty, rein in their conduct. They do not need external impetus. One needs affectionate elders to teach young children the dangers of wanton expression of their natural youthful exuberance. Kusum was fortunate in this regard. At times Gunasundari was frightened by her self-will and her uncontrolled exuberance. At such times Vidya Chatura, who had an understanding of the character of such self-willed persons, taught her patience. He did not want Kusum’s youthful body and mind to be subjected to the rigours of external regime, but argued that her intellect needs to be so cultivated that it provides its own sense of limits without snuffing out the effervescence of youth. Once he counselled Gunasundari: ‘Gunial! Just as a young, infatuated wife is tempered by a cultured husband, not by force but by tact, in a way that deepens their love, we have to cultivate the intellect of a child. If we want our children to be more intelligent than us, we should not place the fetters of our knowledge around them, because a mind that has grown accustomed to obedience does not develop independently. A child’s mind should not be fettered by her parents. That mind should learn to walk, recover from falls and also run if it has that capacity. Parents should not place any obstacles in the path of the autonomous development of their children’s minds. If that intellect has the dexterity to dance, it should be allowed to. Education feeds that intellect, thought is an exercise of the mind, independence is the breeze that nurtures it, enthusiasm is its playground; and observation of the world is the water that nourishes it. It is the duty of the parents to ensure that the water remains pure, that the breeze is unpolluted and unhindered and no debased elements enter the playground of the mind. Parents should ensure that the intellect does not either become lazy or overexcited and that it is nourished by vital elements. These are the limits of the parents’ power to regulate the life of their children. This has to form the boundary within which a child’s mind must be given the freedom to dance. ‘As they begin to grow up and move out of childhood, the parents should give them abilities which would allow them to chart their own future. They should be made aware that life is the source of both happiness and sorrow. We should ensure that evil winds are purified before they enter Kusum’s chamber. Adolescence brings with it exuberance and the desire for greater freedom. At this age, dry instructions would not work as effectively as affectionate teaching. We must create opportunities for her to exercise her judgement. These opportunities for mental exercise should not be of a lowly type which might induce laziness or create desire for sensual pleasures. Also the burden should not be such that a child feels crushed under its weight. Finally, the experiential world of the adolescent should be as pure, as purifying as the water of the Ganga. It should be universal in its reach and be able to contain reflections of variegated experiences. A child’s intellect should be so nourished that she develops the capability of satisfying the thirst of all beings; it should be as noble and nourishing as the herbs of the Himalayas. The adolescent mind should be trained to observe flows of events as wide as the ocean. The unstated principle should be that the child learns to discern between right and wrong; the intellect must be nourished with morality.

‘Gunial! Such is the path of pure education, and its results are beneficial to all. As a general principle, femininity of the female and masculinity of male children should be taken into consideration as it guides their development as adult men and women. Parents who fail to provide such education and cultivate their children fail in the discharge of their duties. Our people have fallen, are debased and do not comprehend their true obligations. Make sure that you never deviate from the path of this pious duty. You and I share our duties and obligations for right conduct. You are for that reason a partner in my moral obligations. You are a co-sharer of my duties because of the education you have received. I give unto you the responsibility of discharging this duty because my affairs do not allow me the scope for their proper discharge. God has given us all that is required for us to discharge our parental duties; I have given you the necessary education which would enable you to discharge this obligation. Give what you have received and gained to your daughter. I have shown you the path which would make her intellect a cultured, chiseled gem. The success of this endeavour would depend upon your enthusiasm.’ Vidya Chatura had given this advice specifically for Kusum’s upbringing. Gunasundari had noted it down and also memorised it. If she were asked by others about the reasons for giving such variety of education and autonomy to her daughter, Gunasundari always pointed out her husband’s injunctions. If someone were to challenge the wisdom of this course of action, this learned woman had the capability of explicating the meaning of these injunctions and successfully defending her husband.
