Despite this, Gunasundari had fears that are natural to a woman’s heart; she was perturbed by the independence that her daughter enjoyed and hoped that her fears should never come true. Both Gunasundari and Sundargauri lived with this constant apprehension. This apprehension had no immediate resolution; it would unfold gradually over time with Kusum’s growth into maturity. As Sundargauri counselled her niece to conduct herself in a manner that reduced Gunasundari’s anxieties, she was herself overcome with apprehension. This worldly wise widow eagerly awaited Kusum’s response. She wanted to know how a girl who had grown up without any restrictions would respond to her mother’s problems. Sundargauri examined her niece closely, alert to the slightest change in the expression of Kusum’s eyes. She attentively heard every word of this inexperienced but intelligent girl. She observed even the minutest change in her bodily expressions, her gaze moving swiftly from head to toe and back. Kusum held on to her aunt’s sari and asked, ‘Kaki! Do you believe that my actions contribute to Gunial’s worries?’ Sundargauri: ‘No, not your actions, but your thoughts and words do increase her anxieties.’ Kusum: ‘Why can’t Gunial say this to me?’ Sundargauri: ‘Your father has decreed that we should know your thoughts, and that we could mould them but not break them.’ Kusum: ‘Does that not prove that my thoughts are unsullied and free of follies?’ Sundargauri: ‘I am no scholar. But if you were to put your ideas into practice, you are certain to do wrong; you would be unhappy and cause pain to others. When English-educated men begin to run the household, women have to follow their commands, but that does not mean that our hearts do not experience any anxieties as a result.’ Kusum: ‘My father and Gunial have divergent views and have different points of anxiety. What am I to do?’ Sundargauri sat beside Kusum and put her arm around her shoulder. ‘Fathers look after sons, while mothers care for daughters. Your father has no objection if you were to follow Gunial.’ Kusum: ‘Then you should try and mould my ideas. Why do you want me to bend them to the point of breaking? If you force me to marry, what could I possibly do? A cow and a daughter have to go where her parents send her.’ Kusum’s heart welled up with emotions; her large eyes brimmed with tears and her heart pounded in her chest. She put her head on her aunt’s chest and wept softly.

Sundargauri sighed with dejection. ‘Daughter Kusum, we are still repenting the fate of our first daughter. Our hearts tremble when we think of the fate that awaits you. Someone as clever as you is certain to have many apprehensions. But all the problems and pain of married life are certainly less compared to what a spinster faces.’ Kusum looked up and wiped her tears. She had felt weak and powerless against the emotional issue of lessening her mother’s anxieties, but in a logical debate she used all her intellectual prowess. For a while both of them forgot about Gunial’s anxieties and joined the debate. Kusum: ‘Kaki, everyone knows about the suffering of married women. Who can claim to have seen the pain of a spinster?’ Sundargauri: ‘We have seen old, unmarried men, but among us there are no old spinsters. So how are we to know if they are happy or unhappy? We have to guess. Everyone except my crazy little Kusum can see their problems!’ Kusum: ‘If the stupid niece cannot see it, the wise aunt should make it apparent.’ Sundargauri: ‘Listen, not everything can be said to a child, but when a child plays the games of the adults, elders are forced to say what they ought not.’ Kusum: ‘So be it then.’ Sundargauri: ‘You would remain adamant and force me to be shameless.’ Kusum: ‘Yes. But do tell me.’ Sundargauri: ‘The shameless reign over their own kingdom.’ Kusum: ‘Yes, bhai, I agree! But say what you have to.’ Sundargauri: ‘I am not your brother! All right, listen if you must. Why do people get married?’ Kusum: ‘Because it is to their liking. It is a matter of like and dislike. What does it have to do with reasons? Some like sweet things, others like them pungent. Some like to be married while others like to remain unmarried.’ Sundargauri: ‘No, it is not so. Choice of food is a matter of taste. But like hunger for food, all animals have the hunger, the desire to experience married life. Even trees flower according to season and bear fruit, while all animals have the desire for marriage once they reach adulthood; it must happen sooner or later.’ Kusum: ‘But Miss Flora, our Queen’s tutor, is still unmarried. Can I say something more?’ Sundargauri: ‘Say it.’ Kusum: ‘No, it might hurt you and you will scold me.’ Sundargauri: ‘No, I will not take it amiss.’ Kusum: ‘Kaki, even you have not experienced married life, have you?’ Sundargauri did not allow her heartache to show. ‘If that Madam has not felt the desire for marriage hitherto, she will feel the need later; if not now she will get married some four years hence. And my daughter, what is in your Kaki’s heart is known to her and her God.’ Kusum: ‘That means even you must have felt some desires.’ Sundargauri did not know how to respond. She rubbed her eyes, looked around and said, ‘Wherever there is life and youth, God has created desire. Vidhatri, Lakshmi, Parvati are all forms of the Mother Goddess; even they experienced desire. Your Kaki is but a woman; how can she be an exception? Desire comes with youth and goes with it. But the wise and virtuous have to learn to control their desires.’ Kusum felt that she had secured a victory. She got up and laughed. ‘If Kaki could do this good deed, her niece would, too. If only for this small problem one has to marry and be pushed into a ditch, I flatly refuse to be married!’ Sundargauri caught her by her hand and made her sit. ‘Sit down. What are you feeling so triumphant about? Today we have become friends and I have shared something with you, but much remains to be said.’

Kusum: ‘All right, then say it. If you do not get tired of speaking, I am not going to tire of listening.’ Sundargauri: ‘You think it is easy to kill one’s desires. But nothing could be tougher. Great sages and even Lord Brahma have been defeated by their passions and they have stumbled.’ Kusum: ‘But you talk of men. Granted, it must be very difficult to control one’s passions. But then why are there so many pious and virtuous women in the world? I believe that women, more than men, have succeeded in controlling their desires. Therefore, the world remembers the follies of men, while among women the satis are remembered.’ Sundargauri was pleased with her niece’s intelligence. ‘Daughter! You have the god given gift of intelligence which makes up for your lack of experience. The fact that there are more pious and virtuous women could be interpreted in two ways. One meaning is the one that you just gave. There is another way of looking at it. One could say that most men are good and hence the few who err are noticed and remembered, while most women are bad and the few good ones are remembered as examples. The sayings of men and the books written by them consider women lascivious and men are said to succumb to their charms. The fact is that there is some element of truth in both these arguments.’ Kusum: ‘How so?’ Sundargauri: ‘God has put desire in both men and women. God has placed certain restrictions on the free play of desire among women, while others have been placed by society. For a woman, her honour and shame are her true ornaments which also limit her desires. A woman who is conscious of her honour tries very hard to control her passion; hence, it is important to cultivate a sense of honour. Similarly, a woman has a sense of pride and is conscious of her family honour; these also act to restrict her desires.’ Kusum: ‘Are women good because of these restrictions? Is a woman not self-willed?’

Sundargauri: ‘She is. She has self-control and there are these external restrictions. A woman may not possess bodily strength, but she has tremendous power whereby evil men are frightened by her look. Ravan abducted Sita Mata and kept her in Ashok Vatika for twelve long years. He would visit her, but he was frightened by the look of her eyes. The mighty Asura king had the courage to face Ram in a battle, but he could not lay a finger on Sita Mata. Sitaji’s courage was greater than that of Ram; so long as we women have her blessings, men can go and fish elsewhere. There are good and learned men, but they, too, have no control over their passions. In such instances a woman by her inner strength can remain steadfast and show the good path to the man who desires her. In situations where both man and woman are good but desire each other, a self-willed woman can ensure that their mutual desire is defeated. But if the woman were to seduce a man, no man has the power to resist her seductive charms. A man may not always succeed in seducing a woman, but a woman would invariably succeed in seducing a man. Women have such power, but when they do not exercise it, good men rightly abuse them.’ Kusum: ‘Therefore a man can marry many women, but a woman once widowed has to remain like you—I do not want to say more. There are such customs among us which show that when it comes to controlling desire, their own and those of the men, women hold the trump card.’ Sundargauri: ‘Very good! May you have a long life, daughter! Therefore we should not try to do all that the men do. It is for these reasons that the Shastras have placed certain limits on us.’ Kusum: ‘The reformers claim that men have strength while women are weak, and therefore men wrote the Shastras and placed restrictions on a woman’s pleasure, while no such restrictions were placed on men.’ Sundargauri: ‘No. These reformers do not understand the subtleties of this. When a child fights with an adult, the adult cannot break all limits like a child. The adult has to protect the child, if necessary, even give a slap or two but in a way that causes no permanent damage and bring the child under control. This is the duty of the adult. Between the weak and the powerful, between the mature and the immature, the powerful and the mature have responsibilities and also certain limits within which to act. When it comes to passion, women have greater self-control than men and are better able to control their desires. Hence, it is the duty of women to act within Shastric injunctions.’ Kusum: ‘If women are capable of such great self-control, why force me to marry?’ Sundargauri: ‘Not all women are equally self-possessed.’ Kusum: ‘Those who are not self-willed can marry and those who are self-possessed can remain unmarried.’ Sundargauri could not immediately think of an appropriate response. She considered the issue and said, ‘If a self-possessed woman were to remain unmarried, women who do not possess her powers may also decide not to marry because of some other desires. If one woman takes a different path, other women are likely to follow her; it could become a custom. Considering all these factors the Shastras erected some walls, and no water should breach those walls. Daughter, we do not control our destinies; our fates have been determined by men more experienced than us and the wise sages who have knowledge of the past, the future and the present; therein lies our good and the welfare of all. They determined my fate as a widow and they have decreed that you shall marry. Even Maharaj Maniraj cannot alter this fate, so do not have any hopes from your father.’ Kusum: ‘All right. All that is fine. But let us assume that I remain unmarried like so many Jain sadhvis, ascetics and these English madams. How will that cause any harm to anyone?’ Sundargauri: ‘You assume that you have the power and the will to control your passions, but you should not assume that you always will.’ Kusum: ‘What else?’ Sundargauri: ‘Men are worried about their wealth while we women have to protect both our wealth and our bodies. This fear stalks us at every step when we are among people and when we are alone.’ Kusum: ‘What else?’

Sundargauri: ‘God has so created our bodies that countless errors of men go unnoticed, while a single mistake by a woman is announced through her body. She has only two choices then: either kill the foetus or be declared outside the pale of caste, family and honour. Kusum! A widow who has experienced life as a married woman can blame her fate and learn to control her desires. How is a young, unmarried girl, who has never experienced desire, to control her passions and remain free of them?’ Kusum: ‘What else?’ Sundargauri: ‘At present you live under the protection of very powerful and resourceful parents. You have not been exposed to the elements of nature; you have known no hardships. But you will not be able to earn your keep. No one is free from old age, illness and death. One cannot rely forever on the wealth accumulated by one’s parents. The status that your parents have earned is not permanent. When they are no longer alive, you will be alone and without any support; there will be no one to look after you and care for you. You will remember my caution and weep, but there will be no one that you can call your own who will come and wipe your tears.’ Kusum: ‘What else?’ Sundargauri: ‘A widow can either go to her brother or to her brother- in-law for support. My brother and sister-in-law despised me and threw me out of their house, hungry and thirsty. But since I was the widow of your father’s brother, your mother took pity on me. If Sundar is alive, it is only because of Gunasundari. Widows like me find a place to live and are fed for a variety of reasons: the fear of the king or that of society, the goodness of the departed men, sometimes out of true family feelings or just out of pity, widows find a shelter. In some cases the brother-in-law or sister-in-law takes her in, while those who are thrown out by their in-laws are taken in by their brothers. But Kusum, even a brother would find an unmarried sister burdensome! A brother would say that she did not marry when marriage was possible, and now she weighs on me like so many bricks! Do you know that a woman born to poor parents is abused if she delays her going to the in-laws’ house? Which brother is going to like a sister who is going to stay with him for life? If you had a brother and if you were to come back from your in-laws’ for a few days, he would welcome you, but no brother would bear your burden for life; he would dislike the very sight of your face. If you were to remain unmarried, you would forsake the comfort that even a widow like me has.’ Kusum: ‘What else?’ Sundargauri: ‘Why do you keep asking what else? I have said so much. Now you must respond. I keep on barking like a dog, and you do not even care to respond!’ Kusum: ‘Kaki, please do not be angry. You have spoken from experience. I will think about this carefully and find a way out.’ Sundargauri: ‘What way are you going to find? If you do not agree when we try to plead with you and please you, we shall simply tie up your hands and legs and get you married!’ Kusum: ‘You can tie me up and even twist my neck. But there can be no immediate response when the matter needs due thought and consideration.’ Sundargauri: ‘Then do not respond. Kumud was a mild girl; she gave your mother grief by her death. You will remain unmarried and trouble your mother. I know this. When your mother was young her mother-in-law and sister-in-law gave her no respite; why would she be spared by her daughters now?’ Kusum: ‘Kaki, do not say that. I have not said that I will not obey Gunial. You are free to shape and mould my thoughts. And you should try to do that if you can. If you decide to act against my wishes, I will still believe that you are my well-wisher, you have experienced the world and that your actions are in my interest. But I cannot be expected to have any control over my thoughts.’ Just then they heard some footsteps. They got up and walked towards the approaching footsteps.
chapters.summary: Kusum, rejecting marriage and widowhood after her sister's tragedy, fiercely debates Sundargauri about her future, asserting her independent thoughts amidst family pressure.

chapters.title: Flora and Kusum
paragraphs: Flora and Kusum Political policy, when applied by men who are liberal and farsighted, leads to the strengthening of relations between political leaders of different states. If two kings have friendly relations they find ways of coming closer to strengthen these mutually beneficial ties; if they are enemies they seek proximity to find each other’s weaknesses. During the reign of Emperor Akbar, he had friendly relations with Rajput kings and many Rajput women joined the imperial zenana. In the present period the English do not follow this policy. There are many reasons for this. But those kings, or their officials who form relations of inter-dining with the English, derive benefits of this closeness. The Rajputs are free, according to both Shastras and custom, to have social relations within the four varnas and also outside of them. This arrangement has been made to enable such social intercourse as is necessary for the benefit of political policy. The English open up their hearts during dinner table conversations; they are rarely so open on other occasions. Their religious leaders and their women also create possibilities of social closeness, which is otherwise not possible. Mallaraj had therefore advised Maniraj that he should have an Englishwoman as a companion for queen Kamlavati. Maniraj, after he assumed the throne, realised the usefulness of his father’s advice. Shastras place no prohibition on the kshatriyas with regard to inter-dining just as the brahmins are free to acquire knowledge from any source. Kshatriyas are like brahmins when it concerns the acquisition of political knowledge and statecraft. At the present time political education and statecraft are equated with

English education. As a source of knowledge English has a position of primacy and reverence in our palaces. These days many debauched and evil practices are found among our princes and palace officials which are sought to be legitimised and sanctioned by customs. These practices hamper the growth and functioning of native states. Mallaraj had formulated a maxim, that customs are contingent upon time. He had taken measures to ensure that this maxim was followed in his palace and by his officials and that no customs contrary to this maxim were allowed to take root in his court. This was done to ensure that conservative and retrograde practices do not impede statecraft. For this reason the palace of Ratnanagari had instituted Sanskrit learning. Following the same logic Maniraj decided to open the doors to English education. Vidya Chatura welcomed the proposal. The widow of Colonel Brave was approached to send a high-born, virtuous and learned tutor from England. She recommended Miss Flora, who was about twenty-five years of age. For the past one year or so, Miss Flora had been the queen’s tutor. Honouring her husband’s wishes, the queen had enthusiastically participated in this project, willingly abdicating her higher status to adopt the role of a student. Gunasundari, deep in grief after Kumud’s death, had been negligent about nurturing Kusum’s intellectual development. On her frequent visits to Gunasundari, Kamlavati observed this and, with her husband’s consent, sent Flora to Kusum. The Englishwoman was accomplished in various arts, while Kusum was eager to learn them. Flora was keen to learn about native customs, while Kusum was enamoured of the polite ways of English women. Flora found she had much to learn from the wisdom and household skills of native women, while Kusum was eager to know about English social customs and their suitability or incongruity with native life. Their mutual attraction made their meetings joyous for both. Flora was on her way to Kusum’s sitting room. She was in the staircase when from a window she saw Kusum approaching her. She waited for Kusum. They held each other by the hand and started talking. They spoke in Gujarati. Flora had begun to speak some Gujarati and her hesitation and mistakes became a cause for laughter.

Kusum: ‘Behn, not ben!’ Flora: ‘Correct. The orthography and speech in your language are different. Kusum behn—is that right?’ Kusum: ‘Correct, Flora behn! Our names mean the same thing.’ Flora: ‘Yes! Yes, you are Kusum and I, too, am a Kusum. You are a miss and even I am one.’ They came up to the sitting room and sat on a couch. Kusum gave Flora a Chinese fan. Fanning herself with it, Flora asked, ‘What is this called?’ ‘Vinzano.’ ‘Who was with you just now?’ ‘My aunt Sundar. Shall I call her?’ ‘Of course, with pleasure.’ Kusum invited Sundargauri to join them. They sat down. Flora said, ‘Please come. Are you well?’ Sundargauri: ‘Yes. Kusum is all praise for you.’ Flora: ‘She is affectionate towards me.’ Sundargauri: ‘Kusum, Madam Sahib speaks softly like Kumud.’ Kusum: ‘Yes. But she likes to be called Flora behn and not Madam Sahib. Flora means a flower. Kusum also means the same and both of us are unmarried.’ Sundargauri: ‘Flora behn, how long will you remain unmarried? Kusum will have to get married soon.’ Flora: ‘Sundar Kaki, we are still young; you are our elder. Those who wish to marry may do so; those who do not may not. It all depends on one’s preference. Kusum ben—behn—may marry if she wants. I may not marry if I so please.’ Sundargauri: ‘Please advise her to get married. Her mother is very worried.’ Flora: ‘She will marry when her education is complete and when she is in love.’

Kusum: ‘Kaki, you have asked the wrong person for help! Their customs and thoughts are different from ours; you will not succeed with her. But let us satisfy your curiosity. Flora behn, among your people, how long do women’s minds stay away from thoughts of love?’ Flora: ‘Love is in the hands of God.’ Kusum: ‘But can a woman remain unmarried and pure if she so desires?’ Flora: ‘Of course, she can. Those who have will and fear God can; God helps all those people.’ Sundargauri: ‘In England, women like you can work. That is not the custom among us.’ Flora: ‘Yes, that a fact.⟨fn:198⟩ But Pradhanji is a wealthy man. We consider it sinful to marry our daughters by force and against their will. Kusum behn is not yet of marriageable age according to our custom.’ Sundargauri: ‘A father’s wealth is useless for a daughter. Moreover, getting a daughter married is not sinful, not getting her married is. There is no merit higher than the gift of a daughter for parents. The gift of a daughter in marriage is not an act of coercion. It actually secures her future; it is for her own good. Parents who desire their children’s welfare cannot be said to act in a coercive manner.’ Flora did not comprehend this argument. Kusum, of course, did and hence tried to change the subject. ‘Kaki, if you do not mind, we will begin my lesson now. But they will be in English, which would be a problem for you.’ ‘You study, and I will sit here and listen to you speak English.’ The two young women began reading a chapter from an English book. There was a sentence in it: ‘He continued to be a lover, though they were married at least five years back.’⟨fn:199⟩ Kusum could not comprehend this. Flora explained it to her in English. ‘So long as they are not married, a man has a different kind of attraction for a woman. That love has novelty. After marriage the novelty vanishes and gradually, even the attraction decreases. That is the usual pattern. Any deviation from this norm is novel.’ Kusum: ‘There was a song in a Parsi drama which had a similar meaning. It is easy to fall in love, difficult to sustain it.’ Flora: ‘Exactly.’ Kusum: ‘Even those who marry for love and of their own choice, the attraction proves short-lived, is it?’ Flora: ‘Yes.’ Kusum: ‘What is the nature of love after marriage?’ Flora: ‘After marriage, a husband and wife become truly aware of each other’s qualities and follies. If they manage to share qualities they become friends; the rest pass their days in happiness or sorrow or with dissatisfaction. Some even quarrel.’ Kusum: ‘In case of a quarrel, women must suffer? Flora: ‘Of course.’ Kusum: ‘Our customs differ to begin with, but eventually it ends up more or less similarly.’ Flora: ‘That may be. But this is a fact.’ Kusum: ‘Man remains a “lover” until marriage, after which he becomes a master.’ Flora: ‘Exactly.’ Kusum: ‘Is this the key to understanding Lord Tennyson’s poem “Princess?”’ Flora: ‘Have you read that poem?’ Kusum: ‘My sister was engaged to Sarasvatichandra, who had read out parts of it to my sister. I was present when he recited it.’ Sundargauri was startled to hear Sarasvatichandra’s name being mentioned in their English conversation. She did not understand anything else, but made her own conjecture. Flora: ‘Have you read anything else by Tennyson?’

Kusum: ‘I have, but understood it only partially. Sometimes my father explains, sometimes my mother does, and at times I try and make sense of it myself. But some things remain beyond my comprehension. I would be grateful if you could explain it to me when you have some time.’ Flora: ‘It would give me immense joy. If you remember any part by heart, do recite it.’ Kusum: ‘I will recite some lines from In Memoriam.’ My love has talk’d with rocks and trees; He finds on misty mountain-ground His own vast shadow glory-crown’d; He sees himself in all he sees. Two partners of a married life— I look’d on these and thought of thee In vastness and in mystery, And of my spirit as of a wife. These two—they dwelt with eye on eye, Their hearts of old have beat in tune, Their meetings made December June, Their every parting was to die. Their love has never past away; The days she never can forget Are earnest that he loves her yet, Whate’er the faithless people say. Her life is lone, he sits apart, He loves her yet, she will not weep, Tho’ rapt in matters dark and deep He seems to slight her simple heart. He thrids the labyrinth of the mind, He reads the secret of the star, He seems so near and yet so far, He looks so cold: she thinks him kind. She keeps the gift of years before A wither’d violet is her bliss;

She knows not what his greatness is, For that, for all, she loves him more. For him she plays, to him she sings Of early faith and plighted vows; She knows but matters of the house, And he, he knows a thousand things. Her faith is fixt and cannot move, She darkly feels him great and wise, She dwells on him with faithful eyes, ‘I cannot understand: I love.’ Flora: ‘Thank you, my sweet Kusum. I will teach you whatever you want; not just that I would teach even other things to one as beautiful as you. Will you learn?’ Kusum: ‘I will learn everything that you teach me.’ Flora: ‘But some of those may still have not found a place in Hindu customs.’ Kusum: ‘That only my parents can answer. I must obey them, and I have total faith in the goodness of their commands.’ At this point a man entered with Vidya Chatura’s ‘card’ and sought their permission to join them. Vidya Chatura entered with Flora’s consent. They all stood up to greet him and began their conversation in Gujarati. Flora: ‘Please come in, Mr. Pradhanji. We were discussing Kusum’s education.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘And what is the outcome?’ Flora: ‘Her intellect has matured. It will be a privilege to teach so very precocious a pupil, Mr. Pradhanji. I shall also have to learn some things from her. My sweet Kusum! Will you teach me how to translate the word “precocity” into your vernacular?’ Kusum looked down bashfully. Flora: ‘See how very “bashful” and shy she has become in her father’s presence!’ Flora hugged Kusum and kissed her hand in delight. Sundargauri was shocked, but Flora did not notice.

Flora: ‘Mr. Pradhanji! What if I teach your sweet child some of our accomplishments? Say, introduce her to the piano, teach her some singing, some painting and so on? Just turn her into an artist and make her life sweeter?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Does Kusum like these things?’ Flora: ‘She has no likes or dislikes. She leaves all to her father with the boundless confidence of a child.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Well, considering her social surroundings, it is not possible to say that these otherwise good things will also prove to be blessings for her.’ Flora: ‘How?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Perhaps you know that Kusum is bound to marry, and we do not know if her unknown husband and his people will appreciate these things.’ Flora: ‘Why should Kusum be bound to marry? She has a mind to remain single as I am. You mean, you will be cruel to her and force her—such a sweet bird—into marriage? No, no, my good sir, I swear, you shan’t do anything of that kind!’ Vidya Chatura laughed and said, ‘My good lady, you first get your point solved by her and her mother, and then we shall see.’⟨fn:200⟩ They all went down. Flora got into her carriage and went home. Vidya Chatura went for his bath. As soon as he had left the room, Sundargauri caught Kusum’s hand and held it away from her body. ‘That wretch! She touched her lips to your hand. She defiled your hand! Wash it off! Who knows what has not passed through her lips? Today she defiled your hand; tomorrow she will defile your mouth and eventually her preaching will convert your heart!’ Kusum, preoccupied with other thoughts, gave no response and walked away murmuring something to herself with a finger on her lips, paying no heed to her aunt. She remembered some Sanskrit verses told to Gunasundari by an ascetic.

As an enfeebled elephant falls into mire, one attached to son, friend and wife sinks as well.⟨fn:201⟩ ‘A married woman falls into a well; so does a spinster. She has no relatives of her own; even such hopes are futile. I now understand what the swami told Gunial. A kinsman gives no solace or happiness,’ Kusum mused aloud. I know what is deemed to be the joy of family is an illusion, false knowledge. This happiness is like one’s own shadow that gives no protection against summer heat.⟨fn:202⟩ ‘Is there no escaping marriage?’ Kusum asked with her index finger on her lips. ‘It was only yesterday that I heard that the Shastras consider any attachment to be a source of pain!’ She placed a hand over her heart and closed her eyes. One forms relationships which please the mind, but the same become shards of sorrow in one’s heart.⟨fn:203⟩ Kusum opened her eyes, kept her hands on her waist and spoke as if addressing Kumud. ‘Behn! You have become happy in death. Swamiji counsels mother; she listens to him; father already knows all this, and still it makes no difference to Kusum! She must fall into a well even though she has a lamp in her hand! Swamiji has rightly said, “One should be alone in the world, like a woman’s bracelet.” If I were to fall at his feet and ask for what my heart desires, would it be denied to me? Swamiji has shown a path of happiness, a path that I like. O’ forest-dwelling deer! May you be joyous. O’ forest! Every branch of every tree gives health. May no harm come to you. O’ sand-filled river bank! May you flow. O’ rocks! Be happy. As I emerge with great effort from this dark night, my mind now seeks your proximity.⟨fn:204⟩

‘If one could listen to and read such wisdom day and night, if one could live in a place as verdant as this, what more could one want? Will father not fulfill this desire of mine? But a cow and a daughter have to go where they are led. Was I born only to be pushed into this deep well?’ As Kusum walked towards her room, she unmindfully hit her head against the door and yet remained quite oblivious of it. She just stood there and spoke as if she had just emerged out of deep sleep. ‘Yes! He can try as much as he wants, but it will all be in vain! Pitaji can do whatever he likes, but to get me married he has to first find a suitable husband! They are not going to be able to find Sarasvatichandra, and there is no other suitable match! Pitaji may not care about me. But would God, the saviour of the helpless, also not care?’ This new hope enthused Kusum. She felt calmer. She opened the door, entered the room and closed the door behind her. Sundargauri was right behind her and had heard her soliloquy. She beat her chest and cried, ‘Girl, this is the limit! Now you won’t even pay heed to your father!’
chapters.summary: Flora and Kusum find common ground discussing love, marriage, and poetry, forming a close bond as Kusum navigates her own future and unspoken desires.

chapters.title: Saubhagya Devi's Auspicious Death
paragraphs: Saubhagya Devi’s Auspicious Death The problems of a household are as complex as that of a state. Sundargauri says that if Kusum had not been educated, she would never have aspired to remain unmarried! Traditional Hindu social wisdom says a girl should not be left unmarried. The new wisdom says that our children, even when young, are individuals; and even the thought of marriage, by force or otherwise, before they attain the age of consent is a sin. Kusum has ascetic aspirations. For Hindu women the life of an ascetic is possible only after widowhood! If she is allowed her way, given our country and our customs, she will face lifelong misery. Should one consider what is just, or what possible outcome an action might have? On one hand there is the grave injustice of robbing a daughter of her independence; on the other hand are the fearsome possibilities determined by Hindu social customs for a spinster! Like a nut-cracker, wisdom new and old crushes me! One afternoon, post-lunch, Vidya Chatura slumped into an easy chair with these troubling thoughts crowding his mind, and dozed off. When he woke up, he saw Gunasundari seated in front of him. She had with her some letters delivered by that day’s post. She was weeping, but tried to compose herself as her husband woke up. She handed him the bunch of letters and said, ‘Saubhagya Devi has gone to heaven.’ ‘What! What happened?’ Vidya Chatura was shocked. He took the letters from her, his face both eager and sad. ‘The son turned out to be depraved and died. Kumud also died, and only because of Pramaddhan. Surrounded by pain, grief and suffering from every direction, Devi’s soft, affectionate heart gave up! Buddhidhan is now faced with every conceivable loss. They made such a virtuous and affectionate pair; it is now broken. It is God’s will. Our grief cannot be compared with his. God has done something for them—before Devi died, she gave birth to a premature child, a boy. Hopes of his survival hang on a thread,’ said Gunasundari. Vidya Chatura put the letters on a table and sank into the chair; tears filled his eyes. ‘Gunial, this is indeed very sad. One can overcome such a wound when one is young, but as one gets older the wound festers. As husband and wife grow older they desire togetherness and mutual support. Maharaj Mallaraj’s last illness became somewhat bearable only because of Mena Rani’s untiring service. Bhavabhuti has said: Happy is that fortunate man who, somehow, obtains that one thing which is the same in happiness or misery, which adapts itself to all conditions, where the heart finds its solace, the flavour of which is unaffected by old age, and which matures, as the time removes the veil, into permanent deep affection.⟨fn:205⟩ ‘Oh God! This is the worst form of suffering.’ Gunasundari: ‘A man thinks only of another man’s pain, but both walls do not collapse together. Saubhagya Devi died an auspicious death; she did not have to see widowhood. The only unfortunate part has been her children. My dear, I, too, desire a death like her. You would be able to forget me in your affairs of the state. Women do not have that opportunity; Mena Rani’s example bears testimony to it.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘In our country it is possible to make a distinction like  that. Our customs make such generalisation about all men possible.’ Gunasundari: ‘If I contextualise my statement, it would be a betrayal of our love. I firmly believe that if we were born in Europe and were husband and wife, I would have said the same thing.’

Vidya Chatura softened. ‘I know that you trust me and have compassion for me. But our Shastras say that man and woman love each other to realise the fullness of their souls, and your desire to depart before me is because of this.’ Gunasundari: ‘So far I have never lost an argument with you, but today I have. Death is inevitable, my Chatura! But a life that is lived for others should be longer. How useful are the lives of us women as compared to the usefulness of your lives?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Mountains are great, but they become useful only when they are covered with fertile earth. A large mountain in the middle of the sea is useful only for the destruction of ships.’ Gunasundari: ‘I am defeated twice already! Oh my Chatura, I am unhappy. If I am led astray by my selfishness, I would become the instrument of pain for you. But I ask God to grant me a death like Saubhagya Devi. No other thought enters my heart.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘What if you stop thinking about it and just leave it to God?’ Gunasundari: ‘But the thought does not leave me. Kumud has departed. It is up to you to decide about Kusum. If I am not alive I won’t have to think about it. This worldly life is too full of suffering.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Let’s talk about something else. Are all these letters about the same thing? Is there any other news?’ Gunasundari: ‘There is a letter from Alak Kishori and another from Vanleela, which I have read. The others are written by men which I have not opened.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Those two contain the same news!’ Gunasundari: ‘Alak Kishori has sought Kusum’s hand in marriage for her father. Vanleela’s letter also contains the same proposal.’ Vidya Chatura was stunned. ‘Kusum, to marry Buddhidhan!’ Gunasundari spoke with composure, ‘We found Sarasvatichandra, who is now gone. Our daughter is without a match. We have no option but to accept Buddhidhanbhai, even though he is older. There is no other person of our caste who is suitable.’

Vidya Chatura: ‘Gunial, what are you saying? You rejected a slightly elderly match for Dukhba’s daughter, and you suggest that we should accept a much older man for Kusum!’ Gunasundari: ‘That is true. But Kumud’s death has stunned my mind. I am worried about Kusum, which also does not allow me to think straight. But to me this match seems feasible.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘We gave Kumud to Pramaddhan in haste, and we repented in hindsight. That was a mismatch only in terms of their learning. This is a mismatch also in age!’ Gunasundari: ‘Alak’s letter is heart-wrenching; she has true affection for Kumud. She promises that Buddhidhan would love Kusum as much as he loved Saubhagya Devi, that Kusum would be very happy and that this would be her way of repenting for the injustice done to Kumud.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘She may say anything.’ Gunasundari: ‘Vanleela writes that the family has turned upside down; for Buddhidhanbhai the shock of Kumud’s death is much greater than his grief over Saubhagya Devi’s death. This is the only way to bring the family out of grief. This marriage would console many wounded hearts.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘It is preferable that Kusum remain unmarried. The interest of the daughter has to be primary while fixing her marriage.’ Gunasundari: ‘I fail to understand you. Is it in Kusum’s interest to remain unmarried? Either the customs of the world have changed direction, or grief has stunned our minds.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Gunial, even I feel that today both of us have gone a bit crazy!’ Gunasundari: ‘At least read these letters.’ Vidya Chatura threw them on the table. ‘I do not want to read those letters. I do not want to think about it till we have definite information about Sarasvatichandra.’ Gunasundari: ‘That is true. But we should not lose both! No one is going to wait for us forever. We should not be placed in a position where we go pleading to them after having shunned such an affectionate proposal.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘All right. We shall see.’ The door was ajar. Vidya Chatura sensed that Kusum was behind the door and had heard their conversation. He called her, ‘Kusum!’ She moved away from the door in a flash, but before disappearing she made her presence known to her parents. This was the first ever instance that Kusum had not responded to her parent’s command. Her eyes had turned red with anger, tears of helplessness streaked her face. Gunasundari went to the door and called out to Kusum two or three times. And yet, she neither responded nor showed herself. Gunasundari lost her natural calm. She could not bear the fact that her daughter had disobeyed the father. Grief and anger combined to darken her mood. Vidya Chatura prevented her from going to their daughter’s room. ‘Gunial, you are intent upon doing something that is neither within your purview, nor Kusum’s.’ Gunasundari stopped, turned around and meekly said, ‘It is not right to give so much leeway to a daughter.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘A mind cannot be coerced into submission. Parents, who instead of moulding their children coerce them, commit the sin of plunging their children into slavery.’ Gunasundari: ‘My mind is stunned. If you say so, it must be right. I have always acted as per your will, and I will do so even today. But henceforth, you take full responsibility of Kusum’s ideas and her experiments and free me of this burden; otherwise leave everything to me and my woman’s way of thinking and be freed of this burden. But please stop shoving your manly ideas into a woman’s head. If one fills up a tunnel with dynamite, the tunnel itself is destroyed. That is what is about to happen to my head. I fall at your feet and ask this of you.’ Choking on her words, Gunasundari fell into a chair. ‘A man who refuses to coerce and force his daughter, is he now to give a command to a wife as dear as you? Gunial, my love! I understand your perplexity and I free you from this responsibility. I will bear the burden. But you would certainly not have any objection to bearing witness to my endeavours!’ Vidya Chatura walked up to Gunasundari, held her hand and helped her rise. She seemed composed and relieved. She stood up and said, ‘My dear Chatura, you are the embodiment of my vow. Your effort is my effort; this secures our unity, our oneness. If I were to shun the oneness and togetherness that you give me, the sun will have to rise in the west! Until today I have believed that a woman must follow her husband in happiness and in sorrow; my conduct has been in accordance with this belief. In childhood I did not give primacy to my parents over your wish; and at this stage of my life I am not going to consider our daughter primary. God will look after her, and you will look after me.
chapters.summary: Vidya Chatura and Gunasundari grapple with Saubhagya Devi's death and unexpected marriage proposals for Kusum, leading to a tense, overheard family discussion.

chapters.title: Kusum's Cloister
paragraphs: Kusum’s Cloister Shocked by her parents’ talk, Kusum had shut herself in her room. She stood at a window which opened out towards the garden. She was petrified by what she had just heard. The heat of her emotions had dried her tears, which still glistened on her cheeks. The green vistas of Saundarya Udyan before her gave a new tinge to the flaming red of her eyes. The play of light on the trees soothed her fraught mind. Gradually she calmed herself and began to consider the issue from other vantage points. Neither Pitaji nor Gunial are to be blamed. They are worried and perturbed because they have my welfare in their hearts. If they had any inkling about the state of my mind they would be less worried, and I would also be able to have my way. The verdant garden with its shades of green and play of light and shadow has reduced my agitation. Flora says that God manifests Himself in nature and gives us joy and bliss. This is an example of that. Mirabai sang: Mira is devoted to you, O’ Lord, you know all. The image of the Lord that she spoke of must be this. God manifests himself through idols, as also through trees and the rays of the sun. Today I have realised the true nature of that manifest God! Oh my God! You saved Mirabai. Now you must save me! Will you not save me? I too say that, ‘Kusum is devoted to your image! Oh Lord, you know the state of my heart.’

She continued to look out of the window for a while longer. Finally she sat down with her hands in her lap and thought, Pitaji is opposed to my marriage with Buddhidhan, while Gunial is in favour of it. I had heaved a sigh of relief knowing that Sarasvatichandra cannot be traced. From where has this new trouble come? I do not want either! God willing, Gunial will fail in this plan and Sarasvatichandra will not be traced; then I can have my way. I will flatly refuse this proposal for Buddhidhan; which means that Gunial will fail and Pitaji’s view will prevail. If father prevails in this instance, eventually I will have my way! Kusum opened the door and looked around. Her parents were not to be seen. Kusum entered their room. The letters were on the table. ‘Is it a theft to read letters concerning me which are addressed to Pitaji?’ she mused aloud. ‘Even Kumud behn used to read, without anyone’s knowledge, Sarasvatichandra’s letters to father.’ Narbheram had written to Vidya Chatura, pleading for Kusum’s hand for Buddhidhan with a lot of pathetic humility. He had also said that Buddhidhan was not in favour of his remarriage, but everyone including the Maharana had made up their mind. Kusum saw a glimmer of hope. She read Buddhidhan’s letter to her father. Dear Vidya Chaturaji, I have lost two of the finest gems of my family. That stone drowned and dragged the gems along. My daughter and my assistant, moved by their love for me, aspire to get me remarried. You must have seen their letters, which were written against my wish. I could not hold their hands to prevent them from writing, hence the letters. No such desire of theirs can be fulfilled, and that is my promise to you. When Kumud Sundari left my house, I lost everything I had. My depraved son died, which was just punishment for his crimes. I have not grieved for him even for a moment. I have rejoiced at his death, and my joy equals the joy experienced by others at the time of a son’s birth. My home and my life have been purified by that death. Kumud Sundari’s mother-in-law died grieving for her. Your love for Gunasundari would allow you to understand my love for my wife. She was my companion in my years of hardship as also during my years of wealth and prestige. She was a partner. I am proud to have been a husband to a woman like her. She left us because the merit that I had accrued must have been exhausted. I have no desire to begin conjugal life with someone else. I must shun passions, as also a new wife. This is not a fleeting, temporary sense of renunciation that one has at the death of a near one. I am a poor widow’s son who became the Minister of Suvarnapur. Kumud Sundari was a reincarnation of both Lakshmi and Sarasvati; her presence sanctified my house. Her virtuous mother-in-law purified my soul and made it pious. God, who placed me amidst such great souls, has now desired otherwise and there must be a reason for His will. I am unable to snap all ties with my king, Maharana Bhupsinh. There are certain large tasks that need to be completed in the administration of the state. Once they are accomplished, I am going to request him to allow me to go and live in Kashi and make Narbheram his new minister. Renunciation is not seen as desirable for our age. Moreover, I have no right to renunciation without acquiring adequate knowledge. Kashi would give me the opportunity to be with many great souls; I am tempted by that prospect. Narbheram believes that I should forsake that opportunity and remarry. He is a poor soul; he does not understand my innermost desires and makes futile attempts. Devi gave birth to a son before she died. If he lives, his sister shall raise him. If not, I shall not grieve over him. A son that I raised turned out to be depraved and evil; he died. It is difficult to predict if this premature boy will turn out to be a worthy son or not. His mother’s life was fulfilled in every sense. She has gone to heaven; her soul is immortal. To grieve for her is a sign of futile attachment. I experience neither attachment nor grief. Even from a pragmatic point of view, the desire for remarriage at my age seems foolish. This should be apparent to one who has had such wide experience of the world which has enabled him to reach the position of a minister. If I were to believe that Narbheram’s insistence has any validity, it would prove that I am unfit to be a minister and also that I have a very low level of intelligence since I lack the discernment and judgement to learn from the experiences that this high position allows one.

Those who act out of an overwhelming desire for a son are lowly beings. Such desires are unbecoming of a man of my age and experience. A sense of justice would show that it would be sinful to place the life of another man’s young daughter in jeopardy by gifting her certain widowhood. The girl’s father as well as the elderly man who marries her share equally in this sin. I have examined this issue from many points of view and I have reasoned. Not for a moment have I imagined that this act is possible. It is a path of certain folly. Narbheram’s affection for me makes him blind to this. I blessed Chiranjeevi Kusum Sundari with all my heart that she finds a learned, virtuous, handsome, wealthy and young man for a husband. My action cannot be contrary to my blessing. Kumud Sundari’s younger sister is a daughter to me. Kusum read this letter and felt her life return! All her despondency vanished; her eyes shone bright. She hurried back to her room, placed a hand over her racing heart and said aloud, ‘Thank God! The world can go fishing. God heard my prayers! Buddhidhanbhai, may all good things happen to you! Your letter is instructive even for me. I have already understood what a person of your age and experience holds up as truth. Even Swamiji’s teaching bears me out. Flora behn and I are fellow travelers. Sarasvatichandra also thinks alike; he was my first teacher. I now need to win over Gunial and Kaki. I need not worry about father as Sarasvatichandra will not be traced. ‘What are the various objections that Kaki has? First, she claims it is difficult to control one’s passions; second is the Shastric injunction that a woman must marry. Third, that our bodies are so made that our errors are known to all; fourth, that a spinster has no house or money of her own; she is despised by all and must live in constant fear of violation of her body. ‘If I were to become an ascetic, all these problems could be taken care of. Food is free; one stays among women, which acts as a protection from men and the question of being seduced or violated by men does not arise. There are so many groups of ascetic women—is that without the sanction of the Shastras? The major hardship is that one will have to wear coarse garments like them and eat coarse grains like barley and bajra. Nothing can be done about the first. But from tomorrow I will train myself to wear coarse clothes and eat coarser grains. The gardener’s wife has coarse garments and also barley and bajra grains. It is not going to violate any caste norms. I will cook my own meals so the question of defilement would not arise. ‘But to both Kaki and Gunial I will say that who knows what kind of a husband I will get; if he is a poor man, I will have to wear coarse garments and eat barley and bajra. One cannot always expect that the husband would turn out good. I will have to live out my fate. ‘Yes. That is what I will tell them. This will cut both ways. Moreover, even in Flora’s society it is found that initially a man is sweet, but eventually tastes bitter. These things happen among us as well. What would I do if that were to happen? It is best to prepare oneself for any eventuality. Sanskrit learning and experiential knowledge are of equal value to a woman!’ Suddenly, thinking a different thought, Kusum said, ‘Sanskrit has a lot of sringar, which is never explained to a girl. She has to wait for her husband to explain it to her. Even arguments about renunciation are filled with experiences of married life, which can be understood only with experience. ‘Sringar and renunciation both need to be experienced. One cannot grasp the sringar of Sanskrit literature, and comprehending it from the experiences of others is different. One always fails to understand statements of experiential wisdom, like pebbles rattling in an empty vessel. One cannot even understand the noise of these pebbles without prior experience. ‘Flora explained to me a common British experience: a lover does not remain a lover after marriage; he becomes a master. When I understood that, I also understood the meaning of our Sanskrit wisdom: In the first phase our two bodies came together as one. Later, you became a lover and I, your dejected beloved. Now you are my master and I am your wife. What more? Life hard as a vajra does not leave my body, and I bear the burden that is my destiny.⟨fn:206⟩ ‘I always knew this in my heart. Man and woman no longer form one body; they are two—the lover and his beloved—but eventually they become master and servant! Our people seem to have forgotten this. I understood it only when Flora shared with me their experience. Once the interest is served, even a healer becomes an enemy. We have a song which says that woman, who was once called sweet as sugar, becomes a servant.⟨fn:207⟩ ‘Sarasvatichandra realised that this is the fate of all marriages. I will take the same path. Gunial unnecessarily invites suffering. She can see only one side, and who knows what that is! I must put my resolve into practice and get accustomed to wearing coarse garments and eating coarse grains. I should also learn to do all my work myself as if I am a forest dweller without any servants. People will like it for their own reasons, and I will enjoy it for my own. ‘Himachal and Menaka also gave many arguments, but Parvati remained steadfast to her resolve. Eventually everyone had to agree with her. The poet said: Though she gave her daughter this advice, the wish was firm, and Mena could not change her determination. Who can oppose a mind unwavering in its pressure towards something desired, or water on its way to low ground?⟨fn:208⟩ ‘My Gunial is like Mena. I desire penance like Parvati. The elders consider my wish desirable. I shall also succeed like Parvati. Therefore, one should put one’s resolve into practice.’ There was a knock on her door, bringing Kusum’s soliloquy to an abrupt end.
chapters.summary: Kusum, shocked by marriage talks, finds solace and resolve in a letter, leading her to contemplate a path of renunciation and prepare for a life.

chapters.title: Malla Mahabhavan or the Political Observatory of Ratnanagari and the Discourse on Mahabharata
paragraphs: Malla Mahabhavan or the Political Observatory of Ratnanagari and the Discourse on Mahabharata The speech of ordinary sages follows sense; while sense attaches itself to the utterances of the primeval sages.⟨fn:209⟩ The assembly organised for the reception of Rana Khachar had generated a lively debate. It had also raised many issues for which Maniraj sought resolution. He felt enthused when he thought of his father’s foresight, restraint and his statecraft. But the decline of other native states filled him with despondency. The preponderance of depraved officers in the English bureaucracy enraged him. Their stupidity and inebriation filled him with native pride. But similar depravity among native rulers made him sad; their idiocy, unaccountability and disorderly rule made him weep. He had experienced the noble aspects of British officials, which for him offered a ray of hope. British statecraft perturbed him, and yet it was also the source of hope. Maniraj spent four–five days debating with himself. One day at noon, swaying between hope and despondency, this young ruler paced restlessly inside Kurukshetra Bhavan, one of the many halls of the Malla Mahabhavan. It was the late Maharaj Mallaraj who had conceived of the Malla Mahabhavan. These days many native states have departments like ‘building’ and ‘public works’ which are created after the English pattern. These departments are created for the beautification of the state and the city and to use funds for public works. At one time Vidya Chatura held the opinion that the English followed these twin goals and that they gave primacy to the utility of these facilities while beauty and aesthetics were secondary to them. The native states, on the other hand, favoured beautification over utility; they either lavished funds for beautification or tended to neglect both these functions. Vidya Chatura had discussed these ideas with the late king. Mallaraj told him that in majority of the native states the treasury was used to create and beautify palaces for the pleasure of the king or his family. The state’s funds were used for the upkeep of many queens and for holding marriage ceremonies of the princes. He also predicted that those expenses would increase manyfold in the times to come because of three English influences—the need for false grandeur, the lure of flimsy objects and the primacy of appearance over substance. Mallaraj had painted a scenario of degeneration and depravity before Vidya Chatura. He had felt that future rulers might remain thoughtlessly steadfast to the old ways while the new generations of princes might remain bereft of any thought whatsoever. He feared that debauched and pleasure-seeking queens and princesses might suck the princes dry of their nobility and humanity, rendering them incapable of working for the welfare of their people. Just as Bhishma in the Shanti Parva counselled the new rulers about their duty and statecraft from his bed of arrows, the old king shared his experiences and predictions with his heir and his minister. Jarashankar remained Mallaraj’s advisor in this task as well. The two younger members of the group thought of constructing a large building to immortalise the Maharaj, and sought his permission. Mallaraj smiled and said, ‘Vidya Chatura, no person or his name are immortal, and will never be so. Both name and body must perish. But we will find a way of leaving something behind for future rulers— if they are to be capable and wise—so that they can benefit from our wisdom and experience. It should also be a way of spending the wealth received from our people for their benefit.’

Mallaraj visualised a ‘mental design’ of the building; crown prince Maniraj had the design prepared by hand and was responsible for its execution. Mallaraj named it the ‘Political Observatory’ of Ratnanagari, but it was Maniraj who added ‘Malla Mahabhavan’ to its name, which was inscribed on the gates. As one passed through the gates one entered a large and beautiful garden. The garden was richly adorned with flowering creepers, thick foliage, lakes, step-wells, wells and pools with seats around them; some of the bushes were cut and shaped to resemble birds and animals. The old king had created a unique design by way of instruction for the future rulers of Ratnanagari. As one passed through the ‘portico,’ one entered a vast hall named Vidur Bhavan. There were five halls situated behind the Vidur Bhavan. They were named Duryodhan Bhavan, Dushasan Bhavan, Karna Bhavan, Drona Bhavan and Pitamah Bhavan—these five halls were together known as the Kaurava Shala. These opened up into another vast hall named Kurukshetra. This hall was flanked on either side by two other halls called Pandu Bhavan and Dhritarashtra Bhavan. There was another set of five halls—Dharma Bhavan, Bhim Bhavan, Arjun Bhavan, Nakul Bhavan and Sahadev Bhavan, comprising the Pandava Shala—which also opened into the Kurukshetra Bhavan. These five halls on the rear side opened into another hall named Panchali Bhavan. Maniraj was not satisfied with Vidya Chatura’s response to the sharp criticism of Chandrakant and Vir Rao; their words like barbs had entered his heart and remained there as painful reminders. Vidya Chatura had invited these two men to see the Malla Mahabhavan. His idea was to reveal to them the secret of the political observatory, which he hoped would be an answer to their apprehensions, and also alleviate the pain of his king. Chandrakant and Vir Rao’s mutual friend Sarasvatichandra had visited the observatory and had returned with new ideas. This had aroused their curiosity. Maniraj restlessly paced up and down the Kurukshetra Bhavan waiting for his visitors. Vidya Chatura entered with the two guests. There were chairs and couches placed in the centre of the hall. They sat down and exchanged pleasantries. Their conversation veered towards the observatory. Vidya

Chatura narrated its history. Even Vir Rao felt some affection and regard for Mallaraj for this unique conception. ‘What grandeur of heart! Chandrakant, look at the poetry of his late highness’s heart! There is something stern and magnificent in his views, words and acts!’⟨fn:210⟩ Vir Rao exclaimed with pride. ‘Undoubtedly, it is so. And yet a few days back, in this very building, you abused his fellows,’ replied Chandrakant. Vir Rao: ‘Tch! Tch! Tch! Chandrakant, you haven’t understood a thing! A solitary moon waning and waxing in the night sky does not dispel darkness, nor do people give up sleeping because the moon shines bright. Maharaj Mallaraj was disillusioned and dejected. He called out to his countrymen time and again, but to what avail! He kept repeating, “What am I to do alone? What am I to do alone?”’ Maniraj was pleased with the praise of his father, but the tone of dejection perturbed him. His minister knew his heart and changed the topic. ‘Vir Raoji, you have just heard the history of this great building. Now let me take you on a tour of it so you can understand its essence.’ Everyone got up. The group was led by Maniraj and Vidya Chatura. They entered Pandu Bhavan. As they entered the room, marble statues of Pandu and his two queens greeted them. On one side was a golden inscription. How is a king chosen? The king must have a body; a body which creates royal lineage. Dhritarashtra is blind. His younger brother has all the qualities of a kshatriya; he also has sight and he is able. Though younger, he ascends the throne. A king requires authority and valour, represented by Pandu. The royal lineage is carried on by his progeny. If Mallaraj’s heirs nurture their royal seed and cultivate their authority they would be able to regenerate themselves even after a crisis. Pandu, and not Dhritarashtra, is the rightful claimant to the throne. On an adjacent wall, Maniraj had placed an inscription in English. Spirit of Acquisition and Growth! Thou wert born to acquire and to grow and not to enjoy! Thou wert born for Duties and not for Rights! Attempt not to rest from Duties and enjoy any Rights. Power is the sweet charmer by thy side, and awful will be the moment that will tempt thee to her embraces. For, beware if warning can avail it against thy frailty, the moment of thy fruition of her charms will also be the moment of thy Death! Great Spirit of Dominating Growth! Thy moment of Fruition of Power will mean the moment of thy disappearance! So dispersed King Pandu the moment he rushed into the arms of fair Madri! There was a small plaque facing this inscription which said: ‘Kings have no rights. They have duties. Pandu met his death the moment he sought pleasure. Oh Rulers of Ratnanagari, never ever forget this story!’ Having read these inscriptions, Vir Rao stood aside and mused aloud, ‘So is the story metaphorical? I am yet to come across a king who follows this norm. If this norm is followed in Ratnanagari, Vir Rao is bound to take back his words in this one instance.’ Maniraj: ‘Vir Rao, we have come here on a tour of this observatory, and not to ascertain if I have attained the high ideals that this building aspires to cultivate. Please do not consider that I have attained all the high ideals. But I do take pride in the fact that the late Maharaj reached the zenith of this ideal conduct. Moreover, it is my teacher, Pradhanji, who breathed life into my thoughts which have been inscribed here; hence you should not attribute them to me.’ Vir Rao: ‘You embody humility, something which is so difficult for someone of my kind of lineage. I see for the first time the virtues of royalty.’ Maniraj: ‘I did not speak in humility; I spoke the truth.’ Vir Rao: ‘You spoke what you in your heart believed to be true. Your humility is heartfelt and not just verbal.’ Chandrakant: ‘Maharaj, what should the kings of our times learn from Pandu?’ Maniraj: ‘It was Pradhanji who received and embodied all the counsel of the late Maharaj; all his thoughts have been inscribed in a notebook by Pradhanji. You will find a response to your question in that notebook.’ The secretary of Malla Mahabhavan fetched the notebook from the table, opened the relevant page and gave it to Chandrakant. The note was in Vidya Chatura’s hand. ‘Malla Maharaj did not equate the state with territory. In his noble conception territory had no value. For him the state was the essence of royal authority, or in other words it embodied the collective virtues of the royal prince. Just as grass requires only water to grow, authority of the state emerges on the strength of essential virtues of the royal princes. People call this authority the state. The fact is that royal authority resides in the princes and not in commoners. The true meaning of state is royal authority. Territory is the field of righteousness on which the princes perform their duties. A territory is populated because of the exercise of royal authority. It is royal authority which empowers this land. It is possible that a larger territory has less power than a smaller territorial unit. A smaller state which exercises more power has greater royal authority; any increase in royal authority has to be equated with the territorial growth of a state. Native states are constituent units of the British Empire. If they can further their royal authority it contributes to the increase of royal power. Any increase in the power of the feudatory states contributes to the strength of the sovereign. If the native states fail to further their own power, the fault would lie in their infatuation—the fatal infatuation of Pandu for Madri—and not in the sovereign.’ Chandrakant was stunned by this response. Vir Rao’s effervescence also subsided. Both gentlemen were full of curiosity. Chandrakant: ‘How many such notebooks are there? What are they used for?’ Vir Rao: ‘What is that seat in the right hand corner used for?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Each hall has five such notebooks. In one I write all the instructions and advice given by the late Maharaj. The present ruler, as he grows in thought, experience and knowledge, writes down his advice for the future rulers in the second notebook. The third notebook is blank; it is meant for the use of the future rulers of Ratnanagari.

The Prime Minister writes down his reflections and experiences in the fourth notebook, while the secretary of this hall notes down the summary of the books housed in the library of this hall for the ready reference of the King. That seat, called the ‘Vicharasan,’ is meant for the Maharaj’s contemplation. Each hall of this Mahabhavan has a secretary, similar notebooks and a seat for contemplation. The books housed in Pandu Bhavan are specific to the theme of the hall. The notes which are made in these notebooks are also specific to the concerns of this bhavan. There is a specific time fixed every week when the Maharaj sits in this hall on the seat provided for his contemplation, reflects on the subject, adds his own thoughts in the notebook provided and seeks to find solutions to the problems facing the state. This is also an opportunity for self-examination where he ascertains as to what extent he and his administration has put into practice the ideals enshrined in this bhavan. Each hall of this Mahabhavan is used in this way.’ Speechless, Chandrakant and Vir Rao looked at each other and read the inscription below the statue of Kunti. The embodiment of forbearance and forgiveness! Your sons faced hardships for many years, but you did not lose your forbearance or forgiveness. You did the penance required to ensure that your sons acquired the fitness to become rulers; you gave them the capacity to turn defeat into victory. Without you, no state can give birth to rulers like the Pandavas, nor can they be nurtured and made capable without your care and penance. They went out of the Pandu Bhavan and entered the adjacent hall. On the way Vidya Chatura discoursed, ‘Pandu Bhavan is a means of securing the right configuration of all elements that aid in securing the royal power. All other halls pertain to attaining prosperity, security and welfare of the state. The mode of attaining the difficult is called Yoga, but what has been attained needs to be secured and preserved. Statehood cannot be attained without Pandu, but without the Pandavas and Kauravas the welfare and prosperity of the state cannot be secured. The Pandavas, sons of gods, represent the power of the state to bring security and prosperity to the people; these five chambers represent them. Kauravas, born of the blind regent Dhritarashtra, are represented by these halls which are situated opposite the halls of the five Pandavas. The Pandavas represent the head, the power of right thought, while the others represent bodily force which is necessary for securing prosperity and wellbeing. The mind is superior to the body and must exercise control over it. Dharmaraj Yudhishthir is the eldest and the finest among the Pandavas and his hall is adjacent to the hall of Pandu.’ They entered the Dharma Bhavan and stood facing the grave and sober statue of Yudhishthir. The inscription on the marble plaque read: Whether it is the household or administration of the state, Mallaraj finds equanimity from only one element. That element is dharma, right conduct. The idea of righteous conduct as embodied by Dharmaraj has no relationship with religion that goes under various names like Shaiva, Vaishnava, Christianity or Islam. The religion that underlies all these religions, that which belongs to all people, that which remains true and steadfast for all times is the dharma of Yudhishthir. Pandu sought Dharmaraj as his first-born to secure the welfare and prosperity of his state. And that is also the aspiration of Mallaraj. When Draupadi was insulted and disrobed, all the Pandavas kept in check their anger and desire for retribution and submitted their passions to the command of Dharmaraj. Mallaraj also aspires to that for himself, his state and his heirs. Those who wish to understand the true nature and essence of righteous conduct must immerse themselves in the words of Sage Vyasa and emerge purified. Dharmaraj attains heaven; Dharmaraj is ever wakeful and it is Dharmaraj who retains equanimity. Those who sleep on the bed of falsehood sleep on a bed of thorns. On either side of the statue, verses from the Mahabharata were inscribed. The inscription on one side read: Reader! King Pandu asked Kunti to invoke Lord Yama with these words. O handsome one, strive duly this very day to gratify our wishes. Fortunate one, summon the God of Justice. He is the most virtuous of celestials. The God of Justice and Virtue will never be able to pollute us with sin. The world also, O beautiful princess, will then think that what we can do can never be unholy. The son also that we shall obtain from him shall in virtue be certainly the foremost among the Kurus. Begotten by the God of Justice and Morality, he would never set his heart upon anything that is sinful or unholy. Therefore, O thou of sweet smiles, steadily keeping virtue before thy eyes, and duly observing holy vows, summon thou the God of Justice and Virtue by the help of the solicitations and incantations.⟨fn:211⟩ The inscription on the other side of Yudhishthir’s statue read: Arjun, who embodied victory, also submitted to Dharma and had faith in it; he aspired to victory through righteous conduct. When Yudhishthir, faced with the strength of his enemies, lost his equanimity, Arjun reminded him of the power of righteousness with these words. Hear, O king, how soldiers that are few in number may vanquish the many that are possessed of every quality. Thou art without malice; I shall therefore tell thee means, O king. The Rishi Narada knows it, as also both Bhishma and Drona. Referring to this means, the Grandsire himself in days of old on the occasion of the battle between the Gods and the Asuras said unto Indra and the other celestials. —They that are desirous of victory do not conquer by might and energy so much as by truth, compassion, righteousness and energy. Discriminating then between righteousness and unrighteousness, and understanding what is meant by covetousness and having recourse to exertion, fight without arrogance, for victory is there where righteousness is.⟨fn:212⟩ The secretary of this hall opened the notebooks which contained the Minister’s reflections. He showed the relevant page to Vir Rao, who read out the note which was in English: ‘The highest sense of duty and unflinching obedience to the highest Principles of the eternal code of Morality which can illumine the soul of the humblest and the highest for the weal of the world— these have the first rights to command and control Intelligence, power, and All! So sang the Indian sage and Bard, and lucky is the nation where He will be obeyed.’ Vir Rao: ‘What is the political message of this intellectual discourse?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘You can see this door situated right behind the statue of Dharmaraj. The door leads to Panchali Bhavan. Panchali is the goddess of the people. She has five husbands; Yudhishthir is the eldest among them. For Yudhishthir, the sense of right conduct was primary and came before his love for Panchali; this should be apparent to you from the inscriptions. In Pandu Bhavan there was one seat for contemplation. In this hall there are three seats for contemplation in three corners, while the fourth corner has a collection of books. Maharaj Maniraj sits on one seat of contemplation with his gaze fixed on the statue of Yudhishthir and contemplates on the eternal code of morality as it applies to the state, its relations with other states and his personal conduct as well as the conduct of his family. ‘On the second seat, the Maharaj formulates the principles of conduct for his officials. Yudhishthir was an able strategist. The instructions for both the ‘‘military’’ and ‘‘civil’’ officials are formulated here. The Maharaj also keeps a sharp eye on the self-discipline of the officials and holds the ‘‘military reins’’ from this seat. ‘The Maharaj uses the third seat to contemplate upon the disputes among the citizens of the state and the criminal elements who are enemies from within. He ensures that justice is done to all and provides succour to the aggrieved through right conduct and just administration. After such contemplation the Maharaj enters Panchali Bhavan to ascertain whether his conduct has pleased his beloved. This is the conception which the late Maharaj Mallaraj had for this hall.’ Vir Rao: ⟨fn:213⟩‘Happy is the man who comes to this nobly conceived hall and bows in deep humility to the high and sacred thoughts it fills one with! A thousand blessings from this poor heart of mine flow towards your Highness as I witness this stern and holy ideal and its fullest, clearest expression.’ Vir Rao pressed Maniraj’s hand. At this, Chandrakant whispered to Vir Rao, ‘Mind you, you are treating a prince like a private man quite mannerlessly!’ Vir Rao whispered back, ‘Damn your etiquette where I simply give a clear form to my admiration! Is not a prince a man?’ Chandrakant: ‘You are rude, whether you are pleased or pained, like a dog that barks and bites or fawns and licks!’ Maniraj’s intervention put an end to this private argument. He said, ‘Vir Raoji, when I sit in contemplation in this room, I am filled with the presence of Dharmaraj who gives rise to many thoughts. It calms my pride, makes my duties apparent to me. And if I am uncertain about the implementation of one over the other, I consult these books, I take into account the context, I consider the welfare of my state and lastly I ask my poor heart. The late Maharaj had fixed this process. A conclusion so reached can only be for the benefit of the state. The words spoken by the great warrior Arjun are the source of my faith.’ The secretary of this hall opened the notebook which contained Maniraj’s reflections and gave it to him. Maniraj read aloud. This person, O king, deserveth to occupy the same seat with Indra himself. Devoted to the Brahmanas, acquainted with the Vedas, indifferent to luxury and carnal enjoyments, habitually performing sacrifices, steady in vows, this one, indeed, is the very embodiment of virtue. The foremost of all persons endued with energy and superior to everybody on earth in intelligence, devoted to asceticism, he is conversant with various weapons. No other person among the mobile and immobile creatures of the three worlds possesseth or will ever possess such knowledge of weapons. And there is none even amongst the gods, or Asuras, or men, or Rakshasas, or Gandharvas, or Yaksha chiefs, or Kinnaras, or mighty Uragas, who is like him. Endued with great foresight and energy, beloved by the citizens and inhabitants of the provinces, he is the mightiest of car-warriors amongst the sons of Pandu. A performer of sacrifices, devoted to morality, and of subdued passions, like unto a great Rishi, this royal sage is celebrated over all the worlds. Possessed of great strength and great intelligence, able and truthful, he hath all his senses under complete control. Equal unto Indra in wealth and Kuvera in hoarding, he is the protector of the worlds like unto Manu himself of mighty prowess. Endued with great might, he is even such. Kind unto all creatures he is no other than the bull of the Kuru race, king Yudhishthira the just. The achievements of this king resemble the sun himself of blazing effulgence. And his fame hath travelled in all directions like the rays of that luminary. And like the rays following the risen sun of blazing effulgence, ten thousand swift elephants followed him, O king, when he dwelt among the Kurus. And, O king, thirty thousand cars decked in gold and drawn by the best steeds, also used to follow him then. And full eight hundred bards adorned with ear-rings set with shining gems, and accompanied by minstrels, recited his praises in those days, like the Rishis adorning Indra. And, O king, the Kauravas and other lords of earth always waited upon him like slaves, as the celestials upon Kuvera. This eminent king, resembling the bright-rayed sun, made all lords of earth pay tribute unto him like persons of the agricultural class. And eighty-eight thousands of high-souled Snatakas depended for their subsistence upon this king practising excellent vows. This illustrious lord protected the aged and the helpless, the maimed and the blind, as his sons, and he ruled over his subjects virtuously. Steady in morality and self-control, capable of restraining his anger, bountiful, devoted to the Brahmanas, and truthful, this one is the son of Pandu.
