The prosperity and prowess of this one afflict king Suyodhana with his followers including Kama and Suvala’s son. And, O lord of men, the virtues of this one are incapable of being enumerated. This son of Pandu is devoted to morality and always abstains from injury. Possessed of such attributes, doth not this bull among kings, this son of Pandu, deserve, O monarch, to occupy a royal seat?⟨fn:214⟩ Maniraj: ‘Vir Raoji! Without comprehension of the subtle nature of right conduct one can acquire neither foresight nor remain steadfast to truth; without it there is no equanimity nor is there welfare of people. In absence of the comprehension of right conduct there can be no exercise of royal authority. Which of the Pandavas had earned the right to receive wisdom from Bhishma? Dharmaraj. When Pandu desired a son, who did he want as his first born? Dharma. Each moment I seek the high ideal of right conduct, and when I feel tired in this search I seek forgiveness from the late Maharaj because in this hall I clearly see my shortcomings, which point out to me that I am yet to acquire the fitness to sit on his throne. My childlike heart trembles. Whenever my own inability, evil thoughts or other problems become obstacles in the discharge of my duty, I listen to the poem that the late Maharaj composed in praise of Yudhishthir. This gives me courage and forbearance.’ Upon a signal from Maniraj, the secretary of the hall recited a composition of Maniraj: ‘You did not succeed your father to the throne; what you gained you lost in the evil game of dice. The lacquer palace, the disrobing of Draupadi in the assembly of the Kauravas blinded your brothers with rage. But you, son of Dharma, retained your equanimity and did not deviate from the path of rectitude. The Kauravas spun webs of deceit and falsehood to harm you and your brothers. They sought the help of men and demons, sages and princes to wreak destruction upon you. But you, son of Dharma, remained steadfast in your duties towards them. Whenever evil and wrongdoing prevail, whenever destruction looms large, whenever demons of death dance, Yudhishthir, you remain steadfast in the righteous battle. Yudhishthir, son of Dharma, you conquered death and ascended to the heavens. Mallaraj vows to follow your dharma.’ Maniraj bowed before the statue of Yudhishthir. They walked towards the door that connected Dharma Bhavan to Bhim Bhavan. Vidya Chatura: ‘The five halls of Pandava Bhavan are interconnected. Yudhishthir cannot decide on matters of right conduct without consulting his brothers, while the brothers would not act contrary to the advice of the eldest. Their unity can be preserved only when they can freely enter each other’s quarters. By the same logic the Maharaj decides on matters of justice and righteousness after giving due consideration to the ideals embodied in all the five halls.’ They entered Bhim Bhavan and stood before the fearsome statue of Bhim.

Vidya Chatura: ‘Chandrakant, this is the hall of Bhim, son of Vayu. He protects Panchali—that is our people. He represents the “Spirit of Protection, Prestige and Power.” Please read the inscription below the statue.’ Mallaraj’s power does not reside in his army. The army is not meant for the protection of his body or for his family. The army is meant for the protection of Panchali, that is the people of Ratnanagari. The army has power only in so far so it works for the protection of the people. Bhimsen is the soul of this army. If Arjun’s power lies in weapons that travel far, Bhim, your strength lies in weapons that you wield. Your weapons are not only those which can be seen with eyes. But oh Bhim, like your sire, your power is unseen but omnipresent. The internal enemies of the state will be destroyed in the dark like Kichaka, and those royal princes who insult and disrobe our people will be destroyed by your mace. It is your power which will destroy the demons. Whenever Panchali is in distress, your strength will be her protection. You have no elder brother except Dharmaraj. It is your duty to obey him and protect Panchali, alleviate her suffering. You are the force that can lift on your shoulders your mother and brothers and carry them to safety from the burning lacquer palace. Vidya Chatura: ‘This inscription was composed by the late Maharaj. There are two short inscriptions on either side. The one facing Dharma Bhavan reads: “Do not take a step without the permission of the elder brother.” The inscription on the other side reads: “Panchali is right behind you. Keep your eyes on her and remain alert to all her enemies.” Vidya Chatura: ‘Dhritarashtra represents the king’s body. Duryodhana, who represents the sons of the king and his bhayats, was born of this body. He symbolises “royal policy.” Dushasana is the punitive power of the king. If these three take away the kingdom from the rightful and righteous ruler—Dharmaraj—and seek to insult and defeat Panchali, then it is Bhim who stands between them and right conduct. He also carries punitive power in the form of his mace. The notebooks in this hall contain thoughts which pertain to these aspects of statecraft. You can see four seats for contemplation in this hall. The first of these seats is concealed; it is situated right behind the statue. Maharaj sits on this seat to hear reports from his “spies,’’ he reads newspapers there and with other such means he keeps an eye over the Panchali Bhavan to ensure that his people do not suffer any hardship. He also guards against his own conduct against Dhritarashtra, the king’s body, and against the conduct of Duryodhana and Dushasana—state policy. He ensures that the delicate body and mind of Panchali—his people—is not subject to any torture and pain. He also plans his unannounced and secret visits to the city and the state from this seat. The second seat in this corner is meant for the king to think of ways of feeding the big-bellied Bhim. He must ensure that his people are adequately fed, that his servants are nourished and that there are adequate resources in his treasury to feed his people in years of drought and famine. It is from this seat that the ‘‘store keeper’’ and the ‘‘commissariat’’ of our army are administered. It is from this place that the hungry are fed. The king considers aspects of Duryodhana and Dushasana that harass Panchali. The third seat is to implement decisions taken while on the first seat. Bhimsen wields his mace from the third seat. The mace crushes any aspects of state policy or any officials that have turned oppressive. The state officials occasionally experience a cut in their pay while some lose their job. This is the punitive power of Bhim. The exercise of this power is merciless even on the state’s bhayats and any of its officials. Even the royal family fears this punitive power. For several generations the rulers of Ratnanagari have been devoted to the people of the state. But it is possible that someday a future king like Dhritarashtra may turn an enemy of the people and crush Bhim in his embrace. We have to guard against this possibility and make decoy statues of Bhim cast in metal to be offered for destruction. All such future plans are made here so that Panchali does not remain without the husbandship of Bhim. If state policy in the form of Duryodhana and punitive power in the form of Dushasana were to turn against the people, they are crushed by Bhim exercising power from this seat.

‘These three seats allow the ruler to weed out those elements in his state that oppress his people. From the fourth seat the ruler selects the best elements within his army and administration. Panchali is also threatened by enemies arising out of other states and natural calamities like famine. From this seat, the ruler calculates and plots ways of neutralising these enemies. It is from this seat that the ruler also thinks of ways of strengthening his army to fight against such enemies. The son of Vayu is always present, albeit invisibly so, exercising his various powers. This hall and the books housed in its library nurture and further these ideas. All these thoughts are enshrined in the notebooks kept here.’ Chandrakant: ‘In this day and age, why do you need an army?’ Vidya Chatura replied with a smile, ‘In this age we fight battles with words. In matters of disputes with other states or with the sovereign we are required to produce papers, employ the art of advocacy and argumentation. The foresight of the late Maharaj ensured that these means of warfare are also secured by the fourth seat.’ Vir Rao: ‘Don’t you have an army? If you do, what do you do with it?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘In case of war against the sovereign of this land by a foreign power, the native states would be required to contribute their small armies to the mighty force of the sovereign. We are prepared for any such eventuality. We cannot predict the future with any sense of certainty. But the king’s authority requires an army. So we maintain an ‘‘armed police’’; they are properly trained and armed. These aspects are considered from the fourth seat. To summarise, all measures necessary to ensure obedience to the command of Dharmaraj and ways of protecting Panchali from enemies, both internal and external, as also calamities are considered here and appropriate and forceful strategies for such emergencies are planned here. The library also supports this aspect of statecraft.’ Vir Rao: ‘Are there instances where you have to use force against your own officials?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘A great deal of care is taken before making appointments in the state administration. Despite this, due to some weakness, if any official were to work contrary to the interest of Panchali, the matter will not go unnoticed; and then such an official will not go unpunished.’ Chandrakant: ‘The state officials are administered, educated and punished from this hall. But who selects them? How are they inducted?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘They are selected in Arjun Bhavan. Maharaj invites his close advisors and ministers to the Kurukshetra Bhavan. They consider all aspects and after due deliberations Maharaj invests them with specific authority. If an official has to be promoted, the decision is taken after due consideration in the appropriate hall of this observatory. The final decision is left to Dharma Bhavan. Let us now proceed to Arjun Bhavan.’ They entered the hall. Arjun was seated in his chariot with Hanuman residing in his flag. Krishna was his charioteer. This was the largest hall. An inscription in English was inscribed in golden letters on the canopy of the chariot. Hail! Glorious Spirit of Activity, Enterprise, and Progress! Unimpeded, Unbeaten, and All-Powerful! Proceed forward ever and ever over land and sea and through Heaven itself! For thou was Heaven-born! Vidya Chatura: ‘Chandrakantji, this was the favourite hall of the late Maharaj Mallaraj. This hall has five seats called Yogasan, Nitiasan, Kriyasan, Vijayasan and Vibhutiasan. Arjun and Krishna, Nara and Narayana, come together and through their union the ideas of statecraft are considered in this hall. Arjun is that political force, that human endeavour which brought fruition to the efforts of the Pandavas and Panchali; Sri Krishna is his charioteer, his guide. A man without divine guidance is powerless. Let us not forget that Kaba stole even from Arjun.’ Vir Rao: ‘Your allegories have been stretched to their limits. Even metaphors are bounded. All these ideas, the organisational structures required for peace time and the imperatives of English colonial administration are all being expressed through Bhim’s mace and Arjun’s bow and arrow. We cannot accept this.’

When Vidya Chatura remained silent, Vir Rao continued in English. ‘We should be fools without common sense to accept the pedantry of these far-fetched allegories. Surely our hoary Vyasa had no idea of any of these, your interpretations of his simple designs. I am quite sure the bard contemplated neither your Spirit of Prestige and Power, nor your Angel of Progress when he penned his bulky volumes to bring onto one place his heterogeneous mass of fictions, adages and nursery tales, and maybe, experiences.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Vir Raoji, this is not something that one can comprehend in haste. Is it impossible to believe that the poet Vyasa while creating imaginary or historical characters also gave them allegorical attributes? Secondly, has not Valmiki’s conception of Ramchandra inspired various poets to imagine Ram with so many different attributes? If we were to take the entire range of Ram’s attributes, are there not some which are contradictory and mutually exclusive and cannot be found in the same person? The fact remains that a great poet’s conception is altered by subsequent poets, and this is what gives permanence to a great poet’s imagination; it is by this process that a poet’s soul lives on. Even if people plagiarise as much as they wish from the great poets, They are for this never in any way at a loss; Many gems are taken from it by the immortal gods, The ocean even today continues to be a treasure house of gems.⟨fn:215⟩ ‘A poet’s greatness lies in the fact that many others partake of his gems and give them different form and name. A poet is one who dwells deep into the memories of the past and emerges from it with gems for his times. A poet’s imagination recognises no limits. ‘Third, Bhavabhuti has marked the difference between the composition of sages and the poems of contemporary poets. He says that the words of new poets follow meaning, while meaning followed the words of the sages. The sages imbued their utterances with a range of meanings and they continue to excite our imagination. A discerning mind can see a lush tree of words in the seeds sown by the sages. Goldsmith wrote: “Remote, unfriended, melancholy, slow.” He could not explain all the meanings of the word “slow.” But it was Dr. Johnson who elucidated its various meanings; all these meanings were latent in the poet’s mind and hence the word “slow’’ came to be imbued with it. Over time, the poet had no memory of the process of creation, but a sensitive critique brought the entire universe of fragrance that had been conveyed through that phrase. In case of Vyasa, meanings emanate from his words. When we search the meanings of his words, we worship the poet sage. The late Maharaj believed that public weal can be attained by extending the meanings of a poet’s words. We have a group of officials who have been trained in this and have become adept at it.’ Vir Rao smiled and said, ‘Very beautifully put; please explain it from that point of view. We shall see what spirit of progress you can spin out of man Vyasa. Only see that you don’t make things too comical for my prosaic wits.’⟨fn:216⟩ On one wheel of Arjun’s chariot was inscribed the word ‘morality’ and on the other the word ‘action.’ Vidya Chatura pointed this out and said, ‘The chariot of this great soul runs on two wheels of morality and action. The meaning will become clear when you hear the words by which Pandu sought the birth of Arjun.’ The lord of the celestials hath been gratified, and is willing to give thee a son such as thou desirest, of superhuman achievements and great fame. He will be the oppressor of all enemies and possessed of great wisdom. Endued with a great soul, in splendour equal unto the Sun, invincible in battles, and of great achievements, he will also be extremely handsome. O thou of fair hips and sweet smiles, the lord of the celestials hath become gracious to thee. Invoking him, bring thou forth a child who will be the very home of all Kshatriya virtues.⟨fn:217⟩ The secretary brought out Maniraj’s notebook and opened it at the relevant page.

Vidya Chatura:  ‘Arjun’s conception of morality and action are inscribed in gold on a silver plaque placed between the two horses drawing the chariot.’ They read the inscription. At the time of Arjun’s birth, Kunti heard the divine words wherein lie the source of Arjun’s morality and action. This child of thine, O Kunti, will be equal unto Kartavirya in energy and Siva in prowess. Invincible like Sankara himself he will spread thy fame far and wide. As Vishnu (the youngest of Aditi’s sons) had enhanced Aditi’s joy, so shall this child enhance thy joy. Subjugating the Madras, the Kurus along with the Somakas, and the people of Chedi, Kasi and Karusha, he will maintain the prosperity of the Kurus. (Surfeited with libations at the sacrifice of king Swetaketu), Agni will derive great gratification from the fat of all creatures dwelling in the Khandava woods (to be burnt down) by the might of this one’s arms. This mighty hero, vanquishing all the effeminate monarchs of the earth, will, with his brothers perform three great sacrifices. In prowess, O Kunti, he will be even as Jamadagnya or Vishnu. The foremost of all men endued with prowess, he will achieve great fame. He will gratify in battle (by his heroism) Sankara, the god of gods (Mahadeva), and will receive from him the great weapon named Pasupata. This thy son of mighty arms will also slay, at the command of Indra, those Daityas called the Nivatakavachas who are the enemies of the gods. He will also acquire all kinds of celestial weapons, and this bull among men will also retrieve the fortunes of his race.⟨fn:218⟩ Vidya Chatura: ‘Mallaraj saw in these the seeds of morality and action. They provide solace and joy. All the Pandavas are sons of gods; but Arjun, who acts, is the son of Indra. He obeys Dharma and Bhim, but the effort and action through which Panchali is attained is Arjun’s. Sri Krishna is a guide to the Pandavas and Panchali, but he became a charioteer only to Arjun. It is only to Arjun that he gave the discourse of the Gita, the supreme commandment of action. It is only to Arjun that he revealed his universal form. Those who occupy the throne of Ratnanagari must remember that Panchali was partial to Arjun; he was a favourite of Sri Krishna and the very life of the Pandavas. If rulers do not nurture morality and action they will not be able to rule Ratnanagari. Rulers must never forget the past and the future of a man of action, as revealed by sage Vyasa. And let Arjuna, O son of Pandu, go unto Mahendra and Rudra, and Varuna, and Kuvera, and Yama, for receiving weapons from them. He is competent to behold the gods for his asceticism and prowess. He is even a Rishi of great energy, the friend of Narayana; ancient, eternal, a god himself, invincible, ever successful, and knowing no deterioration. Of mighty arms, he will achieve mighty deeds, having obtained weapons from Indra, and Rudra, and the Lokapalas.⟨fn:219⟩ The secretary of the hall read out the commentary from the notes made by the Minister: ‘Arjun favours weapons that reach far. Like his weapons, he has a long reach. Vision, excellence and action are his weapons. At a time when native rulers have become inert and confined to their territories, Arjun’s vision extends to the great oceans that cover the earth; his force and spirit extend beyond the seas and skies. He travels to the heavens and meets Kuber, Yama and all the gods who preside over human destiny and fate. He acquires this vision both through knowledge and experiences gathered during travel in his life as a kshatriya; but in his previous life he was a learned brahmin, a sage. ‘‘He is the old, eternal Spirit of Progress.’’ He aspires to victory. His entire endeavour is towards victory; he personifies victory. Arjun always emerges victorious. No enemy can halt his progress. When Drona faces him, this sage-like man emerges victorious with Krishna’s help; even when Pitamah Bhishma challenges him, this eternal man emerges triumphant. Even Karna, that generous son of Surya, will perish at Arjun’s hands. To achieve these feats this royal prince travelled to heaven and obtained divine weapons from Indra; he battled Mahadev in the Himalayan forests and obtained weapons; he travelled far and wide to the corners of the land and acquired them. Mallaraj clearly saw the greatness of Arjun. He has given the prime minister of Ratnanagari the responsibility of ensuring that Arjun’s character, his power and endeavours flourish among the rulers of the state. This discourse has been written for this very purpose and with the hope that the vision, excellence and action of Arjun will remain alive for times immemorial in the rulers of Ratnanagari.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Such, Mr. Vir Rao, is the Spirit of Progress drawn by our late Master’s hand, if not by Vyasa. The Spirit stops not within Indian shores but invades with mighty enterprise all words at home and abroad with his ever growing Vision, his ever restless Aggressiveness and his all-absorbing Action, and triumphs over all that check the march of progress. This is the ‘‘vision,’’ ‘‘excellence’’ and ‘‘action’’ which far-seeing Vyasa has preserved in his work, like seeds for sowing future crops in the land where his mighty soul had sojourned.’⟨fn:220⟩ Vir Rao: ‘I think I must hold my tongue at least till we reach the end of this curious chapter of your political literature.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Now let us turn our attention to the seats of contemplation placed in this hall. The seat facing the horses of the chariot, adjacent to the door that leads to Kurukshetra, is called Yogasan. That seats accords a clear view of Krishna and Arjun, as also the Pandu Bhavan, Panchali Bhavan and parts of Kuru Bhavan. Yogasan is the seat from which the king considers all those matters regarding which Sri Krishna contemplated in relation to the wellbeing of the Pandavas. Relationship with other states and all other matters which must be considered in order to improve and better the present condition and future prospects of the state and its people are deliberated from this seat. All seats of Arjun Bhavan have to preserve and protect morality and action, the seeds of which are sown here. The growth and nurturance of these seeds is ensured from other seats. But it is from the Yogasan that all processes are monitored and regulated. The triumph of all good qualities like peace, progress, speed, timely action, genius, truth and dharma is ensured by a combination of an all-encompassing vision and righteous means. It is supported by wisdom, observation and exercise of royal authority. This seat, with the blessings of almighty God, brings together all beneficial aspects as per the teachings of Sri Krishna. The universal form—the universality of all good—is seen from here; it negates Arjun’s hesitation and keeps Dharmaraj’s ‘‘superstitions’’ under check. It is from here that Panchali—people of our state—is clothed and her husband—the ruler—is guided. All good men and good qualities come together to install the age of goodness. Sri Krishna’s ‘‘telescopic’’ vision that is apparent in this design was conceived by the great mathematician-like Vyasa. ‘‘Progress,’’ which is the essence of our times and the product of Arjun’s morality and action, is thus encouraged and actualised.’ Vidya Chatura continued in English: ‘This is the seat of Inspirations and Aspirations of the Thinker of the State, of the Thinker that ever watches and thinks out with the largest heart and knowledge the lines of progress that can result in the public weal, of the Thinker that thinks coolly, dispassionately and as if without taking more than the part of the chariot-driver to the Angel of Progress. This angel of thoughts keeps aloof from Action even in the midst of the turmoil of battle and his watchful presence at the centre of the strife is, like that of the unarmed Krishna, intended but to minister to the soul of the State and lead her along the right path as she works on the Body that shrouds her Majesty with power. He is ‘‘Yoga’’ itself in the midst of Action, and it is he who prompts and advises and furthers the cause of Progress on all sides at all times in all the great contests and contingencies that gather round nations and their protectors. ‘Vir Raoji! Chandrakantji! States, small or large, require such a ‘‘Thinker,’’ a Yogi who can with complete freedom guide the state and her people. In absence of such a thinker like Krishna and a doer like Arjun, rulers are rendered effete and the people, orphaned. Therefore, the flag of Arjun’s chariot is inscribed with these lines: Where so ever Krishna, the Master of Yoga, is, and where so ever is Partha, the Bow man, there rest assured are fortune, victory, prosperity and Eternal Right.⟨fn:221⟩

Maniraj smiled gently and said to the secretary of the hall, ‘Please bring the late Maharaj’s notes on the nature of Krishna that we are required to cultivate.’ The notes were brought and read out: ‘Krishna was the guide and mentor to the Pandavas. The rulers of this state should also get a minister like Krishna who should be invited from afar, just as Krishna had come from Dwarka and lived with the Pandavas in Indraprastha. The ruler should benefit from his unarmed, watchful presence, and should have a worshipful attitude towards such a minister. The king who sits on Arjun’s seat of Inspirations and Aspirations should know that a king needs a minister who is conducive to his dispositions. The minister stays aloof from action, but in matters of inspiration, aspiration and statecraft the king must follow the counsel of his minister. Such a minister belongs truly to the Pandavas and Panchali, and never to the Kauravas.’ Maniraj: ‘The ministerial seat is placed adjacent to the seat of Inspirations and Aspirations and on the path that leads to Kurukshetra.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Now let us turn towards Nitiasan.’ Chandrakant: ‘That he does not wish to speak of his role betrays Pradhanji’s humility and it is befitting.’ Maniraj: ‘You have understood correctly. Hence, I will have to explain some aspects of this design though it is difficult for me, a man of few words and little learning. A few matters require explanation. In Dharma Bhavan there was an inscription: “Where there is dharma, there is victory.” That is absolutely true; but dharma is sometimes diseased by Superstition. Dharma cannot bear fruit without the grace of God; and in absence of the Thinker’s counsel the mystery of dharma is not revealed. Therefore, the inscription on the horse on the left reads that Krishna is the source of victory. The other inscription reads thus: Indeed as Narada said—There is victory where Krishna is. Victory is inherent to Krishna. Indeed, it followeth Madhava. And as Victory is one of his attributes, so humility is his other attribute.⟨fn:222⟩ ‘Pradhanji will now take us through the explanations of other seats.’

Vidya Chatura: ‘Niti has to be understood in terms of both rajya niti and rajniti. Rajya niti is ‘‘true statesmanship’’ while rajniti is merely ‘‘diplomacy and political craft or statecraft.” ‘Panchali is the people of the state and the Pandavas are the royal qualities or virtues. A policy that is universal and created for the benefit and welfare of both the people and the rulers is called true statesmanship. Statecraft is what the ruler or his minister employs to strengthen the ruler’s authority. The goals of public weal are decided from the seat of Thought, but it is from the seat of Statesmanship that the means to realise these goals are finalised. What you call ‘‘international law’’ is deliberated upon from this seat. The relationship with the sovereign power is decided from this seat. This is the seat of Statesmanship. The seat of Thought points out the goal. The seat of Statesmanship finds out ways and means of reaching the goal, and here too the seat of Thought watches and guides. Foreign Policy, Treaties and the like are designed, and approved here. Here too the Actions, which the next seat goes through, are designed. This is the seat of perfecting Arjun’s Designs.⟨fn:223⟩ The seat of Inspirations and Aspirations wields a bow; this seat of Statesmanship is that bow. The arrow is provided by the seat of Activity. Victory and Prosperity are the result of this endeavour. Statesmanship is formulated here, while statecraft is formulated in the Kaurav Bhavan in accordance with the norms of statesmanship. ‘This is the seat of large-minded policy for the people and of perfected Design; and the Spirit that presides over it reaches with long arms the Greater Arts of State prevalent in the most distant parts of the world and moving more in that line, utilises and conquers the Power of Nature and the Spirits of the Age. And in all his designs he creates what is noble, good, and great and you can never draw him into anything that is ignoble, bad and mean. Arjun is, therefore, called Vibhatsu.⟨fn:224⟩

I am known as Vibhatsu among gods and men, for my never having committed a detestable deed on the battle field.⟨fn:225⟩ ‘The seat of Statesmanship is situated adjacent to the seat of Inspirations and Aspirations, and it faces the wheel of statesmanship. On the other side of the Yogasan is the Kriyasan, the seat of Activity. ‘The wheel of activity is placed before this seat. What does it signify? The first activity that Krishna and Arjun perform is to obtain divine weapons from Varuna and Agni. These weapons rendered the weapons of Indra, Yama, Vayu, Parvata, Ashvini Kumar, Dhanpati, Rudra, Vasu and other divine beings ineffective. The second activity they perform is to burn the Khandava forest as an offering to Agni, which satiated him. ‘The Angels of Thought and Progress, joined together, subdued all Powers of Nature with arms obtained from fire and water, and to fire were subordinated the other Powers of Nature. This phase of progress has got a meaning in these days and this seat of progress directs our eyes to this.⟨fn:226⟩ ‘It was Arjun who obtained the Pashupatastra. He won over Shiva, the one who has the power of destruction, and obtained weapons from him. And what are these weapons like? In the three worlds with all their mobile and immobile creatures, there is none who is incapable of being slain by this weapon. And it may be hurled by the mind, by the eye, by words, and by the bow.⟨fn:227⟩ ‘Arjun had the power to destroy objects both moving and steady not only through his bow but also through his mind, eyes and words. Arjun, through his valour and industry, obtained all these weapons. As he ascended to heaven, the gods, delighted by his presence, gifted him their divine weapons. Arjun was destined to defeat the Kauravas, who were devoid of statesmanship. The gods saw this endeavour as befitting them. Hence, Yama gave him the power to take life; Varuna the god of water gave him the Varuna pash; Kuber gave him the power to create weapons by thought; Chitra Sen, chief musician of the gods, taught him heavenly dance, song and musical instruments. Arjun thus obtained the means of death, of imprisonment and pleasure from the gods and he returned to earth. All these activities are considered from this seat of Activity. We shall consider the use of weapons against the Kauravas later after we consider the meaning of Bhishma Parva. The arrangement of ports, railways, emigration, foreign trade, aspects of native and foreign knowledge systems, arts, sciences of physics and materials, all of which are required for the welfare of our people are considered from this seat. It also encourages the state of Ratnanagari to strive with the enthusiasm, power and intelligence of Arjun to wield all these means to secure the welfare of Panchali, that is, our people. Arjun obeys only the command of Dharma and Bhim. All his means are pure and unsullied; hence Arjun is also called Shweta Vahana or the white vehicle. Arjun wields his weapons with both the right and the left hand. He is unhampered by ‘‘Habit, Prejudice and Superstition,’’ and hence he is also called Savyasachi. ‘This is the seat of free Activity, of execution of Designs of Enterprise and in short, for preparing and furthering without stint or reserve the means and movements of such Progress Policy as may be matured in the seats of Thought and Statesmanship. This seat sends forth ships, merchants, students, scientists, artists and artisans from Ratnanagari and aspires to import the latest triumphs of art, science, industry, learning and commerce into their country. Even the military and naval education of our cadets, bhayats and others in foreign schools is attended to here. We propose from this place to carry out a programme of giving a general all-sided lift to the subjects of this state in all concerns—physical, moral, educational, economic—and in fact in all matters that can raise their life and status.⟨fn:228⟩ ‘Behind the seat of activity is placed the seat of victory, victory which is assured through endeavour and God’s grace. Arjun is also called Vijay and Jishnu. His conquests are not merely those of arms, but he also makes them by exercising influence over the world outside his kingdom and by extending what people have of late been calling “Spheres of influence.” He exports the power and products of his state to distant fields and brings money. He is, therefore, called the Conqueror of Wealth.⟨fn:229⟩ ‘One of the names of Arjun is also Dhananjaya. He is the one who entices distant lands by the produce of this land and brings their wealth to our shores. In this he casts his influence and his arms across the land. The weapons that he obtained from Agni and Varuna are thus enhanced in his hands. It is from this seat that Pandava statesmanship has to triumph over Kaurava statecraft. Krishna and Arjun, working together, joined Shikhandi in the battle against Bhishma; they defeated the learning of Drona and Ashwatthama when they sided with evil; they destroyed Karna, these are also aspects of statesmanship. ‘This Spirit of Progress conquers Bhishma—the grandfather Spirit of Old Wisdom and Tradition, and quiets, without destroying, Drona, the Spirit of Learning and Knowledge, when these lend themselves to the service of a wrong cause—the royal person as opposed to the weal of the State and people.⟨fn:230⟩ ‘In the fourth corner is the Vibhutiasan, the seat of Higher Life. Higher life is the fruit of victory. Victory in war and consequent peace are brought about by Arjun’s efforts. The Pandavas and Panchali taste the fruits of a higher life; as a result of it other lands are attracted to this land and this faster, higher life. When the finest gems of other lands, both men and objects, are attracted to this land they foster a higher life for the state. It is the Spirit of Progress that imports and attracts freely and without prejudice the best things and men of foreign birth. It is this Spirit of Importation that makes a nation great.⟨fn:231⟩ What all did Arjun attract from foreign lands? Who won Panchali? Who invited unarmed Sri Krishna to become a charioteer? Who sought Krishna’s help when the Khandav forest had to be burnt? Who invited Maya

Danav to build their palace? Who was instrumental in building that palace of illusion? Who obtained weapons? Who ascended to heaven to obtain divine weapons? All these great tasks were accomplished by Arjun. Arjun who travelled all over the land to bring riches and greatness for his people was a favourite character of the late Maharaj. Arjun performed the Rajsuya and Ashwamegha sacrifices, secured Krishna’s presence as a counsellor and friend, increased the wealth of the Kuru dynasty and had the palace of illusion built by Maya Danav. He was the one who imported the best things and men to increase the gifts of his land. The books in this hall instruct the rulers to cultivate the spirit of Arjun. ‘This is the seat of Higher Life achieved and filled by the activities and enterprise of the Spirit of Progress; from the seat of Higher Thought to that of High Design, from High Design to the seat of full and forward Execution, and from that to success, the nation is lifted; and from the seat of Success the nation is ushered on by the Spirit of Progress into this last seat of Greatness and of Higher Life and Higher Fruition.⟨fn:232⟩ ‘Vir Rao! Chandrakant! I have given you an overview of the design and purpose of this political observatory and described to you the royal qualities that the late Maharaja wished to foster. I have committed his sage counsel to memory. The other halls of this observatory are secondary. We shall sit in the Kuru Bhavan, and Shankar Sharma and Pravindas will talk about them in brief. It has been a tiring morning for the two of you. For us, such occasions are an excuse to remember the late Maharaja and provide us with an opportunity to recall his sage counsel. They might be dry and uninteresting for a third party like you. It is your affection for us that you have expended so much energy on this.’ Chandrakant: ‘I have experienced a new kind of joy in this place. There are moments when I forget Sarasvatichandra, and then I see his spirit in this building.’

Vir Rao: ‘Saheb! You attribute this great allegory to Vyasa which mislead all of India. You make this allegory so obtuse! This is dearly hilarious and hence joyful. But, if we forget the old man Vyasa, the idealism of this observatory and the design of the various seats give me pure joy.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘That is sufficient for us. Now let us sit down and conclude the discussion.’ All of them moved to the Kurukshetra and took their appointed places. Pravindas commenced the discussion. Pravindas: ‘Queen Madri, who represents royal power, was blessed by the Ashwins with twin sons: Nakul, the embodiment of beauty and Sahadev, the personification of all knowledge. The Ashwins as healers of the gods provide beauty and nourishment. The state and its people form one body; Nakul is the Spirit of Beauty while Sahadev nourishes its health. ‘Nakul is an aesthete. Materials for the beautification of Panchali are prepared in his hall, Nakul Bhavan; for this purpose state treasury resources are used from here. Sahadev brings in the wealth; Nakul spends it. The first principle of good governance is that the resources of the state are utilised for the people. It is in Nakul Bhavan that designs are prepared for the beautification of our state through arts and construction of beautiful roads. Nakul became the keeper of the royal stables in the court of King Virata. Arjun strives to bring in the best produce and innovations of foreign lands, while Nakul Bhavan fosters our native industries, arts and crafts and cultivates expertise in these fields among our people. Nakul introduces and fosters all our indigenous industries and arts, including what you call the fine arts.⟨fn:233⟩ Nakul trains our painters, singers, sculptors and machinists, provides them with resources and gives them encouragement. He teaches them about novel innovations. Men cannot match women in keeping the house clean, beautiful and comfortable; such tasks have to be performed for our cities and villages. This is best done by the people themselves. It is Nakul’s responsibility to train, cultivate and engage our people in these tasks. He creates, trains and fosters our Municipalities and Local Self-Governments. The spread of Sciences, Philosophy and High and popular educations⟨fn:234⟩ among all our people is Nakul’s responsibility. He also conserves desirable aspects of our traditions and welcomes new aesthetic sensibilities. He also provides for the physical wellbeing of our people by creating gymnasiums. ‘Nakul is our Spirit of Beauty, Arts and Aesthetics and is the Lord Mayor and Chamberlain ministering to the wants and decorations of the towns and chambers of Her Majesty, the Panchali of this state. He looks after our refinements and manners; he is the beautiful Prince of Refinement and Aesthetics. He looks after the physical, mental, sentimental and moral growth of our people, and his anvil is always working out new and beautiful implements of arts and science for the health, hygiene and recreation of sweet Panchali.’⟨fn:235⟩ They moved on from Nakul to the hall of Sahadev, his younger brother. Pravindas continued his exposition. ‘In the court of Virata, Sahadev had worked as a keeper of cows. Cows signify wealth. It is Sahadev’s responsibility to count them, protect them and increase them. He is our ‘‘Surveyor’’ and ‘‘Revenue Commissioner.’’ His knowledge of the past, present and the future are utilised for the welfare of our people. Sahadev has to identify problems relating to land and wealth—in fact, relating to all economic matters—and provide solutions for them. He decides the budgetary provisions for improving the wellbeing of our people; he apportions money between the Pandavas and Kauravas; he allocates money to the king and provides for the people; he thinks of ways of increasing the revenue and savings of the state. ‘Sahadev is our Spirit of Prescience and Prudence. He solves our economic problems and governs and distributes his collections. The taxpayer’s comforts and prospects are at his heart while he gives to the rulers their due.⟨fn:236⟩

‘The mines, forests, agriculture and ‘‘canal irrigation’’ are his departments. Sahadev looks after ‘‘Public Health’’ and ‘‘Sanitation.’’ That Sahadev, the knower of the past, present and future, the seer of our fortune and our healer, is the youngest among the Pandavas and responsible for these domains of the state. The elder brothers consult him in all economic matters; Sahadev calculates the cost of each action. He is a cool calculator—just like a merchant.’⟨fn:237⟩ Vir Rao laughed out aloud and said, ‘Ha, ha, ha! I like that Bania! Yes, but I admit he must be consulted and obeyed too by rash men like myself. Go on, Mr. Pravindas, I am really thankful.’⟨fn:238⟩ Pravindas: ‘The Panchali Bhavan is situated right behind these five halls, each of which opens into the Panchali Bhavan. It is the inner courtyard and bed chamber of Panchali; it is here that she meets with her husbands. ‘‘It is our People’s Hall.’’ In this hall, all sections of society can meet the king in confidence. All the formal meetings between the king and the people, ‘‘the levees, the evening parties’’ are held here. The ruler understands the desire and aspirations of our people in this hall and he gets the Pandavas to act upon these. The Dhritarashtra Bhavan is situated next to the Pandu Bhavan, which represents the king’s body. The Pandavas are concerned about Panchali, while the Kauravas are preoccupied with the king’s body. Dhritarashtra is blind; kings are incapable of seeing the true, inner feelings of people. Hence, he has to see through the eyes of a spy. Dhritarashtra saw through the eyes of Sanjay, who informed him about the doings of the Pandavas and Kauravas alike. Sanjay is not a spy; he observes impartially the activities of the Pandavas and Kauravas on behalf of the people; Sanjay observes intrigues as also the unfolding of statesmanship and statecraft and presents these before Dhritarashtra. ‘He is, like the photograph, an apparatus for recording and reporting the spiritual and the physical voice that fills all atmosphere in the state—like your journals and newspapers. He is the king’s binocle and field glass.⟨fn:239⟩ ‘The duties of the brahmin are discussed and deliberated upon, but no book provides a description of the duties of a vaishya. Therefore, Dhritarashtra adopted Yuyutsu, the son of a vaishya, as his own son to learn about the vaishya mind. If a wife were to see more than her husband, she would become more powerful. This is not desirable in state administration. Therefore Gandhari covers her eyes to become as blind as her husband; this is her wifely devotion. It is the duty of Dhritarashtra—father of a hundred sons—to keep the royal lineage alive. The hundred sons are like his bhayats. The king had only one wife, a rule that is followed in Ratnanagari. In each hall of the Kaurava Bhavan there is one Bhayasan, a seat that points out the dangers inherent in that hall. The lineage survives because of Dhritarashtra, but he represents the danger of attachment. Dhritarashtra was alerted to the dangers of his son Duryodhana’s evil at the time of his birth. This evil became apparent to everyone when Draupadi was dishonored in the assembly. Duryodhana’s evil ways did not allow him to see reason when Krishna came as an emissary to stop the war. In all three instances, different virtuous people told Dhritarashtra that his duty as a king was to denounce Duryodhana. But the father, because of his deep attachment, could not follow this counsel. The Bhayasan alerts rulers to the dangers of becoming like Dhritarashtra and harbouring a son who acts against the interests of the state. The king’s effort must be to nip evil in the seed itself. The injustice committed by Dhritarashtra on Yudhishthir was because of his attachment to an evil son. Shankar Sharma will explain the design of the remaining halls.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘In front of us is the Duryodhana Bhavan. Dhritarashtra personifies the king’s body while Duryodhana, his first-born, embodies statecraft. It is statecraft that brings glory to the person of the king.

Suyodhana is trying to win through policy the world he had won by the dice game ruse.⟨fn:240⟩ ‘If Arjun’s policy and action further the interests of the people, Duryodhana acts for the king. Arjun’s expertise is ‘‘statesmanship’’ while Duryodhana is adept at ‘‘diplomacy.’’ It was because of his diplomacy that he secured the support of a great warrior like Shalya who was the maternal uncle of the Pandavas. He had an advisor like Shakuni to deal with the thieves in the state. He used the policy of ‘‘set a thief to catch a thief.’’ It was Duryodhana’s diplomacy that cemented the friendship with the great and generous warrior Karna, who fought on his side. It was Duryodhana’s statecraft that enticed brahmins such as Drona and Ashwatthama and secured the assistance of their enlightenment, their knowledge and weapons for his side. Even Bhishma’s power remained subject to his statecraft. Drona and Bhishma were devoted to the Pandavas, but they remained subservient to Duryodhana. These knowledgeable and wise people were reduced to sating Duryodhana, who through his control over state funds had made them submit to his power. Arjun, unaided by Krishna, defeated Drona, Bhishma and Karna in the battle fought in the kingdom of Virata; but in the final battle each one of them proved to be more than a match for Arjun and Krishna. This was accomplished by Duryodhana’s diplomacy which ensured that great warriors like Bhishma, Drona, Karna, Shakuni and Shalya fought for him. ‘The rulers of today need to emulate this policy. It was Duryodhana’s diplomacy that kept his hundred brothers—his bhayats—together, he educated them, strengthened their power. Duryodhana protected them and was hence supported by his brothers, the bhayats, the family elders and warriors from distant lands; he was the one who saw the genius of Karna. He was the creator of a grand alliance, but was eventually defeated by Arjun’s statesmanship, which secured the counsel of Krishna. If Duryodhana and Arjun were to come together, they would be invincible. Duryodhana suggests many dangers. Instead of serving the Pandavas and Panchali he opposed them, gave them grief and turned his statecraft on a path of sin. This is his principle failing. Ego is the cause of war. Duryodhana was ruled by his ego till the very end of his life; he could not take any counsel that was contrary to his ego. Ego is not only a sense of pride but a sense of ‘‘I’’ that overpowers reason and justice. Duryodhana alerts us to that danger. ‘A king has no rights for his own personal interests and enjoyment. If he thinks he has them, he vitiates the whole policy of the state, and is unfit as Duryodhana to rule a people.⟨fn:241⟩ ‘The thighs that support the body are finally shattered; similarly Duryodhana’s diplomacy is shattered by statesmanship. Once the elaborate edifice that supports diplomacy crumbles, it is rendered empty and destroyed. He will face the wrath of Bhim and Arjun, Dharmaraj will destroy Shalya and Sahadev will kill Shakuni. He will have to bear witness to their destruction and await his own death. ‘The chicaneries and knaveries, the Jobberies and the manoeuvrings, and bunglings of diplomatic gamblers in promotion of mere personal ends must eventually fall under the persistent hammer of the cool and calculating wisdom of patriotic heads whether wearing the crown or not.⟨fn:242⟩ ‘The diplomacy personified by Duryodhana and his brothers will be destroyed by Bhim’s mace. Those who escape the wrath of Bhim will be killed by the aesthete Nakul. Duryodhana will bear witness to this as well. The Spirit of Aesthetics and Arts will stultify the one hundred cadets and military rulers fallen under the evil grip of an ominous self- centered policy. They will be metamorphosed by the policy of Nakul from the bodies of dangerous cadets and rowdy soldiers into those peaceful and virtuous citizens.⟨fn:243⟩ ‘The next hall is that of Dushasana, who represents the punitive powers of a king. He followed Duryodhana and insulted and dishonoured Panchali instead of serving the rightful claimants to the throne. He will be destroyed by Bhim, who will drink his blood. The Spirit of Power and Protection raised by the Hand Divine for the service of the nation will one day kill this imp of brute physical force, this minion of military and regal power and will, to set an example, drink his blood like a Spirit of Retribution, if not revenge. Let rulers beware!⟨fn:244⟩ ‘Right opposite the hall of Arjun is the hall of Karna. He represents generosity, gift and munificence. This generous one is born of Kunti. A king who is not generous is impotent. A king who is generous to a fault will survive even if he is otherwise foolish and depraved. But Karna is certain to be destroyed when he comes face to face with Arjun and his charioteer Krishna. Bhishma has described Karna’s virtues and follies. O thou of excellent vows, without any reason thou speakest ill of all the Pandavas! Sinfully didst thou come into the world. It is for this that thy heart hath been such. Through pride, and owning also to thy companionship with the low, thy heart hateth even persons of merit!⟨fn:245⟩ ‘In absence of these follies, Karna has great qualities and the potential to be good. I know thy prowess in battle, which can with difficulty be borne on earth by foes! I know also thy regard for Brahmanas, thy courage, and thy great attachment to alms-giving! O thou that resembles a very god, among men there is none like thee!⟨fn:246⟩ ‘The power of generous gifts, patronage and munificence is the greatest prerogative of the crown. A policy that relies upon the power of its generous hand will only fail where it marches against the combined forces of the Progressive and Just principles of public Weal, or degenerates into vanities and jealousies!⟨fn:247⟩

‘After that is the hall of teachers. Drona and Ashwatthama are installed there. A teacher and a brahmin is one who pursues knowledge and the arts for their own sake; he does not use his learning to benefit himself but imparts this knowledge to the one most deserving of it. This is the mark of a brahmin; he need not be a dwija. Those like Armstrong and Krupp who invented the modern canons are also brahmins by this logic. If these brahmins were to join the battle and use their weapon of knowledge on the unlettered people, it would violate the principles of eternal dharma and invite the destruction of the world. Parashurama is the only brahmin to have wielded weapons for the sake of dharma. He had to cease waging war once dharma prevailed. His powers eventually merged into the power of Ram. It was Drona who, through years of effort, acquired the knowledge of weapons and imparted it to Arjun. One noble aspect of state policy is to invite and nurture teachers who spend their life in pursuit of knowledge. But when such mighty warrior brahmins forsake their duty as teacher and join a battle against Arjun—a battle against right on behalf of wrong—Krishna has to counsel Arjun to destroy a teacher who deviates from the path of duty and dharma. ‘When learning abuses its functions and lands its strength to help wicked policies, the Angel of Divine Wisdom must hold up his aegis to protect the Spirit of Progress and, if that Spirit has pious scruples against self-protection, then, to create new agencies for the purpose.⟨fn:248⟩ ‘Arjun will not kill his teacher. How is Drona to be destroyed? A brahmin wielding weapons is capable of greater valour than a kshatriya; but he would never acquire the heart of a kshatriya. A kshatriya would never lay down his arms at the news of his son’s death; but Drona lay down his arms. That is the weak point in a brahmin. His heart is soft there. During the war many sages came to the battlefield and advised Drona to give up fighting on the side of immorality. Can a brahmin’s heart resist an appeal to the eternal principles of Dharma and knock off scruples that his higher nature projects before his eye? This sage counsel shook Drona’s resolve, and Dhrishtadyumna felled him. Dhrishtadyumna, born of the same sacrificial fire as Panchali, was born to destroy a man who had deviated from his duty both as a brahmin and as a teacher. He is the Spirit of Audacious Light— Bold Reform—born of Burning Flames to destroy the overgrowth of Learning’s Power where his power is exerted behalf of Regal Power and against the Angel of Progress and his brothers.⟨fn:249⟩ ‘Bhim taunted Drona: If wretches amongst Brahmanas, discontented with the avocations of their own order but well-versed in arms, did not fight, the Kshatriya order then would not have been exterminated.⟨fn:250⟩ ‘Just as the shudras are forbidden from usurping the functions of a brahmin, the brahmin is forbidden from usurping kshatriya duties. A person who violates this principle deserves punishment. Bhim bears no infringement of Duties and Discipline.⟨fn:251⟩ ‘Ashwatthama is part of the same hall. He represents the potential of a brahmin to be depraved and immoral when motivated by pure revenge. He is an example of a learned man becoming demonic. Ashwatthama coveted Krishna’s Sudarshan Chakra and misused the Narayanastra and Brahmastra against the Pandavas. Krishna, who knew the secrets of these weapons, got Arjun to counter them. In times of political turmoil, when the Kauravas use brahmins to wield the Brahmastra, Arjun has to counter it by equally powerful weapons so that the weapons destroy each other. ‘When the sacerdotal and learned classes yield to being set up in sectarian spirit against the path of what is right and progressive in the state and among the people, the Spirit of Progress may as well raise counter-sects and break the force of the former by allowing them to dash against the latter. This is meeting Brahmastra with Brahmastra. It is what we in these days would call setting up journals against journals and congresses against congresses in order to further the cause of Progress and thrash out superior results.⟨fn:252⟩ This is pitting brahmin against brahmin and Shastra against Shastra. ‘But if Ashwatthama were to use the Narayanastra and not the Brahmastra, it should not be countered and be allowed to burn itself down. If the brahmins lay down their own weapons and use the divine weapon of the Creator, Arjun should not counter it but see in its light where righteousness is and where it is not. It can cause no harm; it will only help distinguish right from wrong. ‘This is the weapon of Divine Learning. The flames of Divine Learning can never hurt the cause of Righteousness if they are allowed to burn themselves away unopposed, for they can only show where Righteousness is and where it is not. Opposition makes them more critical and searching. These flames can only be fanned and rendered more irresistible by such opposition; while left to themselves they pass away into the lights of Nature and leave no vantage to those who had generated them.⟨fn:253⟩ ‘That depraved Ashwatthama was punished. The gem that adorned his head was taken away from him. He roams the dark regions of the world writhing in agony. The gem represents the light of true learning, the only true adornment of a brahmin. What can be dearer to a brahmin? I believe that brahmins of today are like Ashwatthama. They have lost the light of their learning and their utterances are cries of pain. They are, like Ashwatthama, cursed by Krishna. ‘The last hall is Pitamah Bhavan. ‘‘He is the Spirit of the Traditions, Experience, and Wisdom of Ages.’’ Bhishma Pitamah is the embodiment of traditional wisdom. His learning, morality and virtues are a source of hope for this country. But when he leads the forces of immorality, Krishna will take up arms in violation of his pledge and place Shikhandi to fight him. Bhishma cannot fight Shikhandi and will fall to his arrows. There are occasions in the life of nations when Bhishma surrenders his wisdom and experience to the forces that oppose righteousness. Bhishma is required to act in the interest of the country and for dharma. But when he sides with the Kauravas to fight the Pandavas, Arjun must search out Shikhandi-like aspects of his life and place them before him. Bhishma will not be able to fight that and lie willfully on his bed of arrows. ‘The Spirit of Tradition is invincible. But find out an apparition of some of the vagaries that are haunted by this Spirit and unman his heart and keep yourself shooting from behind the apparition. The Spirit of Tradition will then lie prostrate upon a bed of arrows piercing his body through a thousand new holes.⟨fn:254⟩ ‘This is the mode of piercing a body withered by tradition. But Bhishma does not die; he lives on his bed of arrows. Traditions and customs do not die easily. Yudhishthir, the virtuous one, benefits from the counsel of wise Bhishma. The gravity, nobility and crystalline charity of this wisdom is apparent in the Shanti Parva and Anushasan Parva. Imbued with this inexhaustible wisdom, Yudhishthir becomes fit to rule for the benefit of the state and people. ‘What rare wisdom is stored up in the traditions and customs of our nation? While not yielding to what is wrong and rotten in them, it is worth our while to see that we do not allow them to pass away from our midst before some wise and impartial soul-seers extract the stores which the Spirit has preserved so long and is only too willing to hand over to fit and willing souls. In this hall of this Grandfather-Spirit, we try to sit as his apt pupils with His Highness at our head, and ever jealous when the Spirit seems to lean in favour of the Kauravas.’⟨fn:255⟩ With these words Shankar Sharma concluded his discourse. Vidya Chatura: ‘The Vidura Bhavan is situated right behind the Kaurava Bhavan. That is where we meet our visitors and friends. You have been to that ‘‘Visitors and Friends’ Hall.’’ There is another floor above all these halls; right at the back on that floor is Subhadra Bhavan. That hall has four seats: Subhadra Asan, Parikshit or the

Heir Apparent seat, the seat of Wealth and Prosperity and the seat of Special Persons. These seats help us reflect upon and secure the welfare of the royal authority and our people. There are three other halls on that floor: the Manushya Deha Bhavan or the hall of Human Body, Moksha Bhavan or the hall of Salvation and Chakravarti Bhavan or the hall of Sovereign Power. In Chakravarti Bhavan we discuss our relations with the government and our duties and rights as constituent units of the British Empire. The policies of the government, its actions, intentions and advice are collated and deliberated upon in this hall. We also receive and honour British officials in this hall as per their rank and protocol. Moksha Bhavan has four seats: salvation through right conduct and devotion, salvation through freedom, salvation in battlefield and one seat to consider various ways in which death occurs. There is a seat of Vyasa placed at the centre of this hall which is given to a great soul who has conquered life and death. The Manushya Deha Bhavan has four seats: the king’s body, the deviant body, the imprisoned body and the ageing body. ‘Kurukshetra, where we are, is our ‘‘Council Hall.’’ You can see the statue of the late Maharaj on this central pillar. On all sides of the pillar are scenes depicting the history of our state. The statue holds a revolving disc. The grooves in the disc equal the number of halls in the observatory. A telescope lens has been placed in each groove, which allows one to see each hall. That disc is the telescope of this political observatory. The Maharaj and his council of ministers sit around this sacred statue to deliberate upon matters of state administration and Maharaj Maniraj remains conscious to ensure that the purpose of each hall and all the seats is never forgotten.’ Chandrakant: ‘Does that imply that Kurukshetra has a purpose different from the other halls in the observatory?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Kurukshetra is the assembly hall for the king and his council of ministers. The halls are for the ruler’s ‘‘self-training,’’ for him to think about relevant issues in seclusion. The purpose of each hall has been described to you. No matter, no issue should remain unobserved. We have a well-classified library in each hall that aids reflection and decision-making. We have found out and developed the classification of Vyasa sufficiently for our purposes.’⟨fn:256⟩ Chandrakant: ‘You have turned the characters of a poem regarded as historical into allegories. Are you not accused of atheism?’ Vidya Chatura smiled and said, ‘It is not our purpose to dispute the historicity or otherwise of the Pandavas and Kauravas. The truth about their historicity is to be researched by persons like yourself. Why should we assume that the great poet did not include allegories in his historical account? The late Maharaj explored and further classified the seed given to us by Vyasa and created a place of beauty and education.’ Vir Rao: ‘In addition to beauty and wisdom, this must also provide solace to the Maharaj.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘The purpose of Dharma Bhavan is to illustrate the possibility of attaining heaven for an embodied person. Sri Krishna has said: Action alone is thy province, never the fruits there of. This wisdom provides equanimity and solace in each action. The hall of Human Body prepares the king for all stages of life. In the hall of the Sovereign, the king reviews the actions and policies of the Sovereign Power and if there are lacunae in their policies, he considers them in the appropriate hall and formulates a policy of dealing with them in this Council Hall. The ministers execute a policy thus formulated. He also realises that ‘‘action alone is his province, never the fruits there of.’’ He attains equanimity and solace in the hall of Human Body and the hall of Salvation. Here, the Maharaj internalises the wisdom of the ancients and collects it for the future. Here His Highness provides a kindergarten to study what Bacon called “The Wisdom of the Ancients,” and here we also lay the germs for the evolution of a brighter, benigner future for our State and Subjects.⟨fn:257⟩ Vir Rao: ‘I have been cured of my crass humour. Pradhanji, as I think about what you have just told us, I am filled with a sense of relief. It is true, your Highness, what the Pradhanji says. It is of no use leading a fidgety life and be mourning and grumbling over things over which we have no control.’⟨fn:258⟩ Chandrakant: ‘Maharaj, counting the beads of a rosary gives solace, but these halls and each seat therein are more sacred than counting beads. You will certainly secure the future of your people through research, sage advice, experience, knowledge, intellect, morality, the study of Shastras and other books as also deliberate action. Even if you do not succeed in securing their welfare in some aspect, it would not be for the want of effort as the fruits of action are not your province. You will attain fulfillment through such action.’ Vir Rao: ‘My friend is practically blessing your Highness without seeming to do so. It is a political way of doing it, but I do not complain of it after this day’s explanations of politics. I too tender unqualified apologies for the vagaries of my Dhrishtadyumna and join in blessing your Highness openly and definitely though in less refined terms.’⟨fn:259⟩ Chandrakant: ‘Maharaj, you have exerted yourself a great deal for our sake. You are known for your courtesy and civility. But today we feel a special fondness for you as we share in your idealism.’ Vir Rao: ‘I say ‘‘Ditto’’ to all that has fallen from my friend’s lips.’⟨fn:260⟩ Maniraj: ‘Vir Raoji, it is more difficult for a king to know and understand the innermost thoughts of commoners than it is for commoners to know the workings of a king’s mind. Therefore, I am also eager to understand the views of scholars like yourself. You speak as frankly to me as you would to a member of your family. This is a new experience for me and it gives me great pleasure.’ Vir Rao: ‘I must say that if more kings were to cultivate your idealism, the dreams of Shankar Sharma and Pravindas will be realised to some extent, and the British will contribute to the regeneration of our native states.’

Shankar Sharma: ‘If Vir Raoji accepts this possibility, it is a hopeful sign for our state.’ Chandrakant: ‘Maharaj, other rulers may or may not emulate you. But you are making a great effort to follow the duties of a king. So long as you perform your duties, you need not worry even if the world were to turn upside down. Your hopes and aspirations, your enthusiasm and your equanimity are great. This political observatory will assist you in your search for knowledge, experience and action, and with that you will attain all that a native state possibly can through ‘‘true statesmanship.’’ If you achieve this, you must consider your life fulfilled. The rest we leave to Pradhanji.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘It is lunch time, and we must obey that part of our duty as well.’ They dispersed. Maniraj’s sense of despondency and gloom dispersed as well.
chapters.summary: Maniraj, troubled by royal duties, finds renewed hope guiding guests through the Malla Mahabhavan, his father's unique observatory for future rulers.

chapters.title: Chandrakant's Confusions
paragraphs: Chandrakant’s Confusions How was that visit to the Malla Mahabhavan useful for me? How does the discussion about the condition of the native states and a discourse on the Mahabharata aid my search for Sarasvatichandra? Do these diversions not hamper it? Chandrakant was walking about on the ramparts of the Saundarya Udyan, his mind in a whirl. Initially, he had hoped that Vidya Chatura would assist in his mission. But several events—the incident with the outlaws, Kumud’s death, Samant Mulu’s illness—had intervened, and gradually his hope had turned into despair. Chandrakant had decided to go out unaided in search of Sarasvatichandra. Gunasundari had assuaged his anxieties, but that did not further his mission. For two days he had participated in lofty discussions about statecraft, which were of no use for his mission. How was he now to tell Gunasundari—who had such deep affection for Sarasvatichandra—that he no longer needed her help? These questions became a quandary for Chandrakant, and he walked around scratching his head, looking for some solution from the world around him. The ramparts separated the garden from a large, open public square meant for the entertainment and leisure of the citizens of Ratnanagari. The ramparts extended to a set of rooms where Gunasundari received visitors. Below he could see Kusum’s pleasure garden and ponds. Large trees obscured his vision of the rest of the building and the garden. In the distance he could see the fortifications of Ratnanagari and the grand royal palaces.

The public square hummed with activity. Many traders who had come from distant villages had set up makeshift shops in the square; many had come with cartloads of grain and other produce. They haggled over prices with the town’s merchants and their agents. Caravans had set up tents and sold camels, horses, cattle, sheep and goats. Foreign goods that had come via the ports were being sold and bought. Beggars, mendicants and brahmins sought alms in their distinctive styles. State officials could also be seen walking about grandiosely among them. Chandrakant observed this pompous show before him, and thought, is it not possible that Sarasvatichandra is part of this crowd, and is looking for me? Is there no one among these people who could provide some clue about his whereabouts? He languidly put his hand in his pocket; some letters came out. He had already read them. He put them back in his pocket, and mused aloud, ‘Ganga has taken very ill in Bombay. She needs me there. Sansarilal wrote that there is no one in my family who is willing to look after her. Kiki says that her mother will die from lack of care if I did not return soon. ‘My clerk informs that my business has suffered in my absence and is likely to go under if I did not return soon. There is money required for household expenses. These are not more important than Sarasvatichandra. Ganga’s death will be a shock and it would be criminal not to be around her. But no one knows how serious her illness is. Chandrakant cannot abandon the search and return.’ He scratched his head from under his headgear and paced up and down the rampart. In a short while Pravindas and Shankar Sharma joined him. They sat down on a terrace. Chandrakant’s agitation was evident, and they enquired about it. Chandrakant: ‘You know that I have come in search of Sarasvatichandra. My search has not progressed. There is illness in my house and I am required there. I think it is now time for me to leave your company.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘Where do you intend to go?’

Chandrakant: ‘I will manage my home front with the help of friends. But so far I have no firm commitment as to how you would help me in my efforts to find Sarasvatichandra. I will go where God takes me.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘Do you want help from us or from the state?’ Chandrakant: ‘That is up to you.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘There are two ways in which help from the state can be obtained. If there is a crime that has been committed within our territory, the police can investigate the matter. Aarthdas is to be brought before the court, and to that extent our police have been investigating the matter. Second, our ‘‘Hospitality department’’ looks after our state guests. But you are not a state guest. You are not here on a matter concerning the state. Nevertheless, you are a guest of our Pradhanji; he considers you a member of the family, and for that reason the Maharaj and all of us see you as one of us. It is our duty to provide any assistance that you might require.’ Chandrakant: ‘It is certain that Sarasvatichandra is somewhere in this state, probably in disguise. Unless I know how the state intends to deal with the problem, how can I specify the assistance that I require?’ Pravindas: ‘There is still some hesitation in you. Pradhanji felt that since the police are already investigating the matter, there was no need to put you through unnecessary hardship.’ Chandrakant: ‘My anxieties would certainly reduce if I knew more about the police investigation. It would also help me make a specific request.’ Pravindas: ‘That can be known without undue delay.’ Chandrakant: ‘I want to go and search for him myself. Pradhanji should not worry about any hardship that I might face. That in fact will give me peace. I have been sitting around doing nothing, and that agitates me.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘Maharaj Shri himself and Pradhanji are both concerned and to distract you from your worries, they spend time with you in Malla Mahabhavan. They feel a deep familial affinity with a friend of Sarasvatichandra.’ Chandrakant: ‘What I considered to be a lack of concern for Sarasvatichandra in fact turns out to be deep affection. This gives me much relief. But my agitation would lessen only when I roam in search of him.’ Pravindas: ‘We shall not prevent you.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘We shall soon resolve this problem. Moreover, this letter has been received by Pradhanji. He does not know the sender. But the letter mentions Sarasvatichandra; hence he has sent it for you.’ Chandrakant took the letter. It was written by Ganga, but she had forgotten to address it to him and instead sent it to Vidya Chatura. The letter was short. I am unwell, but I do not want you to come back. Your family thinks that if Sarasvatichandra were to die or remain untraced, the money would come to you. Therefore, they use my illness as a pretext to call you back. They will spend all that money, none of which will remain with you or Sarasvatichandra. Sarasvatichandra has true feelings for us, something that your family does not. Therefore, do not listen to your family and keep looking for him. Some persons sent by Dhurtalal visit your family occasionally and give them some money. Do not be misguided by them. I am unwell, but I would not be sorry if I were to die. I have never been happy in your family, and I am not likely to be either. If I were to die, Sarasvatichandra will look after my children and care for them. So don’t worry about me, and keep looking for Sarasvatichandra. Chandrakant perspired; his forehead was covered with sweat. He bit his lips and tried to conceal his feelings. He put the letter in his pocket and said, ‘This letter is for me. Someday I will clarify the matter. For the present, please provide all the help you have promised.’ Pravindas: ‘Very well. We shall discuss the matter with Pradhanji and inform you.’

They both left. Chandrakant was disturbed. Neither the beauty of the garden nor the bustle of the public square could provide any distraction. Then he heard a distant voice singing. The inert moon wanes thinking of the moonstone. He was startled. His eyes searched for the singer.
chapters.summary: Chandrakant grapples with family duties and his quest for Sarasvatichandra, finding his resolve tested by a revealing letter and a mysterious, distant song.

chapters.title: Starry-eyed
paragraphs: Starry-eyed Kumud Sundari, accompanied by Bhakti Maiya and the other ascetics, set out on her journey to Sundargiri. That very morning Sarasvatichandra, accompanied by Viharpuri and Radhedas, came down the mountain to visit Surgram and the sea coast. The western side of the mountain was particularly beautiful. The ‘incline’ of the mountain extended right up to the sea; the ‘gradient’ was almost like well-arranged marble steps. Some parts were invisible from the top and seemed to disappear under the rocks. The waves crashed against these rocks. The verdant forest, the tall green grass, the black rocks with pointed tops and the serpentine pathways filled the eyes. It was the month of Chaitra. The sky was cloudless. The first rays of the sun seemed to bathe the mountain with light. The last of the stars had set. The sky had a pristine blue clarity and, unlike the roaring sea, it was still. It extended beyond the horizon. When this clear, unadorned but glowing sky provided a canopy to the lofty mountain, Kumud Sundari in company of the ascetics had climbed halfway up the steep mountain. She and the other women sat down to rest their weary limbs. The spot where they sat down was on a ‘curve’ on the path. It was situated such that a person coming down the mountain would not be able to see a person at the curve until they were almost face to face, but it gave a clear view of the path below. There were many ‘landing places’ along the way; some were on either side of the path, some were shaped like a circle, while others were built as a rectangular platform. Pilgrims halted at these landing places to take rest and regain their strength. Kumud Sundari had already climbed halfway up the mountain. The ‘bracing’ wind of early morning combined with some unarticulated enthusiasm did not tire her at all. Her cheeks were flushed, her limbs strangely relaxed. She participated eagerly in the banter of her companions, locking and unlocking her fingers as she walked. The slight heaving of her breasts, her halting speech, her shallow breathing, her shy eyes, the crease on her forehead and the slight disarray of her hair and clothes all gave a sense that she was either exhausted by the effort or in a state of great excitement. It was difficult to say with conviction what her true state was. But a careful observer would have surmised that physical exertion and mental excitement had both combined to create the strange sensations she experienced. Kumud’s beauty, her clothes and ornaments made her stand out in the group of ascetics. Bhakti Maiya was tall and broadly built; her complexion was dark and she was ugly to look at. All other women, save one, were taller than Kumud. The one who was shorter was almost dwarf-like and stoutly built. All of them had dark complexions, some a shade darker than others. But if colour is not the only marker of beauty, one or two of them were truly beautiful and luminous. All of them wore ochre clothes. Kumud had worn a silk chunari given to her at the temple. The dwarf-like ascetic had folded her other clothes in a white bundle, which she carried. When she had drowned, she had worn her usual ornaments. They still adorned her body. Kumud surrounded by her companions looked like a sliver of moon in the monsoon sky. Bhakti Maiya caressed her affectionately, and said, ‘Beta Madhuri, you must never have exerted yourself so much ever before!’ ‘That is true,’ said Kumud. ‘But the company of pious women and the hope of entering a sacred space have made my physical pain and mental agonies disappear. Maiya, how far is Yadu Shrunga?’ ‘We have come half way. We have some way further to climb.’

‘Madhuri Maiya, your delicate feet are tired and look like withered lotus stumps; let me press them,’ said the dwarf-like ascetic called Vamini, as she sat down to press Kumud’s feet. ‘Vamini Maiya, your feet and mine are built alike. If my feet are tired, so must yours be. Please do not press my feet.’ And Kumud ever so gently removed Vamini’s hands from her feet. ‘Maiya, my feet are tough as iron pillars. You are trying to conceal the fact that you are tired. But can your lotus face hide your fatigue?’ Vamini continued to press Kumud’s feet. ‘Vamini, unlike you, my hands and feet are not deformed. Let me do your work,’ said Bhakti Maiya, and sat down to press Kumud’s feet. Vamini: ‘If you want to remove all incongruities, you should step aside and let Mohini Maiya press her feet; let beauty be joined by beauteousness.’ The dark but strikingly beautiful Mohini took Vamini’s place. Bhakti: ‘One has to do the right thing. But tell me who of these two is beauty and who is beauteousness?’ Vamini and Bhakti gazed upon Kumud and Mohini with playful eyes. Mohini: ‘We all consider Madhuri beautiful. Hence she is beauty. Like her body her virtues are beauteous, hence her soul must also be a thing of beauty. Thus she is both beauty and the essence of beauteousness. Her body, that which is seen, is beauty and her soul, the unseen, is beauteousness. What do you have to say, Bansari Maiya?’ Mohini asked another attractive companion. Mohini’s face glowed with the allure of quiet love. Bhakti: ‘We will carry her the rest of the way.’ Kumud: ‘Maiya, that would be improper! I cannot be such a burden to these pious women. I will climb up slowly.’ Bansari embraced and kissed Kumud, and said, ‘Madhuri! Mother Goddess has sent you to the sacred domain of Yadunandan. It is our duty to assist you in this pious act. Listen to what the song says. A virtuous one, together with A pious one

Finds the formless one. The formless one awakens And frees one from the Cycle of birth and death. Mohini brought out her sarangi and set the song to tune.
