The melody of the song and the instrument permeated the morning sky. Vamini: ‘The three of you together resemble Brahmani, Mahalakshmi and Rudrani. I am filled with joy. Madhuri Maiya, you are as alluring as this clear sky flanked by the vast sea on one side and the mighty mountain on the other. Last night we all witnessed the agony of your heart. We are personally not unfamiliar with pain such as yours, but we bear our pain as a condition given to us by Yadunandan. We are also familiar with beauty and love. Among householders marriage is consummated before love, but we immerse ourselves in devotion to God; we do not marry a man but remain at the mercy of the formless one. But if we ever experience desire we submit to it and accept marriage. Kamadev, the god of desire was born of Mahalakshmi, and the pain that love and desire cause are alluring. We have experienced joys and sorrows and hence we understand your condition. We will help you overcome this agony. Our love leads us to the formless being. If you ever love again, emulate our ways of loving. Forget your sorrow, your weariness and listen to the song of love that permeates the sacred space where we shall take you.’ ” Vamini stood facing Kumud and, swaying to the tune of the sarangi, began to sing. Bansari joined her voice to the song. Behold the beauty of the Unmanifest, A thing of beauty yourself; The illusion of the manifest plays, And you are the god of love. You satiate with the drink of A man’s presence. Behold the light of the Unmanifest That enters your heart. Awaken the god within Through the love of a man;

Make the unsullied beloved Dance in the joy of Yadunandan. The worldly joy is the True meaning of love; It is the path of salvation Given to the beauteous one. Vamini had a melodious voice. Her dance was beautiful. The song, the singer, the dance and the dancer and the accompanying instrument so merged into each other that it was difficult to separate them. The soft light of dawn, the bracing wind and vast picturesque expanse of land were filled with the enchanting music. The whole group became one with the song and swayed to its melody. But the song had a different impact on Kumud Sundari. She understood nothing of the philosophy of the seen and the unseen, of form and formlessness; but the longing and love of the woman suddenly churned her heart. The man she had managed to momentarily forget came back and reclaimed her attention. She remembered the time when her heart was moved by love for the man and his ideals, when she had aspired to undertake her life’s journey as his partner and wife; she remembered her longing and desire to fill his heart with secret messages of love. Destiny willed otherwise and her lover, so keen to take her on a journey of pure love, turned melancholy. His place was taken by a husband who desired only what her body could provide and whose dreams were confined to their bed-chamber and the household. Even that husband turned an enemy, those dreams were destroyed and in a moment, life showed her many different facets. Vamini’s song produced this collage of images in Kumud’s mind. She was besieged with questions: Why did I leave Suvarnapur? Why was I saved from the outlaws? From the river? The sea? Why was she saved from taking her own life? Why did she begin a new journey to the mountain? Why did Sarasvatichandra join the group of ascetics? Why did he become the chosen one? What was the meaning of her desire to see him? What was her intention? All these questions and possibilities surrounded Kumud like the rocks strewn around her, useless and unbreakably hard. But it was imperative that she walk over them. Should she be surprised that they hurt her delicate feet? All her questions were equally futile, complex and without solution, but they were inevitable; they were thorns in her heart. All these thoughts played with her mind to the rhythm of the song; they extended and dispersed and came together; they remained steady and trembled like the strings of the sarangi. Kumud was petrified by all these forces acting upon her. All she heard were the anguished cries of her own heart. Tears flowed from her eyes. The song and dance came to an end. Bhakti got up, affectionately held Vamini by her chin, and said, ‘Vamini, your song, this morning, this place and these beautiful women—is this not the most apt situation for Sri Krishna’s Ras Lila?’ Before Vamini could respond, Viharpuri and Radhedas turned the bend on the pathway escorting Sarasvatichandra. Surprised to see this group of women, they hesitated and stopped. The women also gathered themselves and stood up. Bhakti came forward and greeted them with the familiar call of the ascetics of Yadu Shrunga, ‘Nandko Nandan ek anand det hai!’ The son of Nand gives unsullied joy to all. Everyone, except Kumud and Sarasvatichandra, responded to the call. The two who had remained unmoved by the call looked at each other. The man clad in unfamiliar ochre robes did not go unnoticed by the eyes that thirsted for his vision—Kumud recognised him instantly. Seeing her, Sarasvatichandra thought that Kumud had suddenly come face to face, but immediately reasoned that Kumud could not possibly be in a place like this. His first instinct was to take his eyes off her, but his heart had its own ways and was drawn to this statuesque presence. Even Kumud’s tearful gaze could not resolve his conflict. Mild as thy cheeks the moon’s new beams appear, And those soft eyes adorn the timid deer; In rippling brooks thy curling brows I see, But only view combined these charms in thee.⟨fn:261⟩

Sarasvatichandra was stunned. The visage in front of him was unattainable even to lovelorn heroes of poetry, but the woman who stood facing him was real! He tried to calm his nerves and struggled to appear resolute, but his restless eyes refused to obey his commands. The ones trying hardest to appear calm were in fact caught in a whirl of emotions. Both groups of ascetics, despite their loud call, had peace and quietude in their hearts. The two ‘‘householders’’ appeared calm, but their hearts were in turmoil. All the women except Kumud came forward and stood in a circle. Bhakti Maiya began the conversation. Bhakti: ‘Viharpuri! Where are you taking this new guest, the one for whom Guruji has desired a long life?’ Viharpuri: ‘Guruji has desired that he should be shown the sacred and beautiful spots of Surgram.’ Vamini: ‘So, is this Navinchandraji?’ Kumud, of course, knew. Still she trembled. Viharpuri: ‘Yes, this is him.’ Mohini: ‘It is for the first time that I have seen in a man the combination of tranquil handsomeness and beauty. Viharpuri, why did Guruji destroy this worldly desire of many by secluding a man such as him away from the gaze of women?’ Viharpuri smiled, and said, ‘Mohini Maiya! It is our Yadunandan who decides one’s place in this world. Guruji imparts the knowledge of the formless one to those who have the fitness to receive such knowledge. The moon and the stars fade away when the sun rises. Whether the light of knowledge dispels the illusion of this world or not depends entirely upon the capacity of the one to whom the knowledge is imparted. Guruji remains aloof and distant from this process.’ Bansari: ‘So has this man’s heart imbibed the knowledge of the formless essence of Sri Krishna who agitated and excited the hearts of the gopis, but remained untouched like a lotus?’

Viharpuri: ‘Bansari, he had heard the call of that flute even before he met Guruji.’ This response delighted the hearts of all the women except Kumud. Kumud’s heart was inflamed. Bansari bowed to Sarasvatichandra and addressed him shyly, ‘Oh pious one! Man and woman are two distinct flowers that grow on the same tree. Their colour and fragrance are different, but their togetherness makes the performance of many duties possible and bears fruits. May you receive the sweetest possible form of togetherness. That is our blessing.’ Mohini: ‘I bless that you attain the most beautiful form of togetherness.’ Sarasvatichandra bowed his head to the two women and smiled in response. Vamini laughed and said, ‘Viharpuri, how long will this silent, statue-like guest of yours remain on Sundargiri? On which hill-top will he reside?’ Radhedas: ‘Vamini Maiya, our guest, who spends his time listening to the discourses and in deep reflection, will stay here as long as he finds Sundargiri attractive. At present, he is a privileged disciple of Guruji. Eventually, he will choose a spot of his liking.’ Vamini: ‘Would we have the privilege of hearing him speak? It is proper that Guruji has left the decision to him. But we should know his will.’ Sarasvatichandra was left with no option. His eyes were drawn to Kumud, his heart was in agony, but he had to play his part. He somehow managed to get his eyes to obey his will, smiled softly and said, ‘When female ascetics immersed in the formless god command, this being will find beauty even in his own speech. Oh virtuous women! Ever since Guruji made a gift of new life to this body, it is subservient to his wish. This mountain is beautiful not only by name, but animate and inanimate life on it is equally alluring. Guruji will determine which of these beautiful spots is fit for my habitation; his will is my command.’ Vamini: ‘Navinchandraji, your speech is as attractive as you are.’

Bhakti: ‘His speech is so alluring that though he gave no clear response, Vamini felt that she had received the response to her query—this is the power of beauty. Radhedas, where do you intend to halt for the night? At Surgram or back on Sundargiri? You can certainly respond to these questions.’ Radhedas: ‘You are defeated in the argument. Is there no third place where we can halt for the night?’ Vamini almost jumped with joy and said, ‘Oh Bhakti Maiya, forget about it! If Chandravali’s mother goddess speaks to Viharpuri, then there is a third possibility.’ All the women smiled. Viharpuri spoke gravely, ‘Radhedas, it is natural that women would emerge victorious in any debate about beauty. These disputes by their very nature lead us astray from the path of duty. It is in our best interest to proceed on our way with our guest.’ Vamini: ‘It is an insult to Sundargiri to show disdain for beauty.’ Viharpuri: ‘You are right. So we heard arguments in favour of beauty from those who are themselves beautiful. We rugged and hardened men should refrain from expressing any opinion about it. Vamini Maiya, as the day progresses the sun will get harsher. These rocks will heat up. It may not affect you, but this delicate flower will wither in its heat. We should proceed on our respective paths.’ As Viharpuri pointed towards Kumud, the women’s attention shifted to her pale, withered face, and their banter abruptly came to an end. As they parted, both groups called out in praise of Yadunandan. ‘Maharaj, this way please,’ the duo guided Sarasvatichandra. As he focused on the path ahead and disappeared with his escorts, the image of Kumud was etched on his mind’s eye. He heard the women calling out to Kumud, ‘Madhuri Beta! Madhuri Beta!’ These words remained with him merely as echoes. Though surrounded by her companions, Kumud’s eyes followed Sarasvatichandra till he had disappeared from view, and her eyes brimmed over. The women looked at each other, concerned, and conversed in whispers. Eventually Bhakti lifted Kumud up. Kumud protested in vain. But Bhakti, superior in strength, did not put her down and began her climb up the mountain. So far their banter had been loud. Now they spoke in whispers. Snatches of conversation made their way to Kumud. ‘A meeting of the stars!’ Bansari whispered to Mohini. ‘Of starry eyes or stars in the sky?’ Vamini butted in. Bansari pushed her aside, saying, ‘The stars know about themselves, but these eyes were in distress and were tremulous.’ Vamini jumped up and said, ‘There was anxiety and distress, and it was the distress of love.’ Mohini spoke in a voice choked with tears, ‘Sri Krishna’s will be done. The steadfastness of a yogi on one side, and the longing of love on the other! But sparks flew when their eyes met.’ Mohini sighed deeply as she walked behind Bhakti. They continued to speak in whispers. Mohini: ‘The yogi is as soothing as the southern wind. A man who would not trample even a creeper, a man as full of compassion as Shiva, why does he destroy her love root and branch?’ Vamini: ‘This is the man she longs for even if he is in an ascetic’s robes. He is afraid of being sullied by her presence like a wind that flows cautiously, having purified itself after being sullied by the touch of the flowering creeper.’ Kumud, who had lain inert on Bhakti’s shoulders, opened her eyes, prompting Bansari to enthusiastically observe, ‘Awakened by the buzzing of the bee drawn by her fragrance, the lotus opened herself as the light dawned.’ Bhakti shifted Kumud from one shoulder to the other. She looked at the rising sun and said, ‘The sun, resting for that ever so fleeting moment, hurriedly views all those who have bowed their heads to him and then rises above the mountains to gaze beyond the horizon.’ Mohini said, ‘Maiya, that sun will certainly come back to rest on the horizon. Please allow me to carry Madhuri.’ And she stretched her arms to lift Kumud onto her shoulder. Helpless, Kumud hesitantly said, ‘Maiya, your arms are bathed in perspiration. Please allow me to walk.’ ‘Madhuri, that is your perspiration, not mine.’
chapters.summary: Amidst a spiritual mountain ascent, Kumud Sundari grapples with deep emotions and echoes of past love, as her companions whisper about a destined, starry-eyed meeting.

chapters.title: Pilgrimage to Surgram
paragraphs: Pilgrimage to Surgram Surgram has many temples. All of them were situated outside the village at the point where the river meets the sea. The village had two streets parallel to each other. All the houses were arranged in three rows. The middle row had homes back to back. One of the streets was known as Guru Marg or the Gaur street, where the brahmins lived. The other street was called Chauta, where all other communities including scavenging communities, traders and peasants lived. A large Shiva temple was situated in the centre of the village. The area around the temple was paved. There were few worshippers at the temple. Most villagers had already offered their morning prayers. Sarasvatichandra and his companions arrived at the temple around nine in the morning. They sat on the platform to rest. Being in a village was a novel experience for one who had grown up in a large, glittering, glamorous bungalow in Bombay. Surgram was even more of a village. The house of the Karbhari of Suvarnapur and even the monastery on Yadu Shrunga had a grandeur of their own. This temple was structurally not very different from the Rajeshwara Mahadev, but its location within the village gave a very different feeling. Sarasvatichandra was still unwilling to believe that he had in fact come face to face with Kumud Sundari, but her image was etched on his mind. He could not erase that image and her presence gave rise to many thoughts and questions. The Shiva temple reminded him of the Rajeshwara Mahadev, and memories of events associated with it flooded his mind. These memories and images did not allow him to participate in easygoing conversation with his companions. Their conversation was punctuated by stretches of silence. In one such moment of silence, a brahmin came to offer his prayers. He rang the bell, bowed his head, threw some rice around, came out, removed his headgear and sat down on the temple steps. There were some young boys who came and sat around him. ‘Boys, listen! And remember that all other gods are full of cunning, except our Shivji who is as naïve as I am. That is why he is called Bhola Nath. Don’t you know the hell that awaits people who do not have a grain of intelligence, cannot control their temper and do not know how to control their heart’s desires? But those who are naïve and gullible are protected by our Bhola Nath. He is the god of the naïve and innocent. He is also round so that we can clasp him with both our hands. He is easy to please; even an offering of water pleases him. Therefore, worshipping Shivji is a sign of wisdom. He is so simple that a tree leaf satisfies him; he needs no home as he sleeps in the crematorium.’ Having had his say, the brahmin got up and approached the monks. ‘Bavaji, what brings you here today?’ ‘Mehtaji, this one in the middle is a guest of ours. Guruji desired that he should be taken to this sacred spot,’ Viharpuri replied. Mehtaji greeted Sarasvatichandra with folded hands and asked, ‘Your name please?’ Sarasvatichandra responded, ‘Navinchandra.’ Mehtaji: ‘The newspapers these days write about some Chandra. Are you him?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What do they write?’ Mehtaji: ‘A scholar from Bombay has left home. His name is also some Chandra.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I can satisfy your curiosity only if I know more. In which newspaper did you read this? Do you get newspapers here?’ Mehtaji: ‘The school and the library are nearby.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Will you take us there?’

All of them got up and walked up to a single-storeyed room. A piece of paper with ‘Library’ written in ink was pasted on its door. There was a box of books, one cushion and some bolsters in the room. A carpet covered the floor. The room did not have either table or chair. There were three newspapers, two sent by the state administration and one bought from the membership fees paid by the local members. The state provided one free newspaper to each village school, but if the members subscribed to a newspaper with their own contribution, the state provided a matching contribution. The same rule applied to the purchase of books. One Bombay newspaper carried a story titled, ‘Search for Sarasvatichandra—No. 10.’ This was published at the instance of Sheth Laxminandan. As Sarasvatichandra scanned the story, his heart raced and he could barely contain his tears. ‘Are there other newspapers?’ he asked. Mehtaji: ‘Yes. There is a newspaper published from Ratnanagari which is full of news about the tragedy in the family of our minister.’ Sarasvatichandra read the story with great trepidation. Pramaddhan is dead, Kumud Sundari has drowned. Saubhagya Devi has died and Buddhidhan has decided on renunciation. Sarasvatichandra was shocked. He rubbed his palpitating heart and could not hold back his tears. He would no longer be able to protect his secret. Mehtaji: ‘This news has pained you so. Are you Sarasvatichandra?’ Viharpuri: ‘Maharaj, knowledge and detachment are the only cure of sorrow.’ Radhedas: ‘Maharaj, if you tell us why this news perturbs you so much, we could find a way out.’ Viharpuri: ‘Guruji himself is beyond the world and its grief. But he does alleviate the pain of those near him. That does not constitute attachment with worldly matters.’ Sarasvatichandra bottled up his grief and somehow controlled his tears. But grief was etched on his face. Wiping the sweat off his forehead, he answered all the questions with one response. ‘Sarasvatichandra’s disappearance does not concern me in the least.

All the stories from Bombay are useless. But I have lived for a while in Suvarnapur and tasted the hospitality of Buddhidhanbhai. Therefore, I was momentarily overcome by grief. But that feeling has now subsided. Guruji has freed me from sorrow; hence we need not trouble him.’ Mehtaji’s curiosity was nipped in the bud. His two companions were also satisfied with Sarasvatichandra’s response. Just then a bania came in. He bowed to Viharpuri and said, ‘Maharaj, I seem to have fallen out of favour with you. You did not even inform me that you are in our village! But God answered my prayers and so I have the occasion to receive your darshan. Maharaj, please oblige this poor wretch by having your meal in my house.’ Viharpuri: ‘Sethji, please have a brahmin cook a meal for our consumption. We will go around, see the spots and come to your house. Mehtaji, can you come with us?’ Mehtaji: ‘I can be with you till school time. Where all do you intend to go?’ Viharpuri: ‘We want to visit all the sacred and beautiful spots.’ Mehtaji: ‘For that you will need two or three days.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Show us representative places which would give us the satisfaction of having seen the rest.’ Mehtaji: ‘That can be done before the sun sets.’ Viharpuri: ‘According to you, which are these spots?’ Mehtaji: ‘You should circumambulate all the temples around the place where the river meets the sea. There are some temples on the way. You should enter the sanctum sanctorum of each. The Ratnakareshwar Shiva temple, the temple of Radhekeshji, the Lakshmi temple and the Jain temple are man-made structures. The place where the river meets the sea, the temple of the mother goddess on the island, the Hari Kund at the foothills of the mountain, the port and the step-well, these are all spots of natural beauty. Sarasvatichandra: ‘You have pointed out temples and nature, but there must be interesting people as well.’

Mehtaji: ‘Yes. Among the people you need to meet, I am one; one other is our village priest while the third and fourth are for householders like us and not for renouncers.’ Sarasvatichandra could not suppress a smile, and said, ‘We already have the pleasure of meeting you. Please get me newspapers of the last five–six days. I will go with you and Viharpuri.’ Viharpuri: ‘Radhedas, instead of going to each and every temple, we should go to the Radhekeshji temple because today they are celebrating their annual festival of installation of the idol.’ Everyone agreed to the suggestion. On the way Mehtaji curiously asked, ‘Navinchandraji, where did you acquire this taste for newspapers? It belongs to our world of new learning.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I have some limited experience of new learning. But pray do tell me what the latest political news is?’ Mehtaji: ‘There are three kinds of political news. You already know of the developments in our state. Kumud Sundari is no more. Samant Sinh is dead. Rana Khachar is on a visit to Ratnanagari. There is a plethora of news about large states. In some the municipalities are bad; in others the English officials are up to no good. In some states the English norms are regarded as bad, while in others their implementation is poor. We can laugh at them, be angry or weep. The third set of news is about other native states. In some places they are praised to the skies while others are made out to be fit to ride donkeys. Everyone likes gossipmongers. Newspapers like scandals; they increase their sales. What can we do? People get the rulers they deserve and rulers get the people they deserve. Their administrators are also like them, and together they form Shivji’s wedding party, the newlywed couple and the motley crowd of pilgrims. Our people are illiterate and poor. They are unjust, jealous and take pleasure in the troubles of others. Officers are selfish, devoted to flattery, lazy and arrogant; they are fearful of men but not God. Kings are idiotic, lazy, proud, debauched, drunkards, oppressive and bankrupt. I am so weary of reading newspapers. Some days I feel like writing to the minister to request him to shut down this library, but other considerations prevent me. There is a saying that the Kazi has withered because he has to worry about the whole town. I have to worry about the whole world!’ Sarasvatichandra turned grave and gave no response. Conversation ceased. They walked on in silence. The condition of the country troubled his heart and mind. My country! My Kumud! My father! My Bombay! Kumud Country! he thought incoherently. As they approached the temples he began to feel calmer. On either side of the path there were temples. Some shrines were just a few feet tall while others were large and as high as two-storeyed buildings. The conversation turned to their architectural styles, their history, their management and their present condition. They switched from one topic to another and the talk clouded over Sarasvatichandra’s this-worldly concerns. Suddenly a question popped up in his mind: will the new age make these temples redundant and will their place be taken by societies and government offices? But before he could formulate a response the question vanished. Surgram was a village and its population did not have the wherewithal to create so many temples. In olden times Surgram was a major centre of pilgrimage and wealthy pilgrims arriving from distant lands had created this grand place. The path was narrow but clean. Just as circumstances of human beings change, this place, too, had seen both good times and bad. Once pilgrims stopped visiting the place and the fairs and festivals stopped, the place became desolate and derelict. There was a time when the temples were covered with moss and small plants grew out of them. Then Mallaraj began the conservation and rejuvenation of Surgram. The temples were cleaned of the overgrowth and grime and repainted. The path had been cleared of grass and pebbles and newly paved. In earlier times, colonies of crows lived inside the temples. Now there were varieties of birds that lived in the surrounding trees. The temple wells had broken and their water had turned putrid. They were now restored and their water was once again pure and sweet. The steps of many temples had broken down. They were repaired, and women devotees had placed offerings of grain on them. And yet the signs of decay had not completely disappeared.

Neem, peepal and banyan trees grew out of many temple walls and roofs. The pious people of the village who believed that trees have life had refrained from cutting them down. Just as we live surrounded by traditions and customs, they had allowed the branches of the sacred trees to remain as part of the structure. Mehtaji provided all this information to Sarasvatichandra. The two monks walked behind them silently. Sarasvatichandra: ‘Mehtaji Saheb, the nobility of the Indian mind is not limited to the preservation of human life alone. Its love of life extends not only to the protection of birds and animals but seeks to protect trees as well. Some may find fault with it. Even so, there is grandeur and nobility in such love. I feel proud to have been born in this land of such great souls. These scenes are a testimony to the compassionate hearts of our ancestors. Viharpuri!’ Viharpuri: ‘Yes, Maharaj.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Is a renouncer allowed to retain such pride and affection?’ Viharpuri laughed and replied, ‘Maharaj! All that resides in the hearts of pious, virtuous men is dear to the formless one as well, because such hearts are a testimony to the glory of the Creator.’ Radhedas: ‘I have learnt from Guruji that when all desires and attachments disappear, the calm mind of the renunciate retains compassion for the poor and meek, desire to reform the wealthy, forgiveness for the acts of evildoers and the longing for the realisation of the formless one.’ Viharpuri: ‘Maharaj, Radhedas’ response is apposite.’ Mehtaji: ‘Navinchandraji, English education will destroy all this.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The conservation of this place has been done during British rule at the hands of a king and his minister who are knowledgeable of English learning.’ Mehtaji: ‘That is absolutely true. I accept my error.’ They reached the temple of Radhekeshji. The temple was built on a plinth; one had to climb about fifteen steps to reach the large ornate temple door. On either side of the door was a platform. The temple had recently employed a watchman who sat on a mat, smoking a clay pipe. The temple’s offerings had also increased; hence it had also appointed a priest as a treasurer and storekeeper. As Sarasvatichandra set foot on the first step, the temple’s bell clock rang out eleven times. They stood and counted the bell. The ringing of the bell at the precise moment of their entry helped the transition to the new world they were about to enter. The temple door led to a paved compound which was walled on all four sides. There were rooms for the use of the administrators and priests. Three intricately carved gateways led to the mandap of the temple, which had a marble floor. The sanctum sanctorum was right at the back, where a throne was placed. Adjacent to it was the bed chamber of the deity and a water room. Sarasvatichandra had spent his childhood in Bombay and was familiar with British architecture. Before he could properly observe the temple’s architecture, devotional songs assailed his ears, adding to the unfamiliarity and novelty of his visual experience. A stout old woman had spread out a mat and she sat on it, singing loudly, beating her thighs and torso in tempo as she swayed to the rhythm of the song. I must go, I wish to go, such going is necessary; The body useless, the eyes without sight— Even the mighty have gone; Even those who rode elephants and horses and owned servants. The waters from the rivers have flown; They will not stay, nor will kings live forever, nor paupers. The pride of the haughty has gone; Even those who feasted on sweets have gone. Pray, pray, for it is all you can do. The song invoked thoughts of life and death. Sarasvatichandra felt like giving her a rupee or two. He searched in his pocket, and realised that he no longer had any money to call his own. He thought, I have no money to give to this woman who is a repository of such cultural wisdom. I have never extended my hand to seek alms, but my heart accepts the gift of culture! Or perhaps a brahmin’s heart is bound to receive the gifts of knowledge and culture. Moving ahead, he heard another song and stopped to receive another gift. Believe me one day To dust you shall return. One day the bird shall fly away That is the destiny of all. These words rang through his heart and churned it. They captivated him. Sarasvatichandra stood deep in thought, oblivious to the song. When he snapped out of his reverie, the singer was on the last stanza. The body is an illusion and false is your attachment; False are all your possessions; False are all those dear to you; Futile was your sojourn— At the hour of death all is futile. You shall repent when it is of no avail. Says Bhoja Bhagat, pray As I pray to Govinda. Believe me one day To dust you shall return. One day the bird shall fly away The body is an illusion. The only truth is the journey of the soul. The pertinent question is whether the journey to the world has been a fulfilling one. But the most significant and difficult question is: What is a life of fulfillment? Mehtaji: ‘Viharpuriji, this song has the teachings of all the religions. Attachment is false; the only certainty is death, and devotion is the path to the Creator. All this is fine, but which god is one to worship? Vishnu, Shankar, Shakti, Christ or Prophet Mohammed? In that temple we prayed to Shiva; in this we worship Radha-Krishna. Which one of these is true?’ Radhedas: ‘Shiva and Vishnu are one.’

Mehtaji: ‘If they are one, why are there so many names, so many different idols, a plethora of puranas and modes of worship? All the differences should be obliterated so that we do not have all this hassle, futile expense and pointless quarrels. My Shivji is pleased with a few leaves and some water; why should I give that up and go through these elaborate and expensive rituals?’ Viharpuri: ‘Mehtaji, God is formless and without attributes. There is only one God. But this realisation comes through the path of knowledge. God who is worshipped as a form is also one, but takes many forms and has different attributes. This is the path of devotion. This path has multiple modes of worship suitable to each form. One can attain devotion through any of these paths.’ Mehtaji: ‘But which of these paths and forms should one adopt?’ Viharpuri: ‘The choice depends upon one’s capacity.’ Mehtaji: ‘What capacity? How does that decide whether one should worship Shiva or Vishnu?’ Viharpuri: ‘Listen, everyone has a different capacity. The worship of idols is like the currents of a great ocean. Which wave do we choose? People follow what is customary. Just as a son follows his father, he also follows his father’s mode of worship. All duties and actions follow this principle of proximity and familiarity. Who is the father and who is the son? Their mutuality determines their reciprocal duties. It is a mother’s duty to feed her child at her breast, and not all those who are hungry. Similarly, it is the family’s duty and also a right to teach their progeny about the family deity.’ Mehtaji: ‘That means one should never forsake the customs peculiar to one’s family.’ Viharpuri: ‘No, one should not.’ Sarasvatichandra had followed this conversation with interest. He joined in with a question. ‘Viharpuri, is there not an error in this response?’ Viharpuri turned to him and asked, ‘What kind of error?’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘Yesterday morning, by the blessings of Guruji, I changed my customary family religious belief. You were a witness to it.’ Radhedas: ‘That is indeed correct.’ Viharpuri: ‘Maharaj, I made an error. Mehtaji, Navinchandraji will respond to your query. This will also give us a chance to learn from him.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘You know the saying that though one may be born a shudra, one’s actions could be that of a brahmin.’ Viharpuri: ‘Yes.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Likewise, one born in a family that follows the path of devotion may through cultivation adopt the path of knowledge.’ Mehtaji: ‘Should those who adopt the path of knowledge necessarily be critical of the path of devotion?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That criticism is unnecessary. Once we ascend to a higher step, we have no relationship with the lower step. We form a new relationship and with it, the old one ceases to be. This morning Viharpuriji had said that the need to worship an idol recedes as the seeker through his striving begins to receive the light of the formless being.’ Viharpuri was truly pleased. ‘Maharaj, I only parrot the teachings of our Guruji. You enlighten them.’ Radhedas: ‘And so doing, you broaden our hearts and minds.’ Mehtaji: ‘Navinchandraji Maharaj, which of the various paths of devotion should one adopt?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘You have little self-volition in the matter. It would depend on what you have been raised to follow, and what appeals to you. You will accept that either willingly or unwillingly.’ Viharpuri considered this statement for a while, searched his memory and said, ‘Maharaj, now I remember the Master’s teaching. What you have just said matches his teaching. Depending upon the space and time, hunger is satiated with different types of food. The hunger for devotion is similar. It is satisfied in some by devotion to Vishnu, in some by Shiva, some follow the Prophet while others

Christ. This is something one receives by birth and by living in a community. By giving up one’s religion and adopting another, one does not automatically acquire a higher capacity; one is often led astray by that. Therefore it is said: “Better is death in the discharge of one’s duty; another’s duty is fraught with danger.” But as a person acquires capacity, he also grows in knowledge.’ Mehtaji: ‘But is there unity even in your path of knowledge? There are followers of Kabir, of Jain philosophy, of Sankhya and Vedanta. Therefore, our path of devotion is better than your path of knowledge.’ Viharpuri: ‘In our system devotion is primary; it is the first step. The path of knowledge comes after that. It depends upon capacity and fitness.’ Mehtaji: ‘That may be so. But it is easy to boast about knowledge. Most of those who are boastful have neither knowledge nor devotion.’ They entered the temple proper. It was time for the school to open. Mehtaji gave the old newspapers to Sarasvatichandra and went to the school. It was almost time for the raj bhog at the temple when food was offered to the deity. Gradually more and more worshippers filled the temple. There had been a marked increase in the village population in recent years. There was also a steady flow of pilgrims, but the temple was rarely crowded. Men and women, young and old hung around the temple; some sat, others stood leaning against the walls, some keenly studied the idol while others chatted or sang devotional songs. Some of the men had taken a ritual bath and walked around bare torso with various religious signs painted over their bodies. Some others walked around in what, in a village setting, must be regarded as beautiful and attractive clothes, albeit for a resident of Bombay they held no charm. The three young visitors in ascetics’ robes entered the temple. Viharpuri and Radhedas bowed before the deity. Sarasvatichandra made no bodily gesture, but his heart bowed to the deity. A devotee on his right stood on one leg and sang praise to the Lord’s beauty. Radhedas: ‘Maharaj, Radha waited all night long for Sri Krishna to appear. Similarly, a devotee waits for the Lord and imitates Radha by singing of love and longing. The Lord appeared before Radha in the morning. Ordinary lovers, moved by desire and passion, meet during the night. The Lord responded to Radha’s call after the darkness of illusion had been dispelled. Radha’s devotion had reached its zenith. This devotee worships the Lord of Radha with feelings and intensity similar to Radha.’ Sarasvatichandra observed the devotee who seemed to have no awareness of anything outside of his song and his devotion. The lotus has withered, denied your visage, The lotus has withered. Love of God kindles my body, The eyes cannot see you, o’ Krishna. Radha plays the veena, her song mesmerises the deer; Her song captivates the moonbeam; She paints tigers with her kohl; The deer and the moonbeam, frightened, Disappear. The sun dawns, But Krishna does not. The devotee lay prostrate before the deity with tears in his eyes. He got up and stood leaning against the wall with his eyes closed. His song had found its way into many hearts. Radhedas: ‘Navinchandraji, this prince among devotees has attained oneness with the divine. His joy is equal to that of Radha. This is the zenith of devotion.’ Sarasvatichandra gave no outward response. But his heart spoke out, ’Tis the yearning for the Beautiful!—for the Beautiful in the Divine. It is the Beauty which the sightseers admire, but to the Bhakta is a trance of intense love. There is a form of beauty floating on the air before his loving eye and singing the sweet melodies of Divine raptures into his wistful ears.⟨fn:262⟩ One elderly woman devotee stood singing before the idol. She had worn a string of basil beads around her neck and carried a basket of basil leaves as offering to the deity. She was emaciated with sunken cheeks and appeared to be in pain. Her clothes were darned and patched at many places. A young child, probably her son, stood clutching her feet and cried out from time to time. But she paid no attention to him; her gaze was riveted on the idol. She sang softly, only for the god. I hear his whispered step and climb hill forts to seek his sight. It’s the time frogs croak and peacocks call, the koel cries, the cuckoo shrills Indra exults, calls down the clouds on all four sides, lightning stops being shy the earth is newly dressed, awaits her meeting with the sky wants to look unready, like any other bride and Meera says to Hari why can’t you arrive.⟨fn:263⟩

Tears flowed uncontrollably from her eyes. She appeared like a woman possessed. She harboured a pain so deep that she was indifferent to the wailing of her child. Eventually a deep sigh escaped her. She picked up the basket of basil leaves and offered them to the deity. Clearly, she believed that her offering had been accepted and when she turned her back to the idol, her face was no longer lined with pain. She appeared calm. She picked up her child, made him pay obeisance to the god and went and sat near a katha vachak who was narrating the Bhagvad. Sarasvatichandra, ever a keen observer, remarked, ‘Viharpuri, this woman has some deep sorrow and grief. Her devotion is nectar to her heart. Today, we realised the healing power of devotion. Let us see what it can do for someone who is happy.’ Viharpuri: ‘Maharaj, we shall witness that as well.’ Before Viharpuri’s words could fall on his ears, Sarasvatichandra remembered Kumud. Kumud! Your grief drowned you. So many beautiful, delicate flowers like you are trampled under the weight of pain. How many like you wither and are ground to dust. This woman is also grief-stricken. But you did not receive the succour and healing balm that she received in this temple. Nothing could assuage your grief, not English learning, not the knowledge of Sanskrit, not your parents and not I. But this poor, unlettered woman received that life- giving nectar in this place. There was beauty in her pain. Was that you on the path? If that was indeed you, would you have received this nectar as well? Would this have lessened your grief? It is not within my powers to bestow such peace upon you. This pledge, this resolve of renunciation does not permit any proximity with you, not even that which we had in Buddhidhan’s house. Pramaddhan is dead. You have been widowed. You have come to Sundargiri. You are now free... It is possible for me to atone for my sins... But this decision to be a renouncer!... Kumud, was that really you? Is it possible? Are there not people who look alike? At any rate, all these are hypothetical issues and completely misplaced here. Sarasvatichandra managed to gain some control over his thoughts. His attention turned to a beautiful young woman who stood singing before the idol. She wore ochre robes; her face and body were delicate and beautiful. A few men stood at a distance and looked at her lasciviously. She was surrounded by women who formed a protective ring around her. This young woman was Chandravali’s niece. She had decided to follow her aunt and resolved to remain unmarried. This was not unusual for ascetics and did not invite any criticism. She had taken Sri Krishna as her husband. Her song and her body both reflected her desire for her husband-god. ‘Girdhari comes to me,’ she sang. Her longing, her desire and her bashfulness at the approaching lover were evident as she enacted the song. Girdhari comes to me, O’ He comes to my abode. She uncovered her face and opened her arms to embrace Sri Krishna. I hide from him. Girdhari comes to me, I, untouched, abashed, Hide from him. She ran towards the idol and kissed its feet, then stepped back and cast seductive looks at the idol. Possessed by her desire and passion for her divine lover she pleaded with him to unite with her. As Radha hid you, Mohan, I found you in Vrindavan. Mohan, beloved, be one with me. Beloved Mohan, be one with me. Suddenly, Sarasvatichandra had an epiphany. I swear—I swear—there is no lascivious note in these lines of our good friend Dayaram in spite of all that libidinous veneer over them which is meant to dazzle and catch into its flame the unlearned, worldly, sinking soul in order that she may rise therefore like the phoenix into the heaven of Devotion. Is then this a lewd religion as they say? Is this mere worship of the fetish as they say? Most certainly not. As I understand and realise the depth of this sweet girl’s heart, she is not more distant from the highest purity and abstractest devotion than Cowper was when he loved and worshipped the Eternal Fair in his Olney Hymn. The girl’s vision is at this moment stretched over the vistas of Infinity and Beauty and Love far beyond this man- manufactured Idol, far beyond this Temple of clay and stone, exactly like the vision of Byron’s Dying Gladiator looking at his distant Dacian dame and children as if they were present before his eyes in the midst of the Roman audience against whom he had closed them. Her ideal is sweet and harmless, and has all the pleasure and sport which they in the West get from their balls and dances! If there be no vice in the latter, surely there is none in this—the former. And have my countrymen a right to object to all this as being a wrong side of religion? No—no—not until the generation that frowns at this can boast of the birth of a new poet of God whose fervour of soul shall be able to soar as high as does the spirit of this song in this child! And—the Christian missionaries? I think I realise what must always make them fail in a country so rich in the light of the Heart. Their only chance lies in waiting until our people become colour-blind on this their lightsome land. Are they destined to be so blind? No—this sweet girl says—No! Keshab Chunder’s last stage, too, says—No! Evil will be that day for India when these temples of divine raptures will have been turned into the soulless laboratories and workshops of materialistic ideals! Science I love—but not at the cost of this—the sweet living heaven of the poverty-stricken angels of my country. Can’t give them up for the highest blessings of Western civilisation! Poor sweet angels! You shall live through the din and the turmoil that the world would wake with!⟨fn:264⟩ His silent soliloquy over, his mind turned once more to Kumud as Madhuri. His curiosity was aroused again. His mind grew anxious and his legs unsteady. He said aloud, ‘Viharpuri, shall we leave?’ ‘Yes, Maharaj. Let us go.’ All except Sarasvatichandra folded their hands before the idol and turned to leave the temple. As they came out, they met Chandravali. Viharpuri walked ahead as he saw her. Chandravali, too, did not look up and walked on. Then she abruptly stopped and asked Radhedas, ‘Radhedasji, did you see Bhakti Maiya on your way down?’ ‘Yes. She must have reached Yadu Shrunga by now.’ ‘Was my Madhuri with her?’ Sarasvatichandra waited for the response. ‘There was a young, unfamiliar householder with them.’ ‘Was she tired?’ ‘When we saw them she was seated, after which they carried her. Who is she?’ ‘A victim of the heartlessness of you men. She had drowned, but was saved by the Mother Goddess.’ ‘For everything we men are to be blamed, is it?’ ‘That is a fact.’ ‘All should not be blamed for the misdeeds of one.’ ‘Radhedas, the desire to rise above folly is not a blemish. I, too, aspire to rise above. How can that be a folly? But we shall not discuss this today. Did you see my niece Bindumati?’ ‘She is in the temple. She was singing and dancing before the Lord.’ ‘Love divine is superior to the love of men.’ ‘How can one refute such truth?’ Radhedas joined his companions as Chandravali walked into the temple. Viharpuri had walked quite some distance ahead. He waited for the others to join him. Chandravali went into the temple and embraced Bindumati. Bindumati asked her, ‘Maiya, who was that newcomer with Viharpuri?’ ‘Why should we bother?’ ‘He was a handsome man.’ ‘You have no use for mere men!’ ‘I just asked casually. I think he is the guest of Vishnudasji.’ ‘Is it? We have to get to know him. Have you heard Madhuri’s story?’ ‘Is this that man?’ ‘It must be him.’

‘When the sun sets, the lotus closes its petals. Now I can understand the sweet intensity of Madhuri’s pain.’ ‘Daughter, will you look after the temple for a few days?’ ‘Yes, but why?’ ‘I was anxious regarding Madhuri. Now my anxiety has increased even more.’ ‘Do you intend going to Yadu Shrunga?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘But Vihar—’ ‘What do I have to do with him? I will meet Madhuri and return.’ ‘All right. Then go.’ ‘I will ask some women to stay with you.’ ‘When will you go?’ ‘That we will decide once we get to the island.’ ‘All right.’ ‘Bindu, you should also come with me. But who will look after the temple?’ ‘Why did you change your mind?’ ‘When one is alone the heart often disobeys; it does contrary to what it should. A person whose heart is in such a state should have a companion, even a child.’ ‘Aunty, do all ascetics have to struggle so to keep their hearts in check?’ ‘All human beings should make that effort, ascetics even more so.’ ‘But a married couple need not exercise such control, isn’t it?’ Chandravali kissed the young girl, caressed her and replied, ‘Daughter, those who have the means of pleasure remain dissatisfied. They are required to cultivate the disposition of ascetics. Someone as young as you, who aspires to achieve fulfillment in union with the formless god, must remain ever alert and awake. Madhuri and you are almost of the same age. She will open her heart to you. You might become instrumental in giving back her joy—that is no less merit earned. Hence, you should come with me. The life of an ascetic finds fulfillment through control over the mind, in union with the Mother Goddess and in being the reason for the joy of others.’
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra arrives in Surgram, where a visit to the local library brings him face-to-face with distressing newspaper headlines that deeply unsettle his journey.

chapters.title: Kusum's Penance
paragraphs: Kusum’s Penance ‘K usum! Oh Kusum! I am tired of looking for you! Why do you do this to me?’ Sundargauri was in Kusum’s pleasure garden. Kusum was not to be found in any of her usual spots. Sundargauri heard some sounds from behind the gardener’s hut. There was someone under the peepal tree. Sundargauri hid behind a tree and looked. Kusum’s back was towards her. She had worn the coarse sari of the gardener’s wife and seemed to be cooking something in a pot. She was almost unrecognisable. Sundargauri crept closer—the same eyes and nose, the same face! She couldn’t breathe. She could make no sense of her niece’s strange attire. Confounded, Sundargauri murmured to herself, ‘Oh God, I am so tired of this girl! I understand nothing of what she does or intends to do. Her grief-stricken mother has gone numb and her father, immersed in his administration, can pay no attention to these developments. If people like them cannot fathom her, how will I? Should I come out and comfort her? No... Let me see how this scene plays itself out.’ A large peepal tree covered the space between the hut and the boundary wall. Kusum had made an open fire under the tree. She had placed a pot over the fire and was cooking khichdi in it. She had placed a brick near the fire and sat on her haunches, tending to the fire. She had removed all her ornaments. In fact, she herself was the adornment of the tree and looked like a delicate creeper. Her fair face and body draped in a black sari resembled the moon shining forth on dark nights. Sundargauri felt like rushing out and embracing her, but she restrained herself. Kusum called out in a voice as melodious as a cuckoo, ‘Jamni! The fire is about to go out, there is so much smoke. How do I tend it with a blower?’ Jamna, the gardener, was cutting the grass with a sickle, and replied, ‘Wait, let me get a blow pipe.’ ‘No, no. Show me a method of blowing into the fire without a pipe.’ ‘All right. But if a gardener like me can get a pipe, won’t you get one in the forest? There are enough bamboos there.’ ‘One would need an instrument to cut the bamboo. Show me how to tend the fire without a blower.’ Jamna got up and came to Kusum. She said, ‘Behn, you are born fortunate. Why do you do things that the less fortunate have to do? Please go home. The smoke has turned your eyes flaming red.’ ‘No, do as I ask you to do.’ Jamna thought for a while and said, ‘You made a fire with some leaves and grass. They get burnt out quickly. You will need more dry leaves to keep the fire going.’ ‘If I go gathering leaves now, the khichdi will either get burnt or remain uncooked. We have to make do with what there is. Show me a way of blowing on to the fire.’ ‘I cannot think. You can’t blow like we do—does your delicate mouth have that strength? If I blow it would make your food impure, and you lack the strength to.’ Kusum thought over the problem and said, ‘If I join my fingers to the thumb and make a tunnel of my palm and blow through it, will the force work?’ ‘Yes, that might work. Just try it out.’ Ash flew into Kusum’s eyes and face. Jamna could not help laughing. ‘See what happened! Now go home. Each one should do the work that they are cut out for. Your fair face has been blackened by ash. It might look good on the dark ascetics, not on you.’

‘How do I look?’ Kusum asked as she continued her attempts to kindle the fire by blowing on it. Before Jamna could think of a response, the dry leaves caught fire. Sundargauri came out of her hiding place and said, ‘Your face resembles the moon covered by white clouds!’ Kusum was momentarily surprised to see Sundargauri, but quickly regained her composure. Stirring the pot with a twig to check if the khichdi was cooked, she replied without looking up at Sundargauri, ‘Kaki, ultimately my face will be reduced to ash. I am just trying to see if they go with each other. I am trying to love something that is going to stay with me till the very end.’ ‘Love, my foot! Now get up. Every day you enact a new scene. It will not be tolerated. Jamni, you be careful, don’t let this girl in here.’ Jamna: ‘Kakiba! I pleaded and tried to reason with her. Does she pay any heed to people like us? She is adamant and does what she likes.’ Sundargauri: ‘Kusum, will you listen to me or not? Will you get up or should I call your grandfather?’ Kusum continued with her cooking. She checked some grains with her fingers and put them back in the pot. She looked up and said, ‘So what, Kaki? Do you think that grandfather will scold me like you do?’ ‘No, of course not. You are the apple of his eyes! Why would he scold you! But your ways will certainly pain him. You have given heart-burn to your mother; now it’s your grandfather’s turn. Let me see how many people you will cause pain to. When men educate their daughters, they are spoilt. Your father does not understand this, but your grandfather does.’ Kusum laughed as she opened the lid of the pot and poured some water into it. ‘Kaki, you make a mistake there. Dadaji will scold me even less than Pitaji. I can’t give a retort to Pitaji, but to Dadaji I can speak freely.’ Sundargauri made a face and replied, ‘You will pay heed to no one! What is one to do with you! But at least tell me what is it that you are up to? I fail to understand.’ ‘Kaki, I am practising how to live, to eat and wear clothes like poor ascetics. I am learning how to live frugally without being a burden on anyone.’ She stood up, showed her sari to Sundargauri and playfully pointed to the pot of khichdi in a manner as if to suggest that she had won the argument. ‘Kusum, do whatever pleases you. But this is not right.’ Sundargauri sighed and sat down on a fallen branch. Kusum checked her khichdi. She collected some dry leaves and thin twigs. She sewed the leaves together with the twigs and made a plate with it. ‘Kaki, come eat with me. It will taste sweet and satiate your hunger as well.’ ‘You have really become unbridled! These grains are coarse, unlike what is cooked in your house. It will give you discomfort, and in the morning you will be forced to take medicines.’ ‘Kaki! I have been eating this khichdi for the past two–three days.’ ‘What? For three days! Kusum, you are the limit!’ Sundargauri got up and approached the pot. ‘Don’t...! Don’t touch it! I have bathed before cooking,’ Kusum almost shouted. ‘I know all about bathing. Jamni’s clothes, her pot, all these have been purified, have they?’ ‘Here, see, I have already washed the sari that I shall wear tomorrow—it is drying on that branch. I purchased this pot from the potter. Kaki, come, at least taste my cooking. Why are you acting like one gone crazy?’ ‘Indeed! Now I am crazy and you are sane! I am going to pick up the pot and carry it inside the house to show it to your parents.’ Sundargauri tried to pick up the pot, but Kusum stopped her. ‘If you do not want me to tell your parents, you have to promise that you shall inform me of all your new fads.’ ‘Okay. But you cannot come in my way.’ ‘I will come in your way if it is so required.’ ‘By force or by persuasion?’ ‘By persuasion. At least agree to this much.’ ‘Promise?’ ‘Yes. Promise.’ ‘All right, I accept.’

‘Then tell me what are you up to?’ ‘See, Gunial would like me to marry Buddhidhanbhai. I will not accept that. He is my sister’s father-in-law, and hence, I consider him as an elder. Pitaji hopes that I will marry Sarasvatichandra. Even that is not acceptable to me. And Chandrakantbhai’s brother has proposed to father that I should marry Chandrakantbhai and become his second wife. That is also not acceptable to me.’ Sundargauri: ‘I can understand your refusal in two cases. But why do you say no to Sarasvatichandra?’ Kusum: ‘I will explain if you promise to support me in these two other proposals and help me persuade Pitaji, Dadaji, Gunial and Jarashankar Mama.’ Sundargauri: ‘If I give you my word, what promise will you give me in turn?’ Kusum: ‘I will explain to you my reasons for not wanting to marry Sarasvatichandra.’ Sundargauri: ‘That is not enough. If I pledge my support, do you in turn promise to marry Sarasvatichandra?’ Kusum: ‘No. A huge No.’ She spread her arms wide to demonstrate how huge and definitive a ‘no’ that was. Sundargauri: ‘Then it is a huge no from me as well. Jamni, this little one wants to take me for a ride.’ Jamna: ‘Kusumbehn, tell her. Why should you keep anything secret from Kaki?’ Kusum: ‘I am willing to concede some ground to you. Let us suppose that Sarasvatichandra is found, and that he changes his mind about me. But that will not change my decision. But, if he permits me to ask him certain questions, and if his response satisfies me, and if both of us begin to think alike, I might consider the proposal. I might just consider it. I cannot be tied down to a promise right now.’ Sundargauri: ‘Look at you! Supposing such and such were to happen and supposing such and such were to do this, Kusum might consider the proposal. She won’t do anything more than just consider the proposal. I am not giving you my word for this.’ Kusum: ‘Then let me eat.’ She put some khichdi on the plate of leaves she had made and began to eat. Sundargauri stood stupefied. Suddenly she remembered something and said, ‘Kusum, you may not be willing to be bound to a promise about other things, but you have to tell me what this new fad of yours is.’ Kusum laughed. ‘Kaki, this food is so inebriating that it makes me forget my promise!’ Sundargauri: ‘So be it. I will induce forgetting by hunger.’ She turned to leave. Kusum: ‘Kaki, wait! Why must you take offence to a little teasing? Jamni, I have shared my ideas with you. Explain them to Kaki. If something needs to be added, I will do so.’ Sundargauri: ‘Jamni, you tell me since she will not do so.’ Jamna: ‘Kakiba, Kusumbehn wants to learn to live like a mendicant and a poor gardener. She wants to know whether she can live like we do.’ Sundargauri: ‘What else?’ Jamna: ‘That’s all I know.’ Sundargauri: ‘You haven’t told me anything new. Kusum, what is your intention?’ Kusum washed her mouth, wiped it with her sari and said, ‘Kaki, let me say it. I wanted to eat, so I played this trick on you. So listen. You said that in our times an unmarried girl without her own income cannot sustain herself. You had also said that a rich man’s daughter cannot live like a poor person. Now I have ascertained for myself that I can wear such clothes, eat coarse grains and moreover, also like it. I can live in a place like this without any problem. Jamni lives on two rupees a month, which includes expenses on clothes, food and earthen pots and even wood for fuel. That makes it twenty-four rupees a year.

If one were to count interest at the rate of four percent, it requires an investment of six hundred rupees. ‘Pitaji will spend at least that much money on my Kanyadan. But he won’t even have to spend it. He can keep that money anywhere he likes in his own name and arrange to have the interest paid to me. I do not need anything more. That is enough to live happily! Miss Kusum will be happier than Miss Flora.’ Sundargauri: ‘Who taught you all this? Let it be. Let us assume that you have the money. What do you propose to do with it?’ Kusum: ‘So long as Pitaji does not face the problem of losing his caste by my conduct, I will stay in the house. When problem arises—’ Sundargauri: ‘What then?’ Kusum: ‘Kusumbehn will go to Godavari.’ She sang out these words. ‘Going all the way to Godavari will cost money. But are there not enough places around Surgram and Sundargiri where a woman can live without fear? There are enough monasteries around. Kaki, Kusum is ready to be a Mirabai!’ Sundargauri: ‘When are you packing your things?’ Kusum: ‘Why does one need anything while setting out on a pilgrimage? My body is my chariot in which my mind shall ride. Kusum will set out on a journey of joy.’ Sundargauri: ‘But you will stay here so long as your father keeps you, isn’t it?’ Kusum: ‘I have no problem with that. But I want to visit all these places and decide on a place where I will eventually go.’ Sundargauri: ‘When will you do that?’ Kusum: ‘When the occasion presents itself.’ Sundargauri: ‘Kusum, do you want to come back to the house or not?’ Kusum: ‘Of course. For Kusum, home and monastery are no longer any different. Pitaji and Gunial are Shiv and Parvati. So long as they keep me in this house, which is a temple to them, I have nothing to worry about. Kaki, Kusum’s life will now be one of penance. Kusum loves the black quilt of Mirabai. No other colour will discolour it; and it protects against cold as well.’ Sundargauri: ‘Kusum, you will provide the example that girls should be married off before they are educated. Parents will take your example and will always be afraid to educate their daughters. Daughters will remain unlettered, and you will be responsible for this sin. You will repent at the pain and misery that you have caused your parents and the world. One day you will remember my words of caution.’ Sundargauri walked away in anger and in tears. Kusum stayed back. She was quite taken aback by this verbal assault. She walked around deep in thought. A cloud floated over and covered the sun, as if the sun had decided not to cause more trouble to this delicate beauty or had gone into hiding ashamed of her light! ‘This is a good omen!’ Kusum said to herself and walked towards the house. She had realised her responsibility today. She entered the room where she had heard Sarasvatichandra discourse on his philosophy of life. She assumed his tone, his manners and spoke gravely as if she were he. ‘Oh beautiful flower of this Saundarya Udyan! Your fate is not similar to that of Kumud who flowered at night. The desire for independence that has arisen in you is novel for our times and country. I am the progenitor of that desire for independence. You have protected and nurtured this seed in your womb unseen and unknown by anyone else. What has a mother like you and a father like me to fear?’ Kusum trembled at the thought of the parentage of her desire. This idea itself was frightening. At this moment of unknown fear she saw Vidya Chatura standing by a window, deep in thought. He was preoccupied with thoughts of the state and its administration. Vidya Chatura also saw Kusum, and his train of thoughts stopped. He was aware of Kusum’s desire to remain unmarried. He liked the aspiration and was glad that Kusum nurtured such an aspiration. He was also aware that the customs of the time and country were hostile to such desires. He had weighed the pros and cons and come to the conclusion that such aspirations were inimical to the girl and likely to cause her grief. He had not yet found a way out of this quandary. He shared Gunasundari’s concern. Sundargauri had apprised him of Kusum’s attempt at self-training, and he was happy at this development. He saw Kusum at the staircase, and silently blessed her with a verse of Kalidasa. May lily-dotted lakes delight your eye; May shade-trees bid the heat of noonday cease; May soft winds blow the lotus-pollen nigh; May all your path be pleasantness and peace.⟨fn:265⟩ Kusum! Your father will make all efforts to ease your path. I do not want to lose you like Kumud. I have committed one painful error and I do not intend to commit one more. Is my love for you so feeble that you harbour fears that your aspirations cannot be nurtured in this house? Is my affection so powerless? A young girl like Kusum aspires to remain single, unattached and free of worldly burdens. And yet her father, the Prime Minister of Ratnanagari, feels powerless to help fulfill these aspirations. Such is the power of customs prevalent in our times and country. I destroyed Kumud’s sense of autonomy even before it could emerge. I destroyed it out of my pride and negligence induced by my ministership. Kusum was born when I was ascendant. I have to protect her sense of autonomy. I see that as my duty. Kumud’s misfortune opened my eyes. Kusum will benefit from it. That is her destiny. I reposed my faith in customs that have degenerated. I remained oblivious to my duty. I proved lazy in discharge of my duty and as a consequence, I lost a gem of a daughter who was cultured and yet meek. I take a pledge that I will not lose Kusum. Gunial has raised her daughters like sons. She is so deeply perturbed by the loss of Kumud. What would happen to her if she has to bear the grief of another one? I have to care for her as well as Kusum. One is my wife and the other, my daughter, and it is my duty to ensure my daughter’s happiness. Kusum’s happiness and welfare can be secured not by destroying her aspirations but by nurturing them.

I cannot decide if my conclusion is right and truthful. Parents by their affection make their daughters weak, meek and dependent. The father of a daughter is a cripple. Even the sage Kanva was compelled to say: My eyes are dim with anxious thought; Love strikes me to the life: And yet I strove for pious peace— I have no child, no wife. What must a father feel, when come The pangs of parting from his child at home?⟨fn:266⟩ The loss of a son must also give rise to such debilitating feelings. Laxminandan and Buddhidhan must be in acute agony. I fear I am, what they call, Doting. A strange weakness is creeping over my soul, and I don’t know what absurd follies I shall commit next while under the magic influence of this awful weakness. Let it be! The weakness, if a weakness, is noble and blessed, and I am not going to be frightened out of it by its being called a weakness. For the sake of this dear innocent child, I shall, like the poet, say to my manlier soul—‘Resist not the weakness.’⟨fn:267⟩ The only support and protection that a child has is the love and affection of her parents. A renouncer like Shankar has spoken of such love in worshipful terms. If parents fail to be the protectors and nurturers of their sons and daughters, who will? The State certainly cannot take care of all its children when parents call parentage an accident and shift all duty from their own heads. It is, therefore, for the parents to look to the preservation and advancement of the cradled world. Parents alone can do this work most efficiently as being placed nearest their little ones and able to study their wants and give them that warmth which can develop the seeds of adolescence. This is a function which parental affection alone can best perform and, therefore, by the logic of final causes, the function is also a duty. And I must perform it best for my little Kusum. When affection cooperates with duty, custom and convention must be ruled out of order!⟨fn:268⟩ Kusum, you shall remain steadfast in your resolve to be free from the burden of marriage. Your father will help fulfill your aspirations. You will not be required to lead a life of harsh penance and you will remain in this Saundarya Udyan of yours and nurture your desires. Your father shall willingly give up his caste and his ministership in discharge of this duty.
chapters.summary: Sundargauri finds Kusum embracing an ascetic life, cooking khichdi, and firmly rejecting marriage proposals, revealing her determined quest for freedom and self-reliance.

chapters.title: The Moon and the Moonstone
paragraphs: The Moon and the Moonstone Chandrakant, on hearing a verse composed by Sarasvatichandra, immediately set out to search for the singer. The poet Premanand has described the state of Sudev as he searched for Damayanti. He listens to none, his heart in pain, Sudev and Damayanti came face to face. It did not take Chandrakant long to understand the play of the words ‘moon’ and ‘moonstone.’ He felt that Sarasvatichandra was somewhere in the crowd. He set out immediately for the public square. His eyes and ears were alert to the song and the singer. He pushed and elbowed through the crowd. There were people who had worn different kinds of attire and headgear. Chandrakant found no one dressed like Sarasvatichandra. He roamed all over the grounds and turned back dejected. He saw four or five mendicants seated on the grass that had grown around the fort. They were smoking a clay pipe and talking away. One of them intermittently sang out the lines about the ‘moon’ and the ‘moonstone.’ Chandrakant heard him and stood transfixed. Certainly this man cannot be my friend, he thought. But the lines are his! He went closer and overheard their conversation. One of them said, ‘Since when have you taken up this new song? What happened to your faith in the Formless One?’ Another replied, ‘My words will reach the ears of the one for whom they are meant and arouse in him devotion for the Formless One.’ ‘My devotion is only to this smoking pipe,’ a third butted in.

‘The Formless One manifests himself in this pipe first as fire and later as joy in our hearts. But that is not something that you who live on Yadu Shrunga will understand,’ another remarked. He got no response. One of them sang: Set fire to the world as if it were a pipe, Spread the message of the Unseen One with this pipe of clay. ‘Brother, give up this pipe. All you need is belief in the Unseen One.’ The man smoking the pipe removed it from his mouth and laughed. ‘Look at this man preaching us! Have you ever experienced the delights of a pipe?’ The singer said in response, ‘Only fools smoke a pipe, not me! The light of Yadunandan burns in my heart.’ ‘So be it. You kindle your light; we shall light ours.’ The singer again sang the lines about the moon and moonstone. Chandrakant could no longer restrain himself. He came forward with folded hands and asked the singer, ‘Bavaji, where do you come from? What is the meaning of these lines?’ ‘One who has the capacity to understand them will do so without any need for explanation. I have been forbidden from revealing their meaning to anyone else.’ ‘All right, but are there more lines to the song?’ ‘Son, what is your name?’ ‘My name is Chandrakant.’ ‘Chandrakant, is it? It is a good name. If you possess the good qualities suggested by your name, you will understand these words. Where do you stay?’ ‘I am a guest of the Pradhanji.’ ‘Did you meet an ascetic like me some days ago?’ ‘Yes, near the pond of the palace garden.’ The mendicant considered the information and said, ‘Chandrakantji, did what I sing touch you at all?’

‘If I have understood correctly, the poem contains all meaning and all my being!’ Chandrakant said despondently. The group of smokers had no interest in this conversation. They also did not want to be around a guest of the minister. They left the two of them alone and went away. The ascetic looked around and spoke cautiously. ‘Chandrakantji, what interests you? What meaning do you infer?’ ‘All that I seek is suggested by the moon.’ ‘If that is so, please listen carefully to what I have to say.’ Chandrakant listened to him eagerly, anxiously and with increasing numbness. ‘Chandrakantji, listen to me and reflect on its meaning.’ The ascetic sang in his gruff but melodious voice about the poet’s first glimpse of Sundargiri; he sang about the path of asceticism. Chandrakant was shaken. ‘What! Have you renounced the world?’ As the song progressed, he had no further doubts about the composer. The final line alluded to the state of renunciation. He could not control his tears and they rolled down his cheeks. ‘Bavaji, has my Chandra become an ascetic like you? You must tell me everything clearly. I am a man of this world. I cannot control my feelings any longer. Tell me, has my Chandra become a mendicant?’ Chandrakant’s tears and the sincerity of his questions convinced the ascetic that he was the rightful recipient of the message. He wiped Chandrakant’s tears and said, ‘Son, do not fear. You will soon be united with your gem of a friend. He is invaluable even to us. He thirsts for you; the song that I sang is his and it came from his parched heart. Listen once more to his words so that you can capture something of his longing for you.’ Chandrakant wiped his tears and said, ‘Bavaji, please convey these words to him: Sweet are the words of my friend even when uttered by someone else.’ Before he could complete his sentence, the ascetic sang the song. As soon as it was over, Chandrakant released a barrage of questions. ‘Bavaji, please tell me clearly. Where on Sundargiri is my friend? How is he? How is his health? What is the arrangement for his food? What is the state of his mind? When will he meet me? Where? I want to leave immediately to meet him. Please give me quick responses to as many questions as you can. Many lives depend on him. He is all that I have.’ ‘Son, I have been asked to work secretively. This time and place are not appropriate to reveal all the secrets that I hold. Your gem is with us and we have kept it safely in a golden box. He is happy in every respect. Do not be anxious and calm down. Just as you are a guest of an important man, your friend is the dearest guest of a great soul. Chandrakantji, look—there is someone looking for you. I do not wish to arouse their curiosity. I will wait for you at this place from dusk to dawn and will provide answers to all your queries.’ Just then Shankar Sharma and Pravindas reached the spot. By then the ascetic had disappeared, leaving Chandrakant standing there, bewildered and greatly perturbed. He could not hide his resentment at this intrusion of these two well-meaning friends. But the ascetic had gone, and he had no choice but to submit to all the waiting that was ordained. He realised that in his anxiety to meet the singer of the song he had come bareheaded, and now felt ashamed at his own state. His new friends also noticed this and they asked with some concern, ‘Chandrakant, what are you doing here in this state?’
chapters.summary: Chandrakant anxiously seeks the singer of Sarasvatichandra's verse, encountering an ascetic who hints at his friend's renunciation, leaving him yearning for more answers.

chapters.title: Prison
paragraphs: Prison Chandrakant could not have answered them without revealing the ascetic’s secret message. At the same time he was expected to give some response. ‘I came here in a hurry because I sensed that some news of my friend would be conveyed to me.’ ‘Did you get any news?’ ‘I got some vague information, probably inconsequential. But I am promise-bound not to reveal even that.’ ‘Do not worry. Please come with us to the prison. The officials there have collected some information which we shall assess and then make further arrangements,’ Shankar Sharma said. Ratnanagari had two prison houses, one for convicted prisoners and the other one for under-trial prisoners. These two prisons were separated by a temple. Under British rule the police have jurisdiction over the under-trial prison. But the police tend to torture prisoners who are under trial. Therefore, a decree from Bhim Bhavan gave jurisdiction over the under-trial prison to the Jail Superintendent. The police could enter it only for purposes of investigation. Shankar Sharma and Pravindas took Chandrakant to the under- trial prison. They were met at the gate by two low-ranking police officials, who escorted them inside the prison. Cells with iron bars were constructed around an open square. Half of these cells were empty while the other half housed under-trial prisoners. Aarthdas was one of the prisoners. The prison official pointed him out to the group. They sat on chairs placed in the open square.

Harbham, Abdullah Khan and Fatehsinh joined them. Sardar Singh, the Chief of Police, came with some letters and books. ‘Sardar Singh, please give Chandrakantbhai all the information with proof about Sarasvatichandra,’ Pravindas said. ‘Yes. I also need to take his testimony regarding certain matters,’ replied Sardar Singh. Shankar Sharma said, ‘Please do so quickly and make sure we do not waste time over unnecessary and inconsequential matters.’ Sardar Singh opened a diary and said, ‘For several months Sarasvatichandra lived as a guest of Buddhidhanbhai in Suvarnapur. He left the place the day after Buddhidhanbhai was appointed the Karbhari. One day after his departure Kumudbehn left Suvarnapur. There is a Shiv temple called Rajeshwar on the outskirts of Suvarnapur. He got into a bullock cart somewhere near the temple. Pramaddhan’s personal messenger called Ramsen met him before he left. Sarasvatichandra had read Chandrakantbhai’s letter. He spoke about it to Buddhidhan and told him that he had to set out immediately to meet Chandrakant.’ Chandrakant: ‘Where was the meeting to be?’ Sardar Singh: ‘At Bhadreshwar. Sarasvatichandra lived in Suvarnapur under the assumed name of Navinchandra. There were some incidents which took place while he lived in Buddhidhanbhai’s house. Pramaddhan was angry because of them, and he committed suicide by drowning in the sea.’ Chandrakant: ‘What caused him to do so?’ Sardar Singh: ‘It is immaterial for the present and in any case it is confidential; our officers went to Suvarnapur and have gathered the evidence. We also have evidence of Sarasvatichandra’s journey by the bullock cart. There were three others in the cart with him. That bania named Aarthdas, his wife and an old brahmin woman. Sursinh and Chandandas robbed them. Sarasvatichandra tried to protect Aarthdas’ wife. Chandandas and his accomplices beat him up and took him away. These are the facts. We have two or three versions of the subsequent events, and until we determine the veracity of these versions we cannot place the case before the court.’ Chandrakant: ‘What are these different versions?’ Sardar Singh: ‘According to one version, Sarasvatichandra was killed by the outlaws.’ Chandrakant’s heart trembled, but he retained his outward composure. Sardar Singh: ‘As per another version, Aarthdas murdered him to obtain his precious ring. The third version says that he is alive and living somewhere under an assumed identity.’ Chandrakant: ‘The third version is the true one. I do not believe in the second hypothesis. The first version could be true only if the third one is proven false.’ Sardar Singh: ‘The first story has been spread by a man called Hiralal of Bombay. According to him Sarasvatichandra has been murdered by the outlaws within British territory. If this is true, the case would be registered by the British authorities.’ Chandrakant: ‘Hiralal is a cunning liar.’ Sardar Singh: ‘So he is. According to the information received by our officials, Aarthdas has murdered him and the crime was committed in our territory. But this is mere information; we have no evidence for it.’ Chandrakant: ‘That you shall not find.’ Sardar Singh: ‘Aarthdas says that Sarasvatichandra is alive, but we have no information regarding his whereabouts.’ Chandrakant: ‘He is telling you the truth. You must search for Sarasvatichandra.’ Sardar Singh: ‘So be it. You and I hold the same opinion. But until we find him, we must take on board all the versions.
