Some Dhurtalal, a relative of Sarasvatichandra, has been imprisoned in Bombay. Hiralal is his man. He is an expert at machinations. He has sent an appeal to the British Collector that the matter should be placed before a British court. The Political Agent has written to us regarding this.’

Chandrakant: ‘Is there any prima facie evidence?’ Sardar Singh: ‘Does not look like it. But if Aarthdas is a subject of British India, and if the crime has been committed in British territory, the Political Agent does not ever bother much about prima facie evidence.’ Chandrakant: ‘He may not bother about it, but do you?’ Sardar Singh: ‘These and similar questions are raised in the hall of the sovereign, and we obey the decision taken there. There are two–three aspects that are puzzling in this case. For some reason, Hiralal wants to prove that Sarasvatichandra has been killed, and so he has thrown money to the British police, who have placed the matter persuasively before the Collector. The Collector’s head clerk has been bribed by Hiralal. The Agency’s head clerk has also been adequately bribed. Hiralal argues that given the fact that Sarasvatichandra broke off his relationship with the Pradhanji, our courts cannot do justice to him; hence the matter must be tried by a court in British India. All the government officials support him. For these reasons, the Agency does not wish to involve us even in determining prima facie evidence.’ Shankar Sharma: ‘If there is paucity of evidence, let the matter be placed before a court in British India. What wrong can they do?’ Sardar Singh: ‘No, sir. Firstly, this suspect Aarthdas does not wish to go before a British judge. Dhurtalal wants Sarasvatichandra declared dead—with or without an accused—because he stands to gain substantially by that. Aarthdas fears that Hiralal will use him as a sacrificial lamb. Hiralal has been trying to persuade Aarthdas to write a petition that his case be placed before a British court; but Aarthdas has hitherto remained steadfast. Hiralal wants that Aarthdas should plead before the court that Sarasvatichandra was killed by the outlaws. He is not concerned if the court punishes Aarthdas for the possession of Sarasvatichandra’s ring. It is absolutely certain that if the British police were to decide to locate Sarasvatichandra, they could do so quite easily. But Hiralal has ensured that they make no such attempt.’

Chandrakant bit his lips. ‘Dhurtalal plays such games even from jail! All right. What have you done to locate Sarasvatichandra that the corrupt British police has not?’ Sardar Singh laughed and said, ‘We, too, are police. If the British police find the taste of Hiralal’s money sweet, will it taste bitter to us?’ Chandrakant: ‘I have made no such accusation against you.’ Sardar Singh: ‘Maybe the language of Bombay has an accusatory tone to it. You may not have intended to accuse us. Let it be. We shall try and satisfy your curiosity to the best of our ability. Look here sir, the hall of the sovereign is concerned that this matter should not be tried in a court within British territory. Usually, we are not so concerned. But this is different. In Bombay and elsewhere the tendency of the police is to punish a person who has perpetrated a crime—the police is not much concerned about the nature of evidence against such an accused.’ ‘It is nice that you certify your own conduct,’ said Chandrakant with a light-hearted laugh. Sardar Singh continued in his grave tone. ‘Yes sir, you lawyers can misguide a judge by your arguments; we are not dazzled by such arguments. But it is profitable to drop this discussion and come to the main point. Sarasvatichandra occupied a room adjacent to Pramaddhan’s room in Buddhidhanbhai’s house. Suvarnapur is agog with rumours about this. Hiralal has unchallengeable evidence of this. If this case were to be tried before a judge in British territory, he will place the evidence before the court and prove the reasons for which Sarasvatichandra was murdered and also suggest as to who ordered his killing. It will be the judge’s task to fix responsibility and punish some accused. But we are not going to allow any court to cast aspersions on the daughter of our minister.’ Chandrakant: ‘This gives me the assurance that you will provide all help in this matter.’ Sardar Singh: ‘Now let us turn to Sarasvatichandra. If we believe Aarthdas, then Chandandas and his associates brought Sarasvati­ chandra to the grassland. Aarthdas, who was in possession of

Sarasvatichandra’s ring, was hiding in the banyan tree that night. The outlaws also spent the night under that tree. Aarthdas heard their talk from where he was hiding. Two of our men were also hiding in the same tree that night. They testify seeing the ring glitter in the light of the fire made by the outlaws. Once the outlaws dispersed, one of our men went to file a report with the headman of Manoharpuri village while the other one followed Aarthdas. That is how we came to be in possession of this ring. We have been able to trace footprints at the place where Aarthdas and Sarasvatichandra met. But these prints merge with other prints at some distance and become indistinguishable. Aarthdas has also identified the cart driver from whom a bundle of papers belonging to Sarasvatichandra was retrieved.’ ‘Is that so?’ Chandrakant said eagerly. Sardar Singh: ‘Aarthdas claims that Sarasvatichandra jumped out of the cart to protect his wife. This bundle was left behind in the cart.’ Chandrakant: ‘Oh, my friend proved his valour! Sardar Singh, Aarthdas’ version appears to be correct.’ Sardar Singh: ‘So it does. But there is a hitch. According to Aarthdas the man’s name was not Navinchandra but Chandar Bhai.’ Chandrakant: ‘That is not a problem. If he changed his name once he could do so again.’ Sardar Singh: ‘That may be so. We have asked all police stations in our territory to look for a man going under the name of Navinchandra or Chandar Bhai. But we have not been able to trace him so far.’ Chandrakant: ‘If there is no trace of him, all this talk is futile.’ Sardar Singh: ‘That is so, but there is a glimmer of hope.’ Chandrakant: ‘How?’ Sardar Singh: ‘There is a way by which we can keep talking and also resolve this problem. If you provide us with your testimony, the matter can be resolved satisfactorily.’ Chandrakant: ‘My testimony? What about? What is all this?’

Sardar Singh: ‘Yes sir. I will be brief. Today you walked out of Saundarya Udyan without your headgear. Did you meet an ascetic in the public square?’ Chandrakant: ‘How do you know this?’ Sardar Singh: ‘That question is unnecessary. Did the ascetic give you some indication about Sarasvatichandra? Have you fixed up a meeting later today?’ Chandrakant was stunned. The ascetic had asked him to keep the matter secret. It was not desirable that he break his promise. If he wanted to keep his promise he must tell a lie, and a lie was not acceptable to him. Sardar Singh was quick to grasp this quandary and said, ‘If you are required to keep the matter a secret, I will not coerce you to speak. But I need to tell you that you can keep your conversation with the ascetic a secret from us. He might ask you to accompany him; if he does so, you should inform us and then go with him without any worry. You should give us the information that you can without breaking your promise. And this information must be timely. You will accomplish much more than four of our detectives would. But allow me to caution you that if you do not give us timely and appropriate information, the matter may slip out of our hands and some innocent man may get killed. All the plans of Sarasvatichandra’s father and his friends would become futile and people would spread poisonous gossip about Sarasvatichandra and Kumudbehn in the courts.’ Chandrakant: ‘It is my duty to seek your support and provide all assistance to you in this matter.’ Sardar Singh: ‘That is correct. I must alert you about two other things. If anyone other than you becomes aware of Sarasvatichandra’s whereabouts, that great man will move to some other place. Hiralal will try and get this information; he has vowed to kill Sarasvatichandra if he were to be found alive. Therefore, this matter must be treated as top secret and I should be informed of his whereabouts well in advance so that I can make arrangements for his security and protection. Finally, if Hiralal takes this matter before a court, Sarasvatichandra should be immediately produced before the court. This would prove

Hiralal’s charge to be completely fabricated and he would not get the opportunity to spread canards. This is my suggestion, and you should secure Sarasvatichandra’s full cooperation in this matter. He has nothing to fear from this state or its police.’ ‘I think I can accomplish this,’ said Chandrakant. As he was about to get up, Sardar Singh said, ‘Chandrakantbhai, do not forget that Hiralal has spread his net even in your own house.’ ‘In my house?’ Chandrakant was shocked. ‘What will he find in my poverty-stricken house?’ ‘Even poor friends of wealthy men are wealthy. Your elder brother and your mother want you to take another wife. Hiralal’s employer has given them money to do so.’ ‘What will Dhurtalal gain from it?’ ‘You will give up your efforts and return home, and that is a clear gain for Dhurtalal.’ ‘That I understand.’ Chandrakant could not help a sardonic laugh. ‘The fools. But they make a mistake. I would not abandon my search even if Ganga were to die. Would I go back to marry another woman?’ ‘Forgive me, but there is one more thing. Those who want Sarasvatichandra dead also want Gangaba dead.’ ‘Why?’ Sweat broke out on Chandrakant’s brow. ‘Because the letters and the key that Sarasvatichandra gave you can be obtained by them in your absence only when Gangaba is no more. If Gangaba does not cooperate with them, she is certain to be killed.’ ‘That seems plausible. Oh dear! This is difficult!’ Chandrakant scratched his head and waved his arms in agitation. ‘But do not worry. Just give us a letter in your own hand that Gangaba should trust the bearer of the letter and accompany him to some able and resourceful person’s house in Bombay.’ ‘Tarang Shankar or Uddhatlal. No, Tarang Shankar is poor. Uddhatlal will be a match for them. Yes, I will give a letter for Uddhatlal, and I will write to her that she should go and live in Uddhatlal’s house.’ ‘All right. But do not write directly to Gangaba. The letter might fall into enemy hands.’

‘You are right. How long will it take you to accomplish this?’ ‘We will finish this task within five days. There is no immediate danger to Gangaba.’ ‘I entrust you with Ganga’s responsibility. You should trust me regarding Sarasvatichandra.’ ‘Done. But you must remember everything that I have cautioned you about. If you fail, you are certain to be defeated.’ They all dispersed. Sardar Singh’s words of caution perturbed Chandrakant greatly. Both Sarasvatichandra and Ganga now faced danger. At last, night fell. Chandrakant anxiously waited for the ascetic at the appointed place. He did not show up. But some wayfarer came and gave him a note, which said: ‘Our meeting has been postponed because there is a danger that our secret is no longer secret. If you speak about it to anyone, the meeting will never take place. But if you are able to keep this secret, we shall reschedule the meeting.’ Handing this note to Chandrakant outside the gates of Saundarya Udyan, the unknown wayfarer ran away. Chandrakant read the note in the light of the lanterns placed over the gate. He was already perturbed. This development confounded him even more. He was frightened, irritated and worried. He decided that in the morning he would set out in search of the ascetic, failing which he would go to Yadu Shrunga. He now had to look not only for Sarasvatichandra, but also this ascetic. Strange are the ways of destiny.
chapters.summary: Chandrakant arrives at the prison, where Sardar Singh reveals conflicting theories about Sarasvatichandra's fate, embroiling him in a complex web of political intrigue and danger.

chapters.title: Passions Unseen and Palpable Vows
paragraphs: Passions Unseen and Palpable Vows Fool, not to know that love endures no tie, And Jove but laughs at Lovers’ perjury! —Dryden⟨fn:269⟩ Let me not to the marriage of true minds Admit impediments. —Shakespeare⟨fn:270⟩ Half a furlong away from Yadu Shrunga, the monastery headed by Vishnudas, there was a math for householders called the Grihastha Math. At some distance from it was a math for women ascetics, both unmarried and widowed, called the Parivrajika Math. The women’s quarters were built on the same pattern as the monastery. The quarters for couples also resembled the general design, but that building had an upper storey where there were rooms for couples and each room had a terrace of its own. This math was also called Vihara. These three buildings were separated by hills and forests in which the ascetics had created spaces for meditation, penance and leisure. A large number of birds nested in these trees. Bhakti Maiya and the others reached the Parivrajika Math at noon. Kumud had withered like a lotus in the heat of summer. The exertion and hunger were too much for her to bear, but the new scenery enthused her somewhat. She had learnt about the three monastic houses and the philosophy of Alakh from her associates on their way up the mountain. She had also enquired about Navinchandra whenever the occasion presented itself. Knowing her intimate desires, her clever associates satisfied all her curiosities and implanted in her a seed of hope. The Parivrajika Math was built around a large courtyard. There was a platform at the centre of the courtyard on which there was a basil plant and a peepal tree. Kumud was seated under the tree. The sadhvis surrounded her, and time went by in their questions and her responses. Finally, they sat down for their meal in a veranda. They sat in different groups and each group talked about different subjects. Some discoursed about knowledge, others about aesthetics while some talked of practical issues. Some read the Adhyatma Ramayana, while someone else sang abhangs of Tuka and explained them to others in a mix of Gujarati and Marathi. Two–three groups sang devotional songs in ‘concert’ to the accompaniment of the ektara and other stringed instruments like the tambura. They passed the afternoon in such innocent, aesthetic and pious activities. Kumud slept for a while. She woke up refreshed by the mountain air and enthusiastically tried to join in the new community. The nuns were also pleased by the change in her disposition. As the moon came up in the sky, Kumud also flowered like her namesake lotus. A window opened out onto the ‘precipice’ where Kumud sat; looking out of the window, her focus shifted between the world outside and the conversation between Bansari and Mohini. The precipice was about fifty hands deep. The path from Surgram took a bend right below the window. From the window only about fifteen metres of the pathway was visible after which it disappeared from view. It was a night of the bright fortnight and the moon shone brightly, lighting up the depths of the precipice; its soothing rays entered the crevices of rocks and boulders and softened their edges. This combination of hard and soft, strong and delicate filled Kumud with a deep silence. Her eyes searched for Sarasvatichandra. He had to take this route up back from Surgram. She was alert to any shadow, any sound, even that of leaves flying in the wind.

Kumud experienced a strange mixture of quietness and anxiety. If the conversation between Bansari and Mohini had not concerned her, her attention would not have been drawn to it. The scene outside was quiet and solemn, but it stirred Kumud’s imagination. The conversation of the two women was serious and calming, and yet it enthused her. Bansari: ‘Mohini, there is a moon in the sky, and Madhuri’s face is also moonlike. The moon is soothing, calm and cool. Does not Madhuri’s face appear aglow, almost feverish?’ Mohini: ‘Oh beautiful Madhuri, know that your moon is here and take solace in this knowledge. Do calm down.’ Kumud: ‘Dear sisters, for me that knowledge itself is the cause of turbulence. We bathe in the moon’s light. But for me any direct contact with my moon is a violation of my duty and morality. I do not lust after him. The fire raging within my heart will subside only after there is nothing left for it to burn.’ Bansari: ‘You are right from the perspective of a householder. Malati had also said with deeply felt dejection: Let the full moon blaze in the nightly sky: Let love rage on, death screens me from his fury. What should exact my love and veneration? My father, and my mother and my race, Of still unblemished honour—not my life; No! Nor the mortal who subdues my heart.⟨fn:271⟩ ‘Literary pieces and observing your condition allow us to comprehend your state of mind. But you have now entered the abode of the unseen, Formless One. All these unnatural ties, these worldly aspirations and apprehensions will now disappear, and you will be free.’ Kumud: ‘Sister, the duty of a virtuous wife is the same in every situation. I am determined that I shall not deviate from it.’

Bansari: ‘Even Malati had made a similar resolve, but her deviation was considered moral and righteous.’ Kumud: ‘Malati did not have my problem. She had to simply decide between her parents and her beloved. She did not have my evil desire to be free of marriage. I have resolved to remain distant from this evil desire.’ Bansari: ‘Maiya, the purity and beauty of your heart allow you to speak such words. But a pure heart that has not glimpsed the true path cannot see the path of righteousness and true conduct.’ Kumud: ‘I must follow the path ordained for a virtuous wife and shun what my heart desires. That is my duty. Bansaribehn, it is your affection for me that wants to see me happy; it wants me to adopt a path by which that happiness can be secured. But for many days now I have resolved to see that path as impure and not to even consider its possibility.’ Bansari: ‘Maiya, that resolve is attractive, but it is not the path of truth.’ Kumud: ‘Why?’ Bansari: ‘You desire virtue! But who is that husband that you aspire to be faithful to? Is what you shun not virtue? Or does virtue inhere in the very act of shunning? Madhuri, in this day and age, so many debauched practices have taken root among the householders that what is wrong and a violation of dharma has come to be regarded as dharma itself. And someone as beautiful and virtuous as you are caught in its net and tortured. Now you have entered the world of ascetics. We have preserved, like the keeper of sacred fire, the ancient, unsullied practice of our ancestors. You will be able to observe and follow these customs here. Madhuri, the wicked ways of the world gave you in marriage to someone, but even before that marriage you had given your heart to someone else. That person is your husband, your only one and true husband. Husband is one who is chosen by a woman, not the man she is married to by her parents. And therefore, Sri Krishna abducted Rukmini, and that is considered an act of great virtue. Madhuri, the man to whom you gave your heart and soul is your true husband, and the man to whom your parents gifted your body is an adulterous paramour. Now you decide where your virtue and duty lie.’ Kumud sighed deeply; tears filled her eyes. She looked out of the window and wiped her tears. Kumud sensed some shadows in the valley; she heard some sounds. Mohini rose and came close to her. Looking down at the valley, she caressed Kumud and said, ‘Madhuri, the world asks you to focus on your marriage. But that is not your vision; it is not even a marriage as far as you are concerned. Your soul has been bound in pure matrimony with your Chandra. Your heart sees none else. Your eyes must be guided by your heart. Madhuri, you are startled by every shadow in the valley. Don’t you see your husband in each of those shadows? Didn’t you come up this mountain to have a glimpse of your Chandra? Your true eyes show you what your heart sees. Your heart has accepted only him as your husband in the purest sense, and you are devoted to him as a virtuous wife ought to be. Hence, you must forsake the man who has sullied your body following the evil customs of society. You must unite with the pure essence of love. Madhuri, your object has to be not what you argue; your goal can only be what I have outlined before you. See, it has already filled you with romance and excitement.’ Kumud: ‘I do not have the capacity to refute your arguments. But my future is not mine. It has been given away as I described. Please do not make any further attempts to deviate and sully me from that path.’ Mohini: ‘Society has filled you with wrong and depraved notions. We do not wish to sully you; we only want you to be pure and beautiful.’ Kumud: ‘I desire neither that purity, nor that beauty. The recipient of my purity and beauty has become the source of my problems. If you truly desire my happiness, please free me from that burden and give me the peace and quiet of being with you.’ Mohini spoke gravely and with great compassion, ‘That, too, will be yours when the time for it comes. Madhuri tell me—who are you? Your body or your soul?’ Kumud: ‘Set fire to that body and that soul!’

Bansari: ‘Mohini Maiya, we should not discuss anything that perturbs and disquiets Madhuri. Let us discuss something that gives her solace and soothes her.’ Mohini: ‘What will make you happy?’ Kumud: ‘Talk of something that allows me to forget my world.’ Mohini and Bansari looked at each other. ‘What shall we talk about? Should we describe all our ashrams?’ Mohini asked. Bansari: ‘Mohini, you are two years my senior. Long ago you had promised me that you would explain the purpose of the Manmath Avatar, the reasons for which the god of love was created. This is an opportune moment.’ Kumud: ‘Is there no other subject?’ Bansari: ‘Some of us live in the Vihar Math, while others live in the Parivrajika Math. We are ever keen to understand what each of us is capable of, why and when our capacities change. The masters of the Alakh Marg have discoursed on the god of love because they were concerned about the status of women. These discourses calm us. Madhuri, you too will be at peace with yourself after hearing these discourses.’ Kumud: ‘If these discourses are such that they do not arouse my passions, please go ahead.’ Mohini: ‘Both of you listen carefully. Brahma, Vishnu and Mahesh are the three forms of the Formless Creator whom we call Sri Alakh Bhagwan. “I am One, I manifest in many.” Brahma the creator is the essence of Kama, desire. Mahesh as Rudra turned Kama to ashes. But Kama remained eternal and immortal, though without a body. Kama did not submit either to the creator or to the destroyer of the world. Sri Krishna, our Yadunandan who preserves all creation, caused Kama to be born as his son, who was called Pradyumna. ‘Kamadev, as Brahma, is god. Shankar burned him to ashes, but his soul remained indestructible, imperishable. Even Shiva had to submit to Kama when he married Parvati. The only one who did not submit to Kama, and who in fact subdued Kama, was Yadunandan; and hence Kama was born as his son. Do you comprehend this?’

Bansari: ‘No.’ Mohini: ‘Vishnu’s action is to preserve creation. Devotees of this god must regard Kamadev as an incarnation of Brahma, as a beloved son of Vishnu, and as even more disembodied and unvanquished than Shankar. That element, the element of desire, is the means of securing the welfare of the world. It also protects women.’ Bansari: ‘How so?’ Mohini: ‘In the animal kingdom species feed on each other; even among them the female of the species is protected for procreation. That is the power of Kamadev. Among the animals, the male of the species is more attractive and ornamental than the female; the peacock and the lion are more attractive than the peahen and the lioness. The male attracts the female and in turn is attracted to her; he protects her and cohabits with her. It is quite contrary in the human race. So long as he is stupefied and ignorant, a man is capable of performing even a Rakshasa vivah where he forcibly seizes and carries away a woman, and in so doing displays his depraved and demonic side. But if and when he acquires true knowledge he also becomes capable, like Shankar, to reduce desire to ashes. Knowledge destroys the lust and attachment that makes men dance like peacocks displaying their feathers and crown. If Kamadev did not come to the aid of beautiful women, all men without exception would follow the path of knowledge and become ascetics. A man who fails to acquire knowledge would turn out to be demonic and depraved like the paramour of Madhuri’s body. Women would either have to submit to such depraved men or remain without any sanctuary. Tell me, Bansari, if the lord of love and desire had come to Madhuri’s aid, would she have been subjected to the intolerable depravity and life without support?’ ‘Of course not,’ replied Bansari. Kumud gave no response. She meekly looked down at Mohini’s feet. It seemed that some new element had found its way to her heart. Mohini: ‘When society became depraved, they came to disdain Sri Krishna’s eldest son, but we worship him through our Vihar Math.’

Bansari: ‘If it is incumbent upon all of us to worship the god of love, why do we need this Parivrajika Math for chaste women? Is the celibate life of the great souls and ascetics futile?’ Mohini: ‘Where Brahma is the embodiment of Kama, chaste virgins like Sarasvati and celibates like Narad also have a place. They spread the message of the Formless God for the welfare of all creation. Celibates like Narad and Sarasvati are precious children of Brahma; they look upon all householders as their brethren. The activities and actions of householders contribute to the growth of creation. Our ascetic brothers, like Naradmuni, are immersed in singing the praise of our Lord. We, like Sarasvati, remain in this math as repositories of knowledge and music. The others live in Vihar Math as householders and submit to Pradyumna and in so doing, serve Sri Yadunandan.’ Bansari: ‘Other householders also submit to Kamadev; how is our submission different from theirs? What is the difference between householders of our sect and other celibate ascetics?’ Mohini: ‘The difference is as vast as the husband of Chandravali’s heart and the paramour of Madhuri’s body. The submission of us ascetics to desire is different from that of other householders. Chandravali’s husband is an ascetic; the man who captured Madhuri’s heart left her without any support. Let’s see what he does now.’ Kumud: ‘The word ‘‘paramour’’ pinches me. I consider that man as having a legitimate right over my body. I will resist any attempt to shake me from this faith. I cannot bear your censure that reviles him.’ Bansari: ‘It is for this reason that you are called Madhuri. Your sweet disposition cannot bear censure of even a depraved man or an enemy. The sweetness of your heart is so deep that the salinity of any caustic remark disturbs it.’ Mohini embraced Kumud affectionately and said, ‘Madhuri! We will not utter anything that is harsh and bitter to you. We will speak only words which give you joy. ‘‘What goodness is there in kindness shown by a man towards those who have obliged him? One who is kind towards those who have done him wrong is described as a virtuous person by the good.’’⟨fn:272⟩ Your heart feels so deeply for a man who gave you so much grief; we will not add salt to your sweetness. In our present discussion we might take some examples from your life. Please forgive us for that. Our endeavour is to attain the Formless God by focusing upon the elements of the manifest world. We consider your life as integral to the manifest world.’ Kumud: ‘If your attempt is to give succour to my heart, please carry on, but do not speak of anything that churns my heart.’ Mohini: ‘Madhuri, so it will be. Regain your equanimity and listen. There was a time when there were eight types of marriages, both pure and impure. With the passage of time, society came to regard Gandharva vivah, a union based upon mutual love and consent, as objectionable. But among us, the followers of Alakh consider this marriage to be most superior to all and in fact the root of all other forms of marriage. We believe that the good of the world can be secured by it. We believe that when two hearts become one with the same desire, it signals the desire of the Formless One to manifest Himself. Those who do not have the capacity or the fitness to experience the Unmanifest One acquire this capacity by receiving the light of Kamadev.’ Bansari: ‘But even this-worldly householders submit to this light.’ Mohini: ‘It is not so. Kamadev does not manifest himself in a singular form. There are three states of desire and countless manifestations. The tree of passion has three states: desire, sexual pleasure and love. Desire is akin to the roots, sexual pleasure is like the trunk, while love is similar to flowers and fruits. ‘Desire and passion manifest themselves in various forms, but there are four principle forms: animal passion, illegitimate passion, passion based on attachment and passion rooted on the desire for a son. Animal passion is clearly what prevails in the animal world. It is neither moral nor immoral; it submits to the senses and instincts. The other form of passion is the depraved, illegitimate passion of many men and women. Mutual attraction and some affinity do play a part in this form of desire, but it is unbridled; it is immoral. It leads to disorder, including the mixing of the Varnas. It hampers man from discharging his other duties. It also destroys the bodily and material wellbeing of women; it uproots the good fortune of their progeny. Its roots lie in uncontrolled, limitless desire for consumption; its poison persists till the very end of life. Passion that is based on attachments remains unseen like a seed under the ground from the time of courtship to marriage. The sensual pleasures are experienced only after marriage. It persists in togetherness as also in separation; it rises and subsides but eventually the couple experience true love. Sometimes it allows carnal pleasure but in a detached way, while at other times it denies carnal pleasure, checks it and allows one to focus one’s energies on the divine. Passion that is governed for a time by the desire for progeny eventually subsides and turns spiritual and the couple is able to perceive each other’s essential qualities by piercing the shell of the body. They are able to take pleasure in each other’s essential qualities. This subtle form is the most superior form of love and desire. The couples who reside in the Vihar Math have attained this state. The householders who are not part of our community at Sundargiri are so depraved and fallen that they cannot even dream of such spiritual love. Madhuri, my Madhuri! If you had remained with the man of your heart, you would have reached this state of spiritual love; you would have experienced this glorious state. But you fell and were deprived of this union because of the man you call your husband! Will your association with us not free you from the decayed, fallen and depraved customs of society?’ Kusum hardened her heart and said, ‘Mohini Maiya, let us drop the subject of an ideal which is unattainable even in a dream. The glory and beauty of this spiritual love reminds me of the superiority of my beloved. I who was fallen became impure; I have made this journey to have a glimpse of that great soul, and therein lies my salvation. Any other form of desire is greed, and greed will not save me but cause me to fall even further. Please do not ask anything in this matter, but do continue with your explanation of spiritual love. The higher state and attainments of your ascetic community, which is governed by norms that are unfamiliar to our debased customs, give me assurance that what I regarded as my incapacity to eliminate the pain of my heart is not caused by its depravity, but in fact it is unblemished, unsullied. This I have realised by your grace.’ Her words expressed the calmness of her heart. Mohini: ‘Madhuri, you will realise much more. Your heart’s desire is not only pure, but your virtue and piety are because of it. If that pain were not alive and ever present in you, we would have considered you wretched, insignificant and also depraved. I described to you the character of passion based on attachment. Before marriage it remains only attachment and after marriage there is consummation of it, there is desire for progeny and the attachment persists. But among you the courtship before marriage has disappeared. After marriage there is carnal passion, desire for progeny and bodily enjoyment. The pleasure is limited to the body and love is called love based upon conviction and agreement.’ Kumud: ‘Kindly explain to me this love, this courtship and attachment.’ ‘That is the job of your beloved! Mohini Maiya has done all that can be done for an inexperienced and ignorant person,’ butted in one woman. Mohini: ‘Pramamta, be quiet. You have no knowledge of Madhuri’s joys and sorrows and have no right to say a bitter word to her. Madhuri, love is of four kinds:⟨fn:273⟩ one, which is rooted in passion; two, which is based on conviction, three, egoistic and four, studied. The love which is based on enjoyment of sensual pleasure to the exclusion of all else is the result of animal passions. A woman who loves a man because he has been selected as her husband by her family, or because she has decided on her own volition that he is the one who should be the object of her love is indulging in love based upon conviction. The sweet affection that you have for the man who is the husband of your body is such. This love is based upon the idea that it is incumbent upon one to love the partner chosen. Love that is rooted neither in passion, nor as a result of conviction but arises from the ‘‘fancy’’ of the mind is called egoistic as it emerges from oneself. Love that considers sensual pleasures secondary, love which is not the result of courtship is often egoistic. Those who choose a partner in a swayamvar often love each other egoistically. We ascetics, whose minds are devoted to either acquisition of knowledge or are immersed in devotion, do not experience such egoistic love; hence I cannot provide an adequate explanation of it. But I know that those who do not have faith in our path of devotion to the Formless God consider our devotion egoistic. If the non-believers and agnostics are firm in their conviction and are truthful to it, they may consider the devotion of someone like Bindumati as egoistic, and they would not be deluded in so thinking. ‘The fourth form of love is studied. It is neither based on passion, or conviction, nor is it egoistic. It arises because one performs certain actions repeatedly. A child who feeds at her mother’s breast has this type of love. The child has no carnal desire for the mother, nor is her affection based upon conviction or ego. She is just accustomed to her mother. There is a custom of child marriage prevalent in society. This child couple, due to repeated and constant togetherness, feels such a studied love. Before arriving at this stage either one or both of them might feel egoistic love; some whose disposition is as pure as yours may even love out of conviction. Sometimes there is absence of love, or even of dislike and conflict. The man to whom you gave love out of conviction gave you the taste of such disaffection.’ Of the women who had gathered around them, one spoke up, ‘Maiya we do not need to know about the customs of householders; nothing will be gained from such knowledge. Please discourse about our path.’ Mohini: ‘If you were my only audience, I would have done so. Madhuri, who has lived among the people, has come to us like a fish of salt water which has been dragged into a pond of sweet water. You will not comprehend what it takes for her to breathe our air. Madhuri, I have described to you the four types of desire, its three states and the four types of love that result from it. You should now understand the pattern through which they relate to each other; we have a distinct understanding of it, which too I shall explain. Before we go to bed this evening, all these will be as accessible to you as that berry in your hand. You will, after many days, have untroubled sleep.’ Kumud: ‘All of you have been very kind to this grief-stricken soul.’ Mohini: ‘Desire, sensual pleasure and love take two forms; if they are focused on the body they remain gross, but if they are about the subtle body then that desire, pleasure and love is also called spiritual. Among us desire, pleasure and love are not merely about the body; they are not gross but usually combine subtle aspects and can take various combinations of subtle and gross, heart and body. Often it is purely spiritual. Just as salvation can be attained through the paths of right conduct, devotion and knowledge, it can be achieved by the latter two forms of desire, pleasure and love. We ascetics do not harbour and nourish desire and passion that is merely bodily. All our senses work together, incessantly, to negate them. But we do not negate subtle forms of desire, passion and love. The decision about celibacy and union are determined not by human volition but through the will of Sri Yadunandan. When we experience desire, when passions emerge in our hearts and we feel attracted to someone who also feels an equal and similar desire and passion, we become alert to them. Both hearts seek to know each other. Their endeavour is to ascertain if their union is acceptable to and in accordance with the will of Sri Yadunandan. Men ascetics court women ascetics. If the woman declines the advances, refuses to participate in this courtship, it is required of the man to curb and eventually give up his desire. If the man were to decline courtship, the woman should likewise give up her desire for union. But if both accept the courtship, they should submit to Kamadev so that this son of Sri Krishna can play out all his possibilities through them. This is also a form of worship, of the manifest form of the Unseen God. This worship commences with courtship, progresses to the state of attachment and if they pass through this stage with their desire for each other intact, we bring this worship to its conclusion through Gandharva vivah as we do not believe in the other seven forms of marriage. Their desire and passion also move beyond mere attachment.’

Kumud: ‘Please explain the meanings of terms like courtship and attachment. Don’t you have rituals of marriage? Don’t you have any form of child marriage? In absence of rituals how can it be called a marriage? If there is no marriage, how is widowhood possible?’ Bansari laughed. ‘Madhuri, you have again become an adolescent. No, in fact a child! What kind of questions are these? You, too, have experienced attachment with Navinchandraji. It is surprising that you should still ask such questions.’ Mohini: ‘Bansari, I have some acquaintance with the people of Surgram. I know that just as we are surprised by the life experiences of someone like Madhuri, they too are equally surprised by our conception of the tree of desire. Our conception of the tree of desire is based upon the texts on love and desire that were written for the wider society. Just as others consider food and drink as nurturing the body, as giving pleasure to the palate, we see all our actions as nurturing our devotion to the manifest god which will eventually give us the bliss of being united with the Formless God. Therefore, our theologians have taken texts like Kamasutra as a basis to understand the real significance of Kamadev and given us the conception of the tree of desire. We have adopted the terminology of Kamasutra but imbued it with a different set of meanings. The word sila means disposition, tendency or inclination; it denotes an orientation, a movement. To be disposed to or habituated to someone means silan. And to have an all-rounded, all-encompassing disposition means attachment or parisilan. This term is used in a variety of ways. It means to know the innermost core of something, to know something in a way that is integral to itself. It also means that a man and a woman should know the deepest, innermost cores of each other. It is used in the sense of being enveloped, as in being enveloped by the blue god. It indicates an orientation and desire for oneness; as one heart merges into another, we merge into the divine. Just as the wind passes through and envelops a delicate creeper, man enters and envelops the heart of a woman and in turn is enveloped by her. Madhuri, Navinchandraji thus encompassed you, enveloped your heart and created a sense of attachment. But he abandoned you, which was a deviation from the path of duty. It was a violation. Wherever there is mutual attachment, merging into each other signifies marriage. Our path will allow you to complete your union and perform your duty, which is the right conduct.’ Kumud: ‘That shall not be. Maiya, please proceed with your discourse.’ Mohini: ‘As you please. But remember that just as the sea waves by their incessant pounding break the resistance of a rock, similarly we shall also break your resistance; we shall break your adherence to a false sense of duty and rectitude and give you bliss. Even in the texts of Kama meant for householders creating such a disposition of desire is prescribed, so are intimacy and familiarity. Similarly, whenever necessary, courtship is also prescribed. It is said that courtship is prescribed if it aids the performance of one’s duty. Even during the exchange of marriage vows, the man says to the woman, ‘‘I have courted you, and let this sacred fire grant consent to it.’’ A marriage without courtship is not possible. Why is a woman called Vanita? Vanita is one who has been conquered and possessed by courtship. Without courtship a woman does not become a beloved. Men are by nature brazen, while women tend to be shy. A man has to open her heart ever so delicately as one would open the petals of a lotus. A man must court a woman. Madhuri, Navinchandraji courted you. Your hearts are attached to each other; they have merged and become one. All that remains is: Look up! Behold the youth who shared your sufferings, Whose eyes first caught the flame; whose heart was next, To thee alone devoted; and whose frame, Like thine emaciate equal passion shows. Behold him here! Dismiss this weak timidity— Be love obeyed and destiny fulfilled.⟨fn:274⟩ ‘We attain the unseen by beholding the forms we assume. If this union is created by desire, is ordained by the god of love, man and woman pass though the phases of attachment and courtship; they experience the feverish heat of desire. This heat purifies them and results in a

Gandharva vivah, a union based on love and desire. The marriage of hearts is concluded, and two hearts become one. But there is a bodily aspect to this union and hence it is appropriate that they should unite through Gandharva vivah. Madhuri, you and your Chandra have been consumed by this fire; you have done your penance. Your beloved is residing on this mountain. God has so willed that you should also come here. We shall make the effort to rid you of your obdurate obstinacy and we shall fulfill the task ordained for your beautiful hearts. Your attachment and courtship were devoid of sensual pleasure, and we shall celebrate your union by worshipping the god of love.’ For Kumud it was sinful to even be used as an example in this narrative. She had repeatedly asked to be kept out of this discussion. These words stunned her. She lost her patience, and said, ‘Mohini Maiya, if that is your intention, please send me back immediately to Chandravali Maiya, where it is forbidden to even utter a man’s name. Your discourse is elevating and instructive, but I find any reference to me or to my husband objectionable. You may freely choose your partner. It might also be true that a girl chooses her husband through her own volition. But the man to whom my father made a gift of me will remain the master of this body till the very end of my life. I have no control over my heart, but my body will only submit to the husband chosen by my father.’ Mohini: ‘“I have no control over my heart”—that is your truth. Madhuri, marriage is not a union of bodies; it is a union of hearts. The union of bodies is subsidiary; it is a coming together of inert forms. We prescribe the coming together of subtle elements. Since the fruit of arranged marriages is intimacy, in spite of being deemed a mediocre union, Gandharva marriage is desirable and respectable. Being pleasurable, without much affliction, and affectionate from the beginning of marriage, Gandharva marriage is considered good.⟨fn:275⟩

‘Madhuri, it is because of love that Gandharva vivah has been considered a superior form of union. After the examples of Shakuntala and such others the law-givers accepted a marriage of the bodies. But this does not make attachment and courtship a nullity. Society did away with these customs and made marriage a union of bodies, thereby debasing itself. Look at your own body—it is weak. Look at your marriage—it is not happy and in fact is a source of grief! Society gave up the path of goodness and adopted debased ways. And they have been facing its consequences ever since. Madhuri, following those societal customs your father gave you in marriage, a marriage only of the body. But this does not preclude a marriage of hearts according to our belief. Let us assume that you were married to Navinchandra, and that during the ceremony the women did not sing marriage songs. Would that marriage be a nullity?’ Kumud: ‘No.’ Mohini: ‘Supposing he did not have a groom’s party or did not hold a feast?’ Kumud: ‘That would not matter. Only the Saptapadi is essential.’ Mohini: ‘We arrive at the comprehension of the Formless One through a process of negation, ‘‘not this, not this.’’ Through a similar process I shall explain to you the true meaning of marriage. Let us assume that during the Saptapadi you misstep once or twice.’ Kumud: ‘That does not matter.’ Mohini: ‘What if, instead of you, the priest had uttered the vows?’ Kumud: ‘But that is the custom now.’ Mohini: ‘Which means that your marriage is not in the rituals, but in the vows that you take.’ Kumud: ‘Yes, my father declared his intention to make a gift of me in marriage and made me take the vows.’ Mohini: ‘Yes, but was it one person who declared his intentions and took the vows or were these two different persons? Your father made the resolve, and you took the vows. Truthfully, the bride and the groom should declare their intent to marry and having done so, take the vows of marriage. No law book or law-giver says that a father should coerce his daughter in accepting the vows of marriage. These are the customs of your foolish and depraved society. The father makes a gift of the bride so that he becomes a witness to the marriage and saves his daughter from the hardships that Shakuntala had to face. The gift of the bride or kanyadan can either be made by the father or even by someone else. It is just like someone holding the stirrup while the rider mounts the horse. A marriage is considered valid even in absence of the father or someone else making the gift of the bride. Not only that, but when depraved parents using their right make a gift of the bride and conclude a marriage, which is in fact not a marriage, and force the girl into customary love, if she were, by the grace of God, to be freed from such marriage and submit to the love of the heart, it is both beautiful and sanctioned by the norms of right conduct. Madhuri, your heart has taken the path of right conduct according to our norms, and we shall provide all assistance and support.’ Kumud: ‘The Shastras say that an eight-year-old girl can be given in marriage and she is ready to take and fulfill the vows taken at the time of marriage. Your attempt to nullify this is a violation of morality and your effort is wasted on me.’ Mohini: ‘It might be futile, but it is not a violation of morality. The Shastras that you refer to were written for a specific context and time. It was useful and appropriate for that limited context. But it is not an eternal principle transcending space and time. The norms that we follow are eternal. The Shastras also make other prescriptions that contradict what you said. The Shastras are against the immoral and depraved customs prevalent in your society. The Shastras say that a husband who cohabits with a wife who has not attained puberty commits the sin of killing a brahmin. According to Shastric injunctions at the time of marriage the bride must give the groom the varmala. If the father’s gift of the bride were sufficient condition for the completion of marriage rituals, this injunction about the varmala would be unnecessary. If this part of the ritual is not redundant, it requires the bride’s consent. Are young girls capable of giving such consent? Do these young girls understand the meaning and significance of marriage vows? Who is responsible when a girl is not capable of giving consent to the marriage—the father or the husband? According to the Shastras there should be a recitation of the Kama-Stuti when the father is performing the ritual of making a gift of the bride. The verse very clearly states that the one making the gift is Kama, the one receiving the gift is Kama and the gift itself is Kama. The husband also says that Soma gave the bride to Gandharva, who in turn gave her to Agni, who in turn gave it to the man.⟨fn:276⟩ Moreover, the groom says to the bride: ‘‘The Saman am I, the Rik thou; the heaven I, the earth thou.”⟨fn:277⟩ Marriage involves performance of duties. Is the young girl who hears these verses capable of performing the duties that are enjoined upon her? Does that girl understand either attachment or sensual pleasures? Madhuri, the ancient sages did not believe so. During the Saptapadi the groom addresses the bride as Sakha, as a companion. May my husband live long; may my relations be prosperous. Svâhâ! These grains I throw into the fire: may this bring prosperity to thee, and may it unite me with thee. May Agni grant us that. Svâhâ! I seize thy hand for the sake of happiness, that thou mayst live to old age with me, thy husband. Bhaga, Aryaman, Sâvitrî, Purandhi, the gods have given thee to me that we may rule our house. This am I, that art thou; that art thou, this am I. The Sâman am I, the Rik thou; the heaven I, the earth thou. Come! Let us marry. Let us unite our sperm. Let us beget offspring. Let us acquire many sons, and may they reach old age. Loving, bright, with genial minds may we see a hundred autumns, may we live a hundred autumns, may we hear a hundred autumns! To thee they have in the beginning carried round Sûryâ (the Sun- bride) with the bridal procession. Mayst thou give back, Agni, to the husbands the wife together with offspring.

One for sap, two for juice, three for the prospering of wealth, four for comfort, five for cattle, six for the seasons. Friend! be with seven steps (united to me). So be thou devoted to me.⟨fn:278⟩ ‘Should a girl who has to perform all these duties be a mere child of eight or ten? In your present day society, it is the good fortune of the girls that they are incapable of saying these vows, or else they would be made to parrot them. What good would that do? The intention of the law-givers was that the bride would comprehend and accept these vows. This understanding and acceptance cannot be realised in absence of attachment. While taking the sixth step the girl says that Vishnu bears witness to our love. This statement is not about the love that is to come in the future, it is indicative of the love that already exists. How vile and depraved are those who make young girls of ten or twelve say these words? The ritual does not end with this. The groom places his hand over the bride’s right shoulder and touches her heart. He addresses her heart and pledges his own heart to the vows taken by her. Into my will I take thy heart; thy mind shall follow my mind; in my word thou shalt rejoice with all thy heart; may Prajapati join thee to me.⟨fn:279⟩ ‘The bride whose heart is so touched should have reached an age fit for attachment and courtship. When the bride affirms her love the husband promises that their love would be eternal. How is this possible without attachment? When the bride and groom speak these pledges with clear minds, it signals that their attachment to each other has ripened. You people arrange marriages where attachment and courtship are absent. This is not a marriage in the pure sense. The man and woman so joined are not a couple. At the time of your marriage your uneducated mind was deceived. That man is not your husband. The man to whom the lord of love gave you, the man with whom you feel united spiritually is the real husband of your heart and body. He is the husband in the moral sense. The gift of your body that your father made was a fraud.’ Kumud: ‘It might be so for other brides. But I carefully listened to and comprehended the vows; I accepted them.’ Mohini: ‘In that case, you made vows to two men. Madhuri, I do not wish to make you impure and sullied. Any endeavour is to make you even purer. We ascetics of the Alakh marg perform a marriage of spirits. Before the marriage of the bodies and its consummation we are visited by the subtle spirits of our hearts. Even in this marriage, the union of subtle elements is performed only after a period of intense mutual attachment. The subtle elements of our couples are thus united and they attain a state of togetherness and love. They also cohabit after this period. They indulge in sensual pleasures and even have progeny. They stay together till the body of one of them withers and dies, while the spirit unites and merges with the Formless God and becomes one with the immortals. We regard that unseen spirit to be immortal and unlike wider society, we do not mourn the body that has withered. A widowed man or woman does not enter into another marriage after the demise of the spouse. They regard the entire domain of love as having become one with the Formless God. Their experience and object of love becomes the Formless One. They remain steadfast and virtuous to this love. Madhuri, among us, widowed ascetics do not forsake adornments like bangles and beautiful clothes. We regard the spirit to be present before us and continue to wear beautiful clothes. We, like Bindumati, devote ourselves to the love of God and experience his presence in our lives. Madhuri, here is the proof. Look at the bangles on my hands!’ Mohini extended her arms. She seemed possessed by an intense experience of love. She stood up, closed her eyes and said, ‘Madhuri, the body of my beloved companion is no more. But the moment I close my eyes, my inner vision can see his spirit. And I adorn myself as a mark of his everlasting presence. I hear his voice, a voice that has no origin. And with his consent I open my eyes.’

Mohini, a widow, was overjoyed with this feeling of union with her spiritual husband. Her eyes were moist with tears of joy. She wiped them and said, ‘Madhuri, only this spiritual, unseen love is true. You have, after a period of attachment and courtship, attained love which is not only beautiful but righteous with a great soul like Navinchandraji. That is the only true marriage. The other marriage was fraudulent. You have to free yourself from that deceit. He aspires and lusts after the beauty of your heart and your body. Is this knowledge not enough to rid you of the love that you have forced yourself to believe in? Can’t you shed it like the serpent’s skin? Don’t you see before you a new dawn?’ Kumud: ‘I do not see the dawn that you describe, nor do I see that as a fortunate turn. My heart worships the love that you have described. I had a fleeting experience of such love, but my fate robbed me of it. I must wander around and face hardships and wait for the time when the body of this soul of fire is consigned to flames. I will spend the rest of my time with the succour that Chandravali Maiya has given me.’ Kumud spoke with a deep but quiet distress. Mohini: ‘But what is the need for it? Do you not have a duty towards Navinchandraji? Has that fraudulent and deceitful marriage of yours freed you from this duty?’ Kumud: ‘I cannot decide what is moral and what is immoral. I cannot decide between right and wrong. But that marriage is not fraudulent. It is not a deception. I took the marriage vows with full knowledge of them. I might have been lazy about reflecting on their deeper meaning, but I cannot deceive the man to whom I gave those vows. In fact, after listening to you recite these vows, I have firmly resolved that this body will remain faithful only to him. Mohini Maiya, just as the moon lights up the valley, your discourses have filled my heart with its soft light. I can clearly perceive two elements. As I see the world bathed in the beauty of moonlight, I can see with equal clarity the beauty of the world of love that you ascetics have created. But my vision is framed by this window; it perceives many elements of the valley. Similarly, I see the various streams that have combined to create my world and the location of love within it. Just as one who is on the other side of the window cannot go out and be a part of the world of the valley, I am bound by my vows and have no right to immerse myself in the stream of love created by my Chandra.’ Mohini: ‘I have no adequate response to these beautiful arguments. You are endowed with intellect. You are the first one to have silenced me in the argumentation about love and desire. But I will continue to make efforts to help free you from this window that imprisons you. I do want you to have the joy of spiritual love.’ Kumud: ‘You may do so. But my Chandra has attained the highest form of asceticism. I do not want my presence to deviate him from his chosen path.’ Mohini: ‘That must be decided by God, not you.’ Kumud: ‘So be it. But why should you insist on taking me down a path that I consider depraved or at any rate not beneficial to me?’ Mohini: ‘I am expert on the subject of desire. I understand your innermost desires.’ Kumud: ‘I have already told you what I desire.’ Mohini: ‘I will have to examine and understand as to what your ego wants, what you want because it is the convention, what your body desires and what the aspirations of your spirit are. Madhuri, I see the beauty of your words as also of your heart. But speech and heart though one are distinct. I shall obtain honey from both and give you a taste of what is yours.’
chapters.summary: Kumud, at the math, intensely debates love and duty with ascetics, upholding her vows as her heart yearns for Sarasvatichandra under the moonlit sky.

chapters.title: Sweet Concerns for Sweeter Madhuri
paragraphs: Sweet Concerns for Sweeter Madhuri In a short time Kumud’s life story became known to all members of the Parivrajika Math and the Vihar Math. The ascetics found the combination of social norms and spiritual love miraculous, and both the maths engaged in lengthy discussions about it. In this context Madhuri’s association with Navinchandra also became well known. His conduct towards Madhuri was held as wrong, but they also found reasons to understand and appreciate Swami Vishnudas’ partiality towards him. There was a general consensus on this issue. The only matter of debate was about the desirability or otherwise of the two lovers uniting according to the tenets of the Alakh Marg. They were also uncertain about the rituals to be adopted for concluding this union. Kumud slept surrounded by other women ascetics. Her mind full of Sarasvatichandra, her eyelids kept opening and closing uneasily in her sleep. Mohini and Bansari, who slept on either side of her, remained awake and watched over her. That morning, Kumud had been shocked to see Sarasvatichandra dressed like an ascetic. During the course of the day she had heard the story told and re-told in the community. She was no longer in a state of shock. She in fact felt unburdened. She had regained her equilibrium; but every time she closed her eyes the image of him in an ascetic’s garb flashed before her. What is better for a man like him, she thought, to be an ascetic or a householder? If he were to live among the people, how much good he would do them. I am unfortunate, but it would be a grave wrong if a gem like him were to be engulfed in this fire and reduced to ashes. What can I possibly say to him? His glorious, handsome face and body appear pale as the early morning moon. He eats and sleeps in a place like this; his body will wither in these hardships. But his face looks as blissful as before. How hard they had to try to draw him into conversation! He barely spoke a few words, that too because the women ascetics cleverly forced him to. Most certainly his grief is deep—very deep. Kumud fell asleep with her beloved’s image in her heart, and she dreamt. In her dream she spoke aloud. Such days as you have passed, such as I have known, Whose fevered flames have raged in every vein, And anguish wrung conscious existence from me— Thy love alone preserved my fleeting life.⟨fn:280⟩ Mohini and Bansari sat up and listened to her. Mohini whispered to Bansari, ‘The treatise on desire speaks of a deeply experienced union— this is it.’ Bansari: ‘Yes. It is. A woman in love has many chambers in her heart, each concealing a deeper secret.’ Mohini: ‘Yes. Madhava has described this state. Love rages tyrant in her bosom, But lavishes his bounties on her form.⟨fn:281⟩ Just then they heard some footsteps. Bhakti Maiya and Vamini entered the math. Mohini and Bansari received them. ‘Everything has been arranged,’ said Vamini. Bhakti Maiya: ‘A tent would be erected near the Yamuna Kund in the Vihar Math. The Ras Lila will commence in the evening at the time of moonrise. Before that Guruji will inspect all the arrangements. Navinchandraji will accompany him. We still have to entice him for the Ras Lila. We have to decide where Madhuri should be taken.’

Mohini: ‘It is not as easy as you imagine it to be.’ Bansari: ‘Her adherence to the conventions of society will not allow her to own up to the spiritual union.’ Mohini: ‘There you make an error. Even Malati broke free from such shackles.’ Bhakti Maiya: ‘Whether she should be freed from the shackles or not will be determined by Sri Alakh Bhagwan. Our task is to bring together two hearts on fire as two hot iron rods are brought together. If what we desire is inopportune, the desire will not have a bodily dimension; Kamadev will not unite with Rati.’ Mohini: ‘That desire is already born.’ Bhakti Maiya: ‘That can be known only to Sri Yadunandan who gives birth to all desires. You and I cannot know that.’ Bansari: ‘What then is our duty?’ Bhakti Maiya: ‘We can determine the truth of their relationship only after they meet, and only then can we decide upon our duty. We must witness what feelings arise in Navinchandra after he meets Madhuri and is acquainted with her condition. Once we know the desires of both, we shall decide if we should play the messenger to unite them or if we should pray to Yadunandan to help them cultivate indifference to each other and yet be at peace with the self.’ Mohini: ‘Bhakti Maiya has spoken wisely. We should create a situation that Navinchandraji and Madhuri meet when Guruji comes out to inspect the arrangements. We should, from a distance, know the desire of Navinchandraji and take a decision based on that.’ Bhakti Maiya: ‘That is appropriate.’ Bansari: ‘But how shall we gain access to the innermost core of Madhuri’s heart? The vows that she took at the time of her marriage and the attachment that her heart feels have torn her asunder. Is it not necessary to know which of the two shall give her greater peace?’ Bhakti Maiya: ‘That is also correct.’ Mohini: ‘We have the rest of the night to consider this.’

Vamini: ‘Have you locked that window?’ Mohini: ‘Why?’ Vamini: ‘She was once saved from drowning in the sea. Her despair might prompt her to throw herself out of this window.’ Bansari: ‘But her heart is no longer grief-stricken.’ Bhakti Maiya: ‘That is true. But the suggestion is appropriate. We have brought with us Chandravali’s heart; we must keep it safe. Vamini, lock that window.’ Vamini bolted the window. All of them spread their blankets around Kumud to sleep. Vamini: ‘Oh lord of love, oh Manmath, how many ways are there in which the Formless God manifests Himself? How many ways are there to save the human heart? But Sri Alakh has so willed that young hearts remain partial to you. In a grove full of the loveliest of creepers laden with buds and flowers, young hearts are but drawn towards the flowering mango tree.’ Bansari: ‘Oh Manmath, you are the lord of desire. Your being is for the benefit of the world. Even the koel favours the mango tree for its life- giving sap, which also ignites desire.’ Mohini: ‘The world may force them to take any number of vows, but young hearts will always be ruled by him. Madhuri, you can be saved only by worshipping this god.’ Bhakti Maiya: ‘It is the lord of love who brought this woman, beautiful and delicate as a flower, to this harsh and inapproachable place. How is one to douse desire when its fires are stoked by clothes drenched in water, lotus stems, moonbeams and sandalwood? The glory of Kama is such that he can transform a humble bamboo hut into a palace, light up the darkest of corners, turn the rough, crusty earth softer than a bed and garbage as fragrant as kasturi.’ As if responding to them, Kumud spoke in her sleep, ‘O’ rain- laden clouds douse the fire that burns this heart, and if not then move away and let the moonbeams soothe me.’

Mohini: ‘Bhakti Maiya, send a messenger to Navinchandra who should clearly tell him that this chataka bird singed by the forest fire seeks your cooling waters. If you do not come, the world is transient and we shall not know where you will be the next moment, where your waters, and where this chataka.’ Bhakti responded in the affirmative and sank back into her world of sleep.
chapters.summary: The ascetics discuss Kumud's spiritual love and plan a meeting between Navinchandra and Madhuri, hoping to discern their true desires amidst societal norms.

chapters.title: Companion
paragraphs: Companion1 Silence in love betrays more woe Than words, though ne’er so witty —Sir Walter Raleigh All the women woke up before sunrise, brushed their teeth and performed their morning ablutions. They wore clean saffron clothes and got busy with their assigned tasks. Bhakti Maiya and her associates took Madhuri to the forest groves created in the Vihar Math. They discussed the programme for the evening’s Ras Lila and explained it to Madhuri. On a large rock on top of a hill a clearing was made. It was open and so could receive the moonlight as also the winds blowing from the south and west. It was on a higher elevation than all the three maths and so situated that it could be seen from all three. A vast kadamba tree occupied the centre space, around which small flowering shrubs were planted. The open square was surrounded by unsurmountable hill tops on which exotic birds nested. There was a pool of water called Yamuna Kund. The Ras Lila was to take place around it. The sea shore was clearly seen from this height. Its foaming waves seemed like the glistening breasts of a fair, young maiden. The group stood watching the sea. Any remark about the beauty of the scene seemed to take away something of that beauty. All of them stood there without speaking or moving. The comforting joy of it permeated their hearts. Vamini broke the silence. ‘Madhuri Maiya, this cool breeze blowing over the sea and rising up the mountain does not seem to give you any joy. This beautiful scene seems to have perturbed you.’ Kumud: ‘The sea reminds me of my past. The master of my heart compared me with moonlight and himself with the sea. He said that the moonlight causes the sea to rise, which was patently false. There is no moonlight and yet the sea waves continue to rise.’ Vamini: ‘But it will rise even more when the moonlight appears.’ Kumud: ‘Some other moon will rise, but my moonlight has been captured in the long locks of Shivji.’ Bansari: ‘The play of desire knows how to bring both the moon and the sea under its sway. This play of desire brings with it the memory of the moon even on a dark, moonless night. The meekness of your heart has shaken your faith. I have seen a similar condition ail many hearts.’ Kumud: ‘Why do you wish to poison my melancholy heart with hope when the heart has come to love dejection?’ Vamini: ‘Do you believe that you have disappeared from Navinchandra’s heart without leaving any trace? Oh dear Madhuri, I observed you both when your eyes met. The desire and attraction present in your eyes were present in his as well. Can you challenge me on this?’ This question broke Kumud’s defences. She was reminded of the meeting of the previous morning. Her innermost feelings became transparent. She could give no response. She was disturbed, felt abashed and looked down. Vamini: ‘What are you so abashed about? Why are you suspicious about the performance of what is your duty? We are willing to be your companions; we will carry your message. You should not have even a moment’s doubt about the state of your beloved’s heart. I have closely observed his eyes. He was filled with new hope the moment he saw you on this mountain. How do I know this? I have watched him carefully. What did I see? All his deep-locked emotions broke when he saw Radha’s face, Like sea waves cresting when the full moon appears. She saw her passion reach the soul of Hari’s mood— The weight of the Joy strained his face; Love’s ghost haunted him.⟨fn:283⟩ ‘That was the condition of your beloved. One look at him revealed this. Hence, your despair is untimely. Your beloved is like the sea and you are his moon. What he said to you when he first met you remains true even today.’ Kumud smiled and said, ‘Vamini Maiya, neither I nor my Chandra are adept at the science of love. You ask me not to forget my duty. But we householders are adept at non-performance of duty. If we, fish of salt waters, were to enter the high, pure life of your hermitage, we are certain to die.’ Bansari: ‘Melancholy and despair have taken possession of you, Madhuri, and deprived you of hope. Just as women’s hearts are hidden within the shell of shame and honour, the hearts of men are covered by layers of ponderous earnestness. You need to pierce through these layers. You will realise that your Chandra’s heart is aflame with love and desire. But that flame is hidden. You have to open his heart and once you do, you will find it echoing yours; you will find an image of your heart concealed within it. It will free both his and your hearts from the knots into which you have tied them. Therefore, take the path of love. Listen to the enticing sounds of honey bees Buzzing to bewilder tender women! Sympathize with a flock of cuckoos. Sing love’s commands like bards. Madhu’s tormentor Is faithful to you, fool. Follow him, Radhika!

A mass of vines with thickly clustered shoots, Quivering in the wind like a hand Seems to be gesturing to your tapering thighs To quicken your pace. Stop loitering here! Madhu’s tormentor Is faithful to you, fool. Follow him Radhika!⟨fn:284⟩ ‘Even your heart is covered with multiple layers. You are not able to erase the distasteful act committed by Navinchandra. You can neither erase it, nor express it. But it expresses itself in various ways. Thus you are deceived by yourself. But listen to the truth within. Your heart is like Chandi, intent on destruction. Get rid of your anger and listen to wisdom. Your friends know your armed body is ready For passionate battle, fierce Radha, By the war-drum beat of your clanging girdle. Meet his rich mood without shame! Madhu’s tormentor Is faithful to you, fool. Follow him, Radhika! As you cling to your friend in graceful play, Nails on your hand are arrows of love— Let your ringing bangles go to him! Wake Hari! Claim his intimacy! Madhu’s tormentor Is faithful to you, fool. Follow him, Radhika!⟨fn:285⟩ Kumud sighed deeply. Her red eyes glistened with tears as she spoke. ‘Bansari Maiya, let the ambers smoulder in their own ash. What you believe to be propitious and joyful is for me immoral and painful. It produces contradictory results. Clearly for you my tribulations are pointless.’

The group of ascetic women laughed at this. But Bhakti Maiya felt pity for her. ‘Beta Madhuri, there are many reasons why the path of happiness appears painful, and it is especially so for women. It is not surprising that someone like you should find this path extreme. We women have soft, delicate hearts, they are easily wounded and they are swift to retort. We have a remedy for your ailment. You have no cause to fear that. We perceive a similar love for you in Navinchandraji’s heart. You appear to disdain that love, but in fact it is not disdain. It is just an appearance of disdain. When he is tender you are harsh, When he is pliant you are rigid, When he is passionate you are hateful, When he looks expectant you turn away, You leave when he is loving. Your perverseness justly Turns your sandalbalm to poison, Cool moon rays to heat, ice to fire, Joys of loveplay to torments of hell.⟨fn:286⟩ Mohini, full of compassion, came closer and caressed Kumud. ‘Madhuri, we have investigated your ailment and provided a remedy that is in accordance with our Shastras. You must have faith in us and our Shastra. The joy which is the cause of your pain will eventually be blissful. Pray, listen to me. Do not entertain any thoughts of abandoning Navinchandraji. If you are unable to approach him, we will bring him to you; we have that much faith in his compassion. Hari comes when spring winds, bearing honey, blow. What greater pleasure exists in the world, friend? Don’t turn wounded pride on Madhava! He is proud too, sullen Radha. Your swollen breasts are riper than palm fruits. Why do you waste their rich flavour? Don’t turn wounded pride on Madhava! He is proud too, sullen Radha.

How often must I repeat the refrain? Don’t recoil when Hari longs to charm you! Don’t turn wounded pride on Madhava! He is proud too, sullen Radha. Why do you cry in hollow despair? Your girlfriends are laughing at you. Don’t turn wounded pride on Madhava! He is proud too, sullen Radha. See Hari on his cool couch of moist lotuses! Reward your eyes with this fruit! Don’t turn wounded pride on Madhava! He is proud too, sullen Radha. Why conjure heavy despair in your heart! Listen to me tell how he regrets betraying you. Don’t turn wounded pride on Madhava! He is proud too, sullen Radha. Let Hari come! Let him speak sweet words! Why condemn your heart to loneliness? Don’t turn wounded pride on Madhava! He is proud too, sullen Radha.⟨fn:287⟩ Kumud gave no response, but her eyes brimmed over with tears. The sea waves gave her no solace; they only reflected her turbulence. The ascetics were pained to see that she was deeply hurt, that her heart was filled not with joy but with grief. They felt that their assessment of her ailment was wrong, and so their remedy was likely to be equally wrong. Suddenly Kumud felt as if she were being gently pulled back, and found herself in Chandravali’s embrace. She wept as Chandravali held her close. ‘My dear Madhuri, I could not bear the separation and so I came after you. I will put a balm over your heart. Mohini Maiya, I heard you. But what ails her is deep and complex. Madhuri is torn between convention, customs and her heart’s desire. There is egoistic love, love due to convention and habit in conflict with the most subtle form of spiritual love. We can decide about the fate of her many loves only after we know the root of her ailment. Is it not possible to give her solace, give her the equanimity that one gets at the feet of the Mother Goddess? Is there not a possibility of being happy in renunciation?’ Kumud freed herself from the embrace and said, ‘That is all I want, Chandravali Maiya, that is all I want! See, the very idea has made my tears dry up.’ Kumud stepped back and looked at Chandravali with clear, dry eyes. Mohini: ‘Chandravali Maiya, your diagnosis is incomplete.’ Bansari: ‘We, too, have entered the depths of her heart.’ Vamini: ‘If you were right, she would not have been so eager to leave the island and come up the mountain.’ Kumud: ‘I accept all these accusations. I am a fallen woman. But the only remedy I want is the one suggested by Chandravali Maiya.’ Mohini: ‘Her fortitude and your strength cannot be compared. The remedy that is tolerated by one can kill another.’ Chandravali: ‘Madhuri, we will find a solution that you like and in which your happiness is secured. It will also be what you can bear. These women have become your companions and like true sakhis they want you to be united with your beloved. Allow them to do their work without any fear or shame so that they can test both their diagnosis and their remedy. Be assured that nothing will be done without your consent. I will protect you like Tamasa who watched over Sita. Bhakti Maiya, I have some knowledge of the remedy proposed by you. You can inform me later of the other means. But ensure that my dear child does not suffer due to your remedy.’ Bindumati came forward and said, ‘Madhuri Maiya, do not be afraid. Your multilayered love is subtle, pure and pious and also mysterious. Indifferent through despair, ruffled by harsh treatment, paralysed as it were on account of the sudden meeting in this long separation, pleased by its inherent goodness, and deeply affected by the touching words of your husband, your heart appears to melt with love, as it were, at this moment.⟨fn:288⟩ ‘Bansari Maiya, is this correct or not? I gave an example from what I have read, but you are experienced in these matters.’ Bansari: ‘Our experience is no match for the arguments of your intellect. So we shall listen to you with attention. But the remedy will come from experience.’
chapters.summary: Kumud, called Madhuri, struggles with her deep melancholy and conflicted feelings for Navinchandra, while her companions try to persuade her to embrace love's path.

chapters.title: Diagnosis and Remedy
paragraphs: Diagnosis and Remedy Your heart, Most holy dame, though from the world estranged, Is softened still with pity and affection Towards these thy children; and thy active love, Howe’er opposed to penance and devotion, Shall like the will of destiny prevail.⟨fn:289⟩ Unmarried girls, widows and ascetics lived together in the Parivrajika Math. Young unmarried girls were taught the Kama Shastra. But if a woman desired a union with a man, that could only take place in the Vihar Math. Only married couples could live in the Vihar Math. Usually a widow presided over the Parivrajika Math. She had to be one who had experienced all three stages—young girl, married hermit and widow—and was learned. A married couple that was learned, generous, ascetic and knowledgeable in the Shastras was appointed as the head of the Vihar Math. At one time Chandravali and Viharpuri were married and they presided over the Vihar Math. Both of them decided to live an ascetic life.
