Viharpuri joined Vishnudas and Chandravali became the head of Parivrajika Math. After a time Chandravali gave up residing on Sundargiri and made the island her home. Mohini had taken her place as the head of the Parivrajika Math. If any young girl was struck by the arrow of love and desire, she had to be cared for till her marriage; sometimes a companion was arranged for her and if necessary even a messenger was appointed to carry her messages. All these were part of the duties of the head. The appointment of companion and messenger was deemed fit only if the love was both bodily and spiritual. The texts on love and desire generally pertain to bodily, sensual pleasure. But the learned men and women of this hermitage had added an aspect of subtle or spiritual love to it. They believed that sensual love must eventually lead to spiritual love just as the worship of the manifest form leads to devotion to the Unmanifest One. Chandravali was skilled and well-versed in this art. At one time she took delight in this art and appreciated its beauty. Vishnudas was appointed Master of all the three maths. Under his guidance the monastery and the path of Alakh rose to new heights. He wished to appoint a worthy successor. A householder was not considered worthy of this responsibility and none of the ascetics living under his tutelage were learned enough to take his place. Vishnudas felt that Viharpuri was a suitable successor, but he was married. Chandravali came to know about this. So, to fulfill the desire of the Master, to ensure that her husband could respond to his true calling and to ensure the continuation of the sect and the hermitage, Chandravali expressed her wish that both of them should become ascetics; Viharpuri should go and become a disciple of the Master and she would live in the Parivrajika Math. The couple forsook their desire for each other as easily as a snake sheds its skin. They blessed each other and separated. Stories of their love and asceticism came to be recounted in the hermetic community. Chandravali became the head of Parivrajika Math. Sometimes, quite unintentionally, she and Viharpuri would meet. She regarded such meetings as an obstacle to their resolve; so she left the hermitage on Sundargiri to live on the island. She decided that henceforth she would not worship God in the male form and became devoted to the feminine aspect of the Unmanifest God. Amba became the manifest form that she worshipped. She had so far remained steadfast in her resolve; but pity and affection for Kumud had brought her back to Sundargiri. Chandravali knew that one of the windows of the Parivrajika Math opened onto the valley. Kumud had once tried to drown herself in the sea. Chandravali feared that she might throw herself out of the window, and hence she had followed her up the mountain. That fear had proved to be unfounded. The women who had accompanied Kumud recounted the events and conversations of the past one day. Chandravali’s loving heart was perplexed. That afternoon, Kumud, accompanied by Vamini and Bansari, was sent to look at the beautiful spots of the mountain. Mohini, Bhakti, Bindumati and Chandravali sat together to discuss their plans for Kumud. Chandravali heard them and for a while she said nothing. All others also remained quiet. A koel’s call broke the silence. Bindumati looked up and recited. ’T was festival in her pure life When budding blossoms showed; And now she leaves you as a wife— Oh, speed her on her road! The trees are answering your prayer In cooing cuckoo-song, Bidding Shakuntala farewell, Their sister for so long.⟨fn:290⟩ Mohini: ‘Bindu, why did you sing this verse?’ Bindumati: ‘I blessed Madhuri.’ Mohini: ‘She is not on her way to her husband’s house, is she?’ Bindumati: ‘She will go.’ Mohini: ‘Who said so?’ Bindumati: ‘The koel did.’ Chandravali: ‘Daughter Bindu, you are right. You asked Madhuri that if not desire, what has brought her to this mountain.’ Bindumati: ‘Yes, I asked her something similar.’ Chandravali: ‘And what was her response?’

Bindumati: ‘She sat with one hand on her knee and the other clutching her forehead. She said nothing, but there was a song on her lips.’ Mohini: With an arm leaning on her knee while resting a cheek On the palm of the inclined tendril of her hand, another woman Demonstrated her yearning by humming a soft, tempered melody Hedged in her throat, never moving up and down the scale of tones.⟨fn:291⟩ Chandravali: ‘Did she not say anything at all?’ Bindumati: ‘No, nothing. I even told her that we will go and make a plea to Navinchandraji. She did not respond to that either. Finally, I told her that if she said nothing, we would say whatever we liked to him under her name.’ Chandravali: ‘And then?’ Bindumati: ‘She said nothing even then. When it became unbearable, she got up with tears in her eyes and went away.’ Mohini: ‘I can understand why.’ When a woman with beautiful eyes was asked “Won’t you give me The message?” she answered nothing at all out of her shame But she kept glancing, with a troubled gaze, at her own body That was thinned by the sharp shafts of the God Who Has No Body.⟨fn:292⟩ Chandravali: ‘Mohini, what was Madhuri’s state of mind before you met Navinchandraji at the landing place?’ Mohini: ‘Her condition was what the messenger said about the heroine to the hero.’ Why the question? Return to her without delay. Listen, how I saw your beloved weep on the path waiting for you. She anxiously looked at each wayfarer, hoping it was you, and wept tears of dejection at her futile search.⟨fn:293⟩

Chandravali: ‘Bhakti Maiya, at what point did you become aware of this?’ Bhakti: ‘Only after Navinchandraji left, and to that extent I was caught off-guard. They went down and we commenced our upward journey. Madhuri’s eyes followed Navinchandra just as the sun’s rays follow darkness.’ Mohini: ‘That is what it was.’ To their lovers the young and artlessly impassioned women Sent out their friends who were like their own glances Versed in how to make love evident, sweetly communicating, And fully able to carry off the hearts of men who were desired.⟨fn:294⟩ Chandravali: ‘Bhakti Maiya, when you described Navinchandra’s virtues, his decision to lead an ascetic life and the Master’s partiality towards him, what was Madhuri’s response?’ Bhakti: ‘When I described his virtues and glory, she was in a meditative state. But when I spoke of his desire for renunciation, she grew perturbed and thoughtful.’ Mohini: ‘I have observed her meditative state. We should tell Navinchandraji.’ Whenever she hears a conversation about you and with the tip Of her finger over and over again scratches her ear, What she is doing is crowding in the swarm of your virtues Which have filled her hearing, because she can’t be satisfied!⟨fn:295⟩ Chandravali: ‘Beta Bindu, when you informed Madhuri that Navinchandraji is certain to come for the evening’s programme of the Ras Lila, what did she say?’ Bindumati: ‘She looked vacantly into space.’ Mohini: ‘Even that I understand.’

A woman who felt a strong longing for the pleasures Of love-making kept measuring the distances between the sun And the Mountain of the Evening, with her eyes turning over And over to the opening in the window that rose before her.⟨fn:296⟩ Chandravali: ‘What was her response to his resolve for renunciation?’ Bhakti: ‘We have not observed that closely, but last night she said that she did not want to cause the eclipse of her Chandra.’ Mohini: ‘That language is not a true reflection of her innermost feelings. That was an egoistic response; such momentary egoism does not destroy the desire for spiritual union.’ Chandravali: ‘But none of you have observed her pain at the thought of Navinchandra’s ascetic frame of mind.’ Mohini: ‘At the landing space, she had wept. She had seen him for the first time in those clothes.’ Bhakti: ‘When she learnt about the organisation of our hermitage and especially about the Vihar Math, her grief lessened and she was at peace.’ Chandravali: ‘That sense of peace may also be because she has understood the significance of renunciation. It is also possible that she regards Navinchandra’s renunciation as superior and hence controls her own passion for him. It is possible that she would support and protect his decision.’ Mohini: ‘Whatever that might be. But if this pair thirsts after each other and remains thirsty on this mountain, it is not right. If we delay any further, it may cause great harm and we would repent later. A pair of deer deeply in love escaped from a forest fire, burning with thirst. A pool had enough water for one, but not for two. Both made a pretence of drinking from it and died of thirst.’ Bhakti: ‘The pair of chakravak birds is separated at night; once the night is over, they meet and converse. It is our duty to get these two birds together. After that if they remain unattached and free of passion they will remain separate; but if they desire each other they will unite. It will be decided according to the designs of the Unmanifest God. We now clearly know our duty.’ Mohini: ‘This pair of deer should not be separated because of the inertness of our minds.’ Bindumati: ‘Please do not forget that even Madhuri waits for night fall.’ Chandravali: ‘I feel that we have considered all aspects; the time for thinking is over. Now all that remains is to find means appropriate to the end.’ Madhuri: ‘What we need to do is what I sang this morning. You have seen Madhuri respond to it with tears. Until the girl meets her husband, their hearts will not open.’ Chandravali thought for a while and said, ‘Bhakti Maiya, all that is required of us is to be the messenger. Who is that person trusted by both?’ Bhakti: ‘There is no one. Navinchandraji associates only with Viharpuri and Radhedas; he is never alone. He discusses issues only with the Master and he sleeps in the cave adjoining the Master’s hut. As for Madhuri, we are her companions.’ Mohini: ‘We will reach the bottom of the well only if we tie two ropes together.’ Chandravali: ‘How?’ Mohini: ‘You hold the heroine’s hand, while Viharpuri holds the hero’s hand.’ Bhakti: ‘But who will hold Viharpuri’s hand?’ Mohini: ‘That can be done only if the two who have separated are brought together by love and compassion. Chandravalibehn, if Navinchandra is the chosen successor, Viharpuri will be able to return to Vihar Math; and if Navinchandra decides to join Vihar Math, Viharpuri will fulfill the Master’s desire. Both outcomes are desirable.

Therefore, you must bring these two together. There is no one else capable of doing it.’ Bhakti: ‘The two of you acting together will be able to know what lies in their hearts. Both are partial to each of them, and Madhuri has special trust in you.’ Chandravali: ‘Is it proper for me to do this now that I have submitted myself to the Mother Goddess?’ Bhakti: ‘The Goddess sent you here so that you could save her daughter. Chandravali, it is our natural responsibility that we become messengers in this spiritual union.’ Chandravali: ‘The day, at my behest, my beloved and I became ascetics, I resolved never to look him in the eye again.’ Mohini: ‘Your renunciation is not so feeble, Chandravali, that the mere meeting of eyes will destroy it.’ Chandravali: ‘Desire, disembodied and reduced to ashes, survives. If that fire is fuelled it might rekindle itself. It is best that either you or Bhakti take this responsibility.’ Mohini: ‘On one hand we have this intellectually endowed beauty; on the other hand there is grave, ascetic Navinchandra. No one but Chandravali and Viharpuri can get them to open up their hearts. The result we desire can be obtained only if they together and jointly perform the role of the messenger.’ Bhakti: ‘Chandravali, why are you so apprehensive?’ Chandravali: ‘The heart, however detached and ascetic, trembles while going closer to the beloved. I do not trust my heart, and Madri’s experience has taught us about the hearts of men. Bhakti Maiya, for the greater good this heart of mine allowed a great soul like Viharpuri to sit at the feet of the Master, while I sought refuge of the Goddess. Should that greater good be forsaken? No, I cannot do that.’ Mohini: ‘Egoistic. Will Chandravali become egoistic? The light of the unseen, Unmanifest God permeates all beings. Have you now forsaken your duty to become a conduit of that light? Does Chandravali now consider the task of a messenger beneath her?’

Chandravali: ‘Pray do not misunderstand. What can Chandravali not do for Madhuri? But do I have any right to destroy a building that I helped construct?’ Mohini: ‘In that case, you should have allowed Madhuri to drown in the sea. You saved her, you gave her life. You cannot now refuse to bring joy and fulfillment to that life.’ Chandravali closed her eyes and considered their arguments. Her heart beat faster; its quickening was evident to all by the movement of the garment covering her breasts. Her tears stopped. Finally, growing calmer, she looked up and said, ‘Madhuri, Chandravali will be your messenger. For your sake I will endanger even my penance. I sent you here with the consent of the Goddess. It was She who sent me here. She will also protect my penance and grant you happiness. Mohini, tell me, what is it you want me to do?’ Mohini: ‘This evening we will accompany Madhuri to the Ras Lila. We will converse with Navinchandraji and Madhuri. Chandravali, you should remain a silent witness to this. Tonight, you should sleep by her side and find out what is in her heart. After some time, Bindumati should join in the conversation. The following morning you should report this conversation to Viharpuri and seek his opinion. Viharpuri should find out Navinchandra’s thoughts. He should also ensure that from tomorrow Navinchandra shifts his sleeping place out of the Master’s cave to some solitary place. The next step would depend upon the outcome of this step. Chandravali: ‘I believe that this can be done. But for some time now I have had no experience of such tasks. I do not trust my own judgement about these matters.’ Mohini: ‘That should not worry you. The second task is that Madhuri has to be freed from the delusion that she is duty-bound to love her husband. You have to either do it yourself or show us a way of doing it.’ Chandravali: ‘Just as the light of the Unmanifest God dispels all doubts and the desire for manifest forms, the emergence of pure love will dispel all delusions from their hearts. That should not worry us. We have to bring the two flaming hearts together. If even after we have removed both outward and inner obstacles, they do not come together, we should understand that one of them was cold to the idea of the union, and that should be taken as the will of God. In that case we should all abide by divine will and I should take Madhuri back to the island.’ Bhakti: ‘If the Goddess so wills, Madhuri will be united with Navinchandraji.’ Mohini: ‘The Vihar Math will welcome them.’ Bindumati: ‘And even if your heart slips, Chandravali, the Vihar Math will welcome you back.’ Chandravali was displeased. She pushed Bindumati aside and walked away deep in thought, followed by others who looked delighted at this prospect.
chapters.summary: Chandravali, Mohini, and others discuss Kumud's longing for Navinchandra and his ascetic resolve, devising a plan to understand their true feelings and potentially unite them.

chapters.title: Subtle Desires of a Subtle Body
paragraphs: Subtle Desires of a Subtle Body True love’s that gift which God has given To man alone beneath the heaven; It is not fantasy’s hot fire, Whose wishes, soon as granted, fly: It liveth not in fierce desire, With dead desire it does not die; It is the secret sympathy, The silver link, the silken tie, Which heart to heart, and mind to mind, In body and in soul can bind.   —‘The Lay of the Last Minstrel,’ Walter Scott. Towards the evening Vishnudas, accompanied by all his disciples went out to inspect the functioning of all the three maths. He inquired from the heads of the maths about their general condition, the inmates and guests, the courses of study and other industries and activities. He gave various suggestions. He also familiarised Sarasvatichandra with the institutional arrangements of the hermitage. As the moon rose in the sky, the women of Vihar Math performed the Ras Lila around the Yamuna Kund. Some women were dressed as Krishna, while others as gopis. One woman played the role of Radha, while five or six others enacted the role of her companions. The first act was about the domestic lives of the gopis. Krishna was unseen. But the gopis were drawn to the song of his flute coming from afar. They pined for him. In the second act, Krishna was on the kadamb tree, playing his flute. The gopis surrounded the tree like bees that hover over a lotus. In the third act Krishna appeared in many forms and played Ras with the gopis. Song, music and dance were beautifully brought together to create harmony. In the fourth act Radha and her companions tore away from the other gopis and in the fifth act Radha and Krishna danced with each other on the banks of the Yamuna. Their union signalled the conclusion of the Ras Lila. Mohini explained the significance of each act to Kumud. She introduced Madhuri to all members of the hermitage and praised her intellect, knowledge and aesthetic sensibility. She also narrated the hardships that Kumud had faced. Bindumati sang a song composed by Kumud. Finally, the festivities came to an end and all went back to their quarters around midnight. They talked about what they had heard and seen and fell asleep. Kumud and the group of women, who had developed a deep fondness for her, remained awake. Every one, except Chandravali, had returned. Vamini and Bhakti had followed Chandravali from a distance. The two returned a few hours before dawn. Calling Mohini aside, they whispered something to her, after which all of them went to sleep. Before sunrise, the women had discussed the previous evening’s Ras Lila, the Guru’s instructions, Madhuri’s song and Navinchandra’s presence. They would have continued to talk about it but for the fact that on that day they were required to go among the people, seek alms and spread the message of Alakh. Hence the math was devoid of those who would have otherwise buzzed around like bees in gossip. When Kumud woke up, Mohini, Bindumati and Chandravali were the only others present. Bindumati helped Kumud in performing her morning rituals of bathing and cleansing. They sat on the steps of the math. ‘Bindu, what shall be the matters of our discourse today?’ Mohini asked. Bindumati: ‘I am wedded to Sri Krishna, our Supreme Lord. What other form of knowledge would I want? But if you know of ways by which I could, like Radha, become more steadfast in my devotion, do teach me.’

Mohini: ‘Mere body, in the gross sense, generates bodily desire and embodied love. One should separate subtle body, subtle desire and spiritual love from bodily desire. Eventually it would lead one to unprecedented feelings of devotion. This great form of art is easily attainable by the subtle body of an adept woman.’ Bindumati: ‘How is that achieved?’ Mohini: ‘Sensual desire has no place in the friendship of two men or two women, but the union of man and woman takes the form of bodily desire. The union of mother and son or brother and sister are determined by birth, but these unions do not manifest as bodily desire; if they do it is the highest form of immorality. Such unions should be of subtle love. Those men and women who do not come together by mere bodily attraction show the capacity for subtle love. In many cases their initial union is due to bodily desire. The prevalent norms of love and desire provide the possibility for such unions. Among us, we believe that manifest forms or idols lead us towards a comprehension of the Unmanifest One. Therefore we do respect bodily desire and attraction but such desire would, we believe, eventually lead us to subtle desire and spiritual love. Our bodies are made up of gross matter; they are nourished by food; they engage in sensual pleasure and experience bodily love. Those who desire to detach and remove themselves from this manifest, bodily existence seek a subtle existence. ‘A subtle body is concealed in our gross body. This subtle body is unseen; when its hidden potential and power is released, it creates the possibility for the subtle desire and love to emerge. The knowledge that all manifest forms have an unmanifest essence nurtures the desire for the subtle body and love. The knowledge of the essence of manifest forms nourishes the subtle body; part of this awareness comes from the external context and environment, while the other part emerges from within. This is the nature of religious quest, of desire for action and longing for the Creator. All these desires emanate from the subtle body and the enjoyment of the subtle body binds master and disciple and friends by subtle love. Among our disciples, those who have attained the middle level are nourished by subtle knowledge of many disciplines and texts. Food as matter arouses bodily desires; similarly the knowledge of subtle forms and their essence arouses subtle desires. Many couples initially enjoined by bodily attraction eventually experience the saturation of these desires. The learning and devotion of the subtle body within them would eventually lead them to subtle desire. Man and woman come together for the enjoyment of such subtle desire; what the man gives through his intellect, the woman nourishes by her instincts. Whenever man and woman come together in intercourse with such desires they are imbued with subtle desire. Animals seek union that is bodily; they want bodies to merge as water and milk merge into each other. But those who desire subtle love keep bodily desires separate from the longing of the subtle body. The subtle desires and union of Ram and Sita were such. The poet Magha has described that the discourse given to Krishna by Uddhava was heard by Lakshmi who resides in Krishna’s heart.⟨fn:297⟩ These are signals to the union and oneness which is the result of such subtle love. Padmavati in her subtle body had heard the compositions of the poet Jaydeva. ‘Bodily desire and attraction wither in old age. The body is gripped and diseased by pain. The body finally withers, and in the process one is tempted to detach oneself from the body that one desired. All bodily desires ultimately subside. This process continues. It destroys the essence of the subtle body; it becomes inert and with the passage of time it becomes dry and painful like the body of an addict. But the desire of the subtle body acts completely contrary to this process. The flame of subtle love remains alight till the very end of life; it remains steadfast in happiness and sorrow and virtuous in all conditions. Time does not destroy it; it destroys only the outer body. With time, love results in deeper love, and the poet Bhavabhuti who spoke from experience testifies that old age does not wither such love. A couple bound by subtle love has no fear of competing loves and debauched conduct is impossible in such love. The enjoyment and fulfillment of such love produces peace and quiet, not turmoil. This desire is never satiated; its flame is eternal. Just as a lamp burns as long as there is oil in it, subtle love and desire remain undiminished. ‘The supreme bliss of the realisation of the Unmanifest One and the experience of subtle desire are similar—both are simultaneous. An expert player of musical instruments learns to play a new instrument with the help of his innate knowledge; similarly one who has experienced subtle love feels the bliss of this union effortlessly, almost instinctively. Moreover, bodily love is subject to death and separation, both of which cause pain. But subtle love persists even under these conditions because it has no desire for the body. Chandravali and I are examples of this. I am a widow in the worldly sense and Chandravali is separated from her husband. But the flame of our subtle love has not diminished in the least. It does not require fuel in form of the body; it remains alight by its own fire.’ Chandravali: ‘Madhuri, even your love is subtle.’ Kumud: ‘And therefore, it remains unbroken even through dark times; it is neither destroyed nor does it allow my destruction. I will keep my body at the feet of the Mother Goddess and allow my subtle body to roam freely wherever it wants to.’ Chandravali: ‘You are dejected.’ Kumud: ‘When hope itself disappoints, dejection is the only hope.’

Chandravali: ‘If you desire to control bodily love and seek the fulfillment of subtle love, this desire is both moral and beneficial.’ Kumud: ‘I do not even see the possibility of bodily desire and I pray that my subtle desire is reduced to ashes in the fire of my grief.’ Chandravali: ‘Madhuri, yesterday I saw the great soul who your subtle body desires. He is a favourite of both Vishnudas and Madhuri. His qualities are apparent from his visage.’ Kumud: ‘That may or may not be. How is that of any significance?’ Mohini: ‘How can you say that? If the subtle desires of persons such as the two of you are fulfilled, it would do you good as also the world.’ Kumud: ‘How can an insignificant one like Madhuri have any right or capacity to do good to the world?’ Mohini: ‘You watched the Ras Lila, but you have forgotten its message. Bindumati, please sing that song, the one in praise of Sri Krishna’s flute.’ Bindumati sang. Oh flute, you are proud, Very proud. I was asleep in my palace; You robbed me of my sleep. Everyone knows your caste, You are a mere piece of wood from the forest. Krishna holds you to his lips And carries you in his hand! Mohini: ‘Madhuri, you become Navinchandra’s flute and sing his songs.’ Chandravali: ‘Sing that other song as well.’ Bindumati complied. The flute sings On the banks of Yamuna. Gods and sages alike Are drawn to its magic; Divine beings swoon over its melody;

The women of Vraja run to it, Forgetting even to clothe fully. Even the cows and calves Forget to graze When Surdas’ lord plays the flute. Chandravali: ‘A mere flute in the hands of a great soul can do so much for the world! What can an intelligent woman like Madhuri residing in the heart of Navinchandra not accomplish?’ Kumud: ‘I do not have that right. Why should we speak of it?’ Chandravali: ‘Are you not partial towards the man who has become the favourite of the Master of this hermitage? Will your heart allow you to forsake him?’ Kumud: ‘It is this wretched heart which is responsible for all the sin and turbulence.’ Chandravali: ‘You are still infatuated, young and inexperienced. But I shall bring the two of you together. You can keep your body for whoever you want to. But you will have to dedicate your subtle body to the husband of your subtle desire. If he frees you, you can come to the abode of the Goddess; if he does not, you shall submit to his desire. There are no restrictions on this. Madhuri, you can write him a letter or send him a message by other means. I understand your most subtle desire. If you do not go to him on your own we shall carry you to him and leave you with him just as Shakuntala’s friends left her with Dushyanta, saying, “You alone, when the king of the world is with you! ”⟨fn:298⟩ If he does not recognise and accept you, the Mother’s abode and Chandravali’s heart are always open to welcome you. You must prepare yourself in a short while.’ Chandravali got up and went out. Bindumati walked with her for some distance, then turned back with a verse on her lips. He ventures in secret to savour your passion, dressed for love’s delight. Radha, don’t let full hips idle! Follow the lord of your heart!

In the woods on the wind-swept Jamuna bank, Krishna awaits in wildflower garlands.⟨fn:299⟩ ‘Madhuri Maiya, you must accept the great soul who desires you,’ said Bindumati. ‘Chandravali Maiya, I am not one of those who would keep a rendezvous even for subtle love,’ Kumud responded as if she had just woken up from deep sleep. Mohini: ‘Chandravali is gone. What goes on in your mind, Madhuri, that you do not see those who are present and call out to those who are not?’ Kumud became alert and said, ‘Forgive me, Mohini Maiya. Does Chandravali Maiya expect me to keep an assignation?’ Mohini: ‘If an ascetic like Chandravali has accepted to be your messenger, who are you to feel abashed at the rendezvous?’ Kumud: ‘Chandravali Maiya is to be my messenger? What are you saying?’ Mohini: ‘I said what you heard.’ Kumud: ‘How so?’ Mohini: ‘She met Viharpuri last night. Viharpuri and Chandravali have decided with the Master’s consent that Viharpuri should set out to seek alms so that Chandravali could meet Navinchandra. Chandravali has gone to meet him.’ Kumud’s face betrayed her agony and confusion. ‘What have you done! Mohini Maiya, show me a way down from the mountain. I have seen Navinchandraji. I do not wish to meet him.’ Mohini: ‘What right do you have to disobey Chandravali?’ Kumud: ‘I do not wish to be a fallen woman.’ Mohini: ‘You are proud of your sense of rectitude. What do you think? That an ascetic like Chandravali met Viharpuri at night risking her own heart and its subtle aspirations and that she walked over fire out of love for you only so that you become a fallen woman? Do you think she does not understand the nature of right conduct as it applies to her and you? Do you think she wants to dilute the standards of moral conduct? She was such an able, righteous and noble head of these two Maths that Vishnudasji, who is the purest of all, believes that all desires of Chandravali’s heart can be nothing but pure. The fear that one as pure as Chandravali would lead you on the path of immorality is futile, misplaced and childish.’ Bindumati: ‘Madhuri, even during this rendezvous, both your body and heart will be protected.’ Kumud: ‘You showed me yesterday that he is revered by all ascetics, that he is regarded as detached and beyond all desire. I do not wish to shake him from his steadfastness. The lotus is content to gaze at the moon from afar. Madhuri will not do anything more than that.’ Mohini: ‘Let your body be as inert as that lotus flower, but set your subtle body free as the chakor bird. ‘Viharpuri knows that your Chandra harbours some deep pain within him. He believes that you are the reason for that pain. Viharpuri described Chandra to Chandravali thus: ‘‘Even before its rays can reach the ten directions, even before the chakor bird can drink its rays, the cruel and mighty Rahu devours the rising moon.’’ He further said, ‘‘The moon who cools all the ten directions, soothes all the three worlds, would not need much exertion to satiate a thirsty chakor.” ‘Madhuri, do not be the cause of his agony. Be his balm, accept the blessings of this pious Sundargiri and give us the debased conduct of your society. Accept the path of pure morality and love. Your husband has violated your body. But Chandravali, who is knowledgeable of your customs and is moved by deep love for you, has arranged a union of your hearts, your subtle bodies. You can consider anyone to be the master of your body, but there is only one beloved of your heart. You have to follow the one who rules your heart. You may call it assignation. But Chandravali knows the duty of your subtle body and she is concerned that you fulfill it.’

Bindumati: ‘Madhuribehn, it will soon be night. And if you continue to play truant, this time will slip away never to return.’ Kumud paid no attention to her. She got up and sat near the window. Bindumati silently placed a paper, ink pot and pen by her side. Then she came back and asked Mohini, ‘What next?’ ‘Keep that window locked. The window next to it is barred; you can keep that open. Make your bed next to hers. Keep an eye on her, but let her be alone. That is all we can do for now. I will go and finish my daily rituals.’
chapters.summary: Mohini and Chandravali guide a dejected Kumud on subtle love, encouraging her to embrace a spiritual union and free her heart, teasing a profound connection.

chapters.title: Sarasvatichandra and Chandravali
paragraphs: Sarasvatichandra and Chandravali Even the adverse turn of fortune of such persons proves very wonderful, since divine personages like these come to minister to their wants.⟨fn:300⟩ It was Sarasvatichandra’s practice to stay back at the hermitage whenever the ascetics went down the mountain to seek alms. Viharpuri, Radhedas and a few attendants would usually stay back with him. But today even Viharpuri had set out to seek alms. Sarasvatichandra walked around the cave situated at the back of the ashram. Radhedas sat reading near the front entrance. The attendants were busy cooking their own meals. Sarasvatichandra’s head was in turmoil ever since he had visited Surgram. On his way down Sundargiri he had seen Kumud, who was almost unrecognisable. The banter of the two groups of ascetics had given wings to his imagination. The old newspapers that the school teacher had made available confounded him completely. The newspapers had reported various stories about the domestic lives of Kumud Sundari, Saubhagya Devi, Pramaddhan, Buddhidhan, Sheth Laxminandan, Samant Mulu and others. These reports had pained him. Last evening a song composed by Kumud had been sung; he was still unravelling its meaning. His mind was full of her. Was this beautiful, delicate Madhuri really Kumud? Manchatura had been unable to find any trace of her. Could this Madhuri who floated to the island merely resemble Kumud? Deep pain has left its marks on her; she is a pale reflection of her earlier self, but the resemblance with Kumud is unmistakable. Has her face withered so much in the short time since she and I left Suvarnapur? There was a barb against me in the song that was sung yesterday. Who but my poor Kumud could have written such a song? I am the cause of her widowhood. She jumped into the river because of me. Did I push her in? Yes, it was me. Oh God! I am still alive, and yet she has become a widow. I have decided to become an ascetic. Now that Saubhagya Devi is no more, Kumud’s existence at her in-laws’ would be terribly lonely. She cannot imagine even in her dreams that Pramaddhan is no more. What immeasurable sorrow would the news cause her? I will not be able to bear witness to her grief. If she is really Kumud, I would take her to Gunasundari’s house. Laxman had left Sita in the forest. When they met again he told her, ‘Mother, the wretched Laxman who caused you so much grief bows to you.’ I will bow to Gunasundari and give her Kumud’s grief-stricken hand. I will face Gunasundari, though I have no right to show my face to anyone anymore. Sarasvatichandra, you are wretched and depraved! That will be my penance. But is Madhuri really Kumud? Chandrakant, I need you and your calm rational mind to support my unsteady heart and lead me out of this quandary. You are wandering around in search of me. I, too, am searching for you, but thus far our search has been in vain. The mendicant who was supposed to meet Chandrakant had gathered that the state police was looking for him, that they had kept watch over his movements and also knew about his meeting with Chandrakant. So the mendicant had quietly returned to the safety of Sundargiri without keeping his appointment. He had told Sarasvatichandra that his meeting with Chandrakant would not be fruitful till Navinchandra’s identity and location were revealed. They had together decided to let the issue cool down for four–five days and meanwhile look for another approach. Sarasvatichandra’s meeting with Chandrakant was thus delayed even as he felt the urgent need of his friend. Sarasvatichandra’s troubled mind was drawn to the soothing whispers of the pond where a thousand lotuses bloomed. He lay down on the soft grass at the pond’s edge, with his arm under his head for support. He looked at the hanging roots of the banyan tree. His attention wavered as he saw some books lying around. He sat up. Sarasvatichandra had been given complete access to the entire library of the monastery. The ascetics of Alakh Marg were familiar with texts dealing with both this-worldly and other-worldly existence. Society had come to believe that these texts should be heard or read but not followed in Kali Yuga, the present dark age. But these ascetics believed that at least in the monastery of Sundargiri, Sat Yuga, the age of light and truth, prevailed and that their conduct was according to the injunctions of the Shastras they believed in. The Shastris or interpreters of the texts usually tend to disregard difficult injunctions as observances unnecessary for the present times, and they do not regard such interpretation as violation. This convenient arrangement also permitted the prevalence of depraved societal customs and rituals. While these ascetics believed that the Shastric injunctions have been created for certain specific purposes and for specific goals. They, from time to time, evaluated the validity of these goals in the context of the principles of Alakh Marg. If the principles were found congruent with their beliefs they kept the practices attendant to them immutable. The philosophy and practice of love and desire were developed by them through this process. Sarasvatichandra had studied these texts with interest, but more interesting for him was the translation of these principles into practice. The previous day he had accompanied Vishnudasji on his inspection of the three maths. He realised that the design of the Parivrajika Math and the Vihar Math were without any precedence in the country and not in prevalence even among Western nations. His study of the texts in the library had given him a sense that during ancient times social practices of the Arya people might have resembled the arrangement at the hermitage. As he compared contemporary times with ancient times, he was filled with pain at the present condition, and as he considered the future, he was filled with dread. What a fall! The nation that created and practised such knowledge has fallen so low! Is it possible that the arrangement and customs preserved like sacred fire at the hermitage could not have been preserved in the country? How are so many people to cultivate and practise celibacy, asceticism and untroubled expression of desire of these ascetics? In absence of this cultivated sense, these practices might prove poisonous for society. Is it not possible to cultivate this higher state in our times? In societies of the West, its beneficial as also harmful effects can be seen. Their men of learning and political leaders have observed this; they also have the expertise to alter the course of their society and nation, and the people have faith in their ability to do so. But how are our people to trust our scholars who vouch by the knowledge of other countries? How are they to trust foreign rulers? Till such time as our scholars and political leaders, through their own endeavour, effort and generosity become fit to gain the faith of our people, it is futile to talk about the welfare of our nation. Dushyanta had to gain the trust of Shakuntala’s favourite deer; until he did so the deer refused the fresh grass offered to it by Dushyanta. My learned brothers say that conservatives do not listen to them and remain wedded to old practices. There is merit in this complaint, but who is to be blamed? Traditions represent the wisdom of ages and have hitherto been considered nurturing; they are the outcome of social churning. This assessment may or may not be correct, but the people harbour deep-rooted faith in traditions and in those who formulate these principles; they do not instinctively trust a group of young natives educated by foreign rulers. Why do my countrymen remain steadfast to traditions which are being destroyed by changing times? O’ my grief-stricken country! Many clouds have burst over your head; many more will burst and create a deluge. The dark moonless night renders everyone sightless. At such a time, my country clings to faith as a child clings to its mother. The sight given by the light of this lamp of faith is unmatched by the countless foreign stars. My learned brothers are mere reflections of these stars; why should it be a surprise that my countrymen’s paths are not enlightened by these reflected lights? The goddess of tradition is like Shakuntala. I see you marching ahead, but I also see the country holding you back. This scene churns my heart.

It is the fawn whose lip, when torn By kusha-grass, you soothed with oil; The fawn who gladly nibbled corn Held in your hand; with loving toil You have adopted him, and he Would never leave you willingly.⟨fn:301⟩ No doubt, we of the new generation have done nothing to deserve the confidence of our uneducated countrymen. We are only echoing voices that have come from the West. ’Tis a foreign voice reflected by our hollow-vaulted brains, and those that perceive it refuse to be led by it. We have never even as much as attempted to find out the wisdom of our ancestors and yet we have condemned them unheard; and if somewhere we have dubbed that wisdom with the name of folly, nowhere have we tried to recognise that wisdom. I think there is more common sense and sounder patriotism in the stubborn and wholesale refusal, by our masses, to consider or even hear and endure the latest fantasies of their seduced boys. When we shall have studied that ancient wisdom and considered both sides, the people will hear us, follow us, and even accept our theories of the follies of our best ancestors. We shall then have deserved the confidence of the people.⟨fn:302⟩ How easy it would be for these ascetics to gain the confidence and trust of our people, whom the new generation of scholars have failed to inspire. They possess worldly knowledge with detachment; they are selfless and have the desire to work for the welfare of others, and they have all the knowledge of these books and an organised sect necessary to purify society. Are all these means not sufficient to secure the welfare of our people? These ascetics have a fear—not a misplaced one—that close contact with depraved society will also corrupt them, and hence they maintain a studied distance from society. But society is deaf; why should it hear their call? Sarasvatichandra, it is your duty to secure for these ascetics their rightful place.

Their conduct is at great variance from societal norms; why do people still repose faith in them? People instinctively trust their intentions. They are not proud; they have no ego and are eager to be of service to society. They have shown so much compassion to someone like me whom they found on the road. They submit to bodily demands; they have a heightened sense of aesthetics; they have perfected asceticism into a pure art and consider selfless service of the people to be their vocation. They regard everyone, companions and strangers, alike and their devotion is only to the supreme Unmanifest God. If Madhuri is in fact Kumud, she would obtain complete peace and quiet among these ascetic women. That will also ease the pain that wrenches my heart. She and I coming closer will prove dangerous— we must maintain distance. What would be better for her? Going home or staying here? But before Sarasvatichandra could consider this question, Radhedas came in, and said, ‘Maharaj, Chandravali Maiya wishes to meet you.’ ‘Me? What for?’ ‘The reason is known to her alone. I have no access to it.’ ‘Please ask her. This dress and this male body do not permit me to meet a woman.’ ‘No ascetic has a right to ask the most pious and pure head of the Parivrajika Math to explain herself. Her soul is not female and your soul is not male. These distinctions are obliterated when the intention is the welfare of others. Maharaj, when Chandravali Maiya accepts any task or performs any action, it is inevitably for the welfare of others. Her means are always pure, moral and aesthetic. She has the right to approach even the Master without any restrictions.’ Navinchandra listened attentively, considered the matter and finally said, ‘Viharpuri—’ ‘His consent was obtained early this morning,’ Radhedas interrupted him. ‘Radhedasji, how am I to receive this person in whom you have such deep faith?’

‘Please give her the same respect as the Master. We the followers of Alakh say, Whether thou art to me a child or a pupil, be that as it may; the super-eminence of thy purity consolidates my affection for thee; thy childhood or womanhood is not the consideration; verily thou art adorable to the (three) worlds: in the case of the virtuous, merits are the object of reverence; neither sex nor age.⟨fn:303⟩ ‘This noble ideal is most suitable. Please lead the way and introduce me to her.’ They came out. Chandravali was seated on a platform. She got up. Radhedas said, ‘Chandravali Maiya, this is our new guest for whom we all desire a long life. He is the one for whom you have come this far. Navinchandraji, this is our mother who is auspiciousness incarnate. You have heard of her glory.’ Chandravali glowed with spiritual beauty. Sarasvatichandra felt mellow and satiated in her presence. He bowed his head and said, Just as a glimpse of the dusk is beauteous and enchanting, so is a glimpse of your visage, O’ Bhagvati. Your presence makes people join their hands in obeisance. The earth’s darkness disappears at the sight of you.⟨fn:304⟩ ‘This heart bows before you. I am eager to know your pious command.’ Chandravali: ‘A virtuous heart recognises another. Radhedas, I wish to speak with him in private.’ Radhedas: ‘I will take myself away and sit under that tree from where I will be able to see you, but not hear your conversation. I will approach you only when asked.’ Radhedas walked away and sat down under the tree. Chandravali watched his movement. Then she turned to Sarasvatichandra, whose eyes were riveted on the ground. Chandravali addressed him, ‘Navinchandraji, I will sit on the platform. You will please sit on these steps. I need to speak with you in absolute confidence about something very intimate.’ Sarasvatichandra sat down. He was eager, anxious and somewhat shy and he felt an inexplicable affection towards Chandravali. He continued to look down as he sat. Chandravali also sat down. Chandravali: ‘Navinchandraji, your glory has spread across Sundargiri like sunlight. But I have also heard the story of your previous life.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Your presence and your glorious life are a source of peace and tranquility, but the story of my life is a source of turbulence and disquiet. Maiya, the history of that part of my life is secret.’ Chandravali: ‘You might wish to keep it a secret, but I have heard it from the one whose heart bears witness to that past.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The pure, pious and sacred body in which that heart resided has been destroyed.’ Chandravali: ‘That temple has not been destroyed; yes, the body has withered. Navinchandraji, I have with me the key to that heart, which I shall give unto you.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘How am I to believe that? I might speak of one body, while you might be speaking of another.’ Chandravali: ‘You have seen that person on this mountain, and yesterday you also experienced the barb of pain afflicting that heart.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘But that person has another name now.’ Chandravali: ‘Navinchandraji, you, too, have changed your name. We have given that sweet, delicate person a new name: Madhuri. It was I who gave her that name.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘If what you say is true, it will release me of one anxiety. Your presence will give solace to that troubled heart, and she will forget me. If you give me the name by which she was called earlier, it will resolve all confusion.’ Chandravali: ‘That name is not known even to me. But apart from that, I have intimate knowledge of her innermost thoughts and feelings.’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘Maiya, I will hear your command. But it is my duty not to reveal any personal details of the one who has concealed her identity.’ Chandravali: ‘That is the way it should be. But there is a condition. If both of you recognise and acknowledge each other, our conversation will have meaning. If you do not, then this is as unreal as a dream.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Please speak, what is it that you want from me?’ Chandravali: ‘You sleep with all the others. From today, you should sleep alone, at a place designated by the Master.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The Master’s wish is my command.’ Chandravali: ‘He may want to know your views. You should accept this arrangement.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘All my actions are at the pleasure of the Master. I do not express my wish.’ Chandravali: ‘You may not express it, but you do have desires.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The heart is its own master.’ Chandravali: ‘Navinchandraji, the thirsty chakor bird longs for her moonlight.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Maiya, please counsel her that the soothing light that Chandravali Maiya gives to Viharpuri will also soothe her anguished heart.’ Chandravali: ‘What have you done! Navinchandra— O you hard-hearted one, fame is dear to you, as I hear; but what infamy, I ask, can be more dreadful than this? What became of the fawn-eyed maid in the wilderness? Tell me, my lord—what do you think of her fate?⟨fn:305⟩ Sarasvatichandra’s eyes glistened with tears. He turned his face towards the wall and said in a voice heavy with dejection and pain, ‘Maiya, your accusation is correct and true. I will now have to seek the boon that Dushyanta sought.’

Chandravali: ‘That I shall obtain for you.’ Sarasvatichandra continued as if she had not spoken. Dear, graceful wife, forget; Let the sin vanish; Strangely did madness strive Reason to banish. Thus blindness works in men, Love’s joy to shake; Spurning a garland, lest It prove a snake.⟨fn:306⟩ ‘With these words, Dushyanta had fallen at Shakuntala’s feet and sought her forgiveness. Maiya, I, too, seek forgiveness. Dushyanta had deserved that forgiveness. But I was not put under a spell or curse. I had not forgotten my beloved. I did not cast off a wreath of flowers fearing it to be a snake. We both loved each other. With full knowledge and awareness I threw away that delicate, beautiful and fragrant garland and left it in the harsh, merciless sun of summer to wither. I have no right to seek her forgiveness. And yet this heathen, fallen heart craves for it. It desires nothing more.’ Chandravali’s eyes welled up with tears of compassion. ‘Navinchandraji, Madhuri’s heart is like an ocean of compassion. It bears testimony to her pure love. The hidden moon of the dark night causes high tides in her heart; each wave brings with it grief and forgiveness. Navinchandraji, do not doubt her capacity for forgiveness.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘In face of her generosity my wretchedness appears even more depraved. My crime seems increasingly undeserving of forgiveness, my penance seems unattainable.’ Chandravali: ‘Oh great soul, my Madhuri apprehends your greatness with greater immediacy, and it tears her heart asunder even more.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Oh God! What am I to do? Maiya, I am not truly penitent!’ Fresh tears rolled down his eyes.

Chandravali: ‘The only penance for those who fall in their duty in matters of love is to submit to the beloved and bring joy to that heart.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Her heart is pious, pure and virtuous. My present condition will give her joy.’ Chandravali: ‘That remains to be seen.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘There can be no doubt about it. Her heart cannot aspire to any other condition.’ Chandravali: ‘Have you accepted your present condition of asceticism and renunciation to please her, or out of the inner joy and need of your heart?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The Master has decreed that I should let the circumstances decide for me.’ Chandravali: ‘Your heart is generous and noble and equally in love. Did my Madhuri climb the mountain to see you unmoved and steadfast in asceticism? Answer this question by reminding yourself of your past and with the knowledge that your mind will bear witness to the truth.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘She believes that I am unhappy and desires to free me from my grief. This desire compelled her to come here.’ Chandravali: ‘Are you not unhappy?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Her forgiveness is the cure for my grief.’ Chandravali: ‘If you can be cured of your unhappiness by her forgiveness, why did you stay at her husband’s house? Did you go there to mock her grief?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘If she considers me so depraved, then that should be accepted as the reason.’ Chandravali: ‘Navinchandraji, in a passionate fit of temper you left your father and showed utter disdain for your love. But your love— pure and deep—did not submit for long to your temper. It was your love that took you to Madhuri. You are so noble that you would immediately accept this reason.’

Sarasvatichandra felt abashed and looked down in silence for a while. ‘My intellect, weighed under sorrow, is no match to your brilliance in the analysis of the workings of my heart.’ Chandravali: ‘Oh great soul, your own nobility and greatness do not allow you to see it. What you are unable to see, Madhuri experiences. Just as we need a mirror to gaze at our own visage, great souls cannot see their own greatness; they need a mirror of the pure heart.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Yes, that heart knows all the forms of depravity that my heart is capable of.’ Chandravali: ‘If my Madhuri could regard you as depraved, she would not be Madhuri. My Madhuri in her love sees you as a great soul. A great soul born ever so rarely upon this earth whose light paints the ten directions, whose glory remains without measure, whose mere presence is auspicious.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Oh God! Her benevolence towards my depravity is beyond measure. Maiya, if her heart cannot see my depravity and follies, how will she grant me forgiveness? Only God can forgive me now!’ Chandravali: ‘Oh learned one, in this hermitage those who know themselves can go beyond grief.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘My grief might abate, but my sins will not be washed away.’ Chandravali: ‘The Master will wash away your sins and you shall realise that those who know themselves, those who are self-realised remain untouched by sorrow and beyond all doubts.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Mother, you are right. But at present I am gripped by false knowledge.’ Chandravali: ‘I wish to ensure that you and Madhuri meet alone, know each other’s true feelings and arrive at a mutual decision to either be united or lead separate lives. We shall aid and assist in you this resolve.’ Sarasvatichandra considered this for a while and said, ‘What will it lead to?’

Chandravali: ‘You will understand her pain, and she will understand yours. If you feel that the remedy for her ailment lies in being together with you, by so doing you would secure her forgiveness. If there is some other remedy, you should act accordingly. That, too, would bring you her pardon. If you believe that her pardon would give you peace, you are duty-bound to act according to my suggestion. If you do not understand the cause of your grief, Madhuri’s heart most certainly will, and provide you succour. Navinchandraji, both your hearts are united by a love that is pure and spiritual. But when this love is disregarded, when the heart is tortured it will break. Such is the nature of love. Follow the dictates of your hearts for some time and together with tact, delicacy and dialogue, disentangle them in a way that it causes no pain.⟨fn:307⟩ If that can be accomplished, Navinchandraji as the new Master of the monastery will provide shelter to Viharpuri, and Madhuri will come to stay with Chandravali. If the ties cannot be broken without causing pain, you should obey the heart and reside together in Vihar Math.’ Sarasvatichandra was shocked. ‘Maiya, if that is the only way to seek forgiveness, Navinchandra will willingly or unwillingly abide by that command. But Madhuri’s heart, her love for her husband and her duty as a virtuous wife—will these three allow for such a path?’ Chandravali: ‘That is for Madhuri to decide, not you.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The principle aspiration of my love is to inspire her to the path of piety and merit.’ Chandravali: ‘Indeed, that makes me very happy. Your love is like the love of the moon and the lotus, which are distant from each other but watch over each other and are united in thought. We have planned that your subtle bodies be united for the sake of this love. We are indifferent to whether your bodies unite or not.’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘Why?’ Chandravali: ‘According to our norms, you are her true husband. The man who married her body is only a paramour for us.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Social beliefs are contrary to this view.’ Chandravali: ‘Yes, they are. You can adopt what you like of our beliefs and what you prefer of social customs. We are indifferent to it. The Unmanifest God can be realised only when the desires of the subtle body are fulfilled. Bodily love is merely instrumental. We have no special preference for it if the desired goal can be reached without it.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘You might be indifferent to it; but for me that act is forbidden and immoral. We must not violate it.’ Chandravali: ‘You need not do so. We believe that the path to the Unmanifest opens up only when the desire of the subtle body is fulfilled.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘But why should we even create the possibility of bodily love?’ Chandravali: ‘The crime that you committed is the primary reason for it. So seek forgiveness. If this penance is truly heartfelt then the suggested course of action becomes necessary. How many more reasons do you want? Fight poison with poison.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘This plan fills me with dread. It is improper for the pious aspirations of this hermitage to place pure beings in such danger of depravity.’ Chandravali raised her brow and retorted, ‘What is not proper? You loved that young, infatuated girl, were betrothed to her, and then pushed her into a well! Is it improper for you now to save her? Or is your selfish heart filled with dread at the thought of being pushed into the well yourself? Navinchandraji, is it not treachery to point out to this fearless girl the path of rectitude only to save yourself from danger? If you are faced with a moral quandary according to your social customs and wish to adopt the path of rectitude, you must not harbour any fears in the path of duty. You must cultivate forbearance to remain fearless in the face of danger. You may fortify yourself with all protective armour of the Shastras and your learning; you may seek to remain secure. But to become fearful and cowardly, to harbour uncertainty regarding questions of propriety and consequently to not perform the penance is not the path of duty. You must not fail in the discharge of your duty; you must not be so perturbed. Do you regard the union of your subtle bodies as intended by me as immoral and harmful?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘There is no other objection but this fear.’ Chandravali: ‘Do you not believe that the union of your subtle bodies and the awakening of your spiritual love is inevitable and mutually beneficial?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Maiya, I am speechless.’ Chandravali: ‘Is there any other way of providing solace to both your hearts?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I do not see any other way. But for the reasons I have outlined, I do not want this union.’ Chandravali: ‘Can you see that the only opportunity to seek forgiveness can be had only if you meet her face to face?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I see no other way.’ Chandravali: ‘Navinchandraji, free yourself from this fear and adopt the path of good. Madhuri, like you, has faith in societal norms regarding marriage. She does not desire union with you. She believes that: The great ocean defines our conduct; without doubt it has precious jewels and the capacity to fulfill all our aspirations. I approached it seeking wealth, but let alone precious jewels I got not even a paisa from it. This is no fault of the ocean; it is the result of my actions of many past lives.⟨fn:308⟩ ‘Our Madhuri, though grief-stricken, does not want you as a cure for her grief. She wants happiness for you. I have come here on my own volition. The other ascetics also inspired me to do so. They know of the strength and steadfastness that you are capable of; they also bear witness to Madhuri’s pain. They weep, and their message for you is one of disdain. They say: I am ashamed even to utter these words. Seafarers traverse the oceans, but to quench their thirst they carry water from the wells to the sea.⟨fn:309⟩ ‘Madhuri objected to my meeting you. I came here at the insistence of my fellow ascetics. They asked me to say to you: Your waves reach up to the sky, your jewels light up the dark depths of the ocean; you envelop the earth—but all your glory is useless as a thirsty man forsakes your shores, weeping tears.⟨fn:310⟩ ‘All ascetics desire nothing more than subtle love; the question of bodily love for them is secondary. Oh swan! It is enough that you take this lotus-like woman who has bloomed in this lake of ethereal love as the beloved of your heart. The head of the Parivrajika Math has a message for you: O’ swan! The lotus came in your contact for a fleeting moment, but cannot forget you. O’ royal swan, do swim in the Manas lake as you please, but forsake not such friendship.⟨fn:311⟩ ‘The head of the Vihar Math has pondered over this question and she has come to the conclusion that of the many manifest paths of the unseen divine, the one you choose will eventually lead to Him and hence it is the path of beauty. Your realisation of the Unseen One and your attainment of the manifest forms are both capable of giving supreme bliss. But there is still a lack, and that lack can be fulfilled upon your acceptance of Madhuri’s spiritual love.

O’ royal swan, whosoever comes to be loved by you is delightfully beautiful. But given your riches, O’ swan, you should remember the play of love you indulge in.⟨fn:312⟩ ‘And lastly, to aid the process by which you can consider right and wrong and decide on the path of duty, I need to add: O’ royal swan, you are the glory of the Manas lake. If you have lost the capacity to discriminate between water and milk, who shall show you that discrimination: this baby sparrow?⟨fn:313⟩ ‘If you accept my advice and are yet moved by the desire to control your senses or by the longing to attain the supreme light, you shun Madhuri without her consent. This would certainly imply that you have not understood the secrets of our path, which I urge you to learn from the Master. The ascetics of this mountain abode follow both the manifest and the unmanifest. They believe that by shunning the manifest, one harms the unity and non-duality of the two. Hence, the manifest form of the unseen is also worshipped. Our ideal is the great soul Janak. Sri Ramchandra said in King Janak’s praise: Maharaj, the pure light that you seek is not covered by your royal parasol, the dark stains of soot do not sully it, and the breeze of fans does not extinguish it. Maharaj, the light that you meditate upon is such a light.⟨fn:314⟩ ‘It is however true that in our present times it is extremely difficult for householders to attain mastery over the senses. It is a subtle art, and many fail in this attempt. But those who attain this mastery acquire great glory and contribute to the good of the people. They acquire the capability to see God face to face. Vishvamitra gave up his kshatriyahood and desired to be a seer. He said in praise of Janak, who straddled both these states:

The palms of your hands bear the marks of your bow, your throat contains the sound of Omkara, your light brightens the earth and your soul is illuminated by your inner light. The golden throne indicates your royal power, the padmasana in which you sit suggests your penance, and such are the virtues of the Master who gives joy to this lotus.⟨fn:315⟩ ‘Navinchandraji, finally I must say that Yagyavalkya and Maitreyi, Vashistha and Arundhati did not desire the riches of state power; they sought and obtained supreme bliss and non-duality in each other. This is also the experience of the ascetics of Vihar Math. Madhuri is most deserving of such a union with you, which is certain to further your desire to experience non-duality with the Unseen One. We will arrange a brief meeting between the two of you, to which you must agree. Both of you are free to choose your own paths at the conclusion of this meeting. If you decide to cohabit at Vihar Math, you are free to do so; and if you decide to live in the present condition, that option will also be available to both. But this decision cannot be reached without verification. Unless you meet each other, your desire for each other cannot be ascertained. Hence, you must agree to our proposal.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Who can disregard the teachings of the goddess of learning herself? But Maiya, even the counsel of a father-like sage Vyasa failed to convince sage Shaka. Similarly, your teaching may fail to erase all my fears. Please forgive me for that. My conscience bears testimony that I am undeserving of your compassion and mercy. What you taught me is truth, it is inevitable and beauteous and it points to me the path of duty. But the love which springs from my desire also compels me to endure this pain.’ Chandravali: ‘Oh great soul, “Such is mostly the state of mind of spirited men who have received an insult.’’⟨fn:316⟩ The time for your penance is over.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I can abide by your commands only if the love that binds us is erased from our hearts.’

Chandravali: ‘“That attachment which springs up without a cause cannot be counteracted; it is a thread formed of affection which links together the inner hearts.’’⟨fn:317⟩ It will never be erased.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘If this love is such that it cannot be erased, then how can I adopt a path that is certain to cause more agony to the unsullied one who suffers because of my folly? The one who has caused this pain should get suffering and the one who has been wronged, unsullied love. If these two hearts are linked by attachment and love, then it is desirable that the one who deserves suffering should get suffering. If that is achieved, all my wants will be met.’ Chandravali: ‘God can decide whether you should receive punishment for your actions or not for He alone determines actions and fruits thereof; but you should ensure that she receives the peace that you desire for her.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘When fire and clarified butter come together, the senses will be aflame. One should always be alert to that possibility. It is the course of nature that bodily desire should lead to subtle love; but if subtle love degenerates into bodily love, it would be unbearable.’ Chandravali: ‘It would be so for one who is egoistical about his subtle body; but one who harbours no such ego regards both the subtle and the gross bodies with equi-mindedness. One is required to move among sense objects with the senses weaned from likes and dislikes. Such a person who is bereft of all ego and attachment attains tranquility. But, if one deals with objects of the sense Not loving and not hating, making them Serve his free soul, which rests serenely lord. Lo! Such a man comes to tranquility; And out of that tranquility shall rise The end and healing of his earthly pains, Since the will governed sets the soul at peace.⟨fn:318⟩

‘Navinchandraji, where renunciation does not bring tranquility, the only path available is to cultivate a state where one deals with objects of the senses without either loving or hating them.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘But the next verse says, The mind That gives itself to follow shows of sense Seeth its helm of wisdom rent away And, like a ship in waves of whirlwind, drives To wreck and death.⟨fn:319⟩ Chandravali: ‘There is no contradiction here. One must move among sense objects with the senses weaned from likes and dislikes. To the extent that one attains such mastery, one gains tranquility. One must not love the subtle body and loathe the gross body. The union of subtle bodies is to be naturally attained, and one must nurture it. And if the gross bodies were to unite, one must not shun it and at the same time one must not allow it to overpower the mind and lead one astray. One should neither have longing for desire, nor should one shun lust. One should be like the ocean where all longings subside just as waters subside in the ocean—that state is one of perfect tranquility, a state where all pride and ego of ‘‘I’’ and ‘‘mine’’ have subsided. And like the ocean, day by day receiving Floods from all lands, which never overflows; Its boundary-line not leaping, and not leaving, Fed by the rivers, but unswelled by those— So is the perfect one! To his soul’s ocean The world of sense pours streams of witchery; They leave him as they find, without commotion, Taking their tribute, but remaining sea. Yea! Whoso, shaking off the yoke of flesh Lives lord, not servant, of his lusts; set free From pride, from passion, from the sin of “Self” Toucheth tranquility, O Pritha’s Son!⟨fn:320⟩

Sarasvatichandra: ‘I am not swelled with lust.’ Chandravali: ‘You desire the subtle body.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Why should I invite bodily lust to a feast? Why harbour that attachment, that desire?’ Chandravali: ‘Both hearts claim that they are desireless. Let us assume that Madhuri has attachment, has desire. But you claim that you have none.’ Sarasvatichandra:  ‘Any invitation to it is akin to harbouring attachment.’ Chandravali: ‘I asked you to cultivate the equanimity of King Janak. A king faces many challenges and dangers due to his kingship; but for that reason great souls do not shun that state. The fear of committing a wrong stems from worldly beliefs and illusions. But this danger is insignificant compared with your steadfastness; you must be indifferent to it. Such indifference is not an invitation to lust.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What if these fears of mine were to prove true? Would one not be lost then?’ Chandravali: ‘No, not everything is lost even then. Great souls who fail in their strivings retain their merit in the next life. You would remember Arjun, too, had this question. Lord Krishna cleared his doubts. Arjun asked: And what road goeth he who, having faith, Fails, Krishna! In the striving; falling back From holiness, missing the perfect rule? Is he not lost, straying from Brahma’s light, Like the vain cloud, which floats ’twixt earth and heaven When lightning splits it, and it vanisheth?⟨fn:321⟩ ‘The Lord in his reply said: He is not lost, thou Son of Pritha! No! Nor earth, nor heaven is forfeit, even for him, Because no heart that holds one right desire Treadeth the road of loss! He who should fail,

Desiring righteousness, cometh at death Unto the Region of the Just; dwells there Measureless years, and being born anew, Beginneth life again in some fair home Amid the mild and happy. It may chance He doth descend into a Yogin house On Virtue’s breast; but that is rare! Such birth Is hard to be obtained on this earth, Chief! So hath he back again what heights of heart He did achieve, and so he strives anew To perfectness, with better hope, dear Prince! For by the old desire he is drawn on Unwittingly; and only to desire The purity of Yoga is to pass Beyond the Sabdabrahm, the spoken Ved. But, being Yogi, striving strong and long, Purged from transgressions, perfected by births Following on births, he plants his feet at last Upon the farther path.⟨fn:322⟩ ‘Navinchandraji, because of the merit that you accumulated in your previous births you have been bestowed with pure desires, virtue and knowledge in this birth. You might achieve its fulfillment in this birth, but if you fail in your strivings you will attain merit in the births to come. A child that falls while learning to walk does not give up walking. The child falls and yet rises again and again and learns to walk. What you fear now will become the cause of earning great merit in the future. This world moves incessantly, ceaselessly like an arrow released from a bow. Its force and direction are subject only to the will of God. Virtue is similar; it will not cease until it gives you the fruits thereof. Hence, the fears that you harbour are futile.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘It requires the affirmation of faith.’ Chandravali: ‘Most certainly.

Let no doubt be entertained with regard to the utterance of Brahmanas to whom the Supreme Light has been revealed. Good luck resides in their speech. They utter not words of false import.⟨fn:323⟩ ‘Seers perceive even the unmanifest; should it surprise one that they can see both the births past and those yet to come? Navinchandraji, if you want to be such a seer, you must strive. You will gain the all- seeing Yog drishti. Once you acquire that vision, you will not need the crutches of faith. The Master will show you the path to achieve such a vision.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The seeker who has failed in his search has been aptly described in the literature of the Alakh Marg.’ Chandravali: ‘Yes. In the Shrutis, God and the human being have been described as two birds. God has been likened to the macrocosm, while the human being has been described as the microcosm. These realities have been compared to the force and direction of an arrow; worldly beings are like the arrow itself. The reasons for the birth of the human and for the creation of the world are in the desire of the primeval being. It is like the bow that releases the arrow. When that and all other desires subside, it is the final release, freedom. God is neither consumed nor consumes, while the human being both consumes and is consumed. So long as the arrow remains in motion, human devotion persists. The human being through constant endeavour seeks oneness and unity with the Supreme Being; till that moment of being united the human being remains enmeshed in the world. When all desires subside, the flow that drags him also subsides. Those who remain steadfast and do not fail achieve this union quicker; those who fail but remain committed to the goal of being one with the Supreme Being eventually attain the union; but those wretched beings who have no such desire move from one life to another, As worms move ceaselessly from one whirl to another in the flowing river, so do they ceaselessly move from one birth to another.⟨fn:324⟩

‘Their condition remains such so long as they do not fulfill all their obligations. Just as the traveller’s pace quickens as he approaches home, likewise with those who are intent on merging with the Supreme Being—as they come nearer their goal not only their pace quickens, their desires also become subtler. As the desires become subtler, the enlightened being is able to gain mastery over the senses till such time that desire itself withers away. Navinchandraji, therefore we believe that for a seeker even desires are beneficial. Just as desires attract one who is ruled by the senses, virtues attract one who is virtuous. The Supreme Being and the human being are part of the same tree. The human being is a sensuous being, while the Supreme Being remains a witness to his strivings. When the human being gazes upon the Supreme and when this gaze is returned, when their eyes meet, the Supreme Being attracts the human being towards himself and endows him with his qualities. This is what is described as the grace of God. The companionship and friendship of these two birds is so constituted. A friend sits down for his meal and hears the call of his friend; he does not give up his food but hurries through his meal and rushes out to meet his friend. Similarly virtuous beings who strive for God do not give up desire all together. Their desire becomes subtler. ‘Navinchandraji, the path we have shown you is the right path. Madhuri’s loving disposition will aid and further your strivings. All of us are convinced of it. Navinchandraji, your love is like the arrow that has been released. It is futile to arrest its force. That attempt is egoistic. You must forsake your ego and with pure intent merge with the flow that beckons you. This course has the consent of all, and it is also the path of rectitude. Those knowing the knowable, and resting in all pervading spirit, and acquiescing alike to their wants and gains enjoy lives of perfect tranquility.⟨fn:325⟩ Sarasvatichandra was surprised by Chandravali’s invocation of the mantra given to him at the time of his initiation. Filled with curiosity, he asked, ‘Maiya, what is action? What is intent?’

Chandravali: ‘During the four months of monsoon the sky is laden with rain-bearing clouds that come upon us like a shower of mercy. These dark clouds cover and envelop the moon. Similarly, the subtle and gross bodies of great souls mature, and then their actions fall upon the world like rain. Till such time these great souls remain hidden behind the clouds and later emerge like the full moon of Sharad. Thereafter the world begins to trust their benevolence. Their intentions are regarded as pure and in the interest of people at large. They relate to all virtuous things and influences around them with pure intent. They do not show disregard for them and their actions are not motivated by any expectations of future, indirect gains. These great souls, moved by their desire for virtue, engage themselves in actions for the welfare of the people. Tamas results in laziness, Rajas leads to action with expectation of fruits thereof, while Satva Guna leads to desireless action for the welfare of others.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘But even desireless action is useless for those who wish to attain a state that is devoid of gunas or attributes.’ Chandravali: ‘Only those who have attained non-duality with the Unmanifest Creator are beyond the gunas. So long as the body exists, all three gunas persist. When the subtle body is made subtler, all other desires disappear; the only desire that remains is to act for the welfare of others and the world experiences the fruits of such pure actions.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What is the nature of this intention? How are actions performed? What harm is caused to the one who does not engage in any action?’ Chandravali: ‘The seed of desire and the causal body of a being remain unaltered from one life to another. With death the outer, gross body changes, while the subtle body grows subtler. The causal body initially develops and subsequently withers with the growth of virtue. The subtle body and the causal body are not destroyed at the time of death. The outer, gross body is destroyed but it does not vanish into nothingness; it returns to the five elements of which it is constituted. A new outer body envelops the subtle body. Householders believe that death signals the end, the destruction. But nothing is destroyed.

Matter returns to its original elementary form. Cotton is spun into threads, which are woven into fabric, which once old and torn returns to its original form. The gross body has a similar orientation. From conception to death it progressively alters form, but eventually it returns to the elements. Vegetation has only a gross body. The seed hides in itself the subtle body, which comes to life through cultivation and gives rise to another plant. Among animals the seed gives life and is subject to animal passions. The subtle body is reborn as an animal after death. Among humans all three types of bodies manifest themselves completely. The subtle body becomes subtler as the human body undergoes transformations related to the age of the body. It also nourishes the causal body. The subtle body retains the imprint of previous lives. It undergoes transformations similar to the changes that occur in food from the raw to the cooked stages.
