So long as the subtle body has not been rendered subtler, the desires persist and also increase. But when the subtle body attains its zenith, desires wane like the moon during the dark fortnight. As desires wither, the energies gathered by the subtle body are transformed into action which is directed for the welfare of others. It grows and spreads like the fragrance of a flower, and with that, ‘‘the inner organism is made subtler.’’⟨fn:326⟩ This passion for the good of others diminishes the ego, frees it from desire for honour and pride and finally merges with it. As desires disappear, the subtle body is made subtler. It is like a lamp that loses its flame because of lack of oil; the gross body becomes like the burnt out wick. If desires persist, if they remain as residue, we describe that as the decay and putrification of the subtle body. It is the suicide of the causal body. Because the causal body and subtle body are similarly described and are subject to similar influences, I have described to you Arjun’s fear of dissipation, of being scattered like a cloud, of not finding any repose in either of the two worlds. This dissipation occurs because of this decay and putrefaction. Such dissipated beings regress to the point of their origin and their future direction remains shrouded in darkness. Therefore, the Shrutis say that those who seek to destroy their desire only through the path of knowledge enter the world of suicidal darkness. Hence, it is right and moral that the gross body is eventually destroyed by the natural processes of ageing and death, while the subtle and causal bodies merge and become one with the macrocosm, having performed all their duties. In our philosophical system we consider this intention to be the source, the golden seed of human life. The Purusha, or cosmic male principle, ascends and becomes an integral part of the immortal being; it is moved by the same intentionality. And when the Unmanifest manifests itself in all completeness and yet remains incomplete, it does so in order to fulfill this intentionality. Tranquility cannot be attained by one who seeks withdrawal from action on the basis of an underdeveloped, impatient need for renunciation. Such withdrawal in fact gives rise to Tamas. Navinchandraji, I have described to you the ritual process by which pure tranquility can be achieved.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘But are not the ritual process and the desire for attaining a state beyond all attributes and qualities mutually contradictory?’ Chandravali: ‘The rituals and injunctions prescribed for actions that are performed for the welfare of others are integral to the intent of the action. The intent itself is pure and remains unsullied. The intent for such actions is oriented towards a state beyond attributes and qualities. Neither the Shrutis nor the Shastras can prescribe rituals or injunctions for that intent which arises out of itself. It is its own force. It does not rise and ebb because of external forces like the moon or the winds. Therefore it is said that pure intent requires neither rituals nor injunctions.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Which of these intentions are required for one who is intent upon the Unmanifest?’ Chandravali: ‘Actions performed by human beings to increase bodily pleasures are divided and particularised; because bodily pleasures are not endless and eternal. Those who seek God continue to strive for it till the end of their lives, but this path is for the learned, for those whose sights have opened. But there are as many ways of working for the welfare of others as there are people in the world; there is possibility of action for everyone, for those who are happy as also for those who are unhappy. The possibilities are inexhaustible. ‘Navinchandraji, one like you who is intelligent, learned, aesthetic, knowledgeable and noble-hearted can point out to others their paths. When persons with wealth and capability aspire to work for others, it takes on a glorious dimension. The nobility of these aspirations cannot be fathomed by anyone; it is not only beyond Chandravali but also beyond our Master Vishnudasji. Even the Shrutis and Smritis do not fathom them. The sun travels through the sky in a day, the Vamana measures the earth in one step, a boat traverses the sea; but what can measure and compare the inner world of men of virtue?⟨fn:327⟩ ‘Because what an ordinary person aspires to cannot match with the imaginations of an accomplished mind. “The aspirations of the large- hearted are unbounded, not limited even by the riches of the world; because they do not allow petty gains to fetter their imagination.”⟨fn:328⟩ These virtuous men incessantly think of ways of doing good to others. Their imagination takes wings and moves ceaselessly. Do we allow our men of virtue to spread their light? Where should their flames spread? In which direction should their efforts flourish? True, Brahma is their creator; but they have been confined to a corner of His creation like a lamp that is covered by a pot. Unfettered, the force of these virtuous men is capable of piercing through the universe.⟨fn:329⟩ ‘The possibility of working for the welfare of others is similarly limitless. A king like Janak had the capability of doing good to a sage like Shaka and even Indra. But Chandravali can only hope to do good to poor Madhuri; her capacities do not extend beyond that. If you,

Navinchandraji, were to be placed in a high position, what could you not do for the good of others?’ Sarasvatichandra let out a sigh of dejection. Chandravali: ‘When your circumstances alter, your aspirations will alter with them.’ When poor, a man longs for a handful of rice; when afterwards he is full (of wealth) he regards the whole earth as straw. Hence we must say that for want of fixity as regards the smallness or largeness of the objects of desire, the position of the wealthy magnifies or lessens things (i.e. their value).⟨fn:330⟩ ‘The aspirations of a virtuous person are limited or limitless depending upon his context. A cow by itself is incapable of doing good to others, but when she is milked she provides nectar; she becomes Kamdhuk, who has the capacity to yield every desired thing. A tree provides rest and nourishment to humans, birds and worms alike. A river nurtures and provides for all living forms that live in it. Rain showers on every one and provides nurturance to all in equal measure, and hence its munificence is greater than that of a river. Rain comes only during the four months of monsoon, but the moon gives its light for all twelve months. But even the moon is subject to waning and waxing, while the sun shines forth every day. The rain, moon and sun thus give increasingly greater benefits. Navinchandraji, they are limited by their context; but an ascetic free from the corruption of the world is satisfied by becoming like a tree. Trees and great souls alike live for others. They provide shade to weary travelers attracted towards them. They do not harbour snakes and other similar dangers which might harm those who come to them. Trees and great souls emerge out of their own volition; neither a gardener nor a farmer is required to tend to them. They provide fruits to all without taking service from others.⟨fn:331⟩

‘Navinchandraji, this ascetic community has neither the riches of the world, nor are they adept in the ways of the world; but they are imbued with right knowledge, noble sentiments and virtues. Maharaj Maniraj and the people of this state have fond respect for our aspirations. Their affection is due to trust. When ants pour out on the paths of the hermitage, young ascetics feed them with flour. The ants moving in a formation create beautiful patterns and delight the eyes.⟨fn:332⟩ ‘Navinchandraji, in a hermitage where even ants are cared for, would you refuse to care for a woman who longs for you?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Her aspirations would be equally noble!’ Chandravali: ‘She longs for only one thing. Her every sigh says, Having abandoned my daughter, as ill-luck would have it, with a burning heart, he now lives by his uncommon fortitude and the meritorious acts of his subjects.⟨fn:333⟩ ‘Navinchandraji, I have said all that I could have said. It is up to you now to accept my request. Just as your heart is imbued with goodness and virtue, so is Madhuri’s. The virtuous heart is described thus: A behaviour full of kindness, a restraint over speech pleasing by its modesty, a mind naturally prone to do good, and a friendship irreproachable—triumphant in this secret of the life of the good, of a sweetness not altered by time past or future, guiltless and pure.⟨fn:334⟩ ‘Navinchandraji, you are a virtuous man; you understand the aspirations of other hearts imbued with virtue. My heart cannot bear Madhuri’s suffering. I, too, am detached; I am an ascetic. But I have broken my vows and come to you for the sake of Madhuri; either for her sake or for my own peace of mind I left the abode of the Mother Goddess and have come to you. Either out of respect for our community of ascetics, out of compassion for Madhuri, out of conviction that I have shown you the path of truth, or simply out of your own nobility and learning, please agree to my request. It is beyond my capacity to say anything more. My limited knowledge does not allow me to make more forceful an advocacy of truth. My intellect cannot provide a purer essence of right conduct. Years of ascetic practices have dried up my aesthetic sensibilities. Viharpuri, the one who gave succour to my heart and my efforts, is now your disciple. It is beyond my capacity to ask him to engage with you on this subject. Navinchandraji, I stand before you, pleading with folded hands. I have no sense of shame in asking for alms from a man of virtue.’ Chandravali was overcome with emotion and her eyes welled up. She clenched her teeth, fought her tears and looked up at him with folded hands. Assailed by conflicting thoughts and emotions, unsure, Sarasvatichandra remained silent and searched within for a response. As he witnessed Chandravali battling with her emotions, her eyes could no longer hold back the tears and, with trembling lips, she said, ‘Oh virtuous man! Hitherto these eyes have not gazed upon any man other than Viharpuri. I see on your face the light and beauty that compassion fills one with. What is your command?’ Sarasvatichandra was still undecided. His eyes turned inwards to his heart. ‘Oh virtuous man! What is your command?’ Chandravali asked once again. Startled, Sarasvatichandra looked up. His eyes were still moist. He folded his hands and said with utmost humility, ‘Maiya you have taken me to be your son and have shown all the forgiveness, affection and generosity that a mother is capable of. Mother, I have no right to disobey your command. Your farsighted proposal combines both pure intent and intellect. I will act according to your proposal. You say that Madhuri is mine. When we meet I will point out to her the path that will secure her welfare.’ ‘You must also accommodate her suggestions about your welfare,’ Chandravali said with some hesitation. ‘I will consider both our thoughts and inclinations,’ replied Sarasvatichandra.

‘Oh virtuous man, may you attain all the goodness that you desire. Is there anything more you wish to say as to how I could be of service to you?’ ‘If I have anything at all to say on this matter, Maiya, it could be said only to you.’ He is the one great asylum of comfort, affection and devotion; and the grace of supreme Duty, as it were, moving in a bodily form.⟨fn:335⟩ ‘You have taught me the secrets of superior morality and rectitude. Hitherto, I have felt a deep intellectual discontent and my heart was in a state of agitation. You have, with great affection, shown me the path of tranquility. You have given me knowledge of a subject that I would have found impossible to ask the Master. Even Viharpuriji would have felt constrained to speak of this subject. You are the only one who could have helped me put balm on that heart that I broke without any reason. This is the greatest favour that you have done unto me. You have given solace to both me and her. Your heart is filled with immeasurable love for us. This love compelled you to break your vows and dragged you into activities not conducive to your heart; you worship the manifest and the unmanifest alike with equal devotion. You embody the most subtle understanding of right conduct and most sublime aesthetic sensibility. You are the repository of love, renunciation and knowledge; you are the embodiment of sublime sensibility.⟨fn:336⟩ ‘It is rare to find a sensibility that is nurtured by the confluence of love, renunciation and knowledge. Most people in this world are incapable of even imagining it. Maiya, you are the embodiment of these virtues and you have given me a taste of their divine nectar. No one before today had given me this nectar of duty, morality and aesthetic sensibility. What can I do to repay you for this benevolence?’ ‘Navinchandraji, there was a time when I needed to hear self- praise. But it is no longer so. It is not conducive to my disposition.

Virtuous men like you speak from the heart, and I am satisfied that I could be the cause for its happiness. I would be greedy if I were to crave more of it. I am satisfied that you have agreed to my request. Your generosity and knowledge will aid you in this activity. My blessings are with you and Madhuri. May your pure intentions come to fruition.’ ‘Hitherto, some dense impenetrable darkness had enveloped my heart. Maiya, you are that light, that goddess of dawn who has freed me from it. I am not indulging in false praise. I experienced what I had only heard about. It is your light that has given me this experience. It is due to your blessings that I am free from darkness.’ Yesterday Vishnudas accompanied by all his disciples had gone for an inspection of all the three Maths. Chandravali was present at that time. Upon seeing her, the ascetic had proclaimed the praise of Alakh, of Yadunandan and even Chandravali. Vishnudasji himself had gone up to Chandravali and asked after her well-being. He also asked her to remain present during the Ras Lila and made inquiries about the abode of the Goddess. Vishnudasji was not present during the Ras Lila. Viharpuri had explained the hidden meaning of the Ras Lila to the community. Chandravali had listened to the discourse with meditative attention. The ascetics had insisted that she stand face to face with Viharpuri. At the completion of the discourse Viharpuri first blessed the ascetics and then bowed to them. When he bowed to Chandravali, the ascetics had cried out happily in their praise. Sarasvatichandra had witnessed these scenes with amazement but with total lack of comprehension. Today, he understood the glory of that moment. He was eager to fall at her feet. As Chandravali sought his permission to leave, he said to her worshipfully, ‘Maiya! I am not completely satiated with the nectar of your wisdom. I cannot say that my thirst has been quenched. But it is your prerogative to set limits to your benevolence towards me. I know that my welfare lies in bowing to you. Today, I have had the privilege of being with the Arundhati-like companion of the Vashistha-like Viharpuri. Your light has redeemed me of my darkness. All I need to say is this:

With my head bent low to the surface of the earth I bow to your reverence, as to the divine Ushas, adorable to the world and the source of blessings to the three worlds, you by whom your husband, though a repository of holy lustre, and though the most to be revered of even the primeval of sages, regards himself as purified.⟨fn:337⟩ As Sarasvatichandra bent down to touch her feet, Chandravali, who had taken a vow not to touch any man, held his hands and said, ‘Navinchandraji, the ascetics of this community reserve such worship only for Yadunandan. Even the Master forbids such worship. Who am I? Time is running away. You go back to your noble thoughts, and I will go away.’ Chandravali left. As Sarasvatichandra watched her walk away, he recited lines from Wordsworth. The reason firm, the temperate will, Endurances, foresight, strength, and skill; A perfect woman, nobly planned, To warn, to comfort and, command.⟨fn:338⟩ His mind in a whirl, his thoughts found expression as he mused aloud. ‘Sundargiri, you are an asylum to such noble and beautiful human beings! Chandravali, there was a time when women like you enlightened this fallen country. There was a time when the confluence of knowledge, aesthetic sensibility and piety ennobled this land! There was a time when the pure love of women like Saubhagya Devi merged with the richness of subtle bodies! That time has gone. That is the reason for the degeneration and fall of this land! ‘Chandravali Maiya, you have also laid before me the true meaning of my initiation! ‘She has shown me the evolution of the individual soul from its first flash to its last goal! And she challenges me to verify its truth by the practice of Yoga! And if we believe in Western science upon mere faith on the ground that it is open to verification if we want, can I refuse some similar reception to so proud a production of my own countrymen? And she has shown me the place of love in economy of nature. She has shown me how ‘‘Life is real! Life is earnest!’’ She has carried me through the transmigration scheme in a novel but tangible way. And she has done it all to console and sweeten a sweet life like my Kumud’s and to settle into some realistic practical form a dreamy vagabond like myself! My Kumud! Ah! I feel fired by the name!⟨fn:339⟩ ‘Yes. Kumud—Kumud Sundari! Chandravali Maiya’s benevolent grace is all for you. I can see the end of my penance! But... He suddenly heard Vanleela’s voice say, ‘Oh friend, doe-eyed and enchanting, you have captivated Mohan,’ and was startled. The moments that he had spent alone with Kumud in Buddhidhan’s house flashed before him; his body trembled. ‘How can one trust the body? Chandravali, like the English poet believes: The same love that tempts us into sin, If it be true love, works out its redemption!⟨fn:340⟩ ‘Would not the restraint that protected me at that moment from transgression come to my aid today? Then the situation was delicate; I was a guest, it was a question of honour and there were other dangers besides. But here these ascetics have laid to rest any such fears. Here, one only needs to guard against immoral conduct. But Chandravali does not regard even that as an impediment. For her I am Kumud’s true husband, and Pramaddhan is the paramour! ‘My associations cannot accept this reasoning, even though ethically the lady has an unanswerable case for truth in the argument that all Hindu marriages are null and void! The law, however, is not with her. The construction of our vast society and the hard facts of life in it make it only vastly and extremely perilous to admit her arguments in practice! Alas, that what seems so sound to unprejudiced reasoning and the unartificial but artistic conscience of refined natural instincts should have so totally lost its once sublime and august position from the ethical pantheon of our modern Hinduism! Blessed be these few sacred remnants of those days of spiritual light and purity of my country!⟨fn:341⟩ ‘The question as to whether I am to be regarded as her husband, or Pramad, has become immaterial with Pramad’s death. My marriage with Kumud is now not immoral from any standpoint—that of the ascetics, of Western beliefs or political jurisprudence. But I do not lust after her. Kumud Sundari has occupied an unsullied and beautiful place in my conscience. Marriage with her would corrupt that image, and that would be unbearable. The gross bodies must never unite; union must only be of subtle bodies. Kumud Sundari should spend her life either at the Parivrajika Math or as a companion to Chandravali— that would be the most appropriate and aesthetic solution. ‘But what right do I have to even consider these options? I have committed a crime against her. The only way I can wash away the stains of my crime is by being a source of comfort and tranquility to her. I do not have the right to consider whether that path is aesthetic, moral or otherwise. She is the only one who has this right. According to the principles of love espoused by the ascetics it is immoral to leave the decision entirely to Kumud. They say that I must court her, find out that hidden desire and act accordingly. Sri Krishna broke his vow and wielded his Sudarshan Chakra on the battlefield to protect Arjun. Similarly I should disregard all customs of society and provide succour to that lonely heart. That is my duty. ‘Oh morality! Will you force me to drag Kumud back into the world of householders? Will you prompt me to convince her to remarry? Would Kumud, who has received unqualified love from Saubhagya Devi and Buddhidhan, forget their love? Pramaddhan might have been undeserving of her, but will it be my duty to give her the news of his death? Will the news not pain her? Will she be able to bear it? How will I watch her suffer? What right do you have to witness her pain, Sarasvatichandra! Will not the curious ways of Sundargiri point out to you the path of duty?

‘What if Kumud Sundari were to put her pain and suffering behind her and desire a marriage with me? What if she were to consider herself free and unencumbered and not have the patience to wait for the marriage? Will that not be a certain fall? What about my own firmness of mind? What capacity do I have? What is my duty? Will I have the equanimity to consider these questions at that moment? What if Madhuri is in fact not Kumud but someone else? What if that person feels a certain attraction towards me? In that case, I will have to say to her that, As my heart ponders whether I could ever Have wed this woman that has come to me In tortured loveliness, as I endeavour To bring it back to mind, then like a bee That hovers round a jasmine flower at dawn, While frosty dews of morning still o’erweave it, And hesitates to sip ere they be gone, I cannot taste the sweet, and cannot leave it.⟨fn:342⟩ ‘In that case, what should I do? ‘I will not give her the news of Pramad’s death. So long as she remains uninformed of it, her virtue would not allow any transgression. But what if she were to transgress even without the knowledge of her widowhood? I know the fact of Pramad’s death. A union with her is not prohibited under these circumstances. I will have to do what is required of me to wash off my crime; therein lays my penance. But I will not give her the news. ‘No. That shall not be, and that too for the simple reason that I cannot bear to see thy soul in anguish. Sweet angel at my helm! I shall neither crush thee with news which can only make thee writhe, nor insult thee with idle conceptions of what thou art not, but shall see thee as soft and sweet and pure as thou always hast been. And if my love believes thee to be that, what fear can my heart harbour from thee and thy soul? Ah! Whither am I drifting? Sweet Kumud!⟨fn:343⟩

My soul is an enchanted boat That, like a sleeping swan, doth float Upon the silver waves of thy sweet singing, And thine doth like an angel sit, Beside the helm conducting it.⟨fn:344⟩ ‘You are an idol carved from Gunasundari’s heart. You have received the love of pious Saubhagya Devi! The path that you would lead me on would be both aesthetic and the right path. I hear the song of your desire, and the song is pure and pious.’ Kumud’s song played in his ears. It enveloped him. O’ yogi, play thy flute. What is written cannot be undone. A householder becomes an ascetic. O’ yogi, play thy flute; She will listen to your song. The flute plays a song of love; All that was unsaid by us it sings; The Unmanifest is made apparent; The flute sings of our union. The Unmanifest, subtle and eternal— O’ yogi, weave Kumud into this garland. You, I and the Unseen Are three, eternal and one. The heart is a boat, and you, A sailor in the sea of the Unmanifest. How can the tongue be afraid of teeth? How can Kumud remain untouched by Chandra? As night falls, The moon reigns. Kumud blossoms in its first ray. The moon cannot harm Kumud; The moon nurtures her. Ascetics desire a union Where both desire and renunciation play;

Where hearts dance in unison to beauty; Sundargiri makes this possible. The world is wretched and fallen; We have been saved from it By our renunciation; We need not ever return to the world. Sundargiri, high abode of ascetics, Its lush creepers proffer solitude Where we roam free of passions, Where the wind cools and soothes. Dear Chandra! I am the fragrance; I bloom, I come alive. My petals open For you to drink nectar. Let this night of Chandra remain forever. Let Kumud’s unseen love remain forever. Radhedas, who had been talking to Chandravali while Sarasvatichandra sat musing to himself and lost in his own world, returned, forcing Sarasvatichandra to emerge from that world back into the real one.
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra grapples with his turbulent thoughts about Kumud's identity and fate, seeking clarity amidst deep personal anguish and societal reflections, as her song echoes.

chapters.title: Vishnudas' Authority or Ways of Attaining Fulfillment of Sarasvatichandra's Subtle Body
paragraphs: Vishnudas’ Authority or Ways of Attaining Fulfillment of Sarasvatichandra’s Subtle Body As a very long highway goes to two places, to one at the beginning, and to another at the end, so do the rays of the sun go to both worlds, to this one and to the other. They start from the sun, and enter into those arteries; they start from those arteries, and enter into the sun. And when a man is asleep, reposing and at perfect rest so that he sees no dream, then he has entered into those arteries. Then no evil touches him, for he has obtained the light (of the sun).⟨fn:345⟩ Whenever Vishnudas was on Sundargiri, his daily routine followed a set pattern. Even when he accompanied the fellow ascetics in their journeys to spread the message of Alakh, his time was spent in scholastic pursuits. He would spend the noon in company of a few chosen disciples while the others would go among the people; in the afternoon, as the sun became less intense he would go and preach at some monastery or sacred spot. Often scholars and men of learning would approach him for advice. All his disciples would come together at dusk, rest and take their evening meal, after which they would return to Sundargiri. Himsar was a large lake situated between Ratnanagari and Manoharpuri. On the day when Sarasvatichandra and Chandravali had their discourse, Vishnudas and his disciples had camped near the lake. Large neem, mango and peepal trees on the bank of the lake made a grove. Vishnudas decided to rest in the grove as other disciples went on their mission. Jnanbharati, the chief of the Vihar Math, Jankidas an old monk, Viharpuri and two other younger ascetics stayed with Vishnudas. These two younger ascetics had lived a life as householders and like Vishnudas they had renounced it to become ascetics. Their age was around twenty, twenty-two; both had facility with the English language and appeared to have cultivated a sense of detachment. One of them had a tranquil disposition and was somewhat thick-headed. He had adopted the name Shantidas. The other one was somewhat carefree and entertained doubts about everything. He had chosen the name Shankapuri for himself. Shankapuri called Shantidas by the name Shankabharati but pronounced it as Shankha (conch) bharati. Shantidas did not make any objection to this. The rules of Sundargiri did not permit new entrants to go out for seeking alms for at least a year. They were required to spend this time of initiation as part of the group of initiates who stayed in company of Vishnudas. Vishnudas sat on a deer skin under a mango tree. Shankapuri and Shantidas went for a swim in the lake while the others sat around the Master. Vishnudas looked towards the lake and said, ‘Viharpuri, your heart is tranquil and cool like this place. It is so because of Chandravali Maiya’s unsullied protective cover. Navinchandra’s heart is like this lake; cool, tranquil and filled with nectar but unfathomable. It is difficult to judge what lies in the deep recesses of his heart.’ Viharpuri smiled softly and said, ‘The lake does not have the protective shadow of the trees. The sun dries up its water. Viharpuri is made of sterner stuff like the crust of the earth; he will not wilt even if the tree cover were gone.’ Jnanbharati: ‘Master, Chandravali Maiya has diagnosed his ailment; it is appropriate that her remedy is applied.’ Jankidas: ‘We shall know of its outcome tonight.’ Viharpuri: ‘The night might bring with itself a new world. It is in the fitness of things that we prepare ourselves for it.’

Vishnudas: ‘Viharpuri!’ Viharpuri: ‘Yes, Master.’ Vishnudas: ‘From tonight Sarasvatichandra’s sleeping quarters should be shifted to Chiranjiv Shrunga.’ Jankidas: ‘It would be more suitable to provide him a space closer to Vihar Math; the remedy for his ailment will then be at hand.’ Jnanbharati: ‘If the plan fails, Navinchandra who is a renunciate will feel offended by the solution suggested by Jankidas.’ Vishnudas: ‘What does Viharpuri think?’ Viharpuri: ‘What was the reason behind your suggestion?’ Vishnudas: ‘Both the reason and purpose are large.’ Viharpuri: ‘That is why I asked the question.’ Vishnudas: ‘All three of you are experts in the customs and traditions of our ascetic community. Who do you think is the most suitable candidate to assume the role of the Master of all the three maths?’ Jankidas: ‘That is your prerogative, Master.’ Jnanbharati: ‘You, with your powers will evaluate as to who is most suitable, depending upon their virtues, knowledge and detachment.’ Viharpuri: ‘That is correct. But it is also true that only one who has experienced the worldly life and deeply felt the life of an ascetic, one who has arrived at his own understanding of both these worlds can hope to do good to the entire monastic community. It is for this reason that you hold this responsibility and occupy this position of virtue.’ Vishnudas: ‘It is my duty to identify my successor and give him all the necessary capabilities to uphold this responsibility. For all these years, all the ascetics unanimously believed that Viharpuri was my worthy successor. But now Viharpuri himself feels that Navinchandraji, with his knowledge of the world, with his natural inclination towards the spiritual, ascetic life is more suitable for this responsibility.’ Viharpuri: ‘I am not deluded in my belief.’

Jankidas: ‘But if Navinchandraji is inclined towards a life in the Vihar Math, his fitness to be the master of the monastic order would be compromised.’ Jnanbharati: ‘Viharpuri’s capabilities came to be recognised when he was the head of the Vihar Math. Our history has examples of persons who were the master of the order, while retaining their position within the Vihar Math.’ Vishnudas: ‘But which of the two is more virtuous?’ Jnanbharati: ‘One who has experienced the worldly life and has also lived in the Vihar Math is the most virtuous candidate. In absence of such a person, a celibate like me could be chosen as a compromise.’ Viharpuri: ‘Master, in your considered opinion Navinchandraji is the most suitable successor. I, too, believe that. Under the circumstances we should disregard whether he is a renunciate or living with a companion. His intellect, his aesthetic sensibility and his knowledge are matchless.’ Vishnudas: ‘In that case the issue is not unsolvable. Let me explain my reasons. According to astrological calculations, Navinchandraji is destined for some large act of renunciation. Yadu Shrunga will benefit from his renunciation. The experience and assessment of all our ascetics also support this astrological calculation. But Viharpuri has sensed some deep pain within him. Pain is caused by desire. This man is also destined to undergo unprecedented renunciation with regard to a woman. If his pain is caused by attachment to a woman, it will evaporate in the fire of his penance. Hence, I do not see any danger in going ahead with the experiment suggested by Chandravali Maiya. Our ascetics also undergo such trials under the watchful eyes of the other members of the community. If Chandravali’s insight is to be believed, they both feel a deep attachment for each other. In that case, we have to say to them that they should cohabit as a couple in Vihar Math. Whether we should say that or not would depend upon the decision that they take after meeting each other. But we need to provide them a space other than Vihar Math for such a meeting and their consequent decision.’

Viharpuri: ‘Your exposition is both intricate and truthful.’ Vishnudas: ‘Chiranjiv Shrunga is the most appropriate place. It is obvious that Navinchandraji has various extraordinary powers. A person like him will most certainly come in contact with other accomplished and emancipated beings. If Navinchandraji indeed has this extraordinary experience, it could only bring unprecedented benefits to the three Maths. Chandravali Maiya will favour this decision for one reason, and you would for another.’ Jnanbharati: ‘This is the most superior proposal. Madhuri Maiya is also an accomplished and highly cultivated being. At the time of their encounter with other emancipated beings their union will be further imbued with aesthetic delight and knowledge.’ Meanwhile, Shankapuri and Shantidas had joined them. Shankapuri could not restrain himself and asked, ‘Can a man’s capabilities and powers acquired at birth result in the acquisition of these capabilities by his woman?’ Vishnudas: ‘You once said that according to Western science there exists a centre of gravity in the universe.’ Shankapuri: ‘Yes. I have acquired some Western learning, and this is a proven fact according to them.’ Vishnudas: ‘In Yoga Shastra, astrology and in the treatise of Alakh, similar such centres have been described. Most accomplished beings are able to perceive these centres. Just like the astronomical centre, the astrological centres are unmanifest but they can be experienced. The human body, intellect, passions and destiny are intricately bound to the position and movement of the sun and the planets. Many constellations come together to form the universe of the stars. This unperceived centre lies somewhere in that web of constellations. The solar system is integrally tied to it. All substantial and insubstantial bodies in this universe, all living and non-living matter, action, destiny, desires and consumption have to move through this web and find its centre. In this centre, there exists a location for love. The householders believe that while performing rituals a woman needs only to touch her husband; that touch completes the ritual action of the man. A couple that is united by pure love is an example of this; they are linked together and pulling one link of the chain pulls the entire chain. An accomplished husband also helps to raise his wife to a higher level of consciousness. They are tied together by one ring; they share similar destinies and receive equal merits. Householders are united by their bodies and couples, according to our belief, are united by subtle bodies. Madhuri Maiya has come to us because some bond, some force has brought her closer to Navinchandraji. It is possible that their union will be celebrated on Chiranjiv Shrunga.’ Shankapuri: ‘If their union is destined, why should a great renouncer such as you strive to bring them together? Is this task not too little for your abilities and aspirations? This is a task fit for the head of the Vihar Math.’ Jnanbharati: ‘Shankapuri, you tease Shantidas by calling him Shankhabharati, but you also seem equally block-headed. Anyone who challenges the authority of either the Master or our philosophy is excommunicated from our monastery.’ Shantidas: ‘That is correct. Parents arrange the marriages of their children. The Master is doing just that. It is an insult to him to find fault with it.’ Viharpuri could not suppress his laughter. ‘Master! The lowly beliefs of the householders have not entirely vanished from their minds. You have experience of that world; kindly use the means that they can grasp to redress their doubts.’ Jankidas: ‘Shantidas’ smile is appropriate. That should satisfy Shankapuri. After all poison is the only remedy for poison.’ Vishnudas: ‘Shankapuri’s doubt is not misplaced. Travellers reach the same destination through various paths. Someone may believe that everyone would have travelled on the same path. This belief is not entirely misplaced. Shankapuri has not yet cultivated such closeness with Jnanbharati that he could comprehend the purpose of Jnanbharati’s endeavour for Navinchandraji. Moreover, he is not entirely free from attachment and ego, which give rise to differences. Society considers women to be lowly beings; for them the union of man and woman is only for bodily pleasure and for the procreation of progeny. Jnanbharati, I, too, have lived as a householder in that society. It took me long years to cultivate the understanding that men, women and children are all manifestations of the same Unmanifest Being. Shankapuri is a recent initiate. You could compare his views with those of Navinchandraji, which would immediately show the great understanding of the latter. Jnanbharati wants Navinchandraji to adopt one path, while I want him to adopt another. But both hope that he would attain even a higher state of being. My path suggests that the best result could be obtained by having him stay at Chiranjiv Shrunga. Jnanbharati’s path also culminates at that point. Shankapuri could not comprehend this and took the rope to be a snake.’ Shankapuri: ‘But the question remains. If, according to the astrological calculations, what you desire for them is anyway destined to happen, why should you make all the effort? Why should you not leave it to their destiny and remain indifferent?’ Shantidas: ‘Master, you are agreeable to the proposal that Navinchandraji and Madhuri should stay in close proximity at the same place. How then is your way different from the path suggested by Jnanbharati?’ Vishnudas: ‘Shankapuri, the astrological sciences bring to light the direction of human destiny and the will of God; they do not preclude the duty that is entailed upon all of us. Destiny decreed that we found Navinchandra’s body in a dark, dense forest. We came to be acquainted with him. Astrological signs show that this man will play a sterling role in our endeavour. ‘In the course of our interactions with him we came to recognise his invaluable qualities and his pure, unsullied character. We saw the light within him. It is the moral obligation of any follower of our path to be open and receptive to the virtues and goodness of all beings. It is because of this moral obligation that both you and Shantidas have received forgiveness and asylum from this community of ascetics. No effort will be too much to light the lamp which would enable Navinchandraji’s inner light to shine forth even more brightly. If his light is likely to benefit this community, if its rise is likely to be ensured by his light, it is the duty of all ascetics to nurture and protect that light as a gardener nurtures a plant. The astrological signs work like fuel for this lamp. Destiny, which brought this jewel among men to us, also places upon us certain obligations.’ Shankapuri: ‘What are we to do if we perceive a conflict between astrological signs and duty as we perceive it? For instance, astrological signs might predict looming death, but social obligations force a marriage upon me the same day!’ Vishnudas: ‘Performance of duty is so arranged that one is required to follow the dictates of the will of the Unmanifest Supreme Being. Some actions and duties appear inevitable, others appear immoral, while certain others appear to be neither moral nor immoral. Moral obligations must be fulfilled even if astrological predictions suggest the contrary. Even the master’s injunction to act otherwise should not deter one from the performance of righteous duty. Prahlad disobeyed his father to perform his duty. What appears immoral must be shunned. That which is neither moral nor immoral cannot be the subject of deliberation; a person acts according to instinct. One should not coerce anyone to act against their natural instincts in such instances. One should allow the person to reach a conclusion based upon his understanding of the relationship between the manifest and the unmanifest. This is an important principal of our belief system. A person whose actions are based upon astrological calculations will face the possibility of both good and bad outcomes. But such possibility and danger are integral to all actions. Ascetics remain detached from such dangers. Asceticism means acceptance of limitations. Ascetics adjust their bodily functions to fit the situation in which they find themselves. They remain unaffected by what is attainable and do not long after what is unattainable. The Vihar Math is organised on this principle. It seeks a union of subtle bodies and does not fear bodily death. If the Supreme Unmanifest Being inspires a couple to come together, they do not pay heed to astrological calculations. The possibility of death does not deter them either.

‘Jnanbharati and I both wish to send Navinchandraji to Chiranjiv Shrunga, albeit for different reasons. If Navinchandraji’s welfare is linked to the destiny of Madhuri, it should be accepted as the will of the Supreme Being. Any attempt to act contrary to this is immoral.’ Shankapuri: ‘Which do you regard as more powerful: the will of the Supreme Being or the inevitable force of the constellations?’ Vishnudas: ‘The constellations and stars are an integral part of the universality of the Supreme Being; they are tied to His will. His will governs all of us as also the constellations. All such forces, be they of Yoga or of the constellations and planets, are ultimately one. His will can make us see this non-duality. But this vision is not the same as the sight of our eyes.’ Shankapuri: ‘But did our people know the real position of stars and planets? We believed the sun to be moving in an orbit around the earth. According to contemporary science it is the earth which has movement. Many new planets have been discovered. The conclusions arrived at during the age of darkness must have been misleading and illusionary.’ Vishnudas: ‘Knowledge about the Unmanifest One is like Him— one and permanent. But knowledge about the manifest self of the Unmanifest Being is fractured and subject to change. It is transient because knowledge of the manifest world is contingent upon the comprehension and observation of many. Astronomy in this country has declined with the decline of native power; it might have grown in other countries. We might be required to change our understanding about the characteristics of some of these constellations, but the course of the new and old matter remains immutable, permanent. So if there are new discoveries regarding the movement of planets and constellations, we will have to make new calculations; this is not prohibited in our system. It is easy to make an argument that the principles established by our seers are like dreams, works of imagination. The same argument can be made about experiential knowledge, which is equally dream-like. Our seers had asked questions about the position of the sun and the movement of the earth.⟨fn:346⟩ If the scholars who followed the great seers had not been confined by their narrow vision, our science would have progressed further to an extent that it would have satisfied your curiosity.⟨fn:347⟩ Before suggesting that the astrological almanacs are faulty, the doubter should have their birth chart cast and compare its predictions; the discussion about the veracity of our sciences should follow subsequently. This is the right approach. Shankapuri, you should get your birth chart cast by Jankidas, study this science and only after that pose your questions.’ Shankapuri: ‘What do the stars foretell with regard to Navinchandraji? How did you arrive at the calculations? You do not of course have his birth chart.’ Vishnudas: ‘I posed a question, compared it with my birth chart, did the comparison, and it was obvious to me that this man through his sacrifice will prove the benefactor of the Math.’ Shankapuri: ‘What does that suggest?’

Vishnudas: ‘Jankidas, please satisfy his curiosity.’ Jankidas: Enduring, generous, observing the sacrificial rituals and endowed with proficiency in many sciences and virtuous thoughts, and one at whose birth appropriate sacrifices were performed, truly he is united with prosperity.⟨fn:348⟩ ‘Moreover, A great man possessing good aspect, knowledge, virtues, renown, and renouncing enmity, remains renunciant and courteous even when bestowed with wealth which is esteemed by Gods themselves.⟨fn:349⟩ Vishnudas: ‘Many of the qualities described above are to be found in this man. If that is so, he will prove to be benefactor of this Math. The combination of wealth and renunciation is possible only for a master of this or some similar Math. A person, though wealthy, treats his wealth as a burden and seeks to free himself from this encumbrance by sacrificing this wealth for the sake of the ascetics. Though a man of wealth, he remains a renunciate. ‘So far the hermitage has been maintained through the gifts of the rulers of this state and the charity of faithful followers. The rulers’ gifts have continued because we have been deserving of these gifts. If we lose our fitness, if we stop being deserving of their largess, it would stop and this would be in the fitness of things. The times in which we live are not conducive for faith. The customs and moral ways of life are in decline. The faith of these people is likewise the faith of people in decline. If we want to retain some measure of their faith, we will have to give up our pristine, original ways and accommodate their base and degenerate customs. The ascetic community of Sundargiri has hitherto resisted such forces; it has not succumbed. We are not likely to be enamoured by the prospect of gathering a flock of followers and thereby keep the forces of decline at some distance. We need to find ways of sustaining ourselves in absence of the faithful and their charity. Only one who has great wealth, unmatched learning and possesses virtue can resolve this problem. He needs to consider the condition of society, find ways of uplifting the people and yet remain detached from their corrupting influence; at the same time he must also ensure that the community at Sundargiri rises even higher. It is for these reasons that I see in Navinchandraji a benefactor of the ascetic community.’ Shankapuri: ‘The Alakh Marg prohibits sacrificial rituals. It is also not something that Navinchandraji favours, but it is an injunction according to these verses.’ Vishnudas: ‘Young man, you doubt everything! Who said that our sect completely prohibits rituals? Our theologians say that when the Unmanifest takes form, He does so through sacrificial rite. Based on the authority of various Shrutis, our text says: “When the gods spread the sacrifice with man as the offering, spring was the clarified butter, summer the fuel, autumn the oblation. They anointed man— the sacrifice born at the beginning—upon the sacred grass. With him the gods, the sandhyas and the sages offered sacrifice.” It further says: “With the sacrifice, the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice. These were the first ritual laws.”⟨fn:350⟩ Purusha was the sacrifice and the one to be sacrificed. Shankapuri, I give you consent that you may understand from either Jnanbharati or Viharpuri the rituals concerning the sacrificial rites. ‘Navinchandraji is certain to offer the highest sacrifice. He will not stop at making the sacrifice of wealth; his renunciation will be more subtle. He will renounce wealth and offer it as oblation and sacrifice. All these would be the means to his subtle renunciation. He is the recipient of Madhuri Maiya’s subtle love. This man will eliminate any trace of bodily desire from it and make this subtle love even subtler. He will demonstrate that even in this field he is capable of making sacrifices and further extend his renunciation. The ascetic community of Yadu Shrunga will one day realise the light that permeates this being; of this I am absolutely certain. Shankapuri, the world of householders that you have renounced sees everything from a gross, physical perspective, while we at Yadu Shrunga seek to understand the spiritual aspects. You must forsake the gross and cultivate the spiritual perspective.’ Shankapuri: ‘Yes, Master. I will reflect upon your teachings and follow the path shown by you. I shall make myself more worthy of your grace.’ Shantidas: ‘Master, will you be so kind as to deal with some of my doubts as well?’ Vishnudas: ‘If the subject is within your grasp, your doubts will be addressed.’ Shantidas: ‘Is it not beyond the capacity of the body to imagine that a man and a woman attracted to each other, living alone, would rise above the temptations of the body? Once they are together alone, all else is futile; only the passions of the body are true.’ Shankapuri: ‘Hear, hear! Shankhabharati has a doubt! Get up and let us go out. I will address your doubts. Let us free the Master from having to answer your questions.’ Shantidas: ‘Who are you to address my doubts? You abandoned your wife and tried to seek Bindumati’s attention. And even in this you failed.’ ‘You are truly Shankhabharati! Now bugger everyone’s head,’ retorted Shankapuri and sat aside in sullen silence. Jankidas could not suppress his laughter. Jnanbharati appeared angry; Viharpuri seemed shocked. Having heard their exchange with equanimity, Vishnudas said, ‘Shantidas, a great soul, aided by a favourable constellation of stars and planets, can remain unmoved even under the circumstances that you describe. Evil men snare women in their clutches; they seek carnal pleasures. You have experienced the world of householders. Most of them are somewhere in the middle. They desire women and progeny. Their animal passions are always aroused. They do not know any other form of desire, recognise no other attachment. Therefore, they bring a man and woman together by way of marriage and seek to satisfy their passions. The world of householders has no awareness of the subtle love that renders bodily love subtler and subject to control. It is for this reason that women and men do not trust each other and are always afraid of each other’s company. The couples of Vihar Math subject themselves to well-defined limits. Householders have no conception of these limits; what they consider limits are in fact transgressions. The couples of Vihar Math follow the limits of the science of medicine as also the treatise on love. Therefore, among us relations between men and women are regarded as spiritual. The spiritual attainment of women is in no form regarded as lesser than that of men. Navinchandraji has come to us from the world of householders, but the finer aspects of spiritual conduct are second nature to him. Subtle love and subtler renunciation have been his nature since birth. The superior constellation under which he was born also gives him strength. You and the likes of you have no knowledge, no experience other than the knowledge of the debased ways of householders. You and your kind are frightened by the very thought of self-control in the company of women. It is my belief, based on astral calculations, that Navinchandraji will be as unmoved in the situation as Arjun was in Urvashi’s presence. The ascetic community of Yadu Shrunga views men and women as spiritual beings. The avenues by which their bodily passions may find an outlet have been closed; but there are no limits on the development of righteous conduct. Therefore at this very moment Chandravali Maiya, with full knowledge of all the ascetics, would have gone for parleys with Navinchandraji. And yet, even someone like Shankapuri has not cast aspersions on her. In the social structure of householders this would have given rise to many rumours. People would have behaved like bees whose hive has been destroyed. They would not have been able to view this man and woman as pure souls. Instead they would have seen their bodily forms and spread unsavoury rumours. It is time that you forsake the attitudes of that society and try to cultivate the pure sentiments prevalent on Yadu Shrunga. Jnanbharati, please instruct some ascetic from your math to initiate Shantidas into our world of purity.’

Shantidas was happy. Once he and Shankapuri had left with permission of the Master, Vishnudas spoke to his closest associates. ‘I have to tell the three of you something in confidence. It is a secret matter and must remain so.’ All three grew alert. Vishnudas: ‘From tomorrow for five days, I will leave my body. You will have to guard over my lifeless body. This must remain secret.’ Viharpuri: ‘Master, for us nothing is greater than your command. We shall not fail in our duty.’ Jankidas: ‘There can be no doubt about that.’ Jnanbharati: ‘We are all conscious and alert to our duty and equal to the task.’ Vishnudas: ‘This body is now old. I must perform one final task to aid Navinchandraji’s ascension to the higher realm of consciousness. He has knowledge of many languages, he is learned in many arts; his intellect is imbued with right knowledge. We are incapable of recognising his subtle desires. His desires have become so subtle that enlightenment is not far. He has the capacity to attain Samprajnata Yoga, a state of being where the consciousness is neither active nor passive, a state where the mind is still. Once his subtle desires are completely erased he will be able to merge his consciousness with the Supreme Unmanifest Being. The next four days and nights are propitious. At the most auspicious moment I will try and enter his body. I will, through my consciousness, try and enter his consciousness. I will endeavour to ignite his mind. At other times, I will be in a state of Yoga for my own sake. During those nights, my consciousness freed from my body will enable Navinchandraji to see the light. To the extent that his inner eyes and mine are in complete harmony, he will be able to see all the immortal beings that I see. These immortal beings will satisfy all those questions, curiosities and desires of Navinchandraji that I in my embodied form cannot satisfy. Even if it accomplishes nothing else, this vision, this coming face to face with the immortals will awaken within him the Ritambhara Prajna.

Viharpuri: ‘How will the immortals deal with his desire for the English people and their language?’ Vishnudas: ‘In that world of immortals, beyond the dwelling of Yama all languages are known; there are no distinctions between Arya and Anarya. The immortals will grasp whatever be the thoughts of Navinchandraji. His mind will be purified; all the dirt and chaos will be sieved out. All his doubts will be resolved. As the sun dispels darkness and illuminates righteousness, Navinchandraji’s mind—according to his capacity—will be freed from darkness.’ Jnanbharati: ‘Master, your capacity and spiritual attainment is much higher than his. You are free from the cycle of birth and death; you have attained freedom, fulfillment and contentment even without this adventure. You have attained all your capabilities on your own effort and merit. Let him acquire his capabilities through his own efforts. What is the need for this great and dangerous sacrifice? Its possible fruits are not equal to the risks entailed.’ Jankidas: ‘If Navinchandraji’s stars foretell that he is to acquire these capabilities, then this effort becomes meaningless.’ Viharpuri: ‘Master, if you and we are all capable of attaining moksha through the path of knowledge, why then should one undertake this arduous, dangerous path of Yoga? Does it not seem futile?’ Vishnudas: ‘If that is my duty, I cannot consider the question of either adventure or misadventure. If we are to think of the essence of the Unmanifest to the exclusion of all else, Viharpuri your argument would have merit. But if we are to consider the duties of the manifest form of the Unmanifest, this endeavour is as much a duty as it was the duty of Sri Krishna to guide and assist the efforts of the Pandavas. The manifest God, who is a manifestation of the divine, by his grace grants divinity to humans. The great souls thus blessed also deal with other fellow beings with equal affection. They strengthen the others through the force of affection and give them equal status. God and human beings are related through such links. These inter-meshed links aid the righteous to rise higher and hasten the decline of those who lack virtue. Navinchandraji and I and other ascetics are thus linked; it is my duty to aid him in his upward journey. Viharpuri, Navinchandraji will experience the pull of this force either in a state of awakening or in dream; and to the extent that Madhuri Maiya is linked to him by the force of truth, she, too, will experience its power. Among those who consider all forms of attachment to be undesirable, the duties of the manifest form are totally disregarded to pursue the goals of being united with the Unmanifest Being. In the acceptance of the attributes of the signified, the signified attribute is itself perceived. He who immerses himself in the unsignifiable attains the knowledge of the soul.⟨fn:351⟩ ‘We, on the other hand, believe that the Unmanifest can be attained only after performing one’s duties. The highest duty is to aid the upward journey of the other. It is my responsibility to fulfill this obligation. No one else has the requisite capacity. Viharpuri, my son, we follow this ideal in Vihar Math. We do not renounce for the sake of renunciation when it becomes a duty. My endeavour to discharge this duty for the sake of Navinchandraji should be considered a duty that would aid the efforts of all ascetics in attaining the vision of the Unmanifest One.’
chapters.summary: Vishnudas and his disciples deliberate on Sarasvatichandra's spiritual journey and a significant shift in his living arrangements, hinting at a profound connection with Madhuri Maiya.

chapters.title: Sanatan Dharma or the Five Elementary Sacrifices of Ascetics
paragraphs: Sanatan Dharma or the Five Elementary Sacrifices of Ascetics The World-honoured spake: “Scatter not rice, But offer loving thoughts and acts to all; To parents as the East, where rises light; To teachers as the South, whence rich gifts come; To wife and children as the West, where gleam Colours of love and calm and all days end; To friends and kinsmen and all men as North; To humblest living things beneath, to Saints And Angels and the blessed Dead above; So that all evil be shut off, and so The six main quarters will be safely kept.   —The Light of Asia, Sir Edwin Arnold. The ‘‘freedom’’ and ‘‘modernities,’’ the ‘‘progress’’ and ‘‘truth’’ of these fellows are not ours. We have nothing in common with them. They wish for self-indulgence; we wish for work. They wish to drown consciousness in the unconscious; we wish to strengthen and enrich consciousness. They wish for evasive ideation and babble; we wish for attention, observation and knowledge. The true criterion by which true moderns may be recognized and distinguished from imposters calling themselves moderns may be this: whoever preaches absence of discipline is an enemy of progress; and whoever worships his ‘‘I’’ is an enemy to society. Society has for its first premise neighbourly love and capacity for self-sacrifice; and progress is the effect of an ever more rigorous subjugation of the beast in man, of an ever tenser self-restraint, an ever keener sense of duty and responsibility. The emancipation from which we are striving is of the judgement, not of the appetites. On the profoundly penetrating words of Scripture (Matt. V. 17) ‘‘Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets, I am not come to destroy, but to fulfill.”   —Degeneration, Max Nordau. Serene will be our days and bright And happy will our nature be, When love is an unerring light And joy its own security.   —‘Ode to Duty,’ Wordsworth. Vishnudas and his disciples returned before night fall. The next morning Vishnudas, his most accomplished disciples and Sarasvatichandra sat together. Vishnudas opened the conversation. ‘Navinchandraji, you declined to bow your head before Sri Yadunandan, but were ready to fall at the feet of Chandravali Maiya. What would your society have to say about that and you?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I have renounced that world and have found refuge in you. I am more curious to know your opinion. I bowed to the unseen soul of that pious mother, to her enlightened being and to her heart concealed in the powerful female form. My heart found that the most appropriate gesture, a sign of my devotion to her. The son’s soul instinctively bowed down to a mother’s soul. I bowed before one and not the other, the cause for which lies in this heart and in her light. Society regards men and women as separate; but I have forgotten all about these distinctions ever since I found refuge at your feet.’ Vishnudas: ‘Navinchandraji, the ascetic community of Yadu Shrunga is attracted by and appreciative of your devotion and goodness.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I experience their goodness at every step.’ Vishnudas: ‘Navinchandraji, with the purity of your heart you have gained knowledge of the conduct of the virtuous. You have done so effortlessly.’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘The company of the virtuous is like the sun that opens the lotus and fills it with light.’ Vishnudas: ‘The rays of the sun fall on all things equally; it is the lotus that derives benefit from this contact.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘It is the will of the Supreme Being that grants different capacities to his creations.’ Vishnudas was pleased with this exchange, and said, ‘Navinchandraji, I am so enamoured of your responses that I forget the subject I wished to discuss! I have a plan for you. For some days starting tomorrow, I will be in a state of Yoga Samadhi. During this period you should remain in seclusion on Chiranjiv Shrunga.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I am ever eager to abide by your command and wish. Moreover, yesterday I have also given my word to Chandravali Maiya. Therefore, I am doubly bound to follow your command.’ Vishnudas: ‘We have firm faith that all thoughts and commands of Chandravali Maiya are righteous and beneficial. She has her own reasons, which she must have shared with you. My reasons are different.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The Master’s desire is our command.’ Vishnudas: ‘This maxim is useful for society for the limited purpose of maintaining order. But for us ascetics, the effectiveness of the command rests upon our own goodness. In this hermitage, the master instructs his disciples only with regard to their spiritual development. The master’s instructions or guidance are not issued as commands. Rather, it is like a parent calling out from a window to a child who responds to the call and comes out of love and curiosity. We guide our disciples with affection. Navinchandraji, I want that you should understand the reasons that guide my wish. Chiranjiv Shrunga is a place of exceptional spiritual significance. Those who have earned the merit to reside there either receive a vision of the immortals or even acquire the status of an immortal. They acquire the capacity for good deeds and become capable of working for the welfare of others. They come face to face with the immortal, great souls of this earth. Some great souls attain Turiyavastha, the fourth and ultimate state of the soul in which it becomes one with the Supreme Spirit. Some great souls experience this in the state of awakening while others do so in a dreamlike state. Some experience a state of deep hibernation and emerge from it free of all three forms of passions. Many old and accomplished great souls have made Chiranjiv Shrunga their abode and given to it these sublime qualities. I ask you to make this place your abode from tonight. If there are any obstacles in your path or if you still lack some spiritual attainment, I shall assist your progress through my Yogavastha. I want you to stay there for the period necessary for your spiritual growth.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘With each passing day you shower me with greater blessings, but you give me more than my capacity and fitness.’ Viharpuri: ‘That is the discretion of the Master. We are not fit to question his judgement. If you feel that he has granted you more than your entitlement, Shankapuri would claim that he has received much less than his capacity. This would create disorder in the ascetic community.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘May God keep such disorder away from this harmonious place. I need some clarification from the Master. I will ponder over it and make use of it during this period.’ Vishnudas: ‘You have the right to ask questions. We restrict the questions of those with less capability, but there are no limits on those who have attained the highest status.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What is superior: renunciation or the state of householder? Who has the right of renunciation and who is fit to be a householder? If the opinions of the father, wife, Master and the person himself were to differ, which of the four should prevail? What penance is enjoined upon a man who abandons a woman without reason? When society, religion and textual authority come into conflict, which of the three has the right to emerge victorious? Renunciation, pleasure and morality: of these three, which has the right to primacy? Should abandoning the state of renunciation be regarded as degeneration, as a fall? Who has this right and who does not? How and when do the piety and purity of this place free us from the bonds of social norm and morality? What should be regarded as right conduct for the large mass of people?’ Before any of these questions could be answered, there was a bustle outside. It appeared that many of the monks had suddenly stood up and walked towards someone. There were simultaneous calls of ‘Yadunandan ki jai!’ and ‘Chandravali Maiya ki jai!’ The temple bells rang as Chandravali accompanied by ten or twelve nuns escorted Kumud Sundari to Vishnudas’ presence. Everyone except Vishnudas stood up in greeting and welcomed her and her companions with folded hands. The women ascetics flushed with shyness, greeted the Master and stood before him with heads bowed in reverence. Chandravali placed some fruits and flowers at Vishnudas’ feet as offerings. Vishnudas raised his hand in benediction and said, ‘We welcome you all. May you attain the Unmanifest One, who is sought by the most superior of beings. Chandravali Maiya, kindly sit down along with your companions. Please tell us how we are entitled to welcome you and receive you?’ All the male ascetics sat on one side, long-haired, strong-bodied and learned. The women ascetics, clad in ochre sarees, sat on the other side. Chandravali and Kumud sat in front of this group. Vishnudas, emaciated with age but full of light, radiance and spiritual presence, sat in the centre; his flowing white hair added to his allure. It was as if the Ganga and Yamuna had emerged out of the Himalayas. Sarasvatichandra found this whole scene strangely grand. His eyes were drawn to Kumud, who sat there as invisibly as Sarasvati, but his gaze did not linger over her. Just as a wayfarer finds his path in a flash of lightning in the sky, Kumud discerned engagement in that fleeting gaze. Chandravali said to Vishnudas in response, ‘Master, your blessings are the only form of welcome that we desire. This is Madhuri. I have a great deal of affection and attachment for her. I had given her the permission to come up the mountain, but my concern for her compelled me to follow her. Since I am here, I thought it proper that she should have the benefit of your darshan as also of your ashram. Please allow us to sit and listen to your discourse. We do not wish to interrupt the discussion, which is a privilege for ascetics. Kindly continue your discourse.’ Viharpuri: ‘Yes Master. You were about to respond to the queries posed by Navinchandraji. This will benefit us all.’ In every instance, all the ascetics of this community speak the truth—large and small. There is no trace of innuendo in their speech, but it is no less clever and subtle. Their speech has clarity and a certain reserve, and it betrays no trace of pride. Bhartrihari has said that the learned are consumed by their ego. Poor Bhartrihari must have never visited a place such as this and must have remained confined to the lower social orders. Sarasvatichandra silently spoke these words to himself as he listened to Vishnudas with rapt attention. Vishnudas: ‘Navinchandraji, great souls such as Manu and others have written a code for the householders. Similarly our theoreticians have formulated principles for the ascetic community. You would have seen a copy of this in our library. A learned man free from other worldly obligations has no duties towards himself; his actions should be directed towards the welfare of people at large. Our text, the Lakshya Dharma Sangraha, has described the modes by which the people’s welfare could be secured. An ascetic by disposition is a contented person; having renounced the world of the householder, the ascetic devotes a lifetime for securing spiritual upliftment. But, a learned ascetic who has attained this state is not required to make these efforts. As obligatory actions wither away, a person can detach himself from worldly obligations, but so long as action itself persists, detachment will not nullify obligatory actions. I have no disturbance nor do I have meditative silence. As meditation and hindrance are signs of a mind gripped by desire. I am novel experience itself. What then is a new experience for me? I have performed all actions and gathered fruits thereof.⟨fn:352⟩ ‘A man of learning has no duties towards himself; but for this reason his obligations towards the world do not cease. “I perform no actions; hence my conduct is governed either by social norms or Shastric injunctions should follow their destiny. I am satiated but my actions performed for the welfare of others should follow Shastric injunctions.”⟨fn:353⟩ ‘Why should an ascetic strive for the welfare of the world? It is true that the vision of the Supreme Unseen One frees one from the cycle of life and death. But this is not the final and total release. One is released only from pain and pleasure associated with both the body and the subtle body; because the soul is neither free nor in bondage. One is free from the consideration of gross and subtle bodies only when all action has become unnecessary. “Making over (the merit of his own) good actions to his friends and (the guilt) of his evil deeds to his enemies, he attains eternal Brahman by the practice of meditation.”⟨fn:354⟩ Householders have friends and enemies, but ascetics have no enemies. Still, there are those who harbour animosity towards them as well. The Shrutis say of them: “Children would inherit his wealth, friends would share in his merit and foes would share his sin.”⟨fn:355⟩ ‘Nothing is ever destroyed in the manifest world; all matter comes to rest in its original form. Therefore, whatever merits or demerits accrue to one as a result of one’s actions have to be offered as oblation. By so doing one is freed from the web of action, and the release of the gross and subtle bodies becomes possible. This can be achieved only by immense patience; the result cannot be obtained either in haste or through the path of knowledge to the exclusion of all else. Another Shruti says: “If a man knows this here, that is the true (end of life); if he does not know this here, then there is great destruction (new births). The wise who have thought on all things (and recognised the self in them) become immortal when they have departed from this world.”⟨fn:356⟩ An ascetic must through his endeavour transfer his power and capability to all beings; in so doing he should acquire a subtle body and surrender the gross body to the elements. This is the purest possible end of the embodied person. When subtle and gross bodies are offered along with all their actions as oblation in the sacrifice for the benefit of all beings, the manifest sacrifice of the Unmanifest Being is concluded. ‘All actions of the householders are for the benefit of the self; this is the result of their condition. Ascetics offer all their desires and actions to the will of the Supreme Unmanifest Being in its endeavour to secure the welfare of all embodied beings. Ascetics offer their oblations in the supreme sacrifice initiated by the Supreme Being and transfer their subtle and gross attainments to all beings; their merits are made over to their friends and evil deeds to their enemies. At the conclusion of this process the ascetics are freed of all attachments, released from the body and attain the Unmanifest Being. ‘Such is the root cause of the manifest actions of our group of ascetics. They consider it their duty to spend their lives for the welfare of all people. This duty abides so long as the body remains. All other religions—be they of the Aryas or the Anaryas—are confined to one people. But our religion by very nature and constitution is universal and eternal, because at all times and in all places the welfare of others has been, and will remain, an ascetic’s primary duty. Navinchandraji, learned or foolish, all ascetics have to perform their duties. Even a renunciate has duties. Hence, it has been said, Giving no pain to any creature, let him slowly accumulate spiritual merit, for the sake (of acquiring) a companion to the next world, just as the white ant (gradually raises its hill). For in the next world neither father, nor mother, nor wife, nor sons, nor relations stay to be his companions; spiritual merit alone remains (with him). Single is each being born; single it dies; single it enjoys the rewards of virtue, single (it suffers the punishment of) sin. Leaving the dead body on the ground like a log of wood, or a clod of earth, the relatives depart with averted faces; but spiritual merit follows the (Soul). Let him therefore always slowly accumulate spiritual merit, in order (that it may be his) companion (after death). For which merit as his companion he will traverse a gloom difficult to traverse.

(That companion) speedily conducts the man who is devoted to duty and effaces his sins by austerities, to the next world, radiant and clothed with an ethereal body.⟨fn:357⟩ ‘These are the duties of a householder. Manu himself has defined the duties of an ascetic. Let him not desire to die, let him desire to live; let him wait for (his appointed) time, as a servant (waits) for the payment of his wages.⟨fn:358⟩ Let him reflect on the transmigration of men, caused by their sinful deeds, on their falling into hell, and on the torments in the world of Yama. On the separation from their dear ones, on their union with hated men, on their being overpowered by age and being tormented with disease. On the departure of individual soul from this body and its new birth in (another) womb, and on its wanderings through ten thousand millions of existences, On the infliction of pain on embodied (spirits), which is caused by demerit, and the gain of eternal bliss, which is caused by the attainment of their highest aim, (gained through) spiritual merit. By deep meditation let him recognise the subtle nature of the Supreme Soul and its presence in all organisms, both the highest and the lowest. To whatever order he may be attached, let him, though blemished (by a want of external marks), fulfil his duty, equi-minded towards all creatures; (for) the external mark (of the order) is not the cause of (the acquisition of) merit.⟨fn:359⟩ Let him recognise by the practice of meditation the progress of the individual soul through beings of various kinds, (a progress) hard to understand for unregenerate men.⟨fn:360⟩ ‘Such are the duties enjoined upon ascetics. A beehive becomes useless once the honey has been gathered from it. Similarly, an ascetic who has learnt all the mysteries of the Shastras finds books useless. With the realisation of the Supreme Soul he finds fulfillment. But his duties do not cease with that. This realised being has to wander from place to place, from village to village and perform his duties as enumerated by Manu. According to Manu, an ascetic must observe worldly affairs, learn more about them, deal with all beings with a sense of equality, and experience the subtleness of the Supreme Soul. The movement of the subtle soul is beyond the knowledge of those who are not realised themselves. Such a renunciate has to understand that movement and teach others; he must share his experiences with the world for the welfare of all. A realised renunciate has these obligations and duties, which have been placed upon him from ancient times. Both the householder and the renunciate have to perform these obligations throughout their lives. ‘The duties of householders are contingent upon time and space, while the path of Lakshya Dharma is founded upon the eternal duties of the ascetic. The duties of householders are contained in five elementary sacrifices; similarly the duties of ascetics are also contained in five elementary sacrifices. While the sacrifices of householders are performed through gross objects and the ritual act is manifest to others, the sacrifice of ascetics remains unmanifest and is performed through subtle elements. The sacrifices of householders are most often contingent upon desires; even when they are desireless they are for the welfare of the self, of the body and one’s own being; for them the welfare of others is only a means for the welfare of the self— Maharshi Yajnavalkya has said that for the householders, not just father and son, but even the Brahman is held dear for the desires of the souls. An ascetic loves neither the self nor the non-self. His duty is to perform a desireless sacrifice for the welfare of all beings. The world is held together by Dharma, and Dharma is held and contained by the manifest form of the Unmanifest Supreme Soul. And hence, the sacrifice intended by the manifest being ignites the sacrificial fires of the ascetics. Brahma is the root of the universe and Shiva is its ultimate destination. Vishnu preserves the world between the points of origin and dissolution. This monastic community worships this form of Vishnu—Vishnu, omnipresent and omnipotent, permeates the universe and upholds religion in the universe. ‘“Vishnu, the preserver, the invincible, stepped three steps, thereby upholding the righteous acts. Behold the past times of Vishnu, through which (the devotee) accomplishes pious activities. He is the worthy friend of Indra.”⟨fn:361⟩ ‘Supreme Man himself is present as the sacrificial fire, and the eternal religion of the Aryas emanates from it. “When the Gods, offering sacrifice, bound, as their victim, Purusa, Gods, sacrificing, sacrificed the victim. These were the earliest holy ordinances.”⟨fn:362⟩ ‘In the most superior form of sacrifice Supreme Man becomes the sacrificial animal; spring becomes the clarified butter while summer becomes the fire and winter becomes the oblation.
