The four Vedas emanate from this sacrifice; gods and seers become the performers of the sacrifice. Our endeavour to become one with the Supreme Man is attained by our participation in this sacrifice. The fruits of this sacrifice are so powerful that the distinction between the individual and the universal is obliterated and they become one. This is a pure, desireless action and offering to the Brahman. The unity of the being and the Supreme Being, of the godly and the godless, is thus attained. This is the first step of attaining a three-fold unity of Brahman, God and human being or the Supreme Unmanifest Being, the supreme manifest man and the human being. All action is dedicated to the manifest Brahman and the ultimate destiny of the manifest Brahman is unmanifest, eternal Brahman. It is through this three-fold unity that all actions are contained in the manifest Brahman and that the manifest finds repose in the unmanifest. The elementary sacrifice is the means of attaining unity with all beings; desirelessness, superior motive and welfare of all living beings are the results of this sacrifice. ‘The five elementary sacrifices of the householders are: Pitru Yajna, Manushya Yajna, Bhuta Yajna, Deva Yajna and Brahma Yajna. The elementary sacrifices of the ascetics are known by these very names, but the soul and body of these sacrifices are different. In the primary sacrifice of the Supreme Man, Man himself is offered as the sacrifice in place of sacrificial animals. Similarly, the ascetics offer their masculinity in the sacrifice as oblations. The soul of the being is subtle while the body is gross; together they are offered as oblation. The gross body becomes the sacrificial altar. A bird cannot consume a fruit without being seated on the branch of a tree; similarly among embodied beings the act of consumption requires the body; one cannot become a sacrificial oblation without entering the altar. Before the sacrifice both the altar and the sacrificial animal have to be nurtured; the offering of sacrifice is possible only subsequently. Of the animal it is said: “He sprinkles it with water, into which he has thrown rice and barley, from head to tail, with (the formula), ‘Grow up, agreeable to the Rudra the great god.’ He should let it grow up. When it has cut its teeth, or when it has become a bull.”⟨fn:363⟩ It is necessary to nurture the animal. The subtle bodies of ascetics are thus kept healthy, pure and nurtured. Aided by mutual attraction and the power of constellations couples merge into each other as their subtle bodies unite and become one. They become ready to offer the sacrifice. The arrangement and norms of Vihar Math are determined accordingly. Those men and women who do not experience such unity can conduct themselves in solitary pursuits and be like the bangles of an unmarried girl. Such persons follow the duties of the renunciates, and the other two maths have been created for them. The sacrificial altar and sacrificial animal are brought together through human effort, and this is a function of time. But the subtle and gross bodies are joined to each other at the very moment of the birth of the body. This unity is willed by the Supreme Manifest Being. From this very moment the sacrificial altar and sacrificial animal are brought together for the eventual sacrifice. This sacrificial animal grows daily, becomes healthy and acquires capabilities in various arts, which depends upon the will of the Supreme Manifest Being, the circumstances of the one offering sacrifice, his family and other such causes. The ascetics consider their first duty to aid and participate in the growth and nurturance of the sacrificial animal. This is also an essential ritual of the sacrifice. Just as the sacrificial animal is nurtured, similarly the sacrificial altar has to be prepared to bear the burden of the animal and the heat of the eternal fire. The care that we take to nurture both the gross and the subtle bodies is for this reason. Any consumption that does not aid this process is considered by ascetics as irreligious and lustful and is shunned. ‘How is this altar, the sacrificial animal and all other matter required for the sacrifice to be gathered? The sacrifice of the householders requires wood, clarified butter and other oblations. The sacrifice of the ascetics requires beauty, aesthetic delight, love, devotion and other such virtues. A householder of Rajsi character gathers worldly objects and capabilities for use in religious actions and also enjoys the fruits thereof. Similarly, an ascetic of Satvik disposition endeavours to collect resources for the sacrifice believing himself to be the consumer. We must now understand as to how the elements for sacrifice are obtained. A foetus has no capacity to feed itself. The mother nurtures the child through the umbilical cord; similarly the sacrificial elements collected in the womb of mother earth nurture the gross body and its senses. The subtle body, through its actions, is similarly nurtured. They strengthen the sacrificial altar, feed the sacrificial animal and stoke the sacrificial fire. The omnipresent but unmanifest fire of the Supreme Manifest Being permeates in all ten directions and it ignites such subtle bodies. Thus, the elementary sacrifice commences. ‘The first sacrifice is the Pitru Yajna. This sacrifice is different for the householders and the ascetics. Householders are bound by relations of father and son. If the father be alive, this sacrifice is offered for his direct gratification and in event of his death it is offered for the indirect gratification of his subtle body. Direct gratification brings merit to the son, but parents covet such gratification and such desires lead to the fall of their subtle bodies. A son who seeks to gratify the greed of his parents fails to perform the other four sacrifices, and the sin of this failure accrues to such greedy parents. Moreover, such covetous gratification impedes the fulfillment of their obligations to perform the five sacrifices. Only when human beings perform the five sacrifices in their due proportion does the elementary sacrifice of the Supreme Man become possible. By failing to perform the other sacrifices parents also fail in their duty towards the sacrifice of the Supreme Man. This is not beneficial for either the parents or the son, and also the universe. Therefore, for ascetics the Pitru Yajna has been replaced by the Matha Yajna. The householders perform sacrifices for the gratification of deceased parents. But, in fact, with death the relationship between father and son also ceases as all beings assume subtle bodies after death. The world of ancestors is gratified by both renunciation and asceticism. The virtues of the ascetics are powerful enough to gratify the world of ancestors. And you know that the Unmanifest Supreme Soul has neither father, grandfather nor great- grandfather. It has no ties of kinship. It abides as pure soul. Seen from the worldly perspective, their gratification happens by “caret”⟨fn:364⟩. Father and other ancestors leave behind all worldly relations forever and abide in the world of ancestors. The offerings made for their gratification are an act of faith. But from a pure perspective it is best to abandon all worldly relations. Therefore it is said: “They call (the names of) fathers Vasus, (those of) grandfathers Rudras, and those of great-grandfathers Adityas; thus (speaks) the eternal Veda.”⟨fn:365⟩ ‘The ascetics, following this higher ideal, do not perform the Pitru Yajna. Virtuous fathers forbade their sons from making this sacrifice. Such fathers have unattached, unsullied love for their sons. They consider the progeny not as a son but as a soul, as part of the self. The shraddha of a virtuous man is done not by rituals but by remembering their virtues and knowledge. ‘We perform the Matha Yajna in place of Pitru Yajna. Parents nurture and care for their sons and daughters till such time that they acquire the fitness for offering sacrifice; once they attain the fitness the parents offer their progeny to the monastic orders and give up all claim to them. Such a son is freed from the obligation of performing the Pitru

Yajna and has to perform the Matha Yajna instead. An ascetic does his duties towards his fellow ascetics, his teacher, his monastic order and to Yadunandan. He spends his life in performance of these various duties. The obligations that parents and children have towards each other are often not met due to selfish desires; but these obligations are fulfilled among ascetics through their spiritual sensibility. ‘An ascetic having performed the Matha Yajna becomes capable of offering the Manushya Yajna. This sacrifice is offered for the gratification of the human being. An ascetic becomes both the performer of the sacrifice as also the sacrificial animal. The performer of this sacrifice seeks to satiate all human beings who come into his contact. Individual beings are created from the Universal Supreme Soul; they assume many forms and inhabit various gross bodies, and subtle bodies reside in them and traverse through the cycle of birth and death. During this journey many beings come into contact with each other. Some are this-worldly, while others belong to the other world. Sons and grandsons come from the other world, while beings from this world come in the form of guests, friends, wife, family and all those with whom we come in contact due to pragmatic considerations of everyday life. There are human beings we come into contact with ever so fleetingly in the course of our journey. ‘For our parents, we are their gift from the other world and we reside in their homes as guests. During our childhood we do not possess the capacity to offer sacrifices, and so long as we are thus incapable we are considered guests of our parents. As we acquire the capacity for sacrifice we are transformed from a guest to a host, the doer of sacrifice, and the parents become guests. Their being guests in their own house is purposive; they invite us into their homes as hosts and themselves become guests. A sacrifice offered for the gratification of parents is Pitru Yajna; but among ascetics one’s father and fellow ascetics are regarded as equal. All are equal from the spiritual point of view; hence amongst us Pitru Yajna has been incorporated as part of Manushya Yajna. Just as parents invite us into their lives as hosts, for ascetics all persons—whether they belong to one’s caste, one’s motherland or inhabit any other part of mother earth—are regarded as guests and deserve the offering of Pitru Yajna. We have incorporated them in the Manushya Yajna. There are several guests who come to us on our invitation. Sons and daughters are invited guests; a husband invites a wife and similarly a wife invites her husband. In the wider society rituals of courtship have almost disappeared, but they remain as a practice among us ascetics. Among us couples are attracted to each other as metal is attracted to a magnet. This attraction is caused by the stars and constellations and the worship of the god of love. Such couples experience a sense of unity. Couples thus united do not regard each other as guests. A couple becomes an equal partner in sacrifice due to such unity and non-duality. There was a time when such marriages were also prevalent in wider society. In such marriages the couples would become equal partners in all aspects of human endeavour—religion, industry, desire and self-realisation. ‘Ascetics do not engage in all aspects of human endeavour. Their goal remains the performance of the five elementary sacrifices. Their attachment to each other as a couple is with respect to the performance of these sacrifices. Our ascetics, to fulfill the purpose of this monastery, perform their individual duties and their collective endeavours further the goal of the monastic community. Among the householders members of a community participate in caste dinners and through mutual cooperation contribute to the furtherance of the common endeavour. Similarly couples united by the experience of non-duality make a joint endeavour for the fulfillment of all five sacrifices. They become partners and co-sharers of burdens, encourage each other with noble ideals and enable each other to offer the most subtle of sacrifices. Navinchandraji, if you want an example of this, look at the fiery sacrifice of Chandravali Maiya and Viharpuri.’ The Master’s praise caused them both to lower their eyes. Vishnudas: ‘A couple makes an offering through the unity of their hearts⟨fn:366⟩, the subtlety of their love and the totality of their commitment to the performance of duties. A sacrifice thus initiated for mutual satiation is described by us as Priti Yajna. We characterise all other forms of Manushya Yajna as Atithi Yajna because the obligatory relationship between the host and the guest defines this sacrifice. The guest in this sacrifice may be invited, uninvited or like our parents who have become guests. One’s duty with regard to one’s parents, the motherland and welfare of all people is lifelong; one cannot cease to perform these duties. Parents, by giving their consent to renunciation, free their son from his obligations towards them. But there is no turning away from one’s duty towards the welfare of fellow beings; even an ascetic is not free from this obligation. Duties towards an uninvited guest are circumscribed by the gratification of the guest and cease the moment the guest departs. But if the desires of a guest are such that they cannot be satiated, then the question of his gratification becomes a contradiction in terms. If the guest has limited virtues then also his gratification becomes an impossibility. Societal norms also make space for the deserving and undeserving guest; among the ascetics this discernment rests on different ground. All human beings cannot be accorded equal status as guests; therefore a guest capable of performing the five sacrifices is considered a worthy guest. Their presence lends strength to the sacrifice and furthers the welfare of all. ‘Among the householders, a dwija or a twice-born has been considered a worthy guest. The ascetics accord respect to celibate persons who are not dwija. Knowledge and virtue are two qualities which are considered worthy of respect in the ascetic community. But such considerations do not apply to one’s parents and invited guests. A couple united by an experience of deep non-duality is not a guest and hence beyond these considerations. “For because he stays (sthita) not long (anityam), he is called atithi (a guest).”⟨fn:367⟩ ‘A father and son are not joined by their subtle bodies; even if they do forge such bonds they are transient and incomplete; the bonds of gross body are by very nature transient. Therefore, these relationships are characterised as the one between guests and hosts. The roots of the Priti Yajna among ascetics are in the non-duality of subtle bodies, and they continue to experience this unity even in absence of the gross body; hence this relationship is beyond the pale of obligations towards a guest. In our society, among the householders, marriage is performed without courtship. This is a marriage only of the bodies; here there is no sense of non-duality but merely a transient sense of being a guest. If such a relationship is destined to move towards subtle love and a determination to attain spiritual unity, and in the event that the couple feels this sense of oneness, their relationship moves beyond the obligations of guest and host and they prepare to offer Priti Yajna. In absence of this, they relate to each other by norms of the guest-host relationship. Among the householders all girls are given in marriage before attaining a mature intellect and hence they are ignorant, while some grooms are immature while others are of proper age. It is obligatory for a mature groom to consider his bride as an invited guest. An immature groom has to consider his bride as a destined guest. All brides should regard their husbands as destined guests. In such a relationship there has to be mutuality of obligatory performances and mutual sacrifice. ‘Priti Yajna is founded upon the permanence of the relationship between subtle bodies. The question of abandonment of the subtle body does not arise. This sacrifice is beyond considerations of the worthiness of partners. These considerations do not apply even to invited and destined guests. The question of worthiness of an invited guest has to be posed prior to the invitation. Once an invitation is given it is immoral to ask questions about the worthiness of the invited guest. One cannot even begin to ask questions about the worthiness of one’s parents. This question has legitimacy only with regard to an uninvited guest. An uninvited guest who is neither learned, nor virtuous is moved out of the rubric of Manushya Yajna and accommodated in Bhut Yajna.

“Let him gently place on ground (some food) for dogs, Kandalas (Svapak), those afflicted with diseases that are punishment of former sins, crows and insects.”⟨fn:368⟩ ‘Persons unworthy of being treated as guests are not accorded companionship, but are to be treated as one would treat a dog; therefore they have to be gratified from a distance, as one would deal with worms. This is part of Bhut Yajna. All these living beings have to be redeemed by our sacrifice, which is done out of compassion for them; for this reason this sacrifice is also called Daya Yajna. But even compassion has limits. If the beings are so lowly that their presence itself is likely to endanger the sanctity of the altar and the sacrificial animal, if compassion for them is likely to nullify the sacrifice itself, one must realise that it is not given to us to redeem them. Hence, it is not obligatory on us to show compassion for the sake of compassion or to view compassion as an end in itself. When Sita Mata forgot this, she fell into the hands of Ravana. ‘The other form of Bhut Yajna is Vyahar Yajna or endeavour required in the everyday, practical domain of life. In order to accumulate resources for other sacrifices all human beings are required to exert both their subtle and gross bodies; one has to earn resources through bodily labour and spend them. When we ask the earth for grains or demand services from a servant or seek wages or even demand that horses drag our chariots, all such actions require an effort, an endeavour. If these activities are for eventual use in a sacrifice, then these everyday actions also become like a sacrificial ritual. These efforts are result-oriented and hence they are called Sakam Yajna or Vyahar Yajna. One is required to deal with both living and non-living beings; hence it has been called Bhut Yajna. All actions of householders are oriented towards certain goals; hence all sacrifices of householders in this sense are Vyahar Yajna. ‘The existential element of the manifest Supreme Man is present in all beings. This existential element is not the consciousness of the Supreme Being. Even worms have this existential element. Humans, too, have it. It is part of our intellect and our conscience. One has to observe this world, to engage and experiment with it, to ascertain its qualities and strengths; one has to create a science of it and comprehend its relationship with the universe. All beings imbued with the existential element of the Supreme are offered as oblation in the great sacrifice. This offering is their redemption. This sacrifice is called Vidya Yajna. It is endless and has no limits. This sacrifice is also Bhut Yajna. Men of learning, scholars, seers and poets are partial towards this sacrifice. An accomplished ascetic may, with the greatest of endeavours, be able to have a fleeting glimpse of the Eternal Universal Being; but those dedicated to the pursuit of Vidya Yajna have visions of it like flashes of light. ‘The Matha Yajna is a necessary means for the performance of all other sacrifices. It is required in order to protect the virtues of renunciates and to limit their contact with society. Human beings accept the superiority of the subtle body. But among householders there are sayings like, “a living man will acquire a wife.” Their effort is to further the lifespan of the gross body while neglecting efforts required for attainment of the subtle body. They say that: One should abandon a kinsman for the clan, abandon the clan for the sake of the village and forsake the village for people at large, but one should give up the earth for the sake of self-realisation.⟨fn:369⟩ ‘Just as householders consider giving up the earth for self-realisation as desirable, ascetics believe that the Matha Yajna is primary and if other sacrifices have to be forsaken for its performance, it should be done because without the monastery ascetics are certain to face extinction. A householder requires the body not only to fulfill his desires and base instincts but also to perform his duties, and hence the care and protection of the body is required. We described this during our discussion on the care of sacrificial animals. ‘What if one sacrifice came in conflict with another? We have described Pitru Yajna and various forms of Atithi Yajna as part of Manushya Yajna. In Priti Yajna the couple is one and non-distinct from each other and hence their actions are performed as one. Their decision to participate or not participate in a sacrifice is taken as a joint decision. Therefore, it is a contradiction in terms to speak of the Priti Yajna coming in conflict with the other sacrifices. Even Brahma the Creator cannot destroy the eternal union of the subtle bodies of a couple joined by Priti Yajna. They might, for greater sacrifice and by mutual consent, choose to live apart from each other’s physical body. Such couples, though two, act as one in the performance of sacrifices. A sacrifice that is by one half is necessarily preferred by the other half. Take the example of Ram and Sita. Sri Ramchandra banished the physical body of Sita for securing the welfare of his people; Sita Mata did not see this as a wrong. It is the most startling example of non- duality in a Priti Yajna. Chandravali Maiya’s example is also before you. ‘But couples who are not united by Priti Yajna are two individuals and cannot act as one. These couples must accept their duality and host each other. Because of destiny or as a result of their actions sometimes a couple may deviate from their non-dual existence. Such couples cease to be unitary beings and become two individuals related to each other by norms of the guest-host relationship. ‘The real normative questions arise in the performance of Atithi Yajna and many of the knotty problems of householders arise from this sphere. In our scriptural treatise, Lakshya Dharma Sangraha the injunctions for us have been clearly defined. We cannot ask questions regarding guests invited by us or those who are our guests because of destiny. Once we invite someone and then nullify it by saying that you are unworthy of my invitation is conduct contrary to religion. It is our duty to welcome and respect the wife or son invited by us. A son, once he acquires the capacity for offering sacrifice, ceases to be an invited guest and is to be regarded as a guest who has come to us uninvited. One cannot ask questions about the virtue of an uninvited guest. A wife, once invited to be a partner, cannot be turned away without her consent. One cannot neglect an invited guest to receive a person destined to be our guest or someone who has come to us uninvited. Any neglect of an invited guest is conduct contrary to religion. It is our duty to care for them.

‘A son has to be regarded as a guest till he acquires the capacity to offer sacrifice. Once capable, he can offer Pitru Yajna. When parents cannot support themselves the Pitru Yajna is inevitable and cannot be forsaken; but under other circumstances it is not so. Generally parents are not guests in the temple of their son; the son is a guest in the temple of his parents. A host cannot forsake his duty towards the guest, but a guest is at liberty to move out of the temple of his host. Under such circumstances which make the performance of other sacrifices impossible, a son can leave the house of his parents, and he would not invite any demerit for so doing. But that departure has to be for the performance of one of the other sacrifices. In absence of this, it is forbidden to neglect Pitru Yajna. ‘One’s duties towards other destined guests are not such. A husband or wife cannot abandon the other person. A guest can depart, but the host cannot abandon his duty and depart to perform other functions. An ascetic is bound to the motherland and humanity; he cannot forsake his duty towards either of them. One is freed from obligations only when one becomes incapable of offering a sacrifice. An uninvited guest remains a guest during the period of his residence with his host or till the host becomes incapable of performing his duties. ‘The Vidya Yajna enriches the Manushya Yajna and so long as it does not impede the latter one may continue to offer Vidya Yajna. Vyahar Yajna is a means to the performance of other sacrifices and it may be abandoned if it ceases to fulfill this function. Daya Yajna is offered for the redemption of other beings. If there are no human beings compassion and redemption are both impossible; hence Daya Yajna must remain secondary to Manushya Yajna. ‘Matha Yajna, Manushya Yajna and Bhut Yajna are primary sacrifices of the Supreme Manifest Being and together they are called Lakshya Yajna. The other two sacrifices are Daya Yajna and Brahma Yajna; we call them Alakshya Yajna. Deva Yajna is a sacrifice offered to the non-dual nature of the Manifest and the Unmanifest Supreme Being. Brahma Yajna is offered to the Unmanifest Supreme Being. These can be offered only by those who have attained the highest qualification and spiritual attainment; but we do allow madhyam adhikaris, ascetics of the second order of attainment, to witness this sacrifice. ‘Intellect is the seat of the devas; hence the term deva is indicative of vital spirits.⟨fn:370⟩ Gratification of the devas lies in the satiation of vital spirits. Therefore, the sacrifice which is for the gratification of both is called Deva Yajna. Truth as perceived by the eyes and other senses is not truth; truth is that which is so perceived by pure intellect. Hence, the Shruti says: “And verily, the gods are the truth, and man is the untruth. Therefore in saying, ‘I now enter from untruth into truth, he passes from men to gods.”⟨fn:371⟩ What is perceived as true by the pure intellect alone is Truth. What is generally considered to be true may not be so regarded by the scriptures. The light of the moon is regarded as that which belongs to the moon, but scriptures consider it the light of the sun;⟨fn:372⟩ hence what is ordinarily regarded as truth is falsehood. The mystery of the Supreme Manifest Being’s creation can be unravelled by the scriptures. The movement of the sun and moon, the movement of atoms and the formation of human social institutions are always dynamic. Those who seek to understand the manifest universe study these movements and create various sciences.

Truth so revealed is called Rita. The root term rit is indicative of movement, unceasing movement. Initially all matter is unmanifest, but it becomes manifest and eventually becomes unmanifest once again. New objects take its place. This cycle of creation, growth, continuity and destruction goes on incessantly and endlessly. This is called Rita. Those engaged in Vidya Yajna seek out elements of this Rita through logic and speculation. Their attempt in so doing is to lend stability to the social order. Therefore learned men have been regarded as yogis. The light of Vidya Yajna may illuminate a part or a fragment of the Rita. The total and complete comprehension of Rita is accessible to seers who have an intellect so cultivated that it can perceive the cycle of Rita in its totality.⟨fn:373⟩ This intellect is called Ritambhara Prajna. A seer who attains this spiritual gift acquires intellect that can see beyond the present, the past and the future. The subject of this ‘seeing’ is Rita. The essence of intellect is its capacity for illumination; it is all seeing. It reveals the true essence of things the moment layers of ignorance and falsehood are removed. Truth destroys falsehood, and all three times—the past, the present and the future—are revealed. This act of revelation is Rita. A seer to whom Rita is revealed does not see God as contingent or limited. Rita reveals the non-contingent, absolute form of the manifest being. Nor does he reproach God with inequality of dispensation or cruelty.⟨fn:374⟩ The universal being that Sri Krishna revealed to Arjun is this Rita. An intellect thus imbued with Rita comprehends the intention and the mystery of creation. This seer attains non- duality in the consciousness and joy of the manifest being. The seer to whom Rita is revealed also knows the paths through which the world could be redeemed and its welfare secured. Sri Krishna, the Supreme Soul and Sri Buddha possessed Ritambhara Prajna. The sacrifice and penance done by ascetics to attain this Ritambhara Prajna are called either Deva Yajna or Rita Yajna. ‘Rita is Truth. But this truth is distinct from the Supreme Unmanifest Truth. The only one Supreme Truth is the eternal, the pure, the formless essence of the Supreme Unmanifest Being. The forms that are revealed to human beings are not Rita, and hence are false. Vidya Yajna reveals only partial or uni-dimensional Rita; as new knowledge is gleaned it has to be accommodated with the earlier partial knowledge. Hence, this form of reason lacks permanence. The Rita revealed to a Ritambhara Prajna is complete and holistic; it is embodied. But the parts that make up the whole are not permanent. The Rita of the universe is permanent and unchanging; but the relationship between various constitutive elements is not permanent. Human beings and other living beings are constitutive elements of the manifest universe. Only an all-seeing intellect can discern their destiny. All manifest sacrifices are made possible by the purity of the Rita Yajna. The unity and the non-duality of the manifest and the unmanifest are known only to the all-seeing intellect, Ritambhara Prajna. ‘The sacrifice offered to the eternal, immutable supreme truth, which is distinct from the truth of Rita, is called Brahma Yajna or Satya Yajna. The Rita deals with the order of the manifest universe, while this quest for truth is directed towards the self. The Supreme

Unmanifest Being is enveloped by a golden lid;⟨fn:375⟩ this lid has to be opened by the combined endeavours of Rita Yajna and Satya Yajna. The tripartite unity of the manifest, the unmanifest and the human consciousness has to be achieved through these two sacrifices. Great souls begin their journey with the manifest sacrifices and move to paths of meditation, reflection and knowledge. At the conclusion of this fiery ordeal and penance both Rita and truth illuminate them. Hence it is said that when a great soul passes through the fiery ordeal, both Rita and Truth illuminate his being. ‘On a tree branch two leaves sprout on opposite sides and flowers and fruits emerge in between the two protective leaves. Similarly, on the path of penance Rita and Truth are together but stand facing each other. What emerges from this is Dharma. With passage of time this Dharma becomes like an all-enveloping rain-laden cloud and showers its nurturing, life-giving munificence on the world. ‘Navinchandraji, Dharma is eternal; it is for all times and spaces. Only the evil-minded and those lacking in all virtues do not come under its sway. Ascetics will initiate their sacrifice with Matha Yajna, and if they are capable they will be able to offer all five essential sacrifices. Eventually they will experience the non-duality of the manifest and the unmanifest; they will be free from rebirth and experience supreme bliss. The seer who developed the understanding of the duties towards the guest and replaced Bhagwan Buddha’s Daya Dharma with Atithi Dharma had realised the necessity and interwoven nature of the sacrifices when he performed the Rita Yajna. The intertwined nature of Rita and Truth is a unique contribution of the Alakshya-Lakshya path. Spirituality is not contained and exhausted by Yajna Dharma. Truth is not exclusive to pragmatic, practical endeavours; Daya Dharma does not have an exclusive and privileged understanding of

Rita. The injunction of performing the sacrifices is upon all people and is valid for all times. ‘All your queries have now been answered, but let me elaborate further. There are many laws that the householders have developed, but they are contingent upon time and space. Manu has given the essence of eternal principle: “Learn that sacred law which is followed by men learned (in the Veda) and assented to in their hearts by the virtuous who are ever exempt from hatred and inordinate affection.”⟨fn:376⟩ This is not contingent upon either time or space, nor is it circumscribed by rituals. He says the Dharma that the learned and dispassionate ascetics preach and more importantly practice is most superior. Such virtuous men are to be found among the Mlecchas and the shudras, and the Dharma that they practice daily is supreme. This Dharma requires no sanction from textual or scriptural authority. If the law-giver is a virtuous man the only sanction that he requires is from his conscience; there is no authority that can supersede this sanction. ‘Manu has ordained practices for those who follow the four-fold Ashram Dharma. A person of virtue has to abide by these: “Let him put down his foot purified by his sight, let him drink water purified by (straining with) a cloth, let him utter speech purified by truth, let him keep his heart pure.”⟨fn:377⟩ The mind and heart of a virtuous person are pure; all thoughts and actions that emerge from them are purged of all impurities. Just as water, ash and fire cleanse a vessel, their mind purifies all thought and action. Their conscience testifies to the purity of only those actions which have emerged from their mind. Their conduct is Dharma; anything contrary, even if sanctified by scriptures, has to be subsidiary; because the only legitimate authority over a person of virtue is conscience itself. ‘Ascetics who live in the Vihar Math are also renunciates. All renunciates are required to perform the five elementary sacrifices. The inhabitants of Vihar Math perform their sacrifices as couples, while those who reside in the other two maths do so as individuals, but their choice of the math does not make them either lustful or desireless. Ascetics by nature are celibate. They are attracted to the Vihar Math only when the god of love so desires. The four-fold Ashram laws were ordained in ancient times; but as Manu said, with passage of time and epochs duties and laws came to be differentiated. For our epoch the four-fold ashram division is inappropriate. Therefore, we have developed a two-fold conception of Ashram—one for the householders and the other for the renunciates. We have replaced the brahmacharya and sanyas by this math. Vihar Math has replaced vanaprastha; all women ascetics have their own math. There are two elements that are common to them; one, detachment from ego and possessions and two, a virtuous life. ‘Manu has said of vanaprastha: When a householder sees his (skin) wrinkled, and his (hair) white, and the sons of his sons, then he may resort to the forest. Abandoning all food raised by cultivation and all his belongings, he may depart into the forest, whither committing his wife to his sons, or accompanied by her.⟨fn:378⟩ Making no effort (to procure) things that give pleasure, chaste, sleeping on bare ground, not caring for any shelter, dwelling at the roots of trees.⟨fn:379⟩ ‘He has said that the fourth stage can be lived only upon completion of the third stage. He has described the qualification thus: “When he has paid the three debts, let him apply his mind to (the attainment of) final liberation; he who seeks it without having paid (his debts) sinks downwards.”⟨fn:380⟩ ‘Jabala Shruti has shown the way to be adopted by those who wish to take the path of renunciation without living through the previous three stages: “After completing the period of brahmacharya one may become a householder. After being a householder he may become a vanaprastha. Having become a vanaprastha he may renounce the world.

Or, alternatively he may embrace renunciation from brahmacharya itself, or from the (stage of) householder, or from forest-life.”⟨fn:381⟩ ‘A householder cannot acquire the right of renunciation unless he is free from three kinds of debts. Manu has shown a path whereby a celibate can become a renunciate. Having performed Ishti, sacred to the Lord of creatures (Prajapati), where (he gives) all his property as the sacrificial fee, having reposited the sacred fires in himself, a Brahmana may depart from his household as an ascetic. Worlds, radiant in brilliancy, become (the portion) of him who recites (the texts regarding) Brahman and departs from his house (as an ascetic), after giving a promise of safety to all created beings.⟨fn:382⟩ ‘These verses describe the qualification required for vanaprastha and sanyas. A person of our times can adopt either of the paths. Such a person acquires the capacity to enter and join our math. A celibate is required to cultivate an ego-less state and also non-attachment. But we have developed a different understanding of some of the elements. A householder is required, for example, to be free from three kinds of debts before he acquires the capacity for renunciation. These three kinds of debts are: acquisition of knowledge, fathering a son and performance of sacrifice. We do not consider procreation of a male progeny as a debt. A couple joined by a deep sense of non-duality has only one desire, and that is to experience their unity. Householders are governed by norms of Atithi Dharma and are integral to Manushya Yajna. Hence, renunciation is not contingent upon procreation of male progeny. Acquisition of knowledge and performance of sacrifices are integral to the lives of our initiates. Thus, we have discarded the injunction regarding debts. ‘We have however defined the nature of debts differently. A householder, who is at heart a renunciate, has no other debt but the performance of the five sacrifices; this is his only duty. Matha Yajna, Deva Yajna and Brahma Yajna are best performed by an initiate. But

Manushya Yajna and Bhut Yajna can be performed both by ascetics and householders with different merit. A householder may not have sufficiently done his duties towards either his parents or his wife. Pitru Yajna is best performed as a householder. Similarly, the performance of duties towards one’s wife is also best accomplished as a householder. Moreover, if the duties towards the motherland and fellow beings require material objects and wealth then these duties should be performed as a householder. Duties towards an invited guest have to be fulfilled by the householder and till one discharges one’s duty one is not free from this obligation. Duties towards an uninvited guest cease the moment we are required to perform higher sacrifices. The obligation to perform Bhut Yajna is akin to one’s duties towards the motherland and fellow beings, and one is required to fulfill one’s obligations. Matha Yajna requires that the initiate is free from these three obligations because those who have not freed themselves of these three debts are not fit to lead the life of an ascetic as their subtle bodies are not sufficiently evolved. Moreover, inconclusive and partial offering of a sacrifice impedes the great sacrifice initiated by the Supreme Manifest Being. Therefore, Manu has decreed that one who is free from debt acquires the right of renunciation. A person who locks up his house and leaves has not paid his debts; all his belongings have to be distributed. All other ashrams depend upon the right performance of duties as a householder. Hence, Manu has said: “As all rivers, both great and small, find a resting place in the ocean, even so men of all orders find protection with householders.”⟨fn:383⟩ ‘Our scriptures have gone beyond this. We believe that if an ascetic is required to participate in some great cause which can be performed as a householder, he should for that period live among householders as one of them. The only injunction upon him is that he should remain celibate. The principal duty of an ascetic is to perform the five elementary sacrifices in a spirit of detachment. Among the householders a sacrifice cannot be offered without fire. But an ascetic contains within the self all forms of sacrificial fires. In this sacrifice, the self is not only the offering, but self is the one that makes the sacrifice as also the fire in which the sacrifice is offered. An ascetic is so evolved that he can go beyond all scriptures and texts. Disregarding not only all the Shastras but also this Lakshya Dharma, he should conduct himself purified by Rita, intellect and truth. Intent upon the performance of Atma Yajna, the Universal Being becomes his guest at such a sacrifice. ‘Now, we are required to understand with examples the types of the performers of sacrifices. First among the trinity is Brahma; he created the universe and continues to create it. The universe includes all beings; all beings created by him are his guests. Brahma, the creator, performs Putra Yajna, a sacrifice for the creation of progeny. A being so created by him is imbued from birth with the capacity to offer sacrifices. A foetus in the womb, an infant nourished by her mother’s breast milk, a child loved by its parents, a youth captivated by the god of love and the ascetic engaged in showing the right path to the ignorant are all examples of Brahma’s creation and the capacity of all beings to sustain, nourish and redeem that creation. Having created the universe, Brahma remains unattached. He hands over the creation to Vishnu and remains uninvolved. All other gods are worshipped but Brahma has not created the impulse in us that we should worship him. How are we to create temples to him? The universe is created by the unending Putra Yajna of Brahma, but this Father does not need us to offer Pitru Yajna to him. ‘Vishnu, the upholder, through his various incarnations offered sacrifices. During his first five incarnations Vishnu gathered all the resources required for the sacrifices. As Kurma (turtle), Vishnu made possible the churning of the seas, and the nectar from it nourished the subtle bodies of all gods; thus he nurtured the sacrificial animal. As Matsya (fish), Vishnu prepared the sacrificial altar; as Narasimha (lion-man), he saved Prahlad from his father and prevented the altar from being desecrated. As Varaha (boar), he protected the earth; and as Vamana (dwarf), he demonstrated how the earth filled with oblations could be measured.

‘Sri Ramchandraji learnt the sacrificial rituals from sages and offered the most subtle of Pitru Yajna. He took Sita with him to the forest and performed Priti Yajna. He upheld his father’s promise. At the conclusion of his Priti Yajna, for the satisfaction of his subjects he offered Sita as an oblation and sent her to the forest. As Krishna, he performed many great sacrifices. He restored to his father the kingdom and performed Pitru Yajna. He freed his motherland from the tyranny of demons. He ensured victory for the Pandavas and secured the people’s welfare; this was Lok Yajna. He caused Arjun to acquire knowledge of various kinds from various places and enabled Arjun to offer Vidya Yajna. He showed his universal form to Arjun and performed Rita Yajna and by his discourse of the Gita, Sri Krishna performed Satya Yajna. He became husband to many women. As Buddha, he spread the message of compassion and performed Daya Yajna. Whenever Vishnu took human form he was accompanied by Maha Lakshmi, thereby continuing their external union. When Vishnu’s task was complete, there was a sacrifice of destruction. Shiva, the destroyer, finally meditates upon the unmanifest truth that is Brahman. Maha Shakti participated in the great sacrifice as Vidhatri with Brahma, as Maha Lakshmi with Vishnu and as Chandi with Shiva. ‘This great sacrifice of the primordial being continues. Ascetics learn from it and perform appropriate sacrifices according to their ability and context. The universe which emerges from the toe nail of the Supreme Manifest Being has countless beings. Some are positioned at the source of this great river while others at the point where the river merges into the great ocean. Some are at the bottom, others float on the water, while some others are caught in the flow. The duties of each being are determined according to their location; this also determines the sacrifices required from each. Navinchandraji, I have given you the essence of the Lakshya Dharma and provided examples of each principle. Rest you can study from the original text. You have to determine what your duties are and what sacrifices are obligatory for you. The great sacrifice that we commence is our dharma and therein lies our penance. You have to decide on the strength of the purity of your heart as to what you should adopt. This Chiranjiv Shrunga will offer the finest of your physical and subtle body to sacrifice. May you receive all the merit due to a person who listens to the discourse of sacrifices. Navinchandraji, a life of sacrifice is a life of brahmacharya where our conduct leads us to truth, and it is also a life of rectitude. This is Rita, this is also the truth, this is the blessing of God. It is also the self, as also the Supreme Soul. This is the bridge to non-duality. “Now that serene being which, after having risen from out this earthly body, and having reached the highest light (self-knowledge), appears in its true form, that is the self,” thus he spoke (when asked by his pupils). This is the immortal, the fearless, this is Brahman. And of that Brahman the name is the True, Satyam.⟨fn:384⟩ “That self is a bank, a boundary, so that these worlds may not be confounded. Day and night do not pass that bank, nor old age, death and grief; neither good nor evil deeds. All evil-doers turn back from it, for the world of Brahman is free from all evil.”⟨fn:385⟩ “And that world of Brahman belongs to those only who find it by abstinence, for then there is freedom from all worlds.”⟨fn:386⟩ “What people call sacrifice (yagna), is really abstinence (brahmacharya). For he who knows obtains that (world of Brahman, which others obtain by sacrifice), by means of abstinence. What people call sacrifice (Ishta), that is really abstinence, for by abstinence he obtains from the Sat (the true), the safety (trana) of the self. What people call the vow of silence (mauna), that is really abstinence, for he who by abstinence has found out the Self, meditates (manute).”⟨fn:387⟩ ‘This sacrifice, this truth, this Brahman, this discourse on sacrificial rites, this exposition on truth is a prerogative of only the most accomplished and evolved ascetics. May all the noble participants in this discourse be blessed. Om Shanti!’

Vishnudasji raised his hand in benediction and became silent. The temple was filled with the sound of conch shell. All got up. Viharpuri and Chandravali led the way. They were followed by a group of women ascetics accompanying Kumud. Vishnudas followed them. Sarasvatichandra and other monks followed Vishnudas. Viharpuri and Chandravali began to sing softly. Women ascetics joined their voices to theirs. Vishnudas and others repeated the words silently. As they reached the threshold of the temple, the song ceased. The assembly dispersed with chants hailing Vishnudas. The place where Vishnudas had given his discourse was left with the silence of trees, creepers, rocks, springs, birds and the dense presence of his words.
chapters.summary: Vishnudas instructs Sarasvatichandra to undertake a solitary spiritual retreat on Chiranjiv Shrunga, while Kumud's unexpected arrival briefly shifts the profound philosophical discourse.

chapters.title: Moonrise on Chiranjiv Shrunga
paragraphs: Moonrise on Chiranjiv Shrunga Chiranjiv Shrunga was the highest peak of Sundargiri. This peak was situated behind Yadu Shrunga. The path to Chiranjiv Shrunga passed through rocky terrain, valleys and thick forest. A natural rock formation fortified its peak. There were several large caves in the mountain side; some of these were natural while others were carved by human hands. These caves numbered around seventy-five. A perennial spring provided pure and sweet water. The spring was surrounded by high rocks which allowed sunlight to fall on the water, but the place remained cool even at noon. The spring flowed through ten or fifteen caves; it encircled some, while many others opened towards the water body. The largest of the caves was two-storeyed. It had a terrace of black stone which looked out on all four directions. The lower floor was supported by thick stone pillars. Images from the Buddhist period were carved on these pillars. This floor was lower than the fortification around Chiranjiv Shrunga. The floor below it had a wall on one side and pillars on the free side. An image of five men armed with bows and arrows but in meditative pose was carved on the wall. Some believed it to be an image of the Pandavas, while others believed they were some great souls from either the Ashokan Empire or a later period. The lowest floor had walls on three sides while the fourth side opened out to the spring. There were steps and a platform made for easy passage from the cave to the spring. Lotuses bloomed in the spring. A stone bridge connected the top floor to another cave. The spring flowed below the bridge. This cave was called Saumanasya Gufa.

Sarasvatichandra was brought to the cave as instructed by Vishnudas. It was dusk when he reached the cave. Sarasvatichandra was accompanied by Radhedas, Jnanbharati and three other monks. They were Sundardas, Surdas and Mayapuri; all three had acquired second order of spiritual attainment. They carried pots for water and fruits and tubers. They entered the cave through the steps and sat on the platform. Jnanbharati spoke, ‘Navinchandraji Maharaj, this is Saumanasya Gufa. This, the lowest floor of the cave is open to all itinerant monks. The top floor is reserved only for these who have the right to communicate with the world of the immortals. If a person who does not have this right were to spend a night on that floor, he would be besieged by evil spirits. He is most likely to go mad, and some even die of fright. Ordinary people find this place scary even during the day and usually avoid it, unless in a group. But it is most appropriate for ascetics engaged in meditation. It gives rise to many supernatural experiences. You are to spend five nights on the uppermost floor in contemplation. We will stay here on the lower floor and are to serve you day and night. We will come up only when asked and carry out your command.’ One of the monks fetched water from the spring and gave it to the others. After sometime they climbed up through a stone staircase that reached the uppermost floor. A stone platform was made on all sides of this floor, and the staircase extended up to the terrace. Some grass had grown on the terrace exposed to rain water. The monks cleared and cleaned the terrace. They brought up a pot of water, and before moonrise they went down with Sarasvatichandra’s consent. While going down, Radhedas said, ‘Maharaj, all sounds in this place are magnified by echoes. But no sound from the upper floor reaches the floors below, so if you need us just look out on to the spring and call out to us softly; we will be able to hear you.’ They went down. Finally Sarasvatichandra was alone. He had carried the bunch of letters with him. He sat on a grass-covered rock on the terrace and said aloud, ‘Now,

I am the monarch of all I survey, My right there is none to dispute.⟨fn:388⟩ ‘What a grand, solitary place! Guruji has one reason to send me here, while Chandravali has another. But my heart is incapable of thinking of either of them. Who all shall I think of? Chandrakant? Ganga? Sansarilal? Uddhatlal? Tarang Shankar? Vir Rao? Of home? Father? Dhurtalal? Gumanba? Or of Kumud who drowns all other thoughts? ‘Kumud Sundari has drowned! How can she be here? Madhuri Maiya resembles her in every way: her song, the subject of her song; her voice is so similar to Kumud’s! But the paths suggested by Chandravali are contrary to Kumud Sundari. It is impossible that she would accept this path. ‘My father has issued advertisements in newspapers seeking information about me! Pramaddhan and Saubhagya Devi are both dead! A teacher in Surgram gave me the newspapers and made me aware of all the problems facing the country. Bombay—I am grateful to you! ‘I want to go away! Go away! Go far, far away!’ The image of the temple in Surgram flashed before his mind’s eye. ‘One day, the bird shall fly away. ‘I, too, am like a bird that flies from one branch to another. I came to Chiranjiv Shrunga like a migratory bird. Dear God! Now where am I to go from here?’ He remembered a couplet he had heard in Surgram which sang of the futility of all happiness in absence of the visage of the beloved, and contemplated in silence. Kumud, is all else futile? Or have I, too, sent you a glass of poison? O’ generous Kumud Sundari! What did you do with the poison that I sent you? Like Mira, you drank it and turned it into nectar! There is no difference between Mirabai’s pain and your pain. I am not surprised that your generous spirit has stirred the heart of an ascetic like Chandravali.

Bindumati’s song echoed in his ears. I met Mohan in Vrindavan, Unknown to beloved Radha, Girdhari comes to my street! Sarasvatichandra was startled and thought aloud, ‘Am I destined to see Kumud Sundari while she tries to conceal her identity? What will she say to me? What advice can I now give her? How will I seek her forgiveness? Both of us are free from the restrictions under which we lived in Buddhidhan’s house. This freedom is dangerous. Are we not capable of a union as attained by Viharpuri and Chandravali? Pramad is no more. We took different paths, and yet were brought together. Societal norms have different injunctions. I have renounced my riches, but I have not renounced societal norms. I am not free from all worldly attachments. Which path will allow me to fulfill my duties? Kumud, what are your thoughts? If you desire physical togetherness, Pramaddhan’s death has made that possible. If the penance of my sins lies in fulfilling your desires, is it not my duty to do so, even against social norms? Would it be right for me to coerce you to give up any such desire that you might have? Or are all these thoughts an expression of my own suppressed desires? ‘Is not my wish father to these thoughts? Or, rather, am I not now succumbing to the rush of my own latent will-power itself? Heaven knows whither I am drifting!’⟨fn:389⟩ The moon rose in the sky. It was the eleventh day of the moon’s passage. A three quarter moon rose above the horizon, and its rays filled the terrace. The eastern side of the foothills and the path to Ratnanagari were clearly discernable in the moonlight. The moonlight spread across the world like a thin veil that neither conceals nor covers a woman’s body. Sarasvatichandra went to the western side of the terrace. He looked at the spring below and the lone window on the opposite cave, connected to his by the bridge. This had a calming effect on him. He looked out at the distant sea. His gaze moved from the cave to the sea and back. He saw a light in the cave facing his terrace.

The light fell on the bridge as well. The bridge made of uncarved rocks was shaped like a cradle. Sarasvatichandra saw for a fleeting moment a female form in the window. An ochre bed sheet was spread for him towards the northern side of the terrace. His bundle was also placed there. Some fruits and water had been placed near his bed. Sarasvatichandra sat down and wondered about what he had seen. He forced his eyes away from the bridge, but his ears were attentive to the slightest sound coming from the other cave. At first all that he heard were the sounds of the sea and the rustle of the forest at night. His eyes focussed on the moon as he strained his ears to hear every sound. He heard human voices from the other side of the bridge. Curiously he got up and approached the bridge. All other sounds were blocked out as he focused on these voices. A lamp lit the window, but nothing else could be seen. Sarasvatichandra stood still as a statue, intent upon any movement in the window facing him.
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra, alone in a mountain cave, contemplates Kumud and his future, then glimpses a mysterious female and hears voices from a nearby cave.

chapters.title: On the Other Side of the Bridge
paragraphs: On the Other Side of the Bridge Kumud was in the cave opposite the Saumanasya Gufa. Ten women ascetics, including Bhakti and Vamini had accompanied her. They showed her the various caves and finally brought her to the cave opposite the one where Sarasvatichandra was. Many birds, including cuckoos, nested in the trees around the cave. It was still spring time, and the group decided to spend the night at this beautiful spot. This cave was called the Vasant Gufa; it was built like the Saumanasya Gufa, but on a low-lying area. For this reason it seemed somewhat lower than the other structures. The women had carried with them night clothes and fruits, which they kept on the lower floor and came up. They sat on the platform and admired the surrounding beauty. Kumud was with them. All conversation stopped as they were captivated by the natural beauty of the place. They remained silent till sunset. One of them lit a lamp and said, ‘Madhuri Maiya, this is the place where Guruji has asked Navinchandraji to spend five nights. He will stay in that cave opposite us. He will be there tonight if he has not already arrived. You will spend the night on this floor, while the rest of us will be on the floor below. We have made a soft bed suitable for you and kept fruits and water. There is a lamp here. We will leave you to your fate and go down.’ Kumud was startled. ‘What are you saying! You have cheated me. How am I to spend the night in this dreadful place? I will come down with you.’ ‘Maiya, ascetics have nothing to fear in this place. If you experience any fear, your heart will point out the saviour,’ said Pritimanini.

‘Madhuri, our hearts become free from fear in such places. We have not deceived you,’ said Bhakti Maiya. Kumud: ‘Why did you bring me here without fair warning?’ Bhakti: ‘You know well that Chandravali Maiya has discerned what ails your heart as also its remedy. Mohini Maiya has suggested that you should approach the beloved of your heart. Chandravali Maiya became your messenger and Viharpuri arranged for Navinchandra to spend some days here. You have heard Guruji. How can you then say that we have deceived you?’ Kumud: ‘Chandravali Maiya had clearly said that nothing will be done without my consent.’ Bhakti: ‘That is exactly what we have been trying to say to you.’ Kumud: ‘Why did you bring me here without my consent?’ Bhakti: ‘Madhuri Maiya, women of such learning as Chandravali and Mohini understand your heart’s desire better than you do—they do not need your consent in words, but can discern the unspoken consent of your heart.’ Vamini: ‘Madhuri, does your heart testify to the accusations that you place on these great women? You are not unaware that Chandravali Maiya and Viharpuriji have together acted as your messenger. Bhakti Maiya recounted to you the commands given by the Master. You came on your own volition to Yadu Shrunga and from there to Chiranjiv Shrunga. What more do you need by way of a consent?’ Deep in thought, Kumud Sundari said nothing and looked down. Pritimanini caressing her, said, ‘Daughter Madhuri, do not be afraid. If you so desire, we shall leave in the morning. This wicked world has created a web of desires in your heart and has not allowed you to exchange even one word with this great soul. It has not allowed you to open your heart even for a moment. Spend a few moments with him, say what you have to and listen to what he has to say to you. We are not asking you to do anything more. You might receive the fruits of your subtle love. And in the morning we will take you back to Chandravali Maiya.’

Kumud looked down speechlessly. A song she had composed while still at Buddhidhan’s house came back to her. The heart reincarnates bonds of love From a life past; The vision falters upon a glimpse Of an idol once beloved; The beloved, though proximate, Says nothing; Where do I lay bare my heart Torn asunder?⟨fn:390⟩ Buddhi Maiya, who was seated behind everyone, said, ‘Madhuri Maiya, you have also heard the discourse on the five sacrifices. Are you not tempted to be a partner of that great soul in his sacrifices? Do you not wish to aid his offerings? Do you not wish to become, along with him, the subtle oblation in these great sacrifices?’ Kumud: ‘All this is futile so long as the only person capable of granting these rights has not done so. I do not wish to go and seek these rights from him.’ Pritimanini: ‘That is true, and hence we shall leave you alone. If you want us to act as a messenger, we shall carry your message and bring you back his response. If you do not want us to do so, all that you say or sing can be heard by Navinchandraji in his cave. He will awaken to your presence. He will come to you either by the force of love or compassion, by the will of the ascetics or as ordained by the stars. If the Manifest God so desires, he will come to you and bring peace and tranquility to your heart. If he does not come, you are not required to go to him. At dawn we will all do what you ask of us. Until then please follow the directions of your heart.’ The women ascetics left Kumud and went down. Kumud made an attempt to get up, but her body, as if fixed to the ground, disobeyed her. She was enveloped by moonlight. Finally she got up, but her feet turned not towards the staircase but towards the window. She sat down on the platform facing the bridge. She did not know what her heart truly desired. She failed to comprehend what she wanted. Her body gave no indication whether she was deep in contemplation or in the grip of desire. She had composed a poem, part of which was composed by Tarang Shankar. He had translated the English poet Goldsmith’s poem called the ‘Hermit.’ Sarasvatichandra had given her a copy of it in Ratnanagari. Kumud had retained some stanzas of it and added her own composition to it. She wanted Sarasvatichandra to hear her composition. But her heart was in turmoil and she decided not to sing. I have gone through a fiery ordeal once, she thought. There is no need for me to enter that fire once again. He is not likely to return to Bombay. He has accepted renunciation. Is he likely to give that up? No. He will be happy here. He is happy without me. I will not be happy without him. But I will find solace at the feet of the Mother Goddess. Kumud got up and moved about restlessly. She looked around. Even the moon startled her. She saw a shadow on the other side of the bridge and, turning away from the window, she sat down on a rock. She kept a finger on her lips and murmured, ‘This opportunity will not return. God has thrust me in his presence. I will submit to His will and take advantage of this opportunity. If my mind is unsullied, what have either of us to fear? It is true that only Sarasvatichandra can untangle the confusion that pervades my heart. In this life I am not going to be happy; he will show me the path of rectitude and tranquility. But he will think of me as a lowly person. Who knows what he thinks of me? God knows. Mother, You gave me life; now show me how to live it!’ She sat for a while breathing deeply, then gathered her courage and began to sing.
chapters.summary: Kumud, placed in a cave opposite Sarasvatichandra's, wrestles with her feelings as ascetics subtly push her to sing and embrace a profound, fated encounter.

chapters.title: Songs of Desire
paragraphs: Songs of Desire More close and close his footsteps wind, The Magic Music in his heart Beats quick and quicker till he find The quiet chamber far apart.⟨fn:391⟩ Oh Virtuous one, these lips cannot utter love The speechless is filled with dreams, and sorrows of that knowledge. Fear nothing, gentle maid; Let not the palpitating breast distress Your slender waist. In me, behold your slave! By your avowed affection, elevated To highest ecstasy.⟨fn:392⟩ Dear reader, Kumud’s song travelled from Vasant Gufa to Saumanasya Gufa. It travelled from the depths of Kumud’s heart to Sarasvatichandra’s heart and found an echo. It is not likely that Sarasvatichandra would not recognise Kumud’s voice. That voice, when she was afar, reverberated in his ears and filled him with its melody, its flute-like sweetness and sonority. And when that voice could be heard from Kumud’s own lips, how the beloved heart palpitated can only be imagined. We cannot even understand it in all its fullness, how is one to describe it? The song of that heart, the delicate sound of those lips and the solitude of the cave at the time of moonrise were all in harmony with the song.

O’ yogi! Wait a while, Guide me to the right path, In this dark forest night I roam alone with no memory of home The ‘I’ in the song indicated that the singer was male. Sarasvatichandra was bewildered and wondered, could it be a man who sings? The song progressed. My legs refuse to move, My tired eyes cloud over, Today the forest path is unending, With each step it unravels further ‘My Lord!⟨fn:393⟩ This is Tarang Shankar’s poem which I had given to Kumud. Who else but Kumud could be singing it? Does she not know that I am here?’ There I spy a distant lamp, I am drawn to its light— A sage must reside therein; He will bring an end to my sorrows. O’ yogi, be merciful! Guide me to that path! ‘Surely, this song is not addressed to me! The next lines will provide the answer to that plea.’ The yogi said: Son, beware! Be not tempted by that light, Know it to be a ghostly fire That lures only to destroy. The famished and the parched find succour In this cave of mine, are fed sparse food; Son, come! Reside here, harbour no doubts. Fruits and grain, Soft straw to sleep on, Pure waters of a clear spring,

Joy, peace and words of solace Abound here inexhaustible. God comes face to face here. Son, to such an abode you have come, Know that your worries will end. ‘How I wish I could give you the same solace,’ said Sarasvatichandra. The song continued. The sorrows are false, Frail is the human mind, A morsel fills the belly, A yard is enough to sleep. Union is but momentary, Yet the mind is not content. God has created joy, Yet the mind finds its own sorrow. Like morning dew, The yogi spoke words of succour. They walked together in silence And entered the yogi’s cave. The dark night moved As the world lay in slumber. The yogi cooked on slow fire, Its embers aglow, Spreading the light Of burning wood. Its warmth spreads; Crickets chirp, mice play, The melodious wind blows And the night passes by. The wind whistled through windows on both sides of the bridge, piercing through two hearts. The night grew dense. The yogi is serene, His quiet words blossom, His soft speech brings laughter And the weary traveller finds repose. He speaks of ought and naught,

His wise words soothe, He feeds and eats food sweet, His presence is a balm to the traveller. ‘Kumud, oh Kumud! Having heard the Master’s discourse on sacrifice, you narrate through this song the duties of a host. But to whom, if not me! Kumud, you are the weary traveller filled with sorrow. The care of the ascetic community has not given you any solace. This is a duty that I must perform.’ But before Sarasvatichandra could further articulate his duties, the song continued. The traveller eats not, He listens not, Deep in his melancholy, He weeps streams of tears. ‘Oh Kumud, is this your condition?’ he asked. And the song responded. Moved by the traveller’s plight, The yogi came to share his sorrows, Leaving his food untouched and Asked him again and again: Son, what pains you so? What wounds of heart remain unhealed? You forsook the riches of home; Did you walk away or were driven out? Did a friend turn traitor? Did you meet a heartless woman? Son, know this truth: Attachment to the world is an illusion; Wealth and woman’s love are transient; They desert one after a game or two. Happiness plays its own tricks And darkness descends unbeckoned. Happiness is a mirage— The closer it seems, the falser it is. Friendships come to a naught; Love is self-seeking— Only the naïve believe in it

And weep tears aplenty. Fame and fortune slip away And friends turn their backs. Those who chase shadows Stumble and fall. A woman’s love is greater falsehood; It snares and entices Only to shun and shoo; She makes the man dance To her haughty moves; She mocks the pain of man And her love is not true. The warmth of love that birds know That love is difficult to find. Fire takes the place of love And man turns to cinders. She is infatuation and magic personified; She allows the man no sleep. Son! Why bear such barbs? Let that love go burn on a pyre. The last lines were sung lustily. The yogi grew in strength, The traveller grew ashamed, Eyes downcast, he wept, His face turned deep red. A cloud floated by Scattering bright colours, Painting the body in strange hues; The yogi is amazed to behold The young traveller anew! Sarasvatichandra moved towards the bridge as his eyes searched for the unseen beauty who sang. The eyes flutter and sparkle, The lips open like buds, A woman manifests; Stunned, the yogi runs asunder.

Sarasvatichandra concealed himself and mused aloud as he looked intently towards the other side, ‘Kumud Sundari, your heart is like the heart of this good woman who sees herself as the source of all folly and is filled with compassion for the loved one. And just as she revealed herself, I see you. But I have never shown disdain for a woman’s love. And if you believe that I forsake you out of contempt, my sense of duty would urge me to free myself of this charge and send me to you.’ He could now see Kumud staring at the ceiling of her cave, one hand over her heart, wiping her tears with the other and singing in roused tones. The young woman pleaded with folded hands, Forgive me, Yogiraj! Pure and desire-free, Of restrained speech art thou Who reside in this hermitage. Sullied and sinner, I am that woman Who has no right to be with you. ‘No, no, Kumud! I know that you are pure. The world may speak ill of you or consider your virtues to be lower than Saubhagya Devi’s. But you have come through unsullied from many a trial and ordeal by fire. I know you to be a woman of pure virtue. I am that sinner who brought this condition upon you and who does not have the courage to free you from it. I stand here like a coward.’ Forgive me, Yogiraj, As I narrate my sins, Hear them with empathy And forgive this wretched one. Your darshan rids me of sorrow, Your wisdom quenches all hunger. ‘This is not Tarang Shankar’s composition! Kumud, you are now singing the pain of your own heart, and mine flickers like the wick of a lamp in a storm. Kumud, you make my heart tremble—my penance has commenced.’

If so fallen as to be unfit for your grace, Oh Lord, forgive this wretched one. I was deceived and fooled, Entrapped by his wise words, They did not awaken me, I was ensnared by him. I met such a yogi Who preached false love. Overwhelmed by his sense of wrongdoing, Sarasvatichandra wept at these words. True love has awakened in me, I have seen also the love of men. Forsaking the false, I cling to the true, But the man donned ochre and turned his back on me. His tears flowed uncontrollably. Sarasvatichandra cursed himself and bit his lips till they bled. The woman’s love must be false, Or why would he leave her to tears? The woman is meek and naïve, Deceived equally by the learned, the yogi and the debauched. The man plays with her, Traps her in the snare of love, Only to shun and discard. ‘This is a sharp retort!’⟨fn:394⟩ Sarasvatichandra said with a hand over his heart. Inebriated with bhang, the foolish one Is made to dance by the wise to his delight ‘I did give you the bhang of love, Kumud, but I do not take delight in your plight.’ Mocking her plight, Deceiving her with dreams,

His heart may be devoid of love But her tender heart is aglow. She knew not love, She knew not desire. He whispered to her, Filled her with dreams, with desire And with love, love, love That like a river in spate flowed. Desire turned to fire, And burned her to ashes. ‘Old dreams float around me even as new ones assault my conscience. Oh desire! You do not give up any opportunity to assail me!’ Kumud’s face seemed aglow with a strange melancholy as also beauty, and the onlooker’s heart trembled. But the song had not ended. Betrayed by love, she walked Over burning coals, Sought the forest to soothe her burns But dejection is her fate. ‘Oh vile me! I still control the reins of Kumud’s hope and her hopelessness, and yet I aspire to an ascetic life!’ She left home for the forest, Her misfortunes followed. Only proximity to a sage like you Would assuage this mind in turmoil. The word ‘proximity’ gave birth to new aspirations. Pure and desire-free, Of restrained speech art thou. ‘Kumud, oh Kumud, I desire the state that you describe. But is this a sign of hope or despair? Your heart is like a deep cave, and I must reach its depths.’ Futile it was to seek his nearness. I am numb with sorrow and filled with desire. God filled a well with nectar

To quench my thirst; I sit at its side, bereft of virtue— God did not make me a fish of that water. I weep and crave the nectar, I die of thirst with a well in sight. Die, I say, yet I live on. I crave death and yet I live, Spurned by all, And yet I roam after him, Without hope and yet not without desire, Without life and yet alive. ‘T’is the severest struggle of the heart,’⟨fn:395⟩ he said. He saw Kumud beating her head against a wall, her face lined with anguish. He wanted to rush to her, but her song continued. Ill-starred and sinful am I, Unmatched are my sins. I and the Yogiraj? He Who is filled with nectar! I knew of the renunciation of Buddha; You are renunciation incarnate. He was delighted at this comparison. Chandra’s gaze savours Kumud From afar, and she blossoms. ‘Kumud! My Kumud! You have revealed your identity. Madhuri and sweet Kumud are the same. I cannot bear to have her pining and writhing in torment any longer. While she was in Pramaddhan’s house, it was righteous conduct that I stood witness to it, but to do so now will be a violation of duty.’ He walked towards the Vasant Gufa. If Kumud were not engrossed in her song she would have seen him from her window, but she was gazing intently at the moon. She brought her palms together in prayer and addressed the moon, Chandra.

Chandra’s gaze savours Kumud From afar, and she blossoms. Forsaking the plea of passion, I worship you, O’ Lord, through sight. My fate would turn And I would receive the nectar of peace and wisdom. I am ashamed and hesitant; Desire subsides and springs forth anew; You are the only one who can Set me free. Sarasvatichandra’s heart was no longer his. He crossed the threshold. Kumud’s gaze was fixed on her moon. He could not gauge if she was conscious or delirious. If she were conscious, would she not have become aware of her Chandra? Yogiraj, I have come not To break your penance. I shall be that wall that protects The hermitage from all beings and animals; Cultivate the mind and soul, and Perform your penance without hindrance. Kumud turned towards Sarasvatichandra, but it was as if her eyes did not see him, and he stood there petrified as she continued her song. From without, I shall receive the nectar Of your wisdom and be rid of my sorrows. It was as if she had become a glass doll that moved with the winding of a key. Kumud moved closer to Sarasvatichandra, folded her palms in pranam and softly said, Yogiraj, ocean of compassion, This is all I seek. ‘Kumud Sundari!’ he said and caught her hand, but the hand appeared lifeless and cold, mere bones. Only her open but vacant, unseeing eyes and her song suggested some life.

Remembering our former life And the secrets and promises we shared, This destitute woman Seeks the embers of love. Her hand, turning stiff as a stone bridge between two bodies, came to rest upon his shoulder. Kumud’s eyes were filled with pain and humility as she looked into his eyes, and yet she appeared like a statue. Her delicate frame remained erect and she sang. Being enmeshed in this world is not for me, A mind filled with impure desires is not for me, The aesthete filled me with nectar— The nectar of renunciation. Her hand pressed hard on his shoulder. The master of this body abandoned it, But Yamaraj did not accept this body. ‘Kumud Sundari!’ he said. In response her song continued. I drowned this body and life with it, Sought refuge in water and in hell; Water refused my body, And the Lord of Hell refused my life. That body now barely alive Lies at the feet of my Lord. Her hand removed itself from his shoulder and joined with the other hand in obeisance and her body bent towards his feet. The body does not desire a union of hearts; Life has to be lived. Lord, keep me alive or grant me death, Grant me joy or deny it, Forgive me or singe with fury, Hold this hand or kick it away, Destiny has so willed it, I have found life in my Lord. ‘Kumud Sundari! Kumud! You—in this state!’

She stopped singing and laughed out aloud. ‘Oh, after so long, I am Kumud once again! And not Kumud Sundari. I have become ‘‘Beloved Kumud!’’ Listen, the heart will speak what lies within.’ ‘Oh! She is still in a state of unconscious as she speaks,’ he said ever so softly. She responded as if she had heard his words, ‘My Chandra has spoken! Chandra, you have spoken to me after so long. Listen.’ Virtue I have not cultivated, Fidelity I have not found, Discernment of pure-impure I know not, My intellect is numb. To impart wisdom and purity, To give succour to the abandoned, In a life past, an aesthete came home. Today, I hold the same hand, Such is the play of fate. Look, the stars, the moon and the chakor! ‘The same hand I hold today. The same man stands before me. Where will he go from here?’ Kumud spoke deliriously. She looked up at the stars and addressed them, ‘Look here stars and moon, my Chandra is now with me! Sarasvatichandra became Navinchandra, but Chandra I have found. He wears ochre robes. Ascetic or not, I will not let go of him.’ She caught the sleeve of his long ochre robe and sang. I have found my yogi, But my hands are sullied And my body cursed. O’ Master, pure and wise Hold not these sullied hands. She let go off his robes, looked at her hands and wept. She stood at a distance from him and sang. The Lord shall protect thy light, And purify this sullied body of mine. You captured this heart, Heal it with your wisdom.

Passions of the body are not pure; Lust is devilish, not godly; It is darkness, not light. The love of a godly heart is different; God manifests as love. What is desire for bodiless love?
