Let love flourish, but not of the body. A union of minds is the root of love sublime. A renunciate and cohort of the virtuous, His love is bereft of the body. The love of man and God Is one of devotion and prayer— I seek such bodiless love. But how do I transcend the body? Heartbroken once, Kumud aspires to divine love. O’ Lord, purge me of sin, purify me, Give me light that soothes, Grant me peace and solitude. Yogi! O’ enlightened one With the depth of oceans, This river has come to your shores Over icy mountains and scorching sands; It has risen in spate; And with that deluge, I await the receding waters, I await a sign from my Lord. Her voice trailed off. As if pulled shut from within her eyes closed, her speech ceased, all activity stopped and her petrified body abruptly folded over as she fell. The floor was made of hard stone, and Kumud would have certainly sustained injury if Sarasvatichandra had not rushed towards her and caught her in his arms. He could not wipe away her tears. He could not decide what he should do. He gazed upon her lifeless face and said, ‘Kumud! Kumud Sundari! Wake up! I am Sarasvatichandra!’ There was no response to his urgent plea. He realised that she was in deep coma. He sat down crossed-legged and brought her body to rest in his lap. Her face, though comatose, was alluring in the moonlight and he gazed upon her unrestrained. The circumstances of the touch were distasteful and yet inevitable. Though inert, the delicate touch of the woman’s body excited him and for a moment his intellect, as if poisoned by a scorpion’s bite, became inebriated with desire. Desire rushed through his veins at this proximity, both of sight and touch. Just then a gust of wind brought him to his senses and he became aware of Kumud’s sorry state, of his own error, of the incident in Buddhidhan’s house. Just as a man belabouring under a heavy burden suddenly collapses, his rising desires were quelled by the thoughts that assailed him. This was a novel experience for Sarasvatichandra that at a moment of intense desire, a contrary thought could suppress that desire. Emboldened by this discovery and seeing it to be a remedy against passion, he dwelled on his thoughts. Her condition is akin to what the doctors describe as ‘hysteria’⟨fn:396⟩ and she needs to be treated accordingly. But how am I to obtain the remedy for it here? It would be proper to wait for her to regain consciousness. The moonbeams and refreshing breeze would help revive her and I should sit in a way that she benefits from them. I have no experience in such matters, but Uddhatlal does. He claims that in England hysteria is found among women before marriage which is cured by marriage, and that in this country hysteria occurs after marriage and lasts till the death of the mother-in-law or the setting up of the nuclear household. He has arrived at a ‘generalisation’⟨fn:397⟩ that in England the desires of women are satiated by marriage and amongst us desires are fulfilled when women are freed from the artificial bonds that bind them. Kumud Sundari, you did not experience any lack on either of these scores, or did you? In one matter fate has freed you, and it is up to me to satiate you in the other. I heard the song of your heart—the desire for subtle love was paramount in that song, and its fulfillment is no longer difficult. But can one understand the innermost cravings of a woman’s heart from a song? Who can understand the arousal and quelling of bodily desires better than these ascetics, but it has become difficult even for them to ascertain if Kumud’s heart harbours any such cravings. Will her cravings and passions be satiated just because she can look at me? Does Kumud know her passions? A woman’s body knows her passions and hidden desires better than her mind does. What am I to do? Is this pure, virtuous and righteous young woman not tormented and ashamed at the arousal of bodily desires? Be that as it may, but Sarasvatichandra, it is you who have caused the deep wound in her heart—of that there is no doubt. But are you the only one responsible? It is certainly not Pramad, and there has never been anyone else. Oh God! What am I to do? What am I to do? If I keep sitting with this pained body in my lap, I am assailed by desires and all other thoughts appear powerless. And the emergence of passions at such a moment is the pinnacle of my fallen state. Kumud, you sang your song. Now I shall sing mine and imbue it with my ideals. Kumud did not hear her own song, has no knowledge of it and did not know if anyone else heard it. What was composed in a moment of stable mind burst forth in my presence. Quite contrary to that, my composition will be an outcome of my disturbed state. I shall sing my song and listen to it, but comatose Kumud will not; it is best if she does not. If my song aids the moonbeams and the gentle breeze in reviving her, it will be my good fortune. But it is in my interest that she should neither hear nor understand it. For a while Sarasvatichandra remained motionless; he said nothing, did nothing but kept gazing at the moon and at Kumud’s face as if trying to compare the two. Her face seemed to be scolding him. A song escaped his heart. Abandoned parents And a beloved, virtuous wife; Left only to return, o’ beloved: What was in the heart remained unsaid. ‘And the customs of the world did not permit me to say anything in Buddhidhan’s house,’ he said aloud. No one but his sighs heard him.

I could not see, could not speak, Could not open this heart; I gave, and you drank, poison; Futile is this sorrow. The wisdom that comes to you now, oh Sarasvatichandra, if only it had come then, such folly would not have been committed, he thought, gazing upon Kumud’s face as a supplicant. O’ generous beloved, O’ delicate beauty, your Heart broke and mine Remained cruel, And turned to stone. Societal customs caused this body to become impure, and for that only I am responsible. Your body, my heart; It was I who committed this cruelty. You fulfilled your obligations in each situation and it is your good fortune, and my misfortune, that you are now in this state. Your intense anguish made you unconscious and free of desire—both of the world and of bodily cravings. My condition is quite contrary to yours. I found you, and found you thus— When you have burnt all desire. Desire. Passions. Just as Shiva allows serpents to encircle his body, gives them a place around his neck and places both the Ganga and the moon over his head, Kumud Sundari gave her body filled with painful cravings to her husband and gave me the nectar-filled heart. Kumud, you knew well the delicate balance between the duties of a householder and the aspirations of ascetics. You are a sati; you are the wise one; generosity and purity are personified in you. Beloved Kumud, you gave birth to purity and nurtured it. You have attained the state of a sati with great penance by immersing yourself in flames. If you are not a sati, if even your wifely virtue and fidelity can be questioned, then which other human being is capable of the power that you possess? The cruel world is critical of you; we left it behind for this abode of ascetics, and even here similar questions are being asked. O’ generous beloved, O’ wise one, you are pure and virtuous. The heart once given remained, The body was given as an offering. Kumud, listen to my words in your coma. The path on which your heart has taken you is a pure path and is considered righteous by the ascetics. You have not climbed the ladder of impurity. How did the warp and weft of our hearts come to be tied together? Was it what your parents willed or was it something that the gods wished? Who had the power to tear apart two hearts that have experienced such unity and oneness? Just as one who has the vision of the universal form of the Supreme Being does not ever feel distanced from the Creator, hearts once united by sacrificial love cannot be separated. This light of oneness has been kindled in our hearts and is permanent. No shastra says that this light shall be extinguished. It has not been extinguished in your heart. That became your duty and path to attainment. The opprobrium of the world could not harm it. Your father gave you to Pramad, who became your husband and guest. Modern Indian women embark upon a sacrifice for the sake of the world of their parents. Marriages of today are Pitru Yajna. Ram kept the pledge given by Dasharath; similarly women today keep their father’s word. Kumud Sundari, you placed yourself in the midst of two fires, one of Pitru Yajna and the other of our unity and oneness. You offered your heart to one and your body to the other. You accomplished this hitherto unseen sacrifice. Kumud Sundari, do not despise yourself and belittle your sacrifice. You have earned the merit of the ancient, unchanging unity of hearts and the sacrifice offered by the women of today. Kumud Sundari, awaken and see! You are married to the duty of the heart And yet you offered a sacrifice to the husband;

You did not forget the unforgettable; All censure of marriage drowned with you. You are not without support and companionship. I am with you in this sacrifice of love; it has remained alive within me as well. Pramaddhan has abandoned you and you are no longer required to play host to him. For you there is only one sacrifice that now remains to be performed, and that is of our union. This, too, shall not be difficult. I had forsaken your body and believed that I would be able to discard your heart as well, and I was wrong. To fulfill our obligations, our old union will assume new form. Kumud Sundari, awaken and see. I have donned these ascetic robes, I have seen a new form of duty, I have forsaken the old bond of societal duties For Kumud. The lecherous force of Pramad Unsteadied Kumud; The guest scorned the duties of a guest. Once abandoned by the guest, Who remains a host and to whom? Freed from conventional duties, Kumud was broken root and branch. He looked at her and addressed her aloud as if she were conscious, ‘Beloved Kumud, the man who became your husband and guest has abandoned you. Awaken from your sleep and behold our reincarnation. Beloved Kumud, see how far we have come!’ We have come to this king of mountains, And sheltered by the love of ascetics, Beloved, let us abandon all fears, Let us institute a sacrifice to eternal love. Like his gaze, the moonbeams covered her body, like his hands they caressed her and yet remained powerless to awaken her. Sarasvatichandra saw his effort as futile and, raising her body slightly in his arms, said,

Your consciousness lies dead, Awaken! Arise! The moon showers his rays, Why do you remain untouched? ‘Perhaps your heart remains untouched by these lifeless moonbeams. But do not my words reach your heart? Does your sense of rectitude prefer these cold boulders to my lap? Tell me, Kumud, what should I do?’ Beloved, you lie in my lap, Why do you not speak a word? Or do you prefer these boulders to My lap, o’ virtuous one? If yes, beloved, say so, Open your eyes and speak! How can I lay this body, Delicate and frail, Upon these cold boulders? Sarasvatichandra gazed at Kumud’s face made bright by the moonbeams. Her clothes were in disarray and locks of her hair fluttered in the wind. He was tempted to touch her face, to rearrange her clothes and tidy her hair. Shocked at this awareness, he overcame his temptation and said, Your clothes have come undone, Your hair flies in the wind, Should I touch them or not? Tell me, o’ my life, speak! ‘Why is it that you perspire in this moon-filled night?’ A film of perspiration lines your forehead Despite this cool breeze; Forgive me if I wipe it, That is if you awaken. He wiped her warm forehead and looked at his hand wet with her perspiration as if it were a thing of great novelty. He could not bring himself to wipe his hand dry, though he did eventually. Perspiration, he reasoned, was a sign of life and he thought of checking her breath. There is no life in this body, Her breath comes in sighs, O’ I cannot bear it anymore! Forgive my touch. As he checked her breath he saw tears roll down her cheeks, and was filled with hope and desire. He hesitated, but her closed eyes, the teardrops glistening on her lotus face captivated his gaze. The eyes shut tight, and yet The tears escape From moist eyelashes Like jewels, They rest upon your cheek. He wiped her tears. As his fingers brushed against her long, wet eyelashes delicate and untouched by man, his heart felt a sharp tug. Beloved! As I wipe these tears, As I gaze upon this lotus face, I know I have no right to wipe them, Nor to gaze upon your face. ‘I had no right to wipe your tears in Pramaddhan’s house, but today I have that right. But I did not have the right to gaze upon that face, to feel drawn to her beauty in that house, nor do I have that right here. Do forgive me, I could not prevent myself, and having once gazed upon your face I cannot take my eyes away. Oh, how this face has changed from the time of our first meeting!’ Unconscious, buried deep in Searing agony of heart, having Drowned in swirling currents this Wasted body mired in pain, Where is that lovely face? The memory of that lovely face, the alluring beauty of it even in her unconscious state made Sarasvatichandra lose his senses, and he bent his face closer to those cheeks and lips, but then he stopped and rebuked himself aloud. ‘Sarasvatichandra! If you be the one who betrays the trust reposed in you by this woman of deep virtue, if you were to fall to temptation, the sin would be unbearable and unpardonable!’ To soothe the burning heart, To subdue raging passions, To heal deep wounds, To let the nectar flow, The Lord of Love came and sat on her lips, Made the cheeks tender and rosy; But for a body bereft of love and life, Like for the dead, Such violation is poison. ‘No! No! These lotus bud-like lips and cheeks are not of a dead body! But their allure and glory is lost and not likely to return. Kumud! Awake and arise and forsake this evil lap of mine! This body has begun to assail my heart.’ His eyes were drawn towards her breasts. He forcefully willed himself to instead look at the moon and the pillars of the cave, but the gaze turned with equal force towards what was pleasing to it. Sarasvatichandra was irate. O’ tender, pleasing creeper, My heart is filled with desire, I watch your stirring breasts and I am tempted to be contained by them. But I have no right to gaze upon you, O’ heart! Tempt me not! Let my latent virtue and all that is good in me Arise and awaken. He regained some measure of calm and said, O’ beautiful, alluring creeper, To seek pleasure in you is easy, I shall fly to a distant branch And not be tempted by the peacock’s plumage.

‘The moment I overcome my temptation and awaken to my duty, desire reasserts itself. How am I to escape from this snare?’ Kumud’s clothes fluttered in the breeze, revealing sometimes her soft heels and at other times her breasts. He made valiant attempts to cover her and to control his thoughts. With each part of her that he covered and each part that was revealed to him, his equanimity was challenged and his vulnerability exposed. This aspirant to the life of an ascetic was assailed by the arrows of the God of Love, which to him were like arrows tipped in poison. Under their vicious and relentless force, he grew unsteady. He said aloud, ‘Dear God! Kumud! Kumud Sundari! Wake up! You are happy in your state of unconscious. Either I should suffer a similar comatose state which will free me from this feverish desire, this poison, or you should wake up and sit away from me so that the light of your unsullied soul destroys the inebriating allure of your body.’ His wrought face betrayed his ire and fatigue, and yet newfound passions flowed through his veins even as he engaged in an impossible struggle to subjugate his passions and bring them under control of his intellect and heart. His impassioned tones, the eyes turning red, the slow heat spreading through his body and the excitement, all betrayed the increasing potency of this poison. At this point the song acted as a protective shield and helped him regain control over himself. He began to understand the pangs of desire expressed in Kumud’s song. He saw that there was only one way out of this suffering—either both should drown or both should swim ashore. He understood her entreaties to God and her plea that He should take control of her life. The breeze was unabated. He continued his valiant attempts to keep her clothes in order as he sang. O’ wind! Do not break your limits! Pray do not disrobe her, Do not fling aside this thin, soft veil, The body is abashed. O’ wind! Let her clothes be! O Lord of Love, let me bear your arrows.

‘Oh God, I cannot bear with it any longer! I do not trust myself any more. O’ wind! O’ Kamdev, spare me! Now have done with your nonsense!⟨fn:398⟩’ His eyes had turned red and moist with tears. He shivered as if afflicted with malaria, and yet he could not look away from her. The flowering creeper, though withered in sorrow, Remains enchanting. From her emerge the moonbeams, And I gaze upon the forbidden. I am greedy and I am tempted, I am unhappy and in pain, I am vicious and spew venom, I fill the beloved’s heart with poison. O’ beloved, I beseech you, awaken! Give up this bashfulness and speak, Why do you carry this burden in your heart? He seemed filled with a new enthusiasm and vigour. To a new land we have come, A new garb we shall don, We fear not society, Relatives and friends we have left behind, Left behind is their disdain. As we walk on the path of ascetics, We shall wear ochre robes And make this mountain our home, The peace and solitude of this place Is not to be found anywhere else. Beloved, let us cohabit in chastity. ‘Kumud Sundari! Even if I have to pass through a fiery ordeal in order to bring you back to consciousness, I will do so. When Ramchandra lost consciousness, Sita who was unseen by all others revived him with her touch. The right that she exercised is the right that I seek to obtain. Please forgive me. I cannot bear witness to your plight any longer.’

Her rigid, petrified body seemed to relax just a little; her veins did not look so ossified. Kumud seemed to be moving from a state of coma into deep sleep. All of a sudden she turned to her side in his lap, brushing her breasts against his chest. He experienced a sudden surge of desire at the moment of her miraculous coming to life. Water-laden monsoon clouds bring in their wake a certain heaviness, cool breeze, a darkening horizon, thunder and lightning all at once before the moment when they open and pour down on earth. Vacillating between desire, hope and duty, Sarasvatichandra experienced something similar. ‘Come what may. Let all that is to happen happen. If we are to swim ashore to purity she needs to awaken through my touch; and if we are to sink in the abyss of passion that touch is essential. If my touch is pure it will be like nectar and she will awaken, and if it is poisonous it cannot be resisted. Kumud! Beloved Kumud! Should I address you as beloved? Whatever is the resolution, you must awake now and save me along with yourself.’ Her inert body was pressed against his. Consciously or unconsciously, he held her close and willed her to be revived by his touch. Beloved! Awaken from your coma, Beloved! Arise from my lap. The river rose in spate: Why did it stop so far from us? Their hearts moved even closer. This ocean awaits you, The rising tide welcomes you. What the Lord said in code, Beloved, we have now discerned. He laid her across his lap, lifted her face gently and sang. Beloved! Awaken from your coma, Beloved! Arise from my lap. Open your eyes and behold The play the Unmanifest has set for us. In this new land and new garb,

The world does not matter. Let us aspire to a new purity, Take me along with you on this path. Placing one hand under her head and another under her feet, he raised her slightly and addressed the tender heart in that delicate body. Beloved! Be free of your coma, Beloved! Arise from my lap. Your days of sorrow are now past, Nectar divine awaits you. As he addressed her innermost being, his inner vision, too, awakened. Beloved! Be free of your coma, Beloved! Arise from my lap. Open the doors, and Make my mind yours. The song stopped, but the condition of both remained unchanged. Kumud lay inert in his lap with Sarasvatichandra holding her. He remained seated at the same place, his eyes shut. The breeze and the moonlight played as before. There was a change, though. It seemed as if Sarasvatichandra had touched the core of his being. And as he grew unaware of his body, the wind played with Kumud’s clothes unbridled. As the song ceased, Kumud experienced a sense of quietude and at last emerged from her coma or sleep. The touch and proximity of the beloved was pleasant and she lay in his lap as if in a dream, savouring it. The rustle of the wind and the flutter of her clothes awakened her fully and she opened her eyes. The face of her beloved loomed over her as the moon looms over the dark earth; Kumud gazed unblinking at that precious, enchanting sight. Moments later at the urging of her conscience, she sat up, rearranged her clothes and savoured the deep inwardness of her beloved. Before she could satiate herself, she grew aware of her body and was besieged by thoughts and questions. Without a doubt, Sarasvatichandra is gripped by fever. I experienced the heat of his body and the quiver of excitement running through him. But why are his eyes shut? Oh, a place like this for the one raised in the luxury of Laxminandan’s home! What else could be expected? Am I the cause of this? I have experienced such fever in the past. Is he, too, gripped by the fever of desire? Are great renunciate souls capable of subjugating their desires through meditative inwardness? Should I awaken him? But if he is in a state of meditation, it would be a great folly to do so. But if he is suffering from bodily ailment, God has sent me here to care for him. In that case I must awaken him. Oh what am I to do? Kumud sat facing Sarasvatichandra, whose eyes remained shut tight. She said nothing. She neither moved nor stirred. Pushing aside all other thoughts and desires, she sat with elbow on her knee as her unwavering gaze remained steadfast on his face. Joining her heart with his in silence, this embodiment of pure love and higher aspirations sat as if each moment thus passing were an aeon.
chapters.summary: Kumud's heartfelt song of sorrow and longing deeply stirs Sarasvatichandra, leading him to her side where she discovers him in a mysterious, feverish state.

chapters.title: Hearts Revealed
paragraphs: Hearts Revealed All precious things, discovered late, To those that speak them issue forth; For love in sequel works with fate, And draws the veil from hidden worth.⟨fn:399⟩ Vaster in being free from toils of sense— Was wisest stooping to the weaker heart; And so the feet of sweet Yashodhara Passed into peace and bliss, being softly led.⟨fn:400⟩ ‘S arasvatichandra! Sarasvatichandra! It is I, Kumud, calling out to you!’ Her soft voice entered Sarasvatichandra’s ears despite the roaring winds. Emerging from his contemplative sleep, he opened his eyes and looked at his lap. The one who had lain in his lap was now seated beside him. Sarasvatichandra: ‘Kumud Sundari, I have given you immense sorrow.’ Kumud: ‘What had to happen has happened. You made an attempt to give wings to my fate, but it had no capacity to take flight. It was destined to fall and it did. I see no fault of yours. When a man like Dushyanta forgets Shakuntala’s love, the reason has to be traced back to Rishi Durvasa’s curse. Chandravali behn has spoken to you about my heartfelt emotion. Please rid your heart of all pain on my account.’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘My stupidity and evildoing cannot be erased from my conscience.’ Kumud: ‘What are you saying? You might have made a mistake, but you are certainly not evil. If there was even a trace of evil in you, you would not wander around to save this evil body of mine. Moreover, in that moment of great attraction, you would have succumbed to desire and made this body go through a different experience.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I did nothing that has not been done previously.’ Kumud: ‘You are greater than me in every respect. But I have been hardened by the sorrows of this world and I, too, have experienced the condition that you went through. I have greater experience of pain.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Don’t you think that by talking about these base feelings, we strengthen them? Wouldn’t it be better not to speak of them at all?’ Kumud: ‘That is supported by experience.’ She trembled as she said this. It did not go unnoticed by him. Sarasvatichandra: ‘As I see your condition I ask myself, where does evil lie? In talking of these things or in not talking of them?’ Kumud: ‘The source of evil is this face of mine which gives so much pain to a renunciate like you. The eyes of women are filled with such poison.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Oh God! Oh God! If the eyes of women are filled with poison, then words of men are poisonous, too. It is the words of men which pushed you into the fiery ordeal.’ Kumud felt abashed and looked down. After a pause she said, ‘Now I realise that when my companions left me, I sang the song I had composed which expressed my pain. I must have continued to sing even when I lost consciousness. It must have entered your ears and pained you like a centipede that crawls into one’s ears. Please forgive me. I had no control over my body.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I had seen your bodily form so very often in Suvarnapur. But it was your song that revealed to me the true condition of your heart; and my selfish instinct holds your state of unconsciousness dear.’ Kumud: ‘Even I have reasons for this belief. When my body lay unconscious in your lap, eroding your purity by my touch, I lay inert having lost the strength even to open my eyes. But even then my ears were alert. An insect caught in a glass jar sees the world outside but remains confined to the jar. My heart was like that insect caught in the glass jar. Your sweet, pure words of endearment entered my ears and my heart and removed all my doubts.’ Sarasvatichandra was taken aback. ‘I must have greatly fallen in your esteem.’ Kumud: ‘Why are you so shocked? In Suvarnapur I had remained ignorant of your feelings, and this had pained me greatly. But your words of endearment have alleviated my pain. To the extent that I am capable of easing your pain, I shall do so. The ascetic community here has also created a possibility of it. Your words will become my pathfinder.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘It is improper to judge me by words uttered in a state of helplessness.’ Kumud: ‘But this judgement is not a blot on you.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Brahma himself gave dark spots to the moon, but they remain concealed behind clouds. Today, the wind has removed these clouds as well.’ Kumud: ‘That wind also freed Chandra to be with Kumud. It was an act of generosity. Sarasvatichandra, what more can I say to you?’ She fumbled between using the formal ‘aap’ and the more personal ‘tamey’ in addressing him. Sarasvatichandra: ‘Pray, do not address me as ‘Aap.’ In memory of our previous association, ‘tamey’ would be most appropriate. Once you do, all that is unsaid will be said.’ Kumud: ‘That previous association, that life has slipped away like a beautiful dream. Those terms of endearment which delighted the speaker and the listener, which were like nectar and ornaments, have to be now given up and forgotten; and that takes effort.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Ascetics gain virtue by renouncing things that are most dear to them. Dushyanta said that when in doubt, the conscience of the virtuous should be taken as the proof and measure of their virtue.’ Kumud: ‘The time when we took poetry as a measure of reality has long passed.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘It is my foolishness which has brought upon us this present condition.’ Kumud: ‘What could you have done? When fate takes a turn, even the intellect of the learned falters. My learned, experienced and intelligent father did not think of waiting for you for some time and arranged a hasty marriage. Faced with such a situation one is forced to say that God’s will is supreme. If men of wisdom and experience falter, how can you be blamed if in a delicate moment you lose your equanimity and reveal your innermost feelings?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Kumud! Kumud Sundari! As I see your generosity and wisdom, my attachment for you grows.’ Kumud: ‘Your eyes flutter, your voice breaks, your body trembles... Share your pain with me.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Kumud, your pain is my pain. I shall be happy when you are happy.’ Kumud: ‘What has brought about this present condition?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I am not aware of my own condition.’ Kumud: ‘Will you do as I ask?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘My penance lies in that.’ Kumud: ‘You must assuage your hunger with these fruits and get some sleep. We will have enough opportunity to heal our hearts during these five nights.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Only if you take these fruits as my offering.’

The fruits were laid out on the one large leaf that they had. Kumud said she would eat after Sarasvatichandra, who refused to accept this. Finally, they ate together from that leaf. They did not speak much while eating, but continued to gaze at each other. Their mutual attraction grew even stronger. Kumud, the more experienced of the two in such matters, was alert to this and tried to divert their attention in other matters. ‘I feel that we should not address each other by our real names but use the names given to us by the ascetic community till such time that you decide to reveal your identity. I should then reveal my identity in such a way that my father’s prestige is not harmed.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That is correct. But there is a problem. Every time I say Madhuri, I am drawn to your beauty and sweetness.’ Kumud: ‘There are many in this world who remain attached even without uttering given names.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That is true. Many couples do not take each other’s names. But if we were to adopt such a practice it would indicate to us a relationship that we do not have, and it would become one more cause of mutual attraction.’ Kumud: ‘Then my Chandra, I shall call you Chandra and you can call me what you like. You become my Chandra and dispel the darkness of attachment that envelops me. I hesitate to call you Navin.’ They stretched out their hands to pick up the same fruit, their fingers touched and both felt a current pass through. They were startled and instantly withdrew their hands. The fruit fell down, but their eyes remained riveted on each other. Kumud picked up the fruit and gave it to Sarasvatichandra. Air envelops us. If we try to push it away it gains force and becomes wild. There is no life in absence of air. Any attempt to move it away is futile. It is best to cover oneself with a cloth. In moments of togetherness, such gestures are like the air that envelops us. It is futile to struggle against it. At best one can put a protective covering around oneself, thought Sarasvatichandra. But he could not think of any diversion.

As if reading his thoughts, Kumud asked, ‘Why did you leave your father? Were you angry with him or with someone else? Were you upset about something? What were your reasons for abandoning me? What brought you to Suvarnapur? How and why did you come here? Where do you go from here? What will you do? For my sake...’ Before she could ask him another question, Sarasvatichandra picked up a piece of fruit that had fallen on her heel. His gaze was fixed to the spot that he had just touched. Kumud covered her heel with her saree. Suddenly aware of his action, he said, ‘My response to all these questions will certainly clarify many doubts, and I will be at peace. But whether this peace will be real or will result in something else is difficult to say, given the experiences of this one night together.’ Kumud: ‘A person of virtue believes that supreme aesthetic delight and unsullied rectitude are like a couple—inseparable. Considerations of danger are misplaced while following the path suggested by it. Following this maxim, I have decided that there can be no other consideration for me if I get an opportunity to serve you. I want to be at your feet, whether it places me higher or lower is of no consequence to me. My Chandra, I have no one else but you. You may consider your Madhuri one more blot upon your face, or take her to be an art that further enriches you. The decision is yours. But do not keep your pain and deepest thoughts secret from me. You have to grant me that one right.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘If I do not grant you that right, whom shall I grant it to? I am ready to disregard not only my self-interest but even my duties if they were to impede your path to happiness. In this situation even if there is some diminution of dharma, public censure, or hindrance to my happiness, I would welcome with my heart all of these, by the mental happiness derived from your happiness.⟨fn:401⟩ ‘Madhuri! Madhuri! If the utterance of your name is to deepen my attachment, so be it. My only desire is to secure peace and tranquility for you by whichever means it might require. If I can secure your happiness by offering all that I have as oblation, I am willing to do that. Your desire to make me happy can be fulfilled only if you are happy.’ Kumud: ‘All right. Do you want my salvation or my happiness?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘If you aspire to happiness, I want happiness for you. If your aspiration is salvation, then that is what I want for you.’ Kumud: ‘What is your aspiration for yourself?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I want neither happiness nor salvation. I want peace and wish to perform my duties without any aberrations.’ Kumud: ‘Does happiness for you lie in peace and salvation in the performance of duties? Do you aspire to both?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I believe in what you have just stated. But as long as performance of duties does not secure peace, I do not aspire to peace as it is immoral.’ Kumud: ‘When will peace be moral for you?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘When I see you tranquil and content.’ Kumud: ‘What are your duties?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The five-fold sacrifice that Guruji enumerated for the two of us. These are also observances that men of virtue in our land and in the West aspire to. My duties are also those which I have held dear since childhood. All other ritual observances are for householders. Not for us.’ Kumud: ‘My Chandra, recount to me the story of your renunciation and the sacrifice that it entailed. You have to respond to all my questions; for the present that will secure my happiness. Please do not harbour any fears of misunderstanding or incomprehension.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘In that case, Kumud Sundari—Madhuri— Madhuri, listen. Recounting my own follies or evildoings is also a form of penance, and penance is what I seek. You ask, why did I leave my father and my wealth? I renounced both to free my parents from sorrow and from the debt of performing Putra Yajna. I accepted my father’s proposal of our engagement even without having met you because I assumed that he was happy at this relationship. You may ask the reasons for this acceptance. Please believe me that at that point I had no other reason but my father’s happiness. You know that since childhood I had harboured a desire to leave home and wander the world to understand the essence of our society. You know that I never lusted after wealth. Hence, you will believe that in the first instance the acceptance of marriage was a form of sacrifice of my subtle aspirations in the Pitru Yajna. One auspicious moment my father told me that our love was not acceptable to him. I had a beautiful portrait of you made, and by gazing at your portrait I used to immerse myself in your love. I visited you. We exchanged letters. I had a ring made for you. All these did not find favour with my parents and they put an unacceptable charge on you. The reason for which I had accepted the proposal of engagement proved false. The reasons for which I had agreed to be a householder and partake in my father’s wealth proved false. I realised that my parents would be happiest with my renunciation. With this realisation my duty was to adopt the path of renunciation. Renunciation came looking for me, and I embraced it. What more do you wish to know?’ Kumud: ‘People say that you could not bear a few harsh words of your father, and that you embraced this misadventure of renunciation in anger.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I have read such stories in the newspapers. People who believe it are stupid. I was not and still am not given to anger. Men of virtue do not err and are eager to pardon errors made by stupid men.⟨fn:402⟩ I cannot blame my parents. This is an essential element of one’s duties towards those who are our guests by destiny. There are many stories regarding the many lives of the Buddha, some of which I have narrated to you. According to one Jatak Katha, Buddha as Bodhisattva resided in the forest with his brothers. Indra stole and consumed Bodhisattva’s food for five or six days. For Bodhisattva, the consumption of food or the act of fasting were one and the same, hence he did not mention this to anyone. He fasted till the others realised that his food was stolen from him. His body withered, but he remained joyous. Madhuri, in a household presided over by my stepmother, I remained happy and did not ever succumb to rage. I might make an error in analysing my own heart, but believe me that till today I am not ready to accept that I renounced my all in a fit of anger. Disaffection does not cause me to be angry. Their pain perturbed me, and by walking away I gave them satisfaction. If they at all insulted me, it was only once, and I am not so ungrateful as to forget their countless favours. But worship bereft of faith, welcome empty of heartfelt feelings and cohabitation without love are like a pond without water and eventually have to be abandoned. All virtuous persons have to adopt the path of renunciation; this path is joyous, easy, available, beautiful and righteous. This is the saying of the enlightened one and must be adopted by all those desirous of following the path of virtue.⟨fn:403⟩ Kumud: ‘Were you even at that time not hurt?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I cannot say there was no pain. But that pain was not due to what happened to me. I felt that my father’s act was unjust, and my affection for him caused me pain that he should act in a manner that was unjust.’⟨fn:404⟩

Kumud: ‘How did you free yourself of that pain?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The idea that my going away would give him peace freed me of pain.’ Kumud: ‘If a child insists on playing with a serpent and cries until allowed to play, what is just—allowing the child to hold the serpent or allowing it to weep?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘If that person is not a child, or that child is not yours, one has no right to force him to do something even if doing so would be beneficial to him. One cannot preach to one’s father unless he asks for advice. At the most a son may suggest something to the father with utmost courtesy and humility. A son’s duty is to perform his duties as a host to his father. If the father develops disdain for his son then the son cannot live in his father’s loveless house.’ Kumud: ‘You wanted him to have peace and tranquility. But do you believe that your walking away caused him no pain? Is it right for a son to be indifferent to such pain and not pardon even one error of the father?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘His pain has transformed his heart, or so the newspapers suggest. But my sense of duty points to me a different path. His disaffection for me without any fault of mine is a good thing for me, as love causes pain. His disaffection reduces his longing for me and to that extent frees me from my obligation for Pitru Yajna. My affection for them has increased. I seek to perform my duties within the rubric of my aspirations. By fulfilling my aspirations I provide them with peace. Society believes that it is immoral to be indifferent to their pain and suffering. But the path of spiritual quest is different. I had considered these issues before leaving Bombay. The relationship of father and son is accidental, transient and hence illusionary. People continue to harbour these illusions even after the death of one’s parents and feel pain on that account. A son freed by his father from his obligations towards the parent is free to adopt his path disregarding the pain of his relatives as transient and illusionary.’ Kumud: ‘But you had no understanding of the sacrifices when you felt insulted by your father. Until today, you had no knowledge of the obligatory sacrifices. You found in that insult a reason to leave the house. If you had not felt insulted, you would not have considered your duties regarding sacrifice.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘It is true that Guruji discoursed on the sacrifices today. But what I have inferred with my sense of morality and duty and what Guruji described as the duty of sacrifice are similar with the sole exception that there is a difference of terminology. I have adopted the language of sacrifice because I felt that you would be more amenable to that language. In response to the other question, I should tell you that even the most insignificant cause, if it furthers one’s duties, should be grabbed by the virtuous. Once the Bodhisattva, the enlightened one, was a trader. By some error, news of his death spread; his wife and other relatives were pained by this. The Bodhisattva used this opportunity to go away to the forest. His grieving relatives later met him in the forest; he assuaged their grief through sweet words of wisdom and turned them back.⟨fn:405⟩ I left the house of my host because his disaffection for me was apparent.’ Kumud: ‘Do you consider your father’s penitent affection false or do you regard love itself to be false? If you consider his love to be false, how do you regard my love? If you consider love itself to be false, and for that reason abandoned both him and me, why do you seek penance? Why do you not go to Bombay to lessen his grief? Are you partial towards me?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Madhuri, a person is considered insignificant or special based upon one’s disdain or attachment for that person. Ascetics decide these matters based upon the other’s virtues and their own morality. Householders make calculations about the importance of the mother vis-à-vis the wife or the other way around. Truly speaking both the mother and the wife are guests. Guruji explained to us the duties of a son and a husband, who though the same person, construes his duties differently. Ram insisted that Kaushalya stay with Dasharath and took Sita with him to the forest. At that point he did not consider whether his parents would consent to this decision or not. A couple is one; but society does not look upon this union with favour because customary norms view a marriage as a coming together of bodies. Society has come to completely disregard the pure union of a couple. Madhuri, if I had considered the wife to be more special than the father, I would have set up a new house and lived with my wife. I adopted a path which I felt would secure both his and your welfare. As regards the question of the falseness of love itself, Chandravali Maiya is better suited to answer that; whatever I have gained is from her. I have not considered either your or my father’s love as false. If I had considered your love to be false, I would have been very happy today. If I had regarded my father’s love to be false, both of us would have been living in some palatial house in Bombay. My love for you makes me want to do a penance, but that does not imply that I do not pass through an ordeal on account of my affection for my father. It is my duty to find a resolution to your pain, which was caused solely by my actions. Similarly, it is immoral to reverse my decision of renunciation which was taken to secure my father’s happiness. Renunciation must stay. An elephant’s tusks cannot be wished away.’ Kumud: ‘Your renunciation is the cause of both your father’s grief and mine. Alleviating my grief is your duty, but doing the same for your father is immoral; why so?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘It is not true that my renunciation is the cause of both your and his grief. I lit the flame of love in your heart, and that is the cause of your grief. My father is also aggrieved because of his love for me; but I did not invite this love, I did not cause his love. Moreover, when he rebuked me, he snuffed out the lamp of love. Now he wants to reignite the lamp. Love that has died need not be harboured in one’s home. That ghost is best left on the branch of a peepal tree.’

Kumud: ‘You harbour a deep, unacknowledged rage in your heart. Your words testify to it. Your father’s love for you was never snuffed out; the lamp fluttered in a gust of wind, and once it passed, now burns ever more brightly. His love never died; it became comatose. You cared for me during my period of unconsciousness, you held me in your pious lap. And now you give me immense joy through this conversation. By the same principle you should have cared and protected your father’s comatose love. Oh my Chandra! Emerge from this eclipse and enlighten your father’s heart. What had to happen to me has happened. But you are the only one who can alleviate his pain—the pain of losing a son in old age. This pain cannot be imagined and it cannot be witnessed. Time once gone will not return, and like Dasharath his body might just give up one day. You will be sorry then, and there will be no way of undoing it by penance. You will repent, and I will be condemned to witness your suffering. If you do not want my grief to deepen, if you want me to be happy, please act now. My Chandra, I am alerting you to this danger. I beseech you.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘You have truly shown me my error. You are right— at this moment, I am indeed angry. But when I left home, I was neither angry with my father or anyone else. My father’s barbs had clearly indicated to me the unhappy state you would have been reduced to had we stayed in his house post our marriage. Now I recollect that at that point, I considered living in his house and marriage to you as mutually exclusive. But that decision was not taken in rage; it was a considered decision. Hitherto, I have not felt the anger that I feel today; not even when I left home. And I have not been angry with my father. My rage has boiled over at our social customs which have crushed a flower like you, which have destroyed gardens of pure love. You are a victim of that disorder that our social customs are. Till today, I had remained unaware of your true beauty—the beauty of your mind and the beauty of your soul. You are a victim of our customs, and I was instrumental in the perpetration of this sin. These thoughts make me boil over with anger. What if these thoughts had occurred to me when I left home? I have no answer for that. But I do clearly recall that at the time, I did not act in anger.’

Kumud: ‘Now you must calmly reconsider as to why you should not return to assuage the hurt of your father.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The questions you ask were also posed to me by my friend Chandrakant, who was with me when I decided to leave home. He argued with me till midnight and I considered his arguments all night. I left the house in the morning after having weighed each of his arguments.’ Kumud: ‘What were your thoughts?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Madhuri, you have lived among ascetics for some time now. You have experienced their love. Their love is desireless and hence worthy of reverence. The love of householders is due to attachment. It is covetous. One responds to such love based on the desire that is present on either side; their love finds fruition. Even if one of the two feels immense desire for the other, that person can experience fulfillment. But when this desire is satiated or realised or abates by degrees, that love dies. Son, wife, lovers, parents—all are subject to desire. Householders believe that one must continue to perform one’s duties even after love has died. Ascetics do not think so; they in fact believe that such a state provides an opportunity to be free from false bondage, and I have adopted that path.’ Kumud: ‘Why did you consider going away as your righteous duty? Is it not your duty to eradicate your father’s sorrow? Did not my father- in-law perform his duties even while administering a state? Did not Gunial fulfill her duties even while being caught in the web of family ties?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘One should perform those duties which are in conformity with one’s nature and character. One’s actions should be in accordance with one’s desires and aspirations. Buddhidhanbhai had intense desire to be the administrator of the state. I am from the very beginning desireless. Your pious mother was placed in the web of family ties. Her virtues enabled her to be an equal partner to your father and her sacrifice enabled them to experience non-duality as a couple. I have no such desires. I have been able to extricate myself from my father’s desire for a son; I consider myself fortunate. My father’s grief is due to the separation or because of repentance. I did not believe that he would never be unhappy at my going away. But if I had stayed on in his house, the conflict with Gumanba would have given him greater grief. If I were to return today, he would be happy for the time being, but the conflict with Gumanba would persist for his lifetime. I set him free from this life-long conflict. But I have no remedy for the present pain that he experiences. Such incidents set one free from social ties and grant an aspirant the right of renunciation. If I were to return he might feel happy, but Gumanba would be extremely unhappy and I do not wish to be the reason for her unhappiness. I do not want riches and luxuries. If I were to go back to that luxurious house of my father, he would be subject to daily hissing from Gumanba. You would not wish me to leave this tranquil space and go to a conflict- ridden existence. It would be wrong to make one or both unhappy in an attempt to make my father happy. When I think of the possible consequences or consider my duty, I am convinced that going back would be undesirable and unjust. What appears to be unjust should not be done and there can be no consideration of possible gains or loss to either my father, to you, to me or to anyone else. So long as it is one’s duty to reside in the family house one should do so; but if it becomes an impediment to the performance of other duties one must renounce it. If residence with the family allows one to perform actions, they should be done with inner tranquility. One whose action or inaction is informed by non-attachment finds tranquility in either of these conditions. Hence non-attachment has been considered the righteous path. One may experience happiness in the observance of familial duties, but if such observance is intended for the pursuit of happiness, that person must renounce home.’ Kumud: ‘You are willing to stretch the limits of morality, even violate norms out of your love for me. But your affection for your father is circumscribed by considerations of morality. Why this difference?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘My action or inaction with regard to my father is not determined by either love or disaffection for him. Similarly, I am not moved only by love in my eagerness to assuage your grief. When I left home I did not do so out of affection or disaffection. What I did or did not do, what I intend to do or eschew are due to considerations of duty. I understand now, and understood then, that my dear ones would be pained by my leaving home, but I subjected their love to scrutiny. Chandrakant, while pleading with me not to leave home, said many harsh and bitter words to me. From his point of view they were just and true, and an expression of his abiding friendship and love for me. His words only deepened my affection for him. But my duty was to act according to what I considered to be the righteous path, a path that I had discerned after much soul-searching. Why do friends like Chandrakant consider my being a householder more beneficial than being a renouncer? Is renunciation a sin? Do they wish to prevent me from committing a sin? And they grieve when I cannot do as they want.⟨fn:406⟩ ‘I can understand the wailing of loved ones when someone is dead, dying or has deviated from the path of duty. Chandrakant and my father grieve for me even though I am alive. I know of their pain. But what is the reason for this pain? I considered all these issues before I left home. They were equally attached to me and to the state of being a householder. I asked myself, which do they like more? If they like being a householder, they should stay at home. Their tears for me are for reasons of love. If they love me more than their state of being householder, they are free to renounce it and join me.⟨fn:407⟩ But if they do not leave home, then one must surmise that they love being a householder more than they love me. They do not want to leave either their home or me; they also want me to be with them as a householder.

This is their view of happiness; there is no consideration of my welfare. Or else, I lack in virtues because my loved ones are unwilling to become ascetics along with me. I must lack in virtue.⟨fn:408⟩ Even a man bereft of all virtues has a few friends in his hour of crisis. A man of virtue has many friends, but even such a man rarely has a friend ready to renounce his home for the sake of friendship. Such renunciation has been considered natural.⟨fn:409⟩ Upon deliberation I realised that if I am virtuous, some friend will follow me. If I am without virtues, no friend will follow me and it will be no fault of theirs. But if I have some virtues and still my wailing family and friends do not follow me, I should surmise that their attraction for the household is stronger and that their tears are because of their love for me. If someone were to actually follow my path of renunciation, I would be forced to reconsider my opinion. But if they do not do so, they would be subject to the vagaries of their fate and societal norms, and I would be free from all attachment and duty towards them. I would be free to wander the world in solitary splendour. It is up to them to be unhappy or happy at my renunciation. It is their decision whether to bite into the fruit that they hold in their hands.’⟨fn:410⟩

Kumud: ‘Why do you consider my love to be differently constituted than the love of all others?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I told you that for me love that would lead a person to follow my renunciation would force me to reconsider my decision. You were not totally free. Your fate was tied to the decision of your parents. I felt that they agreed to the engagement because I was the son of a wealthy father. When I left my home and wealth, I felt that they would consider any relationship with me as undesirable. Hence, I decided to free them from the promised marriage and wrote to you and them.’ Kumud: ‘You have very low estimation of my parents’ virtues.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘They proved me correct by arranging your marriage immediately.’ Kumud: ‘They acted according to prevalent social norms and tried to change my fate. What else could they have done?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I do not wish to imply that what they did was wrong. But I did not err in my estimation that their affection for me was no different from the affection of other loved ones. Their actions proved this. If their affection was different from others, they would have considered me worthy of your love even though a wandering pauper. Their actions would have been different.’ Kumud: ‘It did not occur to them.’ Sarsavatichandra: ‘That is so. Only those who have desireless affection can think of doing things differently. All human beings have two eyes. But desireless love opens the third unseen eye which provides special vision and points out different modes of action. Initially, I did not believe—given your age and your words—that you possessed this third eye. Then I asked myself, what if you possessed the third eye? That thought, that doubt churned my heart and before I could glean butter from this churning your fate offered your body as sacrifice. My churning remained futile. I came to Suvarnapur in the selfish hope of seeing you happy and content, which would have stopped the futile churning of my heart and given me peace in renunciation. The Suvarnapur experiences proved that my fate was not to attain tranquil renunciation but to wander aimlessly as a renunciate. I could not bear your suffering and yet was powerless to change your condition. I tried to give you false knowledge that I had gained in hindsight. I also gave you false advice that you should forget the past—something I had not been able to do myself. I came away from Suvarnapur and was brought here by destiny. Intense pain and pure love opened your third eye, and you, too, reached here! Kumud Sundari, the flames of your third eye have opened my third eye today. I perceive and am enamoured of the beauty not only of your heart but also your body. I do not know where this vision will lead me. I am not going beyond limits in my duty towards you. I am not partial to you, but my performance of duties and my partiality are all governed by the third eye. The light of this vision creates new dreams and aspirations before you and me.’ Kumud: ‘One who has suffered the consequences of one adventure should be doubly careful before setting out on another. You now say that had I followed you, you would have considered other possibilities. What would you have done? Would you have given up the idea of renunciation? Had you considered this possibility then? Where do you intend to direct my destiny after today’s experience? I have asked you all kinds of questions, but my heart trembles while asking you this. Sarasvatichandra, what lack did you perceive in me that you deferred the test of my love for you? Love that you had kindled! My father’s decision was another matter. I was naïve and infatuated. I was tied to you by ever so flimsy a thread. My heart was linked with yours, woven with yours. Was it not your responsibility to think about me? Were you concerned about me at that time? What is the nature of your concern now? Certainly, my test is now over. Tell me how miserably I have failed; be brief but clear. Do not conceal anything. If you hide anything from me, know well that Kumud’s third eye will burn her to ashes. My beloved, you have read so much, have thought so deeply of things. And you made its cruel use on me?’ Kumud’s eyes welled up with tears. Sarasvatichandra: ‘I accept that I have committed a crime against you. So long as you remained unaware of my stupidity and my crime, there could be no penance for me. Today, you have recognised how evil I am. If I deserve to be forgiven, please pardon me and if I am undeserving of it, even that would be some solace to the agony of my mind and give some peace to this unhappy consciousness.’ Kumud: ‘Sarasvatichandra, stop feeling sorry for yourself! If you satisfy my curiosity, I have enough faith in you that we would be able to achieve tranquility for us both and be content in our state. Society is evil; its waters have been muddied. Knowledge is like a chemical; if one knows how to use it, it can purify the dirtiest of waters and if one knows not, it can poison the purest of waters. Knowledge is like fire; both pure and impure waters evaporate in its flames. Love that is desirable and noble purifies the heart of all impurities. My Chandra’s knowledge cheated me. That knowledge was responsible for our separation. Kumud will no longer trust that knowledge. If your learning has now been replaced by divine knowledge and if your ochre robes have destroyed all your father’s aspirations, use that divine knowledge to destroy all my desires. You are not just a learned person; your love is not divorced from learning. I understand your love much more than you do yourself. My hope lies in that love, and that love will induce you to provide the best solution.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘It will do what it has to. But Chandra will be judged by Kumud’s heart. You asked me two questions, isn’t it? One, that what were my thoughts regarding you when I left home and two, what are my ideas at present.’ Kumud: ‘That is correct.’ Sarasvatichandra sighed deeply and continued. ‘In Bombay I had decided to come to Ratnanagari and secretly know your intentions.’ Kumud: ‘What would you have done with that knowledge?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘If your heart was still aglow with love for me, I would have come out in the open and met your father. If he had agreed to the marriage, I would have taken you with me like Ram took Sita and Nala took Damayanti. If your father disagreed, I would have set out on my pilgrimage and come back for you when you attained the age of maturity. But that was not to be. I was travelling by sea; adverse winds delayed my arrival. When I reached Ratnanagari, you were already at Suvarnapur. You know the rest of the story.’ Kumud: ‘What a relief! A deep thorn in my heart has been removed. You were not the one who harmed me. It was destiny. It was hasty of me to have thrown those barbs at you. Today I have realised that your love is righteous and that you love this wretched self. I spoke harsh words without ascertaining the facts. Why did you not say this to me before? It would have saved me from the sin of causing you pain. Why did you not write any of this in the letter or in the verse that you wrote?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That letter was written to free you from all obligations towards me. But if the night were to wait patiently, the moon would return the following day. This window of hope was opened by that verse.’ Kumud: ‘Yes, but I was so stunned that this suggestion was like a song to deaf ears. My fate did not measure up!’ Kumud touched her forehead with her finger. Sarasvatichandra: ‘When it became certain that we would meet, I thought of a few possibilities for you. You will have to think of the rest.’ Kumud: ‘And they are?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Brahmacharya and the fourth ashram are for single persons. A couple stays together as householder and can live together in the forest during Vanaprastha. The efforts and activities of a householder do not allow for conscious, deliberate action towards salvation. Whatever merit one earns, one does so without deliberate effort. One does not cultivate active disdain for happiness during Vanaprastha; at the same time one does not make conscious endeavour to secure happiness and comfort. Immorality, dereliction of duty and sin are forbidden in both the stages. Such a state of Vanaprastha is most appropriate for us. This state of togetherness can have three forms; each allows for non-duality as a couple. The first instance allows togetherness without the need for physical touch. Cuddabodhi and his wife lived in the forest as ascetics.⟨fn:411⟩ The wife served her husband and the husband helped her gain knowledge. They cared for each other without physical touch. Another example of this is of the moon (Chandra) and lotus (Kumud). These couples remain in close proximity; their subtle bodies are offered as oblation in the sacrifice. The second form assumes greater proximity where the couple performs a joint sacrifice through a single altar and fire. This is called Ekagni Yajna. Ram and Sita and Vishvambhara and his wife lived together in the forest in this way. The third condition is to live separately but be united through subtle bodies. Viharpuri and Chandravali exemplify this. Draupadi who lived as Saurandhri in the palace of King Virata is another example. The lights of their souls are united; their actions are for the same purpose but their sacrificial altars are different. I can think of these three possibilities. You might suggest others.’ Kumud: ‘Which of these paths has the greatest danger of the violation of morality? You have considered the moral question in each case. Why have you not considered the possibility of its violation? Which of these is the path to salvation? Is there not a possibility of immoral conduct in what you describe as Ekagni Yajna?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Persons of virtue voluntarily accept bondages which further social organisation and at the same time do not impede self-realisation. For them such bondage is righteous conduct and any violation of it is immoral behaviour. Householders, given their prejudices, attachments and their ignorance, are unable to further their pure duties. Therefore, they are subject to injunctions of scriptural texts. Ascetics can for themselves discern between morality and immorality and therefore have the right to act according to their considered opinion, and that constitutes right conduct for them. Kumud Sundari! Madhuri! None of the paths suggested by me entail the danger of immoral conduct or violation of duties. There is danger of immoral conduct from the perspective of societal norms in what I have described as the Ekagni Yajna. The reasons for which I consider it right to disregard social censure, for the same reasons I prefer to remain indifferent to moral norms of society. Those who renounce society are not bound to live by its norms. Their duty entails cultivating a state of unattached desirelessness and in performance of their duties.’ Kumud: ‘How can desirelessness be possible in a situation which allows for the possibility of desire? It is like saying that a barren woman bear a son.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘It is necessary to nourish and strengthen the sacrificial altar. An altar heated by other fires becomes incapable of withstanding the sacrificial fire. A person whose conscience is tempered and cultivated is capable of creating an altar of his body, an altar that has not suffered other forms of heat. Just as consumption of food douses the fires of the belly and nourishes the body, the dousing of passions nourishes the sacrificial altar. Ascetics, when necessary, undergo fasting and celibacy; those who fail to control their palate and desires are called lowly, lustful persons. Yet at the same time an ascetic who spends his energies in controlling desires to the exclusion of all else fails to nourish his altar, and his sacrifice remains incomplete and inferior. This is a violation of the duty of sacrifice. Therefore, for an ascetic satisfaction of desire is not cultivation of desire; it is neither attachment for nor shunning of desire. It is called desirelessness. No one but an ascetic can attain such a state. Madhuri, the paths that I have suggested are those which have been tried and proven to be righteous by the conduct of our ascetics. You are free to choose a path that to you appears the purest and most unsullied.’ Kumud: ‘Have you not invited upon yourself the conflict that is entailed in the suppression of desire? Was that your duty? Or is it a violation of it? If duty is entailed therein, what is the nature of it?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I invited conflict because for me, therein lies my duty. Such conflict is not contrary to the performance of my sacrifice; not initiating and not engaging in the conflict would be an impediment in my sacrifice. Therefore, this conflict is moral for me.’ Kumud: ‘Would you describe this impediment?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘It is possible among couples that one partner covets bodily passions while the other does not. It would be immoral for the one who desires passions to force one’s will on the other. At the same time it would be immoral for the desireless to impede the fulfillment of the desire of the other.’ Kumud: ‘The morality and duties of a couple must be one. How is it that what is moral for one is immoral for the other?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘When a revered guest visits the house of an impoverished host, it is the duty of the host to accord him a welcome worthy of the guest. At the same time it would be immoral for the guest to further impoverish the host by accepting such a reception.’ Kumud: ‘Respect and disdain together would certainly cause an aesthetic rapture; but this subtle distinction between morality and immorality subsisting in the encounter of the host and the guest is a novel idea for me.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘An aesthetic rapture is caused by inert nature while a violation of duties is caused by evil.’ Kumud: ‘That is true. You are knowledgeable in the ways of conception of pure duties and have cultivated a high sense of aesthetics. My heart is now serene, there is hitherto unexperienced peace; all my desires have been fulfilled. You have placed upon me the responsibility of defining what for me would be righteous conduct.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Each heart is different, its capacities are different and each person has a unique understanding of her ‘‘intuitive perception and instinctive impulse.’’⟨fn:412⟩ Therefore, I made the suggestion.’ Kumud: ‘On the union of subtle bodies, both perception and impulse are also limited.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That is the result of mature love.’ Kumud: ‘I shall await such a state.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That is your right.’ Kumud: ‘In the early days of our love you had recited to me a poem, which I now recollect. Beloved Chandra, the ideals of love that you have narrated have given me a sense of equanimity and satisfaction.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What were those lines?’ Kumud recited for him. Our feet now, every palm, Are sandalled with calm, And the dew of our wings is a rain of balm; And beyond our eyes, The human love lies, Which makes all it gazes on Paradise.⟨fn:413⟩ ‘Chandra, only when I think of our past, my tranquility is shattered.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The poet himself has shown the possibility of tranquility. To suffer woes which Hope thinks infinite; To forgive wrongs darker than death or night; To defy Power which seems omnipotent; To love and bear; to hope till Hope creates From its own wreck the thing it contemplates;

Neither to change, nor falter, nor repent; This, like they glory, Titan, is to be Good, great, and joyous, beautiful and free; This is alone Life, Joy, Empire, and Victory!⟨fn:414⟩ Kumud: ‘You had explained these lines as well to me, and they appear to be true now. You have given me the responsibility of deciding the path of my duties. That is one task that remains for me.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Whatever thoughts and aspirations that emerge from your beautiful heart will be beauteous, Madhuri.’ Kumud: ‘There is no such rule.’
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra and Kumud, amidst emotional turmoil, share a revealing conversation about their past love and present feelings, navigating a powerful, unspoken attraction.

chapters.title: A Journey through the World of Immortals and their Blessings or A Dream of Pure Love
paragraphs: A Journey through the World of Immortals and their Blessings or A Dream of Pure Love Before the starry threshold of Jove’s Court My mansion is, where those immortal shapes Of bright aerial spirits live insphered In region mild of calm and serene air, Above the smoke and stir of this dim spot Which men call Earth, and with low-thoughted care, Confined and pestered in this pinfold here, Strive to keep up this frail and feverish being, Unmindful of the crown that Virtue gives, After this mortal change, to her true servants Amongst the enthroned gods on sainted seats. Yet some there be that by due steps aspire To lay their just hands on that golden key That opens the palace of Eternity. To such my errand is; and, but for such, I would not soil these pure ambrosial weeds With the rank vapours of this sin-worn mould.⟨fn:415⟩ They sat in silence, their eyes on each other. The empty leaf on which fruits had been placed fluttered in the wind and fell into Sarasvatichandra’s lap, where Kumud had lain sometime before. Kumud was quick to snatch away the leaf and got up to throw it. This unintended touch had a forceful effect. As she got up she suddenly felt weak. Her body moved in one direction but her head was turned towards him. Sarasvatichandra’s eyes were riveted on her. He, too, felt himself being pulled along with her, but did not get up. Kumud returned and took her place. She looked up at the sky and the moon, and said, ‘It is past midnight. Would you like to sleep?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘Which place would be appropriate for you?’ ‘That which is appropriate for you would be suitable for me.’ Kumud considered this for a while and said, ‘Does this have a meaning other than the apparent one? How should I view it?’ Then resolving the doubt herself, she said, ‘Beloved Chandra, so long as what is good for me is not also good for you, you should stay in your appointed cave, and I will stay here. You should go back to Saumanasya Gufa.’ ‘That is best.’ Sarasvatichandra got up slowly, his eyes on Kumud. He turned towards the bridge and took slow, deliberate steps. Kumud took her bedding and followed him. He saw her but said nothing. Sarasvatichandra’s companions had spread a sheet for him to sleep on. Kumud spread her bedding and covered it with this sheet and turned back. Sarasvatichandra: ‘If you sleep on this hard rock floor and insist that I sleep in this soft bed, sleep will certainly elude me.’ Kumud: ‘There is one bedding and two persons. The more revered of the two has to use the bedding; that is most appropriate.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Such distinctions are forbidden amongst ascetics.’ Kumud: ‘I am not yet an ascetic; at heart I am still a householder.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘You are virtuous and hence an ascetic.’ Kumud: ‘You are my guest.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I am quite used to sleeping on rocks. I even like it. Or else, I could also argue that you are my guest.’ Kumud: ‘You have promised to do what gives me joy.’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘I am caught. If nothing else please take this sheet and my ochre robes. Please sleep on them.’ Kumud: ‘If that pleases you.’ Kumud went away. Sarasvatichandra lay down. Kumud sat on the platform with his robe in her lap. Sleep proved elusive. She looked at the robe and thought, Kumud! Your impure body found comfort in his lap. Will you be able to sleep on his robes? O’ pious robes, you protect the body of that great soul. Tonight, I shall hold you close to my heart as a special blessing of his. Your warmth will bring me sleep. O’ robes, purify my impure heart. As Kumud lay down on the platform, clutching the robes close to her heart, her mind was flooded by thoughts. This is pure love. It is not in my heart, but the heart of that great soul is imbued with it. What a noble and pure heart! He is totally unmindful of my impurities! How partial he is towards me! Society considers a wife to be secondary to one’s father. The same society believes that a woman should consider her husband to be primary and relegate her father, mother and family to secondary position. Social norms entail no such duties towards the wife. It considers such primacy of the wife as immoral. My Chandra considers the immoral to be moral for my sake, and the ascetics support his view! My body has been wedded to someone else. Chandra wants me to follow my marriage vows. He can suppress his desires despite the fact that this body of mine is under his control. He not only suppresses his desires, but he kills them. What love! How am I to reciprocate? What can I do for him? How difficult it is to kill one’s desires? I have experienced its brutality. I was saved not because of my own strength but by God’s will. But he emerges victorious on his own strength. I was in a state of utter submission, and yet he emerges victorious over his desires. How so? He will commit no immoral act; he is not concerned with social opprobrium. It is immoral for me and hence also for him. Today, I did succeed in controlling my desires. But I have only suppressed my desires; he has killed them. I have experienced bodily passions, but he has hitherto not consummated his desire. The possibilities of sensual pleasure have flowered in his imagination, have filled his heart and yet his heart has the extraordinary strength to not transgress limits. If I had not witnessed it today, I would have never believed anyone to be capable of such strength. O’ pure ochre robes, you are the shroud of such strong will! She pressed them closer to her, and her eyes closed, but she was jolted awake. That body was on fire. His eyes were on me. The heart’s passions were obvious. Just the tips of our fingers had grazed, and yet... That fire, that turmoil and churning is because of me. My lack of willingness to be a partner is the cause of his turmoil. Kumud fell into a disturbed sleep and woke up startled by a dreadful dream. I am heartless! And all my cruelty is directed towards him! Of religion, pity is the root! What if the humours of his body are imbalanced by the feverish encounters in this place? She managed to get some sleep, until she woke up again. Sleep, why are you so elusive today? Today, all my worries have been laid to rest, satiated. Then why does my unrestrained mind wander so restlessly? Kumud rubbed her eyes, sat up with his robes in her lap and thought, let me see if he, too, is in a condition similar to mine. Is he still in a feverish state? She walked across the bridge and stood at the entrance to the terrace, clutching his robes. The platform was about six hand measures in length and one hand wide. Sarasvatichandra lay there, blabbering in his sleep. ‘What can I do, Kumud Sundari? If I had not abandoned you, together with you I would have endeavoured to improve the present condition of our country. An unmarried man is shunned by our women. The salvation of women is impossible without a companion like you. But the tigers and wolves of this forest of desire stand between us and our togetherness. I tremble in their presence.’ He stopped speaking. Kumud approached him and gazed at his face aglow with light. Unable to restrain herself, Kumud softly whispered, ‘Oh, my beloved patriot!’ Her arms reached out to embrace him, but withdrew before they enveloped him. She bent over his sleeping form, her lips hovering inches above his, and pulled herself away just as rain-laden clouds turn away without raining down on earth. She stood erect and resolute, and said, ‘No. I will not destroy this beautiful ascetic image by my sullen touch.’ Sarasvatichandra murmured in his sleep, Oh, summoning stars! I come! Oh, mournful earth! For thee and thine, I lay aside my youth, My throne, my joys, my golden days, my nights, My happy palace—and thine arms, sweet Queen! Harder to put aside than all the rest! ... Now am I fixed, and now I will depart. ... For now the hour is come when I should quit This golden prison where my heart is caged⟨fn:416⟩ Kumud stood still, her eyes filled with tears of joy, and thought, the dream reveals his mental universe at the time of renunciation. The reasons for his great renunciation are so subtle and beautiful; he was moved by the desire for salvation! With a hand over her heart, she murmured, ‘Oh wretched heart! Why did you think that it was given to you to imprison this noble man in the cage of love? If you get even a small space in some corner of his heart, it would be an act of mercy on his part, and your great fortune. I blamed him, I harboured expectations from him and I was block-headed and crass. Oh prince among ascetics, forgive me! Allow me to touch your feet for no other reason but to seek your pardon!
