What you have given me goes beyond forgiveness. You have given me so much without my asking for it. You have done your duties towards me. It is now my obligation to prove worthy of it. I do not wish to desecrate such a beautiful ascetic idol! I shall be satisfied by touching your feet.’ Trembling, Kumud moved towards his feet. She sat down in a narrow space near his feet, but she lacked the courage to touch them. Even society does not consider it a sin to touch the feet of a great soul, she thought; it is a path of purification. Very gently she touched his feet, bowed her head to them and softly kissed the soles of his feet. She put his feet on her lap and held them in her hands. She leaned against the wall and made a pillow of his robes. Thus seated she fell into a deep sleep. Sarasvatichandra, too, was now in deep sleep. The only one awake was Sleep herself, who filled their hearts with dreams. Scholars both Indian and Western believe that the ‘impressions’ gathered through ‘associations’ in the wakeful state emerge as dreams. The science of dreams has not developed much. Some compose poems in dreams, while some others formulate philosophical principles.⟨fn:417⟩ We know of such things, but hitherto we have not known two persons having the same dream. This unprecedented occurrence took place tonight in the Saumanasya Gufa. Sarasvatichandra was asleep; his face glowed in the soft light of the moon. Kumud, though asleep, did not have her eyes shut tight. Some onlooker might think that her unblinking gaze was fixed on his face. They simultaneously and together entered the dream world. They saw the same dream. There could be several reasons for this. The human brain is situated behind the forehead. Dreams emerge in the brain. The rays of Sarasvatichandra’s brain might have emerged from his forehead and moved through ‘capillary attraction’⟨fn:418⟩ into the rays of the moon. These moon rays might have entered Kumud’s brain through her half open eyes, or the dream might have been formed in the moon rays and entered their brains simultaneously. Or else by some chance a force like the newly discovered ‘Rontgen Rays’ might have entered Kumud’s brain, and with these x-rays she might have been able to see through the mind and heart of her beloved. Alternately, the constellations of their respective stars might have brought about this condition. A transmigration of souls could also have brought about this miracle. It is also possible that when Kumud touched his feet, some force could have passed through them and brought about this shared dream world. It is possible that this was the result of Vishnudas’ benediction made possible by the state of meditation he had entered. Whatever the cause or a combination thereof, the same dream took shape in both their brains. Dear reader, we shall leave behind the world of wakefulness and enter the world of dreams, and we shall walk silently behind Sarasvatichandra and Kumud Sundari and witness what our eyes are capable of seeing. The moon was on its westward journey in the sky. Its soft light fell on Sarasvatichandra’s face. The moon hid behind Vasant Gufa and Saubhagya Gufa was enveloped by darkness. The group of ascetics on the lowest floor were in deep, dreamless sleep, while Sarasvatichandra and Kumud had entered the world of dreams. A soft breeze imbued with moonlight wafted around the cave; light dew cooled the earth. The Saumanasya Gufa was enclosed by darkness; nothing that happened inside the cave could be seen from outside of it. At this moment Sarasvatichandra, in his dream, was walking on the parapet near the spring. Kumud Sundari followed him wordlessly. We do not know if he was aware of her presence but he took slow, deliberate steps. We can assume that his slowness was to suit Kumud as he did not want to tire her out. Now all the characters and the world that we shall describe shall be from the world of dreams. Soft moonlight spread across the spring, reflecting the images of the two who walked. Their reflections accompanied them. They walked for quite some distance before approaching a fortress-like wall. They walked towards large city gates and emerged on the other side. They stood in a vast field surrounded by tall trees. A light wind rustled through the leaves of the trees. A full moon rose above them. They looked up. A small cloud floated past and covered the moon. Flowers showered down on them from the cloud. These silver flowers grew in size as they came nearer, and a form became discernible. A goddess was descending on earth. Kumud Sundari sat down with folded hands. Sarasvatichandra drew aside to make way for the goddess. The divine form stood before them. Saubhagya Devi had descended in crystalline form. Kumud was deeply ashamed to see her mother-in-law. She felt that she did not deserve any forgiveness and stood with her head bowed. But Sarasvatichandra came forward and spoke with humility, ‘Oh image of pious Saubhagya Devi! I see your crystalline body descended from the moon. If you are not Saubhagya Devi, please reveal your identity if I have earned the merit to know your identity.’ ‘Sarasvatichandra! I am the immortal body of Saubhagya Devi. I saw the two of you together in this place and came down. Kumud Sundari, come nearer!’ said the divine image. Frightened, Kumud approached her and fell at her mother-in- law’s feet. Her sobs did not allow her to speak. ‘Kumud Sundari, my daughter! Now you are on the edge of the earth. You have earned the merit to leave behind earthly norms and witness the true morality of the world of immortals.’ The divine image spoke these words of solace and embraced Kumud. Kumud pressed her head to her mother-in-law’s bosom and said, ‘Devi, you were a goddess in human form—you were a mother. Today I see your immortal form. I am a fallen woman. I had no right to be in your pure presence even then. Now I am even more sullied. My touch defiles your pious body. Allow me to stand aside, impure that I am.’ Saubhagya Devi: ‘I am aware of your deep-seated emotions and I have come to cleanse and purify your heart. In a short while you will be the guest of the world of immortals and will have the darshan of all those immortal beings that this gem among men aspires to meet. So long as you consider yourself fallen and impure, you have no right to enter that world. The ascetics have explained to you the true nature of religion. But social norms are so deeply ingrained in your heart that you follow what is immoral as moral. Even the teachings of the ascetics could not erase this deeply ingrained image. I have come to erase it. I left behind my mortal body on the earth and now live in the world of immortals. Those with spiritual attainments and those who have performed the pure Priti Yajna acquire the merit to reside in this world. I will be here till my husband joins me. Even now from here I can see him. I will await his arrival, and then we shall both leave behind this body and be free. The social norms became an obstacle in your performance of Priti Yajna. I was a party to that. I did not understand it while I was on earth, but the divine sight of this land has made it apparent to me.

Daughter, my son was undeserving of you. The man with you deserves you, and you are wedded to him.’ Kumud: ‘If that is so, all the women of our land should be considered unmarried and deserving of hell. Devi, wasn’t your marriage also subject to social norms? And still you await your husband in this world of immortals. Why is my condition any different?’ Saubhagya Devi: ‘It is not so. Our girls, subject to the power of their parents and social norms, are bound to what appears to be a marriage. She is sent to her in-laws’ house. She becomes mature and offers her sacrifice. This sacrifice is performed on the altar created by her father. The merits of her penance accrue to her, while her sins accrue to her parents because she undergoes the fiery ordeal for the satisfaction of her parents. Some of these girls, by the grace of God, by their superior fate and by their virtues, are joined to their husbands by love and attain a state of non-duality; they earn this merit for themselves. I ascended to this land on the strength of such merit. But it is immoral and unjust to disrupt a woman’s Priti Yajna that she has begun in association with one man and force her to begin a new one for the sake of her father. Your parents forced you to abandon your Priti Yajna. They suffer the consequence of their immoral conduct. You have been freed from that immoral existence by the ascetics. When you touched his feet, you became a virtuous wife to this man. His merits have given you the right to enter this land.’ Kumud Sundari freed herself from the embrace and stood at some distance from the divine image. ‘I am in a dream. The Devi that I see before me does not speak the language of the Devi who was my mother-in-law. Why should I be deceived by this dream?’ Saubhagya Devi: ‘What is a state of wakefulness for the world is our dream, and what the world considers dream is our state of wakefulness. The Devi you loved has died and now her immortal and subtle body is before you. My thoughts and words would appear to you novel. Yama, the God of Death rips apart the curtain that separates life and death. Those bodies that deserve death descend into unending darkness of death while those who deserve life attain this immortal state. This world represents life at its fullest; compared to this earthly life is only half a life. In this state we attain perfect knowledge. I have received such perfect knowledge and hence my language and thoughts are distinct from those of the Devi you knew.’ Kumud considered this for a while and then looked towards Sarasvatichandra. Saubhagya Devi: ‘The man that you look upon is your true husband. My son is not your husband. There are no other examples of a woman like you in our country—a woman who had given her heart to someone but was given in marriage to someone else. Because girls who are mature enough to have a heartfelt sense of love are given in marriage before they reach this age. Your father allowed you to cultivate a heart of your own, and that was a meritorious act. Kumud, at the time of your marriage with my son, we placed lifeless clothes over your hands and bound you in marriage. In place of them, I now place this unifying light upon the two of you. It has entered both your hearts—perceive it. Instead of bodily holding each other’s hands, your hearts are now joined mystically. Experience this magic. May you receive the power to perceive the light that joins you!’ They looked and saw light folded like cloth enter Sarasvatichandra’s heart, and its other end entered Kumud’s heart. Their eyes shone with new light. Saubhagya Devi’s light enveloped them in benediction. They came together in that light as husband and wife. Saubhagya Devi approached them and kept her hands over their heads and said, ‘I, Pramaddhan’s mother free you of all obligations towards him and give you to your real husband and grant the new couple the right to ascend to the world of immortals. In this world there is no pain, no lust, no attachment, no animosity, no ego, no desire; there are no endeavours and there is neither joy nor sorrow. This world is pure knowledge; its vision is of salvation and there is equability in this world. The only desire is to bring to fruition the sacrifices initiated on earth. The immortals shall fill your hearts with this desire. Your hearts will be purified by the sacred sacrificial fires and make you capable of offering yourselves as oblations. At the conclusion of this sacrifice you shall attain eternal freedom. There is no heaven other than this; there is no other tree of fulfillment; there are no gods other than those who reside here. With my powers I inspire you to undertake a pilgrimage for the welfare of all people. I empower you to journey through this heaven. Kumud Sundari, I have concluded my Putra Yajna; may you receive the fruits thereof. I shall shower upon you, and through you upon your true husband, a light-filled potion. It will envelop your body like a wedding saree. This will protect you against the poison of great snakes living in the world of immortals. You will be able to journey through this world without any apprehension or fear.’ The crystalline image showered flowers upon them and these flowers took the form of a potion which covered their bodies with light. ‘Kumud Sundari, Sarasvatichandra, it is time for me to return. Do you have any questions? Do you want any boons?’ asked the crystalline image. Sarasvatichandra: ‘Devi, we do not know our way through this land. We do not know where we are and where we should go. Would you please enlighten us?’ Saubhagya Devi: ‘Siddhalok—this world of immortals—is located in the space between the sun and the earth. Human eyes are incapable of seeing it. You are standing beneath its Pitamahpur, which floats right above us. I can see it, and you shall be able to do so shortly. I heard your footsteps and came to you. Other immortals will also approach you and give you appropriate means and requisite vision.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Who will they be?’ Saubhagya Devi: ‘Your heart will recognise them. I know that your mother Chandralaxmi was right behind me. She has lived longer in the world of immortals; her penance on earth was much higher than mine and hence her attainments are greater. The sacrifice that she had initiated for your sake is incomplete and hence she will come to you.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘How is it that her penance was greater than yours?’ Saubhagya Devi: ‘I was united by love with my husband even before our eventual marriage and I derived its benefits early on. But Chandralaxmi attained union with your father after a great deal of suffering. She had to undergo many fiery ordeals and deal with its poisonous effects. As her death approached her union with your father came to be eroded. She, in her lifetime, could see that a son like you would have to live with a step-mother; her heart was shaken by this. Despite this, she never harboured any evil thought about your father, never uttered a single harsh word. Her love towards him has been like nectar. She kept her faith and trust in him, urged him to remarry and gave up her life joyously. She had to undergo such harsh penance. Anyone who performs such penance on earth attains greater powers in the world of immortals. Sarasvatichandra, your feet will carry you to all the sacred spaces in this land; hence do not worry about it. Kumud Sundari, I am no longer your mother-in-law. You will meet your real mother-in- law; worship her without any attachment towards me. Her penance is many folds higher than mine. I can hear her footsteps now. I am in her way. I shall not impede the arrival of such a pious person.’ The crystalline form gradually disappeared; they could see that her form reflected the presence of Buddhidhan. Both those forms disappeared. Consecrated by that image, the couple stood with their arms around each other, united by the sacred light bestowed upon them. They anxiously awaited the next event. Soon they felt themselves rising through space as if some unseen force was pulling them upwards. They felt as if their bodies had become lighter than air and floated upwards like a balloon. They were freed from the force of gravity. They rose upwards in the sky and came to halt near silver clouds. Someone emerged from a deer-shaped cloud and approached them. Sarasvatichandra recognised the form of his mother. Kumud Sundari, joined to him by the sacred bond, also recognised Chandralaxmi, whose form was constituted of silver clouds. Together they bowed to her. Chandralaxmi said, ‘My son and daughter-in-law! Saubhagya Devi has consecrated your union. I have attained this form as a result of the penance that she described to you. Son, you abandoned your wife, your wealth and home for the sake of your father. That was your Pitru Yajna. Your renunciation was due to your father’s immoral conduct. He is suffering because of that. He must undergo that hardship and I shall aid his sacrifice from here. Your Pitru Yajna is now over. You have embarked upon Priti Yajna. At the same time I can see a great desire in your heart to work for the welfare of our people—that will be your Manushya Yajna. Today, you will be taken to Pitamahpur to find ways of performing this sacrifice. To aid your progress I shall give you certain means and abilities. ‘That city is situated above this space of clouds. The events that take place on earth are reflected in Pitamahpur. Sometimes they form golden webs while at other times they make mounds of mud. There are many worlds within them. I give to you this divine spade to break open those mounds and this ladder which will allow you to descend into them. I give both of you wings that will enable you to float through those webs as also other spaces. The spade and the ladder shall float alongside you and assist you when necessary. ‘These objects came to me as gifts of my penance. I bestow them upon you. Kumud Sundari, your grandmother Dharmalaxmi awaits both of you. Her penance is greater than mine. She has never experienced love. She has undergone limitless misery in the service of her husband. Her deep, silent and noble suffering and her sense of rectitude in the face of that suffering have granted her a place in the land of immortals. She will soon meet you and, given her superior penance, she will grant you objects that have higher powers than the ones I have given you.’ Chandralaxmi disappeared and merged into the clouds. They flew upwards with the aid of their wings. The spade and ladder floated alongside them. They rose above the clouds into clear space. Dharmalaxmi’s aged body approached them and stood in space unsupported by any ground beneath her feet. She said, ‘Son-in-law and daughter, suffering is a great penance. I have suffered all those hardships which would erode most human beings. Now I have obtained a place among the immortals. I have also obtained two gems. I have crafted them into ornaments, and these I give to you. Revered son-in-law, I give you a ring made from this Chintamani. As you focus your attention on it, it will reveal to you the mysteries of any part of this Siddhalok. It will enable you to see and meet any of the great immortals who reside here. It will light up your path and show you the way. Daughter Kumud, I give you this mangalsutra made from Parasmani, a touchstone that turns everything into gold. It will give you light and still your heart with pious and moral ideals. Its touch and light will give you peace and happiness. You and others such as you suffer many privations through your journey through the world. But this suffering also sows the seeds of salvation. We find a barge to cross the sea of suffering without having to seek it. During this sojourn through Siddhalok you will see divine sights through your husband’s eyes. This mangalsutra will reveal their beauty to you and its light will enable you to see golden dust in great mounds of mud. You will be able to see all those gems that are hidden. Whatever you see will be transferred to your husband through the garment of light given to you by Saubhagya Devi, and he will see those objects with even greater clarity. Sarasvatichandra, you have embarked upon this Priti Yajna with the purest of intentions. Kumud will witness that sacrifice, and its munificence shall shower upon the earth. Chintamani, Parasmani, go and occupy your designated places!’ As soon as Dharmalaxmi had said these words, the ring sparkled on Sarasvatichandra’s finger and the mangalsutra came to rest over Kumud’s breasts and shone like light. Before they could touch her feet in gratitude, her grandmother’s form had disappeared. As they opened their eyes, they saw the high walls of a great city blocking their path.
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra and Kumud navigate a night of profound emotion and shared dreams, receiving mystical blessings from Dharmalaxmi that hint at their entwined spiritual journey.

chapters.title: Reflections of Indian Society in Pitamahpur and the Benediction of the Gems
paragraphs: Reflections of Indian Society in Pitamahpur and the Benediction of the Gems And on her lover’s arm she leant, And round her waist she felt it fold, And far across the hills they went, In that new world which is the old.⟨fn:419⟩ I sat beside a sage’s bed, And the lamp was burning red Near the book where he had fed; When a Dream with plumes of flame To his pillow hovering came, And I knew it was the same Which had kindled long ago Pity, eloquence, and woe; And the world a while below Wore the shade its lustre made. It has borne me here as fleet As Desire’s lighting feet: I must ride it back ere morrow, Or the sage will wake in sorrow.⟨fn:420⟩

‘B eloved Chandra, what is this?’ ‘These are the walls of Pitamahpur.’ ‘How long has it been that we have been as one?’ ‘The time that it takes to move from wakefulness to dream; some call it a moment, others aeons!’ ‘Today, I stand close to you, touching your body, and yet I feel peace and tranquility. Yesterday, even when I touched your feet I felt lust. Why is this?’ ‘Those flames of lust originated in your physical body. Today our subtle bodies are united; they breathe in the pure air of Siddhalok.’ ‘Have you any experience of flaming lust?’ ‘Ask that question of your mangalsutra. Our flaming desires and our strivings to control it are known to us. The thread through which Saubhagya Devi united us would allow you to perceive the history of our desires. Do you see it?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘And you can see the outcome of that churning in your mangalsutra.’ ‘Yes.’ Suddenly, they heard the loud barking of dogs coming towards them from the city gates. About fifty large dogs, snarling, barking and pawing the ground with their feet, came and encircled them. The largest of the dogs came forward and spoke to Sarasvatichandra in human tongue, ‘Oh human being, who are you and why are you here?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The immortals have guided our path. We are their children. Who are you and what powers do you enjoy here?’ Dog: ‘When the Pandavas began their journey to heaven, our ancestor entered the heavens as a companion of Dharmaraj Yudhishthir. Since then we guard many city gates in Siddhalok. Since the time of Dharmaraj, we protect this land from immoral, unjust and irreligious persons.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘How do you protect Siddhalok?’ Dog: ‘The immortals enter this city on their own spiritual attainments. But sometimes human beings such as you also come up here. As human beings approach this land we can smell their presence. We can discern their qualities by their smell. If they are Satvik we allow them to enter the city unharmed; if they are Rajasik we inflict minimal bites on them and allow them to enter the city. If they are Tamasik we eat them up and throw their bones on this heap. This is our food; this is our duty and our right.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What are the reasons for this arrangement and what has been the result of it?’ Dog: ‘Bhishma considered only Yudhishthir worthy of receiving wisdom from him. Only persons of virtue such as Yudhishthir are to be shown the mysteries of Pitamahpur. Those with Rajasik qualities have attachments, hatred, affection and ego. They view the city through a vision sullied by these. Their perspective is one-dimensional and warped. We bite these creatures so that they do not deceive the people on earth on their return. They are infected with rabies and infect those who come in contact with them. People of virtue and learning do not believe their stories about Pitamahpur. Tamasik persons deserve to be killed.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘How can considerations of attachment and hatred influence a viewer’s perspective?’ Dog: ‘Feelings of hatred and attachment nestled in the heart affect conduct and also the perspective of that person. Dogs are considered among you as impure; the Europeans keep us in their homes, while Yudhishthir considered us worthy of being brought to heaven. This is an example of Satvik vision. Sage Vyasa agreed to impregnate the wives of his half-brother; Bhishma look a vow of celibacy; Ram ate the berries tasted by Shabari and Bhim married a demon. All these acts were done out of Satvik vision. Among the householders there are divisions of caste. Humans fail to see the pain and suffering of other castes and are partial to their own type. They divide marriage, food, conduct and thought as belonging to a particular caste. They cling to their own and show distain for others. Their own conduct, even if filled with false egotism, is considered moral and the conduct of others is considered immoral. They consider certain truths unworthy of utterance but are not shamed while speaking lies. They conceal truth, speak lies and favour their own relations, whatever their follies may be. Thus attachments and hatred affect not only conduct but also the vision. What is seen without the layers of attachment, hatred and desire is Satvik. This pure vision is imbued with spirituality.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Is love for one’s own country an example of attachment and desire?’ Dog: ‘Love for one’s country that is informed by a sense of duty and obligation is Satvik. Love that is rooted in attachment is Rajasik, and such love for the country ultimately causes the destruction of one’s own country as also of other countries.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘But all persons are moved by a sense of duty towards their country.’ Dog: ‘But a sense of duty that is not informed by Satva is Rajasik. One who remains indifferent to the external conception of duty and morality but considers duties towards one’s own country primary is moved by a sense of attachment and hatred. Such a person recedes both from truth and Rita. One who follows external duties, whose duties towards the country are informed by these external, immutable laws, is Satvik. Human beings have this twin-fold conception of duties, and they are pardoned among them. Immortals and realised souls remain steadfast to external, immutable laws. Yudhishthir did not conceal his desire for his stepmother Madri; he also accepted his struggle to suppress this desire. This honest acceptance of desire was a sign of his Satvik vision, and hence King Bali appeared before him. The two of you will be ashamed to accept your relationship upon your return to earth—this is not Satvik vision.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘If that is indeed the case, why don’t you bite us without further delay? We are prepared for that punishment.’ Dog: ‘By asking this question you have robbed us of our right.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘How so?’ Dog: ‘A human being who can ask for punishment is Satvik. There is another reason as well; you have with you Chintamani and Parasmani and I could smell from afar that these gems will give you the pure vision required to enter Siddhalok. Your question proved this. Now you must proceed on your pilgrimage without further delay. Please enter the city through this gate.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Oh prince among dogs, who was the last human being to enter the gates of this city?’ Dog: ‘Ratnanagari’s King Mallaraj, who lives among the immortals, once entered the city like you. He built the Bhishma Bhavan based on the conception of this city.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Oh prince among dogs, I have visited it. Do you have any instructions or advice for us?’ Dog: ‘We dogs do not believe in false covering such as clothes. But human beings conceal and are secretive about their speech, thought, impulse and conduct. They create a world of appearances and falsehood. I bless you that you shall be free from any such desire. With this power, you will be able to perceive the joys and sorrows of your people. With this understanding, you will be able to realise your desire to work for their welfare. This island of Siddhalok floats over the earth. You will be able to see the condition of India as reflected in the great ponds of Pitamahpur. You should then proceed towards the great mounds of earth and finally, you shall come into the presence of Bhishma resting in the lap of mother Ganga. Ask him the ways by which the welfare of your people can be secured. One who is acquainted with Mallaraj’s Bhishma Bhavan will easily comprehend his discourse.’ With these words the prince of dogs disappeared along with the rest of the dogs. Sarasvatichandra and Kumud Sundari floated into the city as if they had worn ‘skates.’⟨fn:421⟩ They came to a halt near a banister made of gold and silver rods near a great pond called Pitamah Kund. This pond was about a mile long and wide, and it was filled with light. There were large islands in the pond. Sarasvatichandra looked into his ring and said, ‘Kumud, look! This great pond is filled with the ancient light of our country. This light cannot be seen from earth. One is required to swim through the light to reach the islands. Those who are bitten by the dogs jump into this light, pass through it and fall back on earth. The glitter of this light attracts them and they fall down with the rabies given to them by the dogs. Their only experience of this life is the glittering light; their partial knowledge creates terrible havoc on earth. You can see their reflections there.’ Kumud looked into the light and said, ‘Oh! What great battles! This is an object lesson of that fable of blind men and the elephant. They are at war with each other to establish truth as they perceive it. But my noble husband, even these people are useful. Look below the light. There is an ocean of darkness. That, too, is a reflection of the present state of our country. These beings, bitten by the dogs, float in it like lamps. Even a matchstick gives light in total darkness. These people are like those matchsticks. Oh my husband! Please do not show disdain towards them. They, too, deserve your affection.’ Sarasvatichandra embraced her and said, ‘You spoke the truth, a beautiful truth. It is that beauty that I embrace.’ Kumud, delighted by this intimacy, said, ‘The light springs forth like a fountain from beneath those mounds.’ Sarasvatichandra released her from his embrace and looked at the fountain of light. ‘At the conclusion of the great war Bhishma rested on the bed of arrows and entered the eternal Ganga. His body did not merge with the elements. He has come to rest here in the lap of mother Ganga. These mounds have formed over his body; these fountains of light spring from him.’ Kumud: ‘Shall we go there?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Our union and oneness are such that your thoughts are mine, and mine are yours. Look, we are now afloat; these wings have allowed us to fly. We are flying over this sacred light.’ Kumud: ‘What a wonderful ocean of light, light that gives salvation! This is the ocean of the wisdom of our ancients. We bow to you. Destroy the darkness below you and fill our land with your light!’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘That is my desire as well. That desire will be realised with the passage of time, but that time will come when we have become one with the immortals. Duty also entails waiting for the appropriate time. Kumud, what a fragrant, divine breeze wafts over this ocean! We cannot even dream of such a breeze on earth.’ Kumud: ‘Where have our wings brought us to?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘We have come to the top of the great mound. We will descend to its bottom and we will then be in presence of Bhishma and Ganga.’ They came to rest on a place of stable land on the mound. Sarasvatichandra: ‘This is the only part of the mound that is solid. The rest is hollow; if you were to step on it, you would slip inside.’ Kumud: ‘How were these mounds formed?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Once Bhishma came to rest in the lap of Ganga, without the support of this wisdom the intellect of our people got eroded. These mounds have been made by the eroded intellect.’ Kumud: ‘It is not just mud. There are various layers inhabited by countless ants. And see there—there is some light as well!’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Yes, what appear to be ants are in fact reflections of our ancestors. About twenty to thirty crore creatures survive in these mounds. These mounds are a result of their efforts over several aeons. You can see that the ants are forming newer islands.’ Kumud: ‘What is that light?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘At some places the light is tranquil and white while at others, it is coloured. The paths made for the passage of these creatures by peaceful, virtuous and learned souls are of white light. The paths made by the Rajasik or those with half-formed intelligence are of coloured light. The rest of the mound is filled with little holes and tube-like passageways made by Tamasik persons. There are also termites and spider webs.’ Kumud: ‘How shall we enter the core of the mound?’ In response Sarasvatichandra flew upwards, followed by Kumud Sundari. They entered the mound by the path illuminated by white light that resembled moonlight. A ladder materialised, using which they began their descent. The passage was like a bridge over a river. The bottom part reflected the sky above. Sarasvatichandra: ‘The walls are like transparent glass. Look at the world outside: these ants have human form. The mud has cracked like parched saline land. That mud has life. Lowly creatures have become like mud and they have created their own world in these tubes, holes, webs and chunks of mud.’ Kumud: ‘When one piece of mud cannot tolerate the presence of the other, they crash into each other forming heaps of dust, while some other creatures joined by common understanding have formed themselves into pillars. All these pillars are joined to the bottom.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The gusts of wind that come from outside this land shake up the pillars; they collide into each other and crumble. When all of them come together and become one, the wind will be powerless.’ Kumud: ‘Who knows when such a time would come? On that far side are mounds formed by people of other countries. They are united. The dust falls in heaps and the winds from the West shake everything up. Some are shaken first, others later; that is the only difference.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘How these creatures are crushed by the crumbling pillars! Kumud, look at that!’ Kumud: ‘I am.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Just as ants gather crumbs of grains, so are these crumbs of wealth collected here. Wealth, like so many creatures that emerge from the earth’s crust after monsoon rains, emerges from these pillars and is scattered by the winds. These creatures collect this wealth but scald it with their saliva. Those who collect the wealth remain hungry and lead a life of labour. As the labourers wither and shrivel they are destroyed and so are those who subsist on their labour. Thus both the classes—those who are drowning and those who are trying to save them—drown.’

Kumud: ‘This is Jati Yajna, the sacrificial rites of caste. The saliva of these creatures gives solidity to the pillars and they do not crumble. Otherwise, there are gusts of wind from all sides.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Look at the immorality of caste! The guest forces the host to perform sacrifice. So many creatures, attracted by its fire, are scorched to death by its flames! This is the self-inflicted injury that destroys both intellect and wealth.’ Kumud: ‘One must fight to protect the erosion of the intellect, but wealth that is not in good hands must be destroyed.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Oh Kumud! Your mangalsutra spoke a terrible but beautiful truth. The erosion of intellect would bring about a terrible impoverishment of the land, but that would be an act of God. These creatures themselves are responsible for the impoverishment of the country. Their customs are, like termite, corrosive. On all sides there are forests of them. Fathers do not initiate a sacrifice for the sake of their sons and daughters. Their sacrifices are meant only to satisfy their own wants; they offer their sons and daughters as oblation. Oh God! These creatures who sell their daughters, fathers who live only for their own sake claim that eating meat is a crime and immoral, but they do not shudder at the thought of consuming the flesh of their daughters! What is this we see? Mothers drive a wedge between sons and daughters-in-law and separate them. They throw their immature children into the fire of marriage. Look there! Those creatures offer their women as food to their parents; and there, parents are offered for the consumption of the wives! Their women are crushed under their feet; some are seated on their women and feed themselves! It is selfishness all around. What immorality!’ Kumud: ‘Women and men are alike. A woman, through her intelligence and compassion, should help make her husband pure and attractive.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘How can everyone have a wife as generous and intelligent as Kumud! Kumud, this scene though terrible deserves our pity. They themselves destroy their bodies, their children, wealth and religion; they invite trouble. They burn in their own fires and are crushed under the burdens they collect. How are we to free them from it?’ Kumud: ‘They have no vision; give it to them.’ Meanwhile, they had descended deeper. They found themselves at the bottom of the tunnel. They were in an open space from which four paths emerged. They stood at the crossroads. The roof was made up of large black rocks with large holes in it. Shafts of coloured light hung from them like roots of banyan trees; mammoth serpents swayed on them. Sarasvatichandra: ‘Kumud, we have passed through the present and are now in the age of Emperor Ashoka, the most powerful, the most able and the most virtuous of our kings.⟨fn:422⟩ The country was at its zenith under his rule. For over a thousand years the religion of compassion taught by Lord Buddha prevailed in the country. It grew here, was nourished by this land and spread to other countries, while it became recessive in this country itself. Ashoka, grandson of Chandragupta and son of Bindusar, ruled when Buddha’s religion was at its height. Though a Buddhist himself, he had equal respect for Brahminical religion. He gave grants to both. We are now in the midst of the pure light of this virtuous king.’ Kumud: ‘What are these things that appear like the roots of a banyan tree? And these serpents?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘This white light arises from the pure vision of great souls, and the coloured light comes from these mighty serpents. They hold the earth. Kumud, these serpents, the source of light, have been awakened. In a short time, we shall witness the power of their poisonous flames.’ Large red, yellow, green, black and white serpents encircled than, but were repelled by the divine potion that covered the bodies of Sarasvatichandra and Kumud. The serpents came together in a group and discussed something which was not audible. Finally, one very old, fat and large serpent approached them with great effort. He spewed poison at them. Other serpents also spewed venom at them. They were showered by black venom. The light was filled by its blackness. Infants unaware of the power of serpents attempt to play with them. Similarly, these two stood quietly and watched this shower of poison with curiosity. Finally the serpents stopped spewing venom. The light and air became free of their vicious presence. The serpents spoke to them in divine tongue, ‘Oh, fragile children of the earth! What desire brings you to our vicious world? What power allows you to withstand our fiery poison?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The inspiration of immortals brings us here; we move about and are protected by the power they have bestowed upon us. We do not know if we have come here out of any desire.’ Serpent: ‘If you were not protected by pure power you would have become like these creatures in those mounds because of our poison. If you had any desire our venom would have entered your body. You must have spoken the truth as no such thing happened.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘We are not free from all desires, but no specific desire has brought us here.’ Serpent: ‘Reveal your desires.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Our desire is to observe and know all that is worth knowing in this land, which includes your condition, your powers and the reasons for your actions.’ The land of the serpents went into turmoil. ‘Why? Why?’ the question rang through from all sides. Sarasvatichandra: ‘We descended on this land through a shaft of pure light. We saw many cracks and crevices in this great island. We saw large pillars; we saw the immoral lives of creatures living in it. All of these rest on your heads. You cling to the roots of irreligion. It is our duty to understand you and your conduct.’ All the serpents spewed venom on them. They seemed agitated. The great old serpent stood facing them. His forked tongue quivered and hissed and the hair of his moustache bristled with fire. Green and yellow poison showered on them. The great serpent addressed them: ‘Oh humans! You have the hubris to want to know the follies of us serpents! We are the reflections of the composers of the Shastras, Shrutis and Puranas of your country. The scholars who formulate rules of social conduct determine the origin, preservation and destruction of social norms. We are the reflections of those great scholars and law-givers. This great banyan tree that fills humans with awe holds all these social norms. It is our duty to protect this great tree and we shall continue to fulfill our duties. We do not devour those who through their unsullied vision can discern right from wrong.’ The light around them grew darker. Sarasvatichandra: ‘You do not consume righteous conduct and moral persons. Who or what do you consume then?’ Serpent: ‘Oh naïve human being, listen! We subsist on truth and nothing but the truth. We do not chase morality and righteous conduct because they follow from the truth, and truth does not emanate from them. The universe is composed of three gunas or attributes. To view the world only through the prism of Satva Guna is to conceal a large part of the truth in order to focus on a small part thereof. Your world is brimming over with Rajas and Tamas. Satva is a product of the imagination of some naïve person like you. A fresh water spring in an ocean of salinity will turn saline! Similarly the sources of Satva remain submerged by the rivers of Rajas and Tamas. A Tamasik is like a blind man, unable to perceive reality. Similarly a Satvik who remains tolerant and forgiving of Rajas and Tamas is to that extent unseeing. You might consider love between a man and woman to be pure and unsullied, but with experience you will realise your folly. The two of you, given some divine accomplishments, might remain pure, but that will not turn the rest of the world into a pure thing. Animals will not cease to devour each other, conflicts of families will not subside and one righteous person will not stop battalions of sinners. Kings will not cease to be greedy and irreligious conflicts will not be resolved by religion. As in the animal world so among kings, bigger kingdoms will feed on smaller ones. Any edifice of religion created on the basis of blindness towards immorality will be like an edifice built on sand. The way of the world is besmirched by grime and soot; it is false belief and egotism to assume that those who walk on it will remain untouched by its filth. ‘We do not deny these aspirations for purity, but we are ready to abandon them when necessary. We have been created realistically out of the three-fold division of gunas prevalent in the world. You can see that the pure, moral vision of Lord Buddha and Emperor Ashoka has vanished into dust, while our realistic perspective subsists even today. Like the great Himalayas we withstand the foreign winds. We have destroyed marriages as conceived in your Vihar Math. We marry infant girls and forbid widow remarriage. We persist with the joint family system and do not allow any sapling to take root outside the field of its caste. We pitch the unrestrained love between man and woman against ties of kinship. Many such social customs have taken root here and we nurture them, allow them to grow unhindered. Our poisonous fumes destroy anyone who hampers us in our discharge of duties. Our flames are capable of reaching down to the earth and scalding anyone who seeks to destroy this three-fold division of the world. These norms have been established to save society from various passions, deformities, pain and fear. Our venomous flames rise up like vapour against its enemies, internal and external.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Have you improved or weakened the condition of our country? Have you mixed poison or nectar in the hopes and aspirations of our country?’ A torrent of poison rained over them. The great serpent entwined them both in his coils and opened its cavernous mouth to engulf them. Kumud clung to Sarasvatichandra and said, ‘Husband, look! The head of this great serpent is filled with divine gems!’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Beloved, Sita saw a golden deer. Are you not similarly deceived? Where do you see light and gems amidst this shower of poison?’ The serpent crushed them even more, bringing their bodies together as if in a light embrace. Kumud’s mangalsutra pressed against his heart, and he immediately spoke up, ‘Kumud! Kumud, you are right! These serpents are the true and eternal rulers of the land of Aryas. Our rulers and emperors are rulers only for namesake. Their gems and stones are all false. The true, pure gems are in the crowns of these eternal kings. I see them now. Oh, what a beautiful light!’ As soon as he uttered these words, the great serpent freed them. The poison showers stopped and the serpents went back to the roots from which they hung. The great serpent also disappeared, leaving behind a heap of divine gems. Kumud and Sarasvatichandra’s eyes were dazzled by the light of the gems and within moments, the world around them was transformed magically. The dark, black stone ceiling made way for a ceiling of translucent coloured glass. The roots of the tree also became glass. Priceless divine gems hung from the tree like so many chandeliers. Beautiful verdant orchards sprung up around them. Heavenly trees, ponds, fountains, springs and brooks, creepers with amazing flowers and delicate shrubs emerged in place of the dark, venomous world of a moment ago. The scene filled their eyes with wondrous joy. Kumud: ‘Oh my beloved heart! Where has that frightful world of serpents gone? What is this transformation? We are in the same land, but in completely different surroundings. What is this miracle?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The serpents who spewed venom on us are also the bearers of these gems. Those whose visions are poisonous are greeted with venom, as poison kills poison. Those whose vision is aglow with divine light are bestowed with this divine sight. Those with Satvik vision see both the poison and the gems simultaneously. As humans we were first greeted with poison. Our hearts, united as one, could withstand that dark world, and we came even closer. In the moment of embrace we were joined by the Parasmani of your mangalsutra, which allowed us to see these divine gems.’ Kumud: ‘Beautiful, colourful images filter from the translucent ceiling on these gems and garden. A web of seven-hued lights is formed by it.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The Chintamani on my ring makes this vision possible for you.’ Kumud: ‘The light is ever more luminous.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The light of Emperor Ashoka Priyadarshi has shone for over a thousand years. The serpents also live in the reflection of this light. This light of the serpents prevails, and the great mounds and pillars are rooted in them.’ Kumud: ‘The roots are countless; at each root I see a sacrificial altar. What is that being offered to the fire?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The subtle bodies of those offering the sacrifice are being offered as oblation. The sacred ash is from scriptures and norms which scatters around and is being received by people. The lives of many sages are being offered in the sacrifice.’ Kumud: ‘Why does the sublime white light that is here not permeate the upper regions?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Lord Buddha’s light slowly permeates out of this orchard. Below us are the golden domes of the temple of Bhishma; some of its light and fresh winds travel upwards. The light we see is a mixture of these two lights of Buddha and Bhishma. This new force pushes some rays of light to move upwards while the rest get scattered.’ Kumud: ‘These gems also reflect many images.’ Kumud filled her palms with gems and looked at their reflection in the ceiling above. Sarasvatichandra: ‘Kumud, look at those images and tell me what you see. Aren’t the courtship and love marriages prevalent in Europe to be found around us as well? In the upper regions there are pillars for every caste, all divided and segregated. Isn’t the world around us united and one? Isn’t this field of righteousness nurtured by renunciation, generosity, virtue and compassion? Are not the people living under it nourished, enriched and enlightened by it? Are they not glorious and powerful as a result?⟨fn:423⟩ Kumud, observe these gems closely and explain what you feel from your heart.’

Kumud: ‘Oh lord of my heart! I see one light—neither weak, nor harsh—permeate the entire land of India. I hear songs of joy coming from villages and cities alike. I see ascetics and persons of virtue move about freely and fearlessly in the forests, on mountains, on river banks and on the sea coast. Their concern for the welfare of all delights my heart. Their physical bodies are healthy, fecund, beautiful and clean. Our present generation in comparison is short, weak and diseased; they appear like children in comparison. The world reflected below and our present world are different in every aspect: in intellect, learning, asceticism, love and all forms of virtue. Oh dear husband, those people are great pilgrims. Scholars and merchants of India are everywhere—in Lanka, Java and Sumatra in the south; in Tibet, China, Kandhar, Tartar and Rome in the north; in Egypt in the west and in Brahmadesh and Siam in the east. Their boats and chariots are constantly on the move. Oh my beloved, how courageous they are! Their households are a world unto themselves. In each village I see couples in love swinging on silver swings, submitting themselves to the arrows of Kamdev, the lord of desire. Scenes of affluence, joy, wealth, consumption and renunciation fill the sight. Couples in love are also engaged in the service of their parents, who are content with their children but do not seek indulgent service. They want the son and daughter-in-law to perform their other vocations of generating wealth and engaging with each other in mutual love and desire. Family strife is completely absent. The destitute are cared for. People might feel tired of earning money but they spend it tirelessly for others. Assemblies of people gather at places to consider issues of importance for citizens and communicate them to the rulers. Rulers take satisfaction in meeting the wants and aspirations of the people. Sages cultivate diverse fields of knowledge and pursue many sciences. Scriptures are meant for the welfare of the people. Children, youth and elders are all happy. Women, men, family, village, king and kingdom are all equally imbued with beauty, knowledge, wealth and an unsullied vision of good; the sacred altars burn with fires that help maintain and uplift Sanatan and Arya dharma. The earth is fecund, beautiful and green. I see many enlightened beings like Kalidasa, Bhavabhuti, Vikram and Shalivahana roam the worlds fearlessly. Oh my dear, the joy of this scene is the culmination of our pilgrimage.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I see all that you see, and I experience the fulfillment that you do.’ Kumud: ‘Now turn your gaze towards the gems that I hold in my hands. Touch the Parasmani that I wear, and show me what you see in your Chintamani. Our coming together, this union is not possible without the full-bodied embrace of male and female hearts.’ Sarasvatichandra held her hands and raised them to his eyes. ‘Kumud, the world above us is divided by many pillars; but below us there are four divisions shaped like the swastika. There are four varnas contained in them—one is white, the second is iron, the third golden while the fourth is black. These are divided and segregated, but at many places they are joined by bridges. These golden bridges cross over the dividing gulf. From the east, the light of the land of Buddha has begun to spill forth, and in this light the four varnas are melting like metal in fire, the dividing walls are crumbling and I see the world as one.’ Kumud: ‘Why then did we see those fissures and divisions?’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘If there are scenes of beauty, there are also scenes of open grossness.⟨fn:424⟩ In the name of love, libidinous sensualism destroys the altars of Pitru Yajna and gives free play to passions. Under cover of pure sacrifice by some, crowds of men and women driven by animal passions roam with abandon.⟨fn:425⟩ The serpents are spewing venom on them to quell the passions of these debauched couples. If their passions cannot be brought under control, the serpents are determined to destroy them. Oh, the poisonous showers are annihilating! The foundations of desire and the aspirations of women crumble with a touch of this potent venom. I see their world of love vaporise. Parents are eager to marry off their children even before they understand the idea of love. The venom has turned a deathly green. It corrodes the social body to such an extent that it flows through the atrophied veins of immorality and finally destroys the social body. The serpents have become the doctors of this diseased body. They lash it with their tails, bite it and with their venom seek to destroy the inherent sickness and poison of the social body. They infuse it with new strength and health. Kumud, your Parasmani enables us to see the beneficial aspects of this poisonous world.’ Kumud: ‘Dear husband, the serpents must have discerned some such disease in us, too, and hence they spewed venom on us.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That is correct.’ Just then a sweet but grave voice spoke up from the gems. The gems that Kumud held in her hand also joined in this divine voice: ‘Oh humans, you have the fitness to acquire Satvik vision. Those capable of seeing their own shortcomings and the virtues of others are bestowed with this vision. Such vision has been granted to you both. Pray listen to what we gems have to say. You saw the poison of the serpents restoring the health of the diseased social body. That potion of health is composed of a combination of venom and gems. Its light and health-restoring powers extend beyond the clouds of smoke arising from the sacrificial fires. Our rays give potency to that light, and the serpents’ venom has the power to destroy its enemies. But you can now see layers of black soot darken that light. Those layers of soot have been formed by Tamas. Neither the serpents’ venom nor our rays can reach that height and destroy it. Earlier the venom destroyed darkness; but now under the protective layers of soot, darkness and Tamas grow unchecked and unhampered. You saw the mounds of darkness that have formed as a result. The corrosive powers of this darkness erode the bridges that join the four ancient rocks; the rocks shake and crash into each other and crumble. The divisions of caste and the social distances between them have been created by the power of Tamas. The vision of these serpents extends sky-high. We clearly see the mockery, the disregard, the abuses hurled at us by the people of this age. We are powerless to challenge them from this distance. ‘If you are indeed humans from earth and if you return to that land, please support that restorative venom and our light. If you see patterns of coloured light formed by us, please make them come into contact with the light of our gems. If you see earthworms—who have descended from us but are in a fallen state—make them aware of our light and the potency of the venom; teach them to cull out the essence of our traditions. Other creatures of that dark world feed on the dust and eventually merge into that dust. Feed these creatures, drop by drop, the essence of our light and restorative venom. So long as our vision extends to that world and so far as the fame of our capacities is known among the people, we retain the hope that our efforts will bear fruit. So long as we remain hopeful, the serpents shall cling to the roots of the banyan tree, and we shall throw up like a fountain our restorative venom and rays of light. For millennia we have survived on air and held on to this position; we will not abandon our duty for fear or any other unseen reason. Some day these mounds will crumble and block our vision completely. Sometime in the future, humans of a new age will remove these mounds of earth and formulate norms that are higher than the ones we formed. Till such time we, the serpents, will continue our penance. At the conclusion of our penance, we shall go to the roots of this great banyan tree and merge into the great serpent, the Shesha Nag. Till such time we shall not abandon either our endeavour or our sacrifice. Oh humans, if you do not fear the impurities of excreta and the poison of the world above us, please travel there before you visit Bhishma. But if you fear their impurities, you will be able to see some of that world through the shaft of our light.’ The voice disappeared, but the shaft of light remained; it carried the light of the gems to the higher regions. The two of them stood at the centre of this shaft of light and rose upwards on their wings. They emerged at the place from which they had begun their descent. Open sky and breeze comforted them. Waves of light emanating from Bhishma encircled the island. They sat quietly watching these waves. Sarasvatichandra kept his hand on Kumud’s shoulder and said, ‘Kumud, the ground beneath us seems to be moving.’ ‘Yes.’ They stood up. They saw a spade dig the ground and make a hole. They saw some creatures inside the hole. The area around them was aglow with the light of the gems. Sarasvatichandra recognised some of those forms. ‘Kumud! Kumud! This is a reflection of our reformist friends! Look how they endeavour to breathe some life into the other petrified creatures? But alas, the mud remains untransformed, the darkness grows unabated. And there are some strange noises!’ Kumud: ‘Look how their lives are soiled in the mud and disappear! What can we do for them?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘These are mere reflections. It is pointless to have any pity for reflections. But the cacophony has become shrill; these creatures are surrounded by mud and venomous flames.’ Kumud: ‘That I see. Now look at these creatures minutely. They have fully formed mouths and tongues. But they have only one eye. The monkeys carry divine potions in the sky. Drops of this potion fall into the eyes of these creatures and layers are formed, which give them myopic vision. Oh my dear! Help them by removing these layers and have them granted the other eye as well.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Their vision will be restored only when the light of the gems from the crowns of serpents falls into their eyes. The restoration of both eyes would require even rarer, purer light.’

Kumud: ‘What is this noise about?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Some of these creatures are one-eyed while others are blind; some even have inverted eyes. They crash into one another, they fight, quarrel and kill. The noise comes from their screams.’ Kumud: ‘Who are the creatures with inverted eyes and who are the blind?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The creatures with inverted eyes can perceive the world created by the serpents only as inverted; they cannot see it as it is. The others have been blinded by their own Tamas. They form pathways through the mud, and other creatures follow them blindly. They subsist on the mud; it is their life. Some follow the creatures with inverted eyes by their smell. They cannot tolerate the venom that surrounds them. They remain in pain till the end of their lives, and their decomposing bodies further sully the mud.’ Kumud: ‘It is a terrible sight.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Even in this terrible world, there are patterns of Satva and those creatures which come under its sway due to fate remain happy and content for a time.’ Kumud: ‘Yes, these patterns are formed by white light.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘But the mud rushes in from all sides to cover it.’ Kumud: ‘Oh! That white light will be completely covered. Dear husband, do save it!’ Sarasvatichandra smiled and said, ‘The white light cannot be subdued so easily. The light pierces through the mud and the mud makes way for it. Look Kumud, shafts of light are emerging from those two places.’ Kumud got up startled. ‘Oh my beloved, those are the images of my Gunial and my father! How are they here?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘They are followed by the image of Buddhidhanbhai! They have emerged here because of the power of the spade. They are approaching us.’ Gunasundari and Vidya Chatura approached them. Vidya Chatura held a globe in his hand with the map of Ratnanagari engraved upon it. As he walked, his eyes were on the map. Gunasundari walked beside him, and at times behind him. At times she also walked ahead of him. Her eyes were fixed on Vidya Chatura. She ensured that the globe did not fall from his hand and that he did not tire out with the effort. Their shadows accompanied them. In the shadow was a beautiful image— of Gunasundari’s household. Gunasundari was seated on an altar at the centre. Her body was on fire. Fountains of nectar emerged from her body. Gunasundari tried to feed the creatures with this nectar. The creatures clung to her body and tore into her. The flames of her penance extended to the sky. Gunasundari and Vidya Chatura came close. Kumud bowed to them with folded hands. The images walked away. Gunasundari’s words, ‘Kumud! My Kumud!’ echoed through their ears. Kumud turned fearful. She was about to say something to Sarasvatichandra, when Buddhidhan’s image approached them. A web of small and large creatures engulfed his image. Jadsinh’s court, Shathrai, Bhupsinh and Buddhidhan’s retainers clung to him like so many leeches. Buddhidhan’s image shone through the web. He held a creature in his hand, who was unmistakably Pramaddhan. Buddhidhan flung him into darkness and said, ‘Kumud Sundari, your enemy has been thus punished.’ Buddhidhan was followed by the immortal body of Saubhagya Devi who drew some images with light. These images walked past them and towards the pond filled with light. They walked over the light. Many other images emerged from the mound of mud. Mena Rani dressed in black garments emerged, followed by the immortal body of Mallaraj. He held a lotus in his hand. Mallaraj touched Mena’s heart with the lotus. The lotus sang: ‘The lord of the universe holds a conch that drives fear through the hearts of enemies; for the succour of his devotees he holds a lotus, too. Mena, your love is alive!’ Chandralaxmi’s immortal body floated past them holding the withered reflection of Laxminandan. She was trying to breathe life into him. Many other images emerged from the mound. A mysterious voice was heard: ‘Oh humans, you wish to destroy the mounds! Many such pure images fill our heart. They have been created and nurtured by the light from the crown jewels of serpents. If you destroy us, they, too, will be destroyed. Think before you act. You can destroy us only after you create such images with your endeavour. The images will survive only if the mounds survive. If you do not act with pure intention, these gems will not come to your hands again and you shall not have the powers bestowed by the serpents.’ The voice subsided. The hillocks seemed to roar with laughter. Sand and stones spewed out of them. The eruption subsided and a voice said, ‘Oh gems! You are feminine and hence tremble at this fake danger. If you want to see the power of your destroyer, look at the condition of these one-eyed creatures!’ This voice also receded. They could see many forms with iron spades attack the hillock. They struck hard but mud rushed into crush them. The attackers were buried under the mounds of mud; someone’s hands, someone’s head or a part of the spade jutted out of the mounds. It was a heart-wrenching sight. A voice from the skies issued a warning: ‘Martyrs of Truth, Righteousness and Purity! It is resultless and needlessly dangerous to delve these hollow, crumbling all-absorbing hillocks. Follow rather the lights that have created them; and the hands that have evolved them by some stern decree of fate will help you right royally in transforming them into such purer, sounder and beneficent shapes as all will hail. Bring but the rich chemicals that will melt and not destroy these sandy piles. Bring but the patience, the perseverance, the skill, the art and the science that will melt these ancient sands and earth works, which a seeming maniac has laboured to build up for ages, and out of them this nation will find a vast auriferous yield, and the sandy alloy will evaporate.’⟨fn:426⟩ Sarasvatichandra’s heart palpitated as he heard the stern warning. Kumud’s heart also trembled. Both of them got up, the voice subsided and one after another, the images also receded. The images of Laxminandan, Buddhidhan, Vidya Chatura and Gunasundari lingered on with the immortal bodies of Chandralaxmi, Saubhagya Devi and Dharmalaxmi. Vidya Chatura held Gunasundari in his arms and sang. Sarasvatichandra and Kumud stood with folded hands, listening to the song. Is God in penance? Is God in telling the beads? Neither worship nor pilgrimage Attain Him! O’ beloved, find Him! You bore hardships, gave joy in return, You alleviated the sufferings of all. You did not seek praise, You bore heart-piercing wounds. You pushed aside all selfishness, You shunned even pleasures of youth. You did not indulge your daughter, Nor remembered your mother. Your penance was unending, Your worship was Action. O’ fulfilled, ascetic woman, I nurture your action with love. Kingdom of God is within you, That is your worship. God of others is without, Gunial subsists on God within. If your aspiration forever is To bear pain and give joy, Beloved God will never be Distinct from you. There is no other duty, No other meaning of God, No other path to salvation, You remain my beloved for this. We are one for lives to come. Gunial is true to her pledge. May God ever reside in you. I am thou and thou art me. As the song began, Gunasundari could be seen cleaning utensils, sweeping the floor, as the torn pages of her books were scattered around. Vidya Chatura collected these pages and stood by Gunasundari in a subservient pose. Dharmalaxmi’s immortal body appeared. Her gaze turned the utensils golden, the broom turned into a book, the ash used to clean utensils turned into gems and the dirt transformed into letters of the alphabet. The torn pages in Vidya Chatura’s hands became a pearl necklace around Gunasundari’s neck. Dharmalaxmi addressed Kumud in a sombre voice, ‘Daughter! The penance of your mother is many folds greater than mine. I worshipped the gods, but the gods favoured the worship offered by your mother. You behold its power before you. For her, God and worship have come to embody service—service to her parents-in-law and husband’s family. She has received the fruits of this great worship and will receive much more. Your mother joined in the Pitru Yajna of my son as one with him. She has harboured no anger towards those who despised her; praise gave her no joy, and she did not succumb to sorrow in times of hardship. Neither knowledge nor wealth made her proud. She has lived in the midst of the pure light in which the two of you have undertaken this pilgrimage. Daughter, let this pious presence grant you peace and knowledge. Though immortal in body, I am fit only to be her servant. Your grandfather has known this from the very beginning. He worshipped your mother Gunasundari with this attitude; hence all his sins have been washed away. That pure soul will one day be here in his immortal body. I understood this only after I came to this land. I am like the dust of her feet. Your father, too, has been purified through service to her.’ Dharmalaxmi’s voice subsided and the images became blurred. Buddhidhan’s image shone forth. He was now in the garb of an ascetic. Alak Kishori was with him. She said, ‘Bhabhi! Bhabhi, come back! Devi is gone, but you must come back!’ The image of Laxminandan wept, his tears sparkled in the light. His heartfelt cry rang through the skies, ‘Bhai! Bhai! I will not live if you do not return within this month!’ All voices receded. The rustle of wind on the waves was all that could be heard. Suddenly, lightning struck with terrible thunder to match the firing of a thousand canons. Its reflection in the pond was a terrifying sight. The moon set. Darkness prevailed. The play of lighting and darkness made a frightful spectacle. The breeze turned into a fierce gale and the waves rose and fell with it. The darkness spread everywhere and with it, the roaring wind. Sarasvatichandra and Kumud could no longer see each other. She held him in a tight embrace. Lightning struck again and again with terrible claps of thunder. Finally, darkness prevailed over lightning. They saw their elders submerge in the pond of light and heard the final terrible cries: ‘Kumud! Bhai! Bhabhi!’ Sarasvatichandra found a tearful Kumud holding him tightly. As the lightning ceased, their wings lifted them up and propelled them towards the terrible cries at a speed faster than the speed of light. Their bodies were lifted up and dropped into the pond of light, the Pitamah Kund. They sank to its bottom and with that, their combined dream came to an end. Kumud was asleep in the Saumanasya Gufa with Sarasvatichandra’s feet cradled in her lap. At that time the moon set here on earth as well, and darkness prevailed. Neither Kumud nor Sarasvatichandra could be seen. And now dear reader, we must wait for their illumined inner worlds to create a new universe.
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra and Kumud journey to Pitamahpur, encountering wise talking dogs and witnessing India's reflections in a mystical pond before a dream-shattering storm.

chapters.title: Host or Guest? Or the Authority of Selfless Intellect in Considerations of Virtue and Vice
paragraphs: Host or Guest? Or the Authority of Selfless Intellect in Considerations of Virtue and Vice Thyself and thy belongings Are not thine own so proper, as to waste Thyself upon thy virtues, they on thee. Heaven doth with us as we with torches do, Not light them for themselves: for if our virtues Did not go forth of us, ’t were all alike As if we had them not. Spirits are not finely touch’d But to fine issues: nor Nature never lends The smallest scruple of her excellence, But, like a thrifty goddess, she determines Herself the glory of a creditor, Both thanks and use.⟨fn:427⟩ Their sleep did not last much longer. The last hours of a Chaitra night on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight usually give sound sleep. But Kumud woke up. The pleasure of the touch of Sarasvatichandra’s feet neither allowed her to open her eyes, nor allowed her to sleep. A cuckoo cooed from some tree, and with its call her heart awakened. She awoke to the realisation that his touch had become alluring, a touch of pleasure. She was a little confused, but soon her confusion turned to shame, and shame turned to fright. She tried to lift the beloved’s feet and felt them to be feverish. She imagined their warmth to be the heat of desire; love and compassion filled her heart and she, too, was tempted to prolong the touch. She could not get up. In all this confusion she remembered her dream, which deepened her confusion. The images of her mother, father and parents-in-law flashed before her eyes again. She was startled by that memory. She regained possession of her senses; she gently placed his feet on the platform and moved to one side. She lay down as if asleep and in fact did fall asleep as well. Sarasvatichandra, unaccustomed to her delicate touch, was in a state of incomprehension; his memory of the dream and the pleasure of her touch pulled him along to an unfamiliar world. As the cause of the dreamlike state was removed, he sat up alert. He looked around; as his eyes grew accustomed to the pre-dawn darkness, he saw Kumud asleep at some distance. ‘Is that Kumud Sundari?’ he was about to ask, but instead he gazed upon the lovely form. If there was darkness, there were stars as well. His mind was torn between the desire for pleasure and the knowledge of its undesirability. Kumud woke up from her light sleep and saw Sarasvatichandra. At that very moment the eyes of that fortunate man opened and the question: ‘What should I do? What is my duty?’ washed away all traces of desire. ‘Kumud Sundari! You slept here? Are you awake now?’ he asked. At the same time Kumud asked, ‘Sarasvatichandra! Didn’t you get any sleep?’ She sat up. ‘I was alone in Vasant Gufa and thought of you. Sleep eluded me, so I came here,’ Kumud clarified before Sarasvatichandra could say anything. ‘Did you spend the night sitting on the platform?’ he asked. Kumud felt abashed, confused, but finally mustered the courage and said, ‘Yes. I felt that you had fever. That worry brought me here. I could not have ascertained it without touching you. I felt that touching your feet would purify me and also allow me to know the state of your fever. So I took your feet in my lap and fell asleep. When I woke up, I moved away and lay down to sleep. I woke up when I heard you move.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I disturbed your sleep, didn’t I?’ Kumud: ‘The one who showed me what deep, undisturbed sleep could be like also has the right to weave new patterns into it.’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘The touch of my feet defiled your pure aspirations.’ Kumud: ‘Purity and impurity are contingent upon the state of mind. I fell asleep and thereby defiled both our pure aspirations. You might have disturbed my sleep, but I would have caused a rupture in your penance. I am fated to be impure, but I have defiled you.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I have surrendered all rights to you. You have every right to take away anything from my destiny and make it yours to satisfy your aspirations. Therein lies my penance.’ Kumud: ‘You must not speak of penance. The word itself fills me with dread.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I am willing to do even that.’ Kumud: ‘Yesterday you said that I had to determine for myself my duties. I wish that you would clarify the means available to me.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That can be clarified through the questions you pose.’ Kumud: ‘Are you in the role of a host vis-à-vis me?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I am a host to the extent that you are a host to me.’ Kumud: ‘Who then is the host and who the guest?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘For you I am a guest and for me you are one as well.’ Kumud: ‘Is this how Priti Yajna is concluded?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘No. There, two hearts are united as one. Imagine two mirrors placed exactly opposite each other; they reflect each other. Similarly couples thus united reflect each other’s thoughts and aspirations and attain a non-dual existence.’ Kumud: ‘Is there any objection to us attaining such non-duality?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The state of non-duality cannot be forged by us mere humans. It is the will of God.’ Kumud: ‘My aspiration is salvation for both of us. I despise happiness that can be obtained through material comfort. But desire itself does not leave me.’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘Desire can be erased only through a mutually attained non-duality. When a lump of sugar is placed on the tongue, it is the nature of the tongue to soften it with saliva and push it down the throat to the stomach. This is inevitable. When the tongue is desireless and the hand that places the sugar remains tight-fisted, the task of non-consumption of sugar is achieved.’ Kumud: ‘Desire is like gun powder; the mere mention of it ignites desire, but without expressing it two hearts cannot be opened to each other. To eradicate desire one must open the heart and speak of it frankly.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Some desires can be satiated even by silence. Take for instance two wayfarers going through a forest. They meet a thief and both are frightened. If one were to share his feelings with the other, the other would also begin to experience fright whereas initially he was not frightened. And if the other one had also been scared, his companion’s fright would intensify his fear. If they were to open their hearts, both would be weakened. But if they were to keep their fright to themselves and make an outward show of courage, both would be emboldened. Silence in this instance destroys fear. Similarly, if a man and woman do not open their hearts, but in fact conceal their desire, eventually desire would erode and become powerless like a wick without oil.’ Kumud: ‘Desire increases with the knowledge that it is possible to satisfy it.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘This knowledge is dangerous.’ Kumud: ‘If one is destined to experience this fear, what should one do?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Fate can only be countered by fate. It needs the grace of God. Human pride is nothing but false ego in this case.’ Kumud: ‘That is correct. But what is a human being to do? What means are available to us?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Erasure of desire, shame at the idea, cultivation of virtuous thought and firm resolve are the means which push away desire. But its complete eradication depends upon the spiritual attainments of the subtle body.’ Kumud: ‘Desire erupts suddenly; is it not doused equally suddenly?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Wind fans fire; it also smothers it. A sudden realisation of the undesirability of desire can cool passions. A learned person in a moment of amnesia might experience attachment; but at the moment of realisation of such folly, attachment disappears.’ Kumud: ‘Why did God create this web of desires and passion? That snare shakes the world upside down for no reason whatsoever. Its pleasure and pain are both false.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Pleasure and pain may be false, but no creation of God is without a cause.’ Kumud: ‘Desire ultimately brings pain and deserves to be eradicated.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Come and sit with me on the platform and let me explain to you that desire also has its use.’ Kumud: ‘No, I am better off where I am. Fire has to be kept away from ghee.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘You have said the right thing. You have brought it to my attention, and therein lie the seeds of eradication of your desires. Kumud Sundari, you have grasped the true meaning of eradication of desire, and God will bestow upon you the strength necessary for it. Now let me explain to you the necessity of desire. An inanimate object has neither knowledge nor desire. It acts according to its innate properties and subsists in the world. Animals, birds and other creatures possess knowledge about their survival and have passions. They are able to survive and feed on each other. Human beings in their barbaric state were similar to animals; with evolution their intellect and passions also evolved and grew subtler. Humans developed pure intellect and subtle desires. Subtle desires gave rise to the sense of duty, rectitude and religion. Other animals have desires and aspirations to fulfill those. Some humans wish to assist and aid the process of fulfillment of these desires; the sense of moral obligation towards others emerges from this impulse. In absence of this sensibility all beings, whether sentient or inanimate, would be equal. Inanimate objects do not have a sense of duty; similarly human beings would neither be guests nor hosts.
