A person of knowledge perceives duties and obligations that remain unknown to the human eye. This sense of duty nourishes the world and social order. ‘God places desire in all humans—even before they acquire any knowledge or awareness of it. The purpose of desire is the nourishment of the world. In absence of desire why would parents nourish their children? A mother knows the helpless state of her child; she nourishes it with her milk and gives her child shelter and care in this harsh, crude world. Desires of men and women nurture their hearts. The Kama Sutra describes desires as duties akin to the consumption of food; it is required for the body. To an undiscerning eye this might appear true for individual human beings. To an extent this is true, but that is not the principal intent. This statement is addressed to the collectivity. Human passion adds to the numbers of human beings and allows the continuation of the human race. Even for the human collectivity, lust and desire are akin to food; by shunning them completely, humans harm collectivities. But fasting is necessary both for the individual body and the collectivity. Similarly, renunciation of desire by some is beneficial to the collectivity.’ Kumud: ‘If desire is akin to hunger and thirst and hence beneficial, is it not detrimental to seek its eradication out of fear of the happiness and pain it causes?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Metaphors of hunger and thirst are inappropriate to describe desires. The causes and reach of hunger and thirst are universal; they are independent of human beings and integral to the daily subsistence of creation. Desire is related to the instinct of the senses. The sense of perception receives knowledge and craves a certain type of knowledge. The ears desire songs and knowledge that is communicated through words; the nose desires aroma; the eyes desire beautiful forms and the tongue desires taste. The senses and the inner world of a person inspire entry into a new world. The senses and the conscience of a person together churn the knowledge that is received, and impregnate it with aspirations. Just like the foetus in a mother’s womb, some instinct nourishes it with affection and feeds it breast milk. This affection, this breastfeed nourishes desires. This instinct is the aesthetic root of desire. Just as the tongue salivates, instincts intent upon desires grow. But desire by its nature is like a flooding river. A dam controls floods; the unrestrained flow of desire results in debauched conduct. Farsighted and intelligent persons curb this instinct at its root. The causes of desire are avoidable; their flow can be arrested and obstacles to limit its reach can be placed in its path. Both knowledge and aesthetic pleasures have this kind of autonomy. It is due to this autonomy that the possibility of both controlling them and also submitting to them are open. Just as the sword both protects and kills a person of virtue, desire both creates and destroys social order. When desires turn destructive, it is incumbent upon us to seek to destroy them; so long as they are beneficial it is our duty to nurture them. Where questions of merit and demerit of virtue and vice do not arise, human instinct is autonomous. But where instincts are not autonomous, where they are bound by considerations of right conduct, it is sinful to disregard these considerations.’ Kumud: ‘Is the passion of a couple subject to only their self-control or are there other limits, too? When can these become an impediment?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The givers of our scriptures have provided for ritual observances like Ekadashi, and the wise still follow these injunctions. What the ascetics describe as subtle love is like molten lava that stays hidden beneath the crusts of the earth and at the ripe moment, bursts forth and spreads. We have no control over its movement or force. What is described as love by society is nothing but bodily passions, but they can be modulated—as the ascetics do—through penance.’ Kumud: ‘The ascetics believe that love is the root of marriage. I cannot understand the views of the householders. But if the ascetics are right, why are marriage rituals, like Saptpadi, regarded as essential? If the views of householders were valid, courtship would be immoral. If the ascetics were right, our marriages should be regarded as immoral. Divorce and remarriage to a partner one loves would be moral. I fail to understand both the norms of marriage among ascetics and the rituals of the householders. Can a couple, not married in the worldly sense, control their passions, and if yes, how?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘All creations of the Creator are purposeful and have an order. He created humans and allowed them to create some of their own norms, while other norms have been created by non-human agencies. Ascetics and persons of virtue glean for themselves a sense of duties and norms from creation itself. They preserve, maintain and live by these duties and norms in all times and spaces. This is called the Sanatan Dharma. Wise and able persons develop for their own times and context a set of norms and organisations. These are specific to their times and its imperatives. These specific duties are also for the welfare of people. The rituals of Sanatan Dharma are eternal and meant for healthy consciences. But if consciences were to become diseased, specific norms are formulated for them. As people become healthier and robust, the specific norms make way for the eternal norms. Sanatan Dharma is like food, while the specific norms are akin to remedial medicine. The rule is that food and medicine have to be kept apart and consumed according to need. Courtship is a ritual of eternal validity. When two hearts come together in pure love, marriage is solemnised. The ritual of marriage is an embodiment of this subtle love. Ascetics and virtuous persons in all countries have formulated similar principles for the wellbeing of their people. An ascetic couple that accepts such a marriage of the heart performs the ritual of marriage to signal their union to others. It acts like a boundary that others should not cross and seek to disrupt their sacrifice. According to eternal immutable laws the cause of marriage is love and the result of it is also love. The beauty, pleasure and growth of society are also because of love, and ascetics accept love as an integral aspect of the world created by God. A child’s body grows into youth. Similarly, love also grows. Love, like body parts, cannot be discarded. In our country, at some point, the ground from which love grows and the roots of the tree of love were found wanting and diseased. Hence, the ground and the seed of love came to be neglected. Some saplings and plants are grown in pots; their roots cannot enter the ground because they are bound by the pot. In this land the sapling of love has been planted in the pot called child-marriage, and its caretakers are content with its bounded growth. They find this remedy for the disease beneficial. ‘Kumud Sundari, so long as we live among our people, our and society’s welfare can be best secured by following their norms; therein lies our duty. If we renounce society and become ascetics, we would be governed by eternal laws. All the ascetics after due examination have decided that we are one among them. Hence, we have been freed from societal norms and have acquired the right to follow the eternal laws.’ As he spoke these words, Kumud got up and sat beside him on the platform. She was careful to keep some distance from him. She said, ‘You have come to this conclusion after careful consideration. It is my duty to sit beside you.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Why?’ Kumud: ‘Desire that is not immoral should be satiated; therein lies peace and tranquility. Compassion is also a desire.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Whom do you wish to be compassionate towards?’ Kumud: ‘I felt a fever in your body; it is my duty to remedy it.’ Sarasvatichandra laughed out loud and extended his arm. ‘You have been cheated. Take my hand—is it cool or feverish?’ Kumud held his hand and replied, ‘At this point your hand is steady, tranquil and cool. What a surprise! It was not the case at night.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Your hand is warm, but it has begun to cool down.’ Kumud: ‘And now your hand also feels warm.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Kumud Sundari, as you release my hand from your grasp it will begin to cool down; yours has become cooler now. These are momentary passions; they arise due to transient reasons. It is not your duty to feel compassionate towards what is not permanent. Our constant and permanent desire is salvation. We do not desire momentary pleasure, nor do we want to eradicate passing sorrows.’ Kumud released his hand and said, ‘You are right. My touch brings fever to your body and it cools down when that touch is removed. I feel feverish when I feel pity for you.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That pity is misplaced.’

Kumud: ‘Whether it be misplaced or well-placed, whether it is my duty or not, clearly it cannot be immoral?’ Sarasvatichandra considered this proposition for a while and said, ‘That is also a fact. Kumud Sundari, a king makes laws for the collectivity that is his populace. It is the duty of all virtuous persons to abide by these laws even when the authority of the king is not immediately present. Therein lies the welfare of social order.’ Kumud: ‘Which command of the king are we likely to disobey?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘According to the law you have not yet attained the age of maturity, and not you but your father has control over your fate. Without his consent our being together or married is forbidden as per the royal command. If you stay with Chandravali or become an inhabitant of the Parivrajika Math for at least two years, the king and his laws cannot stop our journey together to the Vihar Math. It is the duty of the king to make laws that are beneficial to society and the laws so formulated are accepted even by the ascetics. The ascetics believe that laws formulated for the larger good ought not to be violated as such violation would lead to disorder and harm. A path that can cause harm is forbidden for the ascetics. Hence, with regard to the laws they accept the kingly command as they would a command of their Master.’ Kumud: ‘So had you forgotten about this prohibition till now?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘No. That prohibition does not apply to you. It applies only to me. I would be the criminal and punished for it, not you. I am prepared to accept the king’s punishment as penance. But I have no intention of committing that crime; and so long as I do not challenge that law on the basis of some other norms, I am not guilty in the eyes of God. If my actions hold me guilty in the eyes of God, I will accept the punishment thereof as penance. I crave that punishment and therefore, I did not mention the prohibition to you. But as you expressed your desire and fears, it was incumbent upon me to speak the truth.’ Kumud: ‘So long as this body persists, compassion will abide. Last night you spoke of three options. For the next two years we will stay apart from each other like Chandravali and Viharpuri. During the next five days and nights we will think of the future; we could stay in a grass hut or live in the Vihar Math or some other arrangement could be conceived. We shall during these five days also decide our conduct towards each other during this period of enforced separation. I will do nothing that will place your precious body in any danger of being held guilty by the king.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Our moral conduct is essential not only for us. I am not in the least afraid of inviting the wrath of the king. But the prestige of this pious ascetic community might suffer and invite censure both from the king and the society. It would be a cruel response to the generosity they have shown us.’ Kumud: ‘You strengthen my heart by your desire to seek the welfare of others by moral conduct. Your desire not to endanger the prestige of the ascetics will reduce all my passions to ashes.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘It is a new dawn.’ Kumud: ‘And with it, there is a new light and awakening within us as well.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What that light and awakening should be is your decision.’ Kumud: ‘The execution of this decision is like household work, and I should formulate it. My companions must have woken up. I should meet them, and so should you meet your companions. We have been brought together by the ascetics; with their consent I shall come back here and be of service to you. I still need to know from you as to how you intend to spend the rest of your life, what actions you wish to perform for your own welfare as also the welfare of the people and through what means I could be of assistance in your endeavours. I will cherish with all my love the wisdom and pleasure that you give me. Now please wear your robes. I seek your permission to leave for the time being.’ The couple, brought together by subtle love, separated. Kumud walked away towards the bridge. Before she left, the two subtle bodies, keeping apart their physical selves, embraced each other.
chapters.summary: Kumud and Sarasvatichandra awaken to a profound dawn discussion, grappling with desire, duty, and their complex relationship, as they seek to define their spiritual path.

chapters.title: The Social Aspects of Subtle Love
paragraphs: The Social Aspects of Subtle Love And we shall sit at endless feast, Enjoying each the other’s good; What vaster dream can hit the mood Of love on earth?⟨fn:428⟩ This lovely maid, The soft light of your eyes, assuredly, Regards you bound to her in love’s alliance. What should prevent your union? Fate and love Combined seem labouring to effect it.⟨fn:429⟩ Kumud Sundari came down to the lowest floor of Vasant Gufa. Her ascetic companions were busy with their morning routines. Two sadhvis had gone to the adjoining forest and brought back fresh twigs for brushing the teeth, which they distributed to the rest. Two were considering the most suitable spring to bathe in. Two others were cleaning the cave, while the rest were debating the best way of securing the welfare of women. Bhakti Maiya saw Kumud descend the stairs. As their eyes met she said, ‘Madhuri Maiya, after you clean your teeth, we shall bathe in the pure spring water.’ Kumud: ‘I will follow after the ascetics.’ Pritimanini: ‘The joy on your face suggests that.’

Yamini: ‘Madhuri, last night there were dark clouds of accusations upon the ascetics; the moon must have dispelled it.’ Kumud: ‘Only the goodness and audacity of the ascetics could have purified a wretched householder like me. Like an owl, I was blinded during the day. But at night I saw it clearly.’ Yamini: ‘Has that audacity⟨fn:430⟩ made you happy?’ Kumud: ‘That audacity has made me pure and tranquil.’ Bhakti: ‘Madhuri, your contentment will be a balm on Chandravali’s heart.’ A sadhvi named Buddha said, ‘Madhuri Maiya is at peace. She will also be content. So long as the beautiful flames of her union are not known to the world, she will spend time in great romance. Her contentment can come only when the great soul brings everything to a finale.’ Pritimanini: ‘Oh sweet Madhuri! The ascetic and virtuous force that has purified you and made you serene will also secure your welfare.’ Kumud: ‘Your wisdom can only lead to my welfare.’ Yamini: ‘Madhuri, we can be happy only when we know that you are happy. You seem to be in doubt still.’ Kumud: ‘I tremble at the fear of pain, but I seek salvation more than happiness. This desire makes me uncertain.’ Yamini: ‘When will you enter the Vihar Math? When will you become an ascetic?’ Kumud remained silent. Pritimanini: ‘Yamini! You are transgressing your limits. Madhuri Maiya has, as a result of the great endeavour of our leading ascetics, embarked upon a sacrifice of non-duality. Neither you nor I have any right to know what that sacrifice would entail. Once the two hearts meet, our task is over. One cannot raise the curtain and peep into their world of love. Among the ascetics it is considered a sin. Once love matures it manifests itself. This sense of limits is beneficial for all.

Navinchandra has taken to heart matters of her welfare. If we were to show undue concern for her, we would be accused of pride. Therefore, Yamini, your curiosity is unbecoming of an ascetic and you ought to curb it. We have been relieved of our debt and you must resist the urge to act. Madhuri Maiya, you are wise and you will receive gifts greater than just a happy state of mind. You will also contribute to the riches of our Alakh Marg. The leading ascetics diagnosed your malady and suggested a remedy. It has begun to take effect. You will emerge from this pure, tranquil and fit for salvation. This is no small achievement for our meagre capacities. On this auspicious day we should in secrecy convey the good news to Chandravali Maiya.’ The group went out to bathe and returned only at noon. Sarasvatichandra went down soon after Kumud left. He met his companions and came up after completing his morning routine. He obtained a large, blank note book from his companions and wrote the description of his strange dream. The dream that had lasted a few hours took four hours to describe. He read what he had written, leafed through some of Chandrakant’s letters. After the passage of a long time, Kumud Sundari returned. She sat down on the platform. Sarasvatichandra: ‘How did you pass your time thus far?’ Kumud: ‘I was with my companions and have brought with me a meal of fruits.’ She took out a plate of fruits, which she had covered with the end of her saree, and placed it near him. She got up and returned with a pot of pure milk. ‘What have you been writing?’ she asked him. Sarasvatichandra: ‘I had a strange but instructive dream; I have described it in this note book.’ Kumud took the note book from him and was engrossed in reading what he had written. Sarasvatichandra gazed unblinking at her face and her beautiful features. Kumud felt his eyes on her, though he was oblivious of this. She looked up at him with a smile and broke his trance. ‘The wall that separates bodily passion and subtle desire is like a fortress, but there are many secret passages that lead one to the other.’

He composed himself. ‘It is true. It is like walking on a sword’s edge.’ Kumud: ‘Yes. Where is the source of attraction? We see a person daily, and still feel attracted to them by a force so powerful it cannot be pushed away even with great effort.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Some of us make an effort to fight this impulse, but others see it as their duty to welcome it. They say, “Resist not the weakness!”⟨fn:431⟩ The ascetics understand this distinction. Kumud Sundari, with experience and caution we, too, shall cross these troubled waters.’ Kumud: ‘My compassion led me to forget the marriage vows I had pledged myself to. But I will not forget the pledge taken in your presence.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Did you read through the description?’ Kumud: ‘I wonder if I should read it through to the end or not.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What prevents you from doing so?’ Kumud: ‘It appears that you have described the great dream that I had. There were enchanting moments in it. If they emerge from the dream world into reality, the pledge would be violated.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Did you, too, have the same dream? Is there no difference between our dreams?’ Kumud: ‘There is no difference. You have not named your companion in the description. If you were to name me, it would be my dream.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The miracles of the science of dreams are strange! Kumud Sundari, there is a great lesson in this dream.’ Kumud: ‘Yes. Your aspirations and learning are expressed in such dreams without distortion. Subjects that merit scholastic treatises came to you in form of this dream due to the grace of the Master; and your love enabled me to witness it. My ascetic companions had suggested some such possibility, and hence I held on to your feet.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Kumud Sundari, I am deeply unhappy.’

Kumud: ‘You eradicated my pain. If I cannot do the same for you, I can at least be a partner and co-sharer of your sorrow.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The pain that I felt on your account was like a scorpion’s bite; it corroded me from within. This pain is like a wind that encircles and binds me.’ Kumud: ‘What is this deep sorrow?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The condition of our country and our people is the only source of this pain. My heart trembles at the mere thought as to how to be free from it.’ Kumud: ‘The dream world that the Master has promised to create will either eradicate it or show us a path of its alleviation.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘These are ascetics living a life of seclusion. Our country is caught in a whirlwind. How are they to be reconciled? What shall I tell you about it?’ Kumud: ‘I am unfit to hear of these concerns and lack the capability to understand them. But as an act of mercy, you have to make me capable.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That would depend upon the nature of our togetherness.’ Kumud: ‘Don’t you think that the norms of our togetherness have already been agreed upon?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What is accepted as order for the ascetics can be turned to disorder by society.’ Kumud: ‘I have no one but you. If your purity and piety can be ensured by the arrangements made by the ascetics, you shall have no reason to curtail the privileges already granted to me.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I will never withdraw them; but I cannot tell in which way your duty and morality will pull you.’ Kumud: ‘We shall see when that happens. No one apart from you has any use for me now. People believe that I have drowned; my parents and in-laws also believe that and mourn my loss. Gradually, I will recede from their memory. I have pushed away that world from my consciousness, and you should do likewise. So long as we are far from the path of immorality, is it not unnecessary invitation to trouble to speculate on future hardships?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That, too, is correct.’ Kumud: ‘Let’s drop that subject. How do you intend to pass your time in this monastery? How would you free yourself of this great unhappiness?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘This monastery has ample means to secure my welfare. Duties towards the country require wealth and prestige, which the monastery cannot provide me. But this grand and secluded place is ideal for contemplating ways of enabling our country to rise if one had wealth and prestige. The ability to conceive the welfare of people is rarer than both wealth and prestige. The real question is to acquire that ability. Sundargiri will show a way.’ Kumud: ‘It is your intellect that sees and comprehends these things. How can Sundargiri contribute to it? Social problems can only be resolved by society, and this place has turned its eyes away from society.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Learning exercises the intellect and endows it with ability. Society is the subject of that mental exercise. People in the West believe that such places provide the space and opportunity to cogitate over such matters. Our ancients also believed the same.⟨fn:432⟩ We experience a new robustness in our intellect that is also a gift of this mountain. Sacred spaces and some specially endowed places because of their beauty, tranquility and grandeur are permeated with specially charged air which enters our physical and subtle bodies. Consequently, we experience a fount of purity, wisdom and equanimity.’ Kumud: ‘That must be true. My own intellect seems to have benefited from it.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Consider this. Many of my learned but poor friends are condemned to live in the hustle and bustle of a thickly populated city like Bombay. Unlike the English, they have neither the resources nor the opportunity to come to a place such as this and reinvigorate their body and mind. What pain this must cause me? This mountain has given me many gifts; one of them is this pain.’ Kumud: ‘Your generous heart that is imbued with love for this country must be pained. But why do you consider this pain a gift?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Why do I think of it as a gift? While I was in Bombay I could never imagine as to what I should do with my immense wealth. This mountain and this bunch of letters have told me that if nothing else, I could make it possible for men of learning to stay at such places and enhance their intellect and health.’ Kumud: ‘Devotees and brahmins occupied a special place in the heart of Sri Krishna. These scholars occupy a special place in your heart.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Yes. There are only two classes of people who can secure the welfare of our country and her people—the British and these scholars.’ Kumud: ‘The British are powerful.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘When scholars become capable of making use of their learning, they would be inspired to serve their country. When they and the British, by mutual cooperation, adjustment and trust, work together this capacity will rise in both and they would become worthy of reverence of our people. Kumud, the trust and accommodation that your wise father reposed in Gunial Ba is what the British will need to cultivate in their relations with our men of learning. Gunial Ba with her generosity, forbearance, sacrifice and intelligence cared for your father’s family. Our scholars will also have to cultivate these qualities in caring for the country. Only then will the welfare of all be secured.

I have faith in them. Hence, our scholars have a special place in my heart. They are constantly in my thoughts.’ Kumud: ‘What are your aspirations for them?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I would like women such as Gunasundari, Kumud Sundari, Saubhagya Devi and Chandravali to be in their homes. I want them to be wealthy. I want them to be free of worries and disease. I want goddesses of learning and wealth to shower blessings on them. I want them capable of love and virtue. I want the desire for the welfare and upliftment of the country take firm roots in their hearts. Last night in our dream we saw great hillocks of mud. I want them to be free of the dust of these hillocks and want that they be protected by the dust of the golden clouds. I want that those hillocks turn golden, that all creatures within it find white light and all places become as beautiful as the bejewelled garden in which we stood. These are the cravings of my heart.’ Kumud: ‘What are the means available to fulfill these aspirations?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I had wealth that could have been the seed of this effort, but that I have thrown away.’ Kumud: ‘Once while quoting Austen you had said, “It is a truth universally acknowledged that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.”⟨fn:433⟩ Is this also no longer available to you?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘It is and it is not.’ Kumud: ‘You often said that it was your aspiration that the women of our country should rise and be capable. Do you still harbour this desire?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What shall I say? The means to secure this desire is even rarer than the object of desire. I remember all the pictures I used to paint in my thoughts, and the possibilities of what it could have been to have you by my side flood my mind. I am forced to say:

In the first place, Love smites my mind, which is difficult to turn away from its longing after an unattainable object; what then, when the mango-trees in the garden, the seared leaves of which have been plucked off by the southerly wind, present to my view their tender sprouts?⟨fn:434⟩ Kumud: ‘You are certainly not so impatient to believe that what is going to be available after a few years is completely unattainable. The time may come, you need not fly.⟨fn:435⟩ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Time will make that possible, but who knows where our sense of rectitude will take us? If I had not abandoned Kumud Sundari, through her I would have gained access to the pain and pleasures of our women. Oh my pure beloved! I am apprehensive that such access is no longer available to me. An unmarried medicine man cannot hope to examine the maladies of the subtle bodies of our women. Such an attempt is also improper. A doctor who, while examining the pulse of a female patient, feels a rush of blood either in him or her must terminate the examination. We experienced today the effort involved in defeating the god of desire. If I had not had your unwavering support, lust would have broken my resolve and the mast on which the flag of righteousness flies would have broken down. Without such pure, unsullied cooperation no attempt to remedy the ailment of our women could be undertaken. And yet I cannot free myself of this aspiration, and to that extent I am a fool. Whenever I see a woman, I see you and the suffering of our women comes before me. But each time I think of you, the god of desire stands before me with his arrows of love pointed at me. This fear makes me abandon all thoughts of you instantly. And yet, the divine images that we saw yesterday are constantly present before me.’ Kumud: ‘The tears that stream from your eyes pierce my heart. Please control yourself. I will assist you in your aspirations, and this assistance will be on the righteous path.’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘Kumud Sundari, these letters of Chandrakant reached me due to some quirk of fate. My heart breaks as I read them. My dear friends and the true gems of our country are lying in dust. I was unaware of their condition. These letters have given me a glimpse of it. How much more has escaped my attention? If Pramaddhan had secured your happiness I would have been personally very happy. But his conduct was contrary to it. Because of that I became aware of some of the pains of our women. How many of our women are drowned in sorrow, how their delicate hearts are being crushed, how they weep rivers of tears. I read letters, painful letters to Chandrakant; but do they capture all the pains of our women? If these pictures were present before me when I renounced you and my wealth, I would have determined a different notion of my duties. I freed myself from the mire, but with that I also blinded one of my eyes and lost the capacity to see half of our people. I destroyed with my own hands the one possibility that could have allowed me to alleviate the condition of our orphaned people. It is true that I squandered the one chance I had. But when I think of my duties with regard to them, when I consider as to how I should learn of their pain and what remedies are available, I weep. The tears are beyond my control; I take satisfaction in them. What is beyond my capacity does not involve considerations of right and wrong. I take satisfaction in controlling my desires, and I seek satisfaction in these tears.’ Kumud: ‘If your renunciation was a moral act, is it not immoral to be pained by its unintended consequence?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Considerations of morality and immorality apply when one does not do what one is capable of. What is beyond one’s capacity is neither moral nor immoral. Ramchandra saw that it was his duty to renounce Sita, but his love made him weep. Kumud Sundari, we might kick our love away from within the ambit of our activity, but it is beyond our capacity to free our hearts of love. Just as the emergence of love is inevitable, its waning is equally impossible. And for this reason your compassion towards Sarasvatichandra in the house of Pramaddhan was a righteous act.’

Kumud: ‘Effective ointment clears the vision. Similarly pure knowledge removes all remnants of love; this is the experience of great souls.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That is true. But fatalism and knowledge both are capable of being misused. When some action is enjoined upon us as duty, recourse to fatalism at that moment is a violation of duty. Destiny can be used to rid oneself of pain and pleasure but not to shun duty. Similarly, knowledge is meant for the attainment of the Unseen One, not to seek renunciation from action; knowledge is a means to destroy ego and attachment, and not the essential unity of creation. The use of fatalism to justify inaction, to interpret action as inaction by people like those creatures with inverted eyes have arrested our country and created moulds of clay. They have misused knowledge. Their fires of self-sacrifice have gone out from their souls and have come to the present sorry condition. Knowledge can rid us of desire and lust that arise from ego and attachment. When egoless and detached action becomes the means of sacrifice, the oblations of that sacrifice become pure and bring the sacrifice to its completion. Just as Being, God and Brahma are a trinity, action, duty and knowledge form a trinity. Duty is a right enjoined upon those who perform their actions. Knowledge is the fruit of righteous duty. Till such time as the performance of duties remains incomplete, knowledge in all its aspects does not flourish. Knowledge in absence of morality is like an eclipsed moon. A person who pursues knowledge to the exclusion of all else will be on a dark path. They will attain a land of darkness. Knowledge that is not eclipsed and darkened is pure knowledge, and virtuous persons attain oneness with the Creator through such knowledge. The ascetics of this community understand the meaning of this knowledge. Their sacrifice for the sake of humanity is imbued with love. Kumud Sundari, all my sacrifices, be they for you or for this country, are imbued with the nectar of love. An English poet said: ’Tis better to have lov’d and lost Than never to have lov’d at all.⟨fn:436⟩

Kumud: ‘Isn’t love also desire?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Love that takes bodily form is desire. It arises in lust and wanes with the waning of lust. Desireless love is like a flame; it is like the pull of gravity that joins earth and the moon. It arises out of itself. The only force that weakens its pull is knowledge. But when love is pure and righteous it cannot be weakened even by knowledge. No form of knowledge can take away the love of parents. The reason lies in its purity. Our people consider love between a man and woman to be lowly because they imagine it to be lustful. Our society has become so debased that it cannot imagine that love between a man and woman can also be desireless. This was Chandrakant’s assertion. Who knows if this is indeed true?’ Kumud: ‘At the time of your renunciation how did you imagine you would serve the country without money?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Wander, observe and teach...’ Kumud: ‘Like Lord Buddha?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Something like that.’ Kumud: ‘Why have you changed your decision?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The mounds of mud are so solid and petrified that light would not melt them, fire would not burn them and the spade would not dig them out. When the gems and poison of the great serpent fails, what can my mere words achieve? Lord Buddha’s words permeated through enlightened beings. In our age words do not even echo through these lifeless mounds.’ Kumud: ‘Which of your capacities could be put to use?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Knowledge, virtue and wealth are the three capacities that are necessary. I do not possess the third, and you know that the fourth is in your heart.’ Kumud: ‘Cannot one do without the third and the fourth?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That would depend upon the ambrosia that I drink.’ Kumud: ‘What kind of ambrosia?’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘In a sacrifice for the country, love for one’s country is ambrosia.’ Kumud: ‘When would you know?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘When the churning of this heart is complete.’ Kumud: ‘Today, we consumed our meal of fruits without any desire.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Faced with love for the country, bodily desire becomes nullified.’ Kumud: ‘I will nurture and cherish this love for the country and let the other one drown.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I told you that all your actions will be pure and beautiful.’ Kumud: ‘I will do so out of my selfish desire to be with you.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Your subtle desire will work for the welfare of others. This is an example of it.’ Kumud: ‘We should not even mention either subtle or bodily desires. The term desire itself is suggestive and exciting.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘It appears to be so.’ Kumud: ‘I should now go and read your notes.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘When will you return?’ Kumud: ‘I will assist my companions and return in the evening.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The word evening is also suggestive and exciting.’ Kumud: ‘Your hand is caught in the folds of my saree.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The power that kept the purity of that hand in my encounter with Alakbehn will also protect my purity today.’ Kumud: ‘You have let go of my saree. Your control and capacities are greater than mine.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Our oneness enables us to remain pure.’ Kumud: ‘That is true. But are we so powerless and wretched that we have to make this incessant endeavour?’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘Order emerges from renunciation of greed and pride, from long and subtle penance, from great caution and through discerning wisdom. I have been taught that by giving up pride and ego the intellect moves on the path of welfare.’ Kumud: ‘May that come true. I seek your leave now.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Are you in a hurry to leave?’ Kumud: ‘When one cannot trust oneself, it is best to perform one’s duties without further delay.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I pushed you into suffering, and yet you have my salvation in your heart.’ Kumud: ‘And mine, too.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘May God grant you success.’
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra and Kumud Sundari explore a profound shared dream, navigating their subtle desires and unique togetherness amidst the monastery's sacred spiritual duties.

chapters.title: Arjun's Chariot and the Forest Fires
paragraphs: Arjun’s Chariot and the Forest Fires⟨fn:437⟩ For while the tired waves, slowly breaking, Seem here no painful inch to gain, Far back, through creeks and inlets making, Comes silent, flooding in, the main.⟨fn:438⟩ Thus addressed both by Dasarha and Arjuna, the illustrious god then put forth his most energetic form, and prepared to consume the forest. Surrounding it on all sides with his seven flames, he began to consume the forest of Khandava, exhibiting his all-consuming form like that at the end of the Yuga (cycle). Then those foremost of car-warriors (Krishna and Arjuna), riding in their cars and placing themselves on opposite sides of that forest, began a great slaughter, on all sides, of the creatures dwelling in Khandava.⟨fn:439⟩ “Manifold is the prosperity of him who is weary, So, have we heard, O Rohita; Evil is he who stayeth among men, Indra is the comrade of the wanderer. “Flower-like the heels of the wanderer, His body groweth and is fruitful; All his sins disappear, Slain by the toil of his journeying. “The fortune of him who sitteth also sitteth,

But that of him who standeth standeth erect; That of him that reclineth lieth down; The fortune of him that moveth shall move indeed. “Kali he becometh who lieth, Dvapara when he riseth, Treta when he standeth erect, And Krta when he moveth.”⟨fn:440⟩ Sarasvatichandra and his companions went on a tour of one part of Chiranjiv Shrunga, while Kumud Sundari and her companions went in the other direction. Outside the ramparts of the hill top there was a small lake. Sarasvatichandra and his companions were strolling on its embankments when Shankapuri and Shantidas turned up at the spot. Shankapuri came up close to Sarasvatichandra and said to him in a whisper, ‘Navinchandra! You are doing such things in the garb of an ascetic? Be warned that you shall repent. See how you dissipate under this mask.’⟨fn:441⟩ Sarasvatichandra was surprised both by his words and his English. He quickly regained his composure and replied, ‘Brother! I believe that as you understand the deeper meaning of asceticism, you shall understand me better; these words will then pain you. Therefore it would be better if you give up the scheming ways of the world and cultivate the patience to see the world from the perspective of Sundargiri. You should judge me only after that.’ Surdas and Mayapuri heard this exchange and came forward in anger. Mayapuri caught Shankapuri by the hand and said, ‘An ascetic who cannot observe the humility required to converse with an ascetic of the highest spiritual attainment is not fit to be an inhabitant of Sundargiri. If you repeat such behaviour I would be forced to advise the Master to send you back to the society.’ Shankapuri gave no reply and walked away in company of Shantidas. They came where Kumud Sundari and her companions were sitting. He sat at some distance from them and stared at Kumud. Kumud was startled. Her companions surrounded her and sent Bhakti and Yamini to confront Shankapuri. Yamini: ‘Are you the one who harasses Bindumati?’ Shankapuri: ‘What right do you have to ask me this?’ Bhakti: ‘The women ascetics forgave you once because you are a novice. It might be considered innocent to gaze at women ascetics among householders, but we see it as a lack of virtue. We not only have a right to question you but even to throw you down from this mountain if necessary. We have both the numbers and the strength to exercise that right. Hence, please go away from here or we shall exercise our full rights.’ Shankapuri: ‘Please forgive us. We were just sitting here. We shall go away.’ By the time the two groups returned to their respective caves, they had forgotten these incidents. At sunset, Sarasvatichandra was on the topmost floor of the cave, looking intently at the beautiful world surrounding him. He did not hear the rustle of Kumud Sundari’s footsteps. She waited for a while and then softly said, ‘Sarasvatichandra.’ He turned around and saw her. She sat down and both of them looked at the surrounding beauty. As the dusk settled into darkness, a pale moon rose in the sky. The day had not yet ended. The mountain tops, the trees in the distance turned grey and finally became silhouettes. Birds had returned to their nests; a rare bird could be seen fleetingly. As the day slipped away, moonlight enveloped the earth. When Kumud spoke, it was unclear if her words added to the stillness or disturbed the tranquility. ‘During marriage rituals the groom says to his bride: I am the sky and you are the earth. Why? What is the meaning of this aspiration? How does marriage contribute to its fulfillment?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The sky envelopes the earth, it showers rains, which the earth receives.’ Kumud hesitated, bit her lips and finally said, ‘Is the meaning so entirely gross?’

Sarasvatichandra became attentive. He thought for a while and said, ‘No, of course not. Water, an essential part of the earth, rises to the sky; it takes the form of rain which showers on the earth. Earth collects that water and gives birth to the beauteous, multihued world, thereby fulfilling the sacrifice of the Supreme Man. The aesthetic aspirations of a woman’s heart rise up to the man and stay there in embryonic form and eventually are planted in the heart of woman. She, thus impregnated with aspirations, gives birth to a new life. Kumud Sundari, the subtle desires first arise in the hearts of women and then eventually come to reside in her heart. Man is that interlude who receives these aspirations, only to return them to her.’ Kumud: ‘Are all these ideas contained in one metaphor?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘There is another metaphor: woman is Rig while man is Sama. Sama emerges from the ocean that is Rig Samhita. Similarly, the earth that bears water makes rains possible. Man’s heart likewise emerges from the heart of a woman.’ Kumud: ‘The saline water of the earth turns sweet only because it ascends to the sky. Sama turns Rig into a song of knowledge. A woman’s heart turns sweet with the attainment of a man’s heart and with the power of such a heart her song turns melodious.’ Sarasvatichandra smiled, ‘It seems that the mangalsutra of our dream still empowers your heart. What you say is correct. Hence, man and woman are like two horses that pull the chariot. Their sacrifice requires mutuality.’ Kumud: ‘Marriage, thus, is the coming together of two persons to perform this sacrifice, isn’t it?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘It is.’ Kumud: ‘What disorder must prevail in our country with regards to marriage?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Your question reawakens my pain. Kumud Sundari, a couple that compliments each other is as rare as the divine images we saw in our dream; the rest are like the creatures in the mounds of mud.’

Kumud: ‘The two of us are free from the existence in the mounds.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Our subtle bodies are nourished by your aspirations.’ Kumud: ‘Will these mounds never make way for a lake filled with light? Will the bejewelled paths never emerge in their place?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What is impossible for God? It will take a long time before these mounds are transformed into light. I cannot even imagine what the foreign winds will not do to these mounds and the rocks that appear so stable! Our wretched creatures will never match the speed of trains and when the winds shall blow from all sides, everything shall shake up. The western winds will blow away our mounds. The dust of these mounds will cover the sky and only the moon and darkness shall prevail.’ Kumud: ‘Moonlight brightens up a dark night and as the moon sets, the sun invariably rises.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Your mangalsutra sees a glorious future and fills my vision with new possibilities.’ Kumud: ‘The statues from this cave seem to have come to life and they seem to be flying. My eyes are heavy with sleep.’ Kumud and Sarasvatichandra fell asleep. Moonlight played on their bodies. The moon was covered by a white cloud. Dew fell on them as they began to enter the dream world. Kumud was awakened by its wetness, and said, ‘There is dew here. Let us go down and sleep there.’ Sarasvatichandra followed her as if still in sleep. Kumud and he lay down on a large platform. Soon they were fast asleep and in the world of dreams. Once again, they saw the same dream. As soon as they entered the dream world, the immortals bestowed upon them all their powers and gifts. They were joined together by the garment of light and with the help of their wings they flew towards the moon. In a short time, they were far from the earth. A stray owl and a solitary chakor were the only birds they saw. They passed through the blanket of clouds as they neared the stars. They stopped to admire the beauty of the earth beneath and the sky above them.

Just then a form attired like a kshatriya approached them—it was the image of Samantraj. Sarasvatichandra recognised him, but before he could say anything Samantraj addressed him, ‘Sarasvatichandra! My devotion to the king and his kingdom has enabled me to reach this space. Only those with pure vision can enter the world of immortals. Till such time that I acquire the right, I roam in this outer periphery. You have earned this right, which I have not obtained even after death. Please do me a favour. Kindly take my parrot with you. The parrot knows all my aspirations and desires. He will accompany you and pose questions on my behalf at the appropriate time. If no one answers his questions, I pray that you provide the answers. He will repeat those answers to me, and that will fulfill my aspirations and curiosity. That will also purify my vision. This has been said to me by the immortals.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I will do so gladly. But could you please tell us where we are at present?’ Samantraj: ‘At this point the atmosphere of the earth ends. As you rise higher you will enter the domain of the sun. The immortals who have shaped our destiny reside there. Shortly they will appear before you. You will witness the destiny of all humankind there, along with the destiny of our country.’ The image disappeared with these words. Soon a large aircraft shaped like a balloon approached them. Countless chains of gold, silver and other metals hung from the aircraft. They extended towards the earth and pulled the earth towards them. Various figures, shining in their own light and holding bows and arrows, were seated in the aircraft. Sarasvatichandra: ‘Kumud, Maharaj Mallaraj had seen the great Arjun face to face; he had gone on to conceive of and build the political observatory. We see that great soul Arjun in the aircraft. Look at his divine face!’ Kumud: ‘The world believes that the wielder of the Gandiva is no more!’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘He is no more alive in his body, but like the eternal sun and the moon he circumambulates the earth.’

Kumud: ‘Which part of the earth does he light up today?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘If you look down to the earth, you will realise that. The part of the earth where the chains extend is lit up by him.’ Kumud: ‘Many figures seem to be pulling at the chains. Are they humans or other beings?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That we will know only when we descend to earth. From this distance they appear to be strange creatures. What we see as the earth is not the earth, but a reflection of it in the Pitamah Kund. The chains extend only up to that reflected earth, but its impact is felt on the real earth below.’ Kumud: ‘Who are those pulling the chains?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘On one side is the East; on the other is the West. There are different creatures on either side some of which pull the chains, while the others do not.’ Kumud: ‘What is that area further away?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That is the Mediterranean Sea. That great mountain divides the East from the West. Arjun’s chariot is oriented towards the West. It has turned its back to the East.’ Kumud: ‘Who lives in the East and which people live in the West?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘In earlier times, this chariot was oriented towards the East and the South. But at present its orientation is westward. There, further West is an island where the monkey-people live. They are pulling the golden chains towards them. That great bird that you see is an eagle during the day and is transformed into a chakor by night. We are able to see both its forms because of the Chintamani we have. On the third side a great elephant is pulling the chains, while a peacock is pulling the chains towards the South.’ Just then Samantraj’s parrot flew up and began to sing. Alas! the peafowl, as he dances wild With rapture, drowns my sorrows with his cry— With rolling eyeballs the chakora flies After his mate—the ape his female’s cheeks,

Besmears with flowery dust. Whom should I sue to? Vain the request unseasonably proferred.⟨fn:442⟩ Kumud: ‘What does this old parrot say? Who does he refer to? What does he want?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The aspirations of our noble, patriotic kings are embodied in this ancient parrot. His concern is the welfare of our country and he repeats it day and night. He craves to fulfill his aspirations and pleads for their fulfillment.’ The parrot spoke up, ‘I do not plead before all and sundry. I only approach those who have the capacity to hear and fulfill my aspirations. All persons are engrossed in their activities and have no capacity to hear me. Therefore, with my old wings I fly from one tree to another. That ancient peacock was at one time the vehicle of Kartikeya Swami. Earlier, whenever the people of Rome spoke ill of it, Arjun showered arrows upon them. Kartikeya Swami is no longer present, but the peacock is eternally alive. He plays with his feathers; at times he makes a grand display of them while at times he sheds them. In the present times the feathers are meant only to please and attract the peahen; they have lost their other capacities. How can I plead before him? What can I learn from his country? The peacock can no longer fly high. It is beautiful, attractive and pleasing. Many such peacocks came to life and died in my country.’ The peacock retorted, ‘Oh stupid parrot! Those who know where to look will find something to learn in each place. A person capable of self-examination learns from his life. At some point in the past your country was like mine. But can’t you see that your land has petrified? Many rocks and hillocks have formed there; they arrest the movement of your people who have become like animals; your people are blinded; they have turned deaf and are no longer capable of high aspirations. What right does your country have to receive Arjun’s benedictions? We have removed such maladies from our land. I have fallen, raised myself again and lived through many sunsets, but I am alive and have the strength to fly alongside Arjun’s chariot.’

The parrot turned his attention to the chakor who was pulling another chain. ‘Oh chakor! You belong to the city of Paris and that country. During the day you have the speed and strength of an eagle, and at night you transform yourself into a chakor and fly towards the moon. You have both strength and high aspirations. At one time my country was similarly able. What ails my country today that we have become so feeble that we cannot even hold on to one of these chains?’ The chakor stopped flying and replied, ‘Oh wise parrot of the East! The high aspirations of my independent, liberal people of the West are like the chakor at night and like an eagle during the day. The future of the world is tied to the future of my people. That is our belief; it does not matter if it is true or not. But our faith and our aspirations are of the highest order. It is our faith that empowers us to pull these gem-studded chains in our direction. We represent the collective brains of all people on earth. We will transmit our cultural aspirations to all through electrical wires, and those who have the capacity shall receive them and come to life. We have no desire to rule over your lifeless country; our flight is towards the moon. If you want similar aspirations for your country, you have to obtain the means through your own endeavour. Oh parrot, free yourself from the net of false religiosity and thoughtlessness and then free your country from them.’ Parrot: ‘Oh vile chakor! I had hoped that the peacock would teach me to make a fan of my wings and that you would teach me the modes of acquiring the ability to be a republic like you. Both of you have dashed my hopes. And instead you blame me!’ Chakor: ‘Foolish parrot! If you want to be like the eagle you must know all your faults and learn to introspect. I bestow the capacity of introspection and self-examination to my children with their mother’s milk.⟨fn:443⟩ You must do likewise. Do not be enamoured of my republic. I assume this form to drink from the moon. But when great courage is required, a Napolean transforms me into an eagle. If you want to be like an eagle, sit on the shoulders of the monkey-people and go wherever they take you. The monkey-people are the emperors; they rule over many kings. Why do you crave to be eagle-like? If you aspire to drink from the moon, you should know that moon rocks also drink from the moon’s rays. You do not have to assume my form; you only have to know where to look for moon rays.’ Parrot: ‘We are people devoid of weapons. What use do we have of moonlight?’ Chakor: ‘Have patience. The people and animals that bear arms today will one day be without them; their weapons will automatically drop from their hands. There will be a time when all life on earth will bathe in moonlight and no human shall harm another. Valour is not about the capacity to injure, but to conquer through forgiveness. This wisdom of your land shall prevail as truth all over the earth, and an age of truth and peace shall prevail. That is my aspiration! Listen to what this chain of Arjun’s chariot has to say.’ The chain shook and a quiet white light sprang from it. It said in English: ‘In the twentieth century, there will be an extraordinary nation. This nation will be great but its greatness will not prevent it from being free...In the twentieth century, the country of this nation will be called Europe, and in after centuries, as it still and ever develops, it will be called Mankind...Throughout historical times, the world has ever had a city which has been The City. The brain is a necessity. Nothing can be accomplished without the organ whence come both initiative and will. Acephalous civilisation is beyond conception. It is from three cities, Jerusalem, Athens, Rome that the modern world has been evolved. They did their work. Of Jerusalem there now remains but a gibbet, Calvary; of Athens, a ruin, the Parthenon; of Rome, a phantom, its empire. Are these cities dead, then? No. A broken eggshell does not necessarily imply that the egg has been destroyed; it rather signifies that the bird has come forth from it, and lives. From out of those shells lying yonder—Rome, Athens and Jerusalem—the human ideal has sprung and soared. From Rome has come Power; from Athens, Art; from Jerusalem, Freedom; the great, the beautiful, the true...And they live anew in Paris, which in one way has resuscitated Rome, in another Athens, and in another Jerusalem; for from the cry of Golgotha came the principle of the Rights of Man. And Paris also had had its crucified; one that has been crucified for eighteen hundred years—its People. But the function of Paris has been to spread ideas. Its never- ending duty is to scatter truths over the world, a duty it incessantly discharges. Paris is a sower, sowing the darkness with sparks of light. It is Paris which, without a pause, stirs up the fire of Progress. It casts superstitions and fanaticism, and hatred and folly and prejudice on to this fire, and from the darkness comes a blaze of light...Moreover, Paris is like the centre of our nervous system; each of its quivers is felt throughout the world. And, further it is like a ship sailing on through storms and whirlpools to unknown Atlantides, and ever towing the fleet of mankind in its wake. There can be no greater ecstasy than that which comes from the perception of the universal advance, when one hears the echoes of the receding of tempests, the creaking of the rigging and the panting of the toiling crew, when one feels the straining of the timbers, and realises the speed with which, in spite of all, one happily travels onward. Search the whole world through; it is ever upon the deck of Paris that one may best hear the flapping and quivering of the full-spread, invisible Sails of human Progress.’⟨fn:444⟩ The voice stopped. The chains grew brighter; the chakor’s wings seemed to transform into those of an eagle. Finally the bird said, ‘Parrot! Do not be afraid of the monkey-people. The age of peace and tranquility shall prevail due to our strength and noble power. But before that, there will be a great war. A lamp before going out burns brightly and a dying man shows signs of vigour; similarly this great war shall tear the people apart. ‘‘We shall then witness war’s last agony and war will kill war and the spirit of war.”⟨fn:445⟩ When the world shall pass through these birth pangs, a new age shall emerge. All people of the world shall pull these chains. Parrot! At that time even your country shall rise; to attain that salvation neither arms nor ammunition are required. Ask the history of your land if it has the wherewithal to acquire salvation by any other means. Ask the aspirations of your people; ask the monkey-people who captain your ship. If you do not have faith in the hopes of all humankind, pose your questions to the immortals of your land who reside in this city. Do not make the mistake of blaming others because you have lost the capacity for self- examination.’ The chakor swung around as if on a swing. The parrot remained silent. Sarasvatichandra and Kumud flew towards the golden chains. They held on to a chain with both hands. The chain transformed into many rope-like structures which extended all the way to the earth, their ends dipping into the oceans. The roaring ocean appeared before them, its foamy waves gleaming in the moonlight. Soon, the waters of all the great oceans of the earth filled this ocean. Sarasvatichandra: ‘Oh my companion of this divine dream! Behold the glory of these oceans! So many islands! So many continents! And countless rocks and waves!’ Kumud: ‘Oh beloved! The oceans are surrounded by the monkey- people. On every island I see monkey-people of divine capabilities. They have control over air, waves, fire and electricity.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Varun, Vayu, Agni and Indra assist Arjun. Arjun has turned his chariot towards their country. Kumud, where there is Arjun, the age of truth prevails—this is the promise of Arjun’s father Indra.’ Parrot: ‘Compared to other people, why are the monkey-people so powerful?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Arjun is the protector of monkeys. Our immortals will reveal this mystery to you. The monkey-people roam free and fearless. Arjun’s partiality towards them is natural. Our people are asleep and hence we are in the dark ages. These people are industrious and hence the king of heavens is their friend. “Indra is the comrade of the wanderer.” Who but Indra’s son should undertake such journeys?

Kumud, my companion of this divine dream, behold the truth! This chakor and peacock fly because they have wings. In the distance you can see the bear⟨fn:446⟩ and the elephant; they possess great strength. The monkey-people are supple; they cross the seas and they bear great hardships. They tolerate the heat of Africa and the snow of the Himalayas. They can live wherever they land. Kumud, the bear and the elephant walk, while the monkey jumps from trees to mountains to deserts and across the oceans. From all directions they pull the chains of Arjun’s chariot. You can see that the monkey-people captain all the ships that sail across the seas.’ Kumud: ‘I am filled with awe. Arjun in fact pampers them!’ Parrot: ‘Why is Arjun so partial to the monkey-people?’ ‘Ask your immortals that question,’ said a voice from the sky. Sarasvatichandra: ‘Look what they have done to the chains! What are they doing?’ Kumud: ‘The monkeys have separated each thread of the chain. Some of them are as thin as my arm. From some threads knowledge pours out, while from others wealth. There are countless actions taking place. I watch them, I am enamoured of them, but I cannot describe them in words. Who are those bears and elephants?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The bears are Russians, while the ancient elephants represent the German Empire. The monkey-people are ruled by Panchali, while Duryodhana rules over the bears and the elephants.’ Kumud: ‘Why don’t they pull the chains of Arjun’s chariot?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Duryodhana makes supreme efforts to capture the reins of Arjun’s chariot. But where Panchali is unhappy, Arjun’s chariot moves slowly. The women of the bear-people are not endowed with Panchali’s riches. The love between men and women among the elephant-people is deep, but not ennobling.’ Kumud: ‘How?’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘Listen to what the elephant has to say. The savoury morsels of the lotus stalk, With which thou erst hadst fed her—then in sport Thou scatterest with thy trunk the silvery spray Upon her brow?—Ah shame! Why wav’st thou not The straight-stemmed lotus over her, as a shade Against the sun?⟨fn:447⟩ Sarasvatichandra: ‘We have spent a lot of time here. We should go and see the immortals without further delay.’ Kumud: ‘Correct, but the parrot has something to say.’ Parrot: ‘Oh monkey-people of the islands and of America, don’t you have the time to satisfy my curiosity?’ From each rope groups of monkeys exclaimed, ‘England expects every man to do his duty. Do thou thine!’⟨fn:448⟩ Parrot: ‘When will my country become a big country? Draw her birth chart.’ One monkey came up to him and said, ‘Parrot! We told you to know your duty and to act upon it. Therein lies the welfare of your country. Why don’t you understand this simple maxim?’ Parrot: ‘This chakor gave a long discourse and praised himself. Finally, he predicted a great war. But he did not tell me what I ought to do. You fight everywhere, perpetrate immorality on others and yet tell me to know and do my duty. Is this not treachery?’ Monkey: ‘What immorality have we perpetrated? It is our duty to pull the chains of Arjun’s chariot in the direction of all the countries. Those people who do not pull the chains are cajoled, coerced and tempted by us to do so. We see no immorality in this. Look at Arjun’s actions in your own country. He brought many kings and their kingdoms under his control. If his was an immoral act, ours is also immoral; but if he did his duty, we too are doing our duty. Foolish parrot! Arjun, whose chariot we pull, was born in your country. He abandoned it because it has become fallen and depraved. Arjun considers us worthy. His morality and actions were a seed in your country; we have nourished it into a tree. Even your country has begun to taste its fruits. And yet, if we so much as drive a nail through the hillocks your people cry and wail. Ask your immortals if what you consider to be duty is moral, or if our conception is moral.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Oh king among monkeys! There appear to be two groups among you. What is the reason?’ Monkey: ‘Like Vali and Sugriv among you, we too have two factions. Our Vali and Sugriv both serve our Panchali, but the difference is in the ritual of service. The Sugriv faction abides by our eternal religion, while the Vali faction wants to make modifications in it to suit the changing times. The aspirations that were articulated by the chakor are regarding their principal city, their capital. The rest of the aspirations pertained to the Sugriv faction. I belong to the Vali faction.’ Parrot: ‘Who would listen to religious teachings by someone like Vali?’ Monkey: ‘Our aspirations centre around the welfare of Panchali. The Pandavas of your country have served Panchali from times immemorial. The two of us, Vali and Sugriv, have not served Panchali from times immemorial, but we serve her and try and fulfill her desires. Sugriv’s faction serves Panchali; for them the human race itself is Panchali, and they chase mirages. ‘We believe in the survival of the fittest and labour to be fittest. They believe in their power of making the unfit fit and fail, and by failures fall among the unfit class. Unless the vigorous nation or race can continue, as throughout history, to expand and grow stronger at the expense of the decaying nation or race, the fundamental condition of human advance will not be fulfilled, and a stage of stagnancy ending in social death will be substituted for a State of Progress. The only means, revealed to us by past experience, whereby the vigorous people has supplanted the weaker, has been war, without which change and movement must have ceased. Thus viewed, it will be seen that war appears simply a phase in that tremendous and ceaseless process of competition which prevails alike on sea and land—in the ocean- depths, in the paths of the air, in field and forest, throughout insect and animal and vegetable life. The recoil from war, which is felt by so many minds, is only another instance of the eternal contrast between the upward trend of the human spirit and the physical environment by which that spirit is conditioned. But to strive to reach the ideal by a short cut is not only to fail to attain it, but also actually to postpone its arrival.’⟨fn:449⟩ Parrot: ‘The cat is out of the bag at last. Enough! I can hear or bear no longer. My country has no hope from thee.’ Monkey: ‘Nor from thee and thy people either.’ Parrot: ‘You wish my extinction, then?’ Monkey: ‘It is not a question of my wish but a matter inevitable in the long run unless you strive to benefit by our society which I am sure you won’t.’ Parrot: ‘Would you struggle then to hasten my extinction—if you believe in my doom as an inevitable result of an inexorable law? Why waste your strength to achieve what is sure to come to you without that waste?’ Monkey: ‘You are a fatalist; I am not.’ Parrot: ‘You would commit a sin because it is destined.’ Monkey: ‘I do my duty even when I know the result.’ Parrot: ‘I am undone.’ Monkey: ‘I can’t help it. It is your own doing.’⟨fn:450⟩ An old monkey came up through a golden rope and joined the verbal skirmish. Old monkey: ‘Meek parrot! I am an old monkey of the Sugriv faction. I am here in your support.’

Parrot: ‘You are all cheats. Do you consider our interest higher than yours? How many of our native kings have been deceived by promises made by your people? With each passing day they are ruined. How many hopes and promises given to our people have you dashed? How many pledges have you undone?’ Old monkey: ‘The acute pain of unfulfilled aspirations has turned you mad. During the lifetime of a human being it happens that certain promises and pledges remain unfulfilled and certain actions turn out to be immoral. It is said that among your people even Krishna and Dharmaraj failed to adhere to their promises. You are mistaken in the belief that one generation ought to fulfill the promises made by their ancestors. Our people have formulated principles by which we should deal with promises given to your so called kings and princes. These principles would be told to you by the Vali faction.’ The golden thread held by the monkey of the Vali faction said in English, ‘In truth, there are the seeds of decay in every protectorate, however light is the controlling hand and serious at the outset is the desire to keep alive the native Government. Insensibly goes on an attenuation of authority and a paralysis creeps over the native administration when a civilised power, strong and ambitious, daily confronts a weak, apathetic Government, and efficient and honest European officials press reforms on functionaries incapable, dilatory and corrupt. Insensibly a protectorate approximates to annexation and all the more quickly if the agents of the protecting power are active and capable. Not necessarily from ambition or bad faith, but in obedience to an inexorable law, the weak power becomes weaker and an education goes on fitting the subject for continued subjection. Legal forms refuse to lend themselves to the contradictory conditions such as are found arrayed against each other in conflicts between facts and documents, and diplomacy has to recognise facts to see what is really good for the people.’⟨fn:451⟩

Old monkey: ‘It is egotism to hold steadfast to pledges during such times. If for instance one has taken a vow not to give food to someone, morality does not lie in holding on to such a pledge even unto the death of that person. It is eternal law that one should speak the truth and shun untruth. Your immortals will teach you that taking a pledge of truth and speaking the truth are two different things. Arjun is a servant of dharma, but dharma serves Krishna; Krishna was the giver of dharma. This, too, you should ask the immortals.’ Parrot: ‘It is possible that these are not questions of morality, but what is that duty that your Arjun follows and makes you abide by?’ Old monkey: ‘You heard what the Vali faction had to say. Arjun’s valour is an embodiment of that wisdom. Arjun, with the help of Krishna, set fire to the Khandav forest and many lives were consigned to the flames. The same forest fire has encircled all creation today. Arjun, with the agency of Agni, got arms and a chariot from Varuna, lord of the seas. The same arms and chariot have been gifted to our Arjun. He moves in his chariot, setting forest fires in this age. We the monkeys along with our ‘‘British Lion’’ sit on his flag.⟨fn:452⟩ Other animals also sit alongside us. Brother parrot, if you have the strength to fly, come and sit on the chariot. Arjun is one, not two; he is yours and ours. But Arjun during his journey has left your country and his orientation is towards us. His chariot, and all these chains that hang down from it, has covered all the five great oceans and all the lands in between. If you want to understand the nature of Arjun’s duty you should ask your immortals. What the peacock, the chakor, the Vali faction and I have told you is the truth. If and when the morality and sense of duty that we abide by also prevail in your country, you shall acquire the capacity to sit on the flag of Arjun’s chariot. If you fail to acquire this capacity you shall perish in the fire set alight by Arjun; do not blame us for it.

We are pulled along with the chariot; we make joyous noises. If you want to join us, we have sent our monkey-people to your land.’ Parrot: ‘Whom have you sent, the Vali faction or the Sugriv faction? You have become old and the Vali faction is stronger numerically and in the exercise of power. Who values you? Why should they value us at all?’ The parrot wept. His tears fell into the ocean below. The old monkey went down the rope. The chains disappeared. They could see the bottom of the chariot above and the ocean below. The tears of the parrot came down like rain. Kumud grew sorrowful. Sarasvatichandra felt compassionate towards the parrot and Kumud. He embraced Kumud and said to her for the benefit of the parrot, ‘Kumud! Beloved Kumud, be happy! God will show mercy on our country. King Pandu asked for five sons; his first born was Dharma. Dharma is Arjun’s elder brother. Our country is poor, unhappy, quarrelsome, immoral, without arms, stagnant, fatalistic but without destiny and ignorant. And its destruction appears imminent. And yet there are signs of hope. Dharma, whom this Western Arjun considers his elder brother, is the first born of Pandu.⟨fn:453⟩ Yesterday, we saw his incarnation in Pitamahpur.

The political observatory of Mallaraj also seeks him. When that pious being is incarnated in our hillocks, Arjun’s chariot will turn towards us.’ Kumud clung to him and said, ‘Oh my dearest! Oh giver of solace! I have no such hope. Dharma has to incarnate in our country; only after him will Arjun take birth. Ages will pass and we will all be consumed by the fire; neither this parrot nor you nor I shall survive. Our scriptures say that God is the protector of the orphaned and the saviour of the meek. The scriptures will also be destroyed in Arjun’s great fire. It is futile to hope of marriage after one is dead.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Kumud, why are you afraid? The parrot cannot understand that by doing one’s duties the country can be saved. The parrot is a kshatriya. A kshatriya observes the orientation and force of waves in the ocean of power; he is disappointed by the powerlessness of our country. But as we embrace each other, your mangalsutra rubs the Parasmani on my finger and produces a vision entirely different— behold that vision. Our wings have brought us to a different land. We are on the top of the great Himalayas. Look! The animals pulling the chains of Arjun’s chariot in the north are crushing each other to death; their cacophony deafens our ears. But to the south of the great mountains, fertile, verdant orchards have grown in our country. The people cannot perceive it; but the clever monkey-people have brought the chains of Arjun’s chariot to our land and with it, its fruits; these fruits will amaze us in a short time. Our country has put up more alluring displays than the dance of that peacock, but Panchali is in coma. Those alluring displays are dreams of the past. But look! Those monkey-people are so enthused by the possibilities of our peacock’s dance. When our seers and serpents cared for Panchali’s health and beauty, we were capable of putting up such alluring displays! The aspirations of the chakor may or may not come true, but look there—Sarasvati has emerged from those mud hillocks and she is fighting the fires. Her aspiration is to get Arjun to our side. Not just that, the cooperation between the monkey-people and our Arya race now affects not only the monkey-people, but also the peacock and the chakor. The chakor must be content with a distant moon. Our Lord Buddha resides on the moon and he has given a place on the moon to countless of our people. Parashuram destroyed the age of kshatriyas; the fratricidal wars also hastened its end. Similarly the chakor sees that in our age the eternal laws shall bring about the dissolution of our times. Do you think it is an impossibility? Look! Look! All the people in the world shall become brahmins, including our brahmins who have become shudras. All people will be imbued with the essence of brahminical life. The unmanifest shall become manifest. Look there! The internal conflict of the monkey-people creates a deafening noise. The monkey-people have taken away our arms; our best men are with them; many of our best men are crushed under them; they also take away our food! Despite all this you must understand, as the monkey said, that Arjun is one. That Arjun is the brother of Dharma. They and we both believe that where there is Dharma, there is victory. In spite of all that we have and all that we know, if we are burnt in the fire caused by Arjun, who is to be blamed? The monkey-people? They have factions of Vali and Sugriv, but all we have are these hillocks. The creatures living in them are wretched, feeble and lifeless. Our enlightened beings are buried under these hillocks of mud. We shall bring them out, Kumud! The oneness of our hearts will remove the dust from these gems, and their light will melt these hillocks. At the end of the great earthquake many new bejewelled mountains shall rise. Kumud! Kumud! Stop seeing the pains and pleasures of our people, stop making the futile effort of counting the waves; instead with the help of your gem look at the sparkling Milky Way and let us proceed to the Kurukshetra of our immortals. Let us go there. Time gone by shall never return. Today I am the clay, and you the earth. Kumud: ‘Let this night be endless!’
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra and Kumud Sundari navigate a tense encounter, then share a profound philosophical discussion and a vivid dream journey into the world of immortals.

chapters.title: The Immortals of Kurukshetra and the Future of India
paragraphs: The Immortals of Kurukshetra and the Future of India⟨fn:454⟩ Such is the aspect of this shore; ‘Tis Greece, but living Greece no more! So coldly sweet, so deadly fair, We start, for soul is wanting there. Hers is the loveliness in death, That parts not quite with parting breath, But beauty with that fearful bloom, That hue which haunts it to the tomb, Expression’s last receding ray, A gilded halo hovering round decay. The farewell beam of Feeling past away! Spark of that flame, perchance of heavenly birth Which gleams, but warms no more its cherish’d earth! * * * Approach thou craven crouching slave! * * * These scenes, their story not unknown, Arise and make again your own; Snatch from the ashes of your sires, The embers of their former fires!⟨fn:455⟩ And thou Delhi, whom I am looking down upon from the top of a minaret! Delhi, the barbarous, the cultivated, the heroic! What do I see? A fortress, a mosque, a plain! A fortress where through centuries of glorious deeds or fearful crimes, dark plots and secret tragedies, the great figures of thine Emperors have retained uninterrupted power. A mosque—the Great Mosque—the Jumma Musjid, the majestic symbol of the Crescent whose conquests thou, less favoured than Vienna, wert unable to arrest. A plain watered with blood, the scene of struggles which have more than once decided the fate of millions of human beings. That is what thou wert. This is what thou art now—a broken mirror reflecting the destinies of India.... But it is not the contingency of Russian aggression that would disturb me, if I were an Englishman. The internal policy to be pursued in India is the subject that would absorb my attention.
