I confess that certain ideas which enjoy great favour in certain quarters would give me food for reflection, and none more than the scheme of welding into a single nation the diverse races which inhabit the peninsula, of creating a new nation, and of creating her in the image of the English....British rule is firmly seated in India; England has only one enemy to fear—herself.⟨fn:456⟩ In their national life the Indians have exhibited down to our days their long-practised and often-tried courage of patience... With this they have retained a costly possession, that inclination towards the highest intellectual attainments which runs through their whole history. This treasure is still vigorous in the hearts of the best Indians, and appears the more certainly to promise a brighter future as the government which now controls the nation has come to an earnest though late resolution to rule with the help of the Indians for the good of the people, while the intellectual force and cultivation of their western tribesmen are disclosing themselves ever more clearly to the eager activity of eminent Hindus.⟨fn:457⟩ “To the Aryans I give the world!’’ So ran the prophecy of an ancient Hindu seer, and on this prophecy, which history attests,

Herr Arnoldson builds his theory as to the fulfilment of the Hope of the Ages—the World’s Peace. ...The Aryans were home together once...The utopia of Victor Hugo’s vision...means no more, no less, than the tardy re-union of the Aryan family divided now against itself.⟨fn:458⟩ Ranged thus for battle in the sacred plain— On Kurukshetra—say, Sanjay! Say What wrought my people, and the Pandavas?⟨fn:459⟩ Sarasvatichandra, Kumud and the parrot of their dreams rose and flew upwards and came to rest on the top of the Himalayas. From there they looked down at the Kurukshetra. Behind them were the lands of Central Asia, Tibet, Tatar and China. Far in the distance, the bears seemed to be moving along on their hind legs; some were walking eastwards, some towards the Himalayas. Weary of the bears, other animals were running about here and there in the east, west and the north. Towards the west there were wolves. Our protagonists stood with their backs to them. Below them was a triangular landmass of the Indian subcontinent washed on three sides by great oceans. The roaring of the ocean echoed in their ears. As they stood watching this scene, they heard a voice from below. They listened intently. The voice was unmistakably clear. The days approach When the long line of clouds shall shed on earth Their amaranthine drops, trembling in the breeze That from the east comes powerful, and embued With the rich odours of the sal and arjuna, Those days that boast the grateful interchange Of heat and moisture, and the fragrant breath The earth bestows, sprinkled with genial showers.⟨fn:460⟩

Sarasvatichandra: ‘Kumud, do you see Kurukshetra in the distance? This grave, sombre voice comes from there.’ Kumud: ‘There is some other divine being present here who watches over it.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘My Chintamani captures the reflection of that being with hitherto unseen clarity and beauty.’ Kumud: ‘Yes, even I perceive it.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘He is Lord Parashuram himself. All other incarnations of Lord Vishnu returned to heaven having completed their Yuga dharma. But this incarnation has remained immortal through the ages in order to save and uplift this country. In his incarnation as Sri Ram, the Lord doused Parashuram’s fiery, burning light. Ever since, Parashuram roams the earth’s atmosphere like nourishing rain. Each night he comes to this battlefield of Kurukshetra and contemplates the future of this country and this battlefield.’ Kumud: ‘I could not comprehend how he has saved and uplifted our country.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘For several ages this incarnation has remained immortal; what is for us a passage of years is for him contained in moments. When obstacles were placed in the path of brahminical sacrifice, this incarnation of Vishnu with powers of destruction to match the power of a thousand Arjuns became necessary. Now Parashuram is a benevolent force; his fragrance is spread by the winds blowing from the west. The waters of the oceans come to our land in the form of rain. Their cool showers bathe the earth. The earth becomes fragrant with rain. Human beings are at times bothered by the heat and perspiration and at times the cool breeze soothes them. Pain and pleasure, joy and sorrow return with unfailing regularity. Parashuram represents this cycle. He watches over Kurukshetra. It was his grave voice that we just heard.’ Kumud: ‘Why is Kurukshetra so dear to him?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘This vast field, situated right below Parashuram’s ashram, is known as Panipat these days. In ancient times this place was known as Kurukshetra. For eighteen days, the Pandavas and Kauravas fought their terrible war here. Hundreds of thousands of brave warriors died on this battlefield. The Stree Parva of the Mahabharata has described the ghostly scenes after their death. When Babar fought Ibrahim Lodi, that great battle was fought on this land. The sounds of the dead wailing continued to haunt pilgrims for years.⟨fn:461⟩ Emperor Akbar’s commander Behram Khan defeated Hemu at this battlefield. Sadashivrao Bhau, the pride of the Peshvas, died a valorous death at this spot; along with him two hundred thousand warriors shed their blood here. The glories of the ancient rulers of Hastinapur and the modern day Delhi have been built upon these rivers of blood; the same blood stains the waters of our ancient rivers such as Indus. This is where the kshatriyas sacrificed themselves, where Arjun triumphed. Is it any surprise then that immortal Lord Parashuram should spend his nights in this battlefield?’ Kumud: ‘What is that light we see?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Just as sun rays bring to light many aspects of the world, the light of Parashuram’s ashram spreads in the regions below it. Right beneath it is Kurukshetra. On one side of the field is Indus and on the other, the Ganga. Many other immortal beings reside in the shadow of this great immortal soul. That shaft of light comes from the body of Bhishma who is reclining in Ganga’s lap; his body is protected by the great serpent, Shesha Nag. That comet- like light is mad Ashwatthama who runs amok from the Himalayas to Kanyakumari. Sometimes he passes through the Kurukshetra, at times he shows signs of sanity, while at others of madness. Sometimes he wails in repentance. ‘The Pandavas ascended to the heavens from the Himalayas. They crossed Mount Meru and travelled through the lands of the Persians and the Yavanas. Panchali also travelled with them. She is goddess incarnate and still abides in this country; her light shines forth in this land. The light of the Pandavas spread from Tibet to this area. All the immortals come for a darshan of Panchali. Even Kunti comes to sit beside Panchali. The immortal Hanuman built a chariot resembling the chariot in which Arjun fought the battle of Kurukshetra. In a short time we shall come face to face with these immortals.’ Kumud: ‘Whom shall we meet first? Do you hear some shouts?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That is Ashwatthama wailing. Parashuram looks on with one eye, while the other eye looks towards Kaunch Randhra⟨fn:462⟩. Sparks of fire burst forth from his body. He is silenced by the condition of Bhishma, Panchali brings tears to his eye and he strives to find a way to alleviate her sorrow. He gives solace to Kunti, says something in a code to the Pandavas and talks to Hanuman.’ Kumud: ‘From which direction will the Pandavas approach?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘They have gone towards Kaunch Randhra. They will come from the western side.’ Kumud: ‘Let us first go to Bhishma Pitamah.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘These wings take us where we wish to go. Look, we are flying. Now we have come to the source of Ganga.’ Ganga emerged from a small hole in the Himalayas. It seemed like a trickle at this point. A thick tree cover lined the source of the river. Sarasvatichandra’s spade just scratched the area around the hole and the rocks moved away. The secret Ganga emerged below it. There was a large lake from which the great river gushed out. Right at the centre of the lake was Bhishma; the Shesha Nag had encircled his body and its hood made a canopy over him. Bhishma’s divine body was pierced by Arjun’s arrows. He rested on the bed of arrows. His body appeared emaciated from age-old thirst and appeared comatose. But the waters of Ganga flowed into his mouth. This water had filled his body with nectar. His veins, his bones and other parts of his body had become transparent and shone like jewels. The arrows that had pierced his body appeared like golden nails. The Shesha Nag protected this precious body. The guests of Siddhalok came to a stop near the great serpent’s fangs. The Shesha Nag was somewhat surprised and said, ‘Humans, why have you come here?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The desire for Pitamah’s darshan has brought us here. We visited the Pitamahpur and the pond of light. We now crave his darshan. For how long and for what reason have you been protecting Bhishma Pitamah?’ Shesha Nag: ‘Pitamah has been here ever since the Pandavas left this country. You saw the serpents who hang on to the great tree. I am their ancestor. I protect Pitamah for the same reason for which they hang on to the tree; such is the command of the Ganga in whom I abide.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘From whom does he need to be protected?’ Shesha Nag: ‘At some distance from here you will see Ashwatthama. That brahmin cursed by Sri Krishna lives a life of madness. The hillocks that you saw are his creations; that disorder is of his making.’ The parrot butted in, ‘Correct, oh King of Serpents. The brahmins drove away the Pandavas from this land.’ Shesha Nag: ‘I, too, am a brahmin. Your hatred for the brahmins is due to the malevolent effects of Ashwatthama. In the age of Pitamah, under his protection the brahmins and kshatriyas assisted each other in their sacrifices. He is now resting on the bed of arrows, and the mad Ashwatthama has created this net of hillocks. Parrot, your mind, too, has been affected by the same person. Let me sprinkle some holy water of Ganga on you which will free you from his influence.’ Ganga water was sprinkled on all of them. Sarasvatichandra: ‘Why don’t you sprinkle Ashwatthama’s body with this holy water?’

Shesha Nag: ‘This water would have an effect contrary to the one desired on an insane immortal. That brahmin and the country will be saved at the right time.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What is the difference between that brahmin and the sages and seers? Why has he gone insane? When will that time come?’ Shesha Nag: ‘These days the brahmins are blamed for all that ails you. These accusations arise due to your one-dimensional knowledge. Violation of duties either by the kshatriyas or the brahmins was equally reprehensible. To begin with the Aryas came to Kurukshetra; they were followed by the Mlecchas, and now the Aryas have returned.’ Parrot: ‘Are these monkey-people the Aryas?’ Shesha Nag: ‘Yes. During all the three yugas, Sat, Dwapar and Treta, the beneficial social orders that were created across the varnas were caused by brahmins steadfast in their duties. There are brahmins among the Mlecchas as also among the demons. Those who have the power of perception can see their achievements. Among the shudra kings, a great emperor like Ashoka became possible because he was a brahmin in the form of a kshatriya. Among the Mlecchas, there was an emperor like Akbar. There are equally capable and endowed rulers among the monkey-people. The chakor you met was a kshatriya, while Ashwatthama was born of the evil aspects of brahmins. That depraved brahmin took the wrong lesson from someone like Parashuram. He and his father fought against righteous kshatriyas. Drona the great soul fought a righteous war. But this depraved brahmin killed immorally; he killed enemies while they were asleep. He destroyed life from Uttara’s womb and he used the Brahmastra, the weapon bestowed by Brahma, for this immoral act. Ultimately, in his pride Ashwatthama sought Krishna’s Sudarshan chakra. Ego and attachment are the roots of demonic power—this power is manifest in this brahmin. He used his demonic powers to interrupt the righteous war of the Pandavas. It was not difficult for warriors like Arjun and Krishna, the Supreme Being, to annihilate him. But these two great souls who understood the fate of our society allowed him to live. Sri Krishna cursed him— and his curse was more devastating than death—because this evil man had killed children and life in a womb. The echoes of Sri Krishna’s curse can still be heard in the Kurukshetra and far beyond. Listen... As regards thyself, all wise men know thee for a coward and a sinful wretch! Always engaged in sinful acts, thou art the slayer of children. For this reason, thou must have to bear the fruit of these thy sins. For 3,000 years thou shalt wander over this earth without a companion and without being able to talk with anyone. Alone and without anybody by thy side, thou shalt wander through diverse countries. O’ wretch, thou shalt have no place in the midst of men. The stench of pus and blood shall emanate from thee, and inaccessible forests and dreary moors shall be thy abode! Thou shalt wander over the Earth, O thou of sinful soul, with the weight of all diseases on thee. The heroic Parikshit, attaining to age and a knowledge of the Vedas and the practice of pious vows, shall obtain all weapons from the son of Sharadvata. Having obtained a knowledge of all high weapons, and observant of all kshatriya duties, that righteous-souled king shall rule the earth for sixty years. More than this, that boy shall become the mighty-armed king of the Kurus, known by the name of Parikshit, before thy very eyes, O thou of wicked soul! Though burnt by the energy of thy weapon’s fire, I shall revive him. O lowest of men, behold the energy of my austerities and my truth.⟨fn:463⟩ The accursed voice ceased. The wailing and terrible screams of children killed in Kanpur could be heard. They pierced their hearts. Shesha Nag: ‘Parrot! The depraved act that Ashwatthama committed in the age of Krishna’s incarnation has been repeated in this age by another Ashwatthama-like brahmin in Kanpur. Listen to the terrible screams and wailings of the women and children he killed. Ashwatthama repeats such acts in every age. You should find out if this Ashwatthama is also diseased like the Ashwatthama of earlier times. In this Kurukshetra, Ashwatthama appears at times as a brahmin and at times as a Muslim. He spends the rest of his time making those hillocks. He enters the minds of brahmins and makes them insane; he turns the kshatriyas into addicts; he gets the vaishyas to make wrong calculations and pushes them into immoral trades and turns the shudras into beggars and thieves. He does not allow the people of this land to unite. He causes money to be spent on unnecessary and wasteful expenditures at times of marriage and death. He ensures that an industrious man continues to labour without reward. Oh parrot, this Ashwatthama has turned children into couples and makes them share a bed; he destroys their bodies. He makes the powerful inebriated, turns the learned into men of greed. These are some examples of his doings. What noble duties have been enjoined upon us by the Pitamah in the Shanti Parva and the Anushasan Parva! This insane Ashwatthama destroys the established order. That Ashwatthama is no longer a brahmin; at times he wears the sacred thread only to destroy it. He turns into a shudra at times and at times into a Mleccha. This insane man expands his reign of disorder each day in the domains of women and children, wealth and duties, knowledge and the arts, the mind and the body, the household and the state, the brahmins and the kshatriyas. He has invited upon this land every malady and ill conceivable and he dances his solitary dance in glee. In each age he sows the seeds of decay, misfortune and evil. At times he succeeds. So long as that madman persists, I protect the Pitamah in these sacred waters of mother Ganga. Can there be any comparison between the noble vision of the Pitamah and the hillocks of this madman? Between that order conceived of by the most subtle minds with the wisdom of experience, and this disorder of blind creatures and their age-old traditions! Whenever that madman comes near, I face him with my thousand fangs.’ Parrot: ‘What if someone were to burn down or destroy these hillocks?’ Shesha Nag: ‘Countless creatures live in these hillocks, which are like nests or beehives for them. Only Shiva-Shakti can destroy them. If some human were to suddenly destroy them, the semblance of order that these hillocks provide will disappear and the creatures that dwell in them will be placed in even greater hardship. Parrot, the monkey- people are slowly roasting them in fire, and Ashwatthama’s life is also approaching dissolution. That would be the most desirable solution.’

Parrot: ‘But it is the brahmins who created this disorder.’ Shesha Nag: ‘No. As I told you, Ashwatthama in his previous birth was a demon. This demon took birth in the lineage of brahmins and he has assumed many forms. The purest of brahmins survive only in my lineage. These two humans have seen them. We believe that one soul permeates all beings. A mother must care for her child in her infancy; similarly we preserve the order of our lineage.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What is the difference between your order and the order envisaged by Pitamah?’ Shesha Nag: ‘Pitamah’s vision was created on the basis of the wisdom of the ancient sages, seers, kings and rulers. His celibate life gave vigour to the body. He was born from the divine Ganga, which descended from heaven. His life was enriched by earthly experiences. A scripture is created based on the experience of certain persons. Bhishma’s experience is as vast as the source of Ganga. His experience and wisdom contain the wisdom of all the Shastras. We the serpents are like the rivers. The son of Ganga is like an ocean. The rains that are formed by the ocean waters fill our course. The rivers are for the ordinary mortals; but the origin of all wells, stepwells, lakes and rivers lies in the Patal Ganga or the Ganga that cannot be seen by mortals. Pitamah was born from that Ganga. When Ashwatthama’s time comes to an end, the sound of Arjun’s Gandiva shall reverberate through this land. These arrows in Pitamah’s body will come to life. They will release themselves from his body and make their way through these hillocks and create a new order in place of the one that they have destroyed. Those arrows shall return to Arjun’s quiver and Pitamah shall attain new youth. He will reside in Pitamahpur and all orders and arrangements will obtain their pure, unsullied form. Pitamah was forced to oppose Arjun for the sake of his vow to protect the seat of the Kurus. The Shadow of the Kauravas shall disappear with Ashwatthama. Pitamah will then care only for the Pandavas. Oh humans, even Dharmaraj is a child compared to Pitamah. It was Pitamah who discoursed to him on his duties. In your country at present Ashwatthama disguises himself as Dharmaraj and leads people astray. With the end of his life, pure eternal religion will be re-established, and Pitamah will with his light make your people twice-born. In such times great sages like Vyasa will consider the country fit for receiving their wisdom. That will herald the age of truth. Oh dejected humans, the seeds of hope for you lie here! Bathe in the Ganga and acquire the art of nurturing these seeds to fruition.’ Shesha Nag stopped speaking. Sarasvatichandra and Kumud were lifted up and immersed into the Ganga. Their wings brought them out again and in the flicker of an eye they were flown to another place. Sounds of wailing, screams of agony and lament tore through their ears. They could see nothing but a flat land bathed in moonlight. Both the barren landscape and the cries of lament were terrible in their distinct ways. They were brought down and put on solid ground. They saw an ancient brahmin lying flat on the ground. He stood up and rose so high that his hair touched the clouds. This demonic man took Sarasvatichandra and Kumud in the palm of his hand, brought them close to his face and spoke in a thunderous voice, ‘Do you recognise me? I am that Ashwatthama. The very same who destroyed the kshatriyas, the brahmins and the vaishyas along with all their arts. Hmm! You have bathed in the waters of Vaitarani, isn’t it? Its odour has gone into the pores of your body. Those who bathe in it go mad. Stay away, go!’ He dropped them from his hand, but they stayed afloat on their wings. Sarasvatichandra: ‘Immortal one! We have bathed in the Ganga.’ Ashwatthama: ‘Mad man! That is my Vaitarani. Those that she considers sane are insane for me and her insane are sane for me. My world is differently constituted than the world created by Brahma. I singlehandedly perform the tasks of Brahma, Vishnu and Mahesh. Now that you are here, watch what I am capable of.’ Ashwatthama sprinted away from their field of vision. The land of ornamental beauty hidden beneath the hillocks appeared before them. The great buildings built by Akbar floated up into the sky, Shivaji seated on his throne materialised and from the Kurukshetra, shouts hailing victorious Arjun could be heard. The divine light of the omnipresent God spread all around. At that instant, Ashwatthama assumed myriad forms and jumped down on the divine creation. In no time endless and limitless disorder and chaos spread all around. The divine order crumbled. The gems crumbled to dust and fell into the sea; scores of serpents were crushed to death while others took shelter in the nether world. Akbar’s magnificent palaces turned to ruins and the wailing of the imprisoned Shahjahan could be heard. Dara Shikoh’s severed head appeared before them on a plate. Shivaji was crushed under his own throne and canopy and one of his descendants frolicked in the harem of the Mughal court, while another appeared as a prisoner in Satara. Ashwatthama destroyed Arjun’s chariot and Arjun himself ascended to the heavens. The Pandava lineage was destroyed. Scenes of terrible destruction and dissolution appeared before them. The place where sage Vyasa had composed the Vedas and the Mahabharata, where divine order prevailed, trembled under the dance of destruction and disorder. The great temple crumbled and parts of the desecrated temple were stolen. Kurukshetra came under the malevolent power of Ashwatthama. The scriptures came to be challenged and their meanings reversed. One scripture got entangled with another and became indistinct. Someone appeared to cut them away with a knife. Wayfarers got lost in the maze and fell head on. When a shipwreck happens the passengers scramble to safety, clinging on to the sinking, broken ship, hoping to stay afloat. Similarly all the wretched creatures of Kurukshetra clung on to one of the many names of God, repeatedly chanted it and hoped to swim to safety. These terrible scenes spread across the seas and chaos prevailed. Ashwatthama then rose from the seas and soared up to the clouds. He thundered, ‘Mere mortals! My powers of destruction are greater than that of Maha Rudra. I displayed them before you. Like Brahma I created my own world of disorder and desolation. I turned the magnificent buildings of Akbar into ruins. There, you can see Aurangzeb standing amid the ruins. Who is he? It is I as a Mleccha. Who are those scrambling to be seated upon the throne of Shivaji? It is I as the Peshwas. I am Raghunath Rao. I am also the Brahma of this world of hillocks. Now let me show you my powers as Vishnu!’

The terrible scenes of Kurukshetra faded and disappeared. It became quiet, almost desolate. Gradually pilgrims, peripatetic merchants, traders, performers, Rajputs, kings, queens, brahmins, beggars, shudras, women and children began to gather together as if in a fair. In the midst of this crowd was a large merry-go-round. An old brahmin rotated the wheel. The brahmin’s emaciated body looked like the trunk of a withered tree. His veins protruded. Repeated genuflections to gods and goddesses had turned his forehead black and there was a bump on it. Some potion given by an ill-trained medicine man had blinded him in one eye, but he kept polishing and sharpening the stick for applying potion. He had applied some bitter remedies in the other eye which had darkened and blurred his vision. All around him were potions made from animal parts and bones. He had with him a dirty ink well filled with ink made from a cuckoo’s blood. He wrote on leaves verses to gods and chants to ghosts without discrimination. He claimed to possess powers to turn metal into gold, and the greedy flocked to him. He regaled his audience with tales of dark magic present in forests and ruined cities. He claimed powers to exorcise persons possessed by dark spirits; their repeated slaps had flattened his ears. He sang tuneless compositions on an old, battered tambura. He buzzed around like a mosquito. He had taken a vow of celibacy, but he gave charm potions to old sadhvis and devout widows to capture their attention and affection. He bared his teeth at anyone who touched the objects of his worship, but had no qualms in mocking the goddess that he worshipped. He fought with wayfarers who sought shelter; one such fight had broken his back. His teeth were broken. He shunned all those devout who showed him respect. Lame and deaf, he shuffled around on one leg and spoke to people in signs. He slept in the ruins of a temple where he was bitten by black serpents and bees. During the festival of Holi, he was carried on a broken string cot in a procession and married to various old women of the servant class. He visited many temples without any benefit. He suffered from all possible aches, pains, maladies and diseases, which he collected and nurtured as one nurtures a family. His body bore marks of repeated beatings, which he showed off proudly. All parts of his body were scarred. The parrot laughed seeing the brahmin, Kumud wept, while Sarasvatichandra pondered about the scene before them. Soon, the festive fair created by Ashwatthama was engulfed by darkness. Suddenly scores of small shrines appeared and the temple lights brightened up the fair ground. From each shrine came sounds of new songs; even the stars joined in. The hillocks turned to light and many enlightened immortals appeared before them. Ashwatthama stood amidst this new world, playing heart-wrenching tunes on his flute. In some time, the tunes became tranquil. Sarasvatichandra said in amazement, ‘Kumud! This old brahmin personifies the description imagined by a brahmin poet some fourteen hundred years ago.⟨fn:464⟩ This is also one form of the immortal Ashwatthama. The incarnation of Vishnu cursed him to immortality. He imitates Vishnu now. This insane man now protects and nurtures the Arya social order. Look there, how many people bow before him in reverence and having contracted his infection, they go away. They in turn spread the disease to others. What sins have our country and her people—of the past, the present and of times to come—committed that we are forced to take birth and live in a society poisoned by this evil, diseased man? For what reason was he made immortal? Why did God poison our existence? I fail to understand this. These beautiful shrines, these enlightened beings and this deeply felt song creates an illusion! I understand neither the insane nor the sane form!’ ‘He is a brahmin like you! You brahmins were so dear to Maharaj Mallaraj!’ the parrot said in obvious glee. The pained couple gave no response to him. Just then a bed came floating like a cloud and hovered over the fair ground. An emaciated Panchali lay comatose on it. Tears streamed down her eyes and fell on the crowd below. They drank her salty tears believing it to be rain. Her body was covered from her toes to her breasts. Her breasts were bare. A great monkey sat beside Panchali and sucked one of her breasts. The old, diseased brahmin came up and sucked the other one greedily. Kunti, the embodiment of forgiveness and forbearance, sat near Panchali’s head. She had white hair, was old and withered with pain. For ages she had looked intently at the lotus-like eyes of her daughter-in-law. Kunti had for years wiped Panchali’s tears. Her hand had turned white and flaky because of this constant touch of liquid. Her torn saree was wet with her own tears. She repeatedly pushed away the monkey drinking at Panchali’s breast. She chided him, but all her attempts to push away the old brahmin were futile. So long as Kunti’s caring hand touched her, Panchali lay still, but if for some reason Kunti removed her hand Panchali muttered some feeble words. Kumud could not bear this. She came forward, sat at Panchali’s feet, folded her hands and pleaded with the monkey. ‘Oh king of monkeys! Mother Panchali’s body cannot sustain two sucking at her breasts. Nothing can be done about this evil creature, but you are a devotee of the Mother!’ Monkey: ‘Oh beauteous child! I am Hanuman. I used to reside in the flag of Arjun’s chariot. For some time I have taken this miniature form and sit beside Mother Panchali. So long as Kurukshetra was haunted by the illusionary powers of Ashwatthama and packs of jackals, I used to roam far away on the sea coast. They have robbed Mother of her life itself. The God who protected her honour in the assembly of the Kauravas has preserved her body and defeated all those who violated her. I have been commanded by God to protect her from those who have become her enemies. We, the monkeys, protect her with all the arts we are adept in. This place has neither roots nor fruits, and we cannot sustain ourselves without her breast milk. There is no one other than us who can protect her and we must keep alive to do so; therefore, we have to drink her milk.’ Kumud: ‘It would be better if you were to observe some sense of limits.’ Hanuman: ‘I observe all possible restraint. But Bhim, the son of Yavu, is a wolf belly. I am also a son of Yavu; in my heart I am a devotee of Arjun’s favourite wife, but I am also a wolf belly.’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘Immortal one! Countless monkeys of your land similarly feed on her milk while her own children die of hunger.’ Hanuman: ‘That is true. But as the Pandavas gain ascendancy in this country, our Vali faction will accept Sugriv. This evil character will be pushed away from this land. Her milk will then be sufficient for us and the rest of this country. Moreover, contact with her husband will also nourish her body to health and she will become an undiminished source of nourishment—like the Akshaya Patra—for all.’ Parrot: ‘What will you do to this brahmin? Arjun guided by brahminical sense let him go alive.’ Ashwatthama thundered, ‘I am no brahmin! Like this monkey I am without varna, or I belong to all four varnas. I am also a Mleccha. Don’t you know how many different incarnations I have taken in Kurukshetra?’ He stopped sucking at Panchali’s breast, assumed his demonic from and circled around her bed. Hanuman also assumed his full form and followed him at every step. He sang, ‘Ram, who is like Kamini, whose gift was repaid with manifold benevolence. ‘Mother Kunti! You are the embodiment of forbearance; please keep your patience for a while longer. Look there! The five brothers are coming closer; on the distant horizon, Lord Ram paces anxiously to change Panchali’s destiny. So long as the God who protected her honour and became Arjun’s charioteer worries on our behalf, lament is without reason.’ Panchali sang: Lord! You have forsaken me! How can my heart find solace? Lord! That demon in guise of a brahmin Slayed my leonine children at night. Kunti: Daughter! Do not be pained, The Lord has not forsaken you. After slaying your leonine children, This brahmin has not had a night’s sleep.

Panchali: They told me I was their beloved. All five left me for dead On the snow-capped mountains, And ages have passed. Kunti: Leaving you and the brothers behind, Dharma ascended to heaven. Those among the Kurus who abandon their duties Still live a life of ceaseless pain. Panchali: I cannot remember any Violation of duty. Even in the assembly of the Kurus, Did he not counsel restraint? Kunti: Daughter, wise one, you Must have in love forgotten some duty. So would have the other four, Thus causing Dharma to lose his little finger. Panchali: Cannot bear this sucking of my breast By the evil ones on either side. If your five sons were alive, They would have taken pity on me. Kunti: Daughter, wise one, Know your duties from Sri Krishna! Hanuman abides on the flag of Gudakesh; He is not an evil one. Panchali: Enemy brahmin slayed my sons; He feeds on my breast;

I am no Putana, nor is he Krishna. Why does the evil one suck life out of me? Kunti: Daughter, wise one, be patient; It is the result of your actions. No one knows the will of the Lord. He feeds on your breast as a twice-born! The ways of the Lord are mysterious; He manifests in every age. When the time is ripe, when order has withered, He takes form as Narhari. Be intent upon the Lord. Ages and aeons have passed, But the Lord’s benediction persists. Ashwatthama took the form of Uttara and sat down on the bed. He abused Hanuman in his song. Oh grandmother, heed my tears, Do not consider this monkey one of us. Krishna and the monkey left my husband Alone in the battlefield and took Partha away. These two vile ones Took soft-hearted Partha’s chariot away. The Kauravas cast their web of deceit. Did not the Lord of the universe see? Why did the wise ones Leave my husband all alone? Know, oh grandmother, Know, oh mother, Krishna and the monkey played a deceit And now he sucks the life out of you. Panchali opened her eyes, but her tear-filled eyes could see nothing. She closed her eyes. Kunti placed her loving hand on her forehead as she sang. Daughter, wise one drowned in sorrow, Do not be deceived by this Uttara.

A demon was born to the Lord’s sister’s womb; Aware of his birth, the Lord threw him away. In the house of Kuru was born an enemy of dharma; He filled the earth with blood. If he had been killed at birth, Both the earth and the Age of Truth would have prevailed. In the house of Kuru was born dharma; He nurtured the earth to life. If God killed his sister’s son, He gave life to a dead womb. In the battle of Kuru rose Ashwatthama; In various forms he plotted the earth’s destruction. In the battlefield of Kuru sprang up the tree of righteousness And spread across the world. The enemy of dharma born in the house of Kuru died; He lives a ghostly life. He like wind permeates everywhere. Don’t be afraid, daughter! He shall be destroyed. The divine trees that flowered in the family of Kurus Are present in every age. The wind thrashes them, But they gain in strength. Oh mother of India! You of divine Birth! Oh revered daughter, Open your lotus eyes— The wind touched by Partha has begun to flow. Wake up, daughter! The chariot of Arjun waits on the horizon. His flag holds up Hanuman And Krishna is his charioteer. Hanuman began his song. I have one faith, that of Ram. He builds the edifice of dharma. The Lord is one, takes many names, For me in all names one is true. I flew with Ram-Sita on my shoulder, I carried the boulders for the bridge,

I carried the flag of Arjun, I killed the warriors of Kuru. With Krishna as the charioteer, Hanuman holds the lion flag. Time moves in a circle. Now we live in times When Ram takes the form of a twice-born And Arjun circumambulates the earth in his chariot. The Lord made me his charioteer, Battles rage on all sides. Kurukshetra remains pivotal; Arjun’s chariot moves all around. Kurukshetra is the axis of the wheel; The monkey and other animals Pull Arjun’s chariot. Charging me with the protection of his beloved queen, The Kuru warrior crosses the seas. I saw Sita weep under the Ashoka tree. I hold up Panchali’s bed. As battles rage around us, The Goddess remains untouched by arrows; Her heart is heavy with ancient sorrow. I pull the reins of the chariot in rage. I shall bring back the five brothers; I have never failed in a task ever. This was the song of the eternal devotee. Hanuman appeared before them. He was engrossed in weaving ropes that stretched from Panchali’s bed to the earth. The ropes were stretched across the seas. On this ropeway sailed ships and steamers. Some ships carried priceless gold, silver and gemstones while others carried cotton, clothes and goods made in other lands. The ropes touched ports and sea coasts, and were greeted with fire crackers. The myriad colours and sparkling lights made for a festive and rich atmosphere. Railways and steam engines crisscrossed the hinterlands like colonies of ants. They reduced the distance and travel time. They ferried passengers, goods and knowledge, and enhanced their value. In all directions, on the mountains and on islands, in the plains and in the valleys, in forests and in cities, in towns and in villages scores of monkey gardeners tended to orchards and gardens and planted flowering and fruit-bearing trees. All these were reflected in a glass-like sky around Panchali’s bed. The breeze carried the fragrance of Sanskrit and English learning and brought it to Panchali’s bed. The monkey-people had rejuvenated studies of the Vedas and glorious histories of these texts. This reawakening had wafted towards the scholars of Varanasi. The same breeze carried scriptural knowledge towards the West. At various places there were training academies in the craft of politics. There were exhibitions of precious metals mined from the crust of the earth. In these ropeways, in the orchards and in the gardens, in the fragrant breeze, in the seas, in the political academies, in the mines the people of this vast country were attracted by the force of the monkey- people who nourished the people, taught them various arts and ways of accumulating wealth. The people found political order and they came to be constituted as a large, unified oceanic form; the people rose up in waves. Ashwatthama’s fairground gave way to this glorious scene and was reflected around Panchali’s bed. It also entered her shut eyes. The picture became larger and stretched across the Himalayas. Clever monkey-people could be seen running all around to complete the picture. Hanuman stayed near Panchali’s bed, but at times he was the Sutradhar, at times the poet, at times an ascetic in deep meditation, at times a labourer, at times like the commander of an army; he electrified the magical scene with his presence. He brought rains as well. Sarasvatichandra and Kumud were delighted and stunned by this beauteous scene around them. The fear and despair caused by Ashwatthama receded. Enthused, Hanuman said, ‘Oh humans! I have created this world at the command of Sri Ram. During the age of Ram our people had built a bridge across the sea. In this age we build roads, bridges and ropeways to carry Arjun’s chariot. We connect the whole earth. This is the great sacrifice of the monkey-people for the sake of Panchali’s happiness and for the welfare of the people of this ancient land. I am the chief priest of this sacrifice.’ The parrot chipped in, ‘Oh king of the monkeys! You have painted this glorious picture, but where are the walls? Oh immortal, your picture is painted on air; it is devoid of walls and roof. What good have your monkey-people done for this country? You are immortal but not permanent. A time will come when you shall fight with the bear people who live beyond the mountains; if you are not a match for them you have destroyed our ability to protect ourselves and assist you. Your power has limits and our abilities have been destroyed. How many enemies will you fight without any help? Your picture has no support of a firm wall. Your colours fade in water and air.’ Hanuman did not reply to these barbs, but from far in the west harsh voices were heard. ‘We are immortal. We are capable of protecting ourselves and also keep you under our control. All the seas and every rock therein roar with our might; we pull the chariot of Arjun. Arjun is because of us the monkey-people; we are not because of him. We have crushed many a flock of birds like you.’ Parrot: ‘Hanumanji, are you listening?’ Hanuman: ‘Just as you have Ashwatthama, we have a Duryodhana monkey. This is his futile boast.’ Parrot: ‘It might be futile, but it hurts our ears, boils our blood. Even my feathers fall away in excitement.’ Hanuman: ‘Poison cures poison. You are at liberty to give a fitting reply.’ Parrot: ‘Oh Duryodhana, listen! Why are you so boastful? The Arjun who allows your people to rule over us will eventually come back to our land.’ (Unseen) Duryodhana: ‘My pride comes from the strength of my arms. Pandavas might save the world, but its ruler will always be Duryodhana. Your hopes rest upon Arjun’s power. Your bodies are lifeless; you have neither arms nor ammunition, and your homes are bereft of wealth. Animals eat plants, smaller animals are eaten by larger ones and impotent people serve the potent races. This is the order of the universe.’ Parrot: ‘The one who judges the order will soon appear. Do you believe in justice?’ (Unseen) Duryodhana: ‘Justice is a charade of the Pandavas. If we do not rob you of all that is yours, who will?’ Parrot: ‘Of course! Duryodhana, be warned. You are in the Kurukshetra. And Panchali has been defeated for the second time.’ (Unseen) Duryodhana: ‘She shall be defeated time and again. Don’t you see that our Ashwatthama is immortal and present in your land? You have neither the Pandavas nor the Kauravas. He is our Satan and Angra Mainju of Zarathustra. They secured our victory and we persist because of them. You are nothing but the dust of Kurukshetra, fit to be trampled under the feet of the Kauravas and Pandavas. The Pandavas are under our control and they are not bothered about your condition.’ Hanuman: ‘Duryodhana! Let me warn you that in the battle of Kurukshetra our blood will be the first to be shed. But in this age of Brahma the land of the brahmins shall be protected like the young of the lapwing. Let the sword of the world be Brandished as it may. It cannot cut one vein Without the permission of God.⟨fn:465⟩ Parrot: ‘What separates your Duryodhana from Vali?’ Hanuman: ‘Duryodhana has three follies: pride, attachment and cruelty. Vali has only the first two. Karna has no attachment but is egoistic. The Pandavas are free from all these follies.’

(Unseen) Duryodhana: ‘In this world people acquire possessions by competing with each other. In a horse race, horses race towards one goal. If the horses have no pride, there would be no competition; all their activities and impulse of life would cease. Attachment is the root of love—it nurtures industry and efforts. A combination of action with fruits thereof makes endeavour meaningful. Cruelty makes war possible; cruelty is inebriating. Hanuman has renounced all these qualities, and this impotent parrot is forced to learn from us by pecking at our flesh.’ Hanuman: ‘You argue for pride, attachment and cruelty. You attack the virtuous from your hiding place in a lake of darkness. Come out and face us. We shall continue to ignore you until you gather the courage to come out in the open either in our country or face us in the Kurukshetra. Your Panchali chooses the one who emerges triumphant in the battle between Vali and Sugriv; but this Panchali has been married to Dharmaraj and his brothers. These brothers and the benediction of God have protected her through the ages, and they shall continue to do so. Her life is longer than the combined lives of many immortals like you and me. Egypt, Greece, Rome, Babylon and Byzantine were like mere fireflies that glowed at night and disappeared in the light of day. Europe is a recent phenomenon. It has opened its eyes not more than four or five hundred years ago. This Panchali was born before all of them and she is present in this age. Her long life is a sign from God that we need to comprehend.’ Another voice came from the skies. It was Kunti. ‘That is the truth, Duryodhana! That is the truth. If you believe me to be mad ask your mother who blessed you before the war by saying, “Let Dharma be victorious.” Do not make the mistake of turning a deaf ear to what I have to say. Lay not that faltering unction to thy soul. That not thy trespass, but my madness speaks.⟨fn:466⟩

‘Know that even in thy country the truth-seers of history and social evolution have realised that the best guarantee for political prosperity in a nation is the growth of the sense of Duty among its individuals; and long before that sense was born in thy country, it was fully recognised in this country with successful yearning by my lord and husband that high Duty was to be the eldest and ruling one among the five Sovereign Spirits whom he had brought down from Heaven to succeed to his glorious inheritance. Nay, the very mother of those who then represented thy party could only venture to bless this Duty— this Dharma—with success, and could not put in a single word to bless thee and thy numerous crew in that terrible conflict, which then shook the earth and has so often been repeated in this battlefield with a singularly uniform result. Short-sighted flash of the National Ego! In vain dost thou believe that India is doomed to destruction. Thou art bound and destined, in spite of thy deep-drawn grunt, to take India up the heights of progress until you can both co-operate in furtherance of the common weal of the still vaster world.⟨fn:467⟩ ‘Daughter Panchali, listen to the harsh words of this evil man, but do not be afraid. Be warned, be cautious. If Duryodhana’s ploy is like a serpent, that serpent around your neck shall become a garland of flowers.’ Kumud: ‘Is it not surprising that mother Kunti speaks English?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘In Siddhalok all languages are known to everybody.’ Panchali: ‘Mother, I see your sons on top of snow-capped mountains.’ Kunti: ‘Yes. They are travelling around the western ocean. Hanuman has placed a mechanism under your bed which captures their reflections and projects them. They look very attractive.’ Panchali: ‘Oh my youngest husband, knower of all times, Sahadev! When will you come this side?’ Sahadev’s voice echoed through. ‘Panchali. We are destined to be united before long. Shakuni causes errors in my calculations of the cows⟨fn:468⟩. Hanuman has erected my image to counter Shakuni. Lord Bhrugu has the first right to infuse life into that image; Hanuman has the second right. You can see that the book of receipts and expenditure kept in your state treasury has my image. Hanuman publishes my image along with the ‘‘budgets’’ of the monkey-people, and your people learn while playing in the shadow of my image. But Panchali, so long as my elder brothers do not come to you, it is impossible for me to do so. So many Mlecchas have entered your land from the north; which man of your domain has had the courage to expose this? Which native or foreign ruler has allowed your people even so much as to touch their treasury, their chariots, their horses or even charioteers? Hitherto, no king has had the courage to perform their righteous duties. Hanuman has inspired the monkey-people to be duty-bound. Soon it will be time for my elder brothers to return, and I shall follow them. Now you see my image, but soon I shall come and reside with you in your temple. Panchali, we have been separated for too long, which you could bear only with mother Kunti’s help. Have a little more patience and let my calculations inspire you to believe that, When Vishnu rises from his serpent bed, The curse is ended; close thine eyelids tight And wait till only four months more are sped.⟨fn:469⟩ With these words Sahadev’s image disappeared. The handsome, attractive form of Nakul came and sat on Panchali’s bed. The image entered her heart and whispered in her ears. Then we shall taste each long-desired delight Through the nights that the full autumn moon illumines brought.⟨fn:470⟩ ‘Panchali, when you resided with me in my palace, what games of pleasure we played! Those days will soon return. In the age after

Buddha how we roamed this country and our pleasure gardens even today amaze our people! We did not have to suffer such a long separation even during the age of Muslims. I have placed various mechanisms and instruments under your bed for our union. You will be able to see them when you descend from your bed. Oh how I wish I could come and be with you and fulfill all your aspirations! But what am I to do? My feet will not turn towards you until my elder brothers return. Moreover, I cannot come without asking Sahadev and until such time that he is able to return. For now you will have to be satisfied with my reflection and approve all the arrangements made by Hanuman for our pleasure chamber. Do not be irate with him when he feeds at your breast; also suggest to him all the arrangements to be made for Sahadev’s return. Only after Sahadev’s welfare is secured could I consider coming to you. Panchali, do not lose faith in my love. At present I wander through the western regions, but when the breeze comes from the Himalayas, Himalaya’s breeze blows gently from the north, Unsheathing twigs upon the deodar And sweet with sap that it entices forth I embrace it lovingly; it came so far, Perhaps it touched thee first, my life’s unchanging star!⟨fn:471⟩ Nakul’s image also disappeared. Gusts of wind began to blow. Bhim had carried his brothers, along with Panchali and Kunti, to safety from the burning Laksha Griha at the speed of wind. Similar forceful winds began to blow, and Panchali grew expectant. Bhimsen’s tall, broad image loomed over the land and the clouds. His thunderous voice boomed across the skies. ‘Panchali! Your people are without arms, but do not be afraid. You can see that Ashwatthama nullifies the efforts of all my brothers. The weapons that should strike your enemies turn against us due to his machinations. Shouldn’t one take away a sword from the hands of a child intent upon harming himself? The fact is that the monkey-people, for their selfish interests, have disarmed your people. But God placed the monkey-people on our Arjun’s chariot. Our interest lies in their success. They have in fact disarmed insane and evil Ashwatthama; pray do not mourn this loss. Today there is a general climate of distrust. At such a time your people have been disarmed. Is it not in your interest? There is a possibility of a great war among the most powerful kings. They will die like the inebriated Yadavas; it was the power of arms that caused them to be intoxicated and kill each other. Your people are without arms. Could it not be that this is God’s will that your people be saved from drunken self-destruction? The monkey-people are not so stupid as to not arm you when they need your assistance, Panchali! I am the son of Yavu, and so is Hanuman. He keeps vigil over you and learns of your suffering as also of your people. Consider him to be a brother of mine. Sri Ramchandra’s army was composed of monkeys and bears; they have divided up the continent of Asia between them. But at a time when the two of them fight, the monkey-people will learn to have confidence in your sons. They will recognise their worth and will arm them as it would be in their interest to do so. Who are your enemies? Ashwatthama? Duryodhana? Drought? Other ailments and calamities that spread across your land with the speed of wind? Panchali, look! To remedy your ailments and misery, Hanuman has created these images of us Pandavas, and soon we shall arrive to take the place of our images. ‘Is not Ashwatthama also an object of your compassion? God will remedy the problem that is Ashwatthama. You prevented his killing at that time; both Krishna and Arjun took his gem and let him go away. That was also the will of God. Trust that God and know that He will find a solution to this problem. No one paid any heed to my opinion in the matter. But I shall destroy the thighs of Duryodhana if he were to come out of hiding. The punishment that I gave him once has not reformed him at all. The seeds of his depraved nature lie in his mind. Dharmaraj has begun to sow the seeds to counter his evil. Until they grow, he will not allow me to use my force. The limits imposed by Dharmaraj have restricted Duryodhana’s actions, and to that extent he accepts the authority of Dharmaraj. But there is no change in his words and speech, which in some ways is good because if his speech were to alter one would not know his thoughts. Duryodhana’s boastful words are harmful only to him; they in fact benefit you and your people. Vali is also another incarnation of Duryodhana. He believes that his primary service should be to Tara and not you, which in some way is the correct path. This neglect causes you pain; but Vali has the mental capacity to cultivate a mind like Sugriv and the chakor, and perhaps for this reason God pardons his partiality for Tara. Drought and disease plague your people and make them feeble. But you know that the evil effects of Ashwatthama’s sins will one day reduce. When the burden on the earth becomes unbearable, that burden has to be shed. The supply of food and clothing should match the number of people needing them. The sages of the East and the economists of the West know that the surplus people must die. Who can say if God’s design of making some wealthy and others pauper is immoral? ‘Despite all this, my brother Hanuman is as alert as I am about the activities of your enemies. Panchali, if you were conscious of his concerns, of his sleepless nights and of his labours at times of drought and disease, you would take pity on him. I roam the Western world to remain alert about the possibilities of Vali issuing commands to Hanuman in the name of Ram. I awaken the hearts of the monkey- people and try to cultivate compassion and right thinking in Tara.⟨fn:472⟩ You know that I have begun to attract your sons to this country for this purpose.⟨fn:473⟩ The land of the East is today meek, wailing and in slumber; even in those lands the newspapers have begun to report the news of awakening in form of the Congress Committee.⟨fn:474⟩ All this is being done with the support of Hanuman. Are you unaware of this? I have granted new rights to your people⟨fn:475⟩ by forging an understanding between

Hanuman and the Sugriv faction. Therefore, they ask questions to the ministers and keep them on their toes. Hence, Panchali have patience, take heart. How can I come to you so long as the eldest Dharmaraj has not become manifest in your presence? Arjun, who won your hand in marriage, and Dharmaraj will come, and I shall follow them. Till such time, I can only be a reflected image!’ As soon as Bhimsen’s thunderous declamation stopped, chains showered down from the skies. The winds carried these chains in all directions except towards the Himalayas. Along with this melodious sounds of the flute were heard. Hanuman jumped around, caught some chains and fastened them to Panchali’s bed. Arjun clearly approved of his effort. He looked down from his chariot and gazed into Panchali’s eyes. ‘Beloved! You know that I have become a wanderer. At present my orientation is towards Varunlok and Vayulok, but our union is imminent. Have patience until I fill my chariot with the riches of all lands. Hanuman has paved the field for me to come and sow my seeds. Have faith in him. Hanuman knows of all the arrangements that are required to be made for the riches I have collected for you. He knows of my aspirations for a long time now. ‘Panchali! Let this immortal Ashwatthama torment you for now. Out of great pity I prevented his death. I declined to behead him and Sri Krishna turned him into a mad man. Was all of this pointless? ‘There is a method in his madness which time and effort only will unravel, and then shall dawn before the civilisation of these days the wonders we had sown in our honeymoon days! His madness will, in the dullness of time, burst like a volcano and pour over this boasting age the contents of that unquenched genius which has been burning all along beneath the surface of this man’s madness. Progress will then be lifted up forever.⟨fn:476⟩ ‘Panchali, I cannot come to you just at present. My travels are yet incomplete, there is much to be done and time is short. And how can I ever come to you before my elder brothers Dharmaraj and Bhim?

If you want to have me sooner, send out your sons to voyage across the seas. Indra is a friend of the industrious. Panchali, you know the scriptural injunctions. I am the son of Indra; I was born of his body, I know his heart. I am his son as also his soul. Your people have gone into deep slumber; awaken them from this age of darkness. Get them moving; make them industrious and active—only then can the age of truth arrive. This is my father’s promise; he taught this to Rohit and it is true for your people. Till such times come, I have no time for leisure. There is much to be done and too little time. We have to suffer the pangs of separation till then. Have patience, Panchali, and be alert. I won your hand and our union is not far away.’ Arjun stopped speaking and his chariot moved on. Just then Dharmaraj Yudhishthir’s statue, not just his reflected image, appeared. He caught the reins of Arjun’s chariot and steadied it. He spoke gravely. ‘Panchali, it is true that the return of all four brothers is contingent upon my return. But you know well that my hands and feet have to obey my conscience. Our love abides in our joint performance of duties. But when this togetherness could not be sustained, I left you and my brothers on the Himalayas and moved on. During our years of forest dwelling I had clearly told you that for the sake of my duties I would abandon even you and when that became inevitable, I did so. Those duties prevent me from coming to you. Your people have been diseased by Ashwatthama. Those people have no right to abide alongside me. You will ask, what duties and righteous conduct do I embody? You might ask why is Ashwatthama impure while I, who have travelled across the Mleccha countries, am the embodiment of right conduct? Listen. This body was born of the light of Yama; it has been nourished by the land over which the great and victorious King Pandu ruled and I have received wisdom from Vyasa, Sri Krishna, Bhishma and other sages and seers. When the Lord incarnated as Buddha, he kept me in his heart as he set out to save the world. I carried these flowers to Zarathustra and the great sage born in Jerusalem. Even there Ashwatthama came face to face with me. From there for some time I went to the country of the Arabs. There, too, Ashwatthama appeared in the form of destructive Raudra, and I left that land. The leading men of Europe and America have driven away Ashwatthama from their land. I took a new form and went there. I have travelled around the world. At present all five of us are together and we think fearlessly of all matters. But that is the land of Virochan and King Bali. At present he has rid himself of ego but he cannot free himself of attachment; when the time comes even that will happen. Panchali! The riches of that land are material, not spiritual. At present you possess neither material nor spiritual richness. How can I come to you? ‘The monkey-people, even when away from their group, remain bound to the discipline of the group. Their group leader knows that the most wretched, most distant and most inebriated of monkeys shall accept their command. “England expects everyman to do his duty.”⟨fn:477⟩ You have no groups that have unity. It is very difficult to create and maintain such groups and even rarer to find leaders. In absence of disciplined rule there can be no order and in absence of order there is no right conduct. You possess neither. How can I come to you? ‘‘Let India’s sons learn, too, to know their duty and to do it.’’⟨fn:478⟩ ‘But Panchali, this is no reason to be dejected. Hope and disappointment are to an extent under your control. Take measures to bring to life the emaciated body of Pitamah so that you can benefit from his subtle wisdom. If there be among your sons even one who could rejuvenate that body and learn from him and from the history of the world, many such able sons shall come forward. When Sri Krishna counselled Arjun to do his duty and fight, Ashwatthama taught your people to forsake their this-worldly duties. And some other being has entered the body of religion and lives in it. Panchali, when ego and attachment disappear, Rajas too disappears, as it should. But to abandon all worldly ambitions and perform one’s duties in a detached way is to invite the slumber of Tamas. Neither Vyasa, nor Krishna, nor Ram nor Janak have advocated this path. So long as such attitudes persist, the seeds of duty grow up to promote laziness. This allows

Ashwatthama to flourish. The present day chaos is also the will of the Unmanifest One. But truth is not the only duty; truth and Rita combined give us true conception of duty. The sign of a great intellect is to know the Rita and to perform all the duties enjoined upon one. This has become clear to this son of yours standing by your side.⟨fn:479⟩ But the rest of your sons are still in darkness. ‘The countries of the West understand the meaning of Rita. Your sons understood it in ancient times, but at present they have forgotten it. The West has not understood the essence of eternal truth. Your country understood it well once and even now has some hazy conception of it, and for this reason I am partial to this country. And yet it has no conception of Rita, something that the West has. How can I take root in your land? ‘Panchali! The West has no conception of the contribution of the great seers of this land in giving strength and depth to my essence. These seers knew that I was born of the light of Yama. These monkey- people do not understand that. You have to learn from the monkey- people the conception of Rita and make all arrangements necessary to make the five of us effective in your country. Queen Tara in turn has much to learn from you. Queen Tara knows well what she needs to teach you.⟨fn:480⟩ But due to your comatose state you have forgotten the teaching of the great seers; you have no conception of what you need to learn. You must become aware of it. It is your duty to make possible cooperation between your people and the monkey-people. When this duty is performed, this battlefield of Kurus will once again become the field of righteousness and from it will grow grains that would nourish my body and make my entry into this land possible. Only subsequently, we will be reunited. Many rivers flow from this land of Kaunch Randhra. I have been nourished by the wisdom of many lands. The Indus and Ganga carry all these rivers with them to the sea. When my body is so nourished, I shall be able to say to you, Panchali, that I am the sky and you the earth. If you love me, I have shown you the path of duty. I, Dharma, born in this land will manifest myself in the West, a land adept in all arts. My manifestation will rid the present age of all its ills. Then, Panchali, your eyes shall shine bright and the light of those eyes will merge into the eternal sacrificial fire burning in your heart. Your soul shall burst forth into flames to fulfill all the great sacrifices. Panchali, you should know your duties and also know as to what abides in God. ‘Panchali, at present both believers and atheists in the West perceive my presence. My commands are obeyed by each heart. I made this possible by churning the butter gleaned from experiences of all the countries. I wanted to prove that Dharma is not confined to this land, and so I travelled across the Himalayas and hence my accomplishments. ‘Panchali, when in the forests and in the cities, in the huts of the poor and in the palaces of kings, in the weapons of the brave and in the conduct of merchants, in the lives of great souls and the joys of a child, in the renunciation of the ascetic and in the passions of the lustful, in the heart and on the tongue, in knowledge as also in action, in men and in women, in the faithful and in atheists such character develops that each of them become capable of recognising the true potential of their subtle bodies when they all work for the welfare of the country and cause no injury to even the last person, then in that character you shall perceive my purest form. Nurturance of such character will bring beneficial order in the lives of individuals, countries and all humanity. These duties are dearer to God than his own worship and devotion. For God, performance of duty is in no way inferior to a person coming face to face with him. Non-duality with God is best expressed by the performance of duties. This is the gist of all knowledge gleaned from the teaching of all incarnations. This has been described as the state of Brahmi, also as Yoga or skill in action. That duty is my soul. You perceive my Brahmi state due to the light of that soul. When your brahmins recognise these duties, I shall return to you and till such time God the Creator will take care of you—but only if you have earned the right to be cared for by him! ‘O’ kshatriya woman! Do not fail to discharge your duties in face of great torture and grief. Do not be afraid of sorrow, do not allow fear to shock you and do not become proud in joy. You have the power to conquer pain, fear and joy. These qualities will eventually unite us. Immortal mother Kunti has been by your side for ages and she will continue to encourage you even in these last moments of our separation. ‘O’ princess born of a sacrifice! I am unchanged. Let my image enter your heart and nourish it. You are not dry knowledge devoid of action; you are not action without knowledge; you are not devotion devoid of morality; you are not morality intent upon the fruits of your actions. I am that flower that grows on the tree of morality nourished by the earth and the waters of the skies. Arjun, the embodiment of action, follows me because I am that sense of duty which makes action possible. ‘I am Duty incarnate and neither more nor less! Born in this sacred land, fed, nourished by its best fruits, but self-developed and matured and enlightened by travelling through the space and time outside our nativity! Gone but to return when thou shalt shake off thy sleep and want me in the heart of thy heart! And not till then! Sleep on, my love, but hear the ditty I whispered in your ears in the hour of our love, and dream of it! Dream on! Until it fills thy soul.⟨fn:481⟩ O princess, I never act, solicitous of the fruits of my actions. I give away because it is my duty to give; I sacrifice because it is my duty to sacrifice! O Krishna, I accomplish to the best of my power whatever a person living in domesticity should do, regardless of the fact whether those acts have fruits or not. O thou of fair hips, I act virtuously, not from the desire of reaping the fruits of virtue, but of not transgressing the ordinances of the Veda, and beholding also the conduct of the good and wise! My heart, O Krishna, is naturally attracted towards virtue. The man who wisheth to reap the fruits of virtue is a trader in virtue. His nature is mean and he should never be counted amongst the virtuous. Nor doth he ever obtain the fruits of his virtues! Nor doth he of sinful heart, who having accomplished a virtuous act doubteth in his mind, obtain the fruits of his act, in consequence of that scepticism of his! O sinless one, these all, equal to the celestials themselves, behold with their eyes what Is written in the Vedas, and describe virtue as the foremost duty!⟨fn:482⟩ Dharmaraj’s face shone like the moon over Panchali. The faces of the four brothers shone like moons in four directions. Panchali’s face brightened and she, too, was radiant in the region between sky and earth. Kurukshetra acquired a new divine beauty. The sky brightened with the light of seven moons. Hitherto unprecedented peace and tranquility prevailed in the sky and on earth. The three oceans also became tranquil as lakes and reflected the glorious sky. Hanuman stood on one side of Panchali with folded hands and on the other side stood Ashwatthama, his sanity restored for the moment. A voice from the sky said, ‘O’ Pandavas, wait! Remind yourself of the words of Vyasa when Kaba had defeated Arjun. Even thus, understanding and prowess and foresight, O Bharata, arise when days of prosperity have not outrun. These very acquisitions disappear when the hour of adversity comes. All this has Time for its root. Time is, indeed, the seed of the universe, O Dhananjaya. It is Time, again, that withdraws everything at its pleasure. One becomes mighty, and, again, losing that might, becomes weak. One becomes a master and rules others, and, again, losing that position, becomes a servant for obeying the behests of others. Thy weapons, having achieved success, have gone away to the place they came from. They will, again, come into thy hands when the Time for their coming approaches.⟨fn:483⟩ ‘You have re-acquired your capacities. For the present you must continue your endeavours in other lands. A time shall come when all the divine weapons shall be restored to Arjun. The time for this is not far.’

Panchali from her bed folded her hands and prayed to the divine presence. Old Kunti caressed her head and spoke with new enthusiasm and vigour, ‘Daughter, get up and have a glimpse of the Divine.’ Let hands be bereft of arms. Let home be devoid of wealth. It has no meaning on the field of Kuru, As the Charioteer Himself is unarmed. Give up attachment, embrace action. The immortals watch over you. They await a future When righteousness shall prevail. A divine image walked towards them over the carpet of clouds. Sarasvatichandra whispered to Kumud, ‘Kumud! The master of all immortals, the Eternal Brighu is approaching us. Bow to him in heartfelt devotion. This great soul is the only one capable of turning our dejection into hope. ‘We are now in the all-hallowing presence of that almighty Spirit of Harmony, whom Shelly hailed as the Life of Life!⟨fn:484⟩ This is the Divine light incarnate as a brahmin.’ In a short time the enlightened image of Parashuram appeared before them. The seven moons shone even brighter in its light. Parashuram stood near Panchali. He cast his life-giving gaze over Panchali’s trembling heart and eyes. His grave words spread across the world. ‘I am much more than all that, my little children!⟨fn:485⟩ Panchali! I am that divine light, the Omnipresent essence that permeates through the universe. Have my darshan and attain tranquility. What you touch is a thread of the unborn, the undying, eternal and timeless divine being who contains within Him all Time. Do not harbour any fear. Dharma will return to this land along with his brothers. I control their movements. I have appeared before you at this auspicious time to ensure that your hope is not shattered.

‘I am the hope of duty, the reins of Rita. I control, I am the embodiment of truth and I am the beginning of all the three orders. I am the aged form of the one who was Arjun’s charioteer in the field of Kuru. I was the one to prompt Arjun to compete for your hand and I was the one who clothed you in the assembly of Kurus. I was the charioteer of Pandava’s victory and I remain so. Hence, have hope. I live as an immortal through the ages so that my benedictions do not go waste. Panchali, witness the sun of hope rise. ‘Do not be afraid of this Ashwatthama. Many battles have been fought in Kurukshetra. But none of them had warriors of the calibre of the Mahabharata war. That battle saw the end of the light that we called Pitamah. Ganga has preserved that body which rests on a bed of arrows. That battle robbed the brahmins of their potency and their light was snuffed out. But that light had to be preserved in some form and hence insane Ashwatthama has been made immortal. When Arjun’s arms are restored to him, this mad man will be the only source of knowledge about the Brahmastra. Arjun’s weapons have potency, but no weapon can match the power of one that derives from the head of a brahmin. The Brahm Shirostra is at present located within the head of Ashwatthama, and in this age Arjun will be unchallenged by the Kauravas. The acquisition of the weapon would give him great benefits. ‘Panchali, Ashwatthama is the bridge between the age of Krishna and the age yet to come. Once Arjun places the gemstone back on Ashwatthama’s head, his intellect will at once regain the ancient light and Arjun will acquire the knowledge of the Brahma Shirostra. Panchali look! My friend Arjun has the divine gemstone with him. Ashwatthama has begun to show signs of life just by the rays of the gemstone. The life of knowledge shall begin. He will work for your welfare. In my incarnation as Krishna I had cursed him to a life of three thousand years. That period shall soon end. How long has it been since I incarnated as Krishna? Three thousand years? Whose? Of the humans, of the gods or of Brahma? Ask the monkey-people. ‘In the past the monkey resided on Arjun’s flag. At present they hang from the chains of his chariot. Once they acquire the fitness to climb the chariot and have a vision of Arjun’s visage, they would be able to make this calculation and share with you. I will make the present time appear before you. Look at it with your eyes. Panchali, those three thousand years are about to end. Panchali, awaken to life. The auspicious moment of the end of one age and the beginning of another is upon you. Be ready to welcome it. The power of the weapons emanating from the head of a brahmin is very different from the arms of the kshatriyas. The non-Aryas believe him to be God’s creation, but they have not acquired the fitness to comprehend that creation. This is also an aspect of God’s will. If the brahmin, despite insanity and injury, has created so many weapons, what beneficial means would he have produced had he remained obedient to the Pandavas and retained his sanity and capacity for joy? Panchali, your breast milk will not go in vain. The next age will be the age of brahmins, and you will experience only the beneficial effects of its intellectual prowess. ‘In this age the arms and weapons of kshatriyas will be ineffective and the pure brahmins will be the upholder of this age. Ever since the monkey-people have disarmed you, the signs of the age to come have begun to manifest. In that age not only your weapons or the weapons of the monkey-people, but all arms and ammunition developed by humans will be rendered ineffective. In that age you shall be without fear. But if you do not have faith in the times to come, or if your woman’s heart trembles at the possibility of a future conflict or if your kshatriya self in fact aspires to a great battle, yet is afraid of the outcome because of your inferior ability and preparation, for whatever reason if the breeze of change and of the coming age of brahmins does not touch you, take solace from the glory of Kurukshetra. ‘I am more ancient than my incarnation as Ram. My life is longer than my incarnation as Buddha. I am immortal and shall remain so. In each age I have created glory in this field of Kurus. I have witnessed that glory and made it perceptible to the unseeing. You know that glory, but I shall narrate it again to reconstruct your memory. If you do not know it, who else will know and listen to it?’ Panchali sat up with folded hands. All the moons and stars, Hanuman and Ashwatthama became alert. The axe on Parashuram’s shoulder glinted in the light of the moons, but Ram’s face was the most glorious of all. His grave, brave and sombre voice resounded across the skies. ‘Kurukshetra! You are the only field of righteousness on this earth. That in every battle fought on your ground Dharmaraj shall emerge victorious is a statement most appropriate and true. Sage Vyasa called you Dharmakshetra, the field of righteousness. This name was not given because logic suggested it or pride dictated it, but because his all-seeing vision bestowed the name on you. Violators of duty—be warned! Kurukshetra is not for leisure and non-performance of duties. Be warned before you wage a war there. This field is immortal. The ancient land of valour begins from the show-capped peak of Kailash where the gods, the brahmins and the kshatriyas commence their journey of valour and glory. This path is shielded by high peaks. The valleys are pathways from which swans representing the divine body, the knowledge of brahmins and the glory of kshatriyas swim. The seers and creators of poetry came to this ground through the same passage. Brahmins have sung praise of Gayatri whose vehicle is the swan. That age was that dawn of this land. Brahma established Dharma and ever since this field of righteousness has been created. I assumed an incarnation to bring moral conduct to the kshatriyas and demonstrate the power of the brahmins. I defeated Kartikeya, the commander of the army of gods. A large crater in the mountains created a passage for the swans.⟨fn:486⟩ And a new land made by the penance of the brahmins came into existence, a land that came to be called Brahmavrata. In this land battles were fought for supremacy between Vishnu’s powers of preservation and Shiva’s power of destruction. The bows and arrows of the Vaishnavas, the worshippers of Vishnu, proved stronger. And it was established that after each war of destruction, righteousness and duty shall triumph. So, the field of righteousness is the most truthful name for this field. You have witnessed a battle that destroyed the kshatriyas and preserved righteousness. This Kurukshetra, this field of righteousness⟨fn:487⟩ has not changed; anyone challenging its power shall be taught a lesson. The signs of destruction from your times were apparent even in the age of Kalidasa. This field that preserves the order of Brahma and righteousness makes no discrimination between Aryas and non-Aryas, between brahmins and kshatriyas. It does not discriminate between gods and demons. It destroys immorality and untruth, and truth and duty always triumph in this field, and the new age that I described begins from here. ‘The Pandavas established a new age and Yudhishthir ruled over it. After that a learned and righteous king, Babar, defeated the Kaurava-like Lodi rulers and so did his son. The gods in the form of Mlecchas defeated Mleccha demons in this land. This field of righteousness showed its powers at the time of the emergence of Babar and Akbar. Panchali, these rulers were incarnations of Dharma and despite being Mlecchas they preserved the order of Brahma. These kings were righteous kings, and your salvation, too, lies in this field of righteousness.⟨fn:488⟩ A time came when from the south kings with brahminical names attacked this land. Their leader had triumphed in the south and he had egoistically assumed my name. That brahmin king either forgot that this was the field of righteousness or failed to understand that he represented untruth. He was the descendant of that treacherous king who had destroyed the righteous rule established by Shivaji. Like Ashwatthama, who in his hubris wanted Krishna’s Sudarshan chakra, this descendant also sought to capture what was not his. This Kurukshetra taught a lesson to that king and his Duryodhana-like commander.
