Panchali, the king who emerged triumphant was not righteous, but he did not have the false desire to establish mastery over you. He had his victory and he walked away with the women of the defeated army. Both armies were immoral. Both sides thrust their hands into fire and were burnt.⟨fn:489⟩ Kurukshetra destroyed immorality and untruth on both sides. What sense of duty and order emerged? Panchali, awake! Bring your memory alive! Kurukshetra killed the egoistic man who had assumed my name. I gave the reins of these people to Madhav Rao who followed my order. But the people were devoid of virtue and that treacherous lineage brought a virtuous life to a hasty end. ‘The fury of Kurukshetra had subsided due to the virtuous brahmin king, but at the end of his life the fury spread wide and far.⟨fn:490⟩ The destruction of immorality on either side sowed the seeds of righteousness. The fruits of these trees were captured by the monkey- people, who came to our land by the sea route. Panchali, Kurukshetra destroyed the immoral and the violators of the code of duty, root and branch, and drew righteous people from afar with its magnetic force.⟨fn:491⟩ Shiva’s weapons wreaked havoc in Kurukshetra, while the powers of Vishnu attracted new and righteous people. ‘After arduous research the scholars of the West have found that if one wants to predict the future of kings, states and people, the main question is to find the location of duty. Panchali, your glorious father-in-law King Pandu, with the help of his spiritual attainments, realised this secret and he asked for Dharma as his first-born son. The ruler of Kurukshetra realised that the land of Kurus was the field of righteousness, while blind Dhritarashtra adopted a policy quite contrary to it and remained true to his blindness. Panchali, if you are afraid of the monkey-people you should never forget this mysterious power of the Kurukshetra. The monkey-people acquired the fruits of righteousness without the use of arms. The reason for this was their own commitment to duty, the power of Kurukshetra and Arjun’s cleverness. Religion and righteousness do not abide in your shrines and temples—the religion of shrines and temples proved futile in Somnath and Vishvanath in Kashi. Your eldest husband Dharmaraj has revealed to you the true nature of duties; Kurukshetra has time and again given an object lesson in it. The path of this field of righteousness is the path of eternal duties and therein lies the welfare and salvation of all people. Panchali, you shall rise once again with the help of these duties that is the destiny and that is what this field of righteousness shall ensure. Why then are you afraid of the monkey-people? Can’t you see that beyond the Himalayas reside the bear-people? During the age of Ram, in his battle against immorality and violation of duty, both the monkey-people and the bear-people fought as part of his army. In this age they have divided the land among themselves. The bear- people are to the north of the great Himalayas, while the monkey- people are to the south. Monkey-people are different from humans, but they share many similarities with your people. They are cleverer and more disciplined than your people. The bear-people are hardy and tough but they are far behind in the conception of human duties. They are superior to all other animals which reside in the land under their control. During the incarnation of Ram monkey and bear were like the two wheels of a chariot. But in this age due to racial difference and different abilities they live away from each other. They are suspicious and uncertain as to their friends or foes. This age of doubt and mistrust also maintains their suspicion. The roots of age of destruction are in suspicion and mistrust. The bear-people and the monkey-people are separated by Kaunch Randhra and this Kurukshetra. If their suspicion leads them to war they will have to wage their battle in this field of righteousness, they will be measured against each other in this land. Panchali, in all the battles fought in Kaunch Randhra, Brahmavrata and Kurukshetra, righteousness and brahminical virtues emerge triumphant. It is the chariots of your husbands which have emerged triumphant. In the battle between the brahmins of Maharashtra and the Muslims, the victory came to the monkey-people who did not even fight this war. In this instance neutrality came to your aid. If the volcano is to erupt in this land once again then, even though disarmed, you shall be the beneficiary. The righteous faction shall triumph. If, at that time the monkey-people have become wiser and have learnt to trust your sons, they themselves will teach the use of weapons to your sons, who shall fight on the side of righteousness and emerge triumphant. But if till such time the monkey-people have not broken free from the shackles of mistrust, Panchali you must remain steadfast to your duties and stay as far away as you are kept from the volcano that is Kurukshetra. Let that field of righteousness perform its duty. Kurukshetra has never harmed you, and it shall not do so in the future. ‘Panchali, this discourse should be sufficient solace to your heart. But if you are still curious, learn what more you need to know. Learn the reason, nature, character and fruits of the age of brahmins that is to come.

‘When the Aryas lived in the land beyond the Himalayas, the Supreme Being in the form of Vishnu took four incarnations for their protection. He also took animal forms for the animal-like Asuras. When the Aryas reached this land the first two incarnations were of Vamana and mine—both incarnations were as brahmins. The incarnation of Vamana was to settle disputes between gods and demons, while my incarnation settled disputes between kshatriyas and brahmins. I destroyed the kshatriyas with their weapons. I gave charge of the earth to brahmins and I ceased my activities. Panchali, this was the first measure taken by Vishnu to establish the age of brahmins. In my incarnation as Vamana I demonstrated the power of brahminhood. In my incarnation as Parashuram I showed the power of brahmins if they assumed kshatriya character. I gave the earth to brahmins, but they renounced it. The poor brahmins declined to rule over the earth devoid of enemies bestowed upon them by Vishnu. They were true to their brahminical self. They gave an example of non-possession. With this example, I established order and tranquility upon earth. I suppressed the quarrelsome and battle-ready kshatriyas, but they lost the powers and the light of kshatriyahood. I incarnated as Ram for their welfare. The two separate domains between brahmins and kshatriyas were established in that age. Using Vishvamitra’s knowledge of arms and Vashistha’s learning, making equitable use of the power of destruction and preservation and by placing limits on brahmins and by killing a monkey like Vali and a demon like Ravana, Ram established order in this land. Ramchandra and I established order by using the weapons of brahmins and kshatriyas. ‘Subsequently, I stopped wielding arms. In my incarnation as Krishna I did not wield arms, but became a guide and a charioteer of the Pandavas. As Krishna I gave an object lesson to the kshatriyas in politics, statecraft, ego and selfishness. In that incarnation I gave birth to the Pandavas. I taught them, endowed them with prowess and performed my duties through their agency. I sent them on voyages beyond the seas. The Pandavas were not gods, but sons of gods; they were not sons of kshatriyas, but protectors of kshatriyas; they were not sons of man, but were born to a human mother; they were not the essence of Brahma’s creation, but like Brahma they created a new order. Panchali, you have known them in their purest form. In the age of Krishna, these great souls slayed kshatriyas like Bhishma and Duryodhana and brahmins like Drona and Ashwatthama. If these two varnas deviated from the norms of right conduct, the Pandavas showed what end they would meet and who shall assume their duties. ‘Krishna was not merely a Yogi. His Yoga addressed both brahmins and kshatriyas and he gave his wisdom for the benefit of all. Krishna did not take up arms for the Pandavas; he was their charioteer. But Krishna was no renouncer. Buddha, while being free from the responsibilities of a charioteer, became the harbinger of a new age. It was Buddha who was the masterful renouncer. Through his renunciation, penance and teachings he established a new age. I gave an object lesson in a social order where both brahmins and kshatriyas violated their duties. In my incarnation as Buddha, I worked for the welfare of all beings and humanity as a whole, and not specific groups like brahmins and kshatriyas. I created conditions for the eradication of those who went under the name of brahmins without performing any brahminical duties. Finally the essence of the brahminical heart triumphed, and the Enlightened Being shined forth in that age. Panchali, I did all these in this land! This new teaching travelled to Kaunch Randhra, Brahmadesh, Tibet and China. It is Aryas who have gone westwards and their various incarnations have adopted the pragmatic aspects of this teaching for their people. ‘Thus, each incarnation performed the duties of his age. Now one incarnation will have to collect the fruits of each age, gather their essence and make it available to a new age. It is for this task that I have remained immortal. Now the seeds of opposition among the four varnas shall be destroyed. Buddha united the four varnas and gave salvation to all humans from immorality and suffering. Jesus performed this duty for the West. Despite this, the divisions and acrimony among the varnas have persisted and they have flourished in this land like ashwastha, the banyan tree. This is the doing of Ashwatthama. They have persisted in the West as well, but Duryodhana’s policies and power have suppressed them. But the demonic, magical powers of

Bhim’s son Gatotkach have sprung up there, which has shaken the foundations of this policy. This illusionary power emerges like the dark shadows of some demon. It has begun to shake Duryodhana’s crown. It emerges from the crust of the earth and the weapons of Karna, the son of the sun, appear powerless. Those people recognise it by names like ‘‘Nihilism.’’ Duryodhana has made his vast army battle-ready and made Dushasana its commander. But the power of Bhim’s son seems to rise with each passing day. ‘Panchali, Buddha taught humanity to seek freedom from all suffering, which in his times was called nirvana. Now I shall make the human race more able; I will show them the path of upliftment and welfare. I shall give them a joyous existence. During the incarnation as Buddha, I set the hearts of brahmins free and commanded them to conquer the world. Now I shall send the intellect of brahmins to conquer the world. The brahmins who wear their sacred threads in their hearts, not on their body, shall rule over many countries under different identities. They shall rule over the world and worship the five fires in form of the Pandavas. Now each human being shall perform the duties of each of the four varnas. In body, in forbearance and in valour, each will be a kshatriya; in terms of pragmatic abilities they will be vaishyas, and they will serve the human race as shudras. They will be brahmins in terms of their mental aspiration, freedom from lust, absence of ego, in learning, intellect, penance and light. I shall abide in the heart of each human being and with all my four hands I shall raise the four varnas of each individual and the five Pandavas. What, but the intellect of brahmins can devise an order that will secure the welfare of all? Panchali, I have remained an immortal to create an order that shall be the culmination of all ages and all incarnations. I have caused the birth of brahmins in each country. In the age to come arms and ammunition will be useless. Arjun will once again regain his subtle weapons, as Vyasa had promised; the sage’s words will come true. The Kauravas shall serve the Pandavas, while Pandavas will serve nothing but their duties. The chakor and Sugriv of the West have already got a glimpse of the age to come. Once your Ashwatthama regains his gemstone and his salvation is ensured, he will work for this age and his deeds will fetch fruits never before seen. Those hillocks will cease to be; the serpents and their gems, Pitamah on his bed of arrows shall rise and your sons will offer oblations in the great sacrifice of the new age. That age will be the age of brahmins. All people living in every country will have the essence of brahmins and their weapons will be mere ornaments. In my earlier incarnation I destroyed each kshatriya. I wielded their weapons as a brahmin. But in the new age the essence of kshatriyahood shall not be destroyed. Each person will retain kshatriya qualities which will enhance and aid their brahminical qualities. The brahminical order shall turn all weapons futile, including the weapons of the monkey-people. You are unarmed, but we are about to enter an age devoid of weapons. Your disarming was the harbinger of this age. ‘Panchali, if you and your sons comprehend your duties, recognise the true nature of righteousness, you would also recognise that your suffering could only end in your welfare. Your eldest husband Yudhishthir is waiting to enter your temple. The hearts of your sons must bathe in his reflection, their morality and action must be cleansed by Arjun, their body and strength must be purified by Bhim and all other parts should be cleansed by the sons of Ashwin. Hanuman shall teach your sons the art of cleansing; so feed him at your breast and nourish him! ‘Panchali! Panchali! Your sons have bathed in the light of these beings! Your sons glow as bright as the lamps at Diwali. Behold this pleasing picture! Awaken and nourish this newfound light of your sons. ‘Panchali, I have described to you the cause of the age of brahmins and the form that it shall take. Comprehend it well and your aspiration ought to be to participate in the welfare of that age. If you acquire the powers of a kshatriya in your body, the weapons of today are to be as harmless as the nails of your toe. What use do you have for those in the age of brahmins? The monkey-people are vaishyas in terms of their mercantile abilities. Your sons must become their apprentices and learn their trade. Will they be in want of anything after that? If you begin a sacrifice of service to all humanity, why would you not attain supreme bliss and secure your salvation in and through service?

The brahminical essence, which is capable of nourishing the qualities of kshatriyas and all other varnas in one body, will shine forth. The world has seen the flames of their great sacrifice before, and it shall do so in times to come. Is it not a matter of your endeavour to secure your lineage, to increase and cultivate its inheritance? Panchali, you are one, but the rays of each of these moons have entered each pore of your body. This is not a dream; it is a fact. If you nurture this truth, this Rita, you shall acquire the fitness for the new age from now. The light of these moons shall impregnate you. If you nourish your womb and give birth to the child, you will worship the age, which is your child and you shall make apparent to all what has been latent so far! ‘Panchali, just as the snow-capped mountains of the Himalayas are clearly visible in the light of these moons and the waters of the three oceans sparkle clearly, are you not able to perceive the tapestry of the age of brahmins? Panchali, you will be required to perform great deeds in that age. That is your duty. The monkey-people are jumping around you like the ocean waves. They will provide your sons with the means to travel to other lands; the oceans shall become mines of riches. You and your sons have become as frigid and lifeless, as calm and cold as the snow of the Himalayas. Your distant, cold snow and the saline, frothing water of the monkey-people are both ultimately water. Together, you shall create a new world. Panchali, your people have become as unmoving as Agastya; but that body shall come to life with the waters of the oceans. If there are inebriated and uncontrolled elements among the monkey-people the Ganga shall turn them tranquil, cool and pure. Panchali, be prepared to unleash the purifying waters of Ganga and Yamuna. Make your endeavour! I, the immortal brahmin incarnation of Vishnu, am prepared to give you that ability and flow! Within a few moments or days of my time you shall acquire the fitness! ‘Panchali! Kunti! Pandavas! Hanuman! Ashwatthama! Bhishma! Serpents! And all the creatures living in the regions between the mountain and the sea! So long as Yama can cause impurity in you, what can even my strength do for you? What use is my knowledge of weapons? What can my devotion do? What is the use of my knowledge of the Vedas? What is the use even of my birth in the enlightened lineage of Sage Bhrigu? Or what can my extraordinary penance achieve? I am plagued by such inarticulate concerns. May these concerns nourish your progeny.⟨fn:492⟩ Parashuram’s voice subsided. All the moons circumambulated Panchali and sang in a melodious voice: Know, O people, that Panchali holds, for the good of the world, the energy implanted by Pandavas as the Sami tree contains fire inside.⟨fn:493⟩ Hanuman came forward and spoke, his words echoing through the mountains and seas: Let Parashuram, Son of Renuka who bestowed the earth surrounded by oceans on three sides to the Dwija, nurture all the Aryas.⟨fn:494⟩ ‘Those only will survive this out-going Age of Destruction who are fittest to live in the in-coming Age of Construction, and the fitness, will consist, not in the mailed fist and its power to destroy, but in the progressive virtues of the brain and the heart. May we be fit for that Age, for there is no hope of survival for those not trying to be so fit!’⟨fn:495⟩ The voice receded and with it all the pure beings disappeared. Kumud and Sarasvatichandra, joined together by the light, flew towards the south, leaving behind the land of the Kurus bathed in white light, the snow-capped Himalayas and the starry skies. Soon, they were flying over Ratnanagari, its port bustling with steamers and a large sea-facing house. The only signs of life there were the burning lamps.

‘Kumud, look! The destiny of the state of your father’s ruler is about to change. A new dawn shall bring great festivities!’ exclaimed Sarasvatichandra. ‘So be it! But each moment of Lord Bhargav contains many human years. My heart cannot wait so long,’ Kumud replied. The dream ended. Both of them were in deep sleep on the top floor of the Saumanasya Gufa. Kumud had her own dream, in which she said, ‘The two years of wait that you have decided is too long! So be it! We women have to learn and find solace in Panchali’s separation and in Kunti’s forgiveness.’
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra and Kumud journey above Kurukshetra, witnessing ancient immortals like Parashuram who contemplate India's profound past and uncertain future, revealing a grand, timeless vision.

chapters.title: The Final Blow on the Sandalwood Tree
paragraphs: The Final Blow on the Sandalwood Tree Woodman, spare that tree! Touch not a single bough! In youth it sheltered me, And I’ll protect it now.⟨fn:496⟩ Sarasvatichandra slept deep and undisturbed. After the conclusion of their dream he passed the rest of the night in dreamless sleep. His eyes opened late in the morning at eight. Kumud had woken up at her usual time. Their divine dream had also entered her private one. She waited for a while for Sarasvatichandra to wake up. She decided not to disturb his sleep. She kept by his side a twig and other objects for him to brush his teeth with, and went down to join her companions. She came back to check on him after a while and found him awake. She exchanged some casual words with him and went away. While she was on the bridge connecting the two caves, Kumud said, ‘For some, togetherness sparks desire. But our desire has subsided! How beautiful, untroubled and pure the day appears!’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The world is a reflection of the state of our minds. The world of that divine dream and your pure, pious mind combine to give us a day such as this.’

Kumud: ‘Dream nourished by your pure, unsullied mind is more of an instructive lesson than reality. It strengthens my mind. Will you write down tonight’s dream as well?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Most certainly. The previous dream had intensified my pain. Last night’s dream has restored my equanimity, and I have now some conception of my duties.’ Kumud: ‘The Master’s endeavour has succeeded.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘His benedictions are always with me. But the dream gave me what his powers could not have given. Kumud Sundari, I will soon be able to formulate my duties towards the country and all my loved ones.’ Kumud: ‘How?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Today, I shall not step out. All day I shall think about it, make a plan and explain it to you in the evening.’ Kumud: ‘The time of dusk is usually spent in pleasure. It gives rise to desires; we have experienced this. It is best that sleep should create a barrier at that time. It is desirable to have this conversation during the day.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The bottle of perfume had tilted, but we prevented the perfume from spilling out. We have firmly placed a seal on it. Are we not free from fear on that account?’ Kumud: ‘I believe that your heart filled with pure dreams shall give no opportunities to such fears. But our lives have not attained sufficient levels of subtleness. We have not reached a stage where no effort is required to keep the physical body in limits.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I need the day to formulate my ideas fully. And the night should be of the type that you describe.’ Kumud: ‘I believe that we shall be able to make the third night even purer than the previous two nights. I seek your permission to leave.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What is the role of permission where two have become one?’ Kumud: ‘That is also true. I am going.’

She left. Sarasvatichandra called her back. ‘Kumud Sundari, stay a while.’ Kumud returned. ‘What is it?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Is your mind tranquil?’ Kumud: ‘Yes.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Is it firm?’ Kumud: ‘This question itself weakens my resolve.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘If I were to share with you some news that pertains to you, will you be able to take it without sorrow?’ Kumud: ‘You know what my few strengths are; you are the only one who can enhance them.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Will your heart remain steady aided by the force of knowledge?’ Kumud: ‘If it is that, there is no reason for any doubt.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Do sit down and read these newspapers.’ Kumud sat down and read. She read with trembling heart and tear-filled eyes the news about the deaths of Saubhagya Devi and Pramaddhan and the news of her own drowning. She put the newspapers aside and sat weeping. She could think of nothing to say or do. A deep, black sense of loss, tragedy and sorrow filled her. Sarasvatichandra: ‘I knew that this would cause you deep pain and hence had kept it away from you. But I felt that in our matured sense of oneness, this concealment was wrong, immoral. Therefore, I steeled my heart and put you through the torment of reading these.’ Kumud’s face withered. She could not control her tears. ‘You will understand my pain with regard to Devi. But truly speaking, my sorrow with respect to my husband is the same; in fact my sense of loss is deeper. He was a man of good character and virtue. He went on the wrong path because of the company he kept. I blamed his intellectual inability; I did not see any depravity in his heart. He was not a man of learning, but he had a heart. And you know that even in your case, I trust your heart more than I trust your learning. Do you believe that he would have never missed me or remembered me if he were alive? Dear Sarasvatichandra, my heart is filled with compassion for you and love for him. I had hoped that eventually you shall return to Bombay and be happy, and that I would have no reason to feel pity towards you. I had hoped to return to him eventually when his heart softened. I had firm belief that such a time would come. But belief and hope lie shattered! I kept this body pure even from your touch for his sake. Now that he is no longer alive, am I to go back to my in-laws or to my parents, and for what? I had once read, Jealous, jealous, yet the heart Loves and weeps when all is past.⟨fn:497⟩ ‘Oh God! Is this what you desired?’ Kumud hid her face in her palms and wept irrepressibly. Sarasvatichandra could not bear her lament. He gave up his self- imposed limits, sat down beside her and caressed her back and head. ‘Kumud, if I fail to understand the purity of your heart, who shall? You are generous, pure and forgiving. Now you have to show that you have the forbearance to deal with such times.’ Kumud: ‘The world will take my wailing to be a charade.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Let the world believe what it wants to, mourning is a condition of one’s heart. How are we concerned if the others believe us to be true or false? Our women make scenes by weeping and wailing, they adopt artificial strategies. Have we done any such thing? Your sense of loss and pain are untainted. But among the ascetics there is no place for this loss and suffering.’ Kumud wiped her tears and moved ever so slightly away from him. ‘What you say is right. But according to social norms there is a different conduct expected from me now. First I have to bathe, I am required to go into seclusion as my touch defiles, and these bangles will have to be broken. I will have to perform all the rituals expected of a widow. But who will guide me and make me perform those rituals?’ She wept again with these words.

Sarasvatichandra: ‘You are not required to abide by the norms of the society which you have renounced. In this holy place, couples joined in matrimony by pure marriage do not even mourn the death of a spouse. What society describes as lifelong widowhood is not regarded as such by the ascetics here. Therefore, you should ask the best among the ascetics and Chandravali Maiya and do what they suggest.’ Kumud: ‘Is it appropriate for me to wear these clothes even for a moment?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Try and see it from the spiritual view point of the ascetics. All modes of dress prevalent in society are based on certain notions. If we disregard these notions and regard all forms of dress as similar, you should not give up the dress that you have adopted. Or else you should adopt the mode of dress considered appropriate by the ascetics for this occasion.’ Kumud: ‘You have adopted ochre robes. I shall do likewise.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘In all such decisions, you should seek the opinion of the ascetics.’ Kumud: ‘What you suggest is both right and proper.’ This young woman, an embodiment of sorrow, a picture of turbulence, got up; her sighs were loud and rapid like a pair of bellows. She looked at the stones around as if they were staring at her and trying to say something. She climbed down the staircase of Vasant Gufa as if she counted each step. Sarasvatichandra watched her receding form intently without blinking once. As she disappeared from his field of vision, he turned reflective. I did not want to see her in pain and mourning, hence I withheld this news from her. But our new relationship has enjoined upon me new duties. So long as I was afraid of the possibility of physical attraction between us, it was best that Kumud remained within the limits of a married woman. Now, that fear has been eradicated from both sides. She regards herself as a widow. If physical desire had awakened in us at this stage, I might have believed that our union was not inappropriate and that our purity and chastity, which was under attack from many other forces and emotions, would have been eroded. We kept our chastity only by the exercise of soul-force. A young woman having lost her husband might have embraced desire! But that is no longer a danger either for her or for me. The immense grace of God and our wisdom has turned our desire to the path of salvation. The subtle love has triumphed over physical desire. Now there are no thorns in the path of subtle love. Kumud, at present you are in pain and in mourning. But this mourning will be your path to salvation. I have done the cruel act of a surgeon. Your other pain and suffering was so intense and acute that your delicate heart had no scope to learn from your suffering. The last blow has been struck; from this you shall move towards a more reflective state. God has created pain and suffering to bring our subtle lives to fruition. Pain and suffering, when they become unbearable, find a way of resolving themselves and take us towards the path of salvation. He that lacks time to mourn lacks time to mend. Eternity mourns that. ’Tis an ill cure For life’s worst ills to have no time to feel them. Where sorrow’s held intrusive and turn’d out, There wisdom will not enter, nor true power, Nor aught that dignifies humanity.⟨fn:498⟩ Kumud, your heart will find a purer state of existence out of this suffering. Panchali, the dreams of the immortals promise your salvation. Kumud will attain her spiritual body through her suffering. Kumud, if society were to consider you the personification of contradictions, could it be blamed? You have immense love for me, and yet your heart grieves for Pramad. Society might consider it the cunning of a woman’s heart or the result of contradictions created by God. What else can they do? For them, Woman’s at best a contradiction still!⟨fn:499⟩

But these ascetics will subject you to the purest test of your ailment and give you the best remedy for it. They will search out the contradictory elements of your heart and make a harmonious melody of it. O’ world! Kumud is like the branch of a sandalwood tree; how many more blows will you strike at her? The fragrance of those cuts has wafted up to Sundargiri. World, stop striking at her! I will not allow your axe to reach that tree. Now I have the right to intervene, and her protection is my duty.
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra gently reveals devastating news to Kumud, leading her to profound grief and a new understanding of her path, as he vows to protect her.

chapters.title: Friend or Lover?
paragraphs: Friend or Lover? A virtuous wife and a respected lord Are each to either all—kindred and friends, Wealth, love and life, and all the heart Should covet.⟨fn:500⟩ Sarasvatichandra stood on the platform of their togetherness and shared dream, wondering how the sandalwood tree that he had raised and cared for would deal with this new and severe blow. He wondered if the strength he had given her would enable her to withstand it. He saw Kumud approach the pool of water. She bathed herself and washed her hair. All her companions stood in silence like statues and mourned with Kumud. The man who stood on the platform of his cave imagined Kumud’s tears adding to the water of the pool. Her waist-long wet hair, the clothes clinging to her body, her withered face and her slow, unsteady movement gave her solace. Desire, compassion and sorrow assailed him and deep sighs of dejection palpitated in his heart. Love flowed through his veins. He sang along with the poet Narmad. Beloved, accept the salam of your Yaar, Do not be careworn, take not to heart the meanness. Many a wounds you have borne, passed through fiery ordeals; Food has become tasteless, waters have flooded your boat.

A union of two alike, desires of both have been slain; Companionship has been broken, both lost the race. Crafted of the same jewel, set in gold, But the union was scowled at, all colours lie scattered. Kumud! My Kumud! Beloved! Stop mourning! Break the shackles! Tell me, what may I do for thee? Why does the heart ache? We are in a new land, We shall roam in different garb. We have nothing to fear of society, We have renounced the ways of the world. We have left our kin behind, They, too, have abandoned us. The way of the ascetics is delightful, Accept these robes if you will. This is the play of the Creator, Beloved! These are the signs He sent. Beloved! Grieve no more, Come, be one with this heart. Beloved! Pine no more, Offer a sacrifice to love. As these words flowed out of his heart, Kumud’s ascetic companions gave her new clothes. Sarasvatichandra could not see if Kumud’s eyes were filled with tears or dry. She wiped her body, changed her red saree and wore the new ochre clothes given to her. Both her seen and unseen body signalled something to the eyes that watched her intently. She now stood in the garb of an ascetic. The body stopped sending signals to the eyes. Kumud stood before him, young in body but the very embodiment of a hermit. Sarasvatichandra watched her with tranquil mind, his heart filled with emotions that were pure. Kumud’s companions chorused in delicate voices, ‘Nandko Nandan ek anand det hai! Vishnudasji ki jai! Chandravali Maiya ki jai! Madhuri Maiya ki jai!’

The group disappeared from his vision into their cave. Sarasvatichandra had just sat down to write the narrative of their dream when he was interrupted by a voice. ‘Maharaj, with your permission, could I come up?’ ‘Of course,’ replied Sarasvatichandra and stood up to receive Radhedas. Radhedas: ‘Maharaj, there is a message from Viharpuriji. Your dear friend reaches Yadushrunga tomorrow morning. Viharpuriji wants to know where your friend should stay.’ ‘Please bring him here,’ Sarasvatichandra replied joyously. ‘As you wish,’ said Radhedas and went away. Sarasvatichandra thought, Chandrakant will be here tomorrow morning. But what should I do with Kumud? Should one suffer separation from the beloved while one is united with a dear friend? No, it is not right to distance Kumud even for a moment, certainly not after her fiery ordeal and our sublime togetherness. But Chandrakant has no inkling of the philosophy of these ascetics. His world view is that of a householder. Who knows what he may imagine? Would that not place an obstacle in our friendship? But why should I speculate about what lies in the future? Beloved Kumud, if you wish to remain away from my friend you will stay in your cave and he will live in the floor below mine. But if you in fact wish to meet him, then the matter shall resolve itself. My friend will subject my purity to test and understand my ascetic life; he will welcome my union with Kumud and provide me with the most able support in this sacrifice of love. And if I am found wanting, he will forsake my friendship. I have abandoned all of them. How am I to blame him if he were to abandon me now? He is a learned man but has knowledge of only societal norms, and if he is guided by them, can his love for me be faulted? A new morality and duty binds me to Kumud. This duty is moral and it has resulted in our union. It is imperative that I remain true to it. I will do my duty towards my friend without in any way violating my duty towards her. The eternal norms of the ascetics point me to this path. There can be no other mode of argument. Oh ascetics, I clearly see the path of eternal duty—this is the path of Peace, Joy and Salvation. Your conception of duty is uncomplicated, and complications, if they arise, find resolution. It is true that performance of these duties is often difficult and painful, but for this reason these observations are like a penance. Penance is natural to ascetics and despised by those who lack virtue. Penance is the only mode through which duty is recognised and followed. Kumud, what sublime beauty and upliftment have we experienced in this penance envisioned for us by Chandravali Maiya!
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra observes Kumud's ascetic transformation, then grapples with how to reconcile their unique bond with his friend Chandrakant's impending arrival.

chapters.title: A Woman's Heart and her Power
paragraphs: A Woman’s Heart and her Power I pass, like night, from land to land; I have strange power of speech; That moment that his face I see, I know the man that must hear me: To him my tale I teach.⟨fn:501⟩ A drooping flower is a woman’s loving heart, Upheld by the stem of hope when two true lovers part.⟨fn:502⟩ Attired in her new ochre robes, Kumud went with her ascetic companions. Sarasvatichandra sat on the platform of the Saumanasya Gufa, a place that had given rise to noble dreams and sublime aspirations. He read the account of his dreams and pondered as to how the welfare of his country and her people could be secured. He also considered the means that would be required to fulfill these duties. As the different elements of his dreams revealed themselves and clarified his duties further, he spent the entire day in this happy frame of mind. The only interruption in his cogitations was lunch; and apart from Kumud no one or no other thought entered his mind. Kumud, the companion of his dreams, became a companion in wakeful state and contributed to his aspirations. He spent his day, till just before sunset, deep in thought. Having arrived at certain clarity and conclusions, he climbed up on the terrace of the cave and looked at the beautiful scenery around. He mused aloud in soliloquy, ‘Bodily strength increases and diminishes with use. Similarly the abilities of the mind expand and contract with use. But when mind and body are in harmony the prowess of both the mind and body increase or diminish together. Consumption in moderation increases both abilities, but when these limits are breached both mind and body wither. This sense of limits is known to these ascetics and the people of the West; our ancestors also had knowledge of it. The welfare of people can be ensured by growth and good use of these abilities. In labour, in penance, in industry, in pleasure, in pain, in enjoyment and in renunciation, this sense of limit has to be recognised and observed. In all these endeavours welfare is secured by observing these limits; any breach leads to harm. Ignorance with regard to this sense of limits has created fires of suffering in my country; it has withered all abilities in my country. All attempts by scholars and statesmen to raise my people from the mires of ignorance have been futile and have failed. Our ancestors believed, and people of the West even today believe, that fire—whether apparent or hidden— is dormant in wood itself. Similarly knowledge and ability in our people lie dormant, unseen. My only aspiration is to reveal what is latent, bring to light what is hidden. That is my duty. I shall perform a great sacrifice to fulfill my duty. My conduct shall be in accordance with my duties and I shall offer oblation in that sacrifice.’ In this land, virtue and ability Have for ages remained dormant; I shall offer a sacrifice To make patent what is latent. I have the capacity for sacrifice, I shall offer my wealth as oblation. People are my body— I wander among them with ash smeared over me. For me, a renunciate, The world is akin to a crematorium. In these ochre robes of a renunciate I bear witness to the play of the divine.

Sarasvatichandra sang the poem aloud with his arms raised to the sky. He did not care if anyone saw or heard him. Kumud heard his soliloquy. She silently came up the steps and stood at the back. She was still deep in sorrow. His words brought forth new thoughts and fresh tears. She looked at his statuesque figure and sighed with dejection. She stood there trembling like a leaf. Finally, she wiped her tears, came forward and fell at his feet. Sarasvatichandra was startled. He held her delicate, trembling form by the shoulders and said, ‘Kumud Sundari, Chandravali Maiya has told us that this is not a practice acceptable to ascetics. Please get up.’ Kumud stood up and said, ‘Please initiate me. Once you destroyed my pain. Do it once again. I am still a householder; these ochre robes have not helped me come out of that mire. Once the touch of your feet allowed me to be your companion in the world of dreams. I touch your feet once again in the hope that you will take me on the pure path of salvation. Point me to a path which will neither be objectionable to society nor to the ascetics. You consider a householder’s life akin to a crematorium. For me, it is a crematorium. The pyre that could burn my sorrows has not been lit. It was ignited once, but gusts of wind have swallowed up that fire. My pain still lies on that pyre, rotting. Please turn to ashes my pain, my desire and the blot upon my person. Give me the strength to rise along with you as ash rises in the wind. I do not want any other life!’ Sarasvatichandra placed his hand on her back and said, ‘Kumud Sundari, your mourning purifies you. A few days ago my hand on your back ignited desire in us; but today we have no such desire. This is the outcome of your pain and mourning. We experience the togetherness of our subtle bodies. Your mourning can do nothing more; hence you must forsake it as it is without reason. Tomorrow morning, Chandrakant will be here, and you and I will not have much opportunity of time with each other. It is best that you douse your suffering and make use of this brief togetherness.’ Kumud looked up perturbed and said, ‘Let Chandrakantbhai come. But I fail to think of what we need to discuss.’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘Calm yourself and sit down. I will tell you what needs discussion.’ Kumud: ‘I will sit down after you do.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Let us sit down together. First, tell me what did your ascetic companions counsel you about?’ Kumud: ‘They do not consider him to be my husband. What use is their advice?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What rituals would they observe in case of a husband?’ Kumud: ‘When a householder becomes a renunciate, s/he has to bathe to signify social death. On occasions of death such as this, bathing is prescribed only for those who have touched the dead body. The ascetics do not mourn the loss of a physical body. Widows consider the subtle bodies of their husbands immortal and see the absence of the physical body as a temporary separation. A widow does not change her physical appearance; hair and bangles are for her memorials of her union with her husband and she continues to cherish these signs. In any case, among ascetics they do not wear ornaments, so the question of their removal does not arise. The ascetics do not show any outward sign of mourning and their inner mourning is contained by union with the husband’s subtle body. Their subtle love makes the subtle body accessible and no special endeavour is required by a widow. I have worn these ochre robes because of my faith in them and your command that I should obey their wishes.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I know that they do not shave their heads at the time of their husband’s death, but keep their hair tied in a single plait. Meghaduta has prescribed this single plait, which is observed here.’⟨fn:503⟩

Kumud: ‘That is true; our married women understand neither the duties of widowhood nor the essence of togetherness. Our cruel society condemns a woman who expresses her love for her husband. If the couple make any obvious sign of love they are condemned, and the woman more so as this is seen as enslavement of the man to the woman. These ascetics have a way that is quite the reverse of the ways of householders. I could not come to any decision as to what I should do, and hence I wore these ochre robes. I have not even thought about my hair. In my inner mourning I have forgotten about all outward rituals.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘These are signs of asceticism. You are an ascetic.’ Kumud: ‘If that is your belief, my sorrow shall slip away.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I say what I believe.’ Kumud: ‘In a man as virtuous as you, no other possibility exists, but pain misguided me momentarily.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Then let us consider and decide as to what our conduct towards each other should be and what norms should guide us. Tomorrow morning Chandrakant will reach here. He knows I am here. Do you want him to know of your presence or would you rather keep him in dark?’ Kumud: ‘Your friend will be a man of virtue like you. But I cannot rid myself of the sense of limits and fear imposed by society. If my parents, who have given me up for dead, were to know that I am with you, what ideas would assail them? Who will believe that with unmatched mental strength you have remained chaste and preserved my chastity? What opprobrium would it bring to this community of ascetics which has sheltered you and me? Such a line of thought gives rise to many such questions and shakes up my heart. I can exercise no control over my heart when I think of the disrepute that my conduct would bring to my parents. I cannot even begin to imagine the pain it would cause my father-in-law. It is best for everyone that the evil world believes Kumud to be dead.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘What you say is correct. There are only two ways of ensuring that your presence remains a secret. You should either live in the Parivrajika Math or live with Chandravali Maiya for the rest of your life. And we should be content with the distant love of the moon and the lotus.’ Kumud: ‘Oh God, Your will is supreme!’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Do not be dejected. This is one way of securing what you desire.’ Kumud: ‘After much thought and careful consideration, we had decided to spend two years away from each other and the rest of our lives together. But now you tell me something different. I have no one else I call my own. I shall do as you decree.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘There is no contradiction in what I have said. All of Sundargiri knows our story, except that they do not know our names. When my true identity becomes known, yours will automatically be known as well. Nothing will be left to the imaginations of our loved ones. Once your parents know that you have been with me they will be pained, something that you wish to avoid. I do not fear either the society or anyone else. The ascetics recognise that we are one. I have enough means to marry you openly and live with you in Bombay after two years—that is the best fruition of my penance. I have nothing to fear. I have only to gain. But your parents will be subjected to social criticism. These are the two options; whichever finds favour with you is acceptable to me.’ Kumud: ‘All your desires lead you to penance.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Why do you entertain such doubts once you have experienced oneness? If one path can give us many possibilities, why should we not take that path? You have experienced both my love and my desire; why do you entertain doubts regarding it? If fulfillment in love also makes penance possible, why should one shun that path? I cannot recollect having done anything to have lost your trust.’ Kumud: ‘You must stop mentioning penance. Your penance, your love and your grace should all consist in forgetting about penance. Please do this for my sake.’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘That is beautifully said. I vow to follow that. Nothing is difficult now that I have the strength of your love.’ Kumud: ‘Till this morning I had believed that we have two years to decide about our future together. What is the haste now? You seem eager to decide on this matter today.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Once my identity is known to people, you will either have to come out in the open or keep our relationship a secret. We have to decide on one of these as a future course of action.’ Kumud: ‘I wish to keep myself and my life a secret. If the world is not convinced about my death, I will live under constant apprehension. I cannot hope to be alive and be separated from you. If I stay with you as a partner in subtle love, the world will create uproar and my parents and father-in-law shall suffer. I do not have the strength to witness their suffering. Death is preferable to their suffering.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Since the time of Bhavabhuti, our people have been suspicious of the virtues of speech and women. You fear that their opinion remains unchanged.’ Kumud: ‘That fear is not false.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘We shall remedy that fear at an appropriate time.’ Kumud: ‘You might be courageous. I am not so in the least.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘We shall endeavour to make our people understand the virtues of our women.’ Kumud: ‘You will be buried under the mud of that hillock. In our dream we had the means to rise out of that mire; but in wakeful state I have nothing. My heart trembles at the mere thought of it. We women are by nature fearful and hence we perform even good deeds without revealing ourselves.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘You have given me that experience today. Do tell me which path would give greater solace to your heart? When my intellect is useless, there should be no obstacle to seeking an answer from your heart. There is no one else we can go to for an answer.’ Kumud: ‘I know where my courage would fail me, but I do not know what I am capable of doing fearlessly. You have the capacity to work for the welfare of our people, but that cannot be done without being among the people. You will, in your endeavours, not gain equanimity without my companionship and you will also need a companion like Kumud to care for your little needs. But Kumud’s companionship will make you an outcaste, and people will throw away the garland that you have made for them like it were a snake. I want you to live in the society and work for its welfare. If you accept my companionship, that would become impossible for you. You will never gain equanimity without me as your companion. And what state would I be in without you? I want you to go back to Bombay with Chandrakantbhai. I would like you to give the benefit of your companionship to another more fortunate and unsullied woman. My depraved body will find some corner in the valley or in the sea. There is no place for me in the world and no place is too small for my dead body. Oh my beloved, what I have told you is the truth and for the good of all. I seek permission to touch your feet one last time and go away. I have given you enough pain. You are generous enough to forgive everything. Beloved, now let me go. At least in this one matter my courage holds.’ Kumud got up and walked towards the staircase, weeping. Sarasvatichandra’s eyes brimmed over. He could not bear this tragic scene and disregarding all notions of right and wrong he got up and held Kumud in his embrace. He wiped her tears. He held her face away from his chest and was about to say something to her when she collapsed and fell like one dead. If he had not managed to hold on to her, she would have fallen some twenty yards down the rough stone steps and her delicate body would have broken. Sarasvatichandra leaned over the young woman he held in his arms, his tears merging into hers. He had no doubts regarding his conduct. He spoke to her inert body, ‘Oh my delicate sandalwood tree! Oh my Kumud! There is no scope for further reflection; you do not have to burden yourself with decisions! Consider yourself free from all social bondage. I fear no one. I have not violated any norms of ascetic conduct. I am yours in every sense without any fear of transgression of norms. I am capable of working for our people’s welfare under any circumstances. Your companionship is in no way an obstacle; in fact, it is auspicious and necessary to my endeavours. Your life is necessary not only for yourself but for me and for the fulfillment of my aspirations. Oh my Kumud, awaken to life! I am yours! You are mine! The ascetics and the divine immortals have all testified to this.’ Either his words or his breath touched her heart, and Kumud came to life as a withering flower comes to life in rain. She opened her eyes and, leaning on his shoulder for support, slowly raised herself. She wiped her tears and said, ‘Forgive me. My brain could not take the pressure. I was not in coma, just in deep thought. I heard everything you said, and an idea has flashed in my mind. I am not going to take my life. I have gained your companionship and also the right to serve you. The ascetics lead a life of truth. I am eager to follow that path of truth and appear before the world as I am. If we are one according to eternal norms, if our hearts have been united without the rituals of marriage, if our union is an imperative, if you are the husband of my heart, then I am like the earth and you are the sky and wherever I look I shall find you. For a woman devoted to her husband, neither her parents nor their joys and sorrows come before her husband. I shall also follow that norm and will refuse to accept social shame or scriptural injunctions. The most superior scripture is our love, and I shall abide by it. It is my father who caused this love to grow between us. He made an error in obedience to social custom and made a gift of my body to someone else. My duties towards the one who received that gift have been performed and have now ceased to exist. My heart has been offered in the sacrifice that my father commenced. A man of virtue and perseverance such as you consider this offering a moral duty. Nothing more is required of me. You should reveal my identity and presence to your good friend. He has come so far in search of you and like you he must also be a man of virtue. He will show us a good and righteous path. My life will be fulfilled by our subtle love and with your support I shall be able to ward off any desire for physical love. I cannot uproot the tree of love from my heart; no one else can do that. I shall be your shadow, the earth to your sun, and I shall be a companion and partner in your sacrifice. I shall hear the barbs of the world and suffer along with my parents, but I shall follow what appears to me as my one and only duty. Oh husband of my life, you should now focus all your energies in thinking about the welfare of our people. Put to rest all your worries regarding me. I do not wish to be the co-wife of the people and of all the aspirations that abide in your heart, but I shall be a partner in the sacrifice you shall initiate for their welfare. Let us spend the night in understanding the rituals of that sacrifice. Call me to meet Chandrakantbhai without any doubt or hesitation. I feel the pure immortals touch my heart, and your Chintamani shall reveal the true meaning of their benediction. Our desires shall turn purer. You should allow your neutral friend to decide about our conduct towards each other.’
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra ponders his country's welfare as Kumud, still sorrowful, seeks his guidance, pledging her unwavering spiritual partnership and discussing their future before Chandrakant arrives.

chapters.title: The Dream World of Duties towards the Country
paragraphs: The Dream World of

Duties towards the Country One in hundreds is brave, one in thousands is learned, one in hundreds of thousands is an expounder, but it cannot be said whether one is a donor. One is not brave merely by winning a battle, not merely by studying scripture is one learned, not by mere eloquence is one an expounder, and not only by giving money is one a donor.⟨fn:504⟩ Convinced as he was that ‘‘success in the modern world has to be obtained only by adaptation to the needs of modern life, he wished his fellow-Hindus to unite an inner light of Divine philosophy, drawn from their traditional sources, and generously interpreted, to a mastery of physical science, and the means of natural improvement.’’ Jurist, statesman, scholar, orator, poet, lover of Nature, and meditative sage, he remains to the West the convincing proof that “it is by the word and example of him and his like that India must be regenerated, and the moral endowments of her children made noble, serviceable for the general welfare of mankind.”⟨fn:505⟩ Year by year the leaders of Indian thought in India spread their influence over ever-widening circles, though what the final result may be when these leaders, infused with all the best of the spirit of the East and West, rise up to proclaim that East and West have met, and from the union new forms of thought, new modes of artistic expression, new ways of viewing life, new solutions of religious, social, and moral problems been produced as they must be, is one that the whole past history of the world teaches us to be watched with hope, not fear or doubt.⟨fn:506⟩ On a poet’s lips I slept, Dreaming like a love-adept In the sound his breathing kept. Nor seeks nor finds he mortal blisses But feeds on the aerial kisses Of shapes that haunt thought’s wildernesses. He will watch from dawn to gloom The lake-reflected sun illume The yellow bees in the ivy bloom, Nor heed nor see what things they be, But from these create he can Forms more real than living man, Nurslings of immortality! One of these awakened me And I sped to succour thee.⟨fn:507⟩ Kumud wrapped herself around Sarasvatichandra’s heart like a creeper to a tree trunk. Her subtle body forgot the existence of the physical one. One heart felt another; her face reflected her innermost feelings. The sun had begun its journey towards the horizon. Its light entered the heart of this couple as the physical world came under the sway of the night. The moon and moonbeams both blossomed to give pleasure to this immortal couple. ‘Kumud! Beloved Kumud! The power of the Primeval Being spreads across the world; similarly these moonbeams have spread their light across all realms,’ Sarasvatichandra said as he looked in all four directions. Kumud: ‘It is so. It is the beautiful result of the moon’s immortality.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘My heart aspires that we shall spend this long night as if it was just a moment.’ Kumud: ‘We shall spend our whole life together as one joyous moment.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Our union shall make all our dreams come true. Oh sweet Madhuri, sing a melody.’ Kumud sang: The Vidhata has written, My life is my husband, Immortal is our union— Like the stars, the moon and chakor! Sarasvatichandra: ‘It is true. The stars and the moon are both immortal. Our life shall ascend towards them and we shall nourish ourselves on moonbeams.’ Kumud: ‘Our people are like the distant stars that we see. Our country is closer and fills our vision. Like the male and female chakor, we gaze upon them.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘It is so.’ Kumud: ‘We are feeble-bodied like birds. Will we be able to secure the welfare of our moonlike country?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I have considered this question all day today and now I feel tired. The moonbeams infuse my body and mind with sleep. Kumud, sleep overtakes me. I do not have the strength to go down.’ Kumud: ‘If these moonbeams have so much power over you, you should sleep here with them enveloping you.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Yes.’ He lay down on the floor on which some grass had grown. Either he himself or Kumud placed his head in her lap. He seemed deep in sleep. Moonbeams played on his face and shut his eyelids even tighter. The breeze rustled his moustache. As Kumud watched him with equanimity, and without any trace of desire, her mind was full of thoughts. Until today, my love was selfish. Lust itself is selfish and love that seeks to satiate lust is selfish. Such love ends with youth. My love no longer desires physical lust. My only desire is to witness the good fortune of my beloved and watch him work for the welfare of our people. This auspicious figure sleeps with his head in my lap. I am like mother Kunti who sat near Panchali’s head. I am alive only to aid his great journey. I will give him rest and repose. Lust! You have been turned to ashes in both our hearts. Wife is the other half of a man; she is his body. But this can be attained in many ways. I shall be his advisor, an assistant in the great endeavour he is about to commence. I shall serve him with all I have. In this journey among and with the people there will be times of great trial, and I shall be his repose. This unfamiliar terrain will perturb him and at such times I shall show the forgiveness and forbearance of mother Kunti. I shall nourish this motherless child and I shall through my virtue help raise his lineage even higher. I shall perform all the duties of a wife. I cannot share his bed and be an enchantress like Rambha. Like Chandravali, I shall eschew what is forbidden. To that extent our conjugality shall remain incomplete. But according to his teaching this is not incompleteness. He has made the country his family. He aspires to work for her welfare, and I shall be a partner in his duties and eschew physical desire. How and for what will society blame him or me? And if the world wants to find fault with me, let it do so. Of sinless sires I boast my birth, And sin in me was never found; Yet if suspicion taints my worth, What boots it though my heart be sound?⟨fn:508⟩ Companionship with this great soul has given Kumud strength of character. Kumud, you have no virtues; you are bereft of beauty and purity. This gem among men attributes beauty, purity and virtue to you. Your only duty is to be fit for his love and his grace. You shall roll his wick so that he can spread his light all around. You must keep this lamp alight. You have attained this right—an unblemished right— and you shall honour it. Kumud caressed Sarasvatichandra’s forehead softly and sang. Oh moon in the sky! This moon is greater than you. He has such love for me! He has come to such a state for me. He was wealthy and learned; He has become a beggar for my love. I care not for mother or father; He abandoned his father for me; He abandoned wealth, home and friends; He sought poor wretched Kumud. Whatever I wish for him would be less, Nothing that I find for him would suffice. Moon! Your lifeless light spreads everywhere My moon is filled with life and light. She sat there for a long time, caressing his forehead. She did not feel the weight of his head in her lap. After about two hours Sarasvatichandra stirred. He woke up and sat up. They went down to his room in the cave. They sat on either end of the platform. Kumud broached the subject, ‘There is nothing that we need to discuss. Please explain to me as to how you wish to spend your life in the service of the country.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I have pondered over this question for years. This place and your companionship have shown me the way. Madhuri, please tell me once, clearly and unambiguously, open your heart to me and tell me whether you wish our union to be only subtle and spiritual or both spiritual and physical. I have a way of fulfilling my aspirations according to the choice you make.’ Kumud: ‘If you have found a way that can accommodate either of the choices, isn’t the question itself meaningless?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘In fact, there are two distinct ways depending upon the choice you make; hence the question.’

Kumud: ‘You know the nature of a woman’s heart. After much deliberation I have arrived at a decision, and it holds true. But our hearts are like the flame of a lamp. How is one to trust it? Our intellect is subordinate to our hearts and the heart’s lamp is subject to the mind. Able and virtuous men like you have to put a protective glass over our flames. We shall burn the lamp of our heart and give you light. You could not decide what kind of protective cover you should forge, and hence you left the decision to Chandrakantbhai. When a ship cannot move with the aid of its sails, the captain gets his sailors to row the ship. When our sails failed, I suggested that you ask your good friend to row our boat. You must tell me the options you have thought of. My woman’s heart is eager to share your light. Just as the earth becomes hot and parched for rain, I am burning with anticipation for your rain. I believe that your rain can only be nurturant and I am eager to accept its showers in my heart. The darkness of society, darker than night itself, has hitherto been an obstacle in our path. But my heart has heard your thunder. You are like a rain-laden cloud made dark by sorrow. But I am parched like the earth to see your light.⟨fn:509⟩ Now tear off the curtain that separates us. Pour all your aspirations into my heart and let us prove that I am the earth and you, the sky. Oh my beloved, dearest among all! Your Kumud—who was meek, ignorant and abashed—has become strong, enlightened and unabashed by some strange power of this place.’⟨fn:510⟩ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Without a doubt the power of our dreams has given you a new character. Or else the golden garment given to us by the immortals still unites us and we experience its power.’ Kumud: ‘Whatever it is, now tell me your aspirations so that we can pull the chariot together. My heart wants to enter your heart.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Madhuri, my beloved! In that case, listen. I received an inheritance both from my mother—whose immortal form we saw—and my grandmother. This is the stree dhan, the wealth of these two women, which I kept with Chandrakant when I left Bombay. This wealth was used in making the precious ring for Kumud and her portrait which was made for keeping in the pleasure house built for her. That portrait has been left behind in Bombay, but a new Kumud is with me. I gave the ring meant for her to a grieving bania after I left Suvarnapur. All that I have is this Chintamani mudra that your grandmother gave me.’ Kumud: ‘Those objects of our physical life have been left behind, and this is good for our spiritual love. All our physical possessions are like these kantha, these tattered clothes. This is most fitting for Kumud who was given a new lease of life by Chandravali Maiya.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Kumud! Kumud Sundari! The force of our spiritual love makes my speech unsteady. I address you with formal respect and slip into the familiar, affectionate address. I say much that is illogical—remove those parts of my blabbering and hold on to the essential. Hitherto, many ideas churned in my mind. But now one idea has taken a mature form. I have faith that you shall become my partner in this duty. My father and grandmother had bequeathed some four lakh rupees to me. I used that money for my business and it has now grown to six or seven lakhs. This amount is not sufficient to fulfill all aspects of my dream world. But over time, in some four or five years, the accumulated amount will become enough for one aspect of my ideal. Till such time it will keep accumulating interest in Chandrakant’s custody; and we shall lead a spiritual life among the ascetics, unknown and unrecognised by society.’ Kumud: ‘What do you intend to do with that wealth?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Your body shall remain untouched, unsullied and pure and I shall receive your spiritual love. Similarly, the body of my wealth shall remain untouched and I will use only the interest it earns. From that interest in one year a learned businessman shall be created while in the other, seeds for the welfare of our poor shall be sowed. Each year the interest shall be used for making some permanent arrangement. A scholar who has passed the B.A. examination and has the inclination and ability to become a businessman shall be chosen through a process of selection and elimination. ‘I plan that each such individual shall be given a capital of at least forty thousand rupees. The chosen man should apprentice with an able and proven businessman for a period, during which he will be paid a small salary of thirty rupees a month. For two years, this person should learn business and learn to live parsimoniously. After this period of apprenticeship he should spend two to three years in Europe or America or divide his time between the two. The interest from forty thousand kept aside from him would take care of his needs there. After that he should spend one year in any other part of the world and two more years acquainting himself with the condition of our country. For this entire period of training he would have to take care of his needs from the interest on the capital when abroad and from thirty rupees a month while in our country. I or my representatives will make these arrangements for him and put him as an apprentice with both English and Indian businessmen of repute. ‘Once his abilities are ascertained he shall be given the amount of forty thousand rupees to start his business and work for the welfare of this country. If he has acquired any special skill or professional ability from abroad he should be given an additional sum of ten thousand rupees. A businessman so trained will be able to pull the chains of Arjun’s chariot—this is my firm conviction. A scholar-businessman who has received training at someone else’s expense will not turn out to be selfish, miserly, concerned only about himself and his sons, or seek foolish pleasures. He would not be idle, subsisting on interest. He would not be a slothful creature. But, like Arjun, he shall travel, be industrious, acquire new skills and use them. He will contribute to the wealth of Panchali and his other four brothers. Kumud Sundari, such men will become able students of the English Hanuman; they will become far-seeing people, formulate morality for their times, perform great deeds and foster other talent like them. In the political observatory of Mallaraj there are five seats for Arjun; these seats will be created by the endeavours of such men. Sage-like in scholarship, politician-like in terms of action and equable like Indra, such men shall be born in this land, this righteous land. Indra is a friend of the industrious. This age—the age of Satya—is the age of industry, not of slothfulness. I have faith that such men shall help us usher in that age of industry.’ Kumud: ‘You think that your six or seven lakhs are insufficient. Will you be able to foster such men with only fifty thousand?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Fifty thousand will provide them with a chariot. They will travel in that chariot and with their own ability they will, over time, earn fifty lakhs. The industry and adventure of these men shall prove beneficial for the country. Poor ignoramuses, poor scholars, rich but unconcerned and selfish men will be replaced by such men who will bring the essence of Arjun’s abilities to us. Many persons cannot think of ways of earning wealth. These learned men shall be examples to such unseeing, unthinking men. Given the paucity of my resources we shall be able to create one such man every two years. But that is God’s will. But the same God has bestowed me with so many ideas and ideals; these seeds will nurture many others. In twelve years we shall foster six such able men. They will cross the seas and bring arts and knowledge from abroad to our land, and with that our country shall awaken to their abilities and genius.’ Kumud: ‘How am I to partner you in this endeavour?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘My Kumud will have to find and cultivate virtuous wives for these foreign-returned men; we shall consider that a little later. The interest of my wealth in one year will be spent to foster such men. Now let me tell you the plan for the other year. Young sons and daughters-in-law are the only support of the elderly and the ageing. Children depend upon their parents. The youth are the mainstay of our states; they must be able and right thinking. Just as the state of being a householder is pivotal for the other three ages, the youthful stage is pivotal for children, the elderly and the state. Similarly, the future of the country lies in the ability of our learned men. The scholarship of men of learning rests upon useful and productive youth. If we can sow these seeds, the trees that shall emerge will be strong and fruitful. We shall tend, like gardeners, the crop of learned men that the British have grown in our land with great foresight and scientific thought. We shall travel to the temples and huts of these learned men. We shall understand their aspirations and know their conscience. I shall be with the men and you should get to know their women. You should observe the problems, the ailments and struggles of the women, while I shall do so for the men. We shall be their friends and work for their and the country’s welfare. We saw the reflections of reality in Pitamahpur; we should find that reality. We should give them support and strength to remove the pain and suffering from their lives. ‘Women will have to become learned, adept in arts, nurturant, healthy, strong, free of disease and beautiful, free from the bondage and strife of family life and be able to work for the welfare of their families, be capable of nurturing the young and caring for the ailing and the elderly. Who else but the favourite daughter of Gunasundari can help them be so able? We shall be able to spend fifty thousand rupees every other year for this task. It’s a small sum, but we shall do with what we have.’ Kumud: ‘Our women are dependent upon the family.’

Sarasvatichandra: ‘For that very reason, I wish to create support for the wives of scholars. If men become able, women shall acquire strength. If a learned man has the means to free his wife from the kitchen and household chores, he would set her free. We will support the families you select; I shall provide the means and you shall imbue these women with high aspirations.’ Kumud: ‘The elderly in the family will disdain these women, while others will be jealous of them.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘If all such groups were to derive some benefits from our resources, they, too, shall come around; you and I alone cannot do this. Therefore, till such time that we have able and learned native women, we shall hire on good salary English women of good lineage and get them to work with our women and teach them through their narratives and companionship. We shall thus reach the Ganga to their door step! We shall get them out of their household work and create spaces where our learned women and women from other countries could meet and discuss. We shall enable our widows and turn them into women of strength and ability like the Parivrajikas here. If we train young girls they will grow into able, youthful women and take this work further. Kumud, I can do nothing in this field without you. If men enter the domain of women, it would be considered immoral by our people and our endeavour would be destroyed even before it has begun.’ Kumud: ‘Cannot the ascetic women of this place join in?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The ascetics consider society depraved and wish to maintain their distance from it. Are they wrong? Our spiritual union will be labelled a re-marriage by society, and with that we would meet with such infamy that our endeavour would collapse. And these ascetics believe that the union of our minds is the true marriage. It is good if society stays away from these ascetics. Otherwise these ascetics would be regarded as immoral. Take for example Shankapuri who pursues Bindumati and views our relationship as immoral. This light that has survived through the turbulence of time will be snuffed out and great damage will be done. It is for this reason that I have planned our lives differently. Moreover, we shall train and strengthen our traditional scholars and through them spread the message of our ancient culture and learning in each house. The combination of Western learning brought by their scholarly women and the knowledge of our scriptures given by our traditional scholars will act like water and fire, and that steam shall help move our family trains with greater speed. ‘We shall hitch steam engines to our trains and lay tracks for them and build stations for their rest. Our families will travel through these routes and enter the land of new knowledge. They will learn new arts and acquire new riches. They are barely aware of our scriptures and stories of exemplars, but with new vision they will acquire a subtle understanding of these. The gems and serpents we saw in Pitamahpur will give them purity of character, and the hillocks made by Ashwatthama shall begin to melt. Today our people turn blind as bats when faced with the fiery light of Western learning; but over time we shall be able to open our eyes and learn from that knowledge. We shall work for the welfare of all—children, women, youth and elderly—and provide them with the means for a long and fruitful life. We shall commence this experiment from capital cities and gradually spread it like a banyan tree to districts and villages. I can see the seeds of all-encompassing welfare and wellbeing in this. Kumud, the aspirations of all the immortals shall thus take real shape! Eventually the sum of fifty thousand rupees will be too little, but it will make for a good beginning. Kumud, Sarasvatichandra cannot do this all by himself. In this endeavour I need the union with Kumud blessed by the immortals! I have outlined in brief our shared future and the use of my limited wealth.’ Kumud: ‘Your aspirations have been constrained by your limited wealth. What would be the amount required to fulfill all your aspirations and what means would you employ to do so?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘My father’s accumulated wealth is much greater than what is generally believed. If I had accepted it, my aspirations would not have been damaged. But that has happened. I did what was my duty. If I had inherited that wealth, I would never have come here. If I had not come here, my aspirations would have remained limited as then they would not have been nourished by our dreams. I would have worried about what to do with the wealth and this problem would have been a thorn in my side. The question as to what I would have done with that wealth or what I would do if I were to inherit it even now is like the daydream of the Panchatantra character Soma Sharma. It is true that I had mapped out all my aspirations and then curtailed it to match the resources I have. My complete map would have required slightly greater resources than what my father’s wealth would have permitted. I have shared with you what is feasible; the rest is futile imagination.’ Kumud: ‘It might be futile. But curiosity natural to women makes me eager to know, and hence the question.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘All right, then listen. What appears laughable to others delights the lover’s heart. Your only desire is to know what is in my heart, and it is my duty to give you pleasure through my dream world. Moreover, I think it is not entirely futile to narrate what is not possible for us but within reach of those with superior means. Such narrations would inspire them to action and further the aspirations of those with limited vision. My first idea is to create for our English- educated scholars, our traditional scholars and unlettered artisans a small village like Surgram. I call it Kalyangram. The English travel to places like Simla, Darjeeling, Mahabaleshwar and the Nilgiris to rejuvenate their body and mind. This Kalyangram should be created in some such place, and if that is not possible then on the sea coast. It should be a place of natural beauty that contributes to the physical and mental wellbeing of residents. All the three groups should reside there along with their wives and children, free from all worries and cares. Sundargiri has created three types of maths; similarly Kalyangram will have three kinds of residential facilities. There will be norms on the basis of which aspirants shall be selected. Each year a fixed number of persons shall be invited in residence at the Kalyangram. They will include those who have passed the highest examinations of English- type education, traditional scholars and healers selected through a special screening process and artisans.
