Couples shall reside in Vihar Bhavan, single men in Kumar Bhavan and widows and eventually, if our society is reformed, single women and even nuns will stay in the Stree Bhavan.’ Kumud: ‘What will they do while in residence?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Both modern and traditional scholars should spend their entire life in residence. They will study and research the Vedas, the Vedanta, scriptures, literature, Puranas, religious sects, social customs and all other laws and norms either codified or prevalent in practice. They should wander among our people, observe them and understand the practices and experiences of our people from its source to the present. They must make use of Western learning and research in doing so. They must not engage in factional debates but seek the truth. They must understand every faction, every school of thought, but their eyes must remain fixed on the essential, unbiased truth. They must search out the qualities and defects of both the Pitamah and Ashwatthama. They must enter the hillocks and understand them from within by passing through the lit parts. They must see for themselves both the gems and the poison of the serpents. They must with detached, unsullied vision research all that has been patent as also latent in this land through the ages. They must understand the social and political bodies of our country in modern times. Thus, by an all-encompassing evaluation of the maladies that afflict this country they should prepare a remedy for the future. They must engage in deep research and experimentation to decide as to how Arjun’s arrows could be removed from Bhishma’s body, how Bhishma’s light could spread to all regions, how the arrows could pass through the hillocks without disturbing the sources of light, how the shaking rocks could be made stable, how the gems and poison could be used, how we could benefit from the world of serpents, how Arjun should place the gem back on Ashwatthama’s head and use his mental powers for our benefit. These would be some of the duties of the resident scholars.’ He paused briefly and continued, ‘Kumud Sundari! This is not sufficient. They should know the various social customs and orientation of the society as also its strengths and weaknesses. They should know global patterns, principally the orientations of the English people. This would be the second obligation of the scholars. The chariots of the Pandavas are roaming across the world, and from each spoke of the wheel new forms of knowledge, new inventions, new materials and new forms of pain and pleasure emerge. The physical wellbeing of all peoples, their social and political organisations, religious institutions, their physical and spiritual abilities are transformed by the movement of the Pandavas’ chariots. They assume new dimensions. People who cannot run alongside the chariots fall back, die of hunger, lose their intelligence and strength. They become like animals. They turn into mud hillocks and are finally destroyed. They perish in the forest fire ignited by Arjun. Our scholars must go to the root of all these processes and find new ways of regenerating this ancient land. They must ensure that this does not become the Khandav forest that Arjun will destroy; instead it should be a land that Arjun is partial to, and our people must acquire the fitness to ride on his chariot. ‘We shall create libraries and ‘‘laboratories,’’ create workshops for the regeneration of older crafts and, like Nakul, they shall learn new crafts. We shall bring together new materials so that we acquire the knowledge of new trades and industry. We shall make available all the resources and objects considered necessary by Western and our scholars alike for the advancement of knowledge. This shall be our responsibility. The responsibility of the scholars would be to make appropriate and just use of the resources. This resource centre would need a lot of money. ‘These scholars and artisans should be admitted in residence after they have obtained all available education and training. We cannot take the responsibility of finding teachers for them. They should be invited in residence only after they have gained the capability for independent work in their chosen field. This place is not meant for students but for those who have the ability to create the foundations of new knowledge and direct social organisations onto desired paths. ‘These scholars will have no need to earn their livelihood. They shall be provided for and freed from all familial responsibilities as also from domestic strife. Kalyangram is not for those who are dissatisfied with the provisions we have made for them. ‘‘Those twice-born who are discontented always lead to destruction.’’⟨fn:511⟩ For us, the twice-born are those who are fit to live in this village and do so with contentment. Provisions would be made for the scholar, his wife and their unmarried children. They shall be provided with housing, food, clothing; spaces for physical exercise and leisure shall be created along with meeting halls. All things necessary for them to rise above their present state shall be provided. If their parents are old and feeble, arrangements shall be made for their food and medicine and monetary requirement also. If they are ill and diseased, they shall be housed in our sanatoriums where trained persons shall care for them. Their children shall also visit them and care for them. Resident scholars and their families would also avail the facilities of the sanatorium when unwell. The village would provide facilities for schooling the children of resident scholars, which shall also be available to children of deceased scholars. The scholars must keep away from society. But every year for a few months they should travel across the country for their observation and study as also to spread their knowledge among the people. During this period their conduct, though unmonitored, should be above reproach. The Ashram should provide for the expenses of their children’s weddings once they reach the age of consent, or else their monthly salaries could be enhanced to enable them to bear these expenses. ‘If these scholars and artisans are prepared to live selflessly, they should be paid a monthly salary for the duration of their lives ranging from rupees ten to fifty, over and above paying for all their needs. Initially, when they join the Ashram their salary should be fixed at a lower level and increased according to procedures as and when their capabilities are enhanced. An artisan shall be paid rupees ten and a scholar rupees twenty-five initially. The increase should be determined after a review scheduled after three years and another at the end of ten years. The increased wages for these ten years shall be paid, along with interest, to their wives, children and grandchildren. In case they do not have a family it should be paid as per the terms of their will and in absence of a will it shall go back to the Ashram corpus. After the ten years, the increased wages shall be paid to them as monthly wages and after their death it shall be paid to their heirs as defined by law. They would of course, during their lifetime, be free to use these wages for causes dear to them. ‘A guest house with many rooms and all facilities shall be maintained for the meetings of scholars and artisans. We shall invite all sorts of scholars, artisans and men of virtue at our expense and receive them in the guest house. One part of the guest house should have temples of all sects where men of diverse faiths from across the country shall be received. The parents of our ashramites, when they long to see their sons or daughters, shall be received in these temples; the expenses for their food etc. should be deducted from their children’s salaries and those parents who have the means to pay these should pay them. Apart from parents, ascetics and mendicants should be received with all dignity and honour in temples of their sect. Inhabitants of our Ashram can benefit from their presence. ‘Ashwatthama, the cause of all disorder, sometimes creates for the solace of our countrymen flashes of light in our temples. This light should not be destroyed even inadvertently. Sometimes these lights flash in the sky and at times nearer to the earth. During these brief spells of light, Ashwatthama turns sane and sings songs of rare depth which are like showers of nectar on the trembling hearts of our people. I have experienced this in Surgram. Kumud Sundari, we shall nourish the auspicious aspects of our temples and our resident scholars shall rejuvenate the temples with new ideas and ideals. The visiting guests and our scholars will interact for their mutual benefit. This will create new unity and equanimity in our people. We shall receive all people without bias or discrimination in the temples and the inns attached to them. People from the farthest corners of this land, people of all castes, men, women, youth and elderly, farmers, traders, pilgrims and travellers, people of old and traditional beliefs and those espousing new ideas, ascetics, mendicants and seers, men of experience as also novices shall be welcomed and we shall learn from them. We should know their habits of food and drink, their home life and social practices with all their goodness and follies. We should know their modes of acquisition of knowledge, experience and wealth; we should know their patterns of expenditure and saving. We should know these things and examine them from various perspectives including those of European and native systems of medicine, economics, physiology, moral science and sociology. We should also examine them from the perspectives of a poet and an artisan, from political and philosophical points of view. We should discern what needs to be preserved and protected, what needs to be cut and thrown and what requires reform and modification in accordance with our time and place. ‘The wealth of this impoverished country has been destroyed, it is being destroyed and it will continue to be destroyed in the future. But the art of living with few needs and fewer resources is still alive in the hillocks of Ashwatthama. If this art were to be destroyed by contact with the Western world, it will cause great damage. We have to preserve that art. Our scholars will have to ensure that the meetings with various guests prove to be beneficial for them and us. If our wealth is destroyed, if our industry and craft of wealth creation become feeble and if we lose our capacity to live frugally while making an effort to preserve our arts, our knowledge and essence of religion, the life of this country would near its end. Kumud Sundari, we may or may not be able to free Pitamah’s body of Arjun’s arrows, but we must recognise that this country is no longer wealthy and independent as it was during his times. We have to protect and preserve these age-old abilities before Ashwatthama’s life span comes to an end. Our people say that some seventy-five or hundred years ago our grandparents, though poorer in wealth, had healthy bodies and minds; we are not as strong as our parents and our children are likely to be weaker than us. The new age has lost the art of a healthy life. We might know how to earn a little more money, but our ways are far more expensive and wasteful. Is this the result of our new ways or of amnesia regarding the past? If this is the result of our new learning, its poison must be eradicated from our bodies and if it is an outcome of our amnesia, we must regain and rebuild our memories. This would be a great responsibility on our Ashramites, which they must achieve through their travels and meetings with guest scholars.’

Kumud interrupted him, ‘I see certain images hovering above your head—Ashwatthama restored to sanity, and I also see Lord Parashuram’s feet.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I see Kunti’s hand over your head and I can also hear her song.’ Kumud: ‘I see someone with a large and sparkling jewel standing at some distance from Ashwatthama.’ Sarasvatichandra spoke after deep thought, ‘These images signify the power of this place and the embodiment of our dreams. Kumud Sundari, your Parasmani and my Chintamani are united in our hearts. Look! Look! I see my dream world taking firmer shape in the state of wakefulness. I see wealth manyfold greater than my father’s pass through my hands, and I see myself using it for the welfare of our people. I not only see it but can almost feel it. I, with the help of this miracle, can see myself building new palaces and gardens for our guests! I shall call leading scholars, poets, writers, scholars of scriptures and ‘‘science’’ from all parts of the world as also our country to these palaces. I shall call editors of newspapers, magazines and journals. Scholars of politics and officials, patriots, humanists, great souls, extremely wealthy businessmen and nobles, preceptors of religion and heads of sects, ascetics and all seekers after truth shall be invited and received with respect in these palaces, and all the inhabitants of our Ashram will have the opportunity of close interaction and association with them. I shall call them from everywhere, men, women, native, foreign, Aryas, non-Aryas shall be received equally. Our resident scholars shall find rare gems from this churning of the ocean of knowledge. They shall learn about eternal norms and particular beliefs. They will engage themselves with questions of the welfare and elevation of all unsullied elements. ‘Dharmaraj’s sense of rectitude and duty, Bhim’s incessant mobility and alertness, Arjun’s agency, Nakul’s arts and crafts, Sahadev’s deep knowledge, Hanuman’s sense of fraternity, Kunti’s forgiveness and forbearance and our people’s oneness of heart with the English will be achieved if we sow their seeds in the hearts of our men, women and children. Knowledge and aesthetic sensibility from all over the world shall spring forth in this village. Great wealth shall wander through it like the auspicious feet of Lakshmi. Lord Parashuram has for ages kept the concerns for the welfare of this land alive. The first showers of munificence shall come upon us in this land. Kumud! Beloved Kumud! Panchali awakened and nurtured by this shower shall benefit all humanity. This ability of India has for ages been put through a fiery ordeal, but it survives however frayed. This ability shall flower by Arjun’s association with the monkey-people. For ages, India has preserved in her womb the possibility for the welfare of the world. She shall give birth to that possibility. And that enlightened newborn shall be welcomed by all in this world!’ Kumud: ‘Our chakor birds drink from the moonbeams as also from the light of the stars.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘We were like the chakor, but with newly acquired spiritual abilities we fly over the moon and into the land of stars! They join their song with that of the stars! Kumud, do you hear it? The ashramites of our Kalyangram shall through their scholarship, arts and trade contribute manyfold to the wealth I would have spent on its creation. This would be used in part for the expansion of the village, while the rest of it shall be theirs to use as they wish. This would attract the best among our people to the village; they will contribute to the general welfare, their sensibilities shall be further cultivated and they will be priceless. They would make the country wealthy in resources, in arts and in knowledge; it would make for greater political stability. Their progeny will be strong, handsome, able and learned. Our society at large shall learn from their example and our efforts will take root in a wider field. Autonomy, health, interactions with invited guests shall make our Ashramites virtuous and the virtue nurtured in the village shall bring light to our society as also to English society. And around this virtue shall flourish new light, new joy and new festivities united in one colour. ‘Our people have been entrapped in the multifarious religious sects created by Ashwatthama and are in perpetual conflict in the name of  ‘‘unity, oneness, patriotism, caste pride and reform.’’⟨fn:512⟩ These are illusionary divisions sustained by attachment and ego. Each human being is born with their own values and abilities. If we recognise these they can be helped to maturity. Similarly, our people and our country through the ages and across generations acquired certain values and abilities. These values and abilities are within our grasp; it is auspicious to recognise them and bring them to maturity. Virtues can flourish eternally only when we forsake attachment and ego about ourselves and others. Eternal norms have attachment only for virtues; therefore unity and equanimity flourish in it. We must set fire to all ego and attachment, and from that fire shall emerge the eternal light of virtues and around it we shall experience the festival of oneness and the warmth of equanimity. The immortals and the beings attached to Arjun’s chariot told us clearly that without Dharma, neither Bhim, nor Arjun, nor Nakul and Sahadev shall come to this land. This is what they meant. In absence of eternal norms, the idea of unity and oneness is a meaningless chant and equanimity is only a mirage. We shall in our Kalyangram have a nectar-filled Ganga in place of the mirage. We shall make, like Bhagiratha, a great endeavour to bring Ganga down to earth. ‘Kumud Sundari, in our Kalyangram, able and learned women shall acquire the autonomy, strength of character and virtue to travel among our people. They shall go from village to village, from home to home without seeking alms and through their own learning and example they shall work to elevate our women to a higher plane. Our resident couples and celibate ashramites will also travel among the people and demonstrate to them the victory of the Pandavas. Each village and home shall celebrate this victory and Panchali’s union with her husbands. Each part of her body and soul shall be healthy, equitable, strong and beautiful. People ask what the relationship between woman and the state is. There can be no household without women and no people without women. It is people who constitute a state. Unless the welfare of women is ensured, the temples of states and their rulers are sooner or later destroyed. Unless the condition of women improves, homes become conflict-ridden. A man whose home is torn by conflict remains gripped by worries outside the house. He cannot share his burdens or expect companionship and solace in an ignorant wife. Scholars who despise women claim that great wars have been caused by them, but those who worship women know that no nation can rise without ensuring their welfare. The ascetics of this community neither despise women nor worship them; they see both men and women as spiritual beings and awaken their desire for the Unmanifest God. If those who blame women for society’s ills acquire this perspective they, too, would seek to reform the condition of women like the ascetics. Those who worship women would not be subject to mockery by patriarchal men and would be free from the folly of igniting conflict between men and women. The norms of these ascetics in fact nurture unity and equability, and we shall nourish these further in our Kalyangram. ‘The unity of our people rid of its twin ailments of ego and attachment shall spread across our land and other countries also. Kumud, our oneness and my wealth shall be the foundation of this great endeavour, the building blocks and cement of the new edifice. We shall never permit physical desire to sully our spiritual union lest it restrict our capacity for sacrifice, lest it produce a progeny and deviate us from the path of sacrifice for our people, lest it force us to devote even a part of our lives to personal strivings. Beloved! Oh beloved of my subtle heart, do tell me if your heart has become one with mine! Let us embark on a journey to worship Panchali in the footsteps of Krishna, Kunti and the Pandavas. That would be the conclusion of our spiritual marriage. In this journey across the seven mountains, I see you stand firm and unflinching at each step. I stand behind you, Kumud. We follow each other with steady, determined steps. Our feet rise in unison, we take each other along. Kumud, you are light itself, and your light merges with the light of my heart. Beloved! Oh my companion and partner in sacrifice, our pure wedding has been concluded. Our lights are married to each other.’

Sarasvatichandra ceased to speak and grew quiet. His half-open eyes saw only Kumud’s heart. He was no longer a physical being but pure light. Kumud also acquired that consciousness. The only thing that separated them was moonbeams and the gentle breeze on the terrace of the Saumanasya Gufa. The world itself disappeared in the darkness that enveloped it. They had no desire to speak or even to see each other. Their hearts had merged into one another. Their heartfelt desires spoke in one voice, a voice only their two hearts could hear. ‘Son! Daughter-in-law! I am Panchali. Your union has awakened me. Let my words enter your hearts. I am the Power, the Shakti of all of India. I am the Mother of India. Those who are considered kings and emperors by my progeny are birds of my dream world. They fly in from all four directions and peck at my body; they make an effort to churn my sons and daughters. All those who come to me with a desire to rule over my body eventually become my sons and daughters, and I take them to the grass hut of my husbands and swing them in my cradle. Anasuya turned Brahma, Vishnu and Maheshwar into her sons. I have performed the same miracle time and time again with all those who have coveted my body and I shall continue to do so. The only husbands I have had are the immortal Pandavas. Their father and saviour is Janardan and he is the saviour of all. Foolish Duryodhana residing on the land of Sugriv may make tall claims, but the monkey- people are in fact the bearers of my husband’s flag. You are born of my womb and possess spiritual powers. Do not be afraid to teach Duryodhana his duties. Do not be perturbed by his characteristic insolence. Deal with him with autonomy, intelligence, strength and goodness and let good sense prevail in him. Their Hanuman is in fact a brother of your protector Bhimsen and he gives power to Bhim’s speech. My husband Arjun has conquered all sides. Victory resides in his flag and vanquishes his enemies. The monkey feeds at my breast and so does Ashwatthama. ‘No man can be king or emperor and rule over my body. No man has the hubris to claim to be my husband. No human race for all these four ages can claim to have been my master. Time destroys everything. The dreams of kings and emperors are short-lived, but my husbands are immortal—follow their command and obey their rule. Your only search must be for the immortal ones. Your only penance must be for them. Immortal among immortals, the one who preserves creation is the protector and nourisher of my great and valorous husbands. You should serve no one but Him. Do not believe in this material world, but do not ignore it either. Strengthen your physical bodies so that your subtle bodies can be preserved. Only such a body shall be free from servility and bondage. Be the brethren of all Aryas and non-Aryas alike. You have been born from my womb. I have made the Yavanas and Shakas of former times and Muslims and English of present times my sons and have placed them in the cradle that you shared. Do not get into futile conflict and disputes with them. I have bestowed upon you unity and companionship which shall bring all your aspirations to fruition. Do not ever be separated from each other. Let your virtues and spiritual powers be shared by your associates, let it spread throughout the world. Let your physical prowess grow; but if it is curtailed by the superior strength of others or by divine will, do not forsake the sandalwood-like fragrance of your spiritual strength. ‘Do not allow your hearts to weaken! Oh my children, you reside in the land of righteousness! You are those great souls who have witnessed the path of freedom and salvation. Do not be afraid even if pain and suffering shower over our land. Do not let the roars of evil animals shake you. You are the inheritors of unprecedented spiritual powers and riches. If you walk in the shadows of my husbands and observe the duties enjoined upon you by the immortals, you shall find eternal peace. Peace is yours. Peace is the daughter of our sages; she has remained unattached and unsullied; she is your sister. Your hearts and minds are free; let them be so. Nourish this freedom. What else do the Aryas imbued with spirituality aspire for? Gods willed it and the eternal tree turned barren in this land, but this tree has deep roots in the hearts of Aryas. Nurture it. Whom do you fear? Those from outside or those from within who crave material riches cut away at the branches of this eternal tree; the more they cut, the deeper its roots shall grow!’

The voice receded; so did the presence of the speaker. But as she receded, Panchali’s song could be heard. The power of darkness! Darkness reduced me to this state. My progeny, beautiful, delicate and strong, have withered. What shall I do? What can I do? I am powerless. Many hours have passed. The hours hold firm to the darkness! I hold the hand of God even in the dark. I am nourished, I remain fragrant—forsake not my inner power. I give and receive unperceived by others. My children flourish and grow amidst darkness. Darkness all pervasive has prevailed through the age of Manu. Spread as much as you want, show your strength. Darkness, I shall defeat you in the present. Your ages are my moments, and they too shall pass. Dawn shall break. There—behold! The sun rises. Darkness, you shall be defeated and pushed back. My body, my progeny shall regain their verdant delicacy. Darkness shall be defeated and a victorious future shall emerge.
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra and Kumud share an intimate moonlit night, discussing their spiritual union and their profound commitment to serving their beloved country.

chapters.title: The Power of Justice and the Delicacy of Social Affection
paragraphs: The Power of Justice and the Delicacy of Social Affection Let men versed in policy praise or blame; let the goddess of wealth enter (their house) or go away (from it as she likes; let death come even to-day or in another age; persons of mental calibre do not swerve from the path of justice.⟨fn:513⟩ Fiat Justitia ruat caelem! [Justice shall be done though the heavens fall!]   —A maxim of law O’ sage! That knowledge is no longer dear to my heart.⟨fn:514⟩ Sardar Singh, the Superintendent of Police, pretended to be indifferent about Chandrakant’s meeting with the mendicant. Chandrakant announced that he wished to see the surrounding areas. He borrowed a carriage from Vidya Chatura and set out in the afternoon. He was to meet the mendicant at the eastern foothills of Sundargiri. The day after Chandrakant’s departure, early in the morning, Vidya Chatura requested Gunasundari’s presence in his room. He was seated on an easy chair. Gunasundari, worn out by worries, sat facing him.

‘Gunial, ninety-nine percent out of hundred, Sarasvatichandra is alive. But he has become an ascetic and lives in the Math of Vishnudas. It is futile to entertain any hopes regarding him.’ Gunasundari: ‘He has lost his mother. He needs a mother who would bring him back into our fold. His suffering has grown beyond all limits. I try and forget Kumud, but Kusum becomes a cause of worry. I try to put it out of my mind, but Sarasvatichandra’s suffering pierces my heart. With your permission, I will go to the Math. Neither he nor Vishnudas would decline my plea to bring him back.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘You cannot rid yourself of the idea that Kusum and he would marry, can you?’ Gunasundari: ‘I will rid myself of it when it becomes inevitable. There is no harm in this proposal; we have something to gain and I must make an effort. My heart bears testimony that he will not disregard the plea of my tears.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘What will you gain by bringing him back to our house? What if his happiness lies there?’ Gunasundari: ‘I cannot understand the purport of your words.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘I have some very strange, unimaginable news to give you. I do not know how you will take it. But until I share it with you, you would not understand my view.’ Gunasundari: ‘Tell me whatever it is. My heart has dealt with enough blows; one more is not going to break it.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Words fail me.’ Gunasundari: ‘This is a new experience for me. You are keeping things from me. This distance causes greater pain than the news that you have kept from me. I realise today that a woman is weak and an orphan even though she has her husband’s love.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Kumud is alive.’ ‘What!’ Gunasundari exclaimed in utter joy. Vidya Chatura: ‘Most probably she is alive. She is with Sarasvatichandra.’

Gunasundari’s face withered. She said nothing. She looked down and wept. Vidya Chatura: ‘I knew what this would do to you, therefore I hesitated. Now tell me whether you still want Sarasvatichandra for Kusum.’ Gunasundari’s tears evaporated. She turned red with anger. ‘I am going away. I have nothing more to say. You can do what you like, and others can do likewise. I should have died after giving birth to Kumud. Why do I have to live and bear with all this? I am going. You and your daughter!—I want a release from both of you!’ Gunasundari got up and walked away in rage. Vidya Chatura swiftly followed her, held her in his embrace and sat her down on a table. ‘Gunial, this is not the time for anger. If you do not control your rage and advise me, whom shall I go to? Our prestige, our duties and our own daughter! Would I not have the benefit of your companionship in resolving these matters?’ Gunasundari: ‘What resolution? Our prestige has drowned, our morality has been washed away. Now we have to be together in this mourning. You must give up your ministership. We cannot show our face to anyone. Let us go away to Kashi.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Isn’t it possible that what we imagine could be false? Immoral and debauched conduct is not possible in Vishnudas’ Math. Is it not possible that Sarasvatichandra, moved by duty and morality, gave shelter to Kumud?’ Gunasundari mellowed a little. ‘That is possible. But will the world believe that?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘If we believe in them, we shall make the world believe in them, too.’ Gunasundari: ‘But we have to believe them first.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘If our hearts are pure and our love is true, it is unlikely that our Kumud would do something contrary to the values we have inculcated in her.’

Gunasundari: ‘We have nurtured her with pure values and love. Kumud’s heart was nourished by our love. Would someone like Pramaddhan succeed in making her fall and turn our care to futility?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘We have heard stories about some Navinchandra who was a guest in Buddhidhanbhai’s house. These stories match with your fears.’ Gunasundari: ‘People say all kinds of things, both true and false. Pramaddhan’s bad habits might have brought some social opprobrium even to Kumud. Isn’t our society given to believing in all such rumours? Saubhagya Devi did not believe these stories, and no one has said a lowly thing about Navinchandra. And yet, when he heard these rumours he left Suvarnapur. But if there was even an iota of truth in these stories, he would have stayed there against all odds. Saubhagya Devi kept an eye over her house day and night. Any such thing would not have escaped her attention. If these stories were true, she would not have wailed for Kumud and given up her life. Buddhidhanbhai’s house washed Kumud’s feet in milk. It is possible that she chose to drown herself rather than bear such depraved rumours. But, if she were alive, Sarasvatichandra would have not failed to bring her back to us. That causes some suspicion.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘It is possible that he did not have the opportunity.’ Gunasundari: ‘He might have been concerned about rumours as well.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Possible.’ Gunasundari: ‘If you allow, I will go to Sundargiri.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘What excuse do you have?’ Gunasundari: ‘We had decided to take Kusum to those places, so Sundarbhabhi and I could accompany her.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘And what if the stories are true?’ Gunasundari: ‘Then our destiny is shattered and my mind is as good as locked up.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘I have tried to educate you to the extent possible. I expect more from you, Gunial.’

Gunasundari: ‘You have given me so much, but my dull mind has not retained it.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Gunial, your intellect is glorious, but it has been suppressed by suffering.’ Gunasundari: ‘Possibly. But even then it is of no use to you.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘A sword comes in use only in war. Your knowledge and wisdom are used only at times like these. Gunial, a time has come when I might have to resign the Prime Ministership of Maharaj Maniraj, when I will be a commoner once again with only you as my support. If my Gunial’s wisdom and knowledge do not come to my aid at such a time, Vidya Chatura will have nowhere and no one else to turn to.’ Gunasundari: ‘Women’s brains are in their heels. In such a momentous decision it is not good to be guided by a woman’s intelligence.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘That is what people believe. But our hearts have been cultivated by a different sensibility; we have been united by a different emotion—would my Gunial have the heart to break these bonds? Do you remember, there was a time when my family was torn asunder by strife and disputes, when I was penniless. At that time, you generously and selflessly cared for me and my family. You enabled me and gave me the capability to attain this high position. In those days I was yours, and you were mine. Is that relationship over? Are you no longer mine, Gunial?’ Gunasundari wept on Vidya Chatura’s shoulder and said, ‘Dearest husband, forgive me. I became ungrateful and committed a crime. Pain had muddled my head, but you have cleared the mud. I am now prepared to listen to you and assist you in whichever way possible. Believe me, I shall consider Kumud, Kusum and the whole world secondary, and my mind will be entwined only to yours. Why would you be forced to give up your ministership?’ Gunasundari sat up erect, face to face. Vidya Chatura: ‘Now that you are attentive, I shall open my heart to you. If the stories about Kumud are false, there is nothing to worry, there is no reason to be pained. You, Sundar and Chandrakant through your combined efforts would be able to persuade Sarasvatichandra, and Kusum’s future will become bright. We will seek support from Flora and Kamla Raniji. If they do not succeed, Kusum will not have the heart to go against Kumud. But if what people say is indeed true, I have carefully considered my duty. If Kumud could not stop loving Sarasvatichandra, who is to be blamed? Us. Entirely. We should not be afraid of facing up to the consequences of our mistake. It is our duty to ensure that others are not forced to eat the poisonous fruits of our errors. If Kumud, unable to bear the suffering of her marriage, decided to take her own life, but survived and sought shelter in her love for Sarasvatichandra, as a widow, I believe it is our duty not to be an obstacle in her path and, in fact, to support her decision. All civilised countries consider this to be not only a duty, but the true and final test of parental love. You are not unaware of this. If this is the only way of securing unhappy Kumud’s happiness, we should take that path, and my Gunial should be with me in this decision. I have tried to educate you, and it was for such reasons that you can decide where our duty lies. ‘I know that such an act will bring us infamy; we shall become powerless to work for the welfare of our people. Such a decision by a prime minister shall put the ruler in a quandary. His subjects will not receive such an act with favour, and will brand me as fallen. It is the ruler’s duty to remove such a person from a position of authority. It is my duty to point out the path of rectitude to my king, and I shall do my duty. If this is the only way ensuring Kumud’s happiness, I shall have only you as my companion, if you would still consider me fit to be your companion! ‘In such circumstances I shall also fulfill Kusum’s desire to remain unmarried. If she wants, we shall arrange for her to stay in the Parivrajika Math of Mohini Maiya. If she wants, I shall send her to Europe or America to an institution where single women live, study and work for social upliftment. If she wants, I shall arrange for her to live in Bombay by herself and spend her life pursuing knowledge, morality and the welfare of others. Even this course of action would force me to give up the prime ministership.

‘Gunial, once we pushed Kumud into a well, guided by social customs masquerading as duty and morality. We destroyed her independence. She was enslaved to the paws of a depraved man. All of that was a sin—a grave sin. I have no desire to commit one more sin. The late Maharaj taught us to look at all human beings from a spiritual point of view; this is the lesson that we have been taught by the ascetics of Sundargiri. From this perspective Eastern and Western moralities converge, and we shall not tread the path of sin. If what people say is indeed true, then it is best if Sarasvatichandra accepts Kumud in marriage. It is equally necessary to fulfill Kusum’s aspirations to remain single, especially when there is no suitable husband in sight. These two are our duties. ‘What obstacle could come in the path of our duty? Is the lust for ministership reason enough for us to violate our duties? People can believe what they like. The great Bhavabhuti has described a father who aspires to position more than his duty, which you of course remember. But how can those Feel natural affection for their offspring, Whose souls are sunk in schemes of policy? His only thought is clearly to secure The friendship of the monarch’s chosen friend And boon companion, by his daughter’s person.⟨fn:515⟩ ‘Gunial, parents who give their daughters in marriage moved by lust for ministership or any other object in the world or due to their desire to please the king, society or the country, the love of such parents is false, a nullity and their sense of duty is as good as dust. Parents who take these decisions for their daughter are her enemies. Malati says of such parents: “The King’s regard is all in all with him; his Malati is nothing.”⟨fn:516⟩ She further says: “Alas, my father! Thy ambition spurns a daughter’s happiness.”⟨fn:517⟩ Gunial, most certainly you would not value this ministership more than our love for our daughter and our parental duty.’ Gunasundari: ‘That is indeed true. If I were to consider the ministership and all its accompanying riches primary to our duties, I would indeed be violating the norms. But you have duties towards the King and this state. At the same time, you have a duty towards your daughter. Is it not also duty to sacrifice secondary duty for the sake of primary duty?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘The poet has provided a resolution to this.⟨fn:518⟩ Gunial, if performance of one duty entails violation of another, one must understand that what we consider duty is in fact immorality. To believe that our duty towards our daughter is in any way insignificant compared with our duty towards our parents, country or society is a sign of a rotting mind. Duty is not measured by the prestige or numbers of people involved. If one is required to lie or steal for the good of all humanity, those acts do not cease to be immoral. If the performance of duty or desire to eschew immorality entails destruction of life, such destruction is duty. Sruti, Smriti, knowledge and devotion, social conduct and love are all transient and insignificant compared to our duty.’ Gunasundari: ‘If that is indeed the case, why do men join war and place women in the danger of widowhood? Is it not a husband’s duty to preserve his wife’s married status? Is it not his duty not to turn children into orphans? Why do men praise war as the supreme duty? I do not think it is a sign of your wisdom that you are prepared to give up the ministership for the sake of two daughters and harm the people’s welfare and prove ungrateful to the King. God knows if this is the result of a woman’s thinking.’

Vidya Chatura: ‘You have a discerning intelligence, which is why you can pose these questions. Gunial, duty is not an action; it is the cause of an action. A duty that becomes an imperative does not remain a duty; when we decide to do something or refrain from doing it because of an imperative, we exercise judgement. This judgement becomes a cause of action. When we are guided by nothing but truth, we are rooted in righteousness. We perform three kinds of actions: we renounce or reject some objects, make others happy or unhappy and lead a life of upliftment or fall. All our sorrows and joys emanate from these actions, and for that reason they are not to be considered distinct from each other. The pain and pleasure which result from these actions are our destiny; we have no control over them. We have to welcome them just as we welcome the breeze that flows. When we accept or reject any object for the sake of our minds or body, we have to exercise judgement about duty. When acceptance or rejection of a thing involves our ego and attachment, it is advisable to ask questions about its benefit to one’s parents, the country or to others. We are autonomous while exercising judgement regarding expenditure for a caste feast because that question falls within this class and category. ‘It is within our right to seek pleasure for others by our own actions. But we have no right to perform actions which might harm others or even seek to provide them with joy against their wish. ‘Only those empowered by the social order have a right to cause harm to others by their actions. Social order lies within the ambit of the king’s authority or the officers appointed by him. Parents exercise authority over their children, but that authority is derived from the king. When the king has not given an explicit command to do or not to do something, the authorised functionary has to exercise the authority. But in such instances authority must be exercised for the benefit of others. All other considerations are outside the domain of his authority. An army commander and a judge, in exercise of their authority, punish others and even award capital punishment; but they do not have the right to allow the pain and pleasure of their actions to cloud their judgement. The commander must ensure victory for his army on the right path and the judge must ensure justice. The king derives authority from God. This authority must be exercised for the welfare of his subjects. When a king deviates from his duty, the subjects have the authority to remind him of his duties and bring him on the righteous path. The king exercises authority over his subjects when they deviate from observance of their duties. In all these matters the prime consideration is exercise of legitimate authority to preserve social order. When the judgement fails, the king and his officers have to rely upon the ancient scriptures, great souls and leading men of the realm. Caste as an organisation performs this role for its members. The authority of parents with regard to their children increases and decreases in relation to the maturity and knowledge of the children. Similarly, as human beings mature in knowledge and experience, their authority and autonomy is enhanced and the authority of caste, social customs, scriptures and great souls over them decrease. ‘Our ancestors and law-givers of the past legitimised child marriage. But new knowledge and wisdom has to weigh these prescriptions. I did not realise that I had this authority. I gave Kumud in marriage in Suvarnapur, and that was a violation of my duty and an immoral act. Now I have awakened to my duty and authority. I shall perform my duties. I have no right to confuse my duties as a father with my duties as a minister. A judge ought not to fear while exercising his authority against the state. Similarly, it is beyond my authority to cause harm to Kumud and Kusum in order to secure the interests of the state or retain my position as a minister. If Kumud were to commit a crime against the state and were to be brought before me, I cannot think of my parental duty and hesitate in awarding her death penalty. Similarly, the commander of an army has no authority to consider the fate of his family while going into battle. It is not a matter of a larger or a smaller duty; it is also not dependent upon the consideration of the impact of an action. A person who has been invested with authority to maintain social order must base his action in duty and righteousness. ‘When the question regarding duties towards one’s soul is concerned, the question of anyone else exercising authority is illegitimate. If each soul is able to rise to a higher level, it would lead to overall good. But if violation of duty by one soul leads to overall good, one should be certain that seeds of immorality are sown in that conception of good. Whether one believes that all beings are a part of the Universal Being, or that each being is distinct and unrelated to others, performance of duties by each will lead to the good of all. A person who believes that by violating duties one would do good to others is a fool. Because that wretched person lacks the capacity for universality and in absence of this capacity that person will not have the ability to discern universal good. Such egoistic persons have brought about disorder and strife. History is replete with such examples. Gunial, action which leads to the downfall of a soul are prohibited. Hence, duty lies in upward movement. There can be no conception of duty other than this. ‘God gave us authority over Kumud. If God has willed that her love should lead her to a husband chosen by her heart, we have no authority to become an obstacle to it. If we act without authority and curtail her freedom, we are certain to fall by this violation. Parents cannot abrogate the freedom of their children. Kumud and Kusum are both free. Hence, you should give up all other considerations and worries and think calmly about the path suggested by me.’ Vidya Chatura slumped down in the chair, exhausted. He kept looking at Gunasundari. She was deep in thought and spoke after a considerable lapse of time. ‘You had spoken harsh words about Sarasvatichandra to Chandrakant.⟨fn:519⟩ At that point in time, you wanted to uphold the values of our forefathers. But in a short time those values seem to have fallen out of favour with you. I do not have the capacity to prove that what you have just said is false. But you have moved from old values to new beliefs, and that causes some confusion in me.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘You cannot be faulted for it. Sarasvatichandra acted in haste and caused harm to Kumud. I was feeble and lacked the capacity to deal with it. Hence, I was angry. I held Sarasvatichandra guilty. Once I regained my calm, I thought about Kumud and Kusum’s aspirations, and I arrived at certain conclusions, which I have shared with you.’

Gunasundari: ‘Do you consider the age-old practice of child marriage to be an evil one?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Those who formulated this social practice did not have evil designs. They would have evaluated their time and context and formed this practice for the greater good of people. Even now, if two fathers placed differently were to change this custom, the daughter of one will be happy while the other will be unhappy. If a father who is poor, ignorant and powerless were to break the custom and marry his illiterate daughter late, it would put her in many difficulties. But those who have power in the new order can benefit from the new practice. His daughter would certainly be happier. It is a matter of power and authority. I have the power to make my daughters happy under the new social order. And I know that our daughters have both the capacity and the inclination to be happy under the new order. It is my duty to make this possibility available to them.’ Gunasundari: ‘Have you sought the opinion of our elders?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Sardar Singh sought my father’s opinion, and the Maharaj sought my maternal uncle Jarashankar’s views. Jarashankar Mama was surprised that we should ask such a question. He thought that those who seek such an opinion also expect a favourable answer. He did not want his decision to retire from worldly affairs to be violated; hence he said that the Maharaj and I should take the decision. He did not wish to insult the Maharaj and therefore he said, “I am an old man and for long I have lost touch with the currents of the new age. Younger persons would be best suited to evaluate it. If it were a major crisis in the state, I would have come out from my retirement and shared my opinion. But I have no experience of young ones raised in the new age, and hence I have no authority to make any judgement on this matter.’ Gunasundari: ‘Isn’t his answer an indication of his views?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘That is quite obvious. But father’s opinion was different. He said that a swan placed in a crow’s nest would obviously seek out a swan. This is the vigour of youth. People do not restrain their own youthful impulses but want the children of others to do so. If we follow people’s advice our daughters will be unhappy and if we follow our daughter’s aspirations, society would peck us to death. Therefore the wise thing for us to do is to let people believe that she is dead. We are not bound to dispel this belief. We should let the two of them live happily and without hindrance at Sundargiri. We should neither criticise them nor allow others to do so. Let those who have been given up for dead be happy, and let people be deceived. We do not have to kill our daughters to make people praise us, but we are not required to be so truthful that we have to give up the ministership. Gunial, I have relayed father’s words verbatim.’ Gunasundari: ‘Your uncle who led a life of righteousness and morality wished to uphold social order, and your father who has always played with norms showed a way of playing with society.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘What should we do?’ Gunasundari: ‘As I suggested, let me go to Sundargiri with Bhabhi and Kusum. If the rumours are false, it will be good for all. But if they are true, I will not be able to give opium to my daughter and kill her. If she repents and comes to her senses, I shall hide our shame and take her back to Buddhidhanbhai’s house. But if she does not, we have no option but to follow your father’s advice. People are not openly critical so far, and we should be able to shield ourselves against their opprobrium.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Don’t even think of opting for the second option.’ Gunasundari: ‘To restrain her now is going to be as difficult as raising snakes. When I think of it, my courage gives way. Whether one likes it or not, we will have to do what your father suggested. And I shall have to bear it for the rest of my unhappy life. The path of duty suggested by you appears true to me. I have no valid response to you. But the fire in my heart will not be doused by your wise discourses. You are a man and I am a woman. The Creator made us different; can I undo it? But I give you my word that I shall, to the extent possible, try to live by it. And the rest is up to God, you and my suffering heart!’ Vidya Chatura: ‘That is enough. God is gracious and will have mercy for us in these moments.’
chapters.summary: Vidya Chatura delivers startling news to Gunasundari about Kumud and Sarasvatichandra, sparking a profound debate on duty, reputation, and their daughters' intertwined destinies.

chapters.title: Dust-covered Gems
paragraphs: Dust-covered Gems The drought’s over and clouds thunder My heart has some solace. ‘S ardar Singh, all your inquiries must be over by now,’ Vidya Chatura asked the waiting superintendent of police. They were in the drawing room of his house. Sardar Singh stood up, saluted and replied, ‘They are almost complete.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Do you need to rush to some place to make personal investigations?’ Sardar Singh: ‘No. Last night we had limited information that Kumudbehn is alive, and in Sarasvatichandra’s protection. This morning’s post and information from our messengers have brought more news. The person on Sundargiri is the same man who went under the name of Navinchandra and lived as a guest in Buddhidhanbhai’s house. Some six or seven days ago he, accompanied by Viharpuri, had gone to Surgram. He told the local teacher that his name was Navinchandra and that he had been Buddhidhanbhai’s guest. When asked if he was Sarasvatichandra he did not respond. He is a great scholar of English and Sanskrit, and Vishnudasji intends to appoint him as the head of the monastery after him. At present he is on Chiranjiv Shrunga to acquire higher spiritual capabilities. ‘Pradhanji, our messenger from Suvarnapur has given details of his conduct in Buddhidhanbhai’s house. You can read it from this letter. Pramaddhan and Krishna Kalika had started rumours about him and Kumudbehn, which are not believed by anyone in

Suvarnapur. Buddhidhanbhai has decided to divide his assets in the following manner: one part for his newborn son; one part to be used for the food of ascetics and mendicants in Suvarnapur; one part for Alak Kishori; and one part for Kumudbehn; Pramaddhan’s share has been made out to Kumudbehn. If neither Kumudbehn nor Pramad are alive, Pradhanji, the responsibility of deciding the use of that wealth for righteous purposes will be yours. Buddhidhanbhai is keen to renounce the world, but Maharaj Bhupsinh has bound him in a promise not to do so. ‘A bundle was retrieved from Kumudbehn’s chariot, which is in possession of Gunasundariba, that I am yet to examine. But apparently the bundle contains some poems composed by her, although they do not bear her name. Chandravali saved a young woman whose description matches with Kumudbehn; she has named this woman Madhuri. For the last three or four days, Madhuri has been living in the Parivrajika Math on Sundargiri. She wears the garb of an ascetic, but retains ornaments befitting the daughter of a household such as yours. At present, she, along with some women ascetics, is in the Vasant Gufa on Chiranjiv Shrunga. Navinchandra is in the adjacent Saumanasya Gufa. ‘Madhuri was engaged to Navinchandra, but he left home before their marriage. Madhuri was then married to someone else. This man caused her a lot of pain and grief; hence Madhuri sought to drown herself. But she was saved by Chandravali and other sadhvis of Surgram. Madhuri did not want to be a burden on her parents, nor could she live with her husband. Moreover, she could not bear Navinchandra’s suffering. For these reasons she tried to take her own life. The ascetics could not give her any solace and all their advice and wisdom failed to alleviate her pain. Therefore, as a last resort she was taken to Navinchandra. He gave her the news of her husband’s death. Since then Madhuri has adopted the clothes of a sadhvi. The women ascetics say that she intends to lead a life of asceticism and devotion and spend the rest of her life at Parivrajika Math or with Chandravali Maiya.

‘It was Navinchandra who told Madhuri about her husband’s death. He must have read about Pramaddhan’s death in the newspapers when he went to Surgram. These and other facts suggest that Navinchandra and Madhuri are in fact Sarasvatichandra and Kumudbehn. We will be absolutely certain after Chandrakant’s meeting with him. ‘We gathered this information from the teacher at Surgram and an ascetic named Shankapuri. Shankapuri has very recently joined the Sundargiri monastery, and he has been speaking ill of these two. The ascetics say that Shankapuri is himself impure and that Vishnudasji will excommunicate him as soon as he comes out of his spiritual retreat. It is said that Shankapuri cast an evil eye on Madhuri, who was protected by her sadhvi companions. One should not trust the words of such a depraved man. Our agents suspect that Shankapuri is in fact an informant of Hiralal. We shall deal with him. But the indisputable fact is that all the ascetics revere Navinchandra and believe that Madhuri is suffering from a deep grief, but is unsullied and pure. They are rarely wrong in their judgement about such matters. The ascetics of Vishnudasji’s math smell an impure person as fast as a dog smells prey. Pradhanji, today I see a certain meekness in your eyes.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Sardar, I am grateful to God that my daughter is not only alive, but that her piety and purity are praised by the ascetics. On the other hand, I see that my daughter feels that an ascetic’s life will give her greater peace and happiness than living in my house. She is forced to do this because of our customs and our social order. I see this clearly and I am grieved by Kumud’s pain and by the condition of our country. It is in my hands to secure her happiness and yet, I still feel incapable of doing so. It is all because of the social order that we have created. This is not an inability ordained by God. Some pain and grief are ordained by God, but we have added more to it by our own customs.’ Sardar Singh: ‘If you were to follow your father’s advice, you would be able to straddle both worlds; as we say, keep one leg in milk and the other in curd.’

Vidya Chatura: ‘Neither my Kumud nor Sarasvatichandra would ever agree to a secret marriage and live like thieves. If they were of the type who could have been happy with that arrangement, neither Sarasvatichandra nor Kumud would have sought happiness in ochre robes and food given as alms. If they had preferred a lie over the life of an ascetic, I would have told myself that they are lowly persons and I would not have mourned them as my father suggested.’ Sardar Singh: ‘Pradhanji, your father’s advice is heartfelt; it is out of love for Kumudbehn. But it is not a well-considered decision. At least I think so.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Even I think so. His affection wants to see his granddaughter happy. He seeks a way that will preserve social order by violating it! I have no desire to preserve that social order. I have the power to violate it. I want my daughter’s happiness without societal censure. This is a futile hope. I must act with all my strength and desire without consideration of success or failure—that is my duty. In a matter of such grave significance, I will have to differ from Jarashankar Mama. My father wants me to act in a way that accommodates both Kumud’s wish and social custom. I cannot do that. I will have to choose one path over the other. I will have to either cause pain and displease my elders, or violate my duty towards my daughter. I am confused and feel meek.’ Sardar Singh: ‘All of us are going to be caught in this whirlpool of reform. We will all have to experience this condition.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘I consider it my duty to act even if it means going against the current.’ Sardar Singh: ‘It is natural to feel thus when your daughter has become an ascetic.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘And yet the orders of the Hall of Justice are harsh and inescapable. I tremble at the thought of the evidence that Hiralal might present. That would tear Kumud’s honour to shreds. Today I feel the power of the seat of judgement like an ordinary mortal.’ Sardar Singh: ‘Pradhanji, you have nothing to fear.’

Vidya Chatura: ‘That can be said only when the matter has been concluded. I have always expected the plaintiff and defendant to show patience and forbearance. Today I realise how difficult it is to cultivate those.’ Sardar Singh: ‘Someone like you would be an example to the world as to how to conduct oneself in face of difficulty.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘This experience will make me more compassionate towards evil persons. Ordinary mortals faced with such difficulty, and unable to find a way out, would resort to evil ways.’ Sardar Singh: ‘Exactly.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘I am prepared to deal with ignominy and the wicked pleasure it would give others. Sardar Singh, do your duty without fear or favour and let no other considerations influence your duty towards the state and the people. You must appear as unflinching as vajra to the Bhim Bhavan.’ Sardar Singh: ‘Your daughter is so pure that she has nothing to fear from the bludgeon.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘You should do nothing that in any way compromises the power of that mace.’ Sardar Singh: ‘That is correct and it shall be done. Maharaj and the officials of Ratnanagari have the same wish.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘What are the other developments? How do you intend to deal with them?’ Sardar Singh: ‘Dhurtalal, through his representative Hiralal, has submitted a petition to the Agency that the case against Aarthdas should be tried by an English court. He has argued that Kumudbehn and Sarasvatichandra got involved with each other in Suvarnapur and that you and Buddhidhanbhai instructed either Aarthdas or the outlaws to murder Sarasvatichandra. This matter, they claim, cannot be impartially investigated under your administration, and therefore ask that the case against Aarthdas not be tried in Suvarnapur. They have asked for an investigation to be conducted by a British officer. A letter seeking the response of Suvarnapur State has reached

Buddhidhanbhai. He has sought your opinion before committing himself to a response. Initially the question was one of jurisdiction; now it has taken a larger shape.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘What do you think an investigation of this kind will throw up?’ Sardar Singh: ‘A bundle belonging to Sarasvatichandra came into the possession of the outlaws. In that bundle is a letter and a poem written by Kumudbehn. We have to decide if we should present it before the British investigator.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘If the matter is to be adjudicated by them, then it is our duty to present it. We cannot like commoners suppress evidence from the court.’ Sardar Singh: ‘What if we present the bundle after removing the letter? Which duty binds us to give such material to foreign powers?’ Vidya Chatura: ‘That is the norm of Chakravarti Bhavan, Sardar Singh. What is written in that letter?’ Sardar Singh: ‘The poem is difficult; it can be interpreted in various ways. Here it is, if you would like to read it.’ Vidya Chatura took the letter from him and said, ‘Whatever it is, whatever the consequences, even at the cost of my honour, Sardar Singh, this letter must be presented. Nothing is dearer to Vidya Chatura than justice, and for that he is willing to sacrifice his all.’ Sardar Singh: ‘Please read it.’ Vidya Chatura read it. The poem began with the lines, The vapours that rise from the earth Return from the heavens as rain.⟨fn:520⟩ The poem was written in Kumud’s clear and unmistakable hand. Vidya Chatura felt a surge of pride as he read it. ‘Sardar, this is a pious poem of our pure Kumud. It must be placed before the British court, and if necessary I shall appear before the court and interpret it. This clearly shows how and why Sarasvatichandra left Buddhidhanbhai’s house at the instance of our pure, virtuous Kumud.’ Sardar Singh: ‘That is true. But we will have to face up to all the wicked and false accusations and then present this as evidence. I think in the first instance we need to prove that Sarasvatichandra is alive, and that must be done under our jurisdiction. Hence, the question of his murder or a trial before an English court would not arise. And there would be no occasion to bring Kumudbehn into the picture. You will have enough time to determine if you wish to follow your father’s advice or go according to what seems a duty to you. There might even be some other option.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘If that were to happen, all impediments would be removed. How do you intend to ensure this?’ Sardar Singh: ‘If Navinchandra is indeed Sarasvatichandra, he will have to reveal his identity legally for the sake of Aarthdas’ life and Kumudbehn’s honour. I have asked Chandrakantbhai to pass on this message to him; he has agreed to carry it. After that we will not intervene in the matter. Since the time of Maharaj Nagraj, we have adopted a system that a case involving an ascetic from Yadu Shrunga would first be tried at Yadu Shrunga by the Mahant and an officer appointed by us, and the case will come to us in ‘‘appeal.’’ Brave Sahib had given official sanction to this arrangement. We have no authority to summon an ascetic before any other court of law. We can hand over the case to the government only after the ‘‘prima facie’’ case against an ascetic is proved. Navinchandra is also an ascetic of the order of Yadu Shrunga and we cannot ask him to appear before any court in violation of this arrangement. We shall communicate this to the Agency and it is bound to accept this arrangement. ‘There are no charges against Navinchandra. Vishnudasji and Shankar Sharma will together ascertain his identity. There is no chance of any ignominy in those proceedings. Once it is ascertained that Sarasvatichandra has become an ascetic, Kumudbehn’s honour will be protected and she would not be dragged into the proceedings. This is enough proof to establish beyond reasonable doubt that neither

Aarthdas nor the outlaws murdered a man called Navinchandra or Sarasvatichandra. It would also establish that the precious ring that Aarthdas claims to have been given to him by Navinchandra was indeed a gift from Sarasvatichandra. ‘Once you issue the summons regarding this, we have made arrangements for Sarasvatichandra’s parents and his reputed friends to set out from Bombay for Sundargiri. We shall receive them with honour and once these reputed persons under oath prove his identity, neither the government officials nor Hiralal or Dhurtalal have any argument. If the government is not satisfied with this, they can ask these individuals to appear before a court in Bombay and establish the proof of identity. ‘All clouds of suspicion hovering above Ratnanagari, Suvarnapur and Kumud Sundari shall disperse, and then it will be a matter of your family arrangement, which you will have to resolve in the most appropriate manner.’ Vidya Chatura considered all this for a while and said, ‘Sardar Singh, your plan bears testimony to your foresight and sharp intellect. It takes care of the interest of the state and even the Chakravarti Bhavan cannot find any fault with it. Please explain your plan in detail to the Maharaj. You have to tell me as to how my family can assist you in this judicial matter. Also, I want you as a friend to advise me on the course of action that I should adopt for my family.’ Sardar Singh: ‘That is short and straightforward. You should send Gunasundariba and Sundarba accompanied by your father to Sundargiri. Kusumbehn should also go with them. They will each work on Kumudbehn in their own way. And with your father present there no action which could bring social disapproval would be taken; equally, no decision that needs to be taken on the spot would be missed. You should write to Chandrakantbhai to learn what is in his mind and ask him to speak with Sarasvatichandra accordingly. Miss Flora should go separately. You should share with her your plans and ask her to keep them to herself. Miss Flora should, when the time comes, speak openly with Gunasundariba, Kusumbehn, Kumudbehn, and Chandrakant. If you make these arrangements, you will not need to be present there yourself, nor would you be required to rush there in haste. You are virtuous and pure, and equally pure and virtuous are members of your family. You are fortunate to have them. You will be able to stay here without worry.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Your wisdom is so beneficial. You can see the good path. Sardar Singh, you are also a jewel of Ratnanagari.’ Sardar Singh: ‘Pradhanji, I have the good fortune of having Maharaj and you see me with favour and appreciation. All your officials are like jewel dust around the luminescent jewels like Maharaj and yourself. I do not think I should delay you any further.’ Vidya Chatura: ‘Please go without any worry and do your duty.’ Sardar Singh left.
chapters.summary: Sardar Singh updates Vidya Chatura on Kumudbehn's ascetic life alongside Sarasvatichandra, as they confront societal pressures and a looming legal battle.

chapters.title: A Searing Heart
paragraphs: A Searing Heart Having heard Panchali even in what appeared to them as a wakeful state, Sarasvatichandra and Kumud experienced divine bliss. Late into the night Kumud went down and slept on the middle floor, while Sarasvatichandra slept on the platform. Kumud woke up early next morning and came to Sarasvatichandra. She stood there quietly for a while and then softly said, ‘Sarasvatichandra wake up, it is morning.’ He did not move. She bent down and placed her hand over his forehead. She was about to say something when he woke up, and Kumud withdrew her hand. ‘Kumud, I saw my mother in a dream. She had placed her hand over my forehead and was about to say something when I woke up.’ Kumud smiled and said, ‘Last night I thought to myself that I shall have to fill your mother’s place to the extent possible. I kept my hand on your forehead, and you thought it was your mother’s. It is an auspicious beginning. Now that Chandrakantbhai will soon be here with you, you will remember your—no, our—family even more.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I will either remember them more or forget them even more. I think I should finish my bath and go down to receive him.’ Kumud: ‘Of course.’ Sarasvatichandra was about to say something when they heard voices from below. He looked down and saw Chandrakant along with three ascetics approaching the cave. ‘Kumud, Chandrakant is here!’ Sarasvatichandra exclaimed joyously.

‘You were late; his love made him walk faster. I shall, with your permission, join my companions, and you should go and receive him. Please do not take my name in presence of others. You can tell him about me when the two of you are alone.’ Kumud went away. Sarasvatichandra went down the steps. He heard the familiar greeting, ‘Nandko Nandan ek anand det hai!’ Sarasvatichandra and his companions went out to receive Chandrakant. They moved towards each other in haste, their eyes glued on each other as their feet carried them forward. They almost jumped at each other in joy. Chandrakant held Sarasvatichandra in a tight embrace. His tears bathed his friend’s shoulder. ‘Is it you, my dearest, whom I see in this plight?⟨fn:521⟩ Sarasvatichandra! Sarasvatichandra! What is this? You—reduced to this!’ Chandrakant almost shouted. He stood back to look at his friend, weeping without control or restraint. His face withered. He said to his companion, ‘Bavaji, this is indeed my friend. He cannot hide behind these robes, not from this heart. Sarasvatichandra, what is this?’ Sarasvatichandra’s eyes had brimmed over with tears. His voice broke, ‘Chandrakant, these merciful ascetics have given me a new body, a new life to my soul and a new companion. We will have all the time to talk about all of this. These ascetics are not common mendicants found seeking alms among our people. They are the last repositories of the light of the ancient sages and seers, of Buddha’s monks who lived and moved among the people spreading his light. These are the sages about whom we read in Bhavabhuti! It is my great fortune to be among them. Please revere these ascetics with all the love and faith that you have for me. We will have enough time to speak of other things.’ Chandrakant stood facing the group of ascetics and said with folded hands, ‘I am partial towards this gem of a friend; he is partial towards you. I, Chandrakant, bow to you ascetics with all the love and trust I have for him. I am grateful to you for it is due to your grace that my long quest has come to an end. This gem from the world of learning from Bombay disappeared, and you sheltered him with such care and affection. Many hearts will melt in gratitude for this!’ Radhedas came forward and responded, ‘We ascetics believe that this gem will take us to a higher state. Even you believe that he shall lead to your upliftment. In his previous life, persons like you have helped nurture his values; we have been mere recipients of it. Chandrakantbhai, we ascetics are not acquainted with the lives of householders, but the society that your virtuous friend comes from must be equally noble. We shall receive you among us with all that we have. Please oblige us by accepting it.’ Sarasvatichandra took his friend’s hand in his and said, ‘Chandrakant, this good man Radhedas brought my unconscious body, given up for dead, from the forest to this place. This is Jnanbharati, the head of Vihar Math, which is where ascetic couples reside. A man of learning and deep wisdom, he is an expert in aesthetics and Dharma Shastra pertaining to couples. This is Sundardasji, an expert of our ancient arts. This is Surdasji, a repository of devotional literature, and Mayapuri who is an expert on scriptures pertaining to social order and an exponent of music. These are the real jewels of Yadu Shrunga. ‘My dear Chandrakant, there is nothing in or among these learned saints that is low or vulgar. The very air they breathe is impregnated with the sweet and solemn fragrance of their body and ennobling souls. Their mode of living is simple and yet refined, and their minds are cultured to an extent of which none on our Indian plains has any idea or even a dream. Not you but your heart will love and revere them as you are allowed the rare privilege of living among them, and unhappy and repentant will be the man who thinks of marring the picture of innocence, sweetness and sanctity of life which thrives on these hills and is ever kept warm by these high and unheard of attainments of these modest and simple looking anchorites.’⟨fn:522⟩ Chandrakant: ‘You may rest assured that my fortnight’s residence with that noble lady—your once mother-in-law—whom you have so cruelly wronged, has taught me at least one thing, viz, not to disturb the pictures of peace and innocence such as I found there or many find here as you say. After the hard lesson which your conduct has taught to the world, it scarcely remains for poor Chandrakant to follow your tuition in the rare art of making happy people unhappy—that is the art in which you have excelled as an expert of such superior eminence and unrivalled fame.’⟨fn:523⟩ Sarasvatichandra gave no response. He led Chandrakant towards his cave. The ascetics followed them. The distance between the two groups increased. Sarasvatichandra: ‘Chandrakant, how can I say that what you have said is not true? I have caused grief to many. Even you had to give up your work and Gangabhabhi and wander around looking for me.’ Chandrakant: ‘Of course. This is just a small instance of the fine art of causing pain to your friends that you have cultivated.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Is Gangabhabhi happy?’ Chandrakant: ‘That you would know only when you meet her.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘She must have felt very deeply for me.’ Chandrakant: ‘As if you pay any heed to it.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Tell me, at least.’ Chandrakant: ‘She might be dead or alive.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Why do you say such things? You haven’t lost your habit of saying harsh words.’ Chandrakant: ‘You say that your ascetics are soft and sweet both in word and in conduct. I do not know how to say sweet things, but my conduct so far has not hurt others. You have mastered the art of saying sweet things; you also know how to cause pain by your conduct. I do not possess such twin abilities like you.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Is Pitaji happy?’ Chandrakant: ‘What? Are you still concerned about him? What right do you have now to ask? It was you who had written,

What does the world care for my sorrows and joys There are so many souls upon this earth.⟨fn:524⟩ ‘Do you ever get to read newspapers in this land of enchantment?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Sometimes.’ Chandrakant: ‘Then you should read in them about how the seeds of your adventure have spread and grown.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Chandrakant, who knows my heart, is saying things that are utterly laughable.’ Chandrakant: ‘You want to laugh! You are neither angry nor sorry. I clearly do not recognise your heart, which has further hardened in these winds of asceticism. Your heart is no longer what it was, and I do not know it. But I know the hearts of many others besides yours. I know well the brutal kicks you have given those hearts. Now let me see what your new heart is made of.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Your bitter but truthful words rid me of the poison of my deeds. It gives me solace to hear you. I would have been happier still if Kumud Sundari’s words were as bitter as yours.’ Chandrakant: ‘Shut up! You have no right even to utter her name. Your evil deeds cut her from the stem and her body rotted. That lotus is no more.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That is true, Chandrakant. But it is your good fortune and mine that she is alive. The sadhvis of Sundargiri have nurtured and given a new life to that lotus which had withered. Their virtues and care have made her flower again.’ Chandrakant: ‘What! That jewel among women is alive? Let me meet that pious one without delay so I can seek her forgiveness for being a friend of one as cruel-hearted as you. I will send her parents the good news and plant the tree of hope in their hearts.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘You will meet her soon. That is also her wish. But there is a suggestion; you should not reveal either her name or that of her family to the ascetics without her express permission. No one else should know of her existence without her consent. The ascetics know her as Madhuri Maiya.’ Chandrakant: ‘Clearly, the ascetics are learned; they gave such a sweet name to a delicate person. I will not speak of her to anyone without her consent. But the ascetics made an error in naming you. I made your identity known to them without asking you, which I did deliberately.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I gave this name to myself. The ascetics did not.’ Chandrakant: ‘This is clearly a work of your cleverness.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘How do I look in these robes? I have not looked at myself. I can only see my reflection in the pool of water. But I am sure I do not look as wretched as you suggest.’ Chandrakant: ‘Why should it seem wretched to you? You have to see your reflection in our hearts and in the hearts of your father and Kumud Sundari; only then will you be able to tell us if the colour of your robes matches with the colour of our bleeding hearts.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Even Kumud Sundari has similar robes.’ Chandrakant: ‘She has done the right thing. She wants to burn herself alive on the same pyre on which your dead body is placed! Sarasvatichandra, what is your heart made of? Please take me to that unhappy soul without delay.’ Tears streamed down his eyes; Chandrakant made no attempt to hide them or wipe them. Sarasvatichandra led him towards Vasant Gufa. One ascetic went ahead to alert the women. No one said anything. They walked like dry, rainless clouds of drought. Sarasvatichandra whispered to Chandrakant, ‘They are coming forward to receive us. Do not utter her name even by mistake. Address her as Madhuri Maiya. She is the one standing at the centre of the group; she looks unlike anyone else.’ ‘Just shut up! Who are you to say anything?’ Chandrakant wanted to say, but he swallowed his words, cast a harsh look at Sarasvatichandra and moved ahead in silence.
