In a moment they were face to face with the women. The ascetics stopped and greeted them, ‘Nandko Nandan ek anand det hai! Madhuri Maiya ki jai!’

The life-sized portrait of Kumud Sundari that he had seen in Sarasvatichandra’s bungalow at Walkeshwar flashed before Chandrakant’s eyes. Her delicate beauty, her sweetness and her grave meekness sent his heart into turmoil like a ship being rocked on stormy seas. He wept even more seeing her ochre robes. Sarasvatichandra stepped forward and said, ‘Madhuri, this is my dearest friend, Chandrakant.’ Kumud: ‘Chandrakantbhai, are you well?’ Tears streaming down his eyes, Chandrakant could give no response and fell at Kumud’s feet. Sarasvatichandra picked up his pagdi from the ground. ‘Ku...m... Madhuri Maiya! Please forgive the extreme evil act of my stone-hearted friend. He would not have sought forgiveness. But I seek your forgiveness on his behalf. We have committed an unbearable crime against you; the poison we gave you has spread through the veins.’ Indifferent to her own tears, Kumud tried to lift up Chandrakant, who realised her evident weakness and raised himself up. He wiped his tears with a handkerchief and said, ‘Madhuri Maiya, please forgive him! The crime committed by my friend is as vast as the sky above us. His heart, which we believed was sweetness itself, harbours the salinity of oceans. His salinity has spread all around; I have failed to turn it sweet.’ Kumud wiped her tears and said, ‘Chandrakantbhai, your gem has proved to be a jewel even in the examination set by these virtuous ascetics. Their piety and merit have given him a new form and new values. You shall gradually witness that. With great effort, the ascetics and I have been able to provide some solace to his deeply unhappy and grieving heart. You shall do the rest. He has given solace, support and strength to my poor, orphaned heart. Please do not churn the lake of his heart any further. With great effort the mud has begun to settle in it. With God’s grace, the ascetics, you and I will eventually succeed in our endeavour.’
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra reunites with Chandrakant, whose grief over his friend's ascetic life is profound, setting the stage for an emotional meeting with Kumud.

chapters.title: Summons from Court
paragraphs: Summons from Court Sarasvatichandra and Chandrakant spent the entire day on the upper storey of the Saumanasya Gufa. Kumud came a few times to join them. Sarasvatichandra shared the entire history of his and Kumud’s life; he kept nothing back. As their story, hitherto unknown, came to light, Chandrakant’s mind experienced a plethora of emotions—sorrow, wonderment, joy and confusion. The anger of the morning gave way to hitherto unfelt emotions and thoughts. ‘The two of you have together attained unprecedented spiritual powers in this place. But you have left the crucial decision to me and even explain it to the world! So, all the abuses will come my way! Good! Very good! Kumud Sundari who looks so naïve has set the scene for me!’ Just as he said these words, Kumud came up from Vasant Gufa and stood behind them. Chandrakant, startled by her presence, stood up. ‘Please come in and sit,’ he said. Kumud and Chandrakant sat down. ‘Chandrakantbhai, some men are here. They wish to see both of you,’ Kumud gave them the news. ‘Both of us?’ asked Sarasvatichandra, somewhat surprised. ‘Yes.’ Both friends went down. Kumud waited for them and looked at the surrounding beauty. Sarasvatichandra and Chandrakant saw the ascetics speaking to a man who had come up riding a horse. He had tied his horse to a post outside the cave. His ‘dress’ was that of a rider from the British police and he had worn ‘spurs’ and ‘boots.’⟨fn:525⟩ He saluted Chandrakant and, turning towards Sarasvatichandra, asked, ‘Are you the ascetic called Navinchandra?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Yes sir, I am.’ Rider: ‘Chandrakantji, is he Navinchandraji?’ Chandrakant: ‘He admits that he is. Why do you need to ask further?’ Rider: ‘Navinchandra Maharaj, these are summons for you issued by our judge. Please accept them and sign this duplicate copy with ink and pen. Chandrakantji, these are summons for you.’ Both of them read their summons, exchanged glances and signed their respective copies. The rider asked and noted the names of all the ascetics present and rode away. Radhedas: ‘Maharaj, what is this?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Chandrakant, please read it out.’ Chandrakant read out the relevant portions: ‘Chaitra Sud 10, on this day, under the authority of Maharaj Maniraj and with the benediction of Shri Vishnudasji, the Chief Judicial Officer of the state himself or his representative shall seek the testimony of the ascetic Navinchandra. These proceedings shall take place in the monastery of Shri Yadunandan. On that day, or any other day decided by them, you shall present yourself before any witnesses that are brought forward in this proceeding. Ascetic Navinchandra himself must remain present for this, failing which you shall not be treated as an ascetic and you shall be produced by force before the state officials under the laws which apply to common citizens.’ Jnanbharati: ‘This is in accordance with special rights granted to Guruji. Does the summons mention the reason for this proceeding?’ Chandrakant read: ‘Outlaw Chandandas and others are charged by the State of Suvarnapur that they have murdered a man called Navinchandra. A bania named Aarthdas has been charged by this state for the murder of a man from Bombay named Sarasvatichandra, son of

Laxminandan. The petitioners are Dhurtalal and Hiralal of Bombay. Their plea is that Sarasvatichandra used to wander around under the assumed name of Navinchandra, and that these two persons are in fact one. This matter shall be investigated in either of these states or under British jurisdiction, or in all the three places. Maharaj Maniraj has appointed Shankar Sharma as his Chief Judicial Officer and invested him and Mahant Vishnudasji with the authority to ascertain the identity of Sarasvatichandra and Navinchandra and examine the necessary witnesses to prove his identity beyond reasonable doubt. This summons has been issued in accordance with the special rights granted by Maharaj Nagraj to the ascetics of Yadu Shrunga.’ Jnanbharati: ‘Maharaj Nagraj had promised the ascetics that all judicial matters involving them would be conducted in the presence of their Guruji. If Guruji does not consent to this, all summons are futile. Therefore, there is no reason for you to be perturbed.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Of course, not.’ Meanwhile, another ascetic came and gave a message to Sarasvatichandra. ‘Maharaj! Viharpuriji says that Guruji will emerge from his meditation tomorrow morning, and that you and your friend shall be called in his presence. You must have received the summons issued to you. Guruji will read the letter tomorrow. An ascetic of your piety and attainment has nothing to fear in this place. Moreover, Viharpuriji has sent these letters which were sent by the minister and his family meant for your friend.’ Sarasvatichandra took those letters and gave them to Chandrakant. Ascetic: ‘Most probably Chandravali Maiya will meet you tonight.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Nothing could be better.’
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra and Chandrakant receive surprising court summons from a British police rider, initiating an investigation into Sarasvatichandra's true identity and alleged murder.

chapters.title: Uncertainties
paragraphs: Uncertainties Alas! My friend who will believe it stolen?⟨fn:526⟩ The two friends went up the stairs. Sarasvatichandra: ‘Chandrakant, weren’t you told not to reveal my identity?’ Chandrakant: ‘I was.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Then?’ Chandrakant: ‘You would like to believe that your body, your scholarship and intelligence, your adventures are such that they can be kept a secret.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I have no doubt about it.’ Chandrakant: ‘Pardon me. You will be shocked when you know how I got news in Bombay of your whereabouts and what all the police of Ratnanagari know about you.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘They clearly have traced me. But Kumud Sundari’s presence is a secret, isn’t it?’ Chandrakant: ‘She was no secret for me. I do not know about the others.’ They came up to the terrace where Kumud waited for them. They sat down at some distance from her.

Chandrakant: ‘Kumud, I should get accustomed to your new name. Madhuri Maiya, please read these so that you know why we were called down.’ He gave her the summons issued to Sarasvatichandra. His own summons he gave to Sarasvatichandra. Chandrakant had also received some letters, which he began to read. Sarasvatichandra: ‘Kumud Sundari, Chandrakant was aware of your presence here.’ Kumud: ‘That is somewhat surprising. But we have shed the responsibility of deciding about my identity and our future. It is for your learned friend to decide. He knows your thoughts, my mind, he knows about our dreams and our discussions. He should decide what seems appropriate. Chandrakantbhai is the captain of our ship; we shall set sail in the direction he decides.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘That is the path of equanimity. Chandrakant, it was not I who thought of this solution.’ Chandrakant: ‘That I knew. When you decide something it invariably requires a new churning; there can be no fruits without labour. Without Madhuri Maiya’s wisdom your churning would not produce butter. In her wisdom she found a solution when you stopped making any effort, and your churning has now become my burden! Now Chandrakant is caught in that movement. One leads to one set of problems and the other to another set of problems.’ Kumud: ‘You are a friend, an expert in social customs, you are learned, you know the minds of our parents and all others concerned about our welfare. You have their trust. You are the best doctor of our malady. Who else could we turn to?’ Chandrakant: ‘Of course. Now let me read out a part of your father’s letter.’ He read from Vidya Chatura’s letter. You know what Kumud’s mother desires for her. You know the views of my father. By now you would have gathered what Sarasvatichandra and Kumud want. My own aspiration and inclination is to assist in helping realise any pure choice that Kumud makes. I have no desire other than this. Sarasvatichandra has caused injury to Kumud; he has hurt her and been unjust to her. If he wants to make amends for his actions, he should openly marry Kumud, give her every possible joy and bear with all the censure that our people will heap on them. This is the only path available to a man of his learning and sense of justice. If they are eager to take this path, Kumud’s mother and I will stand by them in face of every social difficulty. My affluence is not dearer to me than Kumud and Kusum. You know that Kusum has this acute desire to remain unmarried. I am prepared to spend all my wealth to fulfill the righteous aspirations of both my daughters. Kusum, her mother and her aunt will come up to Sundargiri tomorrow. Father will also accompany them. So will Miss Flora. Tents for their accommodation have been sent up. The House of Justice has issued summons. Sarasvatichandra, you and others will have to testify before Vishnudasji. I, too, have been issued summons. I will come up to give my testimony. Buddhidhanbhai has also been requested to give testimony. Sarasvatichandra must reveal his true identity. There is no other way. Kumud’s name and presence is a total secret. She can come out in the open if she so desires. Otherwise we have arranged to conduct the proceedings without her presence. You will get other news from the accompanying letters. Let Sarasvatichandra and Kumud read this letter. If Sarasvatichandra feels that he has done wrong and wants to do penance for it, the only righteous path is the one that I have outlined. I, as Kumud’s father, exercising my God-given right ask him that he shall do justice to my Kumud without delay. Sarasvatichandra: ‘Chandrakant, I have told you that if this action would give contentment to Kumud Sundari, I am prepared for it. Her father’s consent clears the path. I have already given my word to Kumud Sundari.’ Kumud: ‘Chandrakantbhai, put aside all considerations about my contentment and do not even imagine the possibility of our marriage in order that he can perform his penance. You are acquainted with our dream worlds and aspirations. What form of union would be best suited for the fulfillment of those aspirations should be the only consideration. A woman has many duties towards her man; which duty should be accepted and which renounced should be decided only on the basis of the fulfillment of his great sacrifice. Which path would allow us to be together and cultivate the same aspirations, which path is the righteous one for securing his prestige and our salvation should be the consideration. In short, which way will enable my union, my friendship with your dear friend to secure his happiness, his equanimity, his honour and his destiny and allow him to fulfill his great endeavour should form the basis of your decision. Do not even think about what will happen to me, whether I will get prestige or dishonour, whether it will endear me to my parents—who are prepared to go to such length to secure my happiness—or if it will cause disaffection, whether I will be happy or unhappy. You are the judge in our dispute; you are the father of the groom. Chandrakantbhai, you are our friend, you are the oblation in our sacrifice and you are the sacred fire as well! Assuming all these responsibilities, make me pure and moral and ensure that the life of the man who has become a renunciate for my sake is fulfilled in every sense. If this is ensured, every condition will give me happiness and contentment. I have no desire other than to see his life’s mission fulfilled, I crave no other riches, and the depravity of others will not in the least perturb me. And this is the truth. If you secure this for me, know that Kumud has no fear of dishonour, immorality and suffering. Chandrakantbhai, be my brother, my advocate and perform your duty. Know that he and I both have complete trust in you.’ Kumud’s eyes turned moist. Chandrakant, also overcome with emotion, replied, ‘Kumud Sundari, your thirst is to ensure that his life be fulfilled. Chandrakant’s fulfillment also lies in that. So do not worry. We also have other letters to consider before arriving at a decision.’ He picked up the second letter. On the envelope was Chandrakant’s name in Kusum’s handwriting. He tore open the envelope, inside which was another envelope. Kusum had written on it, ‘Chandrakantbhai, please give this to Kumudbehn wherever she is. Please keep it with you till you find her. If you do not find her please bring it back. In case you do not come back this side, please tear it up. Kusum.’ Chandrakant gave the envelope to Kumud. She read the letter in silence.

Dear Kumudbehn, I presume that this letter will reach only your hands. Chandrakantbhai will of course tell you all the news from here, but he might keep something from you or he may not be aware of all the developments. Hence, this letter. Everyone was worried about you, but now there is some hope. But after the news of Pramaddhanbhai, people would have preferred you dead than alive. I see this myself and also hear about it. Moreover, the news that you and Sarasvatichandra have been united on Sundargiri has caused not joy but pain. I need not write further on this. When Pramaddhanbhai was alive, Gunial was unhappy because you were unhappy with him. Gunial wants to see Sarasvatichandra happy, but in her heart she would not like that his happiness is secured through you. She will do whatever Pitaji decides only to keep him happy. If you were to remarry Sarasvatichandra, both of you would be dishonoured. Pitaji and Gunial will never be able to hold their heads high again. If Pitaji were to accept your marriage he, too, would be declared an outcaste and will have to step down from the ministership. Jarashankar Mama does not like this one bit, but he is retired and refuses to express his opinion one way or the other. He in any case does not involve himself with the affairs of the caste. Dadaji cannot bear your suffering, but he does not like these developments, so he has found a way by which you keep your and Sarasvatichandra’s identity a secret and spend your life with him on Sundargiri. This would not put Pitaji into trouble, and you could also be happy. Kaki says, why can’t you live like her? If you were to remarry she would not even look at your face, and Gunial would do so only for the sake of Pitaji. Sarasvatichandra’s father has gone mad and craves for the two of you. Pitaji wants you to be happy and is prepared to face every hardship for this. He would have written to Chandrakantbhai about this. It is said that your father-in-law wants to be a renunciate. No one will say all these things to you, hence I wrote about them. If you were to ask me, I would say, please do not get into this trouble. You are free at last; do not get tied down once again. I am not going to be tied down either. Come what may, I do not want to get ensnared by marriage. Hitherto, Pitaji used to say that he would get me married to Sarasvatichandra. By God’s grace, that is no longer a possibility. Pitaji has given his unambiguous consent for me to remain unmarried and celibate. I feel that neither you nor I should get married and the two of us should stay with Gunial till it is possible to do so. Thereafter, we shall stay with Chandravali and Mohini Maiya; we shall study new things and be saved from the ditch that our society is; we shall strive for real salvation. If you are united with Sarasvatichandra, it would be beneficial for me. If you marry him, Pitaji would have to agree that there is no suitable groom for me. If you decide to live a life of widowhood, the wheel will once again turn towards me. Everyone will say there is the groom; marry him. But I am firm in my resolve. Pitaji has given his consent and I shall not allow him to go back on his word. If you and I are both unattached, we could live as we please. We would both like it. In a few days all of us will come there. Your presence has to be kept a secret; hence Gunial has sent a secret message to Mohini Maiya and Chandravali. Flora is to accompany us; I cannot fathom the reason, but I have heard that she is to come to persuade you. She is a good person; you need not worry about her. No one will say such things to you and the two of us may not get an opportunity to speak while we are there, hence I wrote in detail. Sarasvatichandra is a man of virtue and learning. My decision to remain single initially came from him, and he is to that extent my master. Now if he were to go back on it, I would have to say, “Look Machhendra, Gorakh has come!” Kumudbehn, I have learnt much from your sorrow; you should learn from my happiness. We shall not move from our resolve and we will not allow anyone to shake us up. There is much more to be said, but we have our whole lives ahead of us. Kumud’s Kusum, and no one else’s! Kumud’s facial expressions, the lines on her forehead, the movement of her eyebrows, the blinking of her eyes and the changing colour of her cheeks clearly showed that the letter amused her, saddened her and perturbed her heart. The two men watching her were most perceptive. She gave the letter to Chandrakant and said, ‘Chandrakantbhai, the contents of this letter will also help you arrive at a decision.’ The two friends read the letter. Sarasvatichandra turned grave and said nothing. Chandrakant opened the other letters he had received and gave summaries of their contents. ‘Uddhatlal, Tarang Shankar, Vir Rao, Sheth Laxminandan, Haridas, Bulwer Sahib and others will come here to identify Sarasvatichandra and provide testimonies. Sarasvatichandra, this is going to be one festival! If you had not left Bombay and become an ascetic such a time would never have come. It is their and our good fortune that this motley group will come here on a pilgrimage.’ Sarasvatichandra remained sombre and merely asked, ‘Is there no letter from Gangabhabhi?’ Chandrakant: ‘There is. But it needs to be hidden from others.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘At least let Kumud Sundari read it.’ Kumud: ‘Gangabhabhi?’ Chandrakant: ‘She is the one I am married to. But you would be ashamed even to stand beside her.’ Kumud: ‘Is there a problem in letting me read it?’ Chandrakant: ‘There is and there isn’t. Should I give it to you? Anyhow, here it is. What has to happen will happen in any case. Let me read it. Listen. I was not only about to die, but your relatives and dear ones had planned to have me killed through Dhurtalal. You knew this, and yet you did not come back, which was a good thing. Because if I had died but if Sarasvatichandra was found, our children would not have died of hunger. But even if I am alive and Sarasvatichandra is not found, you would not have gone against your family and neither I nor my children would have seen even a false coin from you. Therefore it was good that you did not give up your search to come back.

After your letter came, Uddhatlal took me and the children to his house. There was a big quarrel between him and those whom you call your relatives. But Uddhatlal is not a false gem; he did not give in to anyone. Now I am well again. I became well because I heard that Sarasvatichandra has been found. If that is really true, I will come there with Uddhatlal. It is said that Kumud Sundari is also alive. But all that is futile now. If we belonged to a caste which accepts remarriages, it would be different. You reformers may well get into organising remarriages, nothing can be said about you. But joining that caste and getting our children married will never go together. Uddhatlal says we will all join together—all those castes which allow remarriage, those who have returned from England and those who have been made outcaste—and create a bigger caste. In this new caste no one will be made an outcaste, doors will be open for everyone and thus our caste will grow; only the old will stay in old castes while our caste will have all the youth. I think this is a joke. But there is no way of knowing what you will do; therefore I tell you that this is not correct. It would be a childish caste. I would not like cows and donkeys to be together in one shed. I feel that you men can go to the new caste but we women would prefer to be in our old caste. A caste that does not respect division and is all mixed up is not good. Therefore, please do not bring in the dark ages. Chandrakant was about to fold up the letter and put it back in his pocket, but instead he gave it to Kumud, pointed to a part and said, ‘Please read this—but keep it to yourself—we shall tell Sarasvatichandra at the right time.’ Kumud read the portion: ‘Gumanba’s son Dhanbhai has died. Laxminandan has gone mad, but Gumanba looks after him. She knows that no one but Sarasvatichandra will look after them. Dhurtalal is caught in a criminal case; big and important people take interest in it. The doctor says that Laxminandan will get well when Sarasvatichandra is found. It has been decided to bring him there. If you find Sarasvatichandra get him to take a bath for Dhanbhai. You must give him all the news. Probably Gumanba will also come with

Laxminandan. If you write, I will also come. Sarasvatichandra will need to be scolded to come back, which I can do well, but I cannot persuade an English-educated person; it is like pouring water over stone.’ Kumud gave him back the letter. She went into deep thought. Emerging from it, she said, ‘Chandrakantbhai, all the letters have been read. You have enough to think about. Chandravalibehn will come here tonight and early tomorrow morning Guruji will emerge from his meditation. I will have to go with Chandravalibehn and you will have to go to Guruji. Now we have a few hours to be alone and discuss the matter. If we spend all the time in consideration we will not get the opportunity to formulate a principle and arrive at a decision. It is difficult for us to explain our aspirations and our dream world to anyone else; to get anyone to believe in it is well-nigh impossible.’ Chandrakant thought for a while and said, ‘Then listen. You put the snake around my neck; I will have to put it back on your necks. I consider your union and dream world a miracle of ‘‘psychology.’’ It has a deep message; your aspirations are the fount of it. Chandrakant’s heart cannot even for a moment bear the thought of disturbing this beautiful, pure dream world and distancing you from each other. If your grand and beautiful dreams were to come true for our people, it would create a new, beautiful and happy world for our people, and any delay in its realisation makes me impatient. But in our present society, the light of that beauty would be sullied by your marriage, which is called ‘‘remarriage’’⟨fn:527⟩ by us. People will shun you as if you are untouchables. The dishonour and ignominy you would face would be akin to taking rain-laden clouds to the saline seas; not a drop of your munificence would nourish the earth and it would be wasted. ‘But if you do not get married your beautiful, pure dream will become a nullity, your penance will be futile and the light of your higher aspirations will give way to a dark, moonless night. And unmarried Sarasvatichandra would be without any support in your shared dream of helping raise our society by working among women.

But if you were to marry, Sarasvatichandra would have support which would be as useless as a wooden sword. ‘If you think that you could have only spiritual union, keep aside all physical relations but be together and work among the people, this is your futile imagination. Whenever our people see a man and woman together, they see only a physical relationship; they have no other measure. After hundreds of years of practice and cultivation, men and women of Europe have acquired the art of being with each other while suppressing their desires. This art might be alive among these ascetics and known to our ancestors. But in our present society even the dream of such association has been destroyed. How can we hope for a robust and healthy understanding in such a short time? So, whether you marry or hope for a spiritual union, in either case your guns will fire blank rounds. In a spiritual union you will have to undergo another penance—that of celibacy. ‘Neither of these paths will help you fulfill your aspirations. There is only one path which would allow you to fulfill your aspirations, and that is to follow the path suggested by Gunasundari and Sundargauri. Sarasvatichandra and Kusum Sundari should be married to each other, and Kumud Sundari should assist them by becoming an ascetic. People would praise this arrangement, and Sarasvatichandra would have not one but two partners in his endeavour to help our people rise higher. But there are three obstacles to this. Kusum Sundari wants to remain single; Sarasvatichandra’s heart has become one with Kumud Sundari; he will not be able to forsake one and experience oneness with another. A union of hearts is possible if it does not involve forgetting one and accepting another. When he came to Ratnanagari from Bombay he had neither met you nor got to know you. But when the interest of two persons is tied to one another and when they are brought together, it will lead to some love; some oneness and some sense of unity is attained. Don’t our people experience this? You have just read my Ganga’s letter; we also share some bonds. Kusum Sundari is educated, has aesthetic aspirations and is gifted. Sarasvatichandra would of course feel some bond with her and their union would be manyfold beneficial compared to my union with Ganga. Should there be any doubt about this? But in this case neither the groom nor the bride has any inclination. Moreover, it would involve shattering your unique union. This would be unbearable. It is better that your desire to work for the welfare of people should be consigned to flames. ‘But if your desire and aspirations for the welfare of our people is unshakeable, and still you wish to maintain your union in a way that it does not preclude your great endeavour, there is one way of ensuring both these. Sarasvatichandra should marry Kusum Sundari for the sake of it, and she can, like Chandravali, lead an autonomous life. Both of you can maintain your spiritual love and Kusum can maintain her autonomy without any bonds of either physical or spiritual love. This one path would secure everything: it would counter our social poison, ensure the welfare of our people, your spiritual union shall remain steadfast, Vidya Chatura and Gunasundari shall remain unperturbed. And I would either laugh or be jealous at your penance! That is if it finds favour with you.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘It is immoral to deceive people in order to secure their welfare. I do not even wish to cage birds like parrots and mynahs to ensure their welfare. I would not bind Kusum Sundari to the vows of marriage and then help her violate them! I do not wish to commit this great immoral act of taking false pledges only to violate them. In the Mahabharata, Pitamah tells the great Karna that he met the end he did because he was born in violation of morality. This statement of Sage Vyasa has always appeared true to me. ‘Duty first, and then only our most cherished dreams. To act otherwise is to place the cart before the horse. To believe otherwise is to be under a self-delusion and pernicious fallacy. I have learnt this invaluable lesson in this sacred lodge and have taught it to this dear partner of my dear dreams, and I never promised or proposed to follow an invitation from Chandrakant or any mortal or immortal being to allow any further dissolution of this partnership of mine, whatever name or form you be pleased to give to that dissolution.’⟨fn:528⟩

Chandrakant: ‘I only proposed the adoption of a ceremonial fiction analogous to the thousand and one legal and religious fictions which our people have so often adopted to effect their reforms.’⟨fn:529⟩ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The holy people of this place detest such fictions, and I think their ethics is the purest and highest on this as on several other points.’⟨fn:530⟩ Chandrakant: ‘You have floored me. I have nothing to add.⟨fn:531⟩ Kumud Sundari, only you can decorate his heart with the auspicious designs of a swastika. I have failed in that art.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Chandrakant, we asked you a question as to what our conduct towards each other should be. Answer that specific question, either as a neutral person or as a friend.’ Chandrakant: ‘Kumud Sundari, the intelligence of men will not work in this case. It is your responsibility now.’ Kumud was deep in her own thoughts and did not respond. Chandrakant: ‘Kumud Sundari, come out of your thoughts and engage your mind in this direction. We men have failed. The decision now rests on you. My friend will abide by your decision.’ Kumud: ‘I am grateful to you. I know all that I need to. I will think about this, but Sarasvatichandra do you promise to abide by my decision?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I agree to abide by any decision that you take about the two of us.’ Kumud: ‘Why is your promise qualified?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘This qualification is imposed by our love. In all other matters, your heart and mine will create a joint melody, a duet.’ Kumud: ‘Our music is not separate.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Music is one, but voices are two.’

Kumud: ‘So be it. If I am in your heart, I will emerge through your voice. Chandrakantbhai, I have found a way of arriving at a decision. I have adopted this kantha of an ascetic and my conception of duty will be imbued with ascetic norms. I will not be able to join my family, but I will not remain secluded from them. Ascetics have no secrets except the song of a couple’s heart. I will meet my mother when she comes tomorrow, I will give her solace. My Kusum and I will together find a way and we will consult Chandravalibehn as well.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘I have done and said nothing that the heart with which I feel as one should harbour any suspicion.’ ‘I know that you are a person of virtue and in that sense an ascetic. A person of virtue is one whose thoughts, words and deeds are one. We all strive to attain this ideal of virtue. But society has many places of danger; hence it is said that when dark clouds come, even men of learning who are on the right path lose their way. The place you are about to go to will look after and care for you. But the decision that you are about to make regarding our togetherness will cause uncertainties in your heart; you might feel constrained or following someone else’s wishes might sacrifice your heartfelt desires. Your thoughts, words and deeds might come to face those questions, and how am I to say that I will be there to help you? Parvati had told Lord Shiva that there can be no insult to a daughter in her father’s house; yet she had to face an insult in her previous life for which she was forced to give up her life. You must ensure that you are not faced with that choice. So long as your family is not averse to your thoughts, words and actions, I shall be able to retain my equanimity. You have read the summons issued; I have no fears regarding them. You will also have nothing to fear from your learned and loving parents. But social customs are adverse, and that might endanger your autonomy. I shall not be able to witness any attack on your spiritual or physical body.’ Kumud smiled and replied, ‘Do not worry. These ascetics have given meek Kumud new strength. Her virtues have been nurtured by our togetherness. Why should you be anxious?’
chapters.summary: Chandrakant faces intense pressure from family letters and the heartfelt pleas of Sarasvatichandra and Kumud, who seek his guidance for their future.

chapters.title: Some Decisions and a Resolve
paragraphs: Some Decisions and a Resolve The star of the unconquered will He rises in my breast Serene, and resolute, and still, And calm, and self-possessed.⟨fn:532⟩ Kumud went and joined her companions, and the two friends went out for a walk. Chandrakant spoke of the happenings at Vidya Chatura’s house, Gunasundari’s pain on account of her daughters and Sarasvatichandra, about Kusum’s firm resolve, her intelligence and her defence of Sarasvatichandra’s decision to leave home and finally he spoke about Laxminandan’s sorry condition and Dhurtalal’s cunning and scheming ways. He spoke at length and his words found their mark in the heart of the listener. That night Chandravali met Kumud and recognised her Madhuri as the daughter of the minister of Ratnanagari. Kumud told her about the divine experience which she had because of Guruji’s grace. They went up to Saumanasya Gufa and sat talking with the two friends till midnight. They spoke frankly but with caution. They also discussed the future course of action, but no one could come up with a resolution. Finally Kumud and Chandravali went back to rest in Vasant Gufa. Kumud could not sleep at all. Every time Chandravali woke up, she broached the subject of the decision to be made. In contrast, the two friends slept deeply. Once or twice Chandrakant woke up, laughed about something and went back to sleep.

Early next morning Kumud went to meet Sarasvatichandra; she had worn her kantha. She folded her hands to him and said, ‘I have come to seek your consent to go and meet my unhappy mother. I also request you to meet her and give her solace when you have the time. Now it is time for you to meet Guruji. I do not know where the two of you will be. Please send a message through Chandravalibehn. I will convey the deliberations of the three sisters, Kumud, Kusum and Chandravali, and seek your consent about it. ‘Chandrakantbhai, you have not worn the kantha, but you are a person of virtue. You are acquainted with everything. What more should I say? If you think it advisable please write to my father. We do not have a brother, but the two of us are for him more than a son. We become the cause of his sorrow, but that is also because of his deep love for us. For your friend duty is primary, but for me it is love that is primary. I have neither the knowledge nor the intelligence to understand duty. But his duty and my love lead us on the same path. You believe in love. I will meet my Gunial and Kusum in this kantha. Neither of you have any resolution to offer. My sister and I will arrive at a decision which would be the result of our immature and womanly mind. Please support me, and ensure that that decision finds favour with this great ascetic.’ Kumud stood with her eyes cast down, tears rolling down her cheeks. The two friends looked at each other and responded to her. Sarasvatichandra: ‘So long as your tears have not dried up, the fire in my heart will not go out. The reason is that I fear you would disregard the deepest desire of your heart and eagerly offer yourself as a sacrifice. And therefore, I gave you a conditional promise. You are virtuous, you and I have been united as one, you are the earth and I the sky; after such union you are not required to seek my consent. I will act according to your desire, please know that.’ Chandrakant: ‘Kumud Sundari, go and set forth for the auspicious work. My friend, who was hard as vajra, cannot be separated from your heart. God will grant you the wisdom. Your heart is the fount of pious and noble aspirations. Our blessings are with you.’

Kumud wiped her tears and began to walk away, but she immediately turned back and said, ‘Will you give me the descriptions of our dreams? I will ask Kusum to read those which would allow me to seek her advice. She is young, but her intelligence has flashes of brilliance.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘All right.’ Kumud took the notes, concealed them in her kantha and disappeared. Chandrakant: ‘Sarasvatichandra, shall we go to your Guruji?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Certainly.’ They came down. The two of them and their companions cleaned the cave and cleared all signs of their habitation. Before leaving, Sarasvatichandra filled his eyes with the vision of the cave where he had received benediction. His heart bowed to the cave. The ascetics and the two friends walked wordlessly through the early morning sun, the mountain breeze, verdant forest, black, steady rocks and the sea on the distant horizon. The path was narrow and they walked carefully. Sarasvatichandra experienced a new tranquility and a sense of enrichment. The breeze soothed him and his thoughts were swift as the wind. He walked in peace, greeting the birds and rejoicing in their song.
chapters.summary: Kumud, filled with resolve, seeks Sarasvatichandra's consent for her heartfelt decisions concerning her family, as blessings and support guide her path forward.

chapters.title: Blowing of the Conch in the Temple of the Unmanifest and the Fulfillment of Life
paragraphs: Blowing of the Conch in the

Temple of the Unmanifest and the Fulfillment of Life Tell me not in mournful numbers “Life is but an empty dream!” For the soul is dead that slumbers, And things are not as they seem. Life is real! Life is earnest! And the grave is not its goal; “Dust thou art, to dust returnest” Was not spoken of the soul. Not enjoyment, and not sorrow, Is our destined end or way, But to act, that each to-morrow, Find us farther, than to-day. Art is long, and Time is fleeting, And our hearts, though stout and brave, Still, like muffed drums, are beating Funeral marches to the grave. In the world’s broad field of battle, In the bivouac of Life, Be not like dumb, driven cattle! Be a hero in the strife!⟨fn:533⟩

Vishnudas’ deep, meditative state lasted four days and four nights. During this entire period Viharpuri and two other ascetics of superior attainment kept unblinking watch over his body. When Vishnudas emerged from his meditative state, Viharpuri was present. During the last day and night of his meditation unprecedented bliss illuminated his face. As he emerged from the meditative state his usual tranquility and equanimity returned to his visage. As his senses became oriented with the outer world, his body stirred; noises from without entered his consciousness. Finally Vishnudas opened his eyes and found Viharpuri standing before him with folded hands. He looked at Viharpuri and said, ‘Viharpuri, I was witness to a miracle that I cannot describe in words. It is true that Navinchandraji will raise our monastery to a higher plane, but his sacrifice will not remain confined to this monastery. His light will bring new enlightenment to both this monastery and the wider society; you and I will acquire the fitness only to bear witness to his sacrifice from a distance. Go and bring that great soul here. All our ascetics must study the components of his sacrifice. There should be no shortcoming in this.’ ‘As you wish, Master.’ Viharpuri opened the door and the other ascetics came in to serve their Master in the appropriate way. Viharpuri, accompanied by some ascetics went to meet Sarasvatichandra half-way. Soon he returned with Sarasvatichandra and Chandrakant amidst shouts of glory to God. Sarasvatichandra folded his hands as he saw Vishnudas. Vishnudas stood up to receive him in his embrace. He smelled the top of Sarasvatichandra’s head in benediction and gave him a seat beside himself. Vishnudas: ‘Navinchandra, are you well in body? Is this your friend?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Yes, Maharaj. Your grace has bestowed on me unmatched boons. Wouldn’t my body be well with your grace? And meeting with my dearest friend has filled my heart with joy. This is my learned friend, Chandrakant. I had to trouble my ascetic friends for him.’

Vishnudas: ‘Chandrakantji, your arrival and the power of Chiranjiv Shrunga should have destroyed the deep sorrow of your friend’s heart.’ Chandrakant: ‘This place gives tranquility to all.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘My intense desires and deep attachment have been destroyed. My sorrow was the result of desire and attachment; that, too, has been eradicated.’ Vishnudas: ‘Navinchandra, you have the fitness to perform a great and fiery sacrifice!’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘The seed of this fitness lies in your blessings, and a seed planted by you cannot but flourish.’ Vishnudas: ‘Oh great soul, do not restrict your altar to this small monastic community. Your intelligence will see further than our vision in bringing to fruition the teachings of the great immortals. Your brilliance shall shine forth like the rays of the sun through this world. We, too, shall receive your light and warmth.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Maharaj, I am but a speck in the universe created by the Unmanifest Being. I am prepared to live and work as He wills.’ Vishnudas: ‘Oh dreamer, you have a mind that is free. You must retain this orientation. We believe that those who perform their duties attain equanimity. One has to protect, preserve and nurture our duties towards the manifest world, and by so doing the inner and the outer are brought together in harmony. Lord Krishna taught this as the coming together of Samkhya and Karma in the Gita. This is the independence of the spirit and it is also detached action. Viharpuri!’ Viharpuri: ‘Yes, Maharaj.’ Vishnudas: ‘Do you wish to say something? Is Madhuri Maiya well?’ Viharpuri: ‘A person who has the fitness to live on Chiranjiv Shrunga acquires equanimity. And these beautiful persons acquired equanimity in four nights instead of five as ordained by you. Such is the power of their inner beauty! Yesterday, seeing the bliss on your face we realised that the fifth night would not be necessary. Madhuri Maiya is well in every sense. There are certain questions regarding Navinchandraji’s previous life. The House of Justice has sent queries and issued summons to Navinchandraji.’ Vishnudas: ‘Give this responsibility to Jnanbharati. Navinchandraji, we do not consider our previous life a matter of shame or something to be erased. We consider that seeds of renunciation lie there and do not shy away from its acceptance.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘In this place, all conduct is righteous.’ Vishnudas: ‘The highest among ascetics do not accumulate either honour or ego. Many ascetics from this place have gone back to their previous life in society in order to offer their sacrifice; and as householders they have not harboured the ego that they still retain the spiritual vision of an ascetic. Navinchandraji, it is for this reason we revere both the manifest and the unmanifest. Sarasvatichandra: ‘You initiated me in renunciation of both honour and ego. And today you have clarified for me its essence. This is an act of grace.’ Vishnudas: ‘Ascetics who have renounced both their honour and ego consider their kantha, their ochre robes to be like the copper inscription that authorises them to make a sacrifice for the people. This sacrifice is not intended either to make the ignorant honour them, nor is it to increase the prestige of this monastery. The sense of ego, the sense of having performed a sacrifice is reduced to zero.’ Viharpuri: ‘Maharaj, yesterday I read that the mind becomes feeble when it recognises the multiple arrows that are driven into the soul. Shiva’s wrath turned Kamdev to ashes and his arrows of love became futile. The wielder of the bow that has driven these arrows into the soul also grows feeble; his bow does not remain a bow and his arrows turn blunt. It is the same for the soul whether or not one enacts one’s part in this illusionary play as if one were a witness.’ Vishnudas: ‘Navinchandraji, this is salvation, and is available only to ascetics. Others who claim salvation are in fact in a place like Ashwatthama’s resting place. One must aspire for and seek salvation. But there are those who, like a wasp caught inside a lotus, are bound to salvation; they seek praise for their accomplishments. One has to free oneself, not from the problems of the world which are like arrows piercing the body, but from the power and force of these problems. Those who become thus free, like a child emerging from the womb, become capable of unattached action. For these free beings, unattached action becomes a manifest duty. The desire to merge with the Unmanifest Being is futile without attaining the Supreme Brahman, who is called God by people. Wind and other forces cause sea waves, but they must subside within and be contained by the sea. Similarly, a being must rise and subside within God. This is the only path to attain the manifest God. This path cannot be grasped without unattached sacrificial action. You aspire to be initiated in such action, but your action cannot rest upon people; it must rest in God. People are ignorant, and an ascetic does not crave either their approval or disapproval. Those with superior attainment are only concerned with the welfare of people. Your heart is imbued with this desire; you are on the path to attainment of the Supreme Brahman, and when all aspects of your life converge on that path your endeavour shall cease, it shall subside. ‘Navinchandraji, you have heard the ringing of bells and conch shells during prayer. This worship is symbolic of the manifest sacrifice. This idol is symbolic of that Supreme Being who is the protector and nurturer of life. The pure manifestation of this idol resides in each heart. Devotees through worship offer all that is theirs to the symbolic idol with a sense of detachment. Ascetics and men of virtue offer themselves to the pure essence. In a symbolic temple, fragrance, flowers and other offerings imbue the worshipper with the sense of being in the presence of the pure essence of the Supreme. The devotee offers his purest aspirations and experiences to the divine presence. An aarti is the medium by which the presence of the divine is experienced. Similarly, learned, virtuous men such as you have the vision of the divine in all his embodiments. Ascetics like us ring our spiritual bells in the sanctum sanctorum of our heart. Ascetics of your attainment fill the sanctum with your music and rhythm which fills the being and spreads without.

‘Navinchandraji, the immortals have given you the fitness to perform such a sacrifice, but while exercising this right pray do not forgot this small monastic community and at the same time do not restrict and confine your actions to this monastery. Do not harbour any doubts, do not be afraid of social uproar, do not be cheated by the praise and criticism of wretched ignorant beings, do not be dragged along by people who have a uni-dimensional perspective, do not allow faith that does not respect all paths to constrict your action, do not be afraid of the attack of animal instincts, do not be disdainful of anyone or anything and at the same time do not cease your action on the promise of anyone’s support. Remain steadfast in your spiritual powers and seek the welfare of all those who are guests in your sacrifice. Offer each aspect of your life in your sacrifice! ‘Navinchandraji, such a sacrifice will bring to fruition all the benedictions you have received from the immortals, and you shall at its conclusion attain the Manifest One and move on the path of attaining the Unmanifest. Through Yoga, action and knowledge, you shall attain the Supreme.’
chapters.summary: Vishnudas guides Sarasvatichandra on a path of profound spiritual sacrifice, urging him to embrace unattached action for the welfare of all, transcending monastic confines.

chapters.title: Mohini Maiya's Right
paragraphs: Mohini Maiya’s Right I through the ample air in triumph high Shall lead Hell captive, maugre Hell, and show The Powers of darkness bound.⟨fn:534⟩ Canvas tents for the Minister’s family were pitched in the same garden where the ascetics had alerted Kumud to her heart’s desire. Her family had arrived at Yadu Shrunga even before Kumud had left Vasant Gufa. Four tents were pitched for the family; a kitchen tent was also erected. They had sent a message to Mohini Maiya the previous night. Just as they had sat down to clean their teeth, they saw Mohini Maiya approach. Gunasundari went forward to receive her. The two women greeted each other with ‘Jai Shri Yadunandan!’ and sat facing one another. Mohini Maiya offered Gunasundari the prasad of Yadunandan. Gunasundari: ‘Does tranquility and peace prevail among the ascetics? Are the female ascetics able to perform their religious duties without any hindrance?’ Mohini: ‘So long as the Maharaj rules this realm and Pradhanji protects our interests we have nothing to fear from the world outside, and so long as Vishnudasji is alert the virtues of our sadhvis rise ever higher.’ Gunasundari: ‘Mohini Maiya, I have come here on a mission and I seek your support.’

Mohini: ‘The desire of our Minister’s wife Gunasundari cannot but be virtuous. We feel content even while assisting common people in fulfilling their good desires. We would feel a special joy in assisting your quest.’ Gunasundari: ‘I consider you like my mother and sister.’ Mohini: ‘Receiving and giving such affections has become natural to the head of the Parivrajika Math.’ Gunasundari: ‘I wish to share something confidential with you and ask you about a matter which is secret.’ Mohini: ‘Nothing but the innermost aspirations of a couple’s heart are secret for the ascetics. Moreover, life stories shared by unhappy hearts in confidence are a remedy for them. We ascetics would not fail in our duty as healers. These people are your family. You know best what is confidential from them.’ Gunasundari: ‘There is nothing secret from this group. Mohini Maiya, is a young girl called Madhuri Maiya with you?’ Mohini: ‘She has accepted our hospitality, and become the very life of us ascetics. Day before yesterday, of her own volition she has adopted the kantha.’ Gunasundari: ‘Possibly, she is our daughter whom we had given up as drowned.’ Mohini Maiya: ‘Such fragrance can come only from a lotus.’ Gunasundari: ‘Does any ascetic here know her name or her lineage?’ Mohini: ‘She knows it, and it is believed that Guruji’s great favourite Navinchandraji knows it.’ Gunasundari: ‘If she is indeed my daughter, the ascetics will have to give her back to me.’ Mohini: ‘If that is what Madhuri desires, our ascetic norms will not be a hindrance. But it is not our duty to hand her over to anyone against her will. Our hearts will never accept it. You would certainly not be unaware of the fact that even the ruler of Ratnanagari cannot force an ascetic out of this monastery and take her in his custody.’

Sundargauri: ‘Mohini Maiya, would our Kumud live as an ascetic amongst you? And would you refuse to give her back to us?’ Mohini smiled and replied, ‘Sundargauri, we give shelter to people. We do not forsake them and destroy the hope of others to be given shelter.’ Kusum: ‘Oh good! Kaki has been defeated! Now both Kumud and Kusum shall live as ascetics, and Kaki will be powerless to do anything.’ Sundargauri was about to retort in anger, but Gunasundari prevented her and said, ‘Mohini Maiya, what you say is right. But it is also your duty to give solace to a mother’s heart.’ Mohini: ‘Mohini will assist you in every righteous act. But O’ Gunasundari! It is also a mother’s duty to ensure that her daughter who has given her heart to someone is not separated from him. If Madhuri is indeed your daughter, you caused her to separate from her beloved once; you got her married to a stranger and sent her to live among strangers. This was an immoral, unjust act. If you are intent on repeating such an act, the ascetics will protect Madhuri. If Madhuri of her own volition were to concede to your desire, the ascetics will make every attempt to prevent her from committing this wrong by abandoning her husband. If she were to still persist in her decision, we shall declare her as having violated her duties and we shall forsake her. That is something you would like. If she were to decide to come with you either out of fear or shame or due to inability to express her heartfelt desire, the ascetics will not take her on her word but examine minutely the core of her being, and at the end if we think it would be good for her to join you, we shall not create any obstacles. But if her inner desire is to stay on at Sundargiri, with or without Navinchandraji, we shall shelter her and the ascetics will stand up to any physical force. Just as you kept her in your womb for nine months and protected her from heat and cold, the ascetics shall protect her with all the strength that we have been given by the Supreme Being. Any path that does not involve a violation of duty and morality will be available to you and Madhuri as the benediction of Sri Yadunandan.’

Gunasundari: ‘How and when did the ascetics acquire rights over her? If you consider her to be a widow she should go and live in her father- in-law’s house; if she is considered unmarried, she should come and live with us. This is the social custom. The dictates of Dharmashastra and the laws of Maharaj Maniraj are applicable to all. Ascetics can exercise authority over other ascetics, but if you begin to exercise authority over householders, would you not be violating norms? Please do not be angry.’ Mohini: ‘O’ Minister’s wife, you have merely asked a question. Why should an ascetic be angry about it? This is a valid question. The Dharmashastra is for householders, and it gives no autonomy to women. But our scriptures see a woman as a spiritual being and consider societal injunctions as invalid and lowly. In your society, even a thirty-year-old son is a child for his parents and they do not shy away from giving him orders. In our monastery every mature person is considered capable of recognising an act that is right or wrong, that is beneficial or harmful to them; and any act that prevents a person from acting according to his or her light is an immoral act. The codes of Maharaj Maniraj are essential for social order. But so long as the ascetics of Sundargiri do not violate ascetic norms and duties, the codes of the Maharaj are to be taken only as suggestions—this is a written promise and custom maintained for generations. ‘Chandravali Maiya received your message yesterday, and she informed me about it. I have, at her instance, brought a copy of the promissory note given to us by the Maharaj for you to see. We have no authority over a child born to householders. But when that child, upon attaining the age of maturity, seeks our shelter and if such shelter is given, her parents and the society will have no further rights over her. This is an express injunction of the Maharaj’s promise. Even if Maharaj Maniraj’s child were to, upon maturity, come to us, our right shall be primary. Maharaj’s orders would have no effect.’ Sundargauri looked crestfallen and said, ‘Will Kumud then cease to be our daughter?’

Mohini: ‘Sundargauri, why do you grieve? These are questions of attachment which are futile for us. Our effort is to teach people to give up attachments.’ Sundargauri: ‘Have we lost all rights to secure Kumud’s happiness?’ Mohini laughed and replied, ‘When did you retain the right to ensure her happiness? You mocked her engagement and handed her over to her so-called husband; that day you handed over your rights to him. So where is your right? Truly speaking, you committed a grave crime in believing that you had the right to give her away in marriage, which resulted in a greatly immoral act. Your innocent, darling daughter had to bear grave hardships, which proved that you are incapable of ensuring her happiness. We ascetics secured for her what you as her parents failed to do. If you were to think more closely, the sin of this violation accrues also to the political order that supports this unjust social order and to the king who upholds it as morality. King Dushyant, father of Bharata, said that whenever parents violate their duties, he shall take their place.⟨fn:535⟩ This act of violation is not only caused by death but even by lack of judgement. Thus, when parents cease to act in the interest of their children, the king should act in their interest. Such is the injunction of our ancient law-givers. Our Maharaj does not abide by this code, which might find favour with your depraved society, but we ascetics follow the norms which have been abandoned even by the king. Sundargauri, if your conception of Madhuri’s happiness matches with her own, we shall not snatch away her freedom. But if that is not the case, we shall not allow you to curtail her freedom.’ Gunasundari: ‘My husband had informed me of your special rights and asked me to seek your help within the ambit of those rights.’ Mohini: ‘He is knowledgeable in matters of law and duty.’ Gunasundari: ‘How will you be able to assist us?’

Mohini: ‘As per the wish of the Master, Navinchandraji has spent the last few days on Chiranjiv Shrunga. Madhuri Maiya has, due to our friendly act, benefitted from being in his presence. She has adopted the ochre kantha of an ascetic as a result of this pious union. By now, Navinchandraji must have left to be with the Master. Chandravali will accompany Madhuri Maiya to our monastery. I will send her to you, and if she is indeed your daughter, know her heartfelt desire and convey it to Chandravali. I will confer with her and take a decision.’ Sundargauri: ‘Even if Kumud wants to come back to us, you would prevent her?’ Mohini: ‘If it is a heartfelt consent we will let her go with you, otherwise not. We will decide if her words really express what is in her heart.’ Sundargauri: ‘See Bhabhiji, they will believe what the girl says, but not her mother. Wouldn’t it be better if we were to turn away without meeting her? That meek girl has been turned into a raging bull by these women ascetics.’ Mohini: ‘Whether you like it or not, we have given her strength. You are free to stay or go.’ Gunasundari: ‘Mohini Maiya, what was the nature of Kumud’s proximity with Navinchandra while they stayed at Chiranjiv Shrunga?’ Mohini: ‘This should necessarily remain a secret from all others, but you are her mother. Chandravali might have the true facts and she will share them with you.’ Gunasundari: ‘If Kumud decides to stay here, where would you keep her?’ Mohini: ‘If Navinchandraji decides to join the Vihar Math, she will stay with him; otherwise she will stay with me in the Parivrajika Math or else wherever the Master decides. Wherever she is, she shall be sheltered by Sundargiri.’ Gunasundari: ‘Would it be possible to conceal Kumud’s identity and our relationship with her till we return to Ratnanagari or till such time that we decide? What you describe as a pious union we call it a depravity and fall; would it be possible for you to keep that a secret as well?’ Mohini: ‘It is our duty not to make her previous life public. If her union becomes public we shall remain neutral, but we shall not make it public. It depends upon the capacity of each heart whether her union be seen as spiritual upliftment or fall.’ Gunasundari: ‘That is sufficient for us. Please keep our secret and kindly send her to us.’ Mohini: ‘Do you wish to see the documents granting us special rights?’ Gunasundari: ‘It is better not to see them. Kusum, they are not for you to read. Please give them back to her.’ Kusum read the document aloud before returning it. These anchorites live an innocent, free, unalloyed, holy and refined life which is quite anomalous, not only in this province, but in the whole of modern India. Probably they are a relic of some very ancient stage of the glorious days of Indian civilisation. The Chiefs of this State have always not only extended to them liberal assistance and encouragement, but they have also, with genuine veneration, allowed to them all the sphere and privileges of self-government and all protection against any trespasses by a depraved outside world which a microscopic but nobly planned indigenous republic might have the rare luck of desiring and enjoying in the midst of the semi-barbarous age surging outside their castle walls. The British Government has therefore wisely not only confirmed, but even guaranteed the independence and integrity of this body of holy men, lest a change of views among the rulers of the State should ever tempt any future incumbents of the gaddi to contaminate or crush so noble and well-deserving an institution.   —Extract from the correspondence of the British
Representative to H. H. the Maharaj Nagaraja.⟨fn:536⟩
chapters.summary: Mohini Maiya firmly defends the monastery's special rights and Madhuri's choice, challenging Gunasundari's desire to reclaim her daughter Kumud from the ascetics.

chapters.title: A Curtain Breached
paragraphs: A Curtain Breached Some force whole regions, in despite, Of geography, to change their site; Make former times shake hands with latter, And that which was before, come after.⟨fn:537⟩ Of the four tents one was meant for women, the second for Manchatura, the third for receiving ascetics and the fourth was for other male guests. It was decided to house Chandrakant there. After Mohini left, Gunasundari accompanied by Sundargauri and Kusum slowly walked towards her tent. Manchatura came and inquired, ‘Gunasundari, did you learn anything new from Mohini?’ Gunasundari: ‘Chandravali will bring her here shortly; only then shall we know if our noses are to be cut or they are to remain.’ Manchatura: ‘You grieve and fret unnecessarily. If there is someone powerful enough to swing society one way or another, society swings. Our noses and honour will both remain intact; do not unnecessarily brand your daughter with your harsh words. She survived the outlaws and emerged alive from water. She will merge with the ascetics, and there is no need to announce it to the world. Do not worry. I will straighten everything out.’ Gunasundari: ‘We can make a show of having our noses intact, but the wounds in our hearts will never heal. What is immoral for us is supreme duty for the ascetics. They have done many mad things and will do more such things. We have no means to prevent them. Truly speaking, I do not like to even utter Kumud’s name, I now detest her face and would not like her words in my ears. My heart tells me that my worst fears are about to come true. This girl, who shall bring shame to my womb, did not die nor did she turn to stone!’ Manchatura: ‘You are naïve and do not understand the mysterious ways of the world. You want that girl dead—what are we to do with you women! Her heart was given to one and her body to another, and he turned out to be one such fateless man. Gunasundari, it is easier said than done. Now God has willed that Kumud should lead her life with the man of her heart; if we hold tight to our honour there would be none as foolish as us. Think about it; the outlaws, river Subhadra, the island of the Mother Goddess temple, Sundargiri and Sarasvatichandra—all these are unrelated to each other. So many wheels had to move in unison to get this clock ticking. And now you, her mother, want to break its spring? People set fire to other people’s homes and clap and dance with joy at the spectacle. Should we also stand by and watch our house go up in flames and join the spectacle? Come, gather yourself now and give up this insane insistence. Your daughter has passed through a great and fiery ordeal; her fires have now been doused. Do not singe her when she comes to you, do not scold her, do not keep quiet or speak less and do not go around with a long face. If you do any of this, she is clever and will see your hidden anger and all her fire within shall burn again. Act wisely, Gunasundari, take her into your lap, wipe her tears and give her solace. Be her mother and show her the path to her happiness. Gunasundari, if you do not do this, my death will be upon your head! I know that you have deep affection for me and that you will remain true to my words. With this trust, I am going to receive Kumud midway. I shall bring her here. She will feel shy and constricted in opening her heart to you. Therefore, let her and Kusum be alone together in the tent meant for the ascetics. Both sisters will open their hearts to each other. Daughter Kusum, you must assuage Kumud’s feelings and share her sentiments with Gunial. We will set everything on the right course. And tell your sister that even if no one is on her side, her grandfather will stand by her. He wore arms and rode a horse to save her from the outlaws; now he will take up arms against the whole society for her. Tell her not to worry in the least. Gunasundari, while the two sisters talk, you and Sundar speak to Chandravali, know from her all that needs to be known and seek her advice. Chandravali is a wise, affectionate and caring person. I have sent our people some distance away so that they do not know of Kumud’s presence. I have ordered them not to even look in this direction unless called by you. Now I will go. But be careful, Gunasundari, do not make any error. My life is in your hands!’ Manchatura left. Gunasundari sighed deeply and said, ‘Sundarbhabhi, I cannot fathom what will happen. We are being dragged against the social currents, and both the elderly father-in-law and the wise man of the family are dragging us against our instincts. As a true wife I must follow your brother-in-law, but his wish is totally contrary to our instinct. The elders could have prevailed upon him, but Jarashankar Mama chose silence and father-in-law has climbed onto the bandwagon. If our mother-in-law were alive we would not have been placed in this situation.’ Sundargauri: ‘Bhabhiji, this must be what they call the new age. Now the men have taken over what used to be women’s domain!’ Gunasundari: ‘English education is said to be the means of securing the freedom of women. But this education has begun to cut down our rights root and branch. Now even our daughters have gone over to their father’s side, they are no longer ours.’ Sundargauri: ‘Everyone sides with power and wealth; father-in-law did what his wealthy minister son wanted. Why should we be surprised if our daughters go over to him? Tomorrow he will construct a palace for his daughters; what do we have to give them? People are selfish, and the young ones are enamoured of luxuries.’ Gunasundari: ‘Sundarbhabhi, even to think ill of the husband is a violation of a wife’s duties. Let us stop this. But my heart churns and breaks. I want a release from this. Saubhagya Devi died, and I remained!’ Gunasundari wept copious tears.

Sundargauri: ‘Bhabhi, you are bound by the duties of a true wife. But I am free to persuade Kumud. Would she not listen to me?’ Gunasundari: ‘Sundarbhabhi, didn’t you listen to what Mohini said? Let’s drop that. Now honour and life both will leave us. There is no other way. I will go behind the tent for a while. Let me weep. Don’t come with me. Let me be alone.’ Sundargauri: ‘Yes, go and unburden your heart.’ She sat down on the couch and looked at Kusum who was seated on a chair as if indifferent to everything around her. ‘This is why we gave birth to you! Go! Your grandfather has told you to speak to your sister alone; ask her what you want and tell her what you wish! The two of you are no longer your mother’s daughters. Now go and roam as freely as these bullocks!’ Kusum spoke softly, ‘Kaki, why do you get angry? And why do you unjustly accuse Kumud based only on hearsay? We have not even spoken to her yet and we have no idea what she wants.’ Sundargauri: ‘What is there to be known? What Flora, you, Mohini and Chandravali say will be right, and your mother and I are false. What is left to be known? Neither your mother nor I are so childish as to not know what all of you are going to decide together. You have converted and become unbearable, and that one has become debauched and will remarry. You want to become an ascetic and dance around like Mirabai! That son of Saubhagya Devi was good; at least he caused his mother to die! Now our daughters—the light of our family—will reach Gunasundari to the crematorium. Kusum, we have been defeated. Now mothers will have to do what their daughters want! Now go and do whatever you like!’ Kusum: ‘Yes, I will go. You have all forsaken Kumudbehn, but I will be on her side. None of you ask her, daughter what happened? None of you tell her, daughter do not be afraid. Kaki, I am not worried about myself; even if you were to push me down the valley, Kusum is strong enough to survive. But Kumudbehn has been pushed into the fire, and you do not have one word of solace for her. Instead you brand her and wrongly accuse her. You are incapable of seeing what is just and what unjust. This Kusum will not tolerate.’

Sundargauri: ‘Go, my mother, go!’ Kusum: ‘I am going. But be warned. You are instigating my mother. My mother and my Kaki do not even have the patience to wait and hear Kumud’s side. All of you are going to repent.’ ‘The dark ages are upon us in full glory!’ Kusum heard Sundargauri say as she went out and sat on a chair facing the pathway. A tree- lined path restricted her field of vision. The green canopy of trees, the golden light filtering through it and making a lattice on the red earth path paved with stones soothed her anxious eyes and mind and allowed her to wait patiently. Every shadow, every slight movement alerted her. Kusum would get up every now and then, straining her eyes. Each time her imagination played tricks with her. All that came were some cows, goats, deer and dogs. Sometimes a small group of tribals or ascetics or pilgrims crossed her vision. But her eager eyes did not tire of waiting. Manchatura sat on a milestone, leaning against his stick. He inquired from every passerby about the group that followed them. At last, Manchatura saw Chandravali and Kumud. Kumud had worn an ochre kantha and walked steadily, hand-in-hand with Chandravali. There was not a trace of sorrow on her face. Her visage was tranquil and she appeared to be the embodiment of forbearance, equanimity and resolve. Her forehead was slightly creased. She looked tired but moved with vigour. She looked up and saw Manchatura in the distance. Kumud stopped, grew silent and signalled Chandravali to halt. ‘What happened, my daughter? Why have you stopped?’ Chandravali asked, concerned. Kumud: ‘There is someone who looks like my venerable grandfather.’ Chandravali: ‘That is him. He is the progenitor of your righteous father. You should venerate him. Social customs might force him to say a few harsh words, but you should move along just as the sweet waters of the Ganga pass through the Himalayan rocks.’ Kumud: ‘Just as the Supreme Man, Narayana, keeps watch over the world threatened by deluge, my old grandfather has come to keep watch over me.’

Manchatura approached them and, bending down to look at her, said, ‘My Kumud!’ ‘Yes, Dadaji! Are you well?’ Kumud wept. ‘I have caused all of you untold suffering.’ Manchatura caressed her back and head with his old, wrinkled hands and said, ‘Daughter, have no fear. It was I who saved you from the outlaws. Even if no one else stands by you, I will. But I cannot bear to see you as an ascetic!’ Manchatura’s old eyes filled with tears. Kumud wiped them and said, ‘Dadaji, this ochre kantha is preferable to a widow’s robes. And ascetics like Chandravalibehn have healed the wounds caused by our society. They have given me peace and tranquility. Please compose yourself. When I was young you cared for Gunial, and now you have to worry about me! I don’t like it. All of you have come such a great distance to meet me. If I did not meet you, I would be ungrateful. I have come to meet you all and seek your permission to live my life as an ascetic in this community. Please do not refuse me this.’ ‘Kumud beta, we shall do everything to make you happy. Your Dadaji would not be frightened even if the heavens were to fall. But a tear in your eyes makes my life turn to dust.’ They turned towards the tents. Kusum saw them from a distance and ran towards them like a gazelle. ‘Behn! You are here at last!’ She held Kumud in a tight embrace. Kumud held her close to her heart. Both sisters wept tears of joy. Kumud could contain her joy while Kusum’s joy leapt up to express itself. Manchatura saw the two sisters meet each other with love and joy. His heart though satiated remained thirsty for more. ‘Kusum, you are the only one that your sister has. It will be a test of your intelligence to persuade her out of this ochre kantha.’ Kusum released Kumud from her embrace, looked intently at her sister’s garb and turned her delicate, lotus stem-like neck towards her grandfather and said, ‘Dadaji, you are right; the two of us have to be there for each other now that even Gunial has turned her back to Kumud. But, I like these saffron clothes. May your blessings come true, Dadaji, even I will acquire the fitness to wear them and the two of us will live together. Dadaji, these saffron clothes are a sign of wisdom; forsaking them is not a sign of intelligence.’ All four of them joked and laughed. They were very close to the tents. Kusum said, ‘Dadaji, you counselled Gunial, but it all evaporated the moment you turned your back. Take Chandravali Maiya to Gunial so that she can tell her all that she wants to know. She will be able to cool the tempers of Kaki and Gunial. So that when they meet Kumud they do not burst in anger. If we take Kumudbehn to her now, Gunial would not be able to control her anger and all that is in her heart would come pouring out. Even if she does not show her anger, she will say things that she should not. She will neither speak to nor smile at Kumud. Kumudbehn has just emerged from deep pain, and she would not be able to bear it; her heart will break, and I will get into a fight with Gunial. We shall sit in this tent and talk. You call us when you can trust Gunial to retain her equipoise. We will come when we are done talking. Behn, do not be afraid; these days Gunial goes through these phases and then she calms herself down. We will go when she has quietened down and then we won’t give her the opportunity to get angry. Of course, we will do exactly what we like.’ Kumud turned to Chandravali and said, ‘Chandravalibehn, I feel that Kusum’s suggestion is right. There have been many rumours about me; my Gunial must be perturbed as to what she should believe and what she should not. For me to speak about all this to her is a violation of the customs and norms of our society. Your companionship has taught me to speak frankly without keeping anything concealed behind curtains. But if I were to do that here, it would only turn everything upside down. You and Dadaji go to Gunial and tell her all that you know about me. Her heart is as unsteady as a lamp in the wind. Give her some of your equanimity, and call me when she is ready. I am not afraid of meeting her straightaway, but I will not be able to bear that her love for me causes her so much pain. But she has a deep fondness for you; she will have faith in your words and your unshakable purity; and your kindness would assuage her hurt. ‘Dadaji, it is not necessary to tell you what Chandravalibehn means to me. Twice she has saved my life, and the third time she has pointed to me the path of fulfillment. For the sake of this poor Kumud, she endangered her body and suffered turbulence of mind. What more can I say? Chandravalibehn has etched into her heart all that has happened to me. Please read her heart. And you, Pitaji and Gunial together should decide justly what my duty should be. I do not ask for anything more. I cannot renounce the world more than once. I have attained equanimity and found peace in this community of ascetics. I have accepted this ochre kantha and I cannot abandon it now. Dadaji, now everyone should be free of worry on my account. You have one more responsibility, which you shall hear from Chandravalibehn. Please tell Gunial that Kumud is as meek as ever, but it is her duty to allow me to see her and be in her loving, pious presence. If she feels that I am undeserving of even this much, it would add one more to my ninety-nine misfortunes. Kumud has been counting the fruits of her misfortune, but she does not make a face while eating bitter fruits. Dadaji, this ascetic life will free me from another life of such misfortune. If I go back on my resolve to lead an ascetic life, I will be thrown into a well even in the next life. I do not want that; this is my firm resolve and forgive me for being so resolute. My words bring tears to your aged eyes! Do not let them flow. Dadaji, be happy that I am in a state of bliss.’ Manchatura wiped his tears and said, ‘Daughter, each word of yours pierces my heart. I cannot say anything.’ Manchatura sat down and wept his heart out. Kumud embraced him and wiped his tears. ‘Dadaji, do not love Kumud so much! Never before have you been so feeble in face of difficulty. Your daughter cannot bear to see your heart tremble.’ Manchatura calmed himself somewhat and stood up. ‘Don’t worry. Kumud, if you are determined to be an ascetic, I, too, will accept ochre robes and live among ascetics. I once had such a large family; now only you and Kusum are left. You have taken to a sadhvi’s attire. Who knows what Kusum shall do. Beta, all this talk is useless now. In a few moments or in a few days everything will be decided, and I will not be impatient now. We shall see how the two of you want me to end my life. If a child like you adopts ochre, so will I. I have a few years left. I shall live here, watch over you and die a good death.’ Kumud: ‘Dadaji, if you become a renouncer you shall be happy, and I will be happier if you live here among us. My decision is not because I am weary of the world. It is my heartfelt desire. Have no doubts about it.’ Manchatura: ‘No, daughter. I have no doubts any more.
