Kusum, you take Kumud to that tent and I shall take Chandravali to Gunial.’ Kumud: ‘Chandravalibehn, promise me that you shall not, like Mohini Maiya, attack Gunial with your words. She gave birth to me, and that is the cause of her suffering. I want to free her from all pain and become free from this debt myself.’ Chandravali: ‘Madhuri, you need not ask me for this promise, it is yours. Manchaturaji, we have named your sweet daughter Madhuri Maiya!’
chapters.summary: As Kumud returns, her family grapples with her steadfast decision to embrace an ascetic life, with Manchatura attempting to bridge the divide and offer support.

chapters.title: Daughter
paragraphs: Daughter Mother, why do you weep Tears in heaps? Manchatura, Gunasundari, Sundargauri and Chandravali sat talking in one tent, while Kumud and Kusum sat in another. Chandravali spoke in one tent and Kumud in the other. They spoke till noon. It was almost lunch time. Chandravali spoke at length about Kumud’s life from her time in Buddhidhan’s house till the morning of that day. Gunasundari felt some solace. She put her worries to rest as she realised that her daughter had not fallen into depravity. She was now concerned about Kumud’s future. They decided to worry about it after lunch. Kumud had not yet finished with her story. She was yet to show Kusum Sarasvatichandra’s account of their combined dreams when they were called for lunch. Kusum sent back a message: ‘All of you eat and send two plates for us.’ Sundargauri came to call them. Kusum came out of the tent and said, ‘Behn has not yet acquired the right to show her face to you. Kaki, send our plates here. We shall eat if we want to; otherwise there are many seeking alms on Sundargiri and they will eat. If Kumudbehn is depraved, Kusum is also depraved; if Kumud is given up for dead, Kusum is also dead! Kaki, I have nothing more to do with you.’ Sundargauri: ‘I have come to call both of you.’

Kusum: ‘It is useless to call anyone without purpose, and one should not go where one has no right to go.’ Sundargauri: ‘We are calling you and that is our right, and the purpose is to eat together.’ Kusum: ‘An invitation without honour and a nameless guest should both be kept at a distance.’ Sundargauri: ‘You will not bend. My Kumud will listen to me. Let me in.’ Kusum: ‘You can come in after we are gone. And don’t make this show of calling her “My Kumud.”’ Sundargauri pushed Kusum aside and entered the tent. Kumud came forward. They embraced and wept. Sundargauri held Kumud close to her heart. They sat down side by side. Kusum stood at some distance, not concealing her irritation. No one spoke for some time. Finally Sundargauri said, ‘Kumud, we have given you immense suffering, haven’t we?’ Kumud: ‘No, Kaki. I am very happy here among the ascetics. But I gave you all a cause of concern by coming out alive.’ Sundargauri: ‘Daughter, let us forget the past. Chandravali has half filled Bhabhi’s heart with nectar, and the rest is for the two of you to fill. No one will eat without you. If you want I will send your Gunial, but she has sent me here so please come with me.’ Kumud: ‘I had my meal with my ascetic companions. I have come to ascertain whether my being alive is a source of pain or pleasure for you.’ Sundargauri: ‘That we shall deal with later. Right now just come with me. Surely you are not as hard as Kusum.’ Kumud: ‘Whatever you wish. Behn, let us go.’ They went out. Gunasundari awaited them outside the tent. Kumud went up to her and touched her forehead to her mother’s feet, but could say nothing. Gunasundari lifted her up and said, ‘Get up, Kumud! Don’t be silly. Where there are elders like your grandfather to protect us from heat and rain, women like me should stop worrying about their daughters. You and I should fall at his feet.’ Kumud said in a broken voice, ‘Dadaji’s were the first feet that I touched.’ Gunasundari: ‘Once you have touched his feet, it is equal to having touched mine a thousand times. I must fall at his feet now. I had his shelter, and yet I could not control my heart. After all I am only a woman.’ Manchatura went close and said to Kumud, ‘Daughter, get up. As long as you stay at her feet, you are punishing Gunasundari.’ Kumud stood up. Her face was smeared with tears. Manchatura: ‘Kumud, Chandravali spoke to us of your suffering and of your virtues. Neither Gunial nor I have anything to say. Let us forget what has happened and think of the future. Let us eat together, and then you can tell Kusum what you have decided. Chandravali will eat with us. She is the one who gave you a new life; we shall not fail in our hospitality. Sundar, by that time you should go and call Chandrakant so that he can also join our deliberations.’
chapters.summary: Sundargauri and Gunasundari emotionally confront Kumud, hoping to persuade her to rejoin her family and leave her ascetic life behind after much suffering.

chapters.title: Ganga-Yamuna
paragraphs: Ganga-Yamuna Sister! He is enchanting. He is made only for you. ‘K umudbehn, so Sarasvatichandra left everything because he wanted to see the dark side of our society. And even you travelled with him to the nether regions!’ Kusum said as she paced excitedly around the tent, reading from a sheaf of papers in her hands. She came to a stop and said, ‘Here, take back his writings.’ ‘Yes, I did visit the nether regions with him. I brought these for you,’ Kumud replied from her chair. ‘Why give them to me? And what right do you have to do so?’ Kusum now sat down on a chair facing Kumud. Kumud: ‘I have thought a great deal about this. You have every right to have them. Keep them with you.’ Kusum: ‘Will you at least tell me what you have thought?’ Kumud: ‘This is what I have to say. I have travelled with him and I have seen the deepest, unmanifest aspirations of his heart. I have already told you that I have no right to make what is unmanifest manifest, give form to the formless. I do not have the capacity to be with him and help him fulfill his great desire for the upliftment of our society. Chandrakantbhai would testify to that. He would also testify that you have that capacity.’ Kusum: ‘Oh my God! You are cunning! My naïve sister speaks of this and that and the other and finally brings the ship to anchor at my port!’ Kusum got up, rolling her eyes in disbelief and making faces at her sister. Then she spoke in a firm and clear voice, ‘I understand your intent. But you shall be able to do nothing about it.’ Kumud: ‘Here is a poem composed by an ascetic. Please sing it for me.’ Kusum took the page and sang. The flute has touched my lips I hold the flute to my lips A hundred flutes touch my lips A hundred flutes I hold to my lips ‘Oh, this is just too long! I don’t want to sing it. What are you trying to tell me?’ Kumud: ‘That is the song of what lies in the heart when Krishna holds the flute to his lips and becomes manifest to the world. Kusum, you have seen what lies unmanifest in his heart. I cannot be his flute, and the thought breaks my heart.’ Kusum: ‘I accept that. If you had not experienced the life of a householder, you would not have suffered. An unattached person finds freedom, while love is the root of all trouble. Everyone pushed you into a householder’s life. Now the sign of wisdom is to take it to its conclusion. I have been warned by your example and I shall remain steadfast to the belief that non-commencement of something is a sign of wisdom. Now I will never, even by mistake, go that way.’ Kumud: ‘If my suffering could be eradicated by such sayings, I would have gone to the logical end. But by doing so, everything goes upside down. The desire and ability for this endeavour that this great soul has would be wasted like water on stone. I have only one right and that is to live like Chandravali and Viharpuri. Omnipotent Mahalakshmi takes the form of Jagdamba and plays the garba; during those nine nights that great soul will be like the moon in the sky, and poor Kumud will flower in the mud of a pond. That is the only right given to me by God. Sarasvatichandra will shine like the moon on the forehead of Maheshwara or Maheshwari, and poor Kumud will be placed at the feet of a god of her parent’s choice. Kumud can only hold his moonbeam in her heart. The Goddess comes out to play the garba With the moon on her forehead and lotus at her feet. ‘He would be the moon, and I the lotus. That is our destiny.’ Kusum: ‘Even if that is your destiny, what is wrong with it?’ Kumud: ‘If he remains hidden by the clouds of Sundargiri, Kumud would not be able to see the light of his prestige spread through the world. And if that does not happen, Kumud shall wither. Kusum, when the moon shines in a clear, cloudless sky, Kumud will be able to see him in full glory, and she too shall blossom.’ Kusum: ‘That is correct.’ Kumud: ‘Kusum, will you not be the wind that carries the clouds away? Will you not let Kumud blossom? Kusum, your Kumud has been sullied. I have become worthless and unworthy of offering. My fragrance has vanished. A flower once offered to a god cannot be offered to another. If that were to happen all the greatness of the great soul would come to nothing. Kusum, you are unsullied, faultless, an unsmelt flower. You can keep his greatness intact.’ Kusum went into deep thought. After a while she said, ‘Kumudbehn, none of this is possible. You have not been sullied in any way. Your hearts are one as gem and ring. I will be happy only if your hearts remain as one. And the society which is so blind as to see you as sullied does not deserve to be uplifted. What do you have to do with that society? That society does not deserve you and your work.’ Kumud: ‘Would my Kusum not be that flute which expresses the unmanifest song of that great soul? Will you not be the wind that carries away the clouds that separate me from my moon?’ Kusum: ‘You want for me that happiness which I do not aspire to. You are unhappy and you wish to remain so. I do not have the capacity to give happiness to Sarasvatichandra, and what is considered happiness among our people will not make me happy. I am very happy in my present state.’

Kumud: ‘Behn, are you not selfish?’ Kusum: ‘If remaining unattached is being selfish, I like being selfish.’ Kumud: ‘The freedom that is so dear to you will be ensured by that great soul.’ Kusum: ‘That is good enough to persuade a child.’ Kumud: ‘Despite our togetherness, he left me untouched and pure. Do you believe he would ever violate your freedom?’ Kusum: ‘Such situations are best avoided.’ Kumud: ‘One who has made it possible for me to have an unsullied relationship with him as pure as that of the moon and the lotus, or Chandravali and Viharpuri, would violate you? Don’t you believe that he would never permit a situation that may endanger your resolve?’ Kusum: ‘He might be virtuous. But does that make him capable of such resolve?’ Kumud: ‘I speak from experience. He is a great renouncer.’ Kusum: ‘Kaki told me that men do not have as much control over their passions as we women do. Men may praise themselves, but that is beside the point.’ Kumud: ‘Kaki has spoken the truth. Generally women are shorter than men, but we find some women who are taller than men. Similarly, there are renouncers among men as well.’ Kusum: ‘Behn, you have remained unsullied and pure because of your own resolve. But the love that is in your heart does not allow you to speak in self-praise.’ Kumud: ‘I have told you the truth and I shall repeat it again. I had become like that bottle of perfume ready to spill out. That able renouncer held me firm, and my purity remained unsullied. A person who gave up such wealth, me and the charms of Bombay can walk over the coals of lust without being singed by them. Do you find this surprising?’ Kusum: ‘It is not surprising. I only shared with you what the experienced have told me.’

Kumud: ‘I know his aspirations; I know the endeavour that he wishes to undertake. His wealth falls short of his needs and hence he does not want sons, which also I know. He does not wish to start a married life with me, but he will accept me as part of his penance. I have told you that.’ Kusum: ‘That might be so. But I am tired of this. Let’s talk about something else.’ Kumud: ‘Your tiredness shows that you are not willing to remedy my pain. Why should we talk of anything else? Kusum, our meeting must end here. Kumud shall live in the Parivrajika Math till she wilts. You have dashed my last hope. I had hoped to bring fulfillment to a great soul. But now one who renounced society, love and Bombay will not be able to commence his noble endeavour for the lack of an appropriate partner and co-sharer. He will have to take that as God’s will and live as an ascetic on Sundargiri. That flower shall wither and end its life in dust. Neither he nor I have any other path available to us.’ Kusum: ‘If I act according to your wish, where would you spend your life?’ Kumud: ‘My father-in-law, grieved by my pain and the loss of Devi, is intent on becoming a renouncer. I shall go to him and give him solace. Alakbehn is unlettered, but she is as sharp and affectionate as you. I will spend time with her. Devi has left behind an infant son. I will raise him to be a learned and virtuous man, and that will be my shraddha of your brother-in-law. I will spend time in Suvarnapur and spread among the people of the state the message of your combined endeavour. My father-in-law will provide me with money and state support. Every year I shall spend some time with Gunial, you, Chandravali and Mohini Maiya and will invite both of you and the others to Suvarnapur if possible. I will spend my time reading and in contemplation of the divine. My life would find fulfillment through your and my Chandra’s sacrificial endeavour. I would be happy in your happiness. I wish to see Gunial, Pitaji and my father-in-law happy. What more does Kumud need to fulfill her life?’

Kusum: ‘You told me that according to the ascetics your previous loveless marriage was false and immoral. What about the fact that now you want me to be in a loveless marriage?’ Kumud: ‘It is not as if the seeds of love are entirely absent in you.’ Kusum: ‘That’s not true! That is absolutely not true!’ Kumud: ‘Chandrakantbhai has spoken to Sarasvatichandra about you. I know that when he came to Ratnanagari, you had felt a childlike infatuation for him. During this period God has nourished it, and the seed has sprouted. When I bring the two of you together, the sprouted seed shall become capable of flowering.’ Kusum: ‘What does Chandrakantbhai know of my heart? Everyone blamed Sarasvatichandra, and hence I took his side. Kaki and the others chose to interpret it in ways that they liked. All that is futile.’ Kumud: ‘An unselfish defence is the first sign of love, say the ascetics. Do you deny that your heart leaps up in his defence? Our people get small children engaged to each other, but they provide no opportunity till the time of marriage to cultivate such feelings. Our society has become caught in the mire and does not understand these things. The Lord of Love works through such associations, and when they mature marriage becomes meaningful. This is what the serpents of my dream world told me. Such instances and associations matured our love. Such association has also sown the seeds of love in you, and they must take root.’ Kusum: ‘This is all knowledge from your new scriptures. But there is not a trace of love in me. And even you would have to admit that love for me is impossible for him. Kumudbehn, why do you make these futile attempts?’ Kumud: ‘You wrote in your letter that you have the right to say that the taught has become the teacher. That is what is meant by: ‘‘Dekh Machhendra Gorakh aaya.”’ Kusum shrugged her shoulders and made a face. ‘Okay, so what if I said that? These ascetics have taught you to twist meanings!’

Kumud: ‘I have learnt this from the ascetics. If you think it is misleading, why join them? Go where I point you to.’ Kusum: ‘Shall we close this chapter?’ Kumud: ‘If you close this chapter, close our association as well. Or else both have to go together.’ Kusum: ‘All right. If you, Pitaji, Gunial and Sarasvatichandra all agree on this, I will do as you ask. But even if one of them differs, I shall do what I like. How about that?’ Kumud: ‘That is enough for me.’ Kusum: ‘Watch out! You are about to be cheated. All four of them will never agree. And if they do not, do you give an undertaking that you shall abide by my decision? No, all five; Dadaji’s opinion must also be counted, but not Kaki’s.’ Kumud: ‘I give an undertaking, and so should you.’ Kusum: ‘You are giving a promise. Be careful.’ Kumud: ‘Yes, I give my promise. But you must promise as well.’ Kusum: ‘Neither will I be bound, nor will you. Both of us shall remain free.’ Kumud: ‘You have bound me to a promise. Do you think you can escape?’ Kusum sighed. ‘After all, I too am bound, isn’t it?’ Kumud: ‘Why are you so dejected? Both of us are bound by our promise.’ Kusum: ‘This is not good.’ Kumud went up to Kusum, put an arm around her shoulders and led her out of the tent. ‘Kusum, do you see those rose plants in the hedge?’ Kusum: ‘Yes.’ Kumud: ‘When there is a gust of wind, the dust rises; these roses bound to thorny stems tremble but remain affixed. Which of the two lives is better?’

Kusum: ‘Today, I am unable to think. The wheel has turned towards me and in this quandary I like neither the dust nor the roses.’ Kumud: ‘This dust is free, but the roses which give pleasure to people are bound to thorny bushes!’ Kusum did not reply. Kumud: ‘Most people run after the happiness of such independence, but they get caught in such whirlwinds.’ Kusum: ‘That is true.’ Kumud: ‘The wiser among them crave not for happiness but independence and the wisest consider freedom to be an unbridled play of senses. For them freedom means the freedom of the skies and hence they seek neither asceticism nor renunciation.’ Kusum: ‘That is what I want.’ Kumud: ‘But there are also those beings who wish to fulfill their lives and remain steadfast amidst all troubles like the roses in the thorny bush. They live like a lotus. A lotus grows in water, but like mercury it remains unperturbed by all the turbulence and it makes the water fragrant and attractive. It is not poisonous like mercury but it cultivates the qualities of mercury. Kusum, Sarasvatichandra has no aspirations for unbridled freedom, but he wants to remain untouched and unperturbed by turbulence and engage himself with the welfare of our people. This is the only way by which one could be free and do one’s duties towards others. You want the freedom of an ascetic, while I want you to be like Sarasvatichandra, to be like the lotus and the rose. You have after some consideration agreed to abide by a consensus opinion. Why are you perturbed now? Do tell me, what will you do with your freedom? How will you spend the long life that is ahead of you?’ Kusum: ‘I will read good books, learn more and retain my equanimity.’ Kumud: ‘Would you be satisfied with a selfish life without any engagement with the welfare of others? How will others benefit from your reading and knowledge? What would happen if all the rain-laden clouds were to disperse? Are you not about to waste such a beautiful life? Kusum, from this mountain we can see the place where river Subhadra meets with the sea. Do look.’ Kusum looked in that direction but gave no response. Kumud: ‘Subhadra is filled with sweet water. Only the areas around her bank benefit from her; there is no other way it can be. But her forceful waters meet the sea and merge with it, but they cannot turn it sweet. Her waters turn saline and they cease to exist, while the sea waves continue. But in that lies their non-dualism. Subhadra contributes according to her capacity to the waters of the sea; she adds to the sea, bringing along with her many known and unknown objects. Why does she do that? If you want to understand this, please spend four days at the temple built by Chandravali. Subhadra puts all her gems and pearls into the bottom of the sea—that is what makes the sea a ratnakar. Ships sail across the sea, linking the earth. The waters of the seas shower on all earth as rain, giving life to all living things. Kusum, what would you achieve by remaining single? One thin, solitary stream of water turns to mud, gets trampled under people’s feet and evaporates in the heat of the sun. That is what will happen to your life. It is not an insignificant thing to become the Subhadra of the oceanic heart of this great soul, whose deepest aspirations you know, whose dream world you have glimpsed. You would be his Ganga, Brahmaputra and Sindhu. And no one in the three worlds has this capacity other than you. Kusum, do you not aspire to such a pious, fulfilling life? It is impossible for Kumud to do so. But if you become his Ganga, Kumud will be your Yamuna. If you resist being a Ganga, you and Kumud will both be reduced to a trickle. But if we become Ganga-Yamuna to this Ratnakar, Gunial’s sea of joy shall brim over. Today, both of us have been the cause of her heartbreak. But then we would be the support on which her golden heart could rest. Pitaji has shown willingness to sacrifice his all; we shall be the source of his pride and honour. Laxminandan in his old age will shower blessings on us. You have nothing but good wishes for my father-in-law; we will be the saviours of his family. And we shall be the means of numerous such good deeds; whether you consider them small or big they remain good deeds. And Kusum, we may not take into account all these outcomes, but my hopes and the hopes of this ascetic community rest upon the fulfillment of that great soul’s life—a hope which has also given him a reason to live. Only Kusum can either make his dream world come true or let it shatter. ‘But if you fail to do this and lead a life of unencumbered independence, become like this dust, we—you and I—shall become examples of girls whose parents gave them unrestrained freedom, but who brought nothing but dishonour to their parents. Our example shall be held up to all those girls who want knowledge and freedom. We shall exemplify cruel, uncaring daughters. We shall be the ladder through which the misfortunes of countless young girls shall descend over them. And of course, Kumud’s fate would be to witness, all alone, the ruins of the dream world of this great soul. I do not have the strength to go on. Kusum, you can drown us or carry us across to safety; you can give us life or death. So long as you do not accept him with all your Ganga-like heart, he will not accept my plea. I will never deceive him. If you do not accept him, that swan shall never take flight. Kumud will not be able to see him starve on this earth. I have said all that I wished to. Now Kusum, tell me what is in your heart so I can decide if I must go away forever, or be with you in eternal gratitude. I have not coerced you. I shall not do so. You have agreed to act upon a consensus, and I know that you will be true to your word. And still if there is an iota of discomfort in your heart, your life shall go to waste and I shall not be able to bear witness to it. Therefore, my attempt has been to counsel you, to make your heart accept this. Only then will I take the text step. If you find this distasteful in any corner of your heart, I would prefer to be unhappy rather than see my Kusum unhappy. So tell me, what is in your heart? Tell me, what would secure your happiness? I do not wish to commence the endeavour of securing others’ happiness upon the cornerstone of your grief. I have decided for myself that if I fail to persuade you, I shall spend my life in the Parivrajika Math in a way that brings no dishonour to our parents and assist the great soul from a distance. I will be like the moon that revolves around the earth without ever touching it. Kusum, tell me what is the best way of ensuring your happiness? Kumud was born unhappy, lived unhappily and shall die in sorrow. But you, Kusum, are a fish of a sweet-water lake; I shall not throw you into salty waters. Tell me with a smile, and do not worry about my laughter or tears, as to what you desire. Free me from this agony. I shall not ask you ever again. Please forgive me for saying and asking for so much.’ Kusum: ‘Behn, every word spoken by you is truthful and comes from your experience. I trust you fully; you have nothing but my interest in your heart. I can also see that the path suggested by you shall secure the welfare of all concerned. The only problem is that I do not know what my heart truly desires. A doctor takes our pulse and makes a diagnosis of our ailment. All of you together shall diagnose my heart and suggest a remedy. And that remedy will do me good; I am convinced of this. Just as I do not know what lies within my body, I do not know the pulse of my heart. Find me a doctor or become my healer. I can fathom nothing.’ Kumud: ‘Such examination of subtle instincts is natural to the ascetics of Sundargiri. I shall consult them.’ Both the sisters came out arm in arm and spoke for a long time. The sun had begun to set. Kumud looked in the direction of the path that had brought her to this place. They stopped talking and their eyes absorbed the fading glory of the sun’s last rays. They heard a rustle of feet from inside the tent. They went in to find Chandravali.
chapters.summary: Kumud earnestly persuades Kusum to consider a future with Sarasvatichandra, believing her sister is destined to fulfill his noble aspirations.

chapters.title: Return to Source
paragraphs: Return to Source What am I to quote, where quotation itself is staggered at my situation?   —Anonymous Sarasvatichandra and Chandrakant spent the day in a grass hut provided for them. That day they received many letters including from Bulwer Sahib, Laxminandan, Haridas, Uddhatlal and Tarang Shankar among others. Sarasvatichandra’s identity had become common knowledge among his friends, and all of them were on their way to Sundargiri. Both friends spent the day talking about Bombay and Ratnanagari. At dusk they decided to go out for a walk when there was a knock on their door. An ascetic came and lighted the lamps. Chandravali followed soon after. They stood up to greet her. Chandravali gave an account of all her conversations with Gunasundari and Kumud’s deliberations with Kusum. In conclusion she said, ‘Oh virtuous one, both sisters, with complete freedom, selfless intent and utter pragmatism, have come to the decision that Madhuri Maiya—known as Kumud Sundari in the outside world—shall lead an ascetic’s life, and they have requested you to accept Kusumbehn’s love with all the compassion that you are capable of. Kusum, like Ganga, shall merge with your oceanic self, and Kumud shall be her Yamuna. This is for the good of all. I have examined the hearts of both sisters and have arrived at the conclusion that the welfare of all concerned can be best secured by the remedy suggested by them. This is also the moral and the righteous path. Tell me, what is your command?’

Chandrakant spoke up joyously, ‘Friend, if you wish to retain this kantha, even Kusum Sundari will adopt it. You will be able to realise your dream world and the aspirations of others. Sheth Laxminandan will be here tomorrow. If you accept this request of these two virtuous, learned and cultured women, it would give joy to all hearts, except maybe yours. And the sacrificial fire that you wish to light shall burn bright. If your heart desires to turn down this request, then please offer your aspirations as oblation to that fire. You and Kumud Sundari had initially given the responsibility to me and had asked me to be your judge. Now I command you to accept this proposal. You had agreed to abide by the wishes of the two sisters. Their wish has also been expressed. Someone like Chandravali Maiya testifies to the fact that this is their heartfelt desire and not a false expression. There is no question of asking for your heart’s consent; you are required only to give your verbal consent. This is also the wish of the Master. He told you at the time of initiation that you should forsake ego and prestige. He also told you to forsake, if necessary, this symbolic kantha. Do not commit the misdeed of turning away a seeker like Chandravali Maiya empty-handed!’ Chandravali: ‘Oh virtuous one, I have also obtained the opinions of Jnanbharati and Viharpuri in this matter. They are Guruji’s favourite disciples and have attained superior capabilities. Both of them have given their approval to this proposal. Guruji has narrated to them the divine dream of the immortals that you had. They consider Madhuri Maiya’s aspirations most noble. They want you to accept her sister and give solace to your grieving father. Not just that, they consider this duty a means of performing your sacrifice and want you to acquire more material for your sacrifice. They have sent a message that your sacrifice shall spread joy through the world and enrich our small monastic community as well.’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Maiya, the blessings of those two great souls have always been with me.’ Chandravali: ‘Oh noble one, that day I had described to you the glory of noble aspirations. The time for their realisation has come. Jnanbharati, the head of Vihar Math, has said, ‘‘You are your own fulfillment. Your virtues shine with such light and your glory is so dazzling that it turns to ashes all that is inauspicious.’’ And Viharpuri has said, ‘‘How your horse runs! It renders the wind stagnant, turns the skies into a bowl made of a leaf, it turns rivers into small threads and the oceans into a pond. It turns forests into the branch of a tree, the earth itself becomes small like a clay pot, and it renders mountains into mustard seeds. It crosses the three worlds in one stride. By way of play your horse has acquired such speed; how is anyone to describe your horse in words?’’ O’ great soul! The minister’s father and his wife await your word. What message shall I carry to them?’ Sarasvatichandra: ‘Maiya, please tell them that I am an ascetic who wears a kantha. I am bound by my pledge to give up all my present and future wealth for the welfare of our people. And if the fate of Ratnanagari’s wealthy minister’s daughter were to be joined to mine, she would have to give up her palatial pleasure garden and live in this grass hut, which shall be unbearable! The minister’s elder daughter has suffered great misfortune due to my heartless ways. The example of one daughter is already before them. Hence they have much to think of and consider before they decide to entrust to me another daughter. All the elders must consider this carefully. And even after all considerations, if Kumud Sundari’s heartfelt instruction and Kusum Sundari’s heartfelt desire were to become one, then I shall not deviate from the teachings of our Master.’ Chandravali: ‘What an appropriate message! O’ noble one, my blessings are with you. Now, I must leave.’ They all got up. Sarasvatichandra bowed to Chandravali and said, ‘Chandravali Maiya, you are the embodiment of noble aspirations and duty. I stand before you as a devotee. Do not bring upon me the misfortune that either of these two lamps should be snuffed out by my uncivilised breath.’ ‘So be it,’ blessed Chandravali and left them. Chandrakant was stunned by all that he had just seen and heard. ‘Sarasvatichandra, there is no scope for discussion or deliberation. It is almost night and we cannot go out. Now we must have these fruits and find restful sleep.’ The two friends spent the night without exchanging another word. Chandrakant slept a sound, dreamless sleep. Sarasvatichandra’s sleep was far from restful. He got up many times and found sleep again. Once during the night, he wept and muttered in his sleep, ‘Man is hard as vajra, but a woman’s compassion is limitless. Kumud Sundari, what made you decide to give up what you had considered your duty as a true wife and adopt those prescribed by the ascetics? Out of immeasurable love for me and your inability to bear witness to my condition! You were prepared to go against the wishes of your pious parents. You were prepared to dislodge the images of Saubhagya Devi and Buddhidhan from your heart. You were ready to face ignominy and dishonour. What for? Now you have taken this pledge to lead the life of a widow and an ascetic? What for? You shared my dream world and your heart grieved for our people. You could not see the orphaned state of my dream world. You were moved by your parents’ generosity. You could fathom the real reason for Kusum’s desire to remain unmarried. This is your subtle, spiritual love! This is your compassion, delicacy and pity! Your compassion became the messenger between Kusum and me. You brought our hearts together. Kumud, you are the embodiment of perfect womanhood. Kumud Sundari, only you have understood the meaning of womanhood!’ The night passed and a new day came. Sarasvatichandra was told that Laxminandan and Guman would reach Sundargiri by ten that morning. Before them, Haridas arrived. He met ‘Bhai’ and requested him to remove his kantha and wear the clothes of a householder. Sarasvatichandra looked to Chandrakant for advice. Chandrakant smiled and said, ‘Bhai, Guruji has taught you to give up even the prestige associated with asceticism. Your kantha and these rich clothes and headgear are one and the same. This is the cure for your father’s madness. Accept Haridas’ suggestion and change your clothes.’ Sarasvatichandra removed his ochre robes and wore the clothes that Haridas had brought for him. He said to Haridas, ‘While I am with my father, I shall wear these clothes. At all other times, I shall wear the kantha. Keep this kantha safely as you would a precious jewel, and give it to me whenever I ask for it.’ They went out to receive the Sheth. Father, mother and son embraced on the way, wept and spoke their heart. They went to the tent made for Sheth. Groups of ascetics came out to see this transformation of Sarasvatichandra. Joyous shouts hailing ‘Alakh!’, ‘Yadunandan!’, ‘Vishnudasji!’ and ‘Navinchandra!’ could be heard from all sides. Vidya Chatura arrived two days later followed by Buddhidhan. In another two days all the invited and uninvited guests from Bombay reached Sundargiri. The Karna Bhavan of Maharaj Maniraj and Vidya Chatura erected a tent village in Sundargiri. About fifty witnesses were examined by Jnanbharati and Shankar Sharma, and Sarasvatichandra’s identity was established by due process of law. The following day all the people were divided into two marriage parties and Sarasvatichandra and Kusum were married in accordance with the rituals of the ascetic community. All other rituals according to the wishes of their parents were performed. The groom and bride wore kantha and touched Vishnudasji’s feet. Sheth Laxminandan placed a sum of twenty-thousand rupees at the feet of Yadunandan. Vishnudasji decided to spend half of that sum for the temples of Surgram. Buddhidhan made a gift of Pramaddhan’s share to Kusum. Kumud gave her share of the money received from her father-in-law to her sister. Gunasundari and Sundargauri wept while bidding Kusum farewell. Vidya Chatura watched everything in silence. He had purchased the ring from Aarthdas, who had been declared innocent. He put it on Kusum’s finger and tried to divert attention away from his tears. Guman went mad with happiness at the new daughter-in- law. The groom’s party spent some days on Sundargiri. Maharaj Maniraj had sent his gold-embroidered tent for the newlyweds. After Dhananandan’s death Sarasvatichandra was Sheth Laxminandan’s only heir. The Sheth made a ‘trust deed’ and left all his wealth to his first-born. Sarasvatichandra kept aside a small sum for his parents and made plans to use the rest of the money for the realisation of his dream world. Kumud, Kusum and all his friends participated in this planning. Finally, they left for Ratnanagari. When they left Ratnanagari the scene was heart-wrenching. Kusum’s heart was with Kumud. Kumud sat in their chariot and accompanied them for part of the way. Sarasvatichandra remained silent as the two sisters talked. Eventually, Kumud had to turn back. She got down from the chariot and said in a broken voice, ‘Kusum, do not worry. I will come often. We have handed you this gem of the world. Care for him as you would for your life. You have all the capabilities to nurture this good fortune. Enhance your capacity with time!’ They embraced each other and wept. Kumud touched Sarasvatichandra’s feet and said, ‘O’ great soul! I have bound you to the life of a householder—forgive me for this act. You have become the ocean for my Ganga and together may you fulfill your dream world! I shall be the Yamuna to my Ganga. You are knowledgeable, virtuous and adept at performance of duties. You are imbued with love. Open the heart of this gifted but naïve woman with care. What more can I say? I have made our dreams the dreams of my sister. I, a widow, have stopped seeking my fate and opened all doors for this divine virgin. On the fourth morning of our togetherness I had placed my hand on your forehead; at that time you felt that it was your mother’s hand. Now, I have become the mother of your dreams. The dreams we saw together would allow me to be a mother to you and Kusum and shall remain forever present in my heart! Your union shall be beautiful and auspicious. Our society shall be enriched by it. This hope shall be the fulfillment of all my pain and penance. You and Kusum have made this sacrifice for me. If I were to ask for anything more, it would be a sign of greed.’ Kusum stood still, a picture of equanimity. Sarasvatichandra was bathed in his own tears. His voice choked with emotion, ‘Kumud Sundari! I sinned and pushed you into unbearable suffering. In turn you sacrificed your love. You opened the doors for the realisation of my dream world. I stand at its threshold like a cruel, stone-hearted demon! O’ mother! You have performed a mother’s duty, and as your depraved son I seek your permission to touch your feet. A son can be depraved, but not a mother. You forgave me as a mother. Your virtues helped me retain my equanimity and virtue. I pushed you cruelly into suffering and in return, you gave happiness magnified a hundred fold. You have the wisdom of your mother and the compassion of Saubhagya Devi. You embody their generosity and forgiveness. These qualities were nurtured by Chandravali, only to be showered on someone as undeserving as me. O’ mother! O’ Mother India! Allow my unworthy head to touch your pure, blessed feet!’ Sarasvatichandra, having lost the capacity for any more words, fell at her feet. Kumud raised him up. ‘Sarasvatichandra, the ways of God are miraculous. He gives us many lives in one. You and I have experienced that. In each life you called me yours, and I became yours. I have called you my own and I shall remain so. Our hearts are one as before. My life, my heart, my Kusum is the embodiment of that love. Keep her in your heart. Kusum, you will each day worship this great soul in your heart. At each such moment, think of your absent sister.’ The sisters embraced. ‘Kumudbehn, you must come to Bombay! Now I am going to be away from Gunial, Pitaji and you.’ ‘Kusum, you shall reside in the heart of this great soul. You shall be his partner in sacrifice. Mother, father, I and all others are in him. Do not crave for anyone else and do not neglect your service to him. He is your divine strength and he shall consider you to be the same. Do not consider him to be distinct from you and every time you perform his aarti, let Kumud ring through your heart.’
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra faces an emotional dilemma as Kumud and Kusum present a profound proposal, prompting him to reconsider his ascetic vows and embrace a new path.

chapters.title: Aarti
paragraphs: Aarti The flute plays, it plays sublime! And I awaken to its beauty. The Lord of the Universe dances, He makes the world dance with Him To the rhythms of spring I long to watch the Ras, I long to play the Ras, I long to dance the Ras, With my Lord. Dear reader, after a long journey we return to Bombay. One year passed since Sarasvatichandra brought Kusum to Bombay. Gunasundari wrote regularly to them. Her letters showed that Kusum’s happiness and Kumud’s equanimity had filled her cup of joy. Gunasundari spent her days in delight and in the acquisition of knowledge. All day long Sundargauri spoke to her about the joys of her niece; that was the only work and distraction for Gunasundari. Vidya Chatura was engrossed in his administration and could not write as often. But every time he wrote, he enquired about the welfare activities of his daughter and son-in-law and also shared his experience with them. Sundargauri and Kusum’s banter continued through letters. Kusum read out these letters to Sarasvatichandra and shared her pleasure with him. Kusum wrote to her mother and sister as to how her learning, arts and aspirations had grown by her association with

Sarasvatichandra, the scholars, ascetics and the ‘madams’ who came to visit them. Buddhidhan and Narbheram had witnessed the scenes on Sundargiri. They admitted to each other that if Pramaddhan had been restrained in time, as was suggested by Vidya Chatura, the result would have been more auspicious. Vidya Chatura on the other hand felt that if he had been more farsighted, Pramaddhan could have lived a reformed life and Kumud could have been happy. On his return to Suvarnapur, Buddhidhan gave up the idea of renunciation. Kumud and Alak Kishori ensured that he was free to devote all his time to the administration of the state. Together they raised Saubhagya Devi’s infant son and planned his future. Kumud read Sanskrit and English books, including those which dealt with love and romance. She taught the women who flocked to her. She spent time with Gunasundari and also at Sundargiri and at Chandravali’s abode. This was the place which had given her and Sarasvatichandra noble aspirations. She learnt new ideas from the ascetics. At times, Alak Kishori also accompanied her on these journeys. It was almost a year since she had last met Kusum at Sundargiri. Kusum wrote to her often and insisted that she visit them in Bombay. Every two or three days Sarasvatichandra and Kusum wrote to her about Kalyangram. They repeatedly asked her to come and see for herself what had been described in their letters. She also aspired to be the Yamuna that she had promised to be. Alak was also invited to Bombay. Kumud decided to visit them and obtained her father-in-law’s consent to go. Alak wanted to tease Sarasvatichandra for having stayed in her house under an assumed identity. In Bombay Sarasvatichandra’s plan for Kalyangram had been discussed threadbare. Both father and son had signed the ‘trust deed.’ They were looking for a place on the sea coast away from Bombay to establish Kalyangram. A large stone palace in the Fort area was obtained for Sarasvatichandra’s ‘office’. This building also housed Laxminandan’s ‘mill’ office as also the offices of his other businesses. There was also an ‘office’ for the meetings of scholars and patriots from across the world. These offices were called Surya Yantra Kaksha, Vyapar Kaksha and Samaj Kaksha. The palace was named Lakshmi-

Sarasvati Vilas Mandir. Laxminandan’s bust was placed on the gate of the stone palace. On the first floor a special office was made for the ‘architects’ of Kalyangram where expert architects made and unmade plans. Most people called this the Engineering Office. A room adjacent to it was assigned for making plans for the inhabitants of Kalyangram. Businessmen and scholars from across the world joined these deliberations. Right behind these two rooms was a large office, which had two chambers, meant for Sarasvatichandra. From one chamber, he kept watch over the deliberations of other rooms and carried on a learned correspondence with Vishnudasji through the medium of Jnanbharati and Viharpuri. Kusum used the other chamber to receive women visitors. These two rooms opened out to the sea and had an unobstructed view of the sea face. Guman visited the office frequently and understood the plans from Kusum. Every time Laxminandan came to visit, he went through every office and chamber. His main task was to keep an eye over the balance sheet of his son’s great endeavour, and he was grateful that he could participate. The cost estimates were not fully drawn up, but they had an interest of two–three lakhs on assets of some ten–fifteen lakhs. Moreover, they had five lakhs which did not earn any interest and required to be invested. Over and above this they had Sarasvatichandra’s personal wealth and money that Kusum had received. Maharaj Maniraj’s Karna Bhavan had also committed a grant. As per the initial plans made by Sarasvatichandra and Kumud, Uddhatlal had agreed to travel to England and America to learn their business practices. Tarang Shankar and Vir Rao, along with their families, had consented to live in Kalyangram. Chandrakant had given up his legal practice and had become the administrative secretary of Kalyangram. He and his wife Ganga had promised to live in Kalyangram. All the scholars, artists and businessmen who had benefited from Sarasvatichandra’s generosity had come together to support his dream. Sheth Laxminandan owned bungalows outside the Fort area in Walkeshwar and in Mahalaxmi. Whenever Kusum visited these bungalows she gathered women from the neighbourhood and excited them about learning, arts and pleasures. The Walkeshwar bungalow was meant for Sarasvatichandra. Guman spent all her time in planning its decoration. She constantly worried about what Bhai would need and what would please Kusum, and she went from gardener to jeweller and cloth merchant to furnishing merchant. She visited the homes of native noble women, Parsi ‘Banus’ and English ‘Madams’, took notes, made inquiries and made new changes every day. Guman was no longer a jealous stepmother. She was absolutely delighted with her daughter- in-law and happily preoccupied decorating both Kusum and her home. Two English madams were hired as tutors for Kusum to learn various European arts. Kusum’s arrival in their home proved most auspicious for Laxminandan. His joys multiplied and industriousness, happiness and tranquility reigned over the household. Haridas felt that all his hard work and service had finally borne fruit. Amidst all this joy, Laxminandan had one source of deep sadness. Sarasvatichandra often stood before Kumud’s portrait in his ochre kantha and shed silent tears. He also wore his kantha around Kusum and had got one made for her as well. They had a portrait of Kumud done in her ochre kantha, and both of them would stand before her image in their ascetic robes. Some servants had whispered to the Sheth that once they had seen them both kneeling like Padrees before Kumud’s portrait and speaking with folded hands. Laxminandan hoped for a grandson, and these developments were a cause of concern. He was unhappy that his son and daughter-in-law aspired to emulate Viharpuri and Chandravali. Guman also spoke to Kusum, counselled her and sought to excite her youthful imagination and her woman’s heart. Finally, it was the first anniversary of their wedding. Guman organised a Satyanarayan Puja and Katha at the Walkeshwar bungalow. She invited all their friends and staff. English, Parsi and Muslim friends and associates were invited to a ‘party’ where the ‘piano’ was played. Kumud and her companions had gone to Nasik for pilgrimage and were expected to arrive that day. Haridas had accompanied Kusum to the ‘station’ to receive them. When Kusum and Haridas returned with

Kumud, Alak Kishori and others, at a signal from Guman, a ‘band’ began to play in their honour. For Kusum, the whole world seemed to recede and no one existed except for Kumud; she was engrossed in talking to her sister. When the ‘band’ began to play, Sarasvatichandra was deep in conversation with a great scholar from Kashi. He sought his permission and got up to receive Kumud. He followed Kumud and Kusum, watching them from a distance. He chatted with Alak Kishori and played with Saubhagya Devi’s son. Dry fruits, sweets, katha, song and ‘scent’ provided enough entertainment till late into the night. Most of the guests had left, but the women folk of the house were still engrossed in the Satyanarayan Katha. Sarasvatichandra went up to the top floor and lay down in an easy chair. He felt tired after the long day. The windows of the room were open. The cool sea breeze brought along with it sleep. He slipped into a dream where he was seated on the bed, and Kusum stood facing him. He said, ‘Kusum, our country sleeps on the floor, it has not enough clothes to wear or enough food to eat. How can we sleep on this bed, wear such clothes and eat sweets?’ In his dream the bed turned into a stone platform and they both wore kantha. The dream ended there. At the conclusion of the Satyanarayan Katha, the aarti, placed in a large silver tray, was taken around. Everyone present bowed to the sacred light. Guman sent Kusum up with the aarti to Sarasvatichandra. Sarasvatichandra was still fast asleep in the chair. Kusum stood before him with the aarti. The light of the earthen lamp illuminated his sleeping face, and Kusum stood gazing at him, enchanted. Unknown to herself she smiled at the sight of the beloved’s face. The aarti meant for God became in her hands veneration of her husband, who had come to occupy the place of the divine beloved. She held the plate to his face and murmured, Vraj is dear to me! I do not want Vaikunth, For where would I find my Nand Kunwar there? Downstairs, many still awaited the benediction of the aarti. When some time passed, Guman came up looking for Kusum. She saw them both from a distance, and her heart filled with joy. She ran to Sheth to share her joy, but he was busy with other guests and so she murmured this good news in his ears. Kumud also came up searching for her Kusum. Believing her to be alone, Kumud stood at the open door of the room. Seeing before her eyes the fruits of her sacrifice, she remained transfixed at the door. Kusum still gazed in silent delight at her husband’s radiant visage. Her heart swelled with pride and admiration at what he had accomplished, testified by the presence of scores of friends and staff. Suddenly, gripped by emotion, she began to perform his aarti. She softly sang, Wake up, O’ kantha dhari, wake up! She addressed him as Sri Krishna. Because of Your birth, Vraj is more, even more glorious and Lakshmi resides there eternally. Show Yourself, oh beloved, You sustain the life breath Of those who seek You.⟨fn:538⟩ Kusum could no longer restrain herself. She kept the silver tray aside and moved towards her husband, eager and anxious. She bent over his face and was about to place her lips on his lotus petal lips when she sensed his eyes open, and heard a voice from behind that startled her. The sight of this joyful dream made Kumud forget her sense of limits. Unconcerned, she laughed a gentle laugh as tears of supreme bliss filled her eyes. As she was leaving, her lips formed words and she murmured, ‘My silly little Kusum!’
chapters.summary: Performing aarti for a sleeping Sarasvatichandra, Kusum leans in for a tender kiss, startled by his awakening and Kumud's unexpected, observing presence.
